weight of the individual (mg g-1), varied significantly with the tide stage (F = 3.960, P < 0.05), with greater stomach fullness observed on the ebb than the flood tide for both structured and unstructured habitats (Fig. 3). Large fish (82 to 147 mm) show a similar trend as in the pooled data; for both structured and unstructured habitats, stomach fullness is significantly greater on the ebb tide than on the flood tide (Fig. 3). However, small fish (52-81 mm) show a different trend on the structured habitat, and are entering the structured intertidal zone with fuller stomachs on the flood tide and leaving with emptier stomachs on the ebb tide (Fig. 3).  Identified prey were consolidated into 13 taxonomic categories; multivariate analysis of the data shows a statistically significant difference between the prey composition of structured and unstructured habitats (ANOSIM: P = 0.007, R=0.051). The low global R indicates that the prey composition of the sites is very similar, though a MDS plot for habitat suggests that differences may be attributed to greater prey variability on the structured habitat. SIMPER analysis indicates that polychaetes contributed most to the differences, followed by gammarid amphipods. The Percent Index of Relative Importance values calculated for large and small fish on both habitats reveal similar differences in diet between the habitats, with gammarid amphipods making up a significant portion of small fish diets on structured habitats, and polychaetes making up a significant portion of diets on unstructured habitats (Fig. 4).

DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSIONS Evidence from the present study suggests that the predator exclusion structures placed in the intertidal zone at the beginning of the geoduck aquaculture cycle may affect macrofaunal communities, altering migratory and dietary patterns of mobile fish and invertebrates. Significantly more C. gracilis were observed on unstructured habitats than structured habitats and significantly more L. armatus were observed on structured habitats than unstructured habitats. Intertidal migration may serve various purposes for macrofauna; individuals may migrate to increase foraging opportunities, to decrease agonistic activity, or to increase reproductive output9,15. C. gracilis, may preferentially migrate into unstructured intertidal areas to forage9,16, as the limited habitat complexity of the unstructured habitat may increase foraging efficiency and predation17. Although struc- turally complex areas may have higher prey densities than less complex areas15, C. gracilis may be deterred from migrating into these areas by reduced foraging efficiency or by stranding risk of the predator exclusion structures at low tide. The observation of significantly more L. armatus on structured habitats than in unstructured habitats is consistent with past studies of L. armatus that observed a preference of sculpin for more

Figure 4. Percent Index of Relative Importance for large and small Leptocottus armatus across habitats. Percent IRI for 13 major prey categories of large and small L. armatus on structured and unstructured habitats.

complex habitats14. There was a statistically significant difference in the standardized weight (mg prey g-1 fish) of L. armatus observed between ebb and flood tides for both structured and unstructured habitats, with greater stomach fullness on the ebb than the flood tide. Because sculpin are entering littoral areas with empty stomachs and leaving with full stomachs, it is suggested that sculpin are migrating into the intertidal zone to forage. This relationship between tide level and standardized weight was strongest in the unstructured habitats, and there was less difference in fullness between the tides in the structured habitat, suggesting that migration into the structured habitat may serve another purpose in addition to foraging.  Division of the pooled data based upon fish size suggests that L. armatus may be migrating into structured areas in order to seek refuge. When examining the standardized weights for large fish, as for the pooled data, fuller stomachs were observed on ebb tides and emptier stomachs on flood tides. Interestingly, this relationship does not hold for small fish. Small fish were observed to have fuller stomachs on the flood tide and emptier stomachs on the ebb tide. The higher predation risk faced by small fish in conjunction with this observation suggests that L. armatus may find some refuge value in the predator exclusion structures and may migrate into these areas to reduce predation risk.  Prey composition of L. armatus was significantly different between habitats, as the result of greater overall variability in the diet of L. armatus on the structured habitat. The greater diversity of prey available on the more complex surface of the structured habitat is consistent with previous studies correlating increased complexity with increased diversity and density of species18,19,20. The difference in prey composition was dependent upon polychaetes being a significantly greater food source for sculpin on unstructured habitats and gammarid amphipods being a significantly greater food source for sculpin on structured habitats. This difference is important, as the main contributors to the diet of L. armatus on the unstructured habitat, polychaetes, are infaunal, benthic species, while the largest contributors on the structured habitat, mobile gammarid amphipods, consist of a guild of epibenthic species that would not be present in the area if it were not for the complex habitat provided by the predator exclusion structures.  The differences in habitat utilization and diet composition of L. armatus between structured and unstructured habitats suggest that the predator exclusion structures of geoduck aquaculture do affect mobile benthic macrofauna. As the geoduck industry expands, it will be important to consider the implications of altering the diet and migratory patterns of L. armatus and other ecologically and economically important macrofauna. Future studies could develop bioenergetics models of L. armatus to determine if there are benefits to feeding on prey from structured versus unstructured habitats. It would be interesting to see if there is an advantage to utilization of one habitat over the other, and to observe how differences between the two habitats affect L. armatus populations and on a broader scale, the community to which they belong.

ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS I greatly appreciate the support and guidance of P. Sean McDonald in the development of this project. I am grateful to Karl Mueller, Gene McKeen, and Nate Schwark for logistical and technical help, to Brian Bingham for help with statistics, and to Taylor Shellfish Company for providing access to geoduck aquaculture sites. The field assistance provided by volunteers Kirstin Holsman and Hannah Stapleton was also invaluable to the success of the project. Lastly, I would like to thank the National Science Foundation Research Experiences for Undergraduates program and Steve Sulkin of Western Washington University for supporting this project.

title: Interactions Along the Fault Lines of Civilizations; Investigating Literary Transitions and Legacies in Russian Accounts of the Caucasian Conquest (1817-1864)
abstract: My project extends the arguments of Susan Layton’s 1995 book Russian Literature and Empire: Conquest of the Caucasus from Pushkin to Tolstoy. While Layton explores how literature of the Caucasian conquest helped shaped conceptions of Russian nationality and statehood, this paper probes the corollary influences of the war on literature and its associated criticism. Textual presentations of the Caucasian theater contributed to the rise of a literary perspective that emphasized individual consciousness and experiential authenticity within the dynamic progression of the conquest from 1817 to 1864. By contesting fanciful Caucasian storytelling traditions, these innovative narrative methods opposed established conventions of romanticism affirming instead emerging tenets of realism. How then did Russian authors experience the Caucasus and how did they convey their impressions to Russia’s educated elite? What sentiments did writers express and how did their convictions serve to inspire more objective portrayals of the character’s unique deliberations within his complex environments? This paper accordingly examines primary source literary accounts of the conquest to investigate how narrative developments evolved within their simultaneously changing historical contexts. While these works illustrate the remarkable artistic imaginations of Alexander Pushkin, Alexander BestuzhevMarlinsky, and Mikhail Lermontov, they additionally demonstrate cumulatively momentous transitions of descriptive procedure and form. While these three authors subscribed to numerous and even opposing writing traditions, the sum succession and consequences of their Caucasian works promoted a critical legacy that endorsed realism as a preeminent literary style of modernity.
text:
Interactions Along the Fault Lines of Civilizations; Investigating Literary Transitions and Legacies in Russian Accounts of the Caucasian Conquest (1817-1864) MICHAEL M ARSH-SOLOWAY DEPARTMENT OF SLAVIC STUDIES DEPARTMENT OF HISTORY

JOHN BUSHNELL FACULTY ADVISOR, DEPARTMENT OF HISTORY, DEPARTMENT OF SLAVIC STUDIES, NORTHWESTERN UNIVERSITY

GARY SAUL MORSON FACULTY ADVISOR, DEPARTMENT OF SLAVIC STUDIES, NORTHWESTERN UNIVERSITY

BRADLEY ZAKARIN SEMINAR INSTRUCTOR, DEPARTMENT OF HISTORY, NORTHWESTERN

My project extends the arguments of Susan Layton’s 1995 book Russian Literature and Empire: Conquest of the Caucasus from Pushkin to Tolstoy. While Layton explores how literature of the Caucasian conquest helped shaped conceptions of Russian nationality and statehood, this paper probes the corollary influences of the war on literature and its associated criticism. Textual presentations of the Caucasian theater contributed to the rise of a literary perspective that emphasized individual consciousness and experiential authenticity within the dynamic progression of the conquest from 1817 to 1864. By contesting fanciful Caucasian storytelling traditions, these innovative narrative methods opposed established conventions of romanticism affirming instead emerging tenets of realism. How then did Russian authors experience the Caucasus and how did they convey their impressions to Russia’s educated elite? What sentiments did writers express and how did their convictions serve to inspire more objective portrayals of the character’s unique deliberations within his complex environments? This paper accordingly examines primary source literary accounts of the conquest to investigate how narrative developments evolved within their simultaneously changing historical contexts. While these works illustrate the remarkable artistic imaginations of Alexander Pushkin, Alexander BestuzhevMarlinsky, and Mikhail Lermontov, they additionally demonstrate cumulatively momentous transitions of descriptive procedure and form. While these three authors subscribed to numerous and even opposing writing traditions, the sum succession and consequences of their Caucasian works promoted a critical legacy that endorsed realism as a preeminent literary style of modernity.

The Caucasus has been called a dazzling mosaic of ethnic groups and rival clans, a place where the individual struggles with his concep- tion of self  in response to conten- tious considerations of Muslim vs. Christian, Eastern vs. Western, and Asian vs. European identities1. Divided by these fault lines of civilizations, the Caucasian mountain range is a borderland torn between the cultural and political influences of different worlds . More than fifty different indigenous peoples reside in the territory between the Black and Caspian Seas, including Georgians, Circassians, Chechens, Armenians, Dagestani, Iranians, and Turks3. Russian military forces invaded and conquered the region between 1817 and 18644.  Texts describing the Caucasian conquest com- municate the efforts and outlooks of one civilization triumphing over another. Under the pretexts of nation, empire, and ideology, the individual and his society attempt to advance their own hegemonic ascendancies over foreign, feebler others5. Expressing such attitudes after his victorious military campaigns in Gaul, Gaius Julius Caesar proclaimed veni, vidi, vici, to signify that the Roman Empire as embodied in his own personage came, saw and conquered the provinces inferior, un- sophisticated barbarians6. Victors write the history that reveres their own authority as superior to the claims of subjugated counterparts7. But how are these minority voices acknowledged and represented in the literature of the vanquisher? And, how does the course of political and military affairs influence this dialogue?  While overarching national, imperial, and ideological stimuli promoted the conquest, individuals also had specific, personal reasons to travel to the Caucasian frontier. Sizeable Russian populations, for example, came as civil servants, travelers, soldiers, and exiles8. Political and criminal deportees arrived in such great numbers that people started calling the territory "southern Siberia" already in the time of Alexander I9. Some of these individuals undertook literary endeavors to describe their Caucasian experiences to influential literate circles10. Though only an estimated 4 percent of the male population in a certain province could read in 1844, this same minority represented Russias powerful, educated, and governing elite11.  Authors participating in the state's expansion- ary efforts surveyed the empires unknown corners, observed foreign populations, and assigned them cultural ranks in relation to their own societies12. Introducing readers to territories whose geographical and ethnic features were not yet sufficiently known to the nations readership, Russian writers adapted a textual inter- face with Europes renaissance orientale, concentrating initially on the Crimean peninsula, a region seized from Muslim Tatars in 178313. When Catherine the Great traveled to the Crimea on an official state tour in 1787, for instance, she announced the territory a fairy tale land from The Thousand and One Nights14. Although at first the Crimea intrigued readers with its aura of eastern exoticism, the Caucasus soon became the primary setting of the Russian oriental domain15. While numerous individuals reported the events of the Caucasian conquest from 1817 to 1864, this paper specifically analyzes the accounts of three prominent Russian authors: Alexander Sergeyevich Pushkin (1799-1837), Alexander Bestuzhev-Marlinsky (1797-1837), and Mikhail Iur'vich Lermontov (1814- 1841)l6. Although they subscribed to numerous and even opposing writing traditions, by emphasizing the unique deliberations of the individual within his complex environments, these three authors countered established conventions of romanticism affirming instead emerging narrative principles of realism.  No explicit break separated these two movements, which makes the change harder to discern. As the literary principles of realism and romanticism evolved concurrently in the realm of Russian prose, they competed for prominence, especially in texts describing the conquest of the Caucasus. As both military and literary contests unfolded, the transition away from romanticism towards realism occurred with a progression of hybrid texts employing methods and techniques belonging to both narrative styles17. Blending the poetic and the pragmatic, Russian writers attempted to make their fictitious Caucasian tales more believable by presenting facts and embellishments in tandem18.  Pushkins Caucasian texts, for instance, received praise from his contemporary and succeed- ing audiences for presenting purportedly authentic geographical and ethnographic detail [with] technical excellence of verse. instead of writing too didactically and, perforce, too prosaically19. Authors describing the conquest performed the interdisciplinary activities of littérateur, journalist, and scientist in conveying their observations and interpretations of the war to Russian readers20. Although the three writers discussed in this paper accommodated romantic elements in varying degrees, their realist emphasis on the individuals consciousness within his dynamic surroundings attained more pronounced critical praise than their parallel romantic methodologies.  Even though romanticism and realism seem distinguishable, scholars continue to disagree over how to properly classify certain authors and their works in a particular narrative style. Elizabeth Cheresh Allen explains in her 1992 book, Beyond Realism: Turgenevs Poetics of Secular Salvation, that [t]he trouble is most people, or at least most students of realism, do not agree on the works and authors that fall under its rubric. Snow, for example, welcomes Dostoevsky and Tolstoy into the Realist fold, whereas Erich Auerbach, author of the magisterial study Mimesis: The Representation of Reality in Western Literature, categorically refuses to do so21. This scholarly discord emerges from the historical development of realism: the realist narrative style developed gradually over time with the efforts of numerous writers participating in cross-cultural exchanges high- lighting the keen observation of the individual within his variegated circumstances.  Accordingly, definitions of realism tend to rely on features that distinguish it from previous styles. French modernist painter, Fernand Léger, for example, argues "every epoch has its own realism, invented more or less in relation to the preceding epochs22. George Levine asserts supportively that what realism may be at any moment depends both on what it has been and what the culture expects it to be23. The blurring between realism and romanticism has caused academics such as Donald Fanger to uphold a "felicitous compromise between moment and mode," evident in the title of his 1965 book, Dostoevsky and Romantic Realism24. The descriptive conveyances of these two narrative forms can at times seemingly coincide.  Despite the overlap of these literary movements, public acceptance of more objective narrative procedures presented in accounts of the Caucasian conquest advanced innovative approaches of realism at the expense of foregoing conventions of romanticism. Realist descriptions presented the setting of war more legitimately and thereby usually more horrifically, while romantic works falsely upheld its patriotic glorification. As Russian military campaigns expanded into the Caucasus, Persia, and the Crimea, soldiers started perish- ing in greater numbers. Mourning the deaths of family members, loved ones, and fellow countrymen, readers became dissatisfied romantic pomposity. The realist narrative form, alternatively, empathized more sincerely with peoples losses and effectively criticized the state's overbearing imperial endeavors.  Correspondingly, although the three central authors discussed in this paper contributed to the development of realist approaches, their stories and literary perspectives also accommodated romantic elements some of these writers more so than others. While these authors refuse definitively realist or romantic taxonomi- cal categorizations, they undoubtedly cultivated a more objective description of the character's unique perspective within his intricate surroundings.  In such regards, the Caucasian works produced by these three prominent authors promoted realist narrative approaches in the face of adversity from embedded romantic literary conventions.  Before understanding the traditions of realism that emerged in accounts of the Caucasian conquest, it is necessary to explore narrative styles that preceded it. In his 1978 comparative study of Byron and Pushkin, Victor Zhirmunsky categorized the romantic poema by thematic and compositional features such as a disil- lusioned hero, an exotic setting and fragmentariness25. Moreover, romantic Caucasian stories entailed the fanciful and fictitious, the visionary and impractical to impart a tale of extravagant love, adventure, and excite- ment26. As Russian readers gravitated more towards emotional values rather than logical ones, skillful fic- tional romantic presentations of the conquest received immense popularity and public acclaim27.  Romantic narrative styles misrepresented the Caucasian region with either tacit or explicit promo- tions of the states imperial endeavors. As Vissarion Belinsky affirmed in 1845, Caucasian literature appealed unequivocally to Russian armchair travelers, who exhibited an elevated readiness to enjoy the experience of empire28. The elites sense of boredom made tales of Caucasian freedom, adventure, and exoticism particularly appealing29. In this regard, romantic authors draped the Caucasus in magic and mystery, utilizing hy- perbole, and incredible outbursts of feeling to impress audiences with the sensation of "reading as traveling30.

Along similarly persuasive lines, Russians pursued travel as the antidote for the boredom ofmonotonous life31." Calculated or not, the grandiose language of the romantic approach inspired large numbers of Russians to seek passage to the Caucasian frontier32.  Romantic accounts describing the conquest breathed life into Caucasian rivers, cliffs, clouds, and mountains, generating dialogues that read as brooding parables on the themes of violent death, erotic longing, and imperial encroachment33. The early 1814 episto- lary verse, To Voeikov, by Vasili Andreevich Zhukovsky, for instance, illustrated such romantic tendencies in its presentation of the Caucasian mountaintop, Elbrus: [a]nd like a cloud above the rest,/Elborus [sic] gleams in all his glory/ [w]ith dreadful majesty-a hoary/[g]iant capped by a double crest34. Zhukovsky had never even travelled to the Caucasus when he wrote these verses and based his portrayal on pure imagination35. Considering the ramifications of such ostentatious storytelling practices, romantic writers bewildered expectations and perceptions of the Caucasian setting.  Fear of penalty from the state contributed to the general reticence about the nations imperial endeavors. Under Tsar Nicholas I's regime (1825-1855), the secret police became heavily involved in censorship activities36. Opposing mandates and ideologies of the autocratic regime could bring writers sentences of house arrest, mandatory military service, forced labor, imprisonment, exile, or death37.  Trepidation over authoritarian censorship and punishment unquestionably manipulated the formulation and distribution of printed material.  Censor Alexander Nikitenko disparaged the aims and implications of his own profession in his secret 1826 diary. Referring to his nation's literate elite as "rank automatons," Nikitenko described how "the guid- ing principle...of the so-called high society....is not to appear ridiculous. And not to appear ridiculous means to conform slavishly to fashion in one's speech, opinions and conduct38. As Nikitenkos sentiments confirm, concessions made to the status quo, the comme il faut, and the officially directed hegemonic claims of the Russian empire served to suppress the objective perspective of the autonomous individual. Despite the excessive efforts of the state to control the printed word, the voice of the objective author endured39.  In several considerations, the methods of realism addressed the overarching artistic and moral shortcomings of romantic approaches widely purveyed in Russian writing during the time period of the war. Attempting to resolve romantic distortions and exag- gerations, realism asserted unbiased transcriptions of thought, observation, and experience40. Likewise, the emerging tenets of realism affirmed an incurable love of the concrete and the verifiable, an instinctive distrust of the abstract, the impalpable, and the supernatural, while maintaining a scientific and positivist approach, unfriendly to romanticism, intangible formulations, and metaphysics41. Moreover, realist approaches main- tained the individual was not merely a type, but rather a specific, cognizant personality immersed within his miscellaneous surroundings, upholding the study of individuals everywhere as a worthwhile and informative endeavor42. The astute description of every characters distinct perspective encouraged increased self-aware- ness, reflection, and deliberately considered action43. The realist endorsement of individual objectivity over subjectivity challenged established Russian literary and political traditions throughout the progression of the Caucasian conquest.  Throughout the conquest, Pushkin, Bestuzhev- Marklinsky, and Lermontov all undertook initiatives to underscore the significance of every character within his complicated contexts. The works of these three authors exhibited the rise of a realist narrative style that main- tained the individual's autonomous weighing uncon- strained by nationalistic, authoritarian influences. These three authors challenged Russian readers to examine more thoughtfully the conquest's actual occurrences and implications.  The Caucasian texts of Alexander Sergeyevich Pushkin (1799-1837), for instance, indicate the transition away from romanticism towards realism over the course of the conquest's progression. Ultimately, Pushkin's opinions and descriptions of the Caucasian conquest appealed to an elite readership who opposed estimations of western Europe as the apogee of world civilization and voiced sensitivity to occidentalizations negative impact44. To address this demographic of his audience, Pushkin correspondingly voiced his praise and admiration for the regions cultural traditions and lifestyles to counter biased contemplations of Russian superiority. In his glorification of Caucasian peoples, Pushkin wrote in his 1822 Kavkazskiy plennik, (Prisoner of the Caucausus), The Circassian is covered with arms;/ he is proud of them:/ on him there is armor, gun, quiver,/Kuban saddle, dagger, lasso/ and shaska (sword), his eternal companion/ for all labors and leisure45. While he indeed made use of romantic literary techniques, Pushkin expressed his wonder and veneration for the regions proud and free peoples effectively break- ing down the division between the Russian self and the Caucasian other46.  Along similar lines, Pushkin mourned the sup- pression of the territorys proud peoples, questioning his own regard for the conquest in the passage, did he regret days gone by,/ days of disappointed hopes,/ or, curious, did he contem- plate/amusements of bleak simplicity?/Did he read in this faithful mirror/the habits of a wild people?--/He hid the movements in his heart/in deepest silence,/and on his high brow nothing was betrayed47. Reiterating comparable impressions of his Caucasian experiences in an 1825 letter to his friend Nikolai Raevsky, Pushkin asserted here you will find memo- ries/ of days that were, perhaps, dear to the heart,/ the contradictions of passions,/familiar dreams, familiar sufferings/ and the secret voice of my soul48. While this passage did not appear in publication, it still reflected Pushkins meditations about the human and social losses incurred in the civilizing process associated with the conquest49. Pushkins eulogizing of Caucasian geog- raphies and peoples lamented the Russian states efforts to overpower them. Still, Pushkins loyalty to Russian elites made him an advocate of the colonial expansion in the Caucasus and elsewhere50.  This solidarity caused Pushkin to try to justify Russian atrocities through referencing the tribesmens savagery51. Pushkin expressed his outright support for the Russian conquest of the Caucasus as a bloody but ultimately benign necessity, writing in the epilogue of Prisoner of the Caucasus, that

[t]he Caucasian region, the torrid boundary of Asia, arouses interest in all respect. Ermolov has filled it with his name and beneficent genius. The savage Circassians have become timorous; their ancient audacity is disappearing. The roads are becoming less dangerous by the hour, and the numerous conveys are becoming superfluous.52. Pushkins contrasting attitudes towards empire caused his prose to fluctuate between elegiac mourning and odic triumphalism53. His own internal divisions over the necessity of the Caucasian conquest encouraged the autonomous individual to participate in this line of internal deliberating. Pushkin persuaded his readers to decide for themselves how they felt about such issues54.  Alexander Bestuzhev-Marlinsky (1797- 1837) also emphasized Russians relationships to their Caucasian counterparts in his 1830 story, Letters from Dagestan. In this novella, Bestuzhev-Marlinsky inferred repeatedly through rumors circulated amongst troops that the adversarial Caucasian Prince, Gazi- Muhammed, took on the external guise of Caucasian identity only to veil his true personage as the grandson of a Russian turncoat embodying the offspring of anti-Tsarist sentiment in [his] readerships own country55. In such regards, Bestuzhev-Marlinsky provoked his Russian literate audiences to reconsider their own associations to Caucasian peoples effectively countering prevailing discourses that degraded the mountaineers as inferior savages56. Bestuzhev first adapted the pseudonym Marlinsky in an anonymous review of the tsars government in 182057. His real identity only became known to Russian audiences in 1837 when it was announced that the generally forgotten Bestuzhev had written many popular Caucasian tales of the 1830s under the pseudonym Marlinsky58. The name Marlinsky refers to the cultural fashions of marlinism, a highly theatrical, melodramatic, and pseudoheroic mode of behavior that arose in response to the pressures of post- Decembrist Russia59. The connotations of his pen name allude to his primarily romantic literary inclinations. Of the three authors discussed in this paper, Bestuzhev-Marlinsky represents the most categorically romantic. Some might argue, for instance, that Pushkin described the Caucasian setting more realistically than did Bestuzhev-Marlinsky. Accordingly, BestuzhevMarlinskys romantic proclivities reiterate that the development of the realist narrative did not occur in a gradual, linear chronological progression. Instead, writers contributed to the rise of realism in hybrid texts employing forms and methods from both movements, albeit in varying degrees of authorial subscription to one style or the other60.  In his 1834 text, however, Story of an Officer Held Prisoner by Mountain Tribsemen, BestuzhevMarlinsky provided realistic information about the Caucasian region and its peoples. Warning readers, not to dismiss these Caucasian peoples as savages Bestuzhev-Marlinsky offered a trustworthy ethnographic essay about a Dagestani tribe whose community organization operated in a Rousseau- like pristine state61. Such uninhibited freedom must have seemed particularly appealing to Russians who lived under austere autocratic control. Additionally emphasizing his interest in Caucasian cultures and peoples, Bestuzhev-Marlinsky learned Azeri, a Tatar tongue, and even included tribal death songs expertly rendered into Russian verse by the author and discussed in one of his thirty-nine footnotes in his 1832 story, Ammalat-Bek62. He even gave the work the subtitle byl  (true story)63. In spite of these realist tendencies, Bestuzhev-Marlinsky simultaneously portrayed the conquest with a disparate kind to the travelogue, which revitalized the cloying sentimentalist prose64.  Mikhail Iurevich Lermontov (1814-1841) more aggressively criticized Russian imperial efforts.

His 1832 poem, Izmail-Bey, for instance, conveyed the overwhelming atrocities committed in the Caucasus by Russian military forces: [w]here are the mountains, steppes and oceans/ [u]nconquered by the Slavs in war?/And where have enmity and treason/[n]ot bowed to Russias mighty Tsar?/Circassian, fight no more! Likely as not,/[b]oth East and West will share your lot./The time will come: youll say, quite bold,/I am a slave, but my Tsar rules the world./The time will come: the North will be graced/[b]y an awesome new Rome a second Augustus./Aulsi are burning, their defenders mastered,/[t]he homelands sons have fallen in battle./Like steady comets, fearful to the eyes,/[a] glow is playing cross the skies,/[a] beast of prey with bayonet, the victor/[c]harges into a quiet dwelling./ He kills the children and the old folks,/[a]nd with his bloody hands he strokes/[t]he unmarried girls and young mothers65. Such disparaging depictions of action in Caucasia effectively confronted Russian audiences with the conquests sheer inhumanity.  In Izmail-Bey and later in his 1841 work, A Hero of Our Time, Lermontov expressed his contempt for blind romantic glorification of Caucasian military campaigns. Mocking the anti-scientific, improbable aspects of the romantic literary style, Lermontov sarcastically announced his intentions to spare the audience statistical remarks about the Caucasus because he figured nobody would read them anyway66. By challenging and ironically satirizing affected romantic accounts of the conquests violent setting, Lermontov affirmed alternatively a mode of realistic literary transcription that made the reader reflect personally and autonomously on the conquest.  By the time of the Crimean War (1854-56), the fallibility of Russian military might seemed readily obvious. In many ways, the positive discourse of Caucasian victory sharply juxtaposed the depressing dialogue of the Crimean defeat. The modernized skirmishes of the Crimean War bore witness to some of the deadliest fighting the world had yet to encounter. Count Lev Nikolayevich Tolstoy recounts how Russian forces suffered the brunt of these losses in his 1855 text, Sevastopol Sketches. For example, [w]hen [Tolstoy] left for Sevastopol on November 23rd, 1854, he [describes] how 10, 0000 Russians had been slaughtered by the enemy war machine, confirming the horrific physiognomy of war relative to any societys tolerance for violence67. Having also spent time in the Caucasus himself, Tolstoy came to emphasize the consciousness of the individual apart from his imperial, authoritarian state, carrying on an imposing realist legacy established by Pushkin, Bestuzhev-Marlinsky, and Lermontov throughout the conquests progression from 1817 to 1864.

title: A Well-Baby Checkup - A Ghanaian Perspective: Maternal Factors and Childhood Health
abstract: Poor nutritional status during childhood has major effects on long-term health. In the setting of rural Ghana, childhood malnutrition is prevalent, despite the fact proper nutrition guidelines have been incorporated into intervention programs. Thus, barriers may be preventing mothers from using their nutritional knowledge to make healthy decisions in the household. This study assesses the prevalence of malnutrition and the factors affecting it as seen in a sample of Ghanaian women and their children aged 3-24 months (n=33). Anthropometric measurements were collected on the children and interviews were conducted with the mothers. Analysis found that malnourished children were more likely to be the offspring of mothers who were married (p=0.012) and lacked national health insurance (p=0.176). Low maternal nutritional knowledge was not significantly related to low child nutritional status (p=0.221), however a statistical trend was visible. Because marital status was related to other variables including nutritional knowledge (p=0.040) and number of people in the home (p=0.201), it is possible that relationships in the home are a barrier to childhood health. Efforts to improve the home dynamics and increase the use of national health insurance may decrease the level of childhood malnutrition in this setting.
text:
A Well-Baby Checkup - A Ghanaian Perspective: Maternal Factors and Childhood Health SDEPARTMENT ARAH MIHALOV OF ANTHROPOLOGY THOMAS MCDADE FACULTY ADVISOR, DEPARTMENT OF ANTHROPOLOGY, NORTHWESTERN UNIVERSITY

Poor nutritional status during childhood has major effects on long-term health. In the setting of rural Ghana, childhood malnutrition is prevalent, despite the fact proper nutrition guidelines have been incorporated into intervention programs. Thus, barriers may be preventing mothers from using their nutritional knowledge to make healthy decisions in the household. This study assesses the prevalence of malnutrition and the factors affecting it as seen in a sample of Ghanaian women and their children aged 3-24 months (n=33). Anthropometric measurements were collected on the children and interviews were conducted with the mothers. Analysis found that malnourished children were more likely to be the offspring of mothers who were married (p=0.012) and lacked national health insurance (p=0.176). Low maternal nutritional knowledge was not significantly related to low child nutritional status (p=0.221), however a statistical trend was visible. Because marital status was related to other variables including nutritional knowledge (p=0.040) and number of people in the home (p=0.201), it is possible that relationships in the home are a barrier to childhood health. Efforts to improve the home dynamics and increase the use of national health insurance may decrease the level of childhood malnutrition in this setting.

INTRODUCTION

For newborns, breastfeeding is a major determinant of health because of the beneficial nutritional and immunological properties of breast milk1. At six months, proper introduction of complementary foods, as recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO), is critical to health. According to the 2003 Demographic Health Survey data, 25% of children under the age of five years in Ghana are stunted, or malnurished2. High prevalence of malnutrition indicates that there are barriers preventing mothers from following WHO recommendations. Thus, understanding barriers preventing compliance with feeding recommendations has implications for the improvement of policy and intervention programs used globally. While past research has found child nutritional status to be associated with maternal formal education and socioeconomic status3, little research has focused on factors affecting maternal compliance to feeding recommendations.  Recent research has focused on the role of the mother within the household, specifically her ability to make decisions regarding household resources, child- care, and health9. Her actions regarding aspects of child health - introduction and type of complementary foods, perception and treatment of disease - directly affect child health. Evidence shows that a mothers practical knowledge about nutrition is associated with higher nutritional status; yet, her ability to make health related decisions and access to resources are not guaranteed, adding another dimension9. Recent study examined gender dynamics of household decision-making and found that treatment-seeking behavior was influenced by ownership of children, ability to control funds to pay for treatment, norms in payment responsibil- ity, and marital status10. Attainment of these qualities may depend on other factors - formal education and socioeconomic status. While these studies in West Africa demonstrate the influential role mothers play in child health, they do not address the ability of mothers to use their nutritional knowledge. This study examines mothers differences that create the range of nutritional status among their children.  Feeding practices is a primary area of maternal variation. WHO recommends exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months of life after which breast milk is not sufficient source of nutrients. Complementary feeding transitions a child to adult food. In many developing countries, these recommendations are not followed. While mean duration of breastfeeding in Ghana is 23 months, median duration of exclusive breastfeeding is only 3.2 months2. The child does not like the breast or likes food better are common reasons given as to why exclusive breastfeeding was stopped. Further, complementary food typically provided is kooko, a thin, low energy, low protein mixture. Children do not receive the necessary nutrients for growth and immune function. Unhealthy preparation, such as use of contaminated water or addition of spices, causes further problems. Many highly malnourished children are exposed to infection, which exacerbates malnutrition. Thus, wasting is often prevalent at one and two years of age, increasing the risk of mortality4. Findings of this study would contribute to knowledge of barriers to child health and have implications on nutrition policy and interventions.  Growth is an indicator of environmental and social conditions affecting past, present, and future health4 because it is sensitive to changes, adapting to lack or excess of nutrients5. When infants receive inadequate nutrients, they lack energy, resulting in growth retardation, which leads to stunting, an indicator for chronic malnutrition6. Inadequate nutrients causes protein energy malnutrition, which is detrimental to the immune system. Slowing the speed of immunological response puts risk on the child for infection and dis- ease6. Nutritional studies on factors affecting malnutrition have focused on effects of socioeconomic status, maternal education, and birth order3,7,8. Although an understanding of factors associated with child malnutrition exists and used in intervention guidelines, malnutrition continues to be prevalent in developing countries. Thus, other factors may prevent the attainment of higher nutritional status.  Ghana is in West Africa, just north of the equa- tor, and situated on the Gulf of Guinea, with a population of nearly 23 million, according to the World Bank. Figure.

The country is divided into four regions. The Volta Region is the south-eastern region that borders Togo. Ho, the capital of the Volta Region, is the research site. Ethnically, a majority of the inhabitants and Ewe and speak Ewe, the indigenous language. The town has two modern hospitals, numerous clinics, and several education institutions. Study participants are from a range of living backgrounds.  The aim of this study is to examine the relationship between mothers use of nutritional knowledge and the effects on child growth. Associations between maternal decision-making ability, nutritional knowledge, and child nutritional status are examined in the setting of rural Ghana. The three objectives are: describe prevalence of stunting and wasting in the population, examine its relationship with maternal nutritional knowledge, and identify possible barriers to health based on their relationship with nutritional status.

MATERIALS AND METHODS Study Population This study uses data collected during a two-month field study based in the Volta Region, Ghana.  The study sample was recruited from the villages surrounding a health center located in Voradep village, at the edge of the Ho Municipal District. 34 mother-child pairs were recruited, interviewed, and measured.  Recruitment of participants was done by: (1) visitors to the center during the study and (2) in villages near the center after discussions with community leaders.  These sources were used to ensure a random sample of mothers ac- tively seeking treatment for their children and those that are not. Data Collection The study collected anthropometric measurements of body size and conducted interviews with mothers to determine the relationships between offspring growth status and mothers nutritional knowledge. Data were collected in interviews and were obtained under conditions of informed consent and with human subjects clearance from Northwestern University. Interviews consisted of open and closed ended questions and obtained information regarding demographic, home structure, knowledge and perceptions of nutrition and health, and role in the household.  Child anthropometrics were obtained using standard techniques. Trained investigators weighed children on a hanging scale to the nearest 0.1kg. Length was measured to the nearest 0.1cm using an infant stadiom- eter. To determine nutritional status, length-for-age, weight-for-age, and weight-for-length were compared to the WHO Child Growth Standards for appropriate z-scores (WHO 2006). HAZ values below 2SD are indicative of growth stunting or chronic malnutrition, while WAZ values below 2SD demonstrate wasting or acute malnutrition11. Statistical Analysis Nutritional status z-scores were obtained using version 2 of the WHO Anthro software (World Health Organization), with an anthropometric calculator. It used the age of child - as determined from the date of birth and date measured - length in centimeters, weight in kilograms, and gender to calculate the z-scores. All statistical analyses were conducted using version 10 of Stata (Stata Corporation, College Station, TX). Maternal Nutritional Knowledge was coded as an ordinal variable with values ranging from 3 to 7. For analyses, a new dichotomous high/low variable was generated (0 = nutritional knowledge of 3, 4, or 5; 1 = nutritional knowledge of 6 or 7). Nutritional status was analyzed as dichotomous variables. A series of chi-squared tests were run to determine associations between nutritional status variables, predictor variables and potential confounding variables. With this set of relationships, analysis of health in the population is conducted. Analyses were restricted to a subsample of mothers and children for whom all tested variables were present (n= 33). One pair was excluded because length could not be measured accurately at the interview.

Maternal Nutritional Knowledge Scale

Table 1.

Characteristics of mothers and their children.

RESULTS Descriptive Table 1 represents characteristics of the mothers and children in this study.  Of the 33 mother-child pairs included in the analyses, there were 17 male and 16 female children with an average age of 12.6 months (sd= 204 days).  The mothers ranged from 19 to 55 years, 72.7% of whom were married. Table 1 compares mothers of high and low nutritional knowledge, 19 and 14, respectively. Mothers with a high nutritional knowledge were more commonly younger, single, from larger homes, and using cleaner water. They commonly had less control over meals prepared in the home, which could be a potential barrier in the use of their nutritional knowledge. Also, malnutrition is prevalent in the sample - 18.2% are malnourished (WLA<-2SD) on the basis of X criteria while 42.4% stunted (LAZ<-2SD) and 36.4% wasting (WAZ<-2SD). Mothers of low nutritional knowledge more commonly had malnourished children. Bivariate Numerous chi-squared tests examined relationships between nutritional status, predictor variables, and potential confounders. Results are shown in Table 2, 3, 4, and 5. Table 2: Nutrition: Chi-Squared Test Results (p-values) Analysis showed a statistical trend between nutritional status and maternal nutritional knowledge. Stunted children were more commonly offspring of mothers with low nutritional status (p=0.221), which supports past findings that maternal knowledge can affect child health. Malnourished and stunted children were more often fed nutrient poor complementary foods (p=0.083 and 0.010, respectively). Mothers who fed children nutrient poor foods more often had low nutritional knowledge (p=0.090). Even more, mothers with high nutritional knowledge were more likely to give their child colostrum at birth (p=0.006), the initial discharge from the mothers breast a birth. Thus, mothers with low nutritional knowledge generally feed their children nutrient poor food and do not give colostrum, which can lead to poor health. Other predictor variables did not show significant relationships or statistical trends with nutritional status.  Initial findings between nutritional status and maternal knowledge are not significant for outcome growth variables. While small sample size limited the p-values and results, statistical trends were found. Therefore, the method of analysis used to examine Table 2 will be used throughout the study. Also, some of the lack of significance could be due to other factors acting as barriers to proper nutrition. Table 3: Marital Status: Chi-Squared Test (p-values)

Table 2.

Nutrition: Chi-Squared Test Results (p-values)

Table 3.

Marital Status: Chi-Squared Test (p-values)

Further analysis showed that stunted children more often have married mothers (p=0.012). Single mothers tend, on average, to have offspring with higher nutritional status (p=0.04) and fewer people in their home (p=0.201). It can be inferred that something about the household structure or care-giving affects child health. A single mother may live in a very different household than a married couple, which may allow her a different level of decision-making. Perhaps, smaller households allow more resources for each child. Table 4: Decision-Making: Chi-Squared p-values No significant relationships were found between marital status and meal choice or food choice (p=0.805 and p=0.938, respectively). On the other hand, relationships between nutritional status and decision-making were found. Mothers with high decision-making ability about meals to prepare more commonly had malnourished and wasting children (p=0.150, p=0.030, respectively). Similarly, wasting and stunted children were more commonly the offspring of mothers involved in food purchasing decisions (p=0.102, p=0.174, respectively). Although this was not expected, mothers may be unable to make healthy decisions for other reasons, especially lack of resources like money and clean water.

Table 4.

Decision-Making: Chi-Squared p-values

Table 5.

NHIS: Chi-Squared p-values

Table 5: NHIS: Chi-Squared p-values With the set of chi-squared tests, it was found that mothers possession of the National Health Insurance Scheme (NHIS) affected child health. The Ghana Health Services (GHS) instated the NHIS in 2003 with the goal of achieving universal coverage12. Currently, the NHIS costs 12 Ghana Cedi, which is the rough equivalent of $12, per year. This covers outpatient costs (ie. dental and eye-care) and most inpatient costs (ie. hospital stays and medications). However, many people are not members.  Only 56.7% of the sample had purchased the health insurance.  The data shows that there are benefits of NHIS on health. Stunted children were, on average, the offspring of mothers who did not have NHIS (p=0.176).

Also, mothers who possessed NHIS more frequently had high nutritional knowledge (p=0.198) and used clean water (p=0.070). Thus, nutritional knowledge may be the base factor that leads to healthier actions, such as a mothers possession of NHIS, use of clean water, and feeding children nutritious complementary foods, which positively affect nutritional status. These results provide evidence for positive effects NHIS has on the population and could motivate other mothers. Mothers without NHIS frequently stated it was because they did not have money, their husband did not want it, or she did not know it was important.

DISCUSSION Mothers with high nutritional knowledge were often single, feeding their children nutrient-rich foods, and in possession of NHIS. These findings were significant and consistent with previous research. The expected finding that mothers with high nutritional knowledge would have children with high nutritional status, was not significant, but rather showed a statistical trend. However, Appoh et.al found that a mothers practical knowledge about nutrition is associated with higher nutritional status9. Thus, although this study did not find significant relationships between nutritional knowledge and nutritional status, an analysis of potential barriers to health can still take place.  The main objectives of this study were addressed. First, this population has significant malnutrition based on the study sample, which is important to identify specifically for the health center in order to evaluate the progress of intervention programs. In the total sample, 42% were stunted (LAZ<-2SD), 36% wasting (WAZ<-2SD), and 18% malnourished (WLA<-2SD).  Second, analysis found low nutritional knowledge weakly predicts low nutritional status. The scale uses both actions and knowledge related to health. Several factors were confirmed to be related to child health outcome, including: providing colostrum at birth and feeding proper complementary food. Mothers lacking these factors more commonly had malnourished children. This confirms that health-related actions cor- respond to nutritional knowledge, as used by Appoh et.al in the Maternal Nutritional Knowledge Scale9.  The final objective of this study examined potential barriers to health. Marriage was related to low nutritional status in her offspring, which is the opposite of previous study by Appoh et.al in a similar popula- tion9. Findings suggest the need for further research to determine what factors are involved. Analysis showed that single mothers also had higher nutritional knowledge, which is also related to high nutritional status. These results have important theoretical implications for evaluating the role of kinship relations and household structure on child health. The income disparity within the home may affect decision-making ability and, in turn, child health. Fantahun et.al showed that low maternal decision-making capacity and low socioeconomic status were associated with high under-five mortality14, an outcome variable related to child health. In this study, mothers with higher decision-making ability were found to have less healthy children; however, structural barriers may be limiting her choices. She may have to sell their entire groundnut, or peanut, crop because it yields more money in the market even though it is essential to the porridge mothers prepare because of its protein content. When prepared without groundnut, porridge contains only carbohydrates, which could lead to malnutrition. Thus, it may be that the mother is not making unhealthy choices, but that her economic plight has limited her ability to make healthy ones. Results have significant implications for global health interventions. By identifying barriers to health, it is possible to increase program effectiveness at health centers. Programs should address female empow- erment to allow mothers to use their knowledge to make healthy decisions for their families.  The possession of NHIS was found to have positive effects on nutritional status, which has implications on how the GHS campaigns to increase member- ship. Factors, such as: access to care, socioeconomic status, and acceptance of the program, are limiting. Thus, the GHS must address these issues to reach their goal of universal health care.  Small sample size is the major limitation because of constraints it places on obtaining statistically significant p-values.  While significance was found, many relationships demonstrated statistical trends. The small sample size has ruled out logistic regression, which would allow more complex examination of potential confounding variables.  Because mothers self- reported their own actions taking place up to two years in the past, error may have also occurred. A similar, larger study is necessary to confirm the current findings. Because several of the relationships may be related to income inequality, further study should address socioeconomic status (SES).  SES may prevent a mother from taking actions that promote her childrens health, such as: nutritious complementary foods, adequate food, NHIS, and clean water.  Further study should also take place to better understand the dynamics of kinship relations. While this study collected responsibilities women had in the household, it would be beneficial to gain a better understanding of how they spent their time.

CONCLUSION In rural Ghana, prevalence of child malnutrition is related to feeding of nutrient poor complementary foods, marriage, and lack of NHIS.  High nutritional knowledge was more commonly seen in single mothers and those with NHIS. Further study to examine these dynamics will enhance the significant implications of these findings. Anthropology will benefit from greater understanding of pathways leading to desirable child health while global health intervention programs could be made more effective. Potential long-term effects of marriage and nutritional knowledge on child health call for immediate attention in research studies and global health initiatives.

ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS I thank Thomas McDade, my senior thesis advisor, for his continued support and guidance throughout this entire endeavor; Christopher Kuzawa for his statistical analysis instruction and helpful comments; and the Department of Anthropology for the solid foundation it provided.  My study and time spent in Ho, Ghana would not have been nearly as successful without the guidance, support, and motherly love of Margaret Asante. Finally, I am indebted to the people of Ho for their participation, assistance with my activities in town, and continued friendship.  An Undergraduate Research Grant from Northwestern University funded this study.

title: An Analysis of Carbon Dioxide Emissions in Urban Passenger Transportation
abstract: The goal of this research was to determine which modes, drive systems, and fuels produce the lowest CO2 emissions per passenger-mile in urban passenger transportation. The drive system results show that hybrid drive systems and electric vehicles both offered a 30% reduction in carbon dioxide emissions compared to vehicles that use conventional combustion engine technology. text:
An Analysis of Carbon Dioxide Emissions in Urban Passenger Transportation BDEPARTMENT RENDAN HIGGINS OF CIVIL & ENVIRONMENTAL ENGINEERING

JOSEPH SCHOFER

MENTOR, DEPARTMENT OF CIVIL & ENVIRONMENTAL ENGINEERING, NORTHWESTERN UNIVERSITY

The goal of this research was to determine which modes, drive systems, and fuels produce the lowest CO2 emissions per passenger-mile in urban passenger transportation. Using Argonne National Laboratory’s GREET model as well as real world fuel economy data, carbon dioxide emissions were determined for each transportation pathway (combination of mode, drive system, and fuel). The results show that the transit bus mode had slightly higher carbon dioxide emissions per passenger-mile than the automobile mode. The drive system results show that hybrid drive systems and electric vehicles both offered a 30% reduction in carbon dioxide emissions compared to vehicles that use conventional combustion engine technology. Plug-in hybrids released slightly more carbon dioxide emissions than standard gasoline hybrids while hydrogen fuel cell emissions were heavily dependent on the source of the hydrogen. Biofuels such as cellulosic ethanol and B100 biodiesel had the lowest carbon dioxide emissions of any fuel. The results provided a sense of what technologies offer the greatest reductions in carbon dioxide emissions but this information should be used with caution. Many other factors such as cost, system scalability, and consumer preference play a critical role in the viability of each transportation pathway.

1. INTRODUCTION AND SCOPE

In recent years, policymakers have expressed interest in finding ways to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions since it is very likely that these emissions contribute to global warming (IPCC, 2007). Carbon dioxide (CO2) is the most ubiquitous greenhouse gas and was the focus of this research. In 2007, the transportation sector of the US economy produced 2,014 million metric tons of carbon dioxide which is approximately 1/3 of the US total production (EIA, 2008a). While the transportation sector encompasses both freight and passenger transportation in both urban and rural environments, only urban passenger transportation was examined in this study. The goal was to determine which modes, drive systems, and fuels produce the lowest CO2 emissions per passenger-mile traveled.  Two modes, seven drive systems, and ten fuels were analyzed in various combinations to determine their CO2 emissions. Each combination of mode, drive system, and fuel is referred to as a transportation pathway. For example, one pathway could be a transit bus powered by an internal combustion engine that burns diesel fuel.

1.1 Other Considerations The results are not the product of a life cycle assessment of urban passenger transportation since they are limited to one output: carbon dioxide emissions. A life cycle assessment of each vehicle pathway would have accounted for many other inputs and outputs associated with the system including cost, energy, fuel, and criteria pollutants. Furthermore, a life cycle assessment would account for the inputs and outputs from infrastructure construction, vehicle manufacture, vehicle operation, and vehicle disposal (Chester, 2008).  Other important considerations that were ignored are system scalability and consumer preference. Scalability is a measure of a systems ability to handle growth. Consumer preference is a measure of how much demand there is for a particular pathway. Both of these factors are critical when assessing the viability of each transportation pathway.

2. METHODOLOGY Analysis of fuels using Argonne National Laboratorys GREET model (ANL, 2008) as well as published fuel economy data for a mix of vehicles allowed for the computation of carbon dioxide emissions. The GREET model accepts inputs such as fuel type and production methods to create an output of CO2 and other emission data for a hypothetical automobile. Part of the analysis focused on commercially available vehicles which are either currently in use or on the market. Real fuel economy data was used for these vehicles. A number of the vehicles analyzed are not commercially available or lack sufficient data on fuel economy. For these vehicles, GREET model estimates of fuel consumption were used. Combining the relative efficiencies of the vehicles with the carbon dioxide emissions of the fuels provided the carbon dioxide emission per vehicle mile. These values were then divided by average vehicle oc- cupancies (number of passengers) to produce emissions per passenger-mile.

3. MODES The two modes analyzed were transit bus and automobile. While there are many other modes of urban transportation such as rail, biking, and walking, the bus and automobile were chosen because they share infrastructure such as roads and parking facilities. As a result, infrastructure is a less important factor for comparison purposes.

3.1 Transit Bus A 40 foot transit bus with seating for 40 passengers was chosen for analysis. Information on fuel consumption was attained from the Chicago Transit Authority (CTA, 2008a,b) and New York City Transit (Chandler, 2006). Thus, fuel economy estimates were based off of observed fuel consumption by vehicles that were operating on city streets. The vehicles in the NYCT study were Table 1.

from model years 1999 and 2002 while the vehicles for the CTA were based off of fleet averages for 2008 (which includes vehicles as old as those in the NYCT study). 3.2 Automobile One SUV (Chevrolet Tahoe) and two sedan models (Toyota Camry and Volkswagen Jetta) were used to represent automobiles used in urban transportation. One of the primary reasons that these three vehicles were chosen is because they have models that employ alternative drive systems and/ or alternative fuels. Fuel economy data was obtained from 2008 EPA mileage estimates. The EPA tests vehicles in a highly controlled facility with a prescribed driving cycle (EPA, 2008). The differences in vehicle age and testing methods intro- duced error into the comparison between the bus and car modes.

4. DRIVE SYSTEMS The drive systems analyzed are described in Table 1.

5. FUELS The ten fuels analyzed are listed in Table 2.

Drive Systems

5.1 Emissions and Energy Figure 1 shows carbon dioxide emissions by fuel type. The properties and production methods of the fuels are a critical factor in determining the carbon dioxide emissions of the vehicles they power.  There are three phases in the production of each fuel: feedstock production, fuel processing, and fuel consumption all of which either emit or absorb CO2 from the atmosphere. Feedstock production includes the extraction, production, and transportation of the raw materials used to produce the fuel. For biofuels such as biodiesel and ethanol, this includes the carbon dioxide absorbed by the Table 2. Fuels growing plants. Fuel processing is the transformation of the feedstock material into the final fuel and the transportation of that fuel to the vehicle. Fuel consumption is the consumption of the fuel by the vehicle. 5.2 Petroleum Fuels Gasoline and diesel are both petroleum fuels which are derived from crude oil which is a non-renewable resource. Most carbon dioxide production comes from the consumption of these fuels, but fuel extraction, transportation, and refinery processes also produce carbon dioxide. 5.3 Biofuels The two biofuels analyzed were ethanol and biodiesel. Biofuels are derived from biomaterials such as plant and animal matter. Biodiesel is available in several blends, two of which were analyzed here: B20 and B100. B100 is pure biodiesel and B20 is a more common blend of biodiesel and includes 80% petroleum diesel and 20% biodiesel. Biodiesels most common feedstock in the US is soybean oil, however, it can be made from almost any vegetable oil, animal fat, and algae. Only biodiesel from soybeans was analyzed. Approximately 22% of the soybean mass is vegetable oil, while the remaining 78% is soybean meal (Van Gerpen). The GREET model gives a carbon dioxide emission credit for the soybean meal co-product since it is used in animal feed and can displace other sources of animal feed.  Ethanol is made from the fermentation and distillation of biomass. Different blends of gasoline and ethanol can be produced. The mixture analyzed was E85 ethanol which is a blend of 85% ethanol and 15% gasoline. There is disagreement among researchers about CO2 emissions from ethanol production. The majority of research indicates that corn ethanol has a net benefit over gasoline in terms of CO2 emissions (NRDC, 2006). Cellulosic ethanol can be made from any plant material and uses the entire biomass of the plant whereas corn ethanol only uses the biomass found in the corn kernels (NRDC, 2006). The GREET model shows cellulosic ethanol to be superior to corn based ethanol in terms of CO2 emissions. The feedstocks in the model were 50% woody (tree) biomass and 50% herbaceous (grass) biomass. One of the key advantages to cellulosic ethanol production is that most processing plants burn lignin in place of natural gas. Lignin is a component of the cell wall of the plants that cannot be converted into ethanol. 5.4 Natural Gas Natural gas is composed primarily of methane gas and is part of the fossil fuel family. Figure 1 shows that combustion of natural gas yields slightly lower carbon dioxide emissions per MJ of energy than combustion of diesel or gasoline since it has lower carbon to hydrogen ratio. 5.5 Hydrogen Hydrogen gas can be made from a variety of sources but the two most common feedstocks are electricity and natural gas. Hydrogen is made from electricity through the electrolysis process which is about 60-70% efficient (Ivy, 2004). The CO2 emissions of electrolyzed hydrogen are dependent on the source of the electricity. Figure 1 shows that hydrogen made from the current US electricity mix has the highest CO2 emissions per MJ of the ten fuels. Nevertheless, hydrogen from electrolysis has great potential to reduce CO2 emissions if the electricity comes from renewable sources such as wind and solar.  Hydrogen can also be obtained from natural Figure 2.

gas through a reforming process in which the hydrogen is stripped from the methane molecules. 95% of the hydrogen produced in the US comes from steam reformed methane (DOE, 2008b). The process releases carbon dioxide and requires a significant energy input since the reactions take place at 700-1000 degrees Celsius at 3-25 bars of pressure (EERE, 2008b). 5.6 Electricity Electricity can be used directly as a fuel and it is also a feedstock for the other fuels discussed. Figure 2 shows the feedstock mix for US electricity. This mix was taken from the GREET model as an estimate for the year 2010 but matches closely to the feedstock mix published by the US Department of Energy for the year 2006 (EIA, 2008c).  Figure 1 demonstrates that electricity has the second highest CO2 emissions per MJ compared to the other eight fuels. Obviously, changing the electricity mix in the US to include more renewable sources and less coal will change the carbon dioxide profile of electricity. In addition, carbon sequestration technologies employed at coal fired power plants could also have a positive impact on the CO2 emissions of electricity.

U.S. feedstocks for electricity production as projected by GREET model for the year 2010

6. COMMERCIALLY AVAILABLE VEHICLE RESULTS The commercially available vehicles analyzed are listed in Table 3 while the carbon dioxide emissions for the buses are shown in Figure 3 and those for the automobiles are shown in Figure 4.  Several models of transit bus were used from each transit agency (CTA and NYCT). For the CTA, these included fleet averages for buses with internal combustion engines, hybrid drives, as well as the New

Flyer lightweight bus. For NYCT, the models included the Orion V and Orion VII buses. Minimum vehicle occupancy levels were included to reflect single occupancy automobiles as well as underutilized buses. Both cars and buses often operate with low occupancy for significant portions of their driving cycles. A two passenger occupancy level was assumed for the transit buses. Average vehicle occupancy rates were obtained from national averages published in the Transportation Energy Book (Davis, 2006). The maximum vehicle occupancy rate for the transit buses was based off of a seat to standee ratio of 0.72 which equates to 40 seated passengers and 15 standing passengers (Puchalsky, 2005). This data was based off of the Orion VI 40 foot transit bus which is typical of its class. 6.1 Transit Bus Results The CTA fleet appears to have lower CO2 emissions than the NYCT buses but this is likely attributable to the fact that the CTA data came from newer vehicles. The difference could also be attributable to the geography of each city. The results also show that hybrid drives and biodiesel offered significantly lower carbon dioxide emissions than internal combustion engines and diesel respectively. Finally, Figure 3 shows the significant carbon dioxide emission reductions that can be achieved by increasing vehicle occupancy in buses. 6.2 Automobile Results The results show that the transit buses tend to have higher CO2 emissions per passenger-mile than the cars for average occupancy levels. Part of this difference is attributable to the manner in which the fuel economy data was collected for each mode. The age of the vehicles may also play a role since the bus data was collected from older vehicles than the car data. However, the CO2 emissions of the CTAs 2008 diesel lightweight bus were higher than those of every car model except for the gasoline powered Tahoe indicating that vehicle age may not be a significant factor.  The results also show that the spark ignition (SI) internal combustion engine was one of the highest emitters of CO2 regardless of whether gasoline or natural gas was used as the fuel. CIDI diesel engines offered a reduction in carbon dioxide emissions of about 20% compared with SI engines. Use of a hybrid-electric drive system reduced emission approximately 30% when compared to vehicles that only use an internal combustion engine. Cellulosic ethanol and B100 biodiesel produced the least CO2 emissions of any fuel.

Table 3.

Commercially available vehicles used in the analysis

7. NON-COMMERCIALLY AVAILABLE VEHICLE RESULTS

The results for the non-commercially available vehicles were obtained directly from the GREET model since real fuel consumption data was not available. The hypothetical GREET model vehicle is equivalent to a gasoline powered car using an SI internal combustion engine that attains 23.2 MPG (i.e. a typical family sedan). These vehicles are listed in Table 4.  Figure 5 shows that the fuel cell vehicles carbon dioxide emissions were heavily dependent on the source of hydrogen. Hydrogen made from electrolysis produced almost three times as much carbon dioxide as hydrogen made from natural gas. This is largely due to the high carbon dioxide emissions associated with electricity production in the US.  Results for the plug-in hybrid (PHEV) show that plug-in technology actually increases CO2 emissions of a gasoline powered hybrid vehicle if the electricity comes from the grid. Electricity from other sources may produce a different result. The electric vehicle and gasoline powered hybrid vehicle have comparable carbon dioxide emissions. These findings show that unless the electricity comes from sources with low carbon dioxide emissions, investment in electric and plug-in vehicles does not necessarily make sense when similar emission reductions can be achieved with hybrid vehicles.

Figure 4. Carbon dioxide emissions from an SUV (Chevrolet Tahoe), and 2 Sedans (Toyota Camry and Volkswagen Jetta). *Vehicle is not currently offered in this drive system/ fuel combination.

Figure 5. Theoretical carbon dioxide emissions for non-commercially available vehicles. “Grid Mode” driving indicates that the vehicle is running off of a battery that has been charged by grid supplied electricity.

8. CONCLUSIONS The results of this study provide information about which transportation pathways produce the least carbon dioxide per passenger-mile traveled. Such information is useful when selecting modes, vehicles, and fuels with the goal of reducing carbon dioxide emissions. Furthermore, it provides information to policy-makers about which technologies currently offer the most promise in terms of immediate investment. Several fuels and drive systems stood out as offering a clear carbon dioxide reduction over traditional petroleum fuels and internal combustion engines respectively and merit further study. Biodiesel and cellulosic ethanol fall into this category since these two fuels had the lowest emissions per unit of energy. For drive systems, hybrids and CIDI engines offer clear benefits over SI internal combustion engines and these technologies are already making significant headway in the marketplace. In addition to carbon emissions, policymakers and investors will need to take other factors into consideration such as cost, scalability, consumer preference, and technical barriers to mainstream production when evaluating each transportation pathway. 8.1 Further Study Since fuel cell vehicles, plug-in hybrids, and electric vehicles are not yet commercially available, it is unfair to discount them until more data can be collected. As these technologies develop over the next decade, further comparisons to internal combustion engines should be made. In addition, better information on vehicle occupancy should be obtained for transit buses, particularly with regard to low occupancy and maximum occupancy conditions. A distribution of transit bus occupancy levels throughout its route would be helpful rather than relying on a national average occupancy level.  The next step to analyzing the transportation pathways is to account for other factors in addition to net operating CO2 emissions. Ultimately, a life cycle analysis of each of the vehicle pathways should be performed that includes all inputs and outputs of pathway components. Only then will investors have all of the information they need to make intelligent decisions about urban transportation pathways.

ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS I thank Professor Joseph Schofer in his assistance on this project. His thoughtful questions and insight inspired me to re-think my analysis on multiple occasions. I also appreciate Professor David Boyces feedback on vehicle occupancy levels. Thank you to the Civil Engineering Department at Northwestern University.

Thank you to Argonne National Laboratory for making the GREET model publicly available.

title: Tackling Childhood Malnutrition: An Investigation of Innovative Grassroots Approaches Around the World
abstract: As of 2013, approximately 161 million children under the age of 5 years old suffer from stunted growth globally (WHO). Malnutrition has profound, negative consequences on children’s physical and cognitive growth and development. This cross-regional study aimed to investigate the effectiveness of alternative grassroots nutrition interventions for combating childhood growth stunting. The study was carried out over three months across ten case study sites in Guatemala, Peru, Rwanda, Uganda, Nepal and Cambodia. A mixed method, comparative study design was used, and data was collected using interactive interviews and qualitative field observations. The data were analyzed using NVivo qualitative data analysis software, Microsoft Excel software, and manually. The study revealed four elements that were important for improving growth outcomes across the programs. First, agricultural solutions tend to be the most cost effective, sustainable, and high impact nutrition interventions. Second, targeting new mothers produces better nutrition outcomes in young children. Third, group education classes help to establish social bonds that increase program impact. Lastly, government partnerships promote long-term sustainability. This study also uncovered numerous challenges facing the field of nutrition, including vast variability in the efficacy of nutrition innovations, little cohesion in monitoring and evaluation indicators among programs, and difficulty finding ongoing, apolitical funding sources. Further research into how to effectively scale grassroots interventions while preserving their deep impact is needed.
