Khlebnikov also prac- countrys pagan roots. Early Slavs believed in spirits and tices the anticipation and amassing of a single color, deities that protected their land including woods and which he achieves through repetition or by predicting rivers.11 One of the oldest pagan deities was Mokosh or Mother Moist Earththe goddess of soil, fertility, and an event before it occurs even if it is unnecessary to weaving (Hubbs 20). For Russias large peasant popula- do so.9 The illusion of willful crudeness, generated by such devices, evokes a sense of nostalgia for a simpler tion, the connection with the fertile Mother Goddess, time less restricted by rules, social expectations, or the who bears living things with her fertility as a mother borders of a canvas. bears a child, was particularly significant (Hubbs 20). In their Neoprimitist works, the Futurists also Even political leaders, however, gave credence to the strived to blur the distinctions between high and low art authority of the land: The earth, regarded as a ma- by depicting traditionally low subject matter. Despite ternal body creating and nourishing her children, was perceived as the source of political authority, as well as fertility (Hubbs 21). When Christian missionaries converted the Slavic people, they could not subdue the pagan cult of the Mother Goddess. Instead, they used the figure of Mary, the Mother of God, as a replacement of Mokosh. While in the West the virginity of Mary was stressed, in the Russian Orthodox tradition it is her role as mother that is most important (Hubbs 100). The following proverb summarizes the attempts of the Christian missionaries to eradicate the worship of Mother Earth: Your first mother is Mary; your second mother is the earth; and your third mother is your own mother (Hubbs 21). Today, the country itself is still referred to as Mother Russia. It is important to recognize that the female is more than just a symbol of fertility. Because of her connection with land and nature, the woman is also associated with physical and spiritual strength. In Russian tradition, just like nature is beyond human control, there is something authentic, almost primal about female strength that resists control by man, civilization, domestication, or machinery. Even linguistically, the words for nature, earth, planet, culture, homeland, strength, freedom, independence, life, and Russia are all female gendered words. Russian Futurists wanted to build national identity by tapping into internal Russian traits and values rather than by relying on external sources such as machinery and technology. The female, and their representation of her as a cultural hero, allowed the Futurists to express these goals. Not only is the woman the mother from whom Russian culture and history emanate, but this image of the woman demonstrates strength and free spiritedness that could defy the pressures of Westernization and facilitate the construction of an independent national identity. The exploration of the various degrees and layers of strength embodied in the female figure unifies the widely ranging Futurist works that focus on the female form. Khlebnikovs 1912 poem, Venus and the Shaman is a playful work in which the female figures strong and willful sprit are represented through the wanton, unbridled sexuality of the goddess Venus.12 Khlebnikov depicts Venus as fully nude, flirtatious, and arrogant calling herself a river of delights. Her explo- sive sexuality overflows bursting forth like spring fever / all in flower with the sultriness of passion gleaming in her eyes. Permeating through her core, Venus sexuality is so innate and deeply embedded in the essence of her being, that it cannot be restrained even by Venus herself. She finds herself in a dilemma because of her inability to contain her sexuality and societys desire to do just that.

Venuss worshipers abandon her because they are unable to control her eroticism. Gradually turning from polytheism, her followers become more conserva- tive and try to civilize the goddess by forcing her to conceal her nudity. They made me cover my forget- me-nots!...Id rather die / than have to sunbathe on the sly, complains a distraught Venus. Now, no one builds statues in her honor, no one sings her praises, her name has been forgotten, and her breasts, which used to con- quer multitudes, are ignored. Desperate and dejected, Venus seeks shelter with the wise Shaman who has spent his life isolated from society and civilization. In her vulnerable state of abandonment, Venus seems to give into the pressures to overcome her nature and accept domestication. She claims that she wants to lead a simple life like the Shaman and get back in touch with the birds and bees / far from the hum of the pressing crowd. Exerting a genuine effort, she seems to grow more modest and self- conscious. She blushes and questions whether it is polite to show up naked in a strange mans house. When the Shaman throws her a fox-fur jacket she does not resist and is actually grateful for the cover. Venus even seems to become more attune to housework as she crossly chastises the Shaman, instructing him to keep his dugout clean and to stop smoking! She also cuts open the carcass of a deer and prepares one of her favorite dishes: Venison a la Venus. But the domestication and transformation of the goddess of love into an irritable housewife is meant hu- morously and satirically. Where did she learn to cook? Olympus? It is a commentary on the process of domestication and suggests that there is something unnatural about external influences forcibly imposing changes on ones character and impulses. Because it is unnatural, Venus transformation is unsustainable and she doesnt revel in the simple life of housewifery too long. A dying swan delivers a message that her people love and miss her and need her to return. Venus quickly decides to leave the Shaman and asks him to forget my breasts. / Put them out of your mind. / Forget my face, my sweet behind. Simple life is not for her. Instantly, Venus reverts back to what she was when she first came to the Shaman: untamed and uncovered sexuality. She strokes his beard and disappears like a sweet mistake. Venuss journey comes full circle and she embrac- es the sexuality that caused her such grief. Though the simplicity of her life with the Shaman may have been tempting, even enjoyable, it was inorganic to her nature. And just like Venus eventually shakes off her domestication because it is alien to who she is, the Futurists proposed that Russians shake off  the foreign influence of the West and embrace their intrinsic connection to the East and the primitive (Goncharova).

Khlebnikovs Stone Woman, written in 1919, is a more somber piece that like Venus and the Shaman functions as a commentary on the spiritual power of the female figure.13 Here, however, the females sexuality is secondary. Instead, it is her connection with nature and eternity that gives the female figure power and allows her to transcend human life and death. Khlebnikov demonstrates the closeness of the female figure to the natural world by selecting an enchanted place, presumably far from civilization, as the home of the Stone Woman. A Scythian stone idol, she has stood lifeless and breathless in the same spot for generations and is condemned to stand here forever more. Her power is eternal and universal, stretching from sky to sky.14 It is comparable only to the power of the nature that surrounds her: The mountains whirl in webs of snow, / unwindings of millennial sounds. The mountains too are bound to stand here eternally and have incomprehensible knowledge. Thus the Stone Woman is surrounded by a grandiose natural landscape and is one with it. An anguished young man disturbs the stillness and fairytale wonder by approaching the Stone Woman, desperate for the idols comforting presence. He weeps for all those who have died in wars and battles. Helpless in the face of death, he feels like a miniscule speck in the spectrum of time beating like a captured butterfly in the meshes of the Milky Way. In contrast to this one humans helpless position, the Stone Womans power is boundless because of her connection to the earth and so she transcends any single mortal life and death. As the man weeps, a motha symbol of naturesuddenly lands on the idol bringing her to life. Her transformation further emphasizes the connection between the Stone Woman, nature, life, and death. The transformative moment imbues the poem with the vitality of life as the Stone Womans eyes flicker and fill with intelligence while she breaks into a frenzied dance. Khlebnikov describes her birth with imagery of fire, but the life-giving moth is unlikely to survive the flickering cherry stain. Furthermore, the Stone Womans turbulent dance sharply contrasts with her disciples mournful cries for the blood filling the Tisza and Vistula rivers. Death and dance are juxtaposed because the female figures connection with nature, land, and earth allow her to transcend the limits imposed on humanity. Like Mother Nature or Mother Russia who is eternal, universal, and all seeing, the Stone Woman is a seer through the Milky Way. She will remain a source of power, comfort, and inspiration for eternity regardless of how many individuals live or die. This work can be read as a commentary on the connection of Russian people. Even as mortal lives end, their sprits are united by their shared history and idols, which allows the cycle of life and death to continue. The Stone Woman is a very different female figure than Venus. While Venus exudes life and sensuality, the Stone Woman is coarse and lifeless. But they share a common spirita sprit that transcends everyday life and cant be tamed or even understood. And it is this strength of spirit upon which the Futurists believed that national strength and identity should be fashioned. Like Khlebnikovs poem, Natalia Goncharovas 1908 painting Stone Woman also depicts the Scythian stone sculpture. But in Goncharovas Stone Woman she strives to bring the extraordinarythe idolinto everyday life by situating the Stone Woman in the role of a nude model. The Stone Woman, though she is inanimate, has a very dynamic role in this piece as she destabilizes several norms by actively redefining her representation. The Stone Woman is not the traditional Western representation of beauty as she is far from the voluptuous, milk-skinned nude. Instead, Goncharova assigns this role to an inanimate, crude, and distinctly primitive stone sculpture, thereby replacing the Western ideal of beauty with the other. Goncharova uses modernist techniques of flattening and figural distortion to emphasize how distant the Stone Woman is from the Western ideal of beauty. The Stone Woman has no neck and instead her smooth oval head is pasted onto her torso. Her facial features are somewhat blurred, with half-closed eyes that appear as thin slits. A long nose runs down the length of her face and meets thin, slightly pursed lips. Willowy arms extend from comparatively broad and muscular shoulders. The same stark contrast is repeated by the tiny feet, which extend from disproportion- ably full thighs. Unlike the typical female nude, this female figure is desexualized although she is naked. Not sprawled on a bed fully exposed, she is, instead, com- pressed in a fetal-like position with legs tucked up to her torso, arms held protectively over her flattened rather than voluptuous chest. In addition to defying what the nude model should look like, the Stone Woman reimagines the role of the model. Next to Stone Woman appear painters brushes, behind her is a canvas with flowers, and in her hands she holds a small tubepossibly a tube of paint. The canvas and painterly tools suggest that she is both model and artist. Thus the Stone Woman refuses to conform to what is proper and expected; instead she takes a very active role in redefining and reinventing. Not only does she defy the traditional representation of beauty, but she reinvents the role of the passive model by actively participating in the act of creating. The Stone Womans refusal to be confined to a certain kind of representation accurately aligns with the goals of the

Futurists, as this is the same active participation they proposed for the construction of a Russian national identity. Unlike Stone Woman, which straddles the lines between the extraordinary and the mundane, in Planting Potatoes, completed around 1909, Goncharova is fully situated in the world of familiar subject matter. The female figure is no longer the divine being of the Stone Woman or the goddess Venus, but is an ordinary peasant working in the fields. By capturing an indefinite moment in the everyday life of the Russian peasant, Goncharova romanticizes hard work and the ordinary, demonstrating her interest in heroizing and mytholo- gizing the mundane. While the works discussed above primarily explored the female figures spiritual strength, in this painting, the womens physical strength is most significant. Although Goncharova has not adopted total abstraction, in the modernist style, she has rejected traditional realism and distorts the human form to emphasize certain elements of the piece. Without the use of modeling and shading, Goncharova depicts the women as flattened and geometric with disproportionately large hands and feet. Their shovels, on the other hand, appear diminutive in contrast to their towering bodies. The scale and strength of the womens physicality demonstrates that they dont lead lives of leisure but have adapted to long hours of strenuous work. Suggesting that these peasant women are intimately tied to the land on which they work, their feet are like thick roots firmly planted into their domestic soil. In the distance appears the paintings only male figure. Smaller and further away, his inclusion again underscores the womens closeness to the land and implies that they are able to wok independently of men. With olive skin tone and dark eyes, the womens sharp, angular facial feature dont appear to be European or even Eastern European. Closer to the the true face of peasant RussiaAsiatic and Scythian, the women represent the Russian other that the Futurists idolized (State 12). Red headscarves, traditionally worn by female peasantry, explicitly stress their Russianness. Notably, Goncharova is not depicting a portrait of specific women at a particular moment in time. This can be inferred because the womens faces lack detail and individualization, their clothes cannot be dated, and their location cannot be ascertained. In creating an ambiguous time and space within the painting, Goncharova intends these laborers to represent all peasant woman hard at work in the fields at all moments of Russian history. Planting Potatoes is particularly compelling because the peasant women arent overly romanti- cized. They are not lovely, sensuous maidens leisurely sprawled on a luscious pasture as their cattle graze nearby. Neither clean nor pretty, their work demands that they toil with shovels, lug heavy bags of potatoes, and soil their coarse, bare feet. Goncharova is not just idolizing the primitive, she is idolizing and heroizing the hard work of the primitive. Greatly valuing labor, Goncharova reportedly said that Everything passesfriendship and love; the only thing that remains is work, (State 10). Strong, independent, and timeless, these female peasants personify a nation built on hard, Russian work. The binaries of the divine and mundane, established by Khelbnikov and Goncahrova, are reconciled in Larionovs Jewish Venus from 1912. By depicting a naked army prostitute confidently prostrated on a bed, Jewish Venus instills the divine qualities of the untamed sexuality and spirit of Venus into a mortal form. This piece also demonstrates Larionovs interest in blur- ring the distinctions of high and low art by portraying classes, races, and ethnicities typically dismissed by the Academy. Like Goncharova, Larionov plays with realistic representation by rendering the prostitute as flattened with large and exaggerated facial features. She is fully nude yet, like Khlebnikovs Venus, she is not ashamed of her nudity nor is she portrayed in a position of victim- ization. She is defiant, boldly staring at the viewer as she shamelessly displays photographs of soldiersher cli- entstriumphantly pasted on the wall behind her. Her collection of client photographs is empowering because it demonstrates that the prostitute is not ashamed of her position in life. On the contrary, she collects mementos to commemorate her conquests. The photographs can also be read as a commentary on the Nemprimitivists stance on technology and modernity. Although photog- raphy was not a particularly new invention at this time, it nonetheless represents technology and innovation. Its inclusion in this work reaffirms that the Futurists were not interested in rejecting modernization but wanted progress to proceed on Russian terms. According to Parton, the prostitutes defiant gaze and the stark pallor of her skin against a bright green wall are direct references to Edouard Manets Olympia (52). But Larionovs Venus is no frail, high-class cour- tesan. She has a peasants physicality with large, strong arms and feet. A peasant prostitute, she could easily spend her days as one of Goncharovas potato planters. Depicting the female with what Larionov perceived as distinctly Jewish features reveals his interest in exploring the ethnological canons of beauty (Parton 52). Larionov studied ethnography and was particularly interested in the themes of racial characteristics. He wanted to uncover the unique features that different ethnic groups use to measure the standards of beauty.

Armed with this alternative beauty vocabulary, Larionov strives to challenge Western ideals of perfection (Parton 97). The rejection of European high art is further asserted by the single red rose that appears on the wall next to the soldiers photographs. Parton suggests that the rose is a reference to the Greek myth of Venus and Adonis (Parton 109). By referencing the classical Venus, Larionov is emphasizing that he is reimagining the ideal. The divine goddess is brought to earth and becomes the earthly and tangible goddess of love (Parton 52). But not only is the divine or academic Venus made obsolete and the West dusted off, but the notions of love, passion, and sensuality are now embodied in a Russian peasant prostitute (Goncharova). Although the female figure appears in several manifestations in the works I have discussed, she main- tains certain core characteristics in every reincarnation. From the Stone Woman to the Jewish Venus, the female figure is strong, empowered, and authentic. She is represented as raw and unrefined, bears who she is proudly, and is in control of how she is perceived. The construction of national identity based on core, unrefined values is an empowering philosophy and opens up research opportunities in a variety of fields. Conclusion The role of the powerful female cultural hero makes Neoprimitivism a rich period of study for feminist and gender critics because it proposes a new model of feminist identity in which the woman is not just an image of fertility, but an image of strength and power. The Futurist philosophy is particularly interesting because they were not making a comparison of the male and female strength. Rather than propose that the female is as strong as a men, the Futurists asserted that the female is strong independently of men. Unfortunately, the empowered role of the woman can also have destabilizing consequences because of the potential tensions between strength/liberated sexuality and fertility/motherhood. In a world where the role of the woman is to be more than a mother, what happens to the sanctity of motherhood? Can the sexually liberated, empowered Jewish Venus also be a strong mother figure? Beyond the role of the female figure, this project has stakes for Art Historians. Russian Futurism was one of the first times that Russia became a leader and innovator in the visual arts (Gray 94). With the founda- tion established by the groundbreaking and progressive innovations of Larionov and Goncharoav, younger Russian artists had a basis upon which to structure their theories. Some of these theories, including Malevich Suprematism, attained more recognition in the West, but the Futurists were instrumental in introducing Russia to the global art conversation. Additionally, this was a unique period in Russian Art History because the visual arts preceded and led literature, as most innovations were first made visually and then replicated in poetry. Typically in the history of Russian culture, this relationship was reversed and literature paved the way for visual developments (Gray 108). Finally, the study of the Futurists quest for national identity can add value to cultural studies. The Futurists wanted Russia to reject dominant world- views and fashion a national identity based on her own culture and values. They were fully invested in figuring out how to be progressive and forward thinking while preserving Russian culture and history. Maintaining cultural independence is a vital and challenging question even todayperhaps more than ever todaybecause of the homogenization of values and ideas fueled by globalization and global communication. The Futurists offer one empowering method of deriving independence by introspectively identifying sources of national strength such as the female was for Russia. Footnotes 1 2

title: STRANDED IN JORDAN: A Study of Jordans Iraqi Refugee Policy
abstract: The refugee policies of first world countries and the international refugee regime have been popular topics in refugee studies. This research often overlooks that most refugees flee to neighboring countries in the third world and minimizes the impact that these countries’ domestic policies have on the refugees. The literature on host countries’ responses to a refugee influx is based on a different context than is most often found in the developing world. With one of the highest ratios of refugees to total population in the world, Jordan challenges the standard assumptions and theories in the literature. Jordan has an authoritarian regime, a chronic lack of natural and economic resources, an insular and homogeneous society, a complex diplomatic position in the region and vis-à-vis the U.S., and a complicated history of hosting Palestinian refugees. This research traces the historical trajectory of Jordanian policies on Iraqi refugees and explains them as rational reactions to the refugees’ perceived impact on Jordan’s external relations, regime security, and socioeconomic situation. Elements of process tracing, content analysis, and discourse analysis are employed to examine official discourse on Iraqi refugees in speeches, interviews, and press reports. Its findings suggest that despite continued discourse on treating Iraqis as “welcomed guests,” the Jordanian regime’s tightening policies reveal increasing concern that the refugees’ presence is a threat to the security and stability of the regime and Jordanian society. Furthermore, the policies reflect the regime’s chronic fear of weakness and its desire to preserve social and political homogeneity.
text:
STRANDED IN JORDAN: A Study of Jordans Iraqi Refugee Policy Laura Ashbaugh INTERNATIONAL STUDIES PROGRAM

Galya Ruffer FACULTY ADVISOR INTERNATIONAL STUDIES PROGRAM NORTHWESTERN UNIVERSITY

Jacqueline McAllister

Photo by Eva Serna

GRADUATE STUDENT MENTOR DEPARTMENT OF POLITICAL SCIENCE NORTHWESTERN UNIVERSITY

The refugee policies of first world countries and the international refugee regime have been popular topics in refugee studies. This research often overlooks that most refugees flee to neighboring countries in the third world and minimizes the impact that these countries’ domestic policies have on the refugees. The literature on host countries’ responses to a refugee influx is based on a different context than is most often found in the developing world. With one of the highest ratios of refugees to total population in the world, Jordan challenges the standard assumptions and theories in the literature. Jordan has an authoritarian regime, a chronic lack of natural and economic resources, an insular and homogeneous society, a complex diplomatic position in the region and vis-à-vis the U.S., and a complicated history of hosting Palestinian refugees. This research traces the historical trajectory of Jordanian policies on Iraqi refugees and explains them as rational reactions to the refugees’ perceived impact on Jordan’s external relations, regime security, and socioeconomic situation. Elements of process tracing, content analysis, and discourse analysis are employed to examine official discourse on Iraqi refugees in speeches, interviews, and press reports. Its findings suggest that despite continued discourse on treating Iraqis as “welcomed guests,” the Jordanian regime’s tightening policies reveal increasing concern that the refugees’ presence is a threat to the security and stability of the regime and Jordanian society. Furthermore, the policies reflect the regime’s chronic fear of weakness and its desire to preserve social and political homogeneity.

The Middle East’s ‘Other’ Refugee Problem Academics and policymakers alike have been troubled by the dramatic increase in the number of refugees and forced migrants worldwide over the past several decades. Developing countries with limited resources are absorbing massive influxes of refugees without durable solutions to their resettlement or repatriation. Jordan is a prime example of this problem. Between 450,000 and 750,000 Iraqi refugees are estimated to be living in urban areas in Jordan, adding considerably to its small population of six million.1 While receiving minimal international attention, the Iraqi displacement after the U.S. invasion in 2003 is in fact larger than the size of the Palestinian flight in 1948.2  Jordans capital city, Amman, now has the distinction of having the most refugees of any city in the world, according to a 2010 study released by the United Nations.3 Jordanians reactions to the influx of Iraqis have been mixed. Initially, the spirit of Arab brotherhood and the strong historical ties between the people of Iraq and Jordan compelled hospitality. Later, Jordanians blamed Iraqis for inflation, housing short- ages, high food prices, and job scarcity.4 This frustration was expressed not just in public discourse, but also in sporadic violence against Iraqis.5 Until now, much of the focus and research on Iraqi refugees has been on temporary humanitarian assistance and the possibilities of resettlement or repatriation. Researchers, policymakers, and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) consider voluntary repatriation as the ideal solution for refugees. Despite the tenuous security situation in Iraq, there is pressure from around the world to repatriate Iraqi refugees. European countries have begun deporting Iraqi refugees who did not qualify for asylum, and Middle Eastern countries are eager to ease the strain on their resources.6 King Abdullah II of Jordan has repeatedly said that his country does not want another permanent refugee population because of the burden on its resources, water, education, and health systems.7 Despite the increasing clamor for Iraqis to return to their country, few have moved back. In the first six months of 2009, only 150 out of 500,000 Iraqis living in Jordan repatriated with UNHCR assistance, according to a study published in July 2009.8 According to the UN study, Iraqis reportedly felt that current conditions in Iraq prevented them from returning home, and many said they would not return under any circumstance. The study quoted a Jordanian scholar saying, The decision to flee from your own country is always easier to make than the decision to return.  With no end in sight to Jordans role as host to Iraqi refugees, it is crucial to 26 understand Jordans refugee policies and their impacts domestically, regionally, and internationally. There is a plethora of research on international organizations involvement in refugee situations, first world countries responses to refugee crises, and on resettlement processes of refugees in those first world countries. There is much less research focusing on the countries where most refugees flee to: developing countries in the third world. Furthermore, there is little attention on what shapes these countries responses to refugees, and models based on developed Western countries fail to explain the behavior of developing nations such as Jordan.  For example, Myron Weiner, an internationally recognized migration and security scholar, has theorized that a countrys national security and political interests trump its moral willingness to accommodate refugees.9 Weiner posits that when a country perceives a refugee influx as a threat to its security and stability, it will likely respond with economic aid, coercive diplomacy, or armed intervention. Since his analysis focuses on wealthy, industrial countries, however, it does not adequately account for Jordans behavior. Jordans unique historical and geopolitical position prevent it from responding to perceived security threats according to Myrons or other scholars models. Jordan has neither the economic might nor diplomatic capital to prevent a refugee flow, and its relationship with the U.S. makes a military intervention in Iraq unthinkable. Jordans authoritarian government, precarious location in a volatile region, and delicate diplomatic position make it a unique case that defies the mold created by Weiner and other scholars.  Thus, Jordan responds in the few ways that it still can: tightening border controls, discouraging assimilation, preventing political participation, soliciting international aid, and insisting on third country resettlement or repatriation. Since developing countries like Jordan perceive a refugee influx differently from those in the developed world, explaining their behavior in response to a massive influx of refugees requires a different model.  While their policies are often criticized as unnecessarily restrictive and detrimental to refugees, the policies can be explained as rational reactions to a perceived threat. This research aims to offer a new model to explain how we understand Jordans evolving refugee policies and conflicting discourses as a reflection of state interests and rational choices.   Through analysis of Jordanian policy documents, speeches, and interactions with other nations and international organizations, this research traces the evolution of Jordans perceptions of the Iraqi refugees and explains its policy decisions as actions to preserve the regimes security. For this analysis, elements of process tracing, content analysis, and discourse analysis were used. While fully employing these techniques is beyond the scope of this project, the methods have informed the qualitative analysis.  This first research aim provides an analysis of the political and historical context of Jordanian refugee policy, with particular attention to its experience with Palestinian refugees and its complicated relationship with Iraq. Next, this research provides a detailed analysis of Jordans evolving policy responses to Iraqi refugees, dividing them by category and by their adherence to internationally sanctioned recommendations. Finally, it offers an explanation of how these policies were made in response to perceived security and stability threats. Jordans refugee policy choices are reactions to a deteriorating economic situation, growing domestic unrest, continuing terrorist threats, and dwindling resources. Center of the Storm: How Jordan Became the Region’s Safe Haven In order to understand Jordans current predicament with Iraqi refugees, it is necessary to appreciate its history. In just 90 years since its state formation, Jordan has transformed from a sparsely populated desert to an important regional player.  Jordan has been widely called an artificial state that has historically been plagued by dire resource scarcity and weak political power.  With a leader brought in from the Hijaz and a hodgepodge population of Bedouin, its political survival following its creation in the wake of World War I seemed unlikely at best. Jordan has persevered because of the tenacity of its political elites, the loyalty of the East Bank security establishment, and the countrys geopolitical centrality. These are still the three factors that keep the Hashemite regime in power in Jordan today.10 In addition, Jordan has had a tumultuous history with its neighbor, Iraq. Iraqi refugees are only one factor in the power plays between Jordan and the new government in Iraq. Throughout most of its history, Jordan has had close economic and social ties with Iraq, and the Jordanian people have often sided with Iraq even before their own monarch. The break in relations in the decade preceding the U.S. invasion of Iraq and the subsequent change of regime dramatically changed the dynamic. Nevertheless, Jordan was the first Arab country to send an ambassador to Baghdad following the invasion and has constantly rallied support for Iraqs new government in the Arab League.11 The burden of hosting so many Iraqis, however, has increasingly become part of the official discourse between Iraq and Jordan. Eager to repatriate the Iraqis, Jordan has a significant interest in catalyzing the stability and security of Iraq. Jordan has a long history of addressing refugee issues. Since 1948, Jordan has hosted millions of Palestinian refugees, who now make up about 60 percent of the countrys population. In 1950, King Hussein annexed the West Bank and gave Palestinians Jordanian citizenship, making Jordan the only Arab country to confer widespread citizenship rights to Palestinians.12  Like most other Arab countries, Jordan is not a signatory to the United Nations 1951 Convention on the Status of Refugees and its 1967 Protocol, meaning that it does not legally recognize refugees nor offer them the full protec- tion and rights under the convention. Historically, Arab countries did not sign the convention because they argued that the convention did not adequately preserve the Palestinians right of return and self-determina- tion.13 Consequently, many Arab countries have large refugee populations, but lack the formal protections and legal systems to process those refugees. An additional consequence is that Arab governments have an aversion to using the term refugee for non-Palestinian refugees in Middle East: the government of Jordan, for example, officially calls Iraqis guests or visitors, and in the Arab press the Iraqis are often called the displaced or immigrants.14 Humanitarian organizations have sought to draw attention to the current Iraqi refugee crisis by calling it unprecedented, but this obscures the fact that Iraq has a long history of forced migration that is deeply in- grained in the regions political history. This most recent flight of Iraqis into other Middle Eastern countries can be considered to be simply an amplification and con- tinuation of preexisting regional migration patterns.  All of Iraqs neighbors - and especially Iran, Turkey, Jordan, and Syria - have received waves of forced migrants over the decades because of successive Iraqi regimes attempts to exert control over the population by restrict- ing their mobility and fragmenting them along political, ethnic, religious, or ideological lines.15 Since 1991, Iraq hemorrhaged between 4.2 and 4.8 million internal and external refugees, accounting for more than a fifth of its total population.  Millions of Iraqis came into Jordan throughout the 1990s, but due to the expense and difficulty of the journey, those who arrived in Jordan were mainly a self-selected group who were well-edu- cated and upper-middle class.16 Jordan traditionally received those fleeing instability in Iraq as temporary guests, not refugees, based on the regional tradition of Pan-Arabism.17 Jordan also served an important role as a transit country, as many Iraqis left Jordan to seek asylum in Europe or the U.S. Thus, while many Iraqis in Jordan are indeed stranded and living in Jordan illegally, the population is by no means universally static. These migration patterns are important because they contribute to the Jordanian governments refusal to either recognize Iraqis as a refugee population or to treat them according to international standards. Reliable information on the number of Iraqis who returned to Iraq without UNHCR assistance is hard to come by, however, and there are signs of increasing circular migration between Iraq and Jordan.18 Amman is considered by some to be Iraqs second capital and Iraqis regularly shuttle between Baghdad and Amman for weddings, medical treatment, college, and business meetings. Iraqs economic and social elites have sought to capitalize on Jordans security and stability by obtaining Jordanian residency permits for their families, and then commuting between Amman and Baghdad for business.19 Furthermore, the Jordanian government has notoriously incomplete records of foreigners entering and exiting the country, which is problematic since many Iraqis have transited through Jordan on their way to other countries in the Middle East or in the West.20 Estimates of the number of Iraqis in Jordan varies wildly: at one point the UNHCR reported the number of Iraqis in Jordan to be as high as 1 million, a Norwegian nongovernmental organization at one point put the number as low as 161,000, and the Jordanian government officially accepts the number as 450,000- 500,000.21 The estimate now most used by researchers and cited in NGO reports is between 450,000 and 750,000. The Evolution of Jordan’s Iraqi Refugee Policy In order to trace Jordans evolving refugee policies, this research adopts Jacobsens method of categorizing Jordans policies as either positive (UN recommended) or negative, and by their type: legal-bureaucratic, limiting international organizations activities, and the admission or treatment of refugees. These policies were further evaluated as containing positive or negative elements, with positive responses being in perfect accordance with internationally sanctioned refugee policies. Next, the cause of these policies is explained by adopting Weiners framework for analyzing how host countries perceive refugee populations as a security/stability threat. His factors can be condensed into three areas of analysis for this case study: how the Iraqi refugees affect Jordans external relations, the security of the Jordanian regime itself, and the social and economic conditions in Jordan (referred to as absorptive capacity by Gorden- ker22, Stein23, and Jacobsen24). Analyzing Jordan under this combined framework shows that Jordan perceives the Iraqi refugees as a security and stability threat and responds in ways that are not predicted by models based on Western or developed countries. Jordans unique historical context and geopolitical position mean that the responses available to Jordan are discouraging assimilation, preventing political participation, soliciting international aid, and insisting on third country resettlement or repatriation. Jordans policy toward Iraqi refugees has evolved as the crisis has evolved. As part of a well-established regional migration pattern, Iraqi emigration is neither a new nor shocking phenomenon, which is perhaps why Jordan and its neighbors did not respond at first to the 2003 influx with a dramatic change in policy. Instead, the policy only shifted when the Iraqi population began to be perceived as a security and stability threat to the Jordanian regime.  Jordans legal and bureaucratic policies can be categorized as negative because Jordan has not adopted international refugee law and has no legal framework for determining the status of refugees. Although Jordan has a plethora of institutions and agencies to support Palestinian refugees, it lacks a comparable bureaucratic structure to address Iraqi refugee issues. However, this is more indicative of the adverse political implications of acknowledging an Iraqi refugee population than of Jordans lack of experience with refugee matters. Furthermore, Jordan considers Iraqis to be guests, not refugees or asylum seek- ers because of its complicated history with Palestinian refugees.  As for its relationship with IROs, Jordan has generally had positive responses by welcoming their aid and allowing full access, but it has also restricted some of their programming to ensure that it also benefits poor Jordanians. In the third policy category of admission and treatment, Jordan has had progressively more negative responses.  There was no radical shift in refugee policy in the immediate aftermath of the invasion of Iraq, but the practical problems of hosting hundreds of thou- sands of refugees soon required policy responses. Jordanian policies were described generally as quite generous in the period between 2003 and 2005.  Most Iraqis at the border were given visas and allowed to enter. After 2005, social services were extended to Iraqis, particularly public education and reduced costs for medical services. Work permits are hard to come by and about 80 percent of Iraqis lack proper residence permits. As they fell into illegality, Iraqis were reluctant to seek out those social services for fear of deportation. Increasing entry restric- tions, often based on discriminatory factors like age or religion, are other examples of negative responses.  Still, there have been no large-scale deportations or com- plaints of involuntary repatriation. Jordanian Perceptions of Iraqi Refugees as a Security/Stability Threat The evolving refugee policies can be explained as a rational response to the security and stability threat perceived by the Jordanian government. Exploring the internal dynamics of Jordan  the insecurity of the regime, domestic unrest, economic problems, and social tensions  offers an explanation for why the Jordanian regime views Iraqi refugees as a security/stability threat and why it would depart from its period of open door migration and its policy of no policy.  The refugees have impacted Jordanian international relations, the security of the regime, and the socioeconomic climate. The presence of Iraqi refugees has meant that Jordan has a vital interest in restoring Iraqs strength and stability, and has provided a strong impetus for forming close ties with the new Iraqi government. Regionally, the presence of Iraqi refugees has reinforced Jordans self-constructed role as a safe haven for regional refugees and a champion of Arab brotherhood. The Iraqi refugees are an unspoken problem between Jordan and the U.S. because their presence is evidence of the poor security situation in Iraq. The refugees have proved to be useful leverage for Jordan in making the case for increased international aid, which in turn can be diverted for domestic priorities. As for the threat to the unity of Jordanian society, the Iraqi refugees are perceived as visible evidence of the spread of the Shiite Crescent and as a constant reminder of the fact that allowing foreigners into the country can expose innocent civilians to terrorist at- tacks. Furthermore, Weiners theory of security as a social construct proved true for this case study: in a homogeneous society like Jordan where the regime gains its legitimacy from its religious and ethnic leadership, an influx of newcomers destabilizes Jordanian unity, and thus the regimes grip on power.  Since Iraqi refugees are seen as a source of terrorism and political desta- bilization, the Jordanian government has responded by repressing domestic opposition and political participation, which only contributes to the cycle of instability and insecurity. Furthermore, the influx of Iraqis proved to be a convenient, but unfounded scapegoat for socioeconomic woes, allowing the Jordanian regime to deflect blame for the economic hardship caused by the Iraq War (in which the regime was a complicit partner) to the relatively blameless flood of Iraqi refugees.25  Domestic opposition grows as the Jordanian regime fails to solve the high unemployment rates and the rising prices of gas and food. Furthermore, with Iraqis perceived among the general public as the source of all those problems, their continued presence, and the possibility of their permanent residence, provides a flashpoint for domestic unrest. Thus the Jordanian regime uses the foreign aid intended to assist the Iraqi refugees to consolidate gov- ernmental institutions and its own power. Regardless of the degree of their actual impact, the perception of the Jordanian government and its people is that Iraqis threaten their security and stability. Therefore, Jordans departure from its historical approach to migration and refugees is not an unexplainable aberration, but a rational response to perceived threats.

The Future of Iraqi Refugees in Jordan Since the likelihood of an extended, if not permanent, stay in Jordan for Iraqi refugees grows higher with news of every bombing and election snafu in Iraq, Jordans policy choices continue to have a significant impact on the lives and futures of Iraqi refugees. The refugee problem grows more urgent every day; hundreds of thou- sands of Iraqi refugees are still stranded in Jordan, with their personal resources dwindling and with limited access to work, education and healthcare. The majority of Iraqis are living illegally and fear both deportation and the uncertain future. Voluntary repatriation is considered by the UN to be the ideal solution for any refugee population, but it is rarely practical or achievable, and has in fact never been enacted en masse.26  The continuing violence in Iraq, its political instability, and the vast internally displaced population are all challenges to repatriation. Most Iraqis have no desire to return to their country anytime soon because of the continuing violence in Iraq and because many dont have homes to return to: sectarian violence in religiously mixed areas of Iraq led to vast internal displacement and the formation of new, ethnically homogeneous communities. The controversies and alle- gations of fraud surrounding the March 2010 elections have also undermined political stability, and violence still plagues the country.  Local resettlement, considered to be the next best alternative, is problematic in host countries like Jordan with low absorptive capacity, deep political and security concerns, and vocal opposition to such a prospect. Jordan has made it abundantly clear that it is not willing to be host to another permanent refugee population. The potential for a permanent Iraqi refugee population threatens Jordans security and stability, and therefore the Jordanian government has made no plans for long-term resettlement or assimilation in Jordan.  Third-country resettlement, the next best alternative, is also not realistic given the aversion in Europe and the U.S. to accepting a refugee population with whom it has little ethnic affinity. These countries prefer funneling aid to regional host countries over opening their own borders to refugees. Thus, the Iraqi refugees pose a dilemma to which there is no clear solution, and their humanitarian needs are only worsening with the passage of time. An understanding of how Jordans refugee policies are made, however, is crucial to evaluating the future of Iraqi refugees in Jordan. title: Object Identification & Functional Attributes
abstract: People have a fascinating ability to identify individual objects and keep track of them even through dramatic changes over time. In this study, we investigated the identity preservation of individual objects with a specific focus on functional attributes. Participants were asked to imagine a flawed copy machine, which took an object and produced an altered version of it, along with other modified copies. A picture of the original object, which was given a name and a functional attribute, was presented to the participants followed by several of the outputs, and participants were asked to judge whether outputs could be identified as the original object. We found that if the original object and the output shared the same functional attribute, people were significantly more likely to say that it could be the original object and that identity was preserved. We also found that identity was preserved less with increasing transformational distance between the object and the output, a seemingly intuitive trend but one that has not been consistently produced in literature.
text:
OBJECT IDENTIFICATION & FUNCTIONAL ATTRIBUTES People have a fascinating ability to identify individual objects and keep track of them even through dramatic changes over time. In this study, we investigated the identity preservation of individual objects with a specific focus on functional attributes. Participants were asked to imagine a flawed copy machine, which took an object and produced an altered version of it, along with other modified copies. A picture of the original object, which was given a name and a functional attribute, was presented to the participants followed by several of the outputs, and participants were asked to judge whether outputs could be identified as the original object. We found that if the original object and the output shared the same functional attribute, people were significantly more likely to say that it could be the original object and that identity was preserved. We also found that identity was preserved less with increasing transformational distance between the object and the output, a seemingly intuitive trend but one that has not been consistently produced in literature.

Reina Uchino DEPARTMENT OF PSYCHOLOGY

Lance Rips FACULTY ADVISOR DEPARTMENT OF PSYCHOLOGY NORTHWESTERN UNIVERSITY

Linsey Smith GRADUATE STUDENT MENTOR DEPARTMENT OF PSYCHOLOGY NORTHWESTERN UNIVERSITY

Introduction Suppose that you have lost your keys sometime during the day. Later your coworker says she found them, and drops a set of keys into your hand. How do you know if they are your keys? Would it be convincing enough for them to physically resemble your keys? What if they looked different, but could still be used to open your front door? Everyday, people resolve these kinds of problems that require tracking the identity of individual objects. But how do we solve these problems and what kinds of information do we rely on to solve them? Current theories offer competing accounts for how people determine the identity of an individual object. Perhaps the most intuitive possibility is that people rely on perceptual similarity to match a recovered object to the original object. However, previous research has found that from a young age people usually choose a unique individual object that they have formed a personal attachment to over an exact duplicate of it (Hood & Bloom, 2008). This suggests that even young children use more than mere perceptual similarity in identifying individual objects. Moreover, people can often easily tell that two very similar looking objects are different, and that two very different looking objects are the same. For example, identical twin sisters can be identified as two different individuals even though they look extremely similar, and we can also tell that even though we met cousin Laura as a baby, she is still the same cousin now even though she is a teenager.

Another possible criterion for judging the identity of objects could be the basic level category (aka basic kind) of the original object. This category is exemplified by the word that is typically used to name a given object, for example apple or chair (Rosch et al, 1976). By contrast, words like fruit or furniture are not basic kinds, because these more abstract superordinate terms refer to groups of objects, not specific objects. The criterion of basic kind likely influences assignments of individual identity because people are aware that objects usually do not switch from one basic category to another. However, there are examples of dramatic metamorphoses across basic kinds in the world, and people seem to accept them quite readily. In nature, we see eggs turn into chicks, and seeds into flowers. In fiction, we see frogs turn into princes, and straw into gold. The ease with which people accept metamorphoses that cross the boundaries of basic kind suggests that this information is insufficient for tracking identity in some cases. In summary, the seemingly simple process of judging identity preservation of individual objects requires weighing complex criteria, including perceptual similarity and basic kind, and it seems like these different criteria are recruited in different contexts and with different objects. However, regardless of

Figure 1. Identity preservation across perceptual and functional manipulations.

how identity is judged, there is a common prediction that the greater the distance between the original and successor objects, the less likely they are to be the same (Liittschwager 1995; Blok et al 2005). In the presence of so many criteria it becomes challenging to study the effects of individual factors on identity preservation. Research so far has used fictional transformation machines and magical narratives to describe the instantaneous transformations of individual objects. These scenarios allow experimenters to isolate single factors and determine their contributions to peoples intuitions about identity persistence. Peoples judgments about these transformations do not seem to differ depending on the described method of transformation. To help focus participants on individual objects in these studies, experimenters usually provide a proper name for the objects. Because proper names are associated with unique individuals rather than properties or categories (Hall et al., 2003), adopting this convention offers an effective way to highlight individual objects. Previous research on the preservation of object identity has often manipulated basic kinds. For example, Blok, Newman, and Rips (2005) examined peoples judgments of identity preservation for identical looking objects, across basic kind objects, and across superordinate kind objects. They found that as the post-transformational object moved further from the original objects basic kind, its identity was less likely to be preserved. Rhemtulla and Hall (2009) performed a similar experiment but included a new type of transformation: the within basic kind transformation, in which the post-transformational object maintained basic kind information (e.g., cat) of the original object but altered its perceptual similarity (e.g., Siamese cat to Tabby cat). In contrast to previous work, participants gave lower ratings of individual persistence to objects that had undergone within category changes than to objects that had undergone across category changes. Rhemtulla and Hall (2009) suggested that these counter-intuitive results could be explained by the theory of alignable differences (Gentner & Markman 1997). According to the theory, when two objects are structurally similar to one another, their features can be aligned more easily and their differences become more salient. Our main hypothesis in this experiment was that the functional attributes of objects are major criteria that people use to create and maintain the identity of individual objects. These criteria have not been specifically investigated in the extant literature on individual object concepts, which has instead focused more on basic kinds as defining characteristics of individuals. However, in addition to visually assessing recovered objects, people often interact with them to check their behaviors as well. For example, if a person lost the key to a car, no matter how similar a newly found key is, that person would be unlikely to accept it as the original car key if it could not start the car. Functions and behaviors are fundamental parts of object identities, and thus manipulating the function of post-transformational objects should have an impact on whether participants believe identity to be preserved across a transformation. This effect should hold true regardless of whether basic kind information is altered, if functional attributes are a criteria independent of the basic kind and the appearances of objects. In this study, we used a transformation paradigm similar to Blok et al. (2005). Participants were asked to imagine a fictional copy machine that took an object and outputted an altered version of it, along with several similarly modified copies. Participants were presented with a picture of the original object, which was given a name and specific functional attribute, followed by several of the machines outputs. The outputs had either identical (sports car to sports car), within basic kind (sports car to minivan) or across basic kind (sports car to motorcycle) appearances, and either the same function, an unrelated function, or did not perform the same function as the original object. For example, if the original function of a sports car was that it drives, then the functional attributes of the outputs could be that it drives, does not drive, or decorates the showroom. Participants were asked to indicate if a particular output could be the original object with a yes or no response. Method Twenty-six Northwestern undergraduates participated for course credit. Two participants were excluded because they circled no to all of the questions, suggesting that they did not understand the task. The study took the form of a paper and pen survey, with the stimuli presented on laminated cards. A handout had a brief introduction that described a fictional machine called a multiplier machine. Participants were told that when an object is placed into the machine, the machine generated several copies of the object, all of which were faulty in some way. Participants were also told that at least one of the outputs was the original object, although appearance or function could have been altered during the copying process. The stimuli cards all had a picture of the object and a proper name (or a copy number) and a function printed underneath. The stimuli were six different common objects, and four outputs were presented for each object for a total of twenty-four trials. Participants saw all three types of perceptual (identical, within basic kind, across basic kind) and functional (identical, negated, unrelated) changes from the original object in the outputs. The procedure for presenting the stimuli involved three steps. First, the original object was presented. Then, an output was presented. Finally, participants indicated yes or no to the question Could Copy ## be <proper name of original object>? and rated how confident they were about their answer on a scale from 1 to 3. This was repeated for all twenty-four trials. Results The identity ratings showed a linear decline with increasing transformational distance between the pre- and post-change objects as in Blok et al (2005). There was a general effect for perceptual (F(2,597)= 79.96, p<.0001) and functional information (F(2,597)= 4.21, p<.05). Post hoc Tukey tests showed that having an identical appearance made it significantly more likely for identity to be preserved when copies had a negated or an unrelated function, but not when function was preserved across the transformation. For identical looking objects, there was an effect of function (F(1, 148)=17.45, p<.0001), with post hoc Tukey tests showing a significant difference between objects with identical and negated function, and also between objects with unrelated and negated functions. For the within basic kind transformations there was also an effect of function (F(2,222)=11.544, p<.0001) with post hoc Tukey tests indicating that same function objects preserved identity more than objects with negated or unrelated functions. The same effect was seen for across basic kind transformations as well (F(2,222)=14.604, p<.0001). The mean confidence ratings ranged from 2.27 (SD=0.53) to 2.65 (SD=0.64), and did not show any significant trends.

Discussion The results supported the main hypothesis that function is an important criterion people use to determine the identity preservation of individual objects. Maintaining the function of the original object significantly increased identity preservation across all transformations. For identical looking transformations, outputs with an unrelated function also preserved identity better than outputs with negated function. Several participants commented that when considering objects with unrelated functions, they thought that the objects could still potentially perform the original function, thus making it more likely that identity was preserved. This indicates that objects with negated function had lower identity ratings because they could not perform the specific function attributed to the original object, not because they were perceived of as simply broken or generally non-functional. The results also show a linear decline with greater transformational distance between the pre- and post- change objects. Methodological differences might have produced the discrepant results between this study and the findings from Rhemtulla and Hall (2009), therefore each difference should be tested independently in future research. It is possible that functional information also contributed to the linear trend, so the methodological differences should be tested without functional manipulations as well. Another factor to consider is similarity and difference ratings between pre-and post- transformational objects, which may reveal trends supporting the structural comparison explanation offered by Rhemtulla and Hall (2009). This experiment highlights functional attributes as important factors in peoples identification of individual objects. Along with further investigation into different degrees of necessity or typicality in functions, which might make them more or less important for maintaining identity, conceptual and methodological differences with regard to basic kind transformations should be investigated. Clearly, there are many more unanswered questions on this intriguing issue of how people think about and identify individual objects in the world. 34

title: The Effect of Time Lived in the US on Risk Factors for Type II Diabetes among Indian Immigrant Women of Low Socioeconomic Status
abstract: The rate of diabetes among Indian immigrants in America is increasing rapidly, facilitated in part by the adoption of changes in diet and lifestyle. This study attempts to elucidate the relationship between duration of time lived in the US and risk factors for diabetes. The study population consists of low socioeconomic status Indian immigrant women recruited from a Chicago-based health clinic (n=90). Data were collected on biological and lifestyle factors contributing to the heightened diabetes susceptibility of Indian immigrants in America. In addition, the study explores how well Indian diabetics care for their disease. Findings confirm a positive relationship between duration of time lived in the US and diabetic risk. A significant relationship was found between duration of time lived in the US and abdominal obesity (p=0.01), and a somewhat significant relationship with body fat percentage (p=0.09) and body mass index (p=0.09). Finally, diabetics in this sample population (n=39) did not take care of their diabetes in accordance with current standards of biomedicine, with 53.8% having an a1c hemoglobin measurement above 7.0% and 64.1% reporting less than 2 hours of weekly exercise. This study calls for a focus on educational interventions for Indian immigrants about Type II diabetes.
text:
The Effect of Time Lived in the US on Risk Factors for Type II Diabetes among Indian Immigrant Women of Low Socioeconomic Status Anisa Rahman DEPARTMENT OF ANTHROPOLOGY

Chris Kuzawa

William Leonard

FACULTY ADVISOR DEPARTMENT OF ANTHROPOLOGY NORTHWESTERN UNIVERSITY

FACULTY MENTOR DEPARTMENT OF ANTHROPOLOGY NORTHWESTERN UNIVERSITY

The rate of diabetes among Indian immigrants in America is increasing rapidly, facilitated in part by the adoption of changes in diet and lifestyle. This study attempts to elucidate the relationship between duration of time lived in the US and risk factors for diabetes. The study population consists of low socioeconomic status Indian immigrant women recruited from a Chicago-based health clinic (n=90). Data were collected on biological and lifestyle factors contributing to the heightened diabetes susceptibility of Indian immigrants in America. In addition, the study explores how well Indian diabetics care for their disease. Findings confirm a positive relationship between duration of time lived in the US and diabetic risk. A significant relationship was found between duration of time lived in the US and abdominal obesity (p=0.01), and a somewhat significant relationship with body fat percentage (p=0.09) and body mass index (p=0.09). Finally, diabetics in this sample population (n=39) did not take care of their diabetes in accordance with current standards of biomedicine, with 53.8% having an a1c hemoglobin measurement above 7.0% and 64.1% reporting less than 2 hours of weekly exercise. This study calls for a focus on educational interventions for Indian immigrants about Type II diabetes.

O

Introduction ver the last 20 years, the rate of diabetes prevalence has increased dramatically in both the US and around the world (Zimmet, 2001). Diabetes remains an especially pressing issue among Indian immigrants, who have a higher prevalence of overweight/obesity and diabetes in comparison to all other Asian immigrants (Oza-Frank et al., 2009). Research shows that the prevalence of diabetes among Indian immigrants living in America is disproportionately higher than the prevalence of diabetes among Indians in India itself (Diabetes India; Ramaiya, 1991). Previous studies on American immigrants have shown an acculturation effectthe prevalence of diabetes and diabetic risk factors increase with length of time spent living in the US, taken as a rough measure of American cultural and lifestyle adoption (Koya & Egede 2007; Oza-Frank et al., 2009; Roshania & Narayan, 2008). With a better understanding of this relationship, the high prevalence of diabetes within the Indian immigrant population can be reduced. The purpose of this study is to understand the effect of length of time lived in the US, taken as a rough index of lifestyle and dietary change, on risk factors for Type II diabetes among low socioeconomic status female Indian immigrants. Additionally, this study aims to identify which factors are the strongest predictors of diabetes risks among this population living in the city of Chicago. Finally, this study aims to analyze currently diabetic Indian-Americans and assess how well they care for their condition under current standards of biomedicine. For eight weeks I worked with a Chicago- based health center to obtain biographical information, activity profiles, and anthropometric measurements of female Indian-American immigrants of a lower socioeconomic status. Understanding the major cause of diabetes susceptibility for Indian immigrants can aid in the prevention and early detection of Type II diabetes, in turn helping to lower the high prevalence of diabetes among Indian immigrants in the US.

Indian Immigrants in the US over Time For the past few decades, Asian immigrants have consistently shown higher rates of diabetes than any other ethnic group in America (Oza-Frank et al., 2009; WHO). Moreover, the rate of diabetes among Indian immigrants living in the United States is disproportionately higher than the rate of diabetes among Indians living in India (Ramaiya, 1991). These results clearly suggest that there are aspects related to living in the United States that are making Indian immigrants more susceptible to Type II diabetes. This relationship can be explored in both physiological and lifestyle terms, and can provide a basis to test the effects of adoption of American culture and lifestyle through time. Studies have found that with increased duration of time lived in the US immigrants partake in less physical activity than they did in their home country (Goel, 2004; Koya & Egede, 2007; Lieberman, 2003). Interestingly, data show that foreign-born Asians lead more sedentary lifestyles than Asians born in the west, adding to the belief that lifestyle changes of Indian life to American life lead to increased diabetic risks (Goel, 2004, Pollard et al., 2008). Studies have found a direct relationship between duration of residence in the US and overweight/obesity prevalence and cholesterol for multiple immigrant groups (Goel, 2004; Koya, 2007; Oza-Frank, 2009; Roshania, 2008). In fact, US immigrants have lower prevalence of overweight/obesity at arrival to the US, but the prevalence increases with length of residence (Goel, 2004; McDonald & Kennedy, 2005, Roshania et al., 2008). Oza-Frank et al., 2009 found diabetes prevalence correlated with increased length of residence in the US for immigrants of all ethnicities. The data suggest that duration of residence in the US is a rough index of various lifestyle changes that seemingly leave them at higher risk for becoming overweight/obese and diabetic.

Research Questions This study attempts to explore reasons for increased prevalence of Type II diabetes within a population of low socioeconomic status Indian immigrant women (n=90). The main research question is: Does the amount of time spent in the US reflect upon higher risk profiles for diabetes? Based on previous research, this study expects to find higher risk dietary habits and reductions in activity levels with time spent living in the US. It is hypothesized that with increased time lived in the US, the data will show increased BMI, percent body fat, abdominal obesity, cholesterol, blood pressure and decreased activity profiles and weekly exercise rates. The second research question this study will address is: What are the activity, dietary, and lifestyle factors that specifically make Indian immigrant women more susceptible to Type II diabetes in comparison to the general US population? It is hypothesized that the Indian immigrant study population will show a high average body mass index (BMI), percentage body fat, abdominal obesity, cholesterol, and blood pressure. Additionally, the sample population will show a low amount of activity and weekly exercise, indicative of a sedentary lifestyle. Finally, this study asks: How well do diabetic Indian immigrant women care for their condition? It is hypothesized that diabetic Indian immigrants will not care for their diabetes as well as directed under current standards of biomedicine. Therefore they will show elevated levels of a1c hemoglobin, as well as sedentary lifestyles, increased BMI, body fat percentage and abdominal obesity. Materials and Methods Study Population With the help of the Indian American Medical Association Health Clinic (IAMACF) in Chicago, 90 women aged 30 and older who have emigrated to US from the Indian subcontinent were recruited. Of the 90 women, 79 were born in India, 8 in Pakistan, and 3 in Bangla- desh. The women were recruited while waiting to be seen by physicians at the clinic. The most common conditions treated at the IAMACF clinic are Hypertension, Diabetes, and Dyslipidemia (Radhakrishnan). IAMACF only serves patients without health insurance, and it is assumed that the study population is of low socioeconomic status. The women represent a random sampling of activity levels, diet, health condition and duration of time lived in US. The sample consists of a mixture of normal, pre-diabetic, and diabetic women. Northwestern University IRB approved these methods on August 8, 2009, and informed consent was obtained from each participant.
