title: Exploring the Relationship between Children’s Life Stories and the Big Five Personality Traits
abstract:
Life stories are strong predictors of identity, since the specific narratives adults tell about themselves represent individual differences in personality characteristics. One way researchers analyze these life stories in adults is by measuring the story’s coherence, which is comprised of a clear context, a linear chronology, and an explanation of why the specified events are important to the narrator. In doing so, researchers have found that more coherent personal narratives are related to better memory and communication, and stronger understandings of one’s own identity.

In the present study, I explored the relationship between narrative coherence and personality traits in children in an effort to examine children’s ability to tell life stories and how those stories relate to their developing identities. Participants were 367 children (53.1% female) ages 9-14 (Mage = 12.1, SD = 0.80). Children’s best and sad memories were coded for coherence, whereupon I analyzed whether the Five-Factor Model personality traits were associated with more coherent narratives. I also sought to determine whether Coherence was associated with age and gender. Results revealed that Sad Memory Coherence was generally unassociated with personality traits. However, Best Memory Coherence demonstrated some associations with Neuroticism, Openness, and Extraversion. These were variable across measures. Additionally, while age was unassociated with most coherence dimensions, gender was found to associate with most dimensions of coherence, such that girls’ best and sad memories were generally rated as more coherent than were boys’. While these are only preliminary results, they provide important insight into identity development in children.
text:
LIFE STORIES AND PERSONALITY

Exploring the Relationship between Children’s Life Stories and the Big Five Personality

Traits

Abigail Blum

Primary Advisor: Jennifer Tackett, Second Reader: Dan McAdams

Department of Psychology, Northwestern University

LIFE STORIES AND PERSONALITY

Abstract

Life stories are strong predictors of identity, since the specific narratives adults tell about themselves represent individual differences in personality characteristics. One way researchers analyze these life stories in adults is by measuring the story’s coherence, which is comprised of a clear context, a linear chronology, and an explanation of why the specified events are important to the narrator. In doing so, researchers have found that more coherent personal narratives are related to better memory and communication, and stronger understandings of one’s own identity.

In the present study, I explored the relationship between narrative coherence and personality traits in children in an effort to examine children’s ability to tell life stories and how those stories relate to their developing identities. Participants were 367 children (53.1% female) ages 9-14

(Mage = 12.1, SD = 0.80). Children’s best and sad memories were coded for coherence, whereupon I analyzed whether the Five-Factor Model personality traits were associated with more coherent narratives. I also sought to determine whether Coherence was associated with age and gender. Results revealed that Sad Memory Coherence was generally unassociated with personality traits. However, Best Memory Coherence demonstrated some associations with

Neuroticism, Openness, and Extraversion. These were variable across measures. Additionally, while age was unassociated with most coherence dimensions, gender was found to associate with most dimensions of coherence, such that girls’ best and sad memories were generally rated as more coherent than were boys’. While these are only preliminary results, they provide important insight into identity development in children.

LIFE STORIES AND PERSONALITY

Exploring the Relationship between Children’s Life Stories and the Big Five Personality

Traits

Life stories are strong predictors of identity, since the specific narratives individuals tell about themselves help people to make sense of their experiences. These stories also reveal individual differences in personality characteristics, which may predict things such as life outcomes, life satisfaction, overall wellbeing, and psychopathology (Hirsh & Peterson, 2009;

Reese et al., 2011). One way researchers explore the relationship between life narratives and identity is by rating a narrative’s level of coherence. Coherence reflects a combination of a narrative’s clarity on a linear timeline and thematic importance (Reese et al., 2011). Despite the many life story studies conducted with adults and older adolescents, there have been few studies regarding children’s ability to tell life stories and how those stories relate to their developing identities. Due to a lack of coherence in children’s stories compared to those of adults, it is important to study in further detail because previous research suggests that more coherent personal narratives are related to better memory and communication, and stronger understandings of one’s own identity (Reese et al, 2011). Understanding which factors, such as personality traits, may be associated with stronger (or weaker) senses of self at a young age will increase the knowledge surrounding child identity development. The present study sought to examine associations between personality traits and narrative coherence in childhood and early adolescence.

Personal narratives and autobiographical memory

People’s lives are shaped by various events, obstacles, and relationships that differentiate them from those around them. However, those separate events do not lead to an individual developing a meaningful identity until the events can be unified and internalized into a personal narrative, or “life story” (McAdams, 2001). A “life story” is an umbrella term that encompasses

LIFE STORIES AND PERSONALITY both the specific process of describing one’s life (life narrative) and the ability to think about it in terms of autobiographical events (autographical reasoning; Habermas & Paha, 2011). For this reason, a life narrative is more than just a series of unrelated stories but an integration of these episodes that allows individuals to make sense of their past, present, and future by describing their lives in terms of what is important to them. Research on narrative identity and autobiographical reasoning in adults has delineated that constructing these stories leads people to create identities, since it helps them to find meaning from their experiences (McAdams, 2001).

For example, in a study on finding redemptive meaning in suffering and adversity, McAdams

(2001) found that narrators who can deal with this pain through personal agency and exploration enjoyed higher levels of mental health, physical well-being, and maturity.

Underlying narrative identity is autobiographical memory, which is a uniquely human form of socially and culturally mediated memory that goes beyond the specific details of the event (who, what, where, when) to determine what the overarching meaning of the event is and why it is important to the individual’s life (Fivush et al., 2011). For example, a situation in which a child not only describes what pet he received for his birthday but also explains why receiving that pet was an important milestone in his life would be a strong autobiographical memory.

These memories reflect how individuals interact with their environments and partake in various relationships, more than simply representing the veracity of the memories in general (Adler et al., 2017). Instead of solely retrieving memories from long term storage, individuals interpret autobiographical memories on their way to verbalization. The goal of many life narrative studies is to utilize these autobiographical memories as a way to understand how an individual develops a coherent and continuous sense of self over time. Researchers suggest that the past explains the

LIFE STORIES AND PERSONALITY present, which projects into the future and helps to place an individual in both culture and community (Fivush et al., 2011).

Life narratives are critical for understanding identity, since the story is a flexible form that can change to mirror different life transformations, while still accounting for continuity over time (Fivush et al., 2011). Furthermore, narratives are not only ways to express identity, but ways to create identity, since encoding experiences into autobiographical memory involves a process of making sense of one’s experiences and understanding how one’s perception of himself is related across development (McLean, Pasupathi, & Pals, 2007).  In their process model of self-development, McLean and colleagues (2007) assert that not only do selves create stories, but those stories in turn create selves, working together in a formative cycle. In this sense, the autobiographical reasoning associated with life stories facilitates identity development by leading the individual to explore and reflect on himself through the meaning-making process integral to understanding experiences (Fivush et al., 2011).

While autobiographical reasoning is most often studied in adults, research suggests that this skill begins to develop in adolescence (Habermas & Paha, 2011). This is partly because children are not as adept at recounting their personal narratives; they focus mostly on the good and bad memories that they remember best instead of connecting their past memories to more recent memories in meaningful ways (Fivush et al., 2011). Thus, while an individual’s ability to connect specific experiences into more generalized life stories begins to develop in adolescence, this process is not completely developed until adulthood, whereupon the individual is more cognitively advanced (McAdams, 2001). Specifically, elements of overall coherence—causal coherence (the individual’s understanding of how one event leads to another) and thematic coherence (the individual’s ability to extract values and themes from events and apply them to

LIFE STORIES AND PERSONALITY overarching pictures of themselves)—are low in early adolescence but increase in teenage years and early adulthood (Habermas & Bluck, 2000). Research has shown, however, that children collect experiences and develop temperaments and traits along the way that will eventually help them to construct integrative life stories as they become older (McAdams, 2001). There is also evidence that even children in grade school can master the narratives of single events, which may equate with an adult’s ability to tell a life story (Habermas & Paha, 2011). Consequently, when conducting narrative studies with children and adolescents, it is often easier to ask them to describe specific memories, rather than asking them to provide an entire life story.

Coherence

A critical concept across narrative studies is coherence. According to Reese and colleagues (2011), a coherent narrative is one that makes sense to a naïve listener in terms of context (who, what, where, when) and provides an understanding of why an event is important to the narrator. Despite the fact that longer stories do not equate more coherent stories, coherence relies on sufficient contextual orientation and evaluation. Overall, more coherent personal narratives are related to better memory and communication, and stronger understandings of one’s own identity (2011). As a property of narratives, coherence is not a unitary construct, but one that arises from multiple dimensions, each of which contribute to overall narrative coherence

(2011). There are three main types of coherence: temporal (clearly ordering events in time), thematic (noticing themes and trends in one’s life), and causal (understanding both human motivation and the connection between events and personal change). Many researchers deem causal coherence to be the most important type of coherence in single event narratives, since it requires the individual’s understanding of how one event leads to another, which children and adolescents are often able to do (Habermas & Paha, 2011).

LIFE STORIES AND PERSONALITY

While various schemes for coding coherence in verbal life narratives exist, such as the

Baerger and McAdams’s (1999) coherence scheme, or Peterson and McCabes’ (1983) coherence scheme via high point analysis, Reese et al.’s (2011) multidimensional Narrative Coherence

Coding Scheme (NaCCS) is of most relevance to the current study since it focuses on the independent aspects of coherence that develop at different times. The three dimensions of coherence in this scheme are context (the information that situates the listener by providing the where and when), chronology (how well the listener can infer the order in which actions within an event took place), and theme (the overarching point of the story, including evaluation, resolution, and how well the narrator stays on topic). In test samples performed with preschool- aged children, school-aged children, and adults from various data sets collected across five labs, the scheme was found to be highly reliable among independent coders, with an average reliability coefficient of .80 for context, .82 for chronology, and .89 for theme (Reese et al.,

2011). These results suggest that unlike other coding schemes, the NaCCS can be used both to analyze life stories narrated by adults and single memories told by young children.

Reese and colleagues (2011) further suggest that chronology is the first dimension to develop because children’s ability to order events temporally starts from young ages. While this skill inevitably continues to develop in early adolescence with the ability to create more complicated, causally connected narratives developing in line with normal cognitive advancements, preschoolers can create a reasonably ordered event, explaining how one thing happened, which led to another, and so on. Contrastingly, ability to use context does not emerge until middle childhood, and improves even more during adolescence, when the storyteller becomes increasingly able to account for the needs of the listener to be located within the story.

Finally, although researchers anticipate that even preschoolers can maintain a single topic and

LIFE STORIES AND PERSONALITY possibly offer some brief elaborations, theme is the last dimension to develop, since the ability to provide resolution between an event and oneself does not emerge until adolescence, and continues to develop well into young adulthood (Peterson & McCabe, 1983; Habermas & de

Silveira, 2008). Reese et al.’s (2014) study of cultural differences in coherence between individuals aged 12-21 revealed that older adolescents spoke with the most causal coherence

(Mcoherence = 1.18, SD = 0.59), followed by mid-adolescents (Mcoherence = 0.99, SD = 0.57), and then younger adolescents (Mcoherence = 0.67, SD = 0.53). There was also an effect of gender, with female participants demonstrating higher casual coherence than males (M = 1.02, SD = 0.60 vs.

M = 0.88, SD = 0.56). These findings suggest that–due to the different developmental patterns across these three coherence dimensions and the fact that they measure different aspects of coherence–they should be analyzed independently of one another, while accounting for the age of the narrator. For this reason, determining the effect of age and gender on the coherence of children’s best and sad memories is one of the goals of the current study.

Identity and Personality Several theories of identity development posit that identity construction is highly salient in adolescence, as this is a developmental stage where individuals gain the ability to perceive themselves in more abstract ways and social pressures influence them to figure out who they are

(Waters & Fivush, 2015; McAdams & McLean, 2013). Furthermore, identity achievement, wherein individuals overcome a crisis to discover their true sense of self, is consistently related to various indicators of wellbeing (Marcia, 2002; Hofer, Busch, & Kärtner, 2011). Researchers hypothesize that while identity status is often only achieved in young adulthood, there are important early stages of identity formation occurring in adolescence. Unfortunately, there has been a lack of research measuring these early stages, especially the process of exploration.

LIFE STORIES AND PERSONALITY

Realizing the gap in knowledge, recent studies have sought to provide ways to measure identity exploration during early adolescence (Kylm & Cieciuch, 2015). Since coherence is a fundamental component of identity development, researching whether it is possible to measure coherence in early adolescents—that is, determining whether there is enough variation in coherence scores to reveal salient information or if children of that stage have no coherence at all—will provide a way to assess predictors of well-being.

Since personal narratives are characterized by the ways in which individuals make sense of their experiences, they are inherently tied to personality; depending on someone’s disposition, each person may interpret the same situation in different ways.  In McAdams’ model of personality, there are three layers which work together to develop a cohesive personality: traits as the most basic level, goals as the second level, and narratives as the most complex level

(McAdams, 2001). The first level represents the globally stable, linear, and comparable dimensions of human dispositions that make individuals unique from one another. These traits account for consistencies in behavior, thought patterns, and feelings across different situations and varying times in one’s life. The Five Factor Model of Personality is a well-established hierarchical model of trait structure that is useful in predicting important life outcomes, and comprehensive (meaning it accounts for all major dimensions or personality), while still being narrow and specific (McCrae & Costa, 1999). This model is organized into five broad factors:

neuroticism, extraversion, openness, agreeableness, and conscientiousness. The second level of personality encompasses the characteristic adaptations of those traits, including goals, motives, values, and defense mechanisms. Finally, the third level serves as an overall identity, and is defined by the life stories an individual tells. To gain a holistic understanding of an individual person, personality psychologists should understand the intricacies of each level and how they

LIFE STORIES AND PERSONALITY work together, but little is currently known about how traits at the first level relate to overall identity at the third level (McAdams, 2011).

Personality traits may influence or provide a foundation for identity development processes, which is why the current fragmented and intermittent literature on the relationship must be expanded (Clancy & Dollinger, 1993). The few studies that have examined the relationship between personality traits and identity have generally focused on identity exploration (Luyckx, Teppers, & Kilmstra, 2014) or sense of identity (Loundsbury, Levy, Leong,

& Gibson, 2007). For instance, Luyckx, Teppers, and Klimstra (2014) conducted a longitudinal study on identity processes and personality traits in adolescents aged 12-21 years. They found that higher levels of Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, and Emotional Stability were generally positively related to several adaptive identity formation processes. A longitudinal follow-up of a subset of participants indicated that identity formation was facilitated by high levels of

Conscientiousness and Extraversion, and low levels of Neuroticism (Klimstra et al., 2013).

Another study that further provided support for the connection between identity and personality dimensions compared traits to sense of identity (Lounsbury, Levy, Leong, & Gibson, 2007). The

Big Five traits accounted for 34% of the variance in one’s sense of identity, and that sense of identity was significantly correlated with all five personality traits: Emotional Stability (r = .46),

Agreeableness (r = .34), Extraversion (r =.28), Conscientiousness (r = .26), and Openness (r =

.22).

Despite this evidence for a possible explanatory role of traits in broad identity development processes, coherence specifically is rarely studied in relation to personality traits. In a study of 26 adults that focused on the relationships between traits and narrative coherence specifically, researchers found that the average narrative coherence was positively correlated

LIFE STORIES AND PERSONALITY with the trait of Openness, r = .35, as well as with female sex, r = .31 (Adler, Wagner, &

McAdams, 2007). Reese et al. (2014) further studied the connection between trait levels of personality and coherence in a sample of 268 adolescents, ages 12 to 21, from Māori, Chinese, and European cultures in New Zealand. The researchers asked the participants to recount instances of low points, turning points, and high points in their lives, which were used to examine the association between causal and thematic coherence and their self-reported Big Five traits. As in the current study, the coding scheme for the thematic coherence dimension was taken from the NaCCS. Although there were no significant correlations between traits and narrative identity for younger adolescents, for middle adolescents, there were significant positive associations between Thematic Coherence and Neuroticism for low point (r = .28) and high point memories (r = .26), as well as between Thematic Coherence and Openness in high point memories for older adolescents (r = .28). Researchers found weaker but still statistically significant positive associations between Thematic Coherence and Extraversion in girls’ (r = .17)

and older adolescents’ (r = .27) high point memories, as well as negative associations between

Coherence and Agreeableness in boys’ (r = -.19) and mid-adolescents’ (r = -.25) low point memories.

The Current Study

In this current study, I sought to determine whether there are individual differences in dimensions of coherence in late childhood and early adolescence, whether this coherence is associated with personality traits, and whether coherence dimensions differ by age and gender.

Thus, I investigated how narrative coherence (divided into context, chronology, and theme) in children’s discussions of memories relates to age, gender, and Big Five personality traits in a medium-sized (N = 346), sample of early adolescents. I hypothesized that while there may not be

LIFE STORIES AND PERSONALITY clear associations between thematic coherence and personality traits in a sample this young, there would be an overall positive association between Neuroticism and Coherence, and Openness and

Coherence. There would also likely be a weaker, although still significant positive association between Extraversion and Coherence. I predicted there would be no significant association between Conscientiousness and Coherence. Finally, given the contrasting results in previous research examining relationships between Coherence and Agreeableness, I did not advance specific hypotheses about the relationship between Coherence and this trait. I also hypothesized that there would be gender and age effects, with the older and female participants both having more coherent memories.

Method

Participants

The study analyzed de-identified participant responses from 346 children aged 9 to 14

(Mage = 12.10, SDage = 0.80; 53.1% female) and their parents from the Personality Across

Development Lab’s longitudinal study “Child Personality and Behavioral Outcomes Study” conducted in Toronto, Canada. The families were recruited using a community-based participant pool managed by the Department of Psychology at the University of Toronto, and through flyers and advertisements posted near the campus. In order to participate, both caregiver and child had to be fluent in English, and there could be no presence of neurodevelopmental disorders, psychotic disorders, or intellectual disability in the child. Throughout the study, there were three time points of data collection: Intake, Follow-Up 1 (FU1), and Follow-Up 2 (FU2). The current study used data from FU2, since this was the time point where children were asked to report their best and sad memories. Participants consisted of children who already participated in the first

LIFE STORIES AND PERSONALITY two parts of the study, as well as new children who were recruited solely for FU2 to account for participant attrition. Parent-report measures were collected at FU2.

Measures

Best and Sad Memories. In the lab, children were asked by research assistants to describe a time they remember feeling their happiest, and a time they remember feeling “really sad.” They were given three minutes for this task and were prompted to continue if they stopped speaking before the allotted time was finished. Participants were video recorded for later transcription and coding of these memories.

Inventory of Children’s Individual Differences (ICID). In the second follow up portion of the original study, parents were asked to fill out the ICID (Deal et al, 2017). These 144 mother- reported questionnaire responses were rated on a 7-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (much less than the average youth) to 7 (much more than the average youth). Unit-weighted averages were computed for five higher order personality traits: neuroticism, extraversion, openness, agreeableness, and conscientiousness. This measure provided researchers with an instrument that is neutral for both age and culture and is designed specifically to assess personality traits in children and adolescents, ages 2 to 15. In the present study, reliability estimates (Cronbach’s alpha) for the ICID ranged from .89 (Agreeableness) to .95 (Extraversion; Table 3).

Big Five Inventory (BFI). In addition to the ICID, parents also filled out the 44-item BFI survey (John, Donahue, & Kentle, 1991; John, Naumann, & Soto, 2008). The responses were rated on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (Disagree strongly) to 5 (Agree strongly), providing scale scores for five higher order personality traits: neuroticism, extraversion, openness, agreeableness, and conscientiousness. In the present study, reliability estimates

(Cronbach’s alpha) for the BFI ranged from .74 (Agreeableness) to .86 (Extraversion; Table 3).

LIFE STORIES AND PERSONALITY

Narrative Coherence Coding Scheme. To measure the levels of coherence in the children’s best and sad memories, memories were coded based on a coding scheme developed by

Reese and colleagues (2011). This scheme is divided into three sections: Context (“When I was in third grade, we went to Disney World for a family vacation”), Chronology (“First we went on the Spinning Teacup ride, and then we went to the Haunted Mansion, and then we got lunch as a family. After that, we went back to the hotel to swim at the pool and then we saw a show”), and

Theme (“I really enjoyed the trip because I got to spend time with my family and go to a place I had never been before. It is so cold at home, but it was really sunny in Florida, so that was a nice change. It also made me grateful for how fun my family is, and now my brother and I are a lot closer because of all the time we spent together that week”). Each dimension is coded on a scale from 0 to 3; dimensions are averaged to create an overall coherence score.

Procedure

Before the second follow-up of the study, administered approximately three years after intake, families were sent packages that included informed consent documentation and parent- report questionnaires, which were completed and returned by mail. Once in the lab, the children were asked to perform a multitude of behavioral tasks, including to report their best and sad memories. These memories were filmed during the session and later transcribed by research assistants in the lab.

Memories were coded using the Narrative Coherence Coding Scheme (Reese et al.,

2011). Although I used a pre-established coding scheme, I also developed a supplementary protocol to help interpret the coding scheme for cases that proved ambiguous, in order to prevent subjective coding. After I trained three additional undergraduate coders into the coding scheme, we coded 20 memories together. We then coded 10 memories at a time, individually, until we

LIFE STORIES AND PERSONALITY reached an ICC of .70 for reliability. For any codes we did not agree on, we discussed discrepancies until one consensus code was established. The reliability threshold was met after a total of 60 codes were discussed as a group, whereupon coders were split into two teams, one to code best memories, and the other to code sad memories. From that point on, each memory was double-coded, and any discrepancies between codes were discussed by the separate coding teams, until a final consensus code was agreed upon. After screening the relevant data, the data was analyzed by using linear regression and correlation to determine the relationship between each type of coherence and age, coherence and gender, and coherence and the Big Five personality traits. Specifically, I sought to determine which Big Five traits are associated with greater coherence scores in order better to understand the individual differences that may underlie life narratives.

Results

Intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) among coders’ ratings are displayed in Table 1.

Between raters 1 and 2, agreement for all dimensions of Best Memory Coherence ranged from

.74 to .89. Between raters 1 and 4, agreement ranged from .81 to .85. For Sad Memory

Coherence, agreement on all dimensions between raters 3 and 4 ranged from .71 to .80. Finally, for raters 1 and 4, agreement on Sad Memory Context and theme were .84 and .85 respectively, while agreement for Chronology was .35.1

Descriptive statistics for Best and Sad Memory Coherence are presented in Table 2, with their respective histograms in Figures 1 and 2. Eight best memories were missing because the families refused to be videotaped or declined to participate in the task, whereas 22 sad memories were missing for the same reasons. The average coherence score for Best Memory was 1.80 (SD

1 Reliability score between raters 1 and 4 on sad memory chronology was likely low due to only coding 37 memories together, compared to the 136-231 memories that the other raters coded against one another.

LIFE STORIES AND PERSONALITY

= 0.58), while the average coherence score for Sad Memory was 1.99 (SD = 0.55). These results support the hypothesis that there are individual differences in children’s narrative coherence, both for best and sad memories. In other words, some children are rated as having more coherent narratives than others. This was true of all coherence dimensions: Best Memory Context (M =

1.97, SD = 0.97), Chronology (M = 1.91, SD = 0.86), and Theme (M = 1.52, SD = 0.66), as well as Sad Memory Context (M = 1.86, SD = 0.99), Chronology (M = 2.44, SD = 0.58), and Theme

(M = 1.67, SD = 0.73).

Next, I conducted regression analyses to examine associations between coherence dimensions and Five-Factor Model personality traits. These models were run separately by personality measure (i.e., separate models were run for BFI personality traits and ICID personality traits). Traits for a given measure were entered into a regression model simultaneously, so results present the association between one trait and coherence, controlling for all other traits. I predicted that Neuroticism would be positively associated with narrative coherence. Results suggested inconsistent support for this hypothesis. Best Memory Coherence was positively associated with BFI Neuroticism (β = .16, p = .01), but was not associated with

ICID Neuroticism (β = .01, p = .88). Sad Memory Coherence was not associated with BFI

Neuroticism (β = -.06, p = .33) or ICID Neuroticism (β = .07, p = .44). I also predicted that

Openness would be positively associated with narrative coherence. This, too, was met with inconsistent support. Best Memory Coherence was positively associated with ICID Openness (β

= .20, p = .01), but not associated with BFI Openness (β = .02, p = .79). Sad Memory Coherence was not associated with BFI Openness (β = .07, p = .25) or ICID Openness (β = .15, p = .06).

Furthermore, I predicted that while it was likely to be weaker, there would still be a significant positive association between Extraversion and Coherence. Once again, there were mixed results.

LIFE STORIES AND PERSONALITY

Best Memory Coherence was associated with BFI Extraversion (β = .12, p = .04), but not with

ICID Extraversion (β = .03, p = .68). Sad Memory Coherence was not associated with ICID

Extraversion (β = .12, p = .20) or BFI Extraversion (β = .07, p = .27). Lastly, I hypothesized that there would not be a significant association between Coherence and Conscientiousness. The results were consistent with my hypothesis, as there were no significant associations between

Best Memory Coherence and BFI Conscientiousness (β = .04, p = .55) or ICID

Conscientiousness (β = -.01, p = .93), nor were there any significant associations between Sad

Memory Coherence and BFI Conscientiousness (β = .06, p = .32) or ICID Conscientiousness (β

= .08, p = .29). Due to the contrasting results in prior research examining the relationship between Coherence and Agreeableness, I did not advance specific hypotheses about the relationship between Coherence and this trait. Results indicated that there were no significant associations between Best Memory Coherence and BFI Agreeableness (β = .01, p = .89) or ICID

Agreeableness (β = -.06, p = .42), nor were there any significant associations between Sad

Memory Coherence and BFI Agreeableness (β = .00, p = .94) or ICID Agreeableness (β = .02, p

= .78). To summarize, Sad Memory Coherence was generally unassociated with personality traits. However, Best Memory Coherence demonstrated some associations with Neuroticism,

Openness, and Extraversion. These were variable across measures.

Finally, I examined regression models analyzing the effect of age and gender on narrative coherence (see Table 4). Inconsistent with my hypothesis, I found no associations between age and any of the Best Memory Coherence dimensions, with standardized estimates ranging from β

= .03 to β = .08, all p’s > .05. For Sad Memory, Chronology was unrelated to age (β = -.03, p

=.63), while Context (β =.12, p = .045) and Theme (β =.12, p = .045) were positively associated with age. Lastly, consistent with my hypothesis, there was a significant effect of gender (males

LIFE STORIES AND PERSONALITY coded as 1 and females coded as 0), with female participants being more coherent in every dimension, except for Best Memory Context (β = -.16, p = .15) and Sad Memory Chronology (β

= -.09, p = .43). See Table 4 for significant results. In sum, while age was generally unassociated with Coherence, gender was found to associate with most dimensions of coherence, such that girls’ best and sad memories were generally rated as more coherent than were boys’.

Discussion In this study, I sought to determine whether there were individual differences in dimensions of coherence in late childhood and early adolescence, whether this coherence was associated with personality traits, and whether coherence dimensions would differ by age and gender. I was met with mixed results. While there was variability in children’s levels of coherence, Coherence was generally unassociated with personality traits, with some exceptions described below. Additionally, in this sample of children aged 9 to 14, age was unassociated with

Coherence, but there were gender differences in coherence ratings.

The variability in coherence scores across the sample is indicative of individual differences in children’s narrative coherence, even in this young of an age group. These initial descriptive results are in line with Habermas and Blucks’ (2000) research on the developmental trajectory of causal and thematic coherence. Although the ability to tell coherent life narratives is lower in childhood and early adolescence than adulthood, there are variations in children’s levels of coherence, which suggest that the process of autobiographical reasoning, and consequently identity development, begins in childhood. Since there have been relatively few studies examining narrative coherence in children, this trend should be further explored in future studies.

The findings that Coherence and personality traits were largely unassociated is consistent with previous studies. For example, Reese et al. (2014) found that while Coherence was

LIFE STORIES AND PERSONALITY associated with some personality traits in a sample of participants aged 12 to 21, associations were weak and few in number. In the present study, Sad Memory Coherence was not associated with any personality traits, but Best Memory Coherence was associated with a few traits, with associations ranging from .12 to .20. These results are in line with McAdams’ life story model of personality, which splits personality into three distinct layers, with traits as the first level, and narratives as the most complex third level (2001). Under this model, large associations between constructs at different layers would not be expected, as large associations would indicate that personality is better conceptualized as one single layer. McAdams (2004) has asserted that little is known about how traits relate to narrative identity, since while studies have explored the relationship between personality and identity development, few have explored the relationship between coherence and traits, specifically. Thus, although the connection between traits and narrative coherence must be explored further, the general lack of association between traits and narrative coherence found in this current study provides support for the distinction between the three levels of personality.

Nonetheless, some significant associations between traits and narrative coherence emerged. Best Memory Coherence was positively associated with BFI Neuroticism (β = .16, p =

.01), BFI Extraversion (β = .12, p = .04), and ICID Openness (β = .20, p = .01). These significant associations suggest that although the effect size was small, it seems that, overall, children who were more coherent were rated higher in these traits by their parents. These results concur with previous studies, in which small positive associations have been found between Coherence and

Neuroticism, Extraversion, and Openness (Adler et al., 2007; McAdams et al., 2004; Reese et al.,

2014.  A possible explanation for the positive association between ICID Openness and

Coherence in the current study is that the ICID is composed of two dimensions for openness,

LIFE STORIES AND PERSONALITY which include openness to experience and intellect. Because openness is comprised of traits such as imagination and interest in art, and these traits have been found to be associated with intelligence, perhaps children higher in intellect were better able to organize their memories for the given tasks (Ackerman & Heggestad, 1997; DeYoung, Peterson, & Higgins, 2005; McCrae

& Costa, 1997).

An additional finding was that only Best Memory Coherence was associated with any personality trait (with the exception that Sad Memory Theme was associated with ICID

Extraversion). While no previous narrative identity research predicted that best memories

(similar to high point memories) would be more associated with personality traits than sad memories (similar to low point memories), these results suggest that perhaps for children, compared to adults, good memories are easier to conjure, while sad memories may require deeper thought. Fivush et al. (2011) suggest that self-defining memories (those that are personally significant and lead to an individual better understanding who they are) must include a complex evaluation of the specific event or how it affected the self. In the sample used in the present study, the coders noted that children often described their sad memories as a loss of a grandparent or pet, whereas their best memories were described as something they had personally accomplished, such as making a sports team or winning a prize. Since some best memories were described as a result of personal actions (in comparison to the indiscriminate nature of death), they may have been more meaningful in terms of self-defining moments, and thus discussed in more coherent detail. However, it is important to note that this evaluation is based on a qualitative review of the narratives, not on empirical coding of how much agency was ascribed to the child in best versus sad memories. A future direction could include developing a

LIFE STORIES AND PERSONALITY quantitative coding scheme to analyze the differences between best and sad memories, and to see whether these differences are associated with narrative coherence.

Contrary to my hypothesis, there were no significant age effects for Coherence, barring weak associations with Sad Memory Context and Sad Memory Theme. As previously mentioned, there have been few studies that explore narrative coherence in children. The literature that does exist suggests that the ability to tell stories about personal experiences is learned between ages two and six, but the ability to tell a coherent life story is present mostly in adolescence (Habermas & Bluck, 2000; Habermas & Paha, 2001; Reese et al., 2011). That leaves a large age gap, wherein children begin to develop the skills to describe coherent life stories, but the approximate age range in which this skill is acquired remains unknown. Age effects between adolescents and younger children would be expected, but since there were no significant age effects in this particular sample of children aged 9-14, and there were clearly variations in levels of coherence, the onset of the development of coherence can be postulated to occur at even younger ages. This study should thus be replicated with a larger age range to test this hypothesis.

While the children in this sample did not display age-related differences for levels of coherence, they displayed strong gender-related increases in Coherence, such that females told more coherent narratives. This finding is in accord with previous literature, which reveals that even at ages as young as three years, girls spoke about the emotional aspects of their experiences more than boys (Fivush, Brotman, Buckner, & Goodman, 2000). Since best and sad memories are linked to inherently emotional experiences, it is not surprising that females would describe these events in more detail, and thus more coherently. Moreover, in a study of 8-year-old children, girls told more coherent narratives than did boys, which were firmly rooted in a social context, contained more affiliative themes, and described more emotions (Buckner & Fivush,

LIFE STORIES AND PERSONALITY

1998). This gender difference was also found in the present study, such that on average, female participants were rated as .20 points higher on coherence than male participants.

Limitations and Future Directions

While the present study fills a crucial gap in the literature on narrative coherence in childhood, our results should be interpreted in the context of several limitations. A notable limitation of the study is that the interviewers did not always prompt the children in uniform ways. For example, in many interviews but not all, the interviewers asked, “What happened next?” prompting the child to give a chronological account of the events in the narrative, which the child might not have given on his or her own. At times, the interviewers also asked the child to clarify where and when the event took place. These unscripted questions caused some confusion for the coders in determining how to score context and chronology for those who were prompted versus those who were not. To account for these discrepancies, we deducted one point from the child’s Chronology or Context score if he or she were prompted. This may have resulted in lower overall Coherence scores, as it is impossible to determine retroactively if the children would have reported these important aspects of coherence on their own. Although maintaining consistency while conducting qualitative interviews with children is often difficult to achieve, in future studies, the interviewers should strive to use only pre-determined prompts and not stray from the interview scripts.

Furthermore, while the Narrative Coherence Coding Scheme has been proven to be a good quantitative coding scheme for children’s life narratives, it is important to note that quantitatively coding these memories may not always be the most pertinent method of examination. Adler et al. (2017) suggest that many of the most vital questions in studying narrative identity could be better answered through exploring avenues that account for the

LIFE STORIES AND PERSONALITY complexity of individual narratives. For example, instead of quantitatively measuring how often the child mentions contextual, chronological, or thematic information, focusing on the specific content of the memories (i.e. where and when the event actually took place, or how the event made the narrator feel), could reveal differences in the child’s emotional and intellectual abilities.  Finally, our sample was not particularly diverse, and did not account for cultural differences in coherence. Since cultural differences emerge as a result of the distinct cognitive and social characteristics of a particular population, they would likely affect the development of narrative identity and personality traits, which could reveal interesting differences in levels of coherence (Reese et al., 2014).

To conclude, while these results reveal important insight into the development of identity before adulthood, they are only preliminary. Due to the dearth of research exploring the relationship between coherence and personality traits, more research in this field should be conducted. Future directions may include performing longitudinal studies, so that the development of narrative coherence and personality traits can be assessed in the same individuals at different times in their lives; collecting data from a sample of even younger children to better determine when the ability to tell coherent narratives begins to develop; and collecting data from a more socioeconomically, racially, and culturally diverse sample. Additionally, in adults, the specific types of narratives individuals tell about themselves (i.e. redemption narratives) are differentially related to well-being. A future study could explore how these distinct narrative themes develop over time, beginning in childhood. This would help to explore whether narrative identity and coherence is correlated with well-being before adulthood.

Overall, this study found that there was variability among levels of coherence in children’s narratives, but that Coherence was only intermittently associated with specific

LIFE STORIES AND PERSONALITY personality traits. These results lend support to McAdam’s life story model, by providing additional evidence for the distinction between the three levels of personality. However, the significant associations between Coherence and Neuroticism, Openness, and Extraversion suggest that children who are reported by their parents to be rated higher in these traits may tell more coherent narratives. Since similar results have been found in studies on narrative coherence in adults, the current study’s results provide important insight into the development of coherence and its relationship to personality traits before adulthood. Furthermore, the study found that age effects were not significant for this particular sample of children aged 9 to 14, but that females told more coherent narratives than their male counterparts. These results suggest that coherence develops even earlier than previously thought, and varies by gender. Thus, the current study provides a foundation upon which future research can delve into the exact age in which both males and females, respectively, develop the ability to tell coherent narratives. A more extensive study of narrative coherence in a younger population will lead to a better understanding of the developmental progression of identity formation.

title: Assessing the Effect of Liposomal Spherical Nucleic Acid stability on Vaccine Function for Triple Negative Breast Cancer
abstract: The successful development of vaccines for triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) has been hindered because there are no identified tumor-associated antigens. As an alternative to peptide vaccines, the administration of tumor lysates has been investigated in TNBC to activate the immune system against tumors, wherein a mixture of tumor-specific lysates is administered to behave as antigens. The Mirkin group has previously demonstrated the capability of Liposomal Spherical Nucleic Acids (SNAs) to initiate antigen presentation and activate immune cells. Liposome SNA’s consist of a concentric phospholipid vesicle core where the adjuvant is anchored into the bilayer, and the lysate is encapsulated within the core. With this novel delivery method in mind, we proposed a two-pronged investigation. First, we assessed whether changing the stability of the SNA impacts antigen delivery, by comparing four different lipid constituents and their decay rate in serum. Second, we investigated whether changing the hydrophobicity of the DNA anchor affected SNA decay rate. From these investigations, we find that SNA stability is governed by both liposome membrane fluidity and anchor hydrophobicity, and that these parameters are additive. Taken together, our findings will be able to significantly optimize the way cancer vaccines for TNBC are designed and administered.
text:
Leah Broger

Adviser: Chad Mirkin
Subject: Neuroscience
DOI: 10.21985/n2-zyw0-4f51

Over the course of her undergraduate career, Leah developed a deep-seated fascination with the biological interactions that govern higher order physiological phenomena. After attending Dr. Chad Mirkin’s guest lecture on nanomaterials her freshman year, Leah became specifically interested in the novel properties of nanostructures and their propitious biomedical applications. Leah’s curiosity ushered her into her first research experience at a Dutch biotech startup. Here, Leah optimized bacterial extraction for a diagnostic device, by testing capture efficiencies of gold magnetic nanobeads on patient samples. Presently, in Dr. Chad Mirkin’s Lab, Leah is investigating the stability and effects of liposome composition in liposomal spherical nucleic acids (SNA), to increase efficiency of targeted cargo release in triple-negative breast cancers. This past year, Leah was awarded Northwestern’s selective Academic Year Grant to further probe the chemical and structural basis for oxidation-enhanced immunogenicity, as well as the effects of SNA structure and stability on vaccine function. Leah graduated in Spring 2020 with a bachelor’s degree in Neuroscience, Biochemical Engineering, and Biotechnology.

Abstract

The successful development of vaccines for triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) has been hindered because there are no identified tumor-associated antigens. As an alternative to peptide vaccines, the administration of tumor lysates has been investigated in TNBC to activate the immune system against tumors, wherein a mixture of tumor-specific lysates is administered to behave as antigens. The Mirkin group has previously demonstrated the capability of Liposomal Spherical Nucleic Acids (SNAs) to initiate antigen presentation and activate immune cells. Liposome SNA’s consist of a concentric phospholipid vesicle core where the adjuvant is anchored into the bilayer, and the lysate is encapsulated within the core. With this novel delivery method in mind, we proposed a two-pronged investigation. First, we assessed whether changing the stability of the SNA impacts antigen delivery, by comparing four different lipid constituents and their decay rate in serum. Second, we investigated whether changing the hydrophobicity of the DNA anchor affected SNA decay rate. From these investigations, we find that SNA stability is governed by both liposome membrane fluidity and anchor hydrophobicity, and that these parameters are additive. Taken together, our findings will be able to significantly optimize the way cancer vaccines for TNBC are designed and administered.

title: Inequality in America and The Incarceration System
abstract: My research paper focuses on inequality in America specifically covering the incarceration system and the intersection of race and the criminal justice system. This is an important topic to study due to the high number of racially diverse individuals that are disproportionally affected and incarcerated due to the inequalities in the crime and criminal justice system. To investigate the extent of the issue, ethnographic interviews were conducted in a diverse sample of people by asking a set of questions on experience related to race, crime and criminal justice. The qualitative information gathered from the interviews and from an online class database was in line with the literature on the subject, in that there is currently a widespread problem of inequality in America with regards to race in the crime and criminal justice system. Recommendations were made in light of the findings and one of which was the importance of policy adjustments in the incarceration system. Further research is required to look into why policy adjustments are not being made to successfully serve all members of the society.
