title: “It Wasn’t Made for Him”: Examining Female-Led Superhero films Wonder Woman and Captain Marvel and the Internet Commentary that Follows
abstract: Recently, there has been a public push for the film industry to improve female representation; subsequently, DC and Marvel released female-lead films Wonder Woman and Captain Marvel to critical praise and record box office figures. Strictly looking at industry measures of success (critics’ reviews and box office totals) it would appear that the film industry and moviegoing public are demanding more films with similar female representation. However, public opinion cannot be captured by critical interpretation and viewership alone; it is important to understand how audiences feel after viewing a film and which aspects did or did not resonate with them. With my research, I studied a portion of the discourse spread about these films on the internet to uncover an untold aspect of their public reception. I read and coded meaningful sentiments from the first 250 IMDb user reviews for each film to evaluate audiences’ perspectives on themes.
text:
“It Wasn’t Made for Him”: Examining Female-Led Superhero Films ​Wonder Woman ​and Captain Marvel​ and the Internet Commentary that Follows By: Rachel Fimbianti

I muse about the various female role models from media I idolized throughout my young life with both sentimental fondness and the keen awareness that none of them were exactly the image of female empowerment I want for my future daughters. As a child, Aurora (Mary Costa) from ​Sleeping Beauty (Geronimi 1959) caught my attention because of her pink dress, but she is valued for her beauty above her voice, as demonstrated by how much of the film she spends unconscious. Later Kim Possible’s (Christy Carlson Romano) red hair and green eyes reminded me of my own; while she is an active figure in her story who balances academic excellence and her rather unconventional extracurriculars, her character design involves a waistline only attainable with 0% body fat and then still removing ribs and vital organs (Disney Channel 2002-2007). The fantasy YA novels and their subsequent film and TV adaptations of my teen years focused on heroines who were gifted monster hunters and fighters, but had an overreliance on finding handsome boyfriends to love them ad nauseam by the end. Heading into my 20s, I wanted to create a new image for myself about what female characters could be: well rounded individuals who were agents in their stories and who’s entire existence was not defined by a man.

The releases of ​Wonder Woman (Jenkins 2017) and ​Captain Marvel (Boden and Fleck 2019) intrigued me because perhaps these two women could provide a counter to the subpar female representation I witnessed during my adolescence. Both films went on to be well received by professional film critics and financially outperform many of their male-led predecessors. These films proved that female-centric pieces of media could get made and that audiences were prepared to financially support them. I hoped that the film industry had reached a turning point for female representation and perhaps that the upcoming generation of young girls could have it better than I did. But I was quickly reminded that the internet is not always so welcoming a place, and that these two measures of success do not tell a complete tale of how the films are situated in the social zeitgeist. I wanted to believe that these films indicated that some of society’s deep-seated misogynies were on their way out, but could not escape the feeling that my hopes may be optimistic. I crafted a research project where I read through internet commentary for ​Wonder Woman and ​Captain Marvel to better understand how audiences reacted to these releases and decode some of the remaining battles females face in the pursuit of cinematic equality.

These films are by no means the first female-led pieces of superhero media to ever grace the film/television industry. Lynda Carter notably played Wonder Woman on a TV show during the 1970s (ABC 1975-1977, CBS 1978-1978). Supergirl has had multiple outings, including a film starring Helen Slater (Szwarc 1984) and a TV show starring Melissa Benoist (CW 2015-2021). In the early 2000s, Catwoman and Elektra appeared ​in their own respective solo films as portrayed by Halle Berry (Pitof 2004) and Jennifer Garner (Bowman 2005) respectively. Though the existence of these two films paved the way for future superheroines, their female character depictions are not necessarily positive. The Marvel Cinematic Universe released its first film with a female heroine in the title shortly before the release of ​Captain Marvel​, ​Ant-Man and The Wasp ​(Reed 2018). Despite this landmark, Ant-Man is still the center point of the story. Jessica Jones was a notable female addition among the guys’ club of Marvel Netflix with her titular TV show (2015-2019). And, there was the short-lived TV show, ​Agent Carter ​(ABC 2015-2016), based on the adventures of Agent Peggy Carter after the events of ​Captain America: The First Avenger ​(Johnston 2011).

These selections showcase some pieces of female-centered superhero media, but female characters’ existence within the genre is not limited to when their name is in the title. Superhero films/TV shows generally feature at least one central female character, if not more, to varying degrees of importance. But, simply being included does not imply dynamic writing or complex story arcs. Women in the superhero genre have a history of being either neutralized as a bland love interest or sexualized as an object of desire. Frequently, they are a mixture of the two. Dr. Chase Meridian (Nicole Kidman) in ​Batman Forever (Schumacher 1995) clearly has a sexual interest in Batman starting with the very first time they meet despite him calling her written Psychological works “naive” (4:30-5:30). Later she takes this sexual interest to new heights by using the bat signal, a beacon designated for the Gotham City Police Department to alert Batman when the city needs his protection, to summon and attempt to seduce him because she finds his “black rubber” suit and “scarred psyche” to be a turn on (17:30-19:20).

In recent years, there has been marginal improvement in the depictions of female characters; they often have interests (outside of romance) that are not viewed by society as inherently feminine. In ​Man of Steel (Snyder 2013), Lois Lane (Amy Adams) is a passionate journalist who allows no obstacle to stand in her way as she chases down the story behind Superman (Henry Cavill). In the ​Iron Man trilogy (Favreau, ​Iron Man 2008, Favreau, ​Iron Man 2 2010, Black, ​Iron Man 3 2013), Pepper Potts (Gwyneth Paltrow) is a career woman who starts off as Tony Stark’s (Robert Downey Jr.) personal assistant and later becomes the CEO of Stark Industries. In the first two ​Thor films (Branagh, ​Thor 2011, Taylor, ​The Dark World 2013), Jane Foster (Natalie Portman) is an ardent astrophysicist who has a vested interest in pursuing her work of understanding the world. These three characters do not constitute an exhaustive list of any female character who has found a way to break outside of the “damsel in distress” mantra, which is positive. The main remaining drawback is that, for all of these characters, some part of their story exists to support the journey of the lead male character, especially through romantic entanglement. Lois Lane’s passion toward uncovering the truth of Superman shifts into passionate love when she and Superman begin a relationship. Pepper Potts becomes Tony Stark’s girlfriend and helps him escape his self-destructive playboy lifestyle while coping with emotional traumas. Jane Foster aids Thor in abandoning his selfish tendencies and becoming a man worthy of wielding the hammer Mjölnir through the power of romantic love. These women may have a sizable role in their respective films and have some form of character arc, but they are not the center point to the story. That honor, and all of the character development that comes with it, belongs to the men in the films’ titles. Stories where females are the clear center point are, unfortunately, among the minority.

These flawed characterizations may be attributed to the overwhelming presence of male voices in the film industry. In 2018, in front of the camera “females comprised 35% of all speaking characters” and “audiences were almost twice as likely to see male characters as female characters in the top-grossing films” (Lauzen, It’s a Man’s World 1). And, behind the camera “only 1% of films employed 10 or more women” as directors, writers, producers, executive producers, editors and cinematographers while “74% of films employed 10 or more men” in the same roles (Lauzen, The Celluloid Ceiling 1) Women are also still fighting for proper awards recognition. At the time of writing this piece, the Academy Awards have nominated five women nominated for Best Director, one of whom won (Aurthur), and only one woman for Best Cinematographer (Cooney). The only categories women dominate are the ones where only they can get nominated, Best Lead and Supporting Actress, or the ones coded toward ‘feminine interests’, Best Makeup and Hairstyling or Costume Design. The fact that two of the female directors and the one female cinematographer have all been nominated within the last 10 years would perhaps indicate some measure of growth within the industry. Nevertheless, celebrating that there was a woman nominated in these categories at all in any given year does not demonstrate an immense degree of progress for representation. Even if a female director gets lucky enough to get her work recognized by The Academy, the industry is still plainly male-dominated.

This gender disparity extends outside of film production and impacts the critical circuit. In 2019, men comprised 66% of professional critics (Lauzen, Thumbs Down 2019 1) and similar disparity extends into the user space. Specifically with IMDb, the platform collects information about the gender identities of their user commenters. Although users have the option to not report their gender, the data of those who do showcase that, in most cases, male reviewers considerably outnumber females, often by as much as 3:1 (Hickey). The films I studied showcase a similar imbalance. At the time of this writing, for ​Captain Marvel​, men actually outnumber women over 4:1 with declared female reviewers making up just under 16% of the data pool (​Captain Marvel User Ratings). With 19.5% of reviewers, ​Wonder Woman female commenters are not quite so far outnumbered but they still remain far from the dominant voice (​Wonder Woman User Ratings). This gender disparity can mean that females often aren’t even the prominent voices within surrounding films that showcase them.

This blatant imbalance online can affect a film's offline economic performance and perceptions of its stars; ​film reviews have been linked to phenomena known as “influence effects” and “prediction effects”. These detail the tendency of reviews to ​influence what films consumers choose to spend money on and thus, can impact the ​predicted box office earnings (Gemser et al. 44). Lauzen also talks of how “[o]n average, women reviewers award higher quantitative ratings than men to films with female protagonists” (5). A female-led film may not reach its full financial potential if it is not reviewed by other females because it could achieve a lower critical rating. Richard Dyer also writes of how audience foreknowledge impacts how they view film characters. He lists several locations where audiences can acquire this foreknowledge including “familiarity with the story”, “promotion”, and “star/genre expectations”. While any one of these categories can be applied to both ​Wonder Woman and ​Captain Marvel​, the most relevant point for my discussion is the idea that “criticism...by critics and reviewers may also lead us to try and read a character in a certain way” (109). This logic makes critical opinion around these films especially important, because the information audiences take in before viewing impacts the way they perceive the female portrayals in relation to their male-led predecessors.

Despite these regrettable statistics, in recent years there has been a building movement that demands for females to be placed in positions with more agency in the movie making process, both as creators and as stars (Erbland). This movement in part stems from and is encouraged by the Time’s Up and #MeToo movements meant to expose sexual harassment within Hollywood and prosecute those involved. But the demand for female storytellers extends much further back than when allegations of sexual misconduct were first brought against Harvey Weinstein. The recognition of female creators has been a long time coming.

So, DC and Marvel releasing ​Wonder Woman and ​Captain Marvel into their respective cinematic universes seems a timely step in opening up the industry for more female-led stories. But, despite a vocal subset of the filmmaking industry and the filmgoing population advocating for these films, they still constituted a financial risk for their respective studios. Male-led films (in the superhero genre and others) have proven time and time again that they are profitable at the box office. And, as a show of financial promise and market viability, the film industry tends to green-light projects that mirror previously successful endeavors (Thompson). In addition, many of those who greenlight films perceive that male actors lead more profitable films than females (BBC). Whether true or not, this recurring perception hindered the production of female-led properties. The financial success of the Marvel Cinematic Universe was built entirely upon male superheroes until a superheroine finally made her way into a title 10 years and 20 films after the universe’s inception. Out of the 28 DC films released since their first in 1951, two were female-led before the release of ​Wonder Woman in 2017. ​Under some circumstances, the continuation of the superhero genre alone may be enough to repeat previous successes and thus greenlight future superwomen projects. But choosing a female lead over the standard male still constitutes a break in tradition and thus the chance of perhaps making less money in the long run.

But with great risk often comes great reward. Despite the potential pitfalls, these films were both successful within Hollywood’s typical measures of success: critical rating and box office grosses. Critical rating is used to determine whether or not Hollywood succeeded in making a quality film and is often linked to potential financial successes (Gemser et al. 57). Though, quality filmmaking does not ensure financial success nor does making a potentially bad film guarantee financial failure. ​The Lion King live-action remake (Favreau 2019) was the second highest-grossing film of the year (​2019 Worldwide Box Office Box Office Mojo​) but achieved a “rotten” critical rating of 53% on Rotten Tomatoes (​The Lion King Rotten Tomatoes​). Box office grosses not only measure how much money the studio is making off of the property, but also are used to determine how wide the film’s appeal was and whether to produce a sequel. Wonder Woman scored a 93% critical rating on Rotten Tomatoes (​Wonder Woman Rotten Tomatoes​) and an approximately $830 million in worldwide grosses (​Wonder Woman Box Office Mojo​). ​Captain Marvel has a slightly lower, albeit still respectable, Rotten Tomatoes score of 78% (​Captain Marvel Rotten Tomatoes​) but managed to accomplish a major financial milestone when it grossed over $1 billion in the worldwide box office (​Captain Marvel Box Office Mojo​). As of this writing, a ​Wonder Woman sequel was released, ​Wonder Woman: 1984 ​(Jenkins 2020), and a sequel to ​Captain Marvel is in development with director Nia DaCosta, an African American woman (Kroll).

Strictly taking these two measures of success into account, these two films are major achievements. The data would imply that perhaps the film industry is prepared to move toward improved inclusivity for female professionals and spectators are inclined to come along. In short, the subset of the industry calling for improved female representation could assume their desires were fulfilled. Yet, things are never quite so simple. After a movie patron buys a ticket, influencing box office gross, a wide array of sentiments still must be taken into account after the credits roll (if the spectator even made it that far). Critical admiration does not guarantee that general audiences feel the same, and box office gross does not automatically imply a spectator’s approval. Simply because a film had wide appeal does not mean that it will continue to succeed. Both of these factors - audience approval and long-term loyalty - are important in determining the future viability of similar films; just because the film studio got the patron’s money the first time does not mean they will continue to do so. The information held in the ​Wonder Woman and Captain Marvel IMDb comment sections adds another dimension to traditional measures of cinematic success because it’s a facet of what viewers said after they left the theater and impacts the meanings of the texts as a whole.

I analyzed 500 IMDb reviews because users typically leave longer responses on this site as compared to Rotten Tomatoes or Metacritic - paragraphs versus sentences - and thus offer more material for analysis. As for why I chose to study 250 reviews for each film, this figure seemed like both a manageable amount of reading and as though it would produce a wide array of data. These 250 reviews were the first ones listed under what IMDB describes as the helpfulness rating in each film’s comment section. This choice has two advantages: first, the helpfulness rating is a system of upvoting in which commenters can indicate which reviews offered them information helpful to formulating their understanding of the text and second, this ranking system is the default viewing option. The 250 reviews I read are the first 250 users see if they go searching for opinions on the text. While this system of upvoting tends to favor those reviews that have already made their way to the top, it still stands to demonstrate the type of opinions, be they positive or negative, that reviewers wanted to corroborate and deem “helpful”. Thus, these comments are the most applicable when discussing how these reviews helped shape the text’s meaning because they had the widest reach and most unified appeal. 2. Paratextual Privilege: What is it and Who Does it Belong to? While the sentiments expressed about each film vary from person to person, there seems to exist an underlying connection amongst the differences in opinion, a level of animosity toward an opposing force. This does not mean that there are armies going to battle on the IMDb homepage. Rather, to imagine a reviewer and those with similar sentiments to be a singular entity, opposing forces are groups that dare to differ or even attempt to stifle that group’s communal beliefs. These groups include (but are not limited to) fellow user reviewers, film critics, and even the IMDb platform itself. Henry Jenkins talked about a similar phenomenon in relation to the fandom of the ​Beauty and the Beast television series of the late 1980s (CBS 1987-1990). This show built up an extremely strong fan base during its first season, enough to save it from cancellation, but later faltered. During the third season, the fandom divided, surrounding a shift in the writing from primarily romantic themes to darker, more violent content. In general, fans were extremely critical of the show’s production team as they believed that their desires for the show were not in line with one another. Jenkins describes that

“Moreover, these fans saw this conflict not only in personal terms (“You” vs. Us”) but in terms of a set of economic relations (producers vs. consumers) and political categories (male power vs. female desire).” (124) In this quote, Jenkins showcases that factions within a fandom are not altogether uncommon and can come from many different sets of values, power imbalances and expectations. While the controversies observed in the IMDb comments section do not align with these exactly, there are clear similarities, including an assumed power struggle between movie studios (producers) and audiences (consumers) that I will discuss below. Regardless of the media type, spectators have preferences about content they consume, and when producers present something on the contrary, it can often cause friction in the discourse.

While each group at battle in the comments has its own concerns, in most cases the roots of this animosity can be linked-to Jonathan Grey’s ideas about paratextual privilege. Paratexts influence an audience’s perspective about a text from outside of the media’s internal canon (23). These paratexts originate from multiple sources that surround the original text and help create meaning, including studio-run marketing campaigns, spin-off video games and even critical reviews (143). User reviews function in a similar manner to the published thoughts of professional critics. These user reviews expand discourse surrounding Hollywood films because they add a set of opinions contrary to those of the trained eyes of Hollywood scholars and professional critics. Thus, these reviews influence interpretations of a text because they allow viewers to consider more than one set of opinions while forming their verdicts on a film. In turn, paratextual privilege relates specifically to “who [of these reviewers] has the power to circulate their own readings and versions of the text en masse” (144).

In the ​Captain Marvel ​and ​Wonder Woman ​discourses, there was a battle between users over whose opinions were most accurate: professional critics, everyday filmgoers who liked the films and those who didn’t. In a way, this battle makes sense. Reviews, both amateur and professional, shape and inform future understandings of a text. So it stands to reason that only the ‘correct opinion’ about the text should be allowed into the paratextual space, in an effort to perpetuate a unified understanding amongst spectators and control the text’s reception in society. Will the text be placed amongst the great films of a generation or fade into obscurity? Some may argue the former while others argue the latter but only one set of opinions can have the privilege of being the authoritative and therefore “correct” voice for spectators to consider when developing their opinions on a text. The resulting conflict within this idea (outside of the fact that ‘correct opinion’ is an oxymoron) is that each group at battle believes that they are the correct one and will not have their opinions shut out by rivals that easily.

One way that users make their opinions heard above the noise of the opposition is “review bombing”. In this practice, masses of fans leave abysmally low scores for a piece of media, including films, TV shows, or video games, to demonstrate their disapproval to its creators, often before the title is even released (Wordsworth). Noteworthy examples of titles that got review bombed are ​Ghostbusters (Feig 2016) and ​Star Wars: The Last Jedi (Johnson 2017); Ghostbusters faced criticism for being an all-female reboot of the classic film and ​The Last Jedi enraged fans for its perceived political messages and the characterization of Resistance mechanic Rose Tico. This phenomenon is possible because the integration of film review websites into common use gave audiences a newfound accessibility to share their opinions of a text and help shape its meaning. Their opinions are not necessarily given an equitable stake in this pursuit; professional critics still enjoy greater privilege because they provide opinions solicited by Hollywood and therefore, get more authority over the text (Gray 166). Nevertheless, review bombing showcases that user opinions still occupy a massive space in the discussion surrounding new releases. Users waged war against titles that displeased them and the creators involved because they had platforms where this type of discourse is allowed. In short, the emergence of audience participation in the film criticism process created the first set of opposing groups, amateur user reviewers versus members of the film industry (including professional critics and studio executives).

Just as professional critics rarely have a unanimous answer on a film’s quality, user reviewers disagree on whether a film is good or not. These discrepancies create the second type of paratextual privilege conflict ​(fans and haters). This feud, in particular, has an interesting dynamic as both sides often feel as though they should have the privilege to share their views over the opposition, because their antagonists are so ​obviously not thinking clearly as they ​dare to disagree with such​ blatant facts​ as the film’s quality.

In the end, this paratextual privilege brought on by internet sites comes with a caveat, because IMDb is not a completely lawless land; the platform is moderated. This moderation creates the third set of opposing groups, user reviewers against film review forum websites, such as Rotten Tomatoes or IMDb. The conception that these sites are an unmoderated forum leaves the impression that fans can use the space to leave hateful comments and encourages review bombing. ​Captain Marvel marked a turning point for Rotten Tomatoes in their moderation practices. The site adjusted their methods of collecting fan sentiment to help curb outpourings of premature hate. This included eliminating the chance for audience members to rate a film before its release as well as forfeiting the option for people to indicate that they are simply “Not Interested” in a film (Buckley).

Presently, on IMDb, once a movie “[has] been released and/or screened for the public at least once...registered users [may] vote on it” (Ratings FAQ ​IMDb​). However, the site reserves the right to “temporarily or permanently suppress” reviews that are reported by other users for violating community guidelines (Ratings FAQ ​IMDb​). Notable offenses that can be grounds for deletion include “​[p]rofanity, obscenities, or spiteful remarks in either the body or header of [the] review” or “unannounced spoilers” (User Review Guidelines ​IMDb​)​. Throughout this study, several reviews from the sample were deleted from the site in the time between the time when the ​data was collected and later check ins. Several of these deleted reviews were skeptical of how truthful IMDb was about the film’s cumulative star rating. One user posted a second review claiming “[t]​he other review [they] wrote was deleted because [it] called into question the final rate score as compared to the reviews”. This user later doubled down on the fact that “[they] believe the count is intentionally incorrect”, (Tim-gates-522-762722). Overall, in the review pool, accusations of censorship directed at IMDb ran rampant and only fueled the battle for paratextual privilege waged by commenters.

For ​Captain Marvel​, the resounding public opinion was overwhelmingly against any praise the film received from critics and users alike. In fact, there was a sense of ​incredulity ​that the film actually achieved any of the success the industry claimed it did. To put it explicitly, “the 7.2 [user] score [was] done artificially by bots...and [can]not [be] a testament to how extremely and absolutely bottom poor...the taste of general audiences [is] today” (Sumtim3s00n). There were accusations that film review sites, IMDb and beyond, were silencing negative reviews to appease Disney and that the studio bought positive reviews to make up for bad press. One reviewer claimed that “Rotten Tomatoes will refuse to post my review after 5 attempts over a month, yet they allow 5-star reviews to flourish. Let’s see if IMDb is manipulating the narrative as well” (Sylviawarnock). People went as far as to openly state that they intended to rate the film lower than they actually thought it deserved to help compensate for other reviewers rating it highly or to get revenge on Brie Larson for not being a “nice person” in her publicity tour interviews (Lusha12). In the realm of opposing groups, the conflict within was very one-sided and consisted mostly of attacks against the idea that the film was in any way redeemable like professional critics claimed it was. The reviewers rallied around conspiracy theories that IMDb is being manipulated by studio executives to sway public opinion and maximize profits.

The discourse surrounding ​Wonder Woman also has moments when the user reviewers cast an incredulous eye on those who enjoyed the film, including one who stated “...despite the extremely positive reviews and scores both here and at Rotten Tomatoes. I am deeply amazed anyone could give this garbage more than 2 stars out of 10” (Svestoslav-popov). The film also had its own fair share of those who accused Warner Brothers of buying positive reviews (chunk1978) and upvotes in addition to those who admitted to rating the film lower than they believed it deserved to balance out the “hype” (bledibego). However neither of these opinions were an overwhelming majority as they were with ​Captain Marvel​. Across the two films, these moments carry a similar tone and can be analyzed under a similar lens taking into account blatant differences in the film’s content.

However this discourse does bring something new to the conversation ​within the second set of feuding groups: positive versus negative user reviews. This film offers a non-insignificant number of positive reviews to analyze. ​By using the word “positive”, I do not mean to imply that the wording the reviewer used was constructive or without scrutiny regarding the extent of the intelligence of their fellow user reviewers. By my definition, a positive review is solely that the user’s opinion of the film was positive and they are willing to defend the film from those who thought otherwise. In many ways, these reviewers react with similar tendencies to those with negative opinions, just with a different target for their aggression. They often attempt to discredit those who did not enjoy the film by using statements such as “the website [IMDb] exists in an alternate reality, or...has a bunch of angry, bitter, depressed people reviewing on it” (Cochrandarin). Several reviewers went as far as to place a direct target on who they believed those “angry, bitter, depressed” people were: Marvel fans who were unhappy with DC’s newfound success (badalundabaad) or angry male fans who could not accept that a female had directed what they dubbed as DC’s best film (QuantumZebra). Some reviewers ventured to use their Wonder Woman ​review to spite ​Captain Marvel by rating the film higher than they believe it deserved to distance the two film’s cumulative rating scores (mtlabfall). These positive user reviewers steered away from referencing professional critics reviews, presumably because they share similar sentiments so there isn’t the need to ignite that battle between who’s right and who’s wrong.

So, who actually has the paratextual privilege to make claims about these films and have people listen to them? Presumably, most members of these opposing groups would respond “anyone besides the people on the other side of the argument”. Outside of the fact that this mindset creates a never-ending loop of one party telling the other that they cannot have a different opinion without being either daft or paid off, it can lead to some interesting ways in which the reviews shape the texts themselves.

To some respect, critical and user reviews exist within different intellectual spaces: critics’ reviews influence the perceptions and overall success of films and user reviews take that influence one step further by existing in conversation with one another (Gray 166). The discourse pool for critics’ reviews is set in size and content because there are barriers to entry to be classified amongst the professionals (FAQ ​Rotten Tomatoes​). Manners of entry can include finding a job as a critic at a respected news outlet or, in the social media age, gaining enough of an online following that people start taking your opinions seriously and Hollywood gives you privileged access to the content before the rest of the public (FAQ ​Rotten Tomatoes​, Gray 166). Neither of these manners for entry are especially easy to accomplish so the discourse pool is kept to a select few. Specifically for Metacritic, the aggregator featured on IMDb, to ensure that all members keep to a professional standard within their critical publications, there is a vetting process for publications that submit to be part of the expert opinion pool (Doyle). ​Since there is a limited number of professional film critics, the opinion pool is shaped rapidly ​and semi-permanently once the studio-imposed review embargo lifts. Review embargoes allow for a film studio to determine when professional critics can post about their films to minimize the spread potential negative sentiment about the text and thus, maximize opening weekend profits (Singer). The majority of professional critics publish their reviews soon after they are allowed because it increases traffic to their articles and makes them more profitable (Singer). Once all of the professional critics’ opinions are heard, the discourse pool is metaphorically closed and the reviews, in general, do not change in content. Critics’ reviews themselves do not exist in conversation with one another because that is not their job. These reviews exist to provide a baseline for whether or not a film is worth the price of admission from the perspective of someone who has a trained eye for cinematic technique.

However, in this realm of the average user reviewer, often the only barrier to entry often is a free website account and access to a reliable internet connection. Along with this ease of entry comes with infinite time and space to publish comments. Through the power of the internet, there is room in this user-driven space for any and all thoughts related to any film from the moment of its release until the end of time. Films released a century ago such as ​The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari (Wiene 1920) still receive new reviews. Thus, when a user gets the chance to send their thoughts out into the world, they are doing more than simply sending static theories out into a finite space; these users are contributing to an ongoing discussion where they interact with any reviews that came before. Not even the first user review for a film starts from scratch; it builds upon the foundation set by the first professional reactions allowed to hit cyberspace, critics and other industry professionals. Any published user review must balance between two sets of previous thoughts, the ever-changing user space with its plethora of strong opinions and the static critical space with its wealth of knowledge about filmmaking. For ​Captain Marvel and Wonder Woman​, this balancing act places the user reviewer on the defensive from the beginning because they must choose which army to align with. They can either risk going against a horde of angry fans or the professional critics who are ​so obviously​ in league with movie studios.

But, as much as the public discourse pool may want to exist within a lawless land where people are able to attack whoever and whatever they please, IMDb and other similar sites are monitored. Reviews can be taken out of the infinite discourse pool at any time by the site moderators for violating the community guidelines. IMDb and other review sites hold the utmost paratextual privilege over the userspace. Despite the endless bounds of the digital world, only those that IMDb declares have the right to share their opinion may do so. Critics cannot stop users from trashing films that they praised, and users cannot stop other users from disagreeing with their opinions on a film. Those who moderate digital spaces have more sway in the discourse than any of the commenters because they determine what can be considered in the discussion. The commenters can say whatever they wish in this limitless digital space, but there is no guarantee that any of it will get heard.

3. Wonder Woman: A Motherly Image of Militant Feminism For ​Wonder Woman​, fans were fairly evenly split between those who thought Gal Gadot’s performance in the titular role was a cinematic revelation and those who thought she came off as vapid or wooden. In particular, quite a few people were pleased with the focus on emotional sincerity and innate femininity in Gadot’s performance. One commenter praised that

“[h]er tremendous power is counterbalanced with a naivety that reaches beyond comic relief into an often scathing critique of the human leanings toward inhumanity” (Damionis). This comment speaks to the fact that Gadot’s incarnation of Wonder Woman took undeniable influence from the theories formulated by the character’s creator, William Moulton Marston. Marston’s believed that women were the superior sex due to their increased capacity for love and tenderness and created the character to act as a counterbalance for the overwhelming masculinity present in comic books. He wanted to populate the world with a sort of “psychological propaganda” to showcase the type of woman, nurturing and sensitive, that he believed should, and one day would, be ruling the world (Stuller 13-15). Marston’s theories are problematic, to say the least, because they treat the entire female sex as a singular entity with definable communal emotional characteristics rather than recognizing the innate complexities present in each woman’s definition of femininity. However, the idea that traits typically associated with femininity and, by extension, weakness, such as sensitivity and tenderness, can be strengths does have some redeemable qualities. Gadot’s Wonder Woman has an undying belief that the evil god Ares is causing the humans’ desire to wage war because she sees inner goodness within all creatures; the humans are not inherently evil but are being corrupted to commit atrocities by a malevolent force. While she later must learn that the situation is not quite so simple, her ability to see the promise of a better tomorrow and keep faith that the world’s problems can be fixed is novel, both in the film’s internal canon and in present-day politically divided and environmentally compromised America.

This femininity did not necessarily land well; one commenter stated “Wonder Woman is played by the bad but gorgeous Gal Gadot. Nothing but a series of poses for magazines, trying to look innocent but also bold and intelligent” (MovieChopper11). Here, rather than Wonder Woman’s belief in human goodness being a strength, she is belittled for it.

The discourse surrounding Gadot would surely be incomplete if there weren't some reviewers who felt the need to comment on her feminine figure in relation to her acting ability. Gadot was continually objectified in one of two ways, those who found her incredibly attractive and those for whom her looks were just not sufficient. In addition to the above comment about her “gorgeous” appearance, one reviewer expressed distaste in Gadot by stating that “[she] could’ve hit the gym” before filming because “in her current physique ....[she] looks like [she] had to sleep with the coach to make the team” and that “[her] Hamstrings [sic]...swing like jelly” (Good-decision). Once again, Gadot’s sexuality or perceived lack thereof is being connected to her accomplishments. In addition, the comment about the necessity of “sleeping with the coach” is especially relevant in the #MeToo era where influential men in Hollywood are being convicted of manipulating aspiring actresses of exactly that to award them career-changing roles.

While each of these commenters chose to highlight a different aspect of Gadot and her performance, the prevalence of the male gaze is overwhelmingly evident. The male gaze was first conceived by Laura Mulvey in her revolutionary piece ​Visual Pleasures and Narrative Cinema​. It is described as the tendency for female on-screen portrayals to be styled in a way pleasing to heterosexual male desires and females to exist in the cinematic space strictly to be looked at. Thus, the male gaze creates a sort of spectacle out of the very existence of female characters. This phenomenon is often attributed to the result of males being the dominant content-producing force within the film industry (Mulvey 14). Stories get told with what straight men would want to see in mind because male filmmakers have the ability to cater to their own pleasurable desires in their works. Thus, submissive female characters and gratuitous shots of the feminine form often result.

Catwoman is one character in particular who’s film fell victim to a male gaze. This film was directed by a man and takes special care to emphasize the sexuality of its leading female, Halle Berry, in her costuming and choreography. Berry’s titular character goes from being a submissive and meek artist during the day to fighting male criminals in an overtly sexual style and making cat-related innuendos when she takes on her feline alter ego at night. Her character initially allows her male superiors to overpower her and when she makes moves to take that power back, she does so using her sexuality. As Catwoman makes her transition from human to cat, the male gaze moves from pleasure at her domination onto blatant sexual satisfaction at the sight of her in suggestive positions. In either situation, her character fits within a set of conventional male desires.

In the end, Catwoman manages to overpower the men challenging her so there is some overt feminism to discuss in her portrayal because she has some agency in the outcome of her story. However, because the film does so in a male-gaze-forward manner that emphasizes her sexuality first and foremost, it raises questions as to how feminist the text actually is. If the text appeals to conventional male desires before it caters to female empowerment, the feminist message is still subjugated under male power, similar to the women it is supposedly empowering.

The fact that ​Wonder Woman is directed by a woman, Patty Jenkins should, in theory, exempt it from the male gaze of pleasurable desire. This, of course, can never quite be that simple. ​Wonder Woman still contains elements of a male gaze, albeit not quite so overt as Catwoman​, hidden with its moment of female empowerment. Specifically, the scene where Wonder Woman emerges from the trenches into no man’s land demonstrates a blend of feminist imagery combined with remnants of a male gaze (1:12:00-1:17:00).

In this scene, Diana stands up for what she believes in and saves the Belgian town from the Germans despite the male voices around her telling her that it cannot be done. Her powers outmatch both her male compatriots holding her back and the army shooting at her. Wonder Woman is empowered, self-assured, and unwilling to allow anyone to stand in the way of her desire to help the innocent; she cannot be subdued because she is simply more powerful than any of the men around her. In short, Wonder Woman is acting with the kind of agency Mulvey attributes to be only available to a male character. So, to add a feminist reading to the scene is not necessarily unreasonable.

Yet, users still commented on her attractiveness in the scene. One reviewer emphasized that her presence was “like some shimmering version of hotness, to set male and lesbian hearts a flutter” (Bob-the-movie-man). This reviewer’s wording reduces Wonder Woman back to being an object of sexual desire instead of an empowered warrior. Problem being, various elements of the scene contribute to his case. There are slow-motion shots of Diana’s legs, forearms, and calves as she climbs up the ladder and into battle. She walks in gratuitous slow motion into no man’s land with a look of seductive determination on her face. Her armor shows an amount of skin not entirely practical for a battle scenario that emphasizes her chest and tiny waist. Granted, the choice of clothing here does seem much better in comparison to the costuming of her fellow female Amazon warriors in the male-directed ​Justice League ​(Snyder 2017). This is a pretty low threshold to cross when the comparison point has women fighting in two-piece armors with their midriffs and the majority of their vital organs exposed to the elements.

In many ways, the film does improve upon the genre’s predecessors which is a step in the right direction for future female characters industry-wide. However, creating a film that is perfectly feminist may very well be impossible. In a world where the American film industry has been ruled by men since the rise of the studio system in the early 20th century, circumventing oppressive systems that subjugate women into being objects of desire and submissiveness is no easy task. This can mean that while some aspects of the film may take steps forward for female representation, other aspects may constitute a step back. Even films that endeavor to be feminist can still fall victim to misogynistic tropes, such as the male gaze, ​Wonder Woman ​included.

Even for film academics, how to improve female representation in the cinematic space is not always entirely clear. They grapple with differing opinions on how to create a “female gaze” of sorts to counter the overwhelmingly standard male gaze. Teresa de Lauretis details some historical discrepancies within feminist film scholarship. She states that

“Not surprisingly...a...contradiction was also central to the debate on women’s cinema, its politics and its language, as it was articulated within Anglo-American film theory in the early 1970s in relation to feminist politics and the women’s movement, on the one hand, and to artistic avant-garde practices and women’s filmmaking, on the other. There, too, the accounts of feminist film culture produced in the mid- to late-seventies tended to emphasize a dichotomy between two concerns of the women’s movement and two types of film work that seemed to be at odds with each other: one called for immediate documentation for purposes of political activism, consciousness-raising, self-expression or the search for ‘positive images’ of woman; the other insisted on rigorous, formal work… in order to analyze and disengage the ideological codes embedded in representation” (pg. 140-141). In this dichotomy, Wonder Woman sits closer to “immediate documentation for purposes of political activism” than “rigorous, formal work”. The film is more concerned with adding the best feminist figures it can muster into the social zeitgeist over redefining the meaning of cinema. As this feminist film critical debate would insinuate, its manner of accomplishing said task may not be the best and leads to this debate within feminist filmmaking to rage on.

The disagreement about how to create positive images for women on screen does not end in academia; user commenters have their own clashes about what is and isn’t feminist. In the Wonder Woman comment section, viewers clashed over what elements of the film constituted feminist filmmaking and what additions destroyed the message. Some viewers’ interpretations align with Marston’s theories about nurturing feminism: they see Wonder Woman’s ability to be “charismatic and authoritative but not so much that she loses her feminine charm and sense of humor'' as empowering (Politicidal); others note how Wonder Woman’s feminine benevolence does not extend to all and that film “preaches to the audience about pacifism but then hypocritically celebrates ‘heroic’ violence” (WeeClaude). Some audiences appreciate that the film “provides audiences with a female protagonist who is not merely a leader, but the engineer--the author--of her own destiny and story” (RLTerry1); others condemn the idea that Wonder Woman is “just dragged from location to location by Steve [Trevor, the film’s male lead]” (Evaxbos), similar to the theories of female subjugation presented by Laura Mulvey.

It is also worth noting that these moments of contradiction for Wonder Woman’s status as a feminist figure extend outside of the film’s immediate canon. Gal Gadot served as a combat trainer for two years in the Israeli army before going to college and later committing to her modeling and acting career (Al-Mahadin 248). Even after breaking into Hollywood and being awarded some of her highest profile film roles, Gadot has remained vocal about her support of her home country and credits her military experience as beneficial toward her successes (248). In a certain light, Gadot’s military experience is feminist because it constitutes her accomplishing something unconventional for women, especially in the United States where military service is extremely male-dominated. Given the fact that the Israel/Palestine conflict is a complex and delicate issue, how positive this aspect of her history can be put up for debate. Since 2009 alone, there have been over 3,500 Palestinian deaths at the hands of Israeli forces, a much larger figure compared to approximately 200 Israeli deaths (Fatalities since Operation Cast Lead B'Tselem). For those who support Palestine in the conflict, Gadot’s military service is an inescapable detracting factor in determining her and, by extension, Wonder Woman’s, status as a figure of positive societal change, and it challenges merits of “kick-ass” womanhood because it comes at the expense of years of violent conflict and lives lost (Al-Mahadin 246).

Content made with an amount of a feminist gaze in mind can still contribute something beneficial to the cause for equal representation however imperfect it may be. These contributions must be discussed rather than taken on their word alone that they are feminist. ​Wonder Woman may be feminist to some, but not to others, and the reasoning behind these judgments can further complicate the discussion around films made with a feminist lens. The addition of a complicated discussion about these issues encourages representation to further improve. If spectators cease to discuss what they do or don’t approve of in feminine representation, the industry ceases to progress toward a more equitable space for female creators and stars. These audience conversations are necessary as they encourage filmmakers to continue improving their treatment of female characters.

While not all those who contribute to the discussion surrounding feminist filmmaking will do so in a productive manner, those who do can have noticable impacts on righting the misogynistic wrongs of past releases. For example, the year before the release of ​Wonder Woman​, DC released ​Suicide Squad (Ayer 2016), a male directed film featuring a male-gaze-forward portrayal of Harley Quinn (Margot Robbie). In this incarnation, Quinn wore sequin shorts that were more akin to swimsuit bottoms, a tight ripped shirt that read “Daddy’s Little Monster” across her chest, and flaunted a jacket that read “Property of Joker '' in large font across the back (in case somehow it wasn’t clear enough who her paternalistic boyfriend was). DC has since handed the reins for the character over to Kathy Yan, a female director, for their second outing with the character, ​Birds of Prey (and the Fantabulous Emancipation of One Harley Quinn) ​(2020). This film made drastic improvements upon how Quinn was portrayed within a feminist lens​. A major plot point for this film is Quinn repairing herself emotionally after splitting from her toxic relationship with the Joker, in a manner that seems to actively rebel against a male gaze. Quinn and her female compatriots wear costumes that do show skin, such as Quinn’s recurring pink sports bra that she pairs with high waisted jean shorts and a yellow jumpsuit with gold harlequin diamonds. But this costuming treats Quinn’s shown skin as natural and intentional rather than a sexual tease peeking out from under revealing clothing. The difference between the two films (just four years apart) showcase the industry’s ability to break out of old ‘male-gazey’ habits that encourage female sexual objectification and romanticize relationship paternalism. Progress can be made; these archaic habits just must be recognized and addressed rather than accepted as being an inevitable part of the industry.

4. Captain Marvel: The Intersection of Social Justice and Intertextuality This note of positivity is rather fleeting as the comment section on ​Captain Marvel was, once again, a cesspool of negativity. The feminism-directed user commentary for this film tended to take two forms, those who took issue with Brie Larson’s demeanor during the film’s press tour and those who disliked her performance as the titular heroine. Any semblance of respect for the film was minimal to say the least. Outside of slight shifts in the direction where the hatred was aimed, Brie Larson and her involvement in the film were always the standout problem and the reason that fans were angered or offended.

One way commenters found to criticize Brie Larson was to bring up feminist comments that she made during interviews and on social media. Commenters constantly mentioned aspects of her behavior as evidence that Larson has “toxic public opinions” (Aj_schepis) or “is just VERY unlikable as a person” because “she hates men” and just “wanted to spout feminist hate” (Whathappenedmarvel). As a result, this particular commenter “can no longer bring [themselves] to support a company [Disney/Marvel] that sacrifices everything they’ve built up over 15+ movies to push some false absurd agenda” (Whathappenedmarvel). Some commenters “couldn’t imagine why [Marvel] would destroy such a good franchise with [the] SJW [Social Justice Warrior] propaganda” (Lorandxd) that Larson was spreading. This discourse is largely shaped by a speech that Larson gave a year before ​Captain Marvel​’s release and notable themes then bled into the ​Captain Marvel press tour and spurred some of the righteous backlash Larson experienced in response to the film.

Now, as tends to happen with the internet, by the time that details of an encounter reach the current commenter, it is often far away from the events that actually occurred. Keeping that phenomenon in mind, what did Brie Larson actually comment on that made the internet feel the need to unleash complete and utter hell upon her? Strangely enough, she called attention to the scarcity of female critical opinion, particularly with women of color, in the film industry and how it negatively impacts films that star anyone other than the traditional Hollywood white man. During her acceptance speech at the Women in Film Crystal + Lucy award ceremony in June 2018, Larson brought up the disconnect between the demographics of professionals who can see and review films compared to the racial and gender breakdown of the United States. She emphasized throughout the speech that while she “doesn’t hate white dudes,” (Women in Film, Los Angeles 2:44-2:47) the film industry needs to be “conscious of [their] bias and do [their] part to make sure that everyone is in the room” (2:48-2:54) to ensure that all sides of the discussion relevant to the film’s release are heard and considered. Then, during the ​Captain Marvel press tour, Larson stood by her word and ensured that she was interviewed by more than just white male reporters including ​Marie Clare ​contributor Keah Brown, a black woman with cerebral palsy who was often passed up for major interview opportunities (Brown).

This situation speaks to spectatorship theory, the idea that people view media differently based on their diverse backgrounds and experiences. As described by Judith Mayne, “the study of spectatorship involves an engagement with modes of seeing and telling, hearing and listening, not only in terms of how films are structured, but in terms of how audiences imagine themselves” (32). Mayne is addressing that while spectator theory is inherently connected to cinema, the discipline is not limited to solely cinematic study. Instead, spectator theory “has provided a way to understand film in its cultural dimension” (32). For ​Captain Marvel​, spectator theory goes a step further beyond audience response to the onscreen images, by also taking into account how the film affects a wider cultural understanding. By insisting that the discourse surrounding ​Captain Marvel during the press tour be populated by people of diverse experiences and ways of imagining themselves, Larson opened the discourse pool to people whose experiences often get overlooked. This practice is a step in ensuring that the film’s reception would be as accurate as possible to the actual diverse makeup of the United States.

Under this logic of spectator subjectivity, Larson’s comments and actions seem innocent enough, even praiseworthy and as though all the user backlash is just part of a wild misunderstanding. However, there is one other comment from her initial speech that can be easily misconstrued and, as luck would have it, it very much was. During her speech, Larson comments on how she “does not need some 40-year-old white dude to tell [her] what didn’t work for him about ​A Wrinkle in Time (DuVernay 2018)” because “it wasn’t made for him” (Women In Film, Los Angeles 3:50-3:56). This film prominently features a biracial couple and highlights the strengths of their daughter and adopted son. Therefore, when an African American, biracial, or adopted person watches ​A Wrinkle in Time, ​they may feel a stronger impact from the film than those who don’t share those demographic backgrounds. This matters because, while the film’s merits can be debated, the cultural impact of the film for underrepresented groups may outvalue the potential pitfalls. The film was made for groups of people in this country who do not often see themselves portrayed in a positive light on screen, unlike white men from nuclear families.

While according to spectatorship theory this concept is not incorrect, daring to insinuate that a white male is not the only intended audience and, therefore, should not be the only voice surrounding a film turned out to be a dangerous statement on the internet. As mentioned previously, the IMDb review section is heavily populated by male commenters, similar to that of the professional critical opinion circuit. Rather than taking Larson’s comments to heart and working toward a space of increased inclusivity, commenters cited a mutated version of Larson’s stance and went to work trying to discredit her. One commenter claimed that Larson “used this film to promote her own politic [sic] agenda and herself instead of making it what it is- just a movie everyone should be able to enjoy” and that “[they] would suggest [Larson] to shut up and be pretty cause [sic] there’s obviously not much talent there” (Lusha12). One commenter swore off seeing the film because “Brie Larson told [him] not to. She said she didn’t want or need ‘[him]’ (a man in [his] forties) to support it”. This commenter was also upset that there was no subsequent statement from Disney renouncing her comments and apologizing for them (Spotop04). One commenter even claimed that Larson said “white guys shouldn’t be allowed to watch/review movies” in her “controversial, simply insane past comments” (Cinemaloversclub).

In addition to this backlash, there were also commenters who chose to attack her acting performance. There were the straightforward critiques, calling her performance “wooden” (Grantpaulsen), “cringy” (Bloodfalcon64), “lacking in emotional depth” (Nicholsells), or straight-up “unwatchable” (Deztron). Then, there were those who went a bit more creative. One reviewer stated that “Larson looks like she had to go to athletic school for a crash course but didn’t make it past the first jog!” (DudesTheWorld1). This critique is especially perplexing as Larson notably went through a rigorous training regimen to prepare for her role, including posting footage of herself pushing a nearly 5,000-pound Jeep with nothing but her own strength (Saunders).

Outside of this, some of the most common ways that users found to describe Larson’s performance was to negatively compare her to her MCU predecessors including Robert Downey Jr., Chris Evans, Chris Hemsworth, and Scarlett Johansson. Jonathan Gray describes a similar phenomenon in his theories about intertextuality. Gray defines intertextuality as “instances wherein a film or program refers to and builds some of its meaning off another film or program” and that the intertext as the “referenced film or program” (117). I take a slight spin upon one of the ways that he elaborates upon intertextuality and apply it to one of the basic functions of the MCU. Gray explains that “[i]ntertexuality refers to the fundamental and inescapable interdependence of all textual meaning upon the structures of meaning proposed by other texts” (117). In this statement, Gray is referring to how understanding the many nuances of ​West Side Story ​(Wise, Robbins 1961) requires a basic understanding of ​Romeo and Juliet (Shakespeare). In these cases, the texts are connected by allusion, not plot intertwinement. Users pulling knowledge from other texts has taken on new meaning with the integration of the cinematic universe into popular culture. One of the main conceits of this cinematic universe is that each film takes pieces from previous installments to build upon while still, in theory, being comprehensible in its own right (albeit not as well). This process differs from that of a typical chain of sequels by not always featuring the same cast of characters or even being a direct continuation of the previous story. In the MCU, in order to understand any film’s plot in totality, the spectator needs to have seen all of the previous installments and understand them well enough that they can make intertextual connections. Under this reframe, Larson’s performance is the intertext and the intertextuality is her inability to escape the shadow of her Marvel predecessors in the eyes of the user commenters.

Under this logic, commenters comparing Larson’s Captain Marvel and previous MCU characters and stories is not altogether unreasonable; all of their stories are inescapably connected. Beyond the obvious gender connection between her and Scarlett Johansson’s Black Widow, Larson’s Carol Danvers has a witty sense of humor similar to Robert Downey Jr.’s Iron Man, the military experience of Chris Evans’ Captain America, and the incredible physique and God-like power of Chris Hemsworth’s Thor.

Rather than the user commenters adopting these influences to understand the character further, they created an unattainable bar that Larson had to meet to be considered successful. Users claimed that in her portrayal of Captain Marvel “​[t]here wasn't any display of fight IQ or heart, something you see in Captain America or Iron Man” (Htutmaung) or that “​[t]he reason characters like Thor, Tony Stark, and Captain America are so well loved is because they have flaws'' and that Larson’s incarnation was so perfect and overpowered that was not relatable (Rory_woodard). This commenter also claimed that “despite the fact that Brie Larson spent her entire press tour bashing men, she spent the entire movie trying to copy the successful act of Robert Downey Jr….[with his] hilarious one-liners and quips” (Rory_woodard). This review cements the previous point that the MCU’s intertextuality is not always positive, especially when it comes to critique of female characters. Brie Larson could not portray her character with a witty sense of humor without being accused of copying Robert Downey Jr., who was far from the first person to use that character trait in a performance nor will he be the last.

In addition, one user was adamant that they “[d]on't need Captain Marvel for a female role model in super hero [sic] movies” as they “[a]lready have [B]lack [W]idow” (Frisco2007). This comment speaks yet again the prevalence of the male gaze in Hollywood films. In many ways, Black Widow is an empowered female character. She proved time and time again throughout her stint as an Avenger that she could fight her own battles without becoming a damsel in distress. However, this does not mean that her treatment within the MCU was always entirely fair or free from a level of male gaze. She was introduced into the universe as an object of sexual desire for Tony Stark and while this dynamic did not last long, the overt male-gaze sexuality of her character never quite went away. Her combat attire was often a skintight leather jumpsuit with a strategically placed zipper that was always slightly unzipped at her chest. Not even she could escape the series without a potential love interest in ​Avengers: Age of Ultron (Whedon 2015) when she was momentarily paired up with Bruce Banner/The Hulk. And, possibly the most egregious crime of them all, she never achieved a status above secondary character throughout the ten years between her character introduction and death, in contrast to newer male characters getting their own solo films, like ​Doctor Strange (Derrickson 2016). It was not until after she sacrificed herself for the sake of the future of the universe (both the physical universe and the cinematic one) in ​Avengers: Endgame (Russo and Russo 2019) that she was deemed important enough to get a prequel solo film.

However, from the beginning, Captain Marvel presents a female image contrary to those that came before her. For one, she already escaped the fate of Black Widow by appearing in her solo film before any others. Her costuming infuses a level of combat practicality not often seen with previous female heroes. Although she still wears a skintight bodysuit, it mirrors the costuming of her male compatriots and does not emphasize her feminine features outside of acknowledging that she has them and making proper accommodations (not including armor shaped around her breasts or an undone zipper). Outside of her costuming, Captain Marvel also escapes the film without any trace of a romantic interest. Instead, she has a meaningful platonic relationship with a fellow former Air Force pilot, Maria Rambeau (Lashana Lynch) and her daughter, Monica (Akira Akbar). This choice emphasizes Captain Marvel’s ability to have purposeful relationships that deepen her character- she gains strength in being a friend, rather than weakness in being a passive love interest.

Captain Marvel’s story also invites a reading in contrast to Wonder Woman’s journey of self-discovery. They both hinge upon the fact that, in society, women face stereotypes of being less self-composed and rational and more impulsive and emotional than men. Wonder Woman finds her strength in redefining these generalizations. Her emotion and compassion fuel her heroic behavior and uses her immense physical strength to accomplish her goal of saving the innocent. Wonder Woman is heroic because she cares deeply for others but must learn that right and wrong are not always precisely defined.

Captain Marvel takes a vastly different journey. At the beginning of the film, Danvers, or, as she is called at the time, Vers, is held back by her male trainer, Yon-Rogg (Jude Law), and the “Supreme Intelligence” (Annette Bening) of her world. Their training mantra is that, in order to become an effective warrior, she must fight analytically rather than emotionally. However, Vers’ atomic power becomes more effective when fueled by her anger or excitement, and ultimately her suppression of emotion in battle only benefits those controlling her; she can overpower them when she uses her emotions to her benefit. Captain Marvel’s power is linked to her emotional expression and she reaches her full potential when her emotion and logic are used in tandem. The movie is far from subtle in exploring workplace discrimination against women, but it takes more time to highlight the effort involved in resistance than Wonder Woman’s display of idealistic determination.

However, the commenters’ backlash would perhaps indicate that ​Captain Marvel’s views of feminism were not what they wanted. Previous superheroines were praised as feminist (Wonder Woman and Black Widow) simply because they were not damsels, and often remained un-challenging on a fundamental level. And commenters continually harkened back to these standards of feminism in which the heroine upheld an image closer to standard femininity marked by motherly benevolence and inherent sexual appeal. However, Captain Marvel’s feminist journey introduces Danvers as a witty hero who is dirty, angry, and difficult - similar to Tony Stark - and who destroys a male oppressor in an anti-patriarchal beatdown. This femininity requires a balance between physical strength and emotional balance that is unladylike according to ages-old standards.

Spectators in IMDb comment sections were used to passively feminist superwomen, and the new complexity of ​Captain Marvel was not a welcome addition. ​Captain Marvel requires that viewers adjust their schemas for what a female character should be, even more dramatically than they already have for previous women in superhero genres. ​Captain Marvel​’s plot explicitly relies on defying systems of male control and the film rejects traditional male-gazey cinematography to present an empowered woman who possesses physical strength AND emotional expression. Although part of an intertextual web of MCU films, Captain Marvel charts a new course for women, while externally, Brie Larson’s support of spectatorship theory and calls for diversity deepens an industry reckoning with who is glorified on screen. From passive love objects to warriors and scientists, from idealists to gritty comedians, superwomen have transformed via writers introducing new models to audiences, who then accept them as normal after time and continued exposure. However, as shown in the previous discussion of IMDb response, commenters did not welcome this new norm and even praised older schemas (“I don’t need Captain Marvel, I have Wonder Woman”), in hopes of reversing Captain Marvel’s new paradigm in future films.

When the male characters of a universe are maintained as the untouchable gold standard and the female ideal retains a level of the male gaze, it speaks to audience members’ expectations of media and their reactions when that status quo is broken. Male gaze filmmaking is ingrained in Hollywood, as I discussed regarding ​Wonder Woman, and these schemas have only been exaggerated with the addition of the heavy intertextuality of the cinematic universe. To create a feminist character is often a process of give and take, as the filmmakers must balance studio expectations and audience desires on top of making a film even worth watching. ​Captain Marvel strayed the furthest from the male gaze in her first appearance out of most previous female superheroes, including Harley Quinn, Catwoman, Wonder Woman, Black Widow, and beyond. She has enough power and agency to define herself and prove that societal scorn for women’s emotions is misplaced. But these sentiments are not always commonplace in big budget films and perhaps the commenters were not prepared for such a drastic change. And, in a cinematic universe where each text is defined by each of the text that came before, adopting a different filmmaking lens becomes even more prominent and perhaps even more jarring. The creative leadership for the MCU has proven for 12 years and wild success that they are willing to portray female characters that submit to a dominant male narrative, both in the universe’s plot and the Hollywood model. In this process, the MCU has become a box office powerhouse that now holds the record for highest grossing film of all time (Yedroudj). But if ​Captain Marvel and the list of female heroes in their upcoming slate is any indication, Marvel seems to be realizing the error in their ways and is working toward positive change in ridding themselves of overwhelming male gaze.

5. Conclusion

So, if the current MCU formula for character and story is clearly working, why try and change it? To put it simply, female characters and the young people who idolize them deserve better. Their stories should not be written strictly to supplement a male’s journey and their bodies are worth more than existing to satisfy sexual fantasies. To achieve this new state of female respect, it will require escaping the bound of what intertextuality deems acceptable. Just because a previous text deemed a behavior tolerable does not mean it must continue to be. While it may make some spectators angry or uncomfortable, breaking these habits is an important step in redefining a female’s role in cinema. ​Wonder Woman ​is an example of the give-and-take conflict between feminism and patriarchy in Hollywood; the result is neither horrific nor perfect but one that lays the groundwork for future superheroines. ​Captain Marvel showcases an unapologetic attempt at escaping the confines of her intertextual relationship to previous Marvel characters and defining her as a successful character in her own right. However, audience response on IMDb reveals that the online reviewer community still has work to do to fairly critique feminist works.

This research is only a small facet of the wide array of work to be done in making the space equitable for ​all women. LGBTQ and women of color have stories that differ from those of straight, white women, and must be acknowledged on a wide platform. But their stories are often overlooked and addressing this tendency is one way that the industry can improve. In 2019, 20% of female characters from films were black, 7% Asian, and 5% Latina (Lauzen, It’s a Man’s World 5). A study conducted by GLAAD in 2018 found that only 20 out of 110 films selected from the year featured an LGBTQ character of any gender in any capacity (GLAAD). Despite this, inclusion does not equal adequate representation. Women of these backgrounds are both infrequently featured in major box office films, and when they do appear, they are rarely the center point of the story.

Heading into 2020, all films slated for release by both Marvel and DC prominently featured women both in front of and behind the camera. These releases then changed due to COVID-19 but this does not detract from the noticeable changes in gender proportion. In February, DC released female-directed ​Birds of Prey starring a less male-gaze influenced interpretation of Harley Quinn. ​Wonder Woman: 1984 was slated for release in June before being moved to December. Marvel was finally slated to give Black Widow her due in May 2020 with a female-directed solo film ​that got moved to May 2021 (Shortland). And Marvel’s ​The ​Eternals got moved to from November 2020 to November 2021. This film is directed by a Chinese woman (Chloè Zhao) and has an ensemble cast prominently featuring several women of diverse races (Gemma Chan, Lauren Ridloff, and Salma Hayek).

Some of these films also feature queer women and women of color in prominent positions. ​Birds of Prey​’s Renee Montoya (Rosie Perez) is a Hispanic woman who grapples with a troublesome working relationship with her ex-girlfriend, Ellen Yee (Ali Wong). And ​The Eternals ​will feature Makkari, the first deaf superhero in the MCU as portrayed by deaf, biracial actress, Lauren Ridloff. These films' choices to include women of diverse backgrounds does constitute a step forward for representing marginalized groups. But, the space is not yet equitable; the inclusion of non-straight and/or women of color is still often done through secondary characters or as part of an ensemble cast.

In the end, simply putting a female on the screen does not constitute all encompassing representation. The female must be treated fairly and the filmmakers must be attentive about how their decisions may affect the larger feminist film movement. This means dispelling moments of the male gaze whenever possible, giving the female character an active voice in her story, and being conscious about making content that suits people in a way array of dispositions rather than limiting things to a select few. Despite this, all of these tasks often cannot be accomplished in any singular film. Creating the perfect female character who can single-handedly dispel years worth of exclusions and misrepresentations on her own is a tall, essentially impossible, order. No singular film should try to overcome every hindrance because, by doing so, no one gets their due. Underrepresented people deserve more than haphazard attempts to craft a film that pleases everyone; their stories are important enough to warrant the full attention of filmmakers. It often takes numerous films that each tackle some facet of this complex issue to create more equitable representation and even the films that are unsuccessful on some level still have something valuable to offer this discussion.

In an online culture where polarizing reviews are largely male-written, the critique of feminist films like ​Wonder Woman ​and ​Captain Marvel is flawed. Simply proclaiming a film to be terrible and rating it 1-star shuts down potential avenues for improvement. Even flawed films, such as ​Wonder Woman and ​Captain Marvel​, have something valuable to offer the discussion, even if that entrails advice about what not to do in the future. It’s more important to establish a curious and open-minded way of looking at films than to expect creators to make something perfect. This complexity stimulates discussion and a desire to improve - audiences will never be able to just go home satisfied because sexism has been solved by one film. Critics and users have to keep questioning and allowing nuanced dialogue to rise to the top rather than extreme opinions. Creators and executives have to continue creating female characters as powerful, complex beings who are more than girlfriends.

When it comes time to evaluate how well the films did, female voices of all backgrounds should be the main factor considered. Women are the ones who have been subjected to subpar representations of their gender for years; they are the ones who should have the greatest say in how the industry goes about fixing things. Not all women have to agree about the best way to improve representation, but, these characters are meant to legitimize a female’s status as powerful beings suited for more than romantic attraction, and it is not a man’s job to decide the best way to accomplish that, because “it wasn’t made for him”.
