title: Trash Collection Service Participation in La Pista, Guatemala: A Community Survey
abstract:
Objective: Survey residents of La Pista, Guatemala to understand why people do or do not participate in a newly developed garbage collection system and how the system could be improved.

Setting: The aldea1of La Pista2in the Municipality of Nebaj – Quiché Department, Guatemala. According to the La Pista auxiliatura3, the aldea is home to about 3,000 people in 570 families.

Intervention: In July and August 2018, interns for the non-governmental organization (NGO) Soluciones Comunitarias worked with the local government to adapt available political and physical infrastructure to include La Pista in Nebaj’s trash collection service.

Main outcome measures: In December 2018, we conducted 48 surveys (16 business surveys and 32 residential surveys) to survey public perception of the service, participants’ motivations for opting to pay or not to have the truck bring their trash to the dump, and how residents, businesses and community leaders were looking to improve the project.

Results: Participation rates were high: 83.3% of those surveyed had participated in the service at least once. 57.5% of those program participants cited environmental protection as a motivation for paying for the collection service. Of those that did not participate, three said that the service was inconvenient. Suggestions for improvement include a fixed monthly collection date and helping residents carry their trash. Additionally, survey participants recommended educational workshops on relevant topics to increase participation.
text:
Leah Dunlevy and Amos Pomp

Leah Dunlevy is a senior double majoring in journalism and international studies, and Amos Pomp is a junior majoring in american studies. Leah is currently undecided about her plans after graduating, but will most likely be heading to Princeton in Africa or AmeriCorps. Amos has one more year left at Northwestern.

What is your research topic, in a nutshell?

We examined how a newly-implemented trash management system was working in La Pista, Guatemala four months after implementation.

How did you come to your research topic?

We spent the summer working with leadership in La Pista to implement the trash collection system and we wanted to know if and how the project was still functioning, as well as areas for improvement.

Where do you see the future direction of this work leading?

Future research could investigate how community structure and participation influences program sustainability and effectiveness.

Abstract

Objective: Survey residents of La Pista, Guatemala to understand why people do or do not participate in a newly developed garbage collection system and how the system could be improved.

Setting: The aldea1of La Pista2in the Municipality of Nebaj – Quiché Department, Guatemala. According to the La Pista auxiliatura3, the aldea is home to about 3,000 people in 570 families.

Intervention: In July and August 2018, interns for the non-governmental organization (NGO) Soluciones Comunitarias worked with the local government to adapt available political and physical infrastructure to include La Pista in Nebaj’s trash collection service.

Main outcome measures: In December 2018, we conducted 48 surveys (16 business surveys and 32 residential surveys) to survey public perception of the service, participants’ motivations for opting to pay or not to have the truck bring their trash to the dump, and how residents, businesses and community leaders were looking to improve the project.

Results: Participation rates were high: 83.3% of those surveyed had participated in the service at least once. 57.5% of those program participants cited environmental protection as a motivation for paying for the collection service. Of those that did not participate, three said that the service was inconvenient. Suggestions for improvement include a fixed monthly collection date and helping residents carry their trash. Additionally, survey participants recommended educational workshops on relevant topics to increase participation.

Literature Review

Inorganic Waste Production and Disposal

The World Bank’s Urban Development department estimates the amount of “municipal solid waste … will rise from the current 1.3 billion tonnes per year to 2.2 billion tonnes per year by 2025. Much of the increase will come in rapidly growing cities in developing countries” (“What a Waste…”). Despite the saliency of the topic in Nebaj and other growing cities, there are apparently no prior studies that have examined waste production in low-income communities in Latin America and the Caribbean (Martínez Arce et al.).

As more waste is produced, the question of waste disposal becomes increasingly important. For reasons unique to each location, up to 40 percent of the world’s trash may be burned (Thompson). Burning garbage emits greenhouse gases and smoke, which have negative impacts on both human health and the natural environment (WHO). Smoke often contains poisonous chemicals, heavy metals and other particulate matter that harm respiratory systems. Worldwide, ambient air pollution causes 4.2 million premature deaths per year (WHO). The negative health effects of smoke disproportionately affect young children, elderly and women (“Environment and Health Risks”). Though the environmental and health impacts of littering and burying trash may not be as immediate as that of burning, these acts pollute the environment in the long term, contributing to increased environmental contamination and disease (“2 Rubbish and disease”).

Approaching the La Pista Problem: Environmentalism and Trash Management in Low Resource Communities

Carter (2018) defines four common policy instruments for enacting environmental policy. Carter argues that “policy instruments should be enforceable, effective, and educative: they should change the behaviour of target groups, achieve the stated policy objectives and help spread environmental values throughout society” (332). Using the example of recycling, Carter describes how government investment is likely necessary to develop recycling infrastructure. Once physical structures—household recycling bins, collection trucks, and recycling plants—are in place, public voluntary action is required for the systems to be of use. However, for people to actually participate in recycling services, they first must know about them, so it is up to proponents of recycling to enforce voluntary participation with educative campaigning. Making changes in La Pista’s waste disposal habits would require similar community awareness in order to successfully utilize environmental policy to change behavior.

Andrew Dobson discusses the negative aspects of using an “information deficit” model to approach an environmental problem. An information deficit model assumes that people do not know that their actions harm the environment or that they do not know of more eco-friendly options (Dobson 70). Additionally, John Kretzmann and John P. McKnight lay out the theoretical structure for asset-based community development (ABCD), encouraging an understanding of the physical, associational, institutional, economical and individual assets in any given community before making assumptions about what is or is not known or being done (Kretzmann & Mcknight). Dobson’s critique of the information deficit model and Kretzmann and McKnight’s theories of ABCD influenced our approach because we were interested in the motivations of people in La Pista regarding our project above our own thoughts and priorities.

Dobson also argues that “poor people are often forced to degrade their environments in order to scratch a living, but out of sheer necessity they are often also the best stewards of their immediate environment because of their dependence on it for their livelihoods” (110). Approaching our project with this in mind allowed us to see that communities like La Pista often do have the drive to conserve their natural surroundings but are faced with challenges unique to poor areas (Gerber).

A study by Hettiarachchi et al. (2018) on waste management in Latin America also questions how the role of local governance in waste management systems impacts program efficiency. They suggest that “the governance aspects usually explain how society participates in and accomplishes complex tasks to achieve a common goal such as the [waste] management process, which includes many stakeholders because it is closely attached to day-to-day living of the population” (Hettiarachchi 2). Elias Azzi’s 2017 study on responses to Lebanon’s waste crisis similarly concludes that effective waste management requires involvement of all stakeholders, including localized actors and centralized collaboration (Azzi).

Background on La Pista

Since the start of the 21st century, Nebaj and many of its surrounding aldeas have grown quickly, causing a rapid increase in the production of inorganic trash. When we spoke to workers at the municipal dump, they told us that when the landfill was originally created, the edges of Nebaj and La Pista’s development were nowhere near the site. But now, houses are being built closer and closer to the disposal depot. As people produce more waste, the dump needs to expand, but housing developments encroach on potential expansion lands.

Before August 2018, La Pista did not have a public service to collect resident and business trash and deposit it to the municipal dump. Without that option, people burn or bury their trash, or they dump it in the woods, fields or river. In other locations, such methods have been found to negatively affect human health and the natural environment (Thompson, WHO). In La Pista, residents report that water outside their homes filters through drainage systems littered with trash, contaminating sources of drinking water.4 A report by the World Bank concludes that “improving solid waste management, especially in low income countries, is an urgent priority” because it is “arguably the most important municipal service and serves as a prerequisite for other municipal action.” (Hoornweg & Bhada-Tata 2012). We hope this project will contribute to a better understanding of ways to improve trash management systems at a micro level, using La Pista as a case example.

The last 15 years have seen rapid growth in Nebaj’s municipal population, and residents of La Pista, Guatemala have observed a rise in inorganic trash, especially plastic bags, bottles and packaged snack foods. According to Miguel and other community surveys, the rise in convenient plastic packaging, widely available in La Pista’s tiendas, has reduced the traditional use of organic and reusable materials, like leaves and woven baskets, to transport food and other items. Tiendas are the largest consumers and producers of inorganic, disposable waste in La Pista because of packaging and plastic bags, though most homes reported that they also accumulate their share of garbage. As inorganic waste production has increased, the need to invest in and organize trash management infrastructure has grown more urgent. Unfortunately, Nebaj’s municipal trash management planning has failed to keep up with the needs of its constituents. La Pista was facing a mutually reinforcing, two-fold problem including both environmental and policy challenges.

Prior to July 2018, La Pista had had three trash pickup events in which residents helped pick up trash from the streets, demonstrating a collective interest in environmental cleanliness and improved trash disposal options. But, because there had been no continued service, trash always returned to the streets, and people continued to burn, bury and litter.

While the larger Municipality of Nebaj has all the infrastructure for their own trash management system, there had been no coordination for managing the garbage of auxiliary villages like La Pista. The auxiliatura reported that they had attempted to contact the Muni about coordination for a service, but the Muni had been unresponsive. It is possible that coordinating with La Pista would have imposed an additional strain on municipal resources like truck drivers, gas and coordinating schedules, thus deterring Nebaj authorities from responding to La Pista’s requests for support.

It would have also been difficult for the private sector to take ownership for this project because of the high initial startup costs for entrepreneurs. In addition to a truck, an entrepreneur would also need public land for a dump and workers to sort through the trash. Thus, it would have been logistically difficult and expensive for La Pista entrepreneurs to begin this project without Muni support. Furthermore, the venture likely is not profitable enough to even pay off the additional investment, much less receive any sort of revenue, meaning there is virtually no profit incentive for an entrepreneur to assume the fiscal responsibility. Ultimately, it was important that a new system in La Pista be approved by Nebaj authorities and work within the municipal framework.

Intervention

Working with the local community organization Soluciones Comunitarias, we surveyed individuals in La Pista to learn that store and homeowners would be willing to pay for a truck service that would take their trash to the dump. Contrary to the information deficit model, the majority of people we spoke to in La Pista knew that burning trash was harmful and were aware that it would be ideal to consolidate and send their trash to an existing waste management facility such as the Nebaj dump, however they lacked basic trash management infrastructure create a service.

Soluciones Comunitarias held meetings with the community and the auxiliatura to discuss the plan for the trash collection program. Modeling it after the service that had previously been implemented in the main municipality of Nebaj, we met with the government of Nebaj and asked for infrastructural support for a new trash management system in La Pista. The mayor and his Health Commissioner agreed to allow La Pista to contract a municipal garbage truck to deposit their trash in the Nebaj dump, and we scheduled the first trash collection for August 16, 2018.

Leading up to the first collection, we worked with the La Pista auxiliatura to publicize the new service with the hopes that high participation would build momentum for the project to continue. On the morning of August 16th, people piled their trash on the edge of the soccer field in the center of town and paid the secretary of the auxiliatura their collection fee depending on how much they brought. One nylon bag cost Q1.5 In total, 71 participants (families, store owners, and individuals) brought their trash on La Pista’s first collection day.

For more information about the details of the intervention, including our project design process and justification, contact the authors for access to our case study, “Trash Management in La Pista, Guatemala” (Dunlevy & Pomp 2019).

From August to December, excluding November, there were monthly trash collections in La Pista, and the Nebaj Muni has commended La Pista leaders for their achievements and for setting an example for other aldeas. Even so, Muni scheduling issues have caused the program to falter regarding consistent monthly collection, causing a cancellation of the service in November.

The trash collection service in La Pista is an example of a voluntary action policy instrument that requires some level of government expenditure. The government must use the revenue from the service to contract the garbage truck, providing basic infrastructure and communicative signals regarding proper participation methods. However, it is up to the individual whether they pay for and participate in the service.

Methodology/Approach

Four months later, in December 2018, we returned to La Pista for two weeks to learn how the program was functioning and possible ways to improve the service. We considered the question: how has La Pista’s trash collection service developed over its first four months, and what are the community’s perceptions of it? More specifically, we wanted to know program participation numbers, what people’s motivations are to participate or continue to burn/bury their trash, and how people would like to see the system grow and improve.

We conducted three types of interviews with community authorities and leaders, the Health Center and La Pista residents. Questions for community authorities covered participation and general functioning of the program. We also interviewed the Health Center about their role in the project and the potential impacts of the program on the health of La Pista residents. Finally, we interviewed La Pista residents about their participation and their motivation for participating or not and asked for suggestions to improve the program.

We set out to answer these questions by first attending a meeting of community leaders. Later, we surveyed a worker at the Puesto de Salud (Health Center). By talking to authority figures, we gathered general information about the program’s progress.

We spent the majority of our field research time conducting community surveys. Over the course of two weeks, we used haphazard sampling to select survey participants. We walked around different areas of La Pista, knocking on doors and entering stores as we went, to get a sample size of 48 that represented La Pista geographically. Each day in La Pista, we surveyed in a different area. At each home or store we asked the name of the interviewee, asked permission to record the conversation, and conducted the survey, writing notes as necessary. We did not collect any demographic data such as age or gender, as we believed it would be invasive and culturally inappropriate given our position as foreigners. We also did not collect information on the family wealth, which could have been a useful indicator of program participation. Ultimately, we conducted 48 surveys in a town of 550 families. As such, our results may be unrepresentative of the larger population of La Pista.

Our haphazard sampling may also introduce bias into our results. For example, La Pista residents that were willing to talk to us might already value community participation and social service to a certain extent. Therefore, it is possible that people who said yes to an interview were already more inclined to use a social service such as a trash collection program.

Survey questions

Behavior

What does your family/this store do with its trash?

Do you know of the truck that comes to collect trash?

Have you used this service?

Do you bring your trash to the truck monthly?

What did you do with your trash before the service started in August?

Motivation

What is your reason for (not) participating?

Do you know of anyone who does not participate and why they do not participate?

Suggestions/Feedback

How do you know when the truck is coming?

Is the service easy to use?

Are there changes or additions that could be made to improve the service?

Cultural differences make it difficult to ask questions that are hypothetical or too abstract of people in La Pista. Answers to such questions are often either too short to be meaningful or difficult to extract without asking leading questions. For example, asking someone if they participate in community organizations or events might not extol a complete answer. A response might include school functions but exclude church or community gatherings that a family indeed attends. Also, asking someone to rate the trash collection service on a scale of 1-5 proved difficult because it was abstract, did not get at the qualitative information we were looking for and seemed in general to be an arbitrary and relative measurement for program evaluation.

Upon our return to the United States, we listened to our survey recordings and coded them according to the questions we asked and patterns that emerged in the answers.

Results

Due to our small sample size, we pooled survey answers from store owners and employees and residents.

I. Behavior

On collection days, the secretary of the auxiliatura records each participant in a notebook. Figure 1 shows program participation numbers according to the secretary’s notebook. Because we do not have exact population numbers for La Pista, we count participants by number. In addition, a “participant” can be a household, a store or business, and organization or an individual. According to the secretary, one possible explanation for the initial decline in program participation numbers is that when the garbage truck comes more frequently (i.e. once a month), people do not have as much inorganic waste to dispose of. Therefore, they will wait for the next month’s service. This suggestion seems plausible, but more exact data regarding how often the average person or business in La Pista produces enough trash to require disposal would be needed to support the idea.

40 respondents (83.33%) out of our sample of 48 reported that they had participated in the trash collection service at least once. We will call these 40 people “consistent users.” We were unable to determine, based on survey responses, if people had participated once, one-three times, or every time because survey respondents did not explicitly report behavior like, “I brought my trash to the truck in September but not in October.” We also believe it is possible people reported themselves as consistent users having unknowingly missed a service due to the inconsistent timing of the garbage truck service. Our survey potentially could have produced three groups of people–consistent users, inconsistent (one to three time) users, and nonusers–but our data does not identify any one-three time users. Therefore, we include anyone who reports having used the service as a “consistent user,” acknowledging that some of the 40 are likely inconsistent users. Failing to distinguish between consistent and inconsistent users likely skews our results because the rate of participation from our surveys greatly exceeds the rate of participation according to numbers reported the secretary of the auxiliatura. Thus, our record of consistent users is likely inflated when compared to the probable actual proportion of the population that participated.

II. Motivation

Of those 40, 57.5% said that they participated to protect or care for the environment. When coding, we considered desires to keep the streets and the community clean and prevent contamination as environmental protection. Table 2 shows participants’ reported motivations. Some participants mentioned motivations in more than one category, and some participants who reported participating had unclear reasons (shown in the “Unknown” column on the graph).

Health issues include concerns about smoke and dirty water. Some residents expressed concern that water filters through garbage in streams and gutters, contaminating drinking water sources or encouraging breeding of bugs and diseases. It is possible that sometimes residents who cited environmental protection as their motivation were implicitly evaluating the effects of environmental contamination on human health. For example, one store owner said, “It is better to use the truck because there [in the dump] they do not burn it [the trash…]. It is better not to burn because we know it contaminates the environment…. It is important [to care for the environment] because global warming is global. If we do not protect it, in the future it will affect the water, contaminate the soil, the trees, and even the animals.” We coded this response as “environmental protection,” although it is likely that the interviewee had human health in mind when speaking about soil and water contamination, However, we only coded a motivation as health when the interviewee specifically said they participate to protect people’s health. Taking this into consideration, our count of environmental protection motivations may be much higher than health, and all six people motivated by health and other reasons (the orange part of the health column) were also motivated by environmental protection.

If someone reported the authorities as their motivation, one of the reasons they participate is because the auxiliatura has told them to stop burning their trash and bring it to the truck. Other motivations included ease and the idea that “they know what to do with it [the trash]” at the dump.

Among non-participants, inconvenience was cited as a reason for not participating three times. One person said, “I only take out my trash, and there is a lot of it, and burn it. As I am old and very tired, it takes too much effort [to bring the trash to the collection site].” Coding for inconvenience also includes answers that burning trash is more convenient and the truck stop is too far away.

III. Suggestions/Feedback

Our surveys revealed a myriad of ideas for project improvement and expansion, including having someone collect people’s trash door to door rather than having everyone bring their trash to the field. Some wanted the truck to come more often and/or to have a fixed service date for each month. Others want to run capacitaciones (empowerment workshops) to show people why and how they should participate.

One participant involved placing public garbage cans in each sector of La Pista, an idea that had been discussed during the summer but not fully developed due to reservations about dogs and large deposits of trash in the interim periods when the truck has not yet come.

As we got further from the soccer field pickup location, we talked to a few residents who reported not knowing about the service. We recommend that the bocina more thoroughly advertise to residents further away from the central pickup location and possibly providing assistance for them to bring their trash such as subsidizing (or partially subsidizing) the cost of a tuk tuk (moto-taxi).

Analysis

We hypothesize that the trash collection service was successful because residents had previously demonstrated interest in seeing and motivation to make change in La Pista’s trash management practices. Three attempts to clean up La Pista were reportedly successful; all that was lacking was an initiative to create a sustained public trash collection service. When we interviewed residents in December, many articulated compelling reasons why they participated in the trash collection programs, ranging from environment to health, expressing personal investment in the project and belief in the benefits of participating. Additionally, there seems to be a strong sense of community responsibility among residents. As we walked around La Pista with Virgilio, it appeared as though most residents knew one another. They greet each other on the street and recognize each other in stores. La Pista also benefits from a strong leadership structure. Residents of La Pista are receptive to the auxiliatura’s authority and comply with La Pista rules and regulations.

Despite the many benefits of La Pista’s social and political structure, there are weaknesses in the trash collection service. One of the most fundamental weaknesses of the program is its dependence on the Nebaj Muni’s infrastructural coordination. The Mayor of La Pista scheduled a trash collection in November, but the Muni cancelled. In the summer, La Pista authorities directly asked us to meet with the Muni, as they believed that our presence as foreigners would encourage support and hasten action on the part of the Muni. Having foreigners carry out political communication like this is not necessarily the most sustainable way to build relationships, and if the Muni were ever to withdraw their support of the project, it would be quite difficult for La Pista authorities to continue the trash collection service. This potentiality seems less likely now, however, as the Muni has praised La Pista’s efforts.

Further research could investigate how community structure and participation influences program sustainability and effectiveness. It would also be prudent to explore La Pista’s political relationship with Nebaj. What are the sociopolitical effects of an aldea pursuing development projects outside of the Muni’s direct initiative? Over time, another opportunity could be an exploration of how La Pista’s trash management system could influence practices in other auxiliary aldeas of Nebaj.

Beyond Nebaj, surveys of other Guatemalan communities with varying governmental structures, public participation habits and trash management infrastructure to see what makes some programs more “successful” than others could be a significant contribution to waste management literature. For example, some developing cities are making concerted efforts to reduce inorganic waste production. In 2018, in San Pedro La Laguna, a Mayan village and rapidly growing tourist hotspot, the mayor Mauricio Méndez received approval to ban the sale and distribution of single-use, “disposable plastic bags, straws, and expanded polystyrene containers” (“This Mayan Village” 2018). Instead, residents of San Pedro La Laguna use palm leaf baskets and wrap meat in banana leaves, as one resident says her “grandmother used to do” (“This Mayan Village” 2018). Why has this policy been implemented there and not elsewhere in Guatemala?

Statement on Researcher Positionality

We are university students with limited time to travel to Guatemala. As a result, during both site visits we pushed to have trash collection days before we had to return to the States, pressuring local time customs and potentially affecting natural behavior. While it is difficult to parse out the effects of our direct influence on the project, for example whether the December trash collection service would have definitely occurred in December or been delayed until January, it is important to recognize that we certainly may have had such an unnatural effect. However, our positionality as outsiders also had benefits. We were able to genuinely ask questions about how things work in La Pista rather than making assumptions about what could or could not be done, enabling us to approach the problem with a more objective perspective. Also, we were able to schedule a meeting with the Mayor of Nebaj because of our relationship with Miguel. These advantages helped jumpstart the project, demonstrating potential positives of foreign intervention, although we do recognize foreign intervention’s weaknesses which we discuss in the section above.

Acknowledgments

Thank you to our faculty sponsor and advisor Dean Karlan, and to Kim Suiseeya for for providing additional feedback. We would also like to thank our local partners in Guatemala, Marta Verani, Katie Brickwood, Grace Galloway, Luke Burchell, and Greg VanKirk of SEC, CES, and Project X, SolCom and El Descanso staff, and our host families in Antigua and Nebaj. Thank you to Peter Civetta, Patrick Eccles, and Stephanie Marin for helping us return to Guatemala. And, of course, thanks to our GESI team–Jason Kwon, Andie Gomez-Patron, Evan Nixon, and Anamaria Sayre.

The study resulting in this publication was assisted by a grant from the Undergraduate Research Grant Program which is administered by Northwestern University’s Office of Undergraduate Research. However, the conclusions, opinions and other statements in this publication are the authors’ and not necessarily those of Northwestern University or its affiliated programming.

Village, or town.

La Pista, an Ixil community, is the Spanish name for Ak’ Txumbal. Ixil is the indigenous language of the Ixil people, who reside in three Guatemalan municipalities: Nebaj, Cotzal, and Chajul.

An auxiliatura is a mayorship of an auxiliary aldea in a municipality. In Nebaj, auxiliaturas are the de facto decision-makers for their respective aldeas, although the Nubaj Muni can technically override them. Mayors are called alcaldes, and another word for mayorship is alcaldía.

title: Personality Traits and the Narration of Spiritual Experiences among African American and White Adults in Late Midlife
abstract: For over a hundred years, psychologists have sought to understand the role of spirituality in human behavior and experience, and how it might relate to features of personality. This study considered personal narration of spiritual experience and how it relates to the personality traits of Openness to Experience, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Neuroticism. Over 400 narrative accounts of spiritual experiences given by mid-life adults (approximately half of whom were white and half African American) were analyzed and coded for themes of (1) Narrator Agency (NA), which tracks how participants describe their own efficacy and responsibility; (2) Spiritual Action/Intent (SA), which tracks how much participants attribute agency to spiritual beings; and (3) Spiritual Proximity (SP), which tracks how much participants view spiritual forces as omnipresent and accessible. Openness was positively associated with themes of NA, and negatively associated with SA.  Gender and race proved to be strong predictors of narrative themes, with men showing higher scores on narrative agency (NA) than women and African American adults scoring higher on spiritual action/intent (SA) and spiritual proximity (SP) than white adults.  After controlling for demographics, Extraversion predicted greater NA while lower Openness was associated with higher SA. Furthermore, themes of NA and SA were inversely related, which has implications for the importance of spiritual paradigms in understanding how people narrate their lives.
text:
Personality Traits and the Narration of Spiritual Experiences among African American and White Adults in Late Midlife

Ahmadu Simpson

Department of Psychology, Northwestern University

PSYCH 398: Senior Thesis Seminar

Dr. Dan McAdams

May 8, 2021

PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY 2

Abstract

For over a hundred years, psychologists have sought to understand the role of spirituality in human behavior and experience, and how it might relate to features of personality. This study considered personal narration of spiritual experience and how it relates to the personality traits of Openness to Experience, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Neuroticism. Over 400 narrative accounts of spiritual experiences given by mid-life adults (approximately half of whom were white and half African American) were analyzed and coded for themes of (1) Narrator Agency (NA), which tracks how participants describe their own efficacy and responsibility; (2) Spiritual Action/Intent (SA), which tracks how much participants attribute agency to spiritual beings; and (3) Spiritual Proximity (SP), which tracks how much participants view spiritual forces as omnipresent and accessible. Openness was positively associated with themes of NA, and negatively associated with SA.  Gender and race proved to be strong predictors of narrative themes, with men showing higher scores on narrative agency (NA) than women and African American adults scoring higher on spiritual action/intent (SA) and spiritual proximity (SP) than white adults.  After controlling for demographics, Extraversion predicted greater NA while lower Openness was associated with higher SA. Furthermore, themes of NA and SA were inversely related, which has implications for the importance of spiritual paradigms in understanding how people narrate their lives.

PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY 3

Personality Traits and the Narration of Spiritual Experiences

In The Varieties of Religious Experience, William James (1902) famously argued that religious sentiments are so distinct, profound, and universal that they can be considered a unique product of the human mind. Religiosity is expressed through institutional and social organizations, and it is a foundational motivator and emotional component in individuals’ lives.

According to James (1902), considering the motivational and emotional dimensions of religion illuminates why various life events can project a mystical or transcendent significance for some people, while they may seem entirely ordinary to others. In other words, the existence of personal religiosity means that humans have the capacity to experience life events and their associated emotions in one of two ways: as being transcendentally significant or not being so.

James suggested that religious emotional experience is, in many ways, similar to regular emotional experience on the behavioral surface, but religious emotions are always felt in relation to what the individual considers “divine.” This element of divinity causes religious sentiments— and religiosity more broadly—to adopt a tone of severity and urgency (which may be positive or negative in valence) that is not broadly characteristic of secular emotions or experiences.

Many psychologists today believe that religious experience is a natural feature of human life, perhaps unique to our species. Imparting religious significance on life experiences may be an evolutionary product of the human inclination to seek intent and meaning in random, unexplainable events (Bering, 2006; Willard & Norenzayan, 2013).  Religion also functions to bind people together into communities, promoting cooperation and solidarity within groups

(Wilson, 2002). It is clear that personal religious experiences and their associated emotions are widespread and persistent in nearly all contemporary societies. Even as conventional religious observance has waned somewhat in the United States and Europe in the past few decades, all

PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY 4 societies nonetheless showcase strong religious traditions, and billions of human beings today consider themselves to be “religious” and report personal experiences that have a religious or spiritual quality (Baker et al., 2016; Labbé & Fobes, 2009; MacDonald, 2000).

In the current study, we explore people’s narrative accounts of religious experience through a life-story approach (McAdams & McLean, 2013).  In the spirit of James’s (1902)

effort to document the varieties of religious experience, we aim to identify salient themes in different stories people tell about religious or spiritual experiences in their lives. In addition, we aim to discover links between the varieties of religious experiences people describe and their self-reported dispositional personality traits. In what ways do differences in people’s narrative accounts of religious experience map onto their basic traits? Can we predict specific variations in religious narratives from people’s particular trait profiles? In this study we seek to answer these questions and examine how race and gender influence individual differences in the narration of religious experience.

The Study of Spirituality and Religion in Psychology

In modern research, personal religious feelings and their interpretations have come to be broadly referred to as “spirituality,” as such experiences and emotions do commonly occur independent of conventional religion. Different researchers use different meanings for

“spirituality,” but the most common uses of the term are represented by a definition offered by

Baker and colleagues (2016), which defines spirituality as that which is related to a search for

“transcendent connection and sacred meaning.” This definition of spirituality is also very similar to James’s (1902) definition of religion, which he defines as “the feelings, acts, and experiences of individual men in their solitude, so far as they apprehend themselves to stand in relation to whatever they may consider the divine” (p. 31). James (1902) defines divinity quite broadly, but

PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY 5 for him—independent of religion or practice—it also refers to a grand quality of fundamental, transcendent, and all-encompassing interconnectedness and importance. In this study, I use

“spirituality” in place of James’s notion of “religion” in order to maintain specific emphasis on the personal relationship with the “divine” while keeping some distance from discussions of organized institutions and formal practices also denoted by the term “religion.”

James’s (1902) discussion of religiosity is also deeply concerned with the individual differences in spiritual experience and the unique qualities that differentiate spiritual emotions.

He believed that by guiding the way people seek sacred meaning and universal connection, organized religion functions as a powerful, emotive motivator that works uniquely in conjunction with an individual’s conception of the divine. Yet as important as certain emotional experiences may be to a person’s religiosity, it is only once these feelings interact with logical and cognitive factors—normally offered through doctrine or creeds—that religion fully gains its motivational power to guide various behaviors and decisions in daily life (James, 1902). Thus, many formalized aspects of organized religions ultimately become key components in how individuals consciously interpret their religious emotions or mystical phenomena.

James (1902) offered some preliminary illustrations of how varying individual dispositions create different patterns of spiritual experience and emotionality, exemplified by his

“healthy mind/sick soul” distinction. According to James (1902), people with a “healthy mind” are more inclined towards seeking religious experiences that validate and encourage connection to the world around them, which in turn promotes jubilant emotions and feelings of empowerment and acceptance associated with spiritual experiences. On the other hand, those with a “sick soul” are more inclined towards feelings of guilt and angst, so they more frequently seek salvation or an alleviation of internal suffering in their religious experiences.

PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY 6

James (1902) felt that a consideration of personal religious or spiritual accounts would provide the richest insights into the nature and causes of these divergent religious experiences.

He stressed the importance of individual accounts because spiritual experiences are necessarily individualized due to their ineffable and noetic qualities. These features of spiritual experience make them difficult to understand, communicate, or quantify for those who have not had them.

Furthermore, such experiences are transient and hard to induce intentionally, making it a difficult task to study these experiences and their associated sentiments in an objective laboratory setting

(James, 1902).

Nevertheless, psychologists have tried to undertake this task of studying spirituality by employing highly constrained and conventional methodologies. Most commonly, researchers have used self-report questionnaires designed to measure an individuals’ levels of spirituality according to various conceptual dimensions. Examples of these spirituality dimensions include

‘existential well-being,’ ‘cognitive orientation towards spirituality,’ and a tendency to accept paranormal beliefs (Hill & Pargament, 2003; MacDonald, 2000; Saroglou, 2002). Meta-analyses by Saroglou (2002) and MacDonald (2000) show that these, along with a litany of other measures, have been developed to differentiate certain aspects of religiosity, religious participation, and spirituality. Though it is common for researchers investigating the psychology of spirituality to define their own parameters and dimensions, there have been three distinct dimensions of religiosity which have enjoyed more widespread popularity and use: intrinsic, extrinsic, and quest-oriented religiosity (Allport, 1966; Batson, 1993; Saroglou, 2002, 2010).

First proposed by Allport (1966), the distinction between intrinsic and extrinsic religiosity describes different motivations for participating in religious practice. People who are intrinsically religious view connecting with the divine as an end in itself and are motivated by an

PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY 7 internal desire to understand their faith, live by their religion’s moral principles, and maintain a personal connection with the higher force at the center of their belief (Allport, 1966). People who are more extrinsically religious engage in religious practice as a means to procure external benefits such as an organized social alliance or securing basic life needs like food and shelter

(Allport, 1966).

Beyond intrinsic and extrinsic motivations for religiosity, Batson and colleagues (1983)

identified a third orientation, which they named quest religiosity. In quest religiosity, individuals view their religiosity as an ongoing search for truth or supreme meaning. They see spirituality as an adventure to be pursued over time. All of these motivations—intrinsic, extrinsic, and quest— may govern aspects of an individual’s personal religiosity or spirituality, and indeed a great deal of empirical research on spirituality has been organized around these concepts, especially in the field of social psychology (Blaine & Crocker, 1995; Jagers & Smith, 1996).

Religion, Spirituality, and Well-being

Several research studies and meta-analyses have found significant and consistent effects of religiosity on physical and psychological well-being.  Beyond The Varieties of Religious

Experience, research has consistently found that religiosity of any sort is a protective factor against mental illness and psychopathology, promoting positive coping strategies for dealing with negative life events, and predicting physical health benefits, too, likely through the promotion of healthy lifestyle habits. Studies have found that these benefits hold true across different age groups (Berry & York, 2011; Wink & Dillon, 2008), gender and ethnicity/race categories (Blaine & Crocker, 1995; Jagers & Smith, 1996), and different religious traditions

(Hill et al., 2000; Hill & Pargament, 2003). This line of research suggests that the internal and motivational features of religion are largely responsible for its associated health benefits. It may

PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY 8 also be true that the communal aspects of participating in organized religion promote some of these health benefits (Wink & Dillon, 2008), but the social elements of religious practice may not fully account for the tendency of some people to more frequently employ positive, spiritual- grounded coping strategies in their daily lives (Berry & York, 2011).

Indeed, some studies have found that intrinsic religiosity, rather than overall religiosity, is the feature of religion/spirituality primarily responsible for the positive association with well- being (Blaine & Crocker, 1995; Jagers & Smith, 1996). The internal and personalized experiences of religious belief and spiritual emotion offer benefits that ordinary experience and emotion do not. The association between intrinsic religiosity and associated health benefits seems to be especially strong for Black Americans (Jagers & Smith, 1996), who consistently report higher levels of both intrinsic and extrinsic religiosity than whites. African Americans, along with other members of the African diaspora, generally tend to view spirituality as being central to their personal and cultural identities as well as instrumental to much of what happens in ordinary life (Blaine & Crocker, 1995; Jagers & Smith, 1996). Black Americans are also more likely than white Americans to make spiritual attributions in their everyday lives, thereby more frequently inducing their own spiritual emotions and experiences, likely to the benefit of their own health.

Hill and Pargament (2003) argue that the relationship between intrinsic religiosity and well-being is driven by differences in attributional styles, which reflect profound qualitative differences in the spiritual frameworks people use to interpret life events—something James’s predicted with his healthy mind/sick soul distinction. Hill and Pargament (2003) propose that viewing religiosity as a cognitive schema helps explain the effects of different spiritual orientations on health. Cognitive schemas are mental representations of life events that help

PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY 9 people bridge gaps in knowledge or memory to better understand causality and derive meaning from various events (McIntosh, 1995). Therefore, a more intrinsically religious individual would be more likely to employ religiously grounded schemas when trying to understand events in their life and relate them to a divine will or process (Hill & Pargament, 2003). This is exactly what

Hill and Pargament (2003) found in their study, which reports that people who use religion or spirituality to enhance their connection to God, motivate their actions, and frame their individual or interpersonal struggles enjoy more of the psychological benefits associated with religiosity. A schematic implementation of religious belief is also consistent with earlier hypotheses that cognitive components of religious belief interact with one’s spiritual sentiments to motivate and justify behavior (James, 1902).

Employing a religious schema to explain a life event like personal failure or the unexpected loss of a loved one can help individuals attribute the causes of negative outcomes to fundamentally positive spiritual forces, helping people reframe their understanding of random or painful events. In this regard, Spilka and Schmidt (1983) found that people are more likely to make religious attributions in situations of greater importance and personal concern, especially those that are negative, potentially maximizing the benefits of religion as a coping mechanism.

Similarly, Chang and colleagues (2012, 2014) have found that perceptions of one’s own ability and self-efficacy mediate the spirituality–well-being relationship, suggesting that the mental health benefits of spiritual schemas are strongest when employed to help strengthen the perception of one’s own ability to succeed and overcome hardship.

In sum, psychological research into the effects of religiosity and spirituality show that they do serve a special function for the human mind and body by providing people with new schemas through which they can understand their lives and emotions and relate them to what

PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY 10 they believe to be sacred truths. Yet despite the robust benefits of spirituality on health, the nature of its effects varies greatly with the individual’s internal experience of spiritual phenomena and emotion. Thus, as useful as the extrinsic, intrinsic, and quest distinctions have been in organizing quantitative research, scholars have known since James (1902) that the qualitative differences in individual spirituality vary in ways beyond what is described by the motivational paradigm used in modern empirical research. More research is still needed, therefore, to document this variation and to understand what predisposes people towards qualitative differences in how they interpret life events through a spiritual framework.

Personality Traits

Due to the deeply personal and idiosyncratic nature of spiritual experience, the present study aims to examine personal spirituality by analyzing people’s unique narrations of spiritual experiences. This study also aims to examine how dispositional personality traits relate to the characteristic manner in which people narrate these kinds of experiences.  Because intrinsic religiosity is strongly related to an internal tendency to recognize divine or spiritual influence on various aspects of life (Blaine & Crocker, 1995; Hill & Pargament, 2003), we expect that dispositional traits related to intrinsic religiosity will correspond to narratives which portray spiritual or divine forces embodying a more active and normative role in their lives.

Additionally, we expect that dispositional traits related to greater mental-well-being and self- confidence will be associated with narratives that portray spiritual forces which aid and strengthen the self, consistent with findings on the link between perceived self-efficacy, spiritual attributions, and well-being (Berry & York, 2011; Blaine & Crocker, 1995; Chang et al., 2012;

2014).

PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY 11

This study draws on the Five Factor Model of personality (FFM) to assess variation in dispositional traits. The FFM is a widely adopted framework for understanding and distinguishing broad personality differences (McCrae & Costa, 2008). The five traits which comprise the FFM are Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Neuroticism, and

Openness to Experience. Agreeableness captures tendencies toward being compassionate, cooperative, trusting, and compliant, versus their opposites (e.g., lack of compassion, distrustfulness, aggression), while Conscientiousness taps into variation on dimensions of orderliness, industriousness, responsibility, and self-control (John, 2021). Extraversion is about dominance, assertiveness, sociability, and positive-emotionality (John, 2021). Neuroticism measures negative emotionality, emotional instability, and lower self-esteem (John, 2021).

Finally, Openness assesses the overall tendency to seek novel stimuli and engage in fantastical or imaginative thinking, as well greater intellect and cognitive flexibility (John, 2021).

Psychologists have already begun to investigate the relationship between these traits and religiosity using empirical studies that quantify trait personality levels and various aspects of religiosity using self-report questionnaires. The most consistent findings to date have been strong associations of both Agreeableness and Conscientiousness with religiosity (Saroglou, 2002).

Two meta-analyses by Saroglou (2002, 2010) and one by McDonald (2000) found that higher levels of Agreeableness and Conscientiousness consistently correlate with higher levels of general religiosity, intrinsic religiosity, religious fundamentalism, and spirituality.

A potential explanation for these associations may be that since Agreeableness is related to being trusting and compliant, it may also predispose people to be more likely to trust and comply with the authority of a more powerful and knowledgeable spiritual being (Labbé &

Fobes 2009; Womble et al., 2013). However, this explanation is premised on the predominantly

PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY 12

Christian population used for these studies, who may be more likely to view the divine as a willful figure to be obeyed. Likewise, it may be true that people who are higher in

Conscientiousness may be more likely to adhere to the standards of behavior associated with their spiritual belief system, including participating in prayer services, following certain lifestyle customs, and trying to maintain a personal connection with spiritual beings (Labbé & Fobes

2009; Womble et al., 2013).

Extraversion and Neuroticism also relate to religiosity and spirituality, though these relationships are found less frequently and often show weaker associations (Beitel et al., 2004;

Labbé & Fobes 2009; MacDonald, 2000; Saroglou, 2002, 2010; Womble et al., 2013). In fact, the associations that have been found between religiosity and Extraversion and religiosity and

Neuroticism are almost opposite to one another. Extraversion correlates positively but weakly with intrinsic religiosity and a cognitive tendency towards spirituality (MacDonald, 2000;

Saroglou, 2002), but Neuroticism only correlates positively with extrinsic religiosity (Saroglou,

2002). Furthermore, research into the effects of spirituality on stress response and existential well-being has found that Neuroticism is often negatively associated with these benefits of spirituality, though it remains unclear whether this is because highly neurotic people less frequently employ spiritual schemas or because less spiritual people are more likely to have difficulty coping with existential stress and thus exhibit increased neuroticism (Labbé & Fobes

2009; MacDonald, 2000; Womble et al., 2013). On the other hand, these same studies have found that Extraversion is positively associated with the mental-health benefits of spirituality, which may be due to Extraversion’s role as a protective factor because of its connection to positive emotionality and greater self-confidence (Labbé & Fobes 2009; Smillie et al., 2019;

Womble et al., 2013).

PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY 13

With respect to Openness to Experience, the most consistent finding is that Openness is negatively associated with intrinsic, extrinsic, and fundamentalist religiosity, but it is positively associated with quest religiosity (Saroglou, 2002; 2010). People who are higher in Openness are generally more attracted to more complex and abstract ideas (John, 2021), which may explain why they are more to engage with religiosity an inquisitive and curious manner, associated with quest religiosity (Saroglou, 2002). Other findings relating spirituality to Openness are slightly more varied, but a meta-analysis by MacDonald (2000) has found that Openness correlates with a greater tendency to believe in paranormal or supernatural phenomena, as well as a greater tendency to emphasize the experiential elements of spiritual belief. These findings are also consistent with a finding by McAdams and colleagues (2004) that people higher in Openness tend to give more complex narrative accounts of life experiences that include descriptions of unusual or fantastical experiences and sensations. Fantastical and ineffable sensations are also a common component of mystical experiences as noted by William James (1902), so it may be that spiritual people higher in Openness are more likely to accept these types of sensations and incorporate them into a spiritual framework.

Narrative Accounts

In order to investigate how individuals describe the presence and influence of divine forces in their lives, this study will analyze narrative accounts given in response to one section of the Life Story Interview (LSI) dealing with a spiritual, mystical, or transcendent experience. The

LSI was used as part of McAdams and Guo’s (2015) longitudinal study of personality and narrative identity in midlife adults (see also, Manczak, Zapata-Gietl, & McAdams, 2014). One advantage of using autobiographical narratives to study spirituality is that it allows researchers to focus on the internal and personal components of spiritual or religious belief. In the responses

PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY 14 given to the LSI, participants are encouraged not only to describe a spiritually significant event but also to discuss their emotional reactions and interpretations of the event. These added elements of narration can better help researchers understand the varying nature of religious—or spiritual—sentiment in different people, beyond simply measuring their degree of adherence to certain spiritual or religious beliefs.

Another benefit of a narrative approach is that it allows researchers to more easily track how adults describe divine influence in relation to themselves, which is understood to be an important component of the link between spirituality and psychological well-being (Berry &

York, 2011; Blaine & Crocker, 1995; Chang et al., 2012; 2014; James, 1902). Agency is considered one of two primary motivational themes in autobiographical narratives (McAdams,

1996), and is reflected in the way people describe intentionally and effectively initiating change in their lives according to their own goals and motivations (Adler, 2012). Tracking how individuals narrate their own agency in the context of a spiritually significant event allows us to directly observe how and when spiritual schemas are invoked in reference to the self, and whether they describe a strengthening or pacifying impact of divine intervention (Berry & York,

2011; Blaine & Crocker, 1995; Chang et al., 2012; 2014).

The autobiographical narratives used in this study are excerpts of transcribed responses to the LSI used in McAdams and colleagues’ Foley Longitudinal Study of Adulthood (FLSA:

McAdams & Guo, 2015). The FLSA was a nine-year study of personality and narrative identity in midlife adults, where participants, initially aged between 55 and 57, were asked to describe key scenes from their lives three times over the course of nine years. As part of participation, participants also completed a series of self-report measures, including the NEO-FFI, a valid and reliable questionnaire used to measure dispositional personality according to the FFM. For this

PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY 15 study, I focus on each participants response to the section of the interview in which they are asked to narrate key spiritual, mystical, or transcendent experiences. Since participants were asked to discuss such experiences all three times they completed the LSI, data from the all three interviews are analyzed and aggregated in order to create the most robust assessment of how adults narrate spiritual experiences. Then I compare these scenes with FFM personality traits for each participant taken form their NEO-FFI scores.

Because of previous research that finds both Agreeableness and Conscientiousness predict intrinsic religiosity, which is associated with a greater personal adherence to spiritual or religious frameworks (Blaine & Crocker, 1995), I hypothesize that (1) participants higher in

Agreeableness will be more likely to describe divine or spiritual forces that actively and normatively influence their lives, and participants higher in Conscientiousness will also be more likely to exhibit this tendency. I also examine how much participants describe themselves as exhibiting agency, which is strongly linked with well-being (Adler et al., 2008) and is associated with dominance and self-confidence, both of which are positively linked with Extraversion and inversely with Neuroticism (Ghaed & Gallo, 2006). Since spirituality seems to aid well-being through attributions that enhance a sense of personal responsibility (Blaine & Crocker, 1995)

while externalizing blame for failure and hardship (Spilka & Schmidt, 1983), I hypothesize that

(2) participants higher in Extraversion will be more likely to describe spiritual experiences that emphasize their personal agency, while participants lower in Neuroticism will be more likely to emphasize their own agency.

Finally, because of the finding that people higher in Openness narrate more elaborative and fantastical personal experiences (MacDonald, 2000; McAdams, 2004), and because of its negative relationship to religious fundamentalism (Saroglou, 2002; 2010) I hypothesize that (3)

PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY 16 participants higher in Openness to Experience will give narrative accounts that describe divine or spiritual forces as more fluid, flexible, and accessible.

Method

Participants

The participants in this study were the 164 adults who took part in the Foley Longitudinal

Study of Adulthood, aged between 55 and 57 years old. Participants were recruited from the greater Chicago area in Illinois to participate in a study, a majority of whom were female (63.6

% female, 36.4% male), and slightly more than half of whom were White (55%). The rest predominantly identified African American (43% African American, 1% interracial, 1%

“other”). There was significant variation of annual household incomes among participants, ranging from a minimum of under $25,000 a year to a maximum of over $300,000 a year, with the median household income falling between $75,000-$100,000 a year. A large majority of the sample had at least some college education: 44% had some graduate education, 24% graduated college, 27% had some college education, and 5% had only a high school diploma.

Materials

The materials and data used in this study were taken from Foley Longitudinal Study of

Adulthood with the permission of Dan McAdams, the lead researcher in the study. This study worked with a specific section of the LSI dealing with spiritual experiences, which was administered as part of the FLSA. These scenes (S/T scenes) asked participants to describe as spiritual or transcendent moment using the prompt:

“The next question is a religious, spiritual or mystical experience. Whether they are religious or not, many people report that they have had experiences in their lives where

PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY 17 they felt a sense of the transcendent or sacred, a sense of god or some almighty or ultimate force or a feeling of oneness with nature, the world or the universe. Thinking back on your entire life, please identify an episode or moment in which you felt something like this.  It may be an experience that occurred within the context of your religious tradition if you have one, or it may not be connected to religion at all, and it may be a spiritual or mystical experience of any kind.  Please describe this transcendent experience, where and when, who was involved.”

This prompt was used all three times the LSI was administered, during the first, fifth, and ninth years of the FLSA. Here I refer to the first year of the FLSA study as Time 1, the fifth year as

Time 5, and the ninth as Time 9. In order to develop a more robust picture of the what narrative themes are typically included in response to this section, and how they related to personality, this study analyzed responses from all three times the LSI was administered.

Participants also completed a small battery of self-report questionnaires, including the

NEO-FFI-3, which is an abridged version of the NEO personality inventory with generally accepted validity (Guo, Klevan, & McAdams, 2016). The scores on the NEO-FFI-3 indicate the degree to which participants exhibit each of the traits from the FFM. The NEO-FFI contains 60 items, each of which is phrased as a statement about the self to which participants must indicate how much they agree or disagree using a five-point scale (1=strongly disagree; 5=strongly agree). Each of the big five personality traits is measured by set of twelve specific items on the

NEO-FFI, meaning each item corresponds only to one trait. Responses to the twelve items for each trait were used to provide an overall score for that trait, with higher scores indicating that the survey’s respondent exhibits higher levels of that personality trait (Guo et al., 2016). Given

PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY 18 the prior evidence that personality traits are relatively stable in the later stages of adult life (John,

2021), this study only considered data from the responses given at Time 1 of the FLSA.

Procedure

As the first step in deriving thematic categories for the data, I read the S/T scenes from

Times 1 and 5 in order to understand how participants described the experience of spiritually or religiously significant events in their lives. Three major themes were identified relating to how participants characterize spiritual influence, the relationship between spiritual influence and personal action, and the fluidity and omnipresence of spiritual beings. In order to codify how these themes are discussed by each participant, I developed coding schemes using five-point scoring systems in order to quantitatively describe differences in spiritual narration. This approach then allowed for direct comparison of the prominence of these narrative themes with personality data, which has been quantified using the scores on the NEO-FFI-3.

Establishing Interrater Reliability for the Coding Systems

The Spiritual Action/Intent and Spiritual Proximity schemes were developed specifically for the purposes of this study, while the Narrator Agency scheme was merely adapted from a preexisting for use with the S/T scenes. As part of the development of these coding systems, and second coder used the coding systems to score the S/T scenes independently of the primary coder. Initially, 20 of the S/T scenes from Time 1 were coded together by both coders in order to develop the specificity and precision of the coding schemes. Then, five groups of 10 - 15 narratives from Time 1 were coded by each coder independently, and after each round, scores were compared and discussed, and the coding schemes were adjusted for clarity and specificity to achieve more coding consistency and reliability. Afterwards, the rest of the of the Time 1 narratives—roughly half—were coded independently by both coders, and once all Time 1

PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY 19 narratives had been coded twice, all scores completed independently were compared using a

Pearson’s correlation coefficient to establish interrater reliability. The S/T scenes from Times 5 and 9 were only coded by the primary coder.

Spiritual Action/Intent (SA). The Spiritual Action/Intent system was designed to measure whether participants narrate divine or spiritual influence as more active or passive.

Spiritual causality was scored on a 5-point scale (0 – 4), where higher scores correspond to S/T scenes in which spiritual forces are narrated as actively and intentionally influencing the lives of participants. Lower scores corresponded to scenes in which spiritual forces are described as passive or inactive, and the minimum score of 0 was reserved for scenes that attribute no spiritual influence.

The application of the Spiritual Action/Intent scale followed a similar logic for scoring as that of Adler’s (2012) scale for codifying narrator agency, which is discussed in more detail below. This decision was made since some psychologists theorize that humans are innately predisposed to imagine spiritual beings as agentic actors because of our ability to understand and infer the intentions behind the action of others, referred to as the Theory of Mind (TOM) (Bering

2006; Willard & Norenzayan, 2013). Furthermore, many religions do describe divine forces which act intentionally to bring about a specific goal or divine order (James, 1902). Therefore, according to the TOM, if humans invoke the TOM to understand spiritual influence, then they will likely describe spiritual or divine action in a way which mirrors the way they describe human action. The reliability for this scale, containing 139 items, was acceptable (r = .63).

Narrator Agency (NA). The Narrator Agency system was developed so that we can track the way participants describe the relationship between spiritual forces and their own ability to act and affect change. Agency is a common motivational theme used in narrative research,

PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY 20 which relates to how much the participant believes in the efficacy of her own abilities and attributes outcomes to her own intentional actions (McLean et al., 2020). Highly agentic narratives emphasize the protagonist’s autonomy and ability to achieve success primarily through one’s own efforts, while narratives low in agency often attribute outcomes to external causes or factors (McLean et al., 2020). The coding scheme used for this study was a 5-point scale (0 – 4), with 0 given to responses that describe the protagonist as exhibiting practically no agency, and 4 given to responses that depict highly agentic protagonists. The reliability for this scale suggests the adjustments made to fit this study may have limited used elsewhere (139 items; r = .41)

Spiritual Proximity (SP). The Spiritual Proximity scale was used to codify the degree to which participants describe divine or spiritual forces as omnipresent and accessible. Spiritual

Proximity will be scored according to five-point scale (0 – 4). Higher scores will correspond to narratives that depict spiritual forces which can commonly interact directly through ordinary people or are inextricably linked to ordinary life. A narrative with a higher score in the Spiritual

Proximity scale may include more descriptions of personalized contact with spiritual forces (e.g.

a participant believes Jesus spoke with him directly) and specific sensations related to the interaction with spiritual beings. Lower scores were given to scenes in which the divine or spiritual forces were narrated as more rigid, localized, and inaccessible to ordinary people. A minimum score of 0 was reserved for scenes that do not describe any spiritual influence or event.

Results

For the narrative themes of Narrator Agency, Spiritual Action, and Spiritual Proximity, participant’s scores for each coding scale were averaged across Times 1, 5, and 9. A second coder provided independent scores for all coding scales at Time 1, which were combined with the first coder’s scores and then an average was taken for Time 1.

On average, across all time points, participants tended to narrate spiritual experiences with slightly more emphasis on their own agency (NA: M = 2.16, SD = .70), while also being slightly more likely to attribute events and experiences to the deliberate action of spiritual forces or beings (SA: M = 2.19, SD = 1.10). A Pearson’s correlation coefficient revealed an inverse relationship between the tendency to emphasize one’s own agency and an inclination to emphasize the presumed agency of spiritual beings. The correlation coefficient for this relationship is displayed in Table 2. Participants were also somewhat more likely to describe spiritual beings and forces as accessible or proximal to the ordinary world (SP: M = 2.73, SD =

1.00). A Pearson’s test revealed a significant relationship between the themes of Spiritual Action

(SA) and Spiritual Proximity (SP), indicating that the inclination to narrate spiritual beings as proximal and accessible was strongly associated with a tendency to describe such beings as more deliberate and agentic. The correlation coefficient for this relationship, as well as those for SP and Narrator Agency (NA) are shown in Table 2.

On average, women’s narrative accounts were richer in themes of spiritual

3.99, p < .001), SA (t(157) = 2.46, p < .05), and NA (t(157) = -2.71, p < .01) were all significant.
