More women than men voting for SI is not surprising given past trends in which women were more likely to align themselves with conservative values and the marianismo-inspired rhetoric from the regime that praised women for serving their country only in domestic spaces. Overall, however, the power of female electoral participation both in and outside the voting booth was key to the NO victory.

Another way gender stereotypes and politics intertwined during this period is evident in how women were physically represented in the campaigns. In primary documents cited for this analysis, the physical representation of women focused mostly on superficial traits such as physical appearance or generalizing women as mothers. This narrow focus worked to appeal to the “common” woman seeing themselves in the advertisements, to the hopes of those who wanted the idyllic, beautiful future promised by the NO campaign, and to women who wanted to secure safety for their children via the SI campaign. Though each campaign took a different approach, for the most part gender stereotypes for how women should only care about their families and what the “ideal” women should look like were a common theme throughout the campaign process.

The NO campaign presented more women in their video spots instead of in specific, female-targeted pamphlets or posters. In general, the NO campaign franjas have been hailed as impressive achievements in advertising, packaging democracy essentially as a sellable product

Gail 21 with catchy jingles and attention grabbing, humorous shorts. The video franjas, namely the 47 music video for “La alegria ya viene” (the main song of the campaign, “Happiness is Coming”), featured a variety of Chileans in various, everyday situations. According to one of the creators of the campaign, “given the predominance of discursive and rhetorical messages coming from the ruling leadership, it was essential that the sources of information and the actors of the events were the ordinary people, the citizen, the man, the woman or the youth of the popular sectors...whose opinions have never been taken into account by TV”. In this presentation, 48 however, like most advertisements, the campaign ensured those chosen were still physically attractive and representative of the idyllic future they were trying to sell. David Hojman describes how women were physically presented in the NO campaigns as follows:

In the NO ads, women were never portrayed as they usually are in soap powder ads, in traditional female roles, as dutiful mothers and housewives. The NO program makers seemed to be working on the assumption that Chilean women, at least in the key audience groups they wanted to address, hated to be cast into conventional gender stereotypes.

Viewers were shown the real-life mothers or wives of victims of human rights abuses; for example, female relatives of the dead or the disappeared were seen dancing a haunting cueca, the national dance "of women alone." But apart from them, women were always presented as active and fun-loving (aerobic dancers, horse riders), intelligent (Liliana

Mahn, Moy de Toha, and several actresses), and taking the initiative. In a NO comic sketch, a woman warmly and tenderly encourages her man to do something. Her tone, both their attitudes, and everything else suggests that she is after an improved sexual

48Arturo C. Navarro, La Campaña Del NO Vista Por Sus Creadores (Ensayos), (CIS, 1988), 114. (My translation).

47David E. Hojman, “YES or NO to Pinochet: Television in the 1988 Chilean Plebiscite,” Studies in Latin American Popular Culture 11 (January 1992): 171.

Gail 22 performance on his part, but actually she is really encouraging him to say NO. Two of the four flag-carrying riders in the video "La alegria esta en marcha" ["Happiness Is on the

March"] were women. A demonstration of women in front of an army regiment headquarters, singing “it changes, everything changes,” and offering carnations to the soldiers, was also shown . 49

Though Hojman cites a variety of skits and videos from the month long franja campaign, all are consistent with the assumption that Chilean women did not want to be simply boxed in as typical housewives. This point in the campaign ads is subtle and not obviously stated, yet the shot variety and repetition continually reinforces these ideas of female empowerment and autonomy for the viewer.

However, one Chilean newspaper article reviewing the first few franjas noted that the NO spots included “near perfect frames, blonde and brown faces mixed with a specific attractiveness

(that differed from the series of dazed women that were marching...in part of the Sí program”.50

In the writer’s view, the intentional attractiveness of those in the spot does not go unnoticed, especially in contrast to those in the SI. Similarly, a poster that is unaffiliated with a group other than being positive towards the NO continues this objectivization of women. The poster contains various cartoon drawings of a scene with situations all involving the word “no”. The drawing in the forefront of this scene is a group of men following behind a cartoon woman (one man is even drooling while staring at her behind). The woman has a “no” sticker on her breast and is waving her finger, a speech bubble declaring “NO” is drawn out of her mouth. It is suggested she is 51

51Poster, “NO”, 1988, Iconografía, Antonio Bascuñan Collection, Biblioteca Digital of the Museo de la Memoria y los Derechos Humanos, Santiago, Chile.

50“Defectos y virtudes de los primeros programas de Sí y del No en TV,” La Segunda, September 6, 1988, http://30mas.cl/defectos-y-virtudes-de-los-primeros-programas-de-la-franja (My translation).

49Hojman, 171.

Gail 23 telling the men off for ogling at her. Here, the objectiviation of this woman is used for humor, as a caricature of situations in which someone would say no. This cartoon woman has no other purpose than just being a conventionally attractive object. The surface level focus in these documents is an example of how women are often described solely by their physical appearance rather than their contributions, as objects for men to critique and admire.

Other presentations of women in the

NO franjas are less superficial but still emotionally riveting. For example, one spot with women who had a loved one disappeared by the regime dance “La cueca sola”, a national dance of Chile usually performed with a partner. However, these women are dancing alone to symbolize their loss. The women here are grouped by their shared trauma, reminding the 52 general population of the atrocities committed by the dictatorship. Various Chilean (and even

American) celebrities appear in some spots, using their celebrity status to “sell” their product of democracy. These celebrity women included Chilean actresses, political figures (or family 53 members of political figures) and artists, all discussing their reasons for voting “NO” or explaining why they have turned away from supporting the regime.

53“Franja del SI y del NO- Capítulo 26,” September 30, 1988, http://30mas.cl/franja-30-de-septiembre (my translation).

52“Franja de SI y del NO- Capítulo 5,” September 9, 1988, http://30mas.cl/franja-9-de-septiembre

¡¡NO[illegible]

¡NO!

¡NO puedo!

DECIDASE POR... NO-"BIS"

Dile que NO perica

¡NO!

EL NOTICIERO NO

Figure 2. “NO” from the Antonio Bascuñan Collection of the MMDH Library

Gail 24

Overall, the video franjas of the NO campaign presented women through traditional advertising techniques such as celebrity appearances and showcasing traditionally attractive,

“everyday” women as well as highlighting certain groups who had been affected by the traumas of the dictatorship in order to appeal to a wide range of Chileans. Having women presented not just as mothers but simply Chilean citizens is how the NO campaign moved away from reinforcing gender stereotypes put in place by the regime and toward a more inclusive future, even if some spots relayed traditional conventions of beauty and male objectification.

The SI campaign’s presentation of women in both their franjas and other propaganda materials revolved around the idea of women solely as mothers, as one bloc that only cared about family issues. In one campaign poster, photos of Pinochet with adoring women and children are placed around text declaring, “Women say YES, yes to the future, yes to the family, yes to progress, yes to Pinochet, yes to peace, yes to Chile”.54

Another SI poster has photos of a family (mother, father and six children)

above the caption “Chile begins in YOUR family” surrounded by a border of the SI logo and the phrase “Yes to your family, to your Chile”. These 55 photographs group women into one collective that seemingly only cares about family issues, insinuating Pinochet is a true defender of the family.

The phrase “Chile begins in your family” in the second poster also presents women as the first line of naturalization for Chilean children—a good

Chilean mother will raise their children to respect and love their country, and by extension the Pinochet regime.

55Poster, “Chile comienza en tu familia,” 1988, Iconografía, Antonio Bascuñan Collection. (My translation).

54Poster, “Las mujeres chilenas dicen SI”, 1988, Iconografía, Antonio Bascuñan Collection. (My translation).

LAS MUJERES DICEN SI

Sí al Futuro Sí al Progreso Sí a la Paz

Sí a la Familia Sí a Pinochet Sí a Chile

Figure 3. “Las mujeres chilenas dicen SI” from the Antonio Bascuñan Collection of the MMDH Library

Gail 25

Outside of posters, the SI franjas also include women in a few of their spots, though not at the level and representation of the NO franjas. The spot that aired on September 29th is a strong example of two ways in which the franjas physically presented women. The ads begin with what appears to be a reporter interviewing folks at a pro-SI rally, asking them who will win the plebiscite. More women than men are shown in these interviews, spanning various ages, and all of them express confidence in a SI victory. Mixed in with these public questions are staged interviews of women also declaring their support for SI. In one, the scene opens with a woman stirring something in a pot, then she looks up and notices the cameras, introducing herself as a housewife, “as you all can see”. Her on-camera presence is not as strong as an accomplished 56 actor would be, yet she still delivers her message that life with Pinochet is considerably better than with Salvador Allende, since now she does not have to wait in long lines just to buy bread and other necessities. A shopkeeper in another interview also remembers the long lines under

Allende to purchase simple products, and wants things to stay the way they are because “how we are is fantastic”. These women as housewives, shopkeepers and excited citizens interviewed 57 publicly are presented as a reminder for all watching that Pinochet is the right choice for Chile, insinuating a vote for NO would be a return to hardships. The women formally interviewed put it more explicitly; Pinochet saved a disintegrating Chile from Allende and now the country is better than ever. Here, the regime connects NO with governments of the past, using the presence of these women as physical reminders of life under Allende. Women are presented not as ordinary citizens, but as mothers and providers who defend their household and support Pinochet given he makes this task safer and easier for them to carry out.

57 Resumen de testimonios ciudadanos de la Franja del SI y del NO,” September 19, 1988. (My translation).

56 “Resumen de testimonios ciudadanos de la Franja del SI y del NO,” September 19, 1988, http://30mas.cl/franja-29-de-diciembre-testimonios-ciudadanos. (My translation).

Gail 26

Overall, the physical presentation of women in the NO campaign focused on women as citizens of a new, energetic future, rather than perpetuating discriminatory gender roles claiming they must only be wives and mothers. They did, however selectively use women who were conventionally attractive; this choice reinforces other gender stereotypes about what men consider to be desirable in females. The women presented in the SI campaigns were often relegated to their status as caregivers, mothers and as living reminders of the past they were trying to avoid. They also represented the tradition of Chilean women voting more conservatively when presenting women who were decidedly anti-Allende and were affected by his presidency. This selective presentation reiterates stereotypes of women as obedient, morally pure, and as champions for an idealistic, non-radicalized future as propagated by marianismo and the discourse of the Pinochet regime.

The intentional targeting of women by the advertisements and campaign materials from both the SI and NO campaigns is yet another way gender roles played a part in this vote. The materials used by the two campaigns had different overall aims and structures, however, both strongly appealed to women as mothers by emphasizing what each campaign could do for the future of Chile and the future of the family. The idea of presenting women solely as mothers and caretakers as established above is now taken a step further with campaigns and political groups explicitly appealing to what marianismo claims women should care about: the security and well-being of their families above all else.

One of the main tactics of the SI campaign used was to present fear and reminders of the past, such as product scarcity under Allende and lack of childcare resources, to convince voters that Pinochet was the secure choice for a better future. They often falsely painted the NO

Gail 27 campaign, communists and other far-left groups as extremely dangerous and violent individuals.

This fear mongering was then used to communicate to women, the saintly protectors of the home and family, that they must vote for Pinochet and save their families from disintegration. The SI campaign also presented some of the positive things Pinochet had done for the family as reasons to continue supporting his regime. One poster with a drawing of a smiling woman wearing a SI button holding her thumb up contains the text “And what is happening today? Numerous open centers and daycare centers exist to care for, nurture and educate your children while you work.

For these reasons, vote YES”. Another pamphlet drawing features an armed soldier in the 58 foreground and a family standing in the background next to a house and Chilean flag. The caption of the page says “Thanks to the armed forces for caring for the future of our children”.59

One pro-SI cartoon has a black and white drawing of an apartment building on the left side of the page where on each floor is a figure, smiling and cutting a hole in the ceiling with a saw. This hole is directly underneath the person above them, so it seems all will fall through when the sawing is done. On the right side of the page is a bright, colorful drawing of a happy looking family: a smiling mother with an apron, two young kids with backpacks and a male figure at the door. The text of this cartoon says, “to vote NO is to give space to hate and ambition, without respecting your fellow man...to vote YES is to continue in peace; it is a sure path; it is living better”. This comparison the world of the NO to that of the SI paints the NO as selfish and 60 hateful, drawn in dark colors. In contrast, the SI world is colorful and glowing, presenting the

60Pamphlet, “Votar NO Votar SI”, 1988, CLMMDH 659-03-01, Ana Cobos Sater Collection, Museo de la Memoria y los Derechos Humanos, Santiago, Chile. (My translation).

59Afiche, “Gracias! a las FF.AA., 1983-1988,” Archivo Fotográfico y Digital, PF-0338, Biblioteca Nacional de Chile, Santiago, Chile. (My translation)

58Photograph, “Y qué ocurre hoy?, 1988,” Archivo Fotográfico y Digital, PF-0042-b, Biblioteca Nacional de Chile, Santiago, Chile. (My translation).

Gail 28 image of a peaceful, smiling, nuclear family in the SI universe. Even a simple matchbox is adorned with a message from the SI campaign that claims, “we have always wanted chilean families to have continually better health, better housing, better well being”. This phrase on the matchbox explicitly connects the 61 government to the family, insinuating that Pinochet’s patriarchal government structure has always cared for the health and best interests of Chile’s families. These examples demonstrate how the SI collective relied on fear and their continued relegation of women to domestic roles in order to court their vote, claiming this regime was the only way to protect Chile’s families and prevent a return to chaos.

This tactic of appealing to female voters by referencing families and family safety is also found in the television franjas. One spot starts with a sleeping baby and a voiceover explaining to the child that “this country is yours” and it is the adult’s job to protect the child so they “will grow up in peace” with Chile at their side. In the same franja, an unnamed female reporter in a conversation about how children need peace and security to grow up and thrive notes “the

61Matchbox, “Caja de fósforos Si”, 1988, CLMMDH 1080-24-01, Padenas Zuniga Enrique Collection, Museo de la Memoria y los Derechos Humanos, Santiago, Chile. (My translation).

Votar “NO” es dar lugar al odio y la ambición, sin respetar a los seme- jantes.

Votar “SI” es continuar en paz; es caminar seguro; es vivir mejor.

Figure 4. “Votar NO Votar SI”, Ana Cobos Sater Collection from the MMDH

Gail 29 triumph of a child is the best recompensation for a mother. The failure, an immense pain”. SI 62 seems to be appealing to mothers and the need to protect the future, but also putting mothers in a box, impling their most important role is to raise a successful child. The SI propaganda suggests this is something that is only possible with the current government and not, as the same female reporter claims, in reference to the NO coalition ,“an uncertain future”.63

All of these propaganda pieces are extremely diverse in their literal messaging and physical form, yet they share the common tactic of conflating family security with a peaceful,

Pinochet-led future. These examples demonstrate how SI appealed to their bloc of women voters by simultaneously creating violent enemies out of the opposition and speaking directly to their job as mothers in securing a safe future for their children. It is insulated that women should support the government because they have provided resources that families need, such as childcare, not to mention having the armed forces physically protecting families from any harm.

These advertisements are appealing to the stereotypes of how mothers should always have their children’s best interests at heart by conflating the Pinochet regime with ideas of family security and idyllic futures, compelling women to vote SI and avoid the selfish, dark, individualistic world of the NO.

The NO campaign and other female-organized opposition groups also used rhetoric about a better future in an effort to appeal to women and mothers. One pamphlet for the NO addressed workers, young folks and women specifically. In the section targeting women, the text reads,

“Women we call you to say NO to the increases and high prices, NO to hunger, to alchoholism, to child prostitution. Chilean women: Say NO, Vote NO, Defend the NO. For the right to health,

63“Franja del SI y del NO- Capítulo 14”. (My translation).

62“Franja del SI y del NO- Capítulo 14,” September 18, 1988. http://30mas.cl/franja-18-de-septiembre. (My translation).

Gail 30 education, family security, and women’s rights”. This call out simultaneously champions 64 women’s rights while also addressing issues of family security, appealing to the more “feminist” in the ranks and those who are in control of their family’s well being. Another pamphlet also calls out women directly, addressing some of the stereotypes used by the regime’s advertising:

There are those who believe that because we are women they can convince us anything.

Today, a man that has spent 15 years in power asks us for our vote. He promises peace, progress and tranquility. Can we believe him? Us women know to say things by their name. Under this government in Chile today there are 600,000 unemployed. Drug addiction and crime are on the rise...Us women go to work and we do not have nurseries to leave our children. We want to live in peace, in a happy country without violence, where there is work and tranquility. We want a country where our children have opportunities to develop.

This is why we will vote

NO.65

This piece is noteworthy because it specifically counters the regime’s reliance on what they believe to be the obedience and

65Pamphlet, “Por eso votaremos NO,” 1988, Archivo Fotográfico y Digital, PF-0309-b, Biblioteca Nacional de Chile, Santiago, Chile. (My translation, emphasis original).

64Pamphlet, “Chile dice vota defiende el NO,” 1988, CLMMDH 1801-3-01, Dorothea Schilke Collection, Museo de la Memoria y los Derechos Humanos, Santiago, Chile. (My translation, emphasis original).

Hay quienes creen que porque somos mujeres nos pueden convencer de cualquier cosa

¿Cómo? ¿No es así?

¿Quiere volver al pasado? Somos millones [illegible]

Hoy, un hombre que lleva 15 años en el poder nos pide nuestro voto. Nos promete paz, progreso y tranquilidad. ¿Podemos creerle?

¡15 años!

¿Podemos creerle?

¡NO!

Las mujeres sabemos decir las cosas por su nombre

• Bajo este gobierno en Chile hay hoy 600.000 cesantes • Crece la drogadicción y la delincuencia

• 400.000 familias viven allegadas • Si las mujeres salimos a trabajar no tenemos salas cunas donde dejar a nuestros hijos

Este NO es el país que queremos

• Queremos vivir en paz, en un país alegre y sin violencia, donde haya trabajo y tranquilidad. • Queremos un país donde nuestros hijos tengan oportunidades de desarrollo

Por eso votaremos NO

Figure 5. “Por eso votaremos NO,” from the Biblioteca Nacional de Chile

Gail 31 naivete of Chilean women. The targeted audience of this pamphlet is being appealed to with facts and logic rather than relying solely on the emotional appeals cited as Pinochet’s tactics. That being said, the end of the piece reverts back to reminding women that they want a safe, peaceful world for their children to grow up in, which is the same wish the SI campaign promises their female audience. This demonstrates how no matter the ways in which the appeal was made, the apparent end goal for many politically-involved women was a better future for their children.

Another female targeted propaganda piece declares “Voting NO means that we want to participate in the construction of a modern Chile, where as women we are valued not just as mothers and spouses but also as intelligent beings that have contributions to give. Women, vote

NO! We know what we want!”. Here, suggesting the NO vote will create a modern, arguably 66 feminist Chile implies the dictatorship only considers women as mothers and spouses and nothing more, that positive changes will not come with the continuation of the Pinochet regime.

These ads call out women explicitly, using numbers and statistics to justify the need for change rather than fear and emotion. The NO offers the same promises for a better future as the SI but addresses the failures of the current government as well, telling women not to be naive and look at those around them when making judgements.

In the video franjas, as previously discussed, the goals of the spots were to present everyday Chileans participating in normal activities. For women, this meant scenes of actresses dancing, working as nurses, going on picnics, and even riding horses holding the Chilean flag.

Actress Malucha Pinto makes an appearance in one of the spots, explaining that she is voting NO in order to achieve the free, peaceful country she had always dreamed about for her children.67

67“Franja del NO y del SI- Capítulo 11,” September 15, 1988. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=28R7jirO6i0

66“NO, voto de mujer,” 1988, Archivo Fotográfico y Digital, PF-0309-a, Biblioteca Nacional de Chile, Santiago, Chile. (My translation, emphasis original).

Gail 32

Other famous female Chilean figures that appeared throughout the franjas would often appeal directly to the women watching, like in the spot featuring Carmen Frei, daughter of ex-president

Eduardo Frei. Frei, in her jewel-toned teal pantsuit and introducing herself first as a Chilean woman, directly refutes some of the claims regarding family security made by the SI propaganda. She speaks directly to the camera when she says, “Chilean women have the desire to change” and that even though the regime says they represent the Chilean family, they are in 68 fact disbanding it. She concludes, “women want changes, we are tired of all this hate and violence, a future for us women, for our families, for our children”. Frei groups all women into 69 this collective pushing for change while telling them the dictatorship is no friend to women, despite what they claim to have accomplished. A NO future is one without violence or hate and with a future for women and their families.

In comparison to the SI campaign, the NO does not directly appeal to women as intentionally or specifically, but their promises of a better future that will come with a NO victory are very similar to that of the SI. The women's groups that targeted women in their ads reference some traditional gender roles, yet also recognize the power female voters have as individuals that the dictatorship seems to overlook. Opposition advertising appealed to women to fight directly against the injustices of the dictatorship, listing specific failures that can be rectified with a NO vote (unemployment, drug addiction, etc) and are now well within the participatory reach of this once severely marginalized population. The NO campaign also harnesses the power of hope and change when referring to the future rather than the fear mongering of the SI. The overall appeal of the opposition campaign was a promise of a brighter

69“Franja del NO y del SI- Capítulo 11,” September 15, 1988. (My translation).

68“Franja del NO y del SI- Capítulo 11,” September 15, 1988. (My translation).

Gail 33 future for all to interpret how they wanted, and for some women that meant better lives and opportunities for their children, but their hopes were not limited to their role as mothers as they were often in the SI pieces.

Takeaways:

In summary, when examining primary sources regarding how Chilean women participated both formally and informally in the plebiscite of 1988, how they were physically presented in the campaigns for both sides, and how the SI and NO coalitions specifically targeted women in their political materials, the influence of specific gender roles can be seen in a variety of different ways. First, the existence of political materials from women-only action groups highlight how the opportunities afforded to women in regards to political participation often did not involve political party affiliation. This is due to the entrenched expectation that parties were male-only spaces and women should exercise citizenship in more domestic ways. Sources related to the voting process detail how women who aligned with the opposition participated in voter registration drives in and outside of these action groups, a role that challenged the idea that female participation was not meant to be active and formal. In arguably the most impactful form of political participation, women from all factions of the Chilean political spectrum cast their ballots on election day, with 47% of women voting for SI and 52% voting for NO. The expectation going into the vote was that women would vote more conservatively, given past trends and the perception that women aligned themselves with the strict morals and patriarchal expectations set by the regime, though this turned out not to be the case. The physical representation of women in the NO campaign aimed to present women as active citizens from all walks of life, yet would intentionally feature physically attractive women and therefore reinforce

Gail 34 stereotypes regarding traditional expectations of beauty. For the SI campaign, women were presented often solely as mothers and wives, given that was how the regime had viewed and treated women under their patriarchal government structure. Finally, those aligned with the NO campaign appealed directly to women by speaking to their power to change the current way of life while acknowledging the exaggerations and lies of the dictatorship. This approach empowered women as political actors rather than keeping them on the sidelines, contrasting stereotypes of female fragility. The SI campaign relied on fear-based propaganda when directly addressing women, claiming that the current regime was the only way to protect their family and prevent a return to chaos and degradation of morals. Appealing to women in this way was directly perpetuated by marianismo ideals, namely that women should be the moral guardians of society and only focus on caring for their families. Overall, the presence of gender roles and specific stereotypes reveals that the political participation of Chilean women during this intense moment in the history of Chilean democracy was constantly gendered and women were often not seen as intentional, formal political actors, though their impact on the final vote was crucial in securing a NO victory.

Future Steps:

This project presents several future steps for further research. One step would be to examine the same issue but with an intentional, intersectional lens, namely exploring the role of indigenous Chilean women or the LGBTQ+ community during this time. Often these minority groups are left out of the main narratives of a society, especially in a country dominated by a more traditional, Catholic ideology. Looking into the role of less-documented minority groups would provide more context into Chile’s political system during this time while also elevating

Gail 35 groups that are frequently excluded from historical narratives. Another way this research could be continued would be exploring the role of women in the public referendums that have occurred since 1988, specifically the upcoming vote on the possibility of creating a new Chilean constitution scheduled (at the time of writing) for October 25, 2020. Comparing the female presentation and activism in the 1988 referendum and the upcoming vote could provide interesting insights into how women’s political participation has evolved over time and if specific gender roles mentioned in this analysis are still prevalent in the 21st century.

Conclusion:

To conclude, the impact of women in this revolutionary vote cannot be understated.

Regardless of how they were portrayed, how they were and were not able to formally participate, or how they were targeted by propaganda, the almost 3.6 million Chilean women that voted, specifically the 1.8 million who voted NO, played a crucial role in returning representative democracy to the country. Those in charge of the advertising campaigns for the SI and NO resorted to reductive stereotypes and manipulation in their tactics, yet the women in these archives were so much more than what stereotypes painted them to be. They were mothers and wives, but they were also ardent defenders of justice and hopeful for a better future. The women of Chile during this period serve as a reminder of the power women can have in dismantling oppressive forces maintained by rigid, patriarchal societies and that women as political forces cannot be underestimated or ignored.

title: When Women Teach: Female Pedagogues on the Early Modern Stage
text:
When Women Teach:

Female Pedagogues on the Early Modern Stage

Sam Lien Nguyen

Advisor: Professor Kasey Evans

Honors Coordinator: Professor Vivasvan Soni

April 30, 2021

English Department

Weinberg College of Arts and Sciences

Northwestern University

A thesis submitted in partial fulfillment of the requirements for graduation with honors from the

Department of English

To younger Sam, who fell asleep thinking about radicalizing education

Table of Contents

Acknowledgments i

Introduction 1

Chapter 1: The Case of Male Pupil and Female Pedagogue in Love’s Cure 10

Chapter 2: Doctor Rosalind Dismantles Patriarchal Authority in As You Like It 20

Coda 33

Bibliography 35

Acknowledgments

A little bird once quoted E.L. Doctorow: “Writing is like driving at night in the fog. You can only see as far as your headlights, but you can make the whole trip that way.” Actually—it wasn’t a little bird. An angel in the shape of my supervisor, Professor Kasey Evans, said that to me when I was having doubts about my ability to complete this thesis, and I cannot communicate how much those words helped tide me over during moments of intense uncertainty. From sage advice to language exchange to funny robot arm emoji, Professor Evans, your wisdom, endless compassion, and warming sincerity make this process (and in general my experience as an

English student) so much more fulfilling. From the bottom of my heart, thank you.

To the incredibly talented, supportive, and empowering group of women who make up the 2021 cohort: YAS QUEENS! I am so proud to be a part of this team and witness every single one of us persevere through and grow from difficult moments. Thank you, Professor Viv Soni, for keeping us on track with your *generative* comments and accompanying us throughout this journey as our Honors Coordinator.

My sincere appreciation to all the exceptional professors in the English Department, whether or not I have had the honor of working with you. Professor Jules Law’s evident passion for literature inspired freshman me to declare the major two weeks into college. Professor Nick

Davis feels more like a friend who always welcomes more nerdy conversations. Special thanks to Professor Jeffrey Masten, Professor Wendy Wall, and Professor Whitney Taylor, for teaching the classes that helped me realize how much I love Renaissance literature. You make me want to read and write like I’m running out of time: voraciously and unapologetically.

Shout out to the Northwestern Library for all the chapter scans! COVID might keep me

(literally) thousands of miles away from you, but it definitely cannot keep me from knowledge.

Thank you to Josh Honn especially, for your valuable assistance in the purchase of books and other research materials.

Introduction

Growing up in Vietnam, I was haunted by a proverb, Nhất nam viết hữu thập nữviết vô, which roughly translates: “Having one son means having a child, having ten daughters means not having any child.” I learned it from the textbooks; I heard it in conversations; I saw manifestations of it in the way parents relentlessly tried to have more babies in order to beget a son, regardless of their preparedness. The implicit lesson, both inside and outside of the schoolroom: being a girl meant I was deficient compared to boys.

Several years later, in a college Renaissance Literature class, I noticed with both amusement and chagrin that the notion of the defective female not only spans hemispheres, cultures, and eras, but also bleeds into scientific pursuits. According to Galen, the ancient Greek anatomical structures, but “[women’s] lack of vital heat—of perfection—…result[s] in the retention, inside, of structures that in the male are visible without” (Laqueur 4). This means, among other things, that women’s genitalia and men’s are structurally homologous—with the vagina and ovaries corresponding to the penis and scrotum—except that women’s organs fail to extrude. In other words, women are men turned outside in. This model, later termed the “one-sex model” by Thomas Laqueur, makes it clear that maleness is the default, the product of successful gestation, while femaleness is incomplete, defective, faulty.

While this model consolidates male superiority, it also introduces a prominent issue of the early modern period: if men and women are anatomically parallel, how can gender differences be enforced? Jean E. Howard explains, “Because by this [Galenic] account male-female difference was less grounded in ideas of absolute bodily difference than is typical today, much emphasis was placed on behavioral differences and on distinctions of dress” (1619). More specifically, early modern England relied on education to generate these behavioral differences that would distinguish boys from girls: “Renaissance humanists… sought to gender young children through pedagogy” (Wall 61). As Caroline Bowden puts it, “the provision of education in the family was 1 gendered, with girls receiving less tuition than boys, and in some cases it is clear that girls gained only very basic skill” (90). The location and content of their education also differed: while boys left home at the age of seven to receive formal training in Latin, rhetoric, grammar, logic, and mathematics at grammar school, girls remained at home for domestic and religious lessons. As 2 education aimed to condition learners into virtuous citizens, Danielle Clark argues, it “inculcated social values, acculturated the individual, and provided the learning deemed appropriate to the social status held by the pupil,” directing boys toward a vocation and girls toward a “discourse of containment” (19). In other words, the early modern educational model served to produce and reinforce social and gender roles: men trained to become powerful and eloquent state leaders while women prepared to become chaste, silent, and obedient wives, mothers, and mistresses of the house. There was also an emphasis on women’s education not as an opportunity for 3 self-edification but rather as a preparation for fulfilling their matrimonial and household duties.4

Walter Ong specifically examines Latin language training as an enforcement of a gendered education. In his influential paper “Latin Language Study as a Renaissance Puberty

Rite,” Ong considers the early modern teaching of Latin as a “puberty rite” through which young

In essence, the cleavage between Latin and vernacular English mirrors the division between an exclusively male world and a domestic world with (and of) women. To become full members of the learned society, boys must leave the company of women for the social milieu of powerful preceptors.

Implied in Ong’s argument is the notion that masculinity requires socialization in the right environment, while femininity is the state that can be informally taught within the domestic setting. This claim offers another model for understanding maleness and femaleness that may, at 5 first, appear to be in conflict with Galen’s, but Galen’s is a model for sexual, gestational difference while Ong’s emphasizes differences that result from separate gender training. Early modern sex and gender, then, undergo divergent (yet interconnected) processes of construction.

This important distinction between early modern sex and gender resonates with the modern understanding of the sex/gender distinction proposed by Judith Butler, building on Simone de

Butler expounds, “sex is understood to be the invariant, anatomically distinct, and factic aspects of the female body, whereas gender is the cultural meaning and form that that body acquires, the variable modes of that body’s acculturation”

Interestingly, Renaissance playwrights sought to challenge the very education that shaped them and to destabilize the deep-rooted framework of gender through their dramas. It is not difficult to find examples of female characters from this period who “suggest both an awareness of the constructed and performed nature of gender roles, and a desire to problematise and complicate the classifications typically available as ways of seeing women” (Kamaralli 1123). In her investigation of names in The Taming of the Shrew, Laurie Maguire points out that even when

Katherine sanctions Petruchio’s right to name everything, she still finds the space to slyly reassert the full form of her own name, which Maguire interprets as an act of resistance.

Similarly, Patricia Parker contends, Bianca establishes herself as an independent scholar who masters her own masters by flaunting fluency in Latin and demanding to study “as [she] pleases

[herself].” Anna Kamaralli offers an excellent reading of the four female characters in John

Webster’s The White Devil and Shakespeare’s The Winter’s Tale and their performance of traditionally masculine traits, thereby calling into question the definability of womanhood. Janet

Adelman identifies in the characterization of Cleopatra in Shakespeare’s Antony and Cleopatra a tension with the phallogocentric parameters according to which women are faulty men. These characters also invite us to upend the teacher-pupil roles and imagine women not as passive students but powerful instructors, an invitation that I will later take up in this thesis.

These plays, along with copious early modern instructional texts—such as Juan Luis

Vives’s Instruction of a Christen Woman (1529), Roger Ascham’s The Scholemaster (1570), and

William Kempe’s The Education of Children in Learning (1588)—also testify to the inextricability of education, the construction of gendered and hierarchical social configuration, and the (re)production and performance of both masculinity and femininity. The early modern stage was, according to Moncrief and McPherson, a “key pedagogical site” to examine how educational practices disciplined students as representatives of their social station and gender (4).

Nevertheless, scholarly discussions of early modern education until the first decade of the twenty-first century gave only minimal attention to the matter of gender and almost none to the ways in which pedagogy and performance intersect: Rebecca Bushnell’s The Culture of

Teaching: Early Modern Humanism in Theory and Practice offers a thorough discussion of the advent and development of humanism throughout the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries but neglects its interplay with gender; Jeff Dolven’s Scenes of Instruction in Renaissance Romance attempts to formulate a “poetics of pedagogy” by studying instructional scenes in prose romances rather than the drama of the age; and a variety of texts concentrate on women’s literacies in the early modern with little to no consideration of gender and performance. Moncrief and McPherson’s edited collection goes furthest in exploring the rich intersection of gender, pedagogy, and performance. The essays in this collection examine a variety of Renaissance instructional and literary texts to illustrate that early modern pedagogy, especially the teaching of gender, is explicitly performative. Moncrief and McPherson also examine the inseparability of performance on stage and performance of gender in everyday life. As aforementioned, distinctions of dress were meant to signify male-female differences, and crossdressing, “however playfully undertaken, always threatened to expose the artifice of gender distinctions by showing how easily one sex could assume the clothes and ape the behavior of the other” (Howard 1619).

As we know, early modern stage performances licensed crossdressing in plays that do and do not thematize gender, since female parts were played exclusively by young boys during this time.

Nevertheless, not enough attention has been paid to scenes of (sexual and gender)

pedagogy in which women rise to the role of educators and men are relegated to studenthood.

What occasions women to teach? What conditions must be satisfied for women to safely transition into an instructional role? What does it take to educate a man into manhood? In the first part of my thesis, Love’s Cure offers an excellent platform to entertain these questions, especially in its portrayal of budding romantic relationships. The play’s attempt to realign the gender performance of its two protagonists, who are both transvestites, with their biological sex 8 sparks a complex series of educational imperatives that simultaneously deconstruct and reconstruct its understanding of sex and gender. For the purpose of this thesis, I will focus only on Lucio and his relationship with Genevora, for two reasons. First, Lucio regards himself as a woman at the beginning of the play and maintains his femininity almost until the end. As my research aims to examine gender presentation not as equivalent to biological sex but rather as the product of social acculturation partially distinct from sex, I view Lucio as gender-fluid and fruitful for the scope of my study. Second, this relationship features a female pedagogue. In my 9 analysis, I read Genevora as simultaneously a mother, a lover, and a teacher, and thus as a challenge to Walter Ong’s proposition that early modern masculinity was only learned in the closed male schoolroom. Lucio’s character arc illustrates a masculinity taught in the domestic setting by a woman to a male-born student originally alienated from male society. More importantly, I contend that while Genevora adopts a similar pedagogy to other male characters who attempt to transform Lucio, her successful tutelage results from her acknowledgment and encouragement of Lucio’s gender fluidity and performativity. Instead of viewing his femininity

as an ignominious property to be cast off, Genevora is interested in the various gender expressions that Lucio occupies and commands him to assume different gender roles as they suit her needs.

The second part of my thesis shifts into a discussion of Shakespeare’s As You Like It.

Although this is a canonical text, there are surprisingly few materials written on Rosalind’s role as an educator in the play. A large body of scholarship on As You Like It comments on her crossdressing and the effect that it has on surrounding characters and the dramatic plot. My thesis briefly explores her transvestism, but only in the service of a larger investigation into the opportunities that playing a man opens up for Rosalind in her education of Orlando. More specifically, I argue that under the guise of the young man Ganymede, Rosalind performs the dual roles of a teacher and a physician, both versions of the “doctor.” Throughout the play, she assumes these two “doctor” roles in parallel to bolster her authority and to exact a “transgressive reinscription,” to borrow a term from Jonathan Dollimore: using irony or parody as “a mode of transgression which finds expression through the inversion and perversion of just those preexisting categories and structures …; a mode of transgression which seeks not an escape from existing structures, but rather a subversive reinscription within them—and in the process a dis-location of them” (Dollimore 57). In other words, instead of striving for transcendence, this 10 version of transgression takes the form of upending or destabilizing ideological, “natural” categories. For Rosalind, this transgressive reinscription means establishing her position in traditionally male-dominated fields so as to effectively infiltrates the patriarchal order and destabilizes the extant epistemological paradigm.

10 I mention this notion in passing in my examination of Love’s Cure, but will employ it more substantially in my chapter on As You Like It.

As a whole, this project endeavors to disrupt the narrative of uninterrupted early modern patriarchy. Love’s Cure and As You Like It tells the stories of women who upset the power differential between the sexes and claim authority they could not ordinarily assume. These plays explore and interrogate the theater and the classroom as sites where gender performance can vitiate entrenched power structures. By examining the gendered pedagogical dynamics in these plays, I hope to reveal how every instance of teaching and learning offers opportunities for shifting the grounds of power and authority. They always allow for the possibility of resistance, transgression, and subversion—incrementally, perhaps, but no less powerful for that.

Chapter 1: The Case of Male Pupil and Female Pedagogue in Love’s Cure

Who is the average schoolteacher in the United States? A 43-year-old white woman with over a decade of teaching experience, according to data published in April 2020 by the U.S.

Department of Education (Tai and Westat). While it is true that the demographic of schoolteachers (excluding higher education) is now predominantly female, this has not always been the case. Up until the common school movement of the late 1830s, men dominated the teaching profession (Provenzo). During the early modern period, it was at best bizarre and at worst transgressive to imagine women as pedagogues. More often than not, early modern literary works, especially playtexts, position women as students who need instructions from male masters. Highly canonical examples include Shakespeare’s The Taming of the Shrew, which features two sisters as students and three male suitors acting as teachers, and The Tempest, in which Prospero teaches Miranda about the male species for the first time.11

However, the multiplicity of female student figures in literature does not imply that there was no attempt to question the standard male-tutor-with-female-pupil dynamic. Just as modern society questions the pay gap between men and women undertaking the same work, or the tendency for women to end up in lower-ranking and untenured positions in higher education, several early modern dramatists interrogate the gender dynamics and politics in their scenes of instruction through educational, social, and ontological lenses. One salient example appears in

Francis Beaumont and John Fletcher’s Love’s Cure, or The Martial Maid. The main plot deals with the gender transformation of two siblings—Clara and Lucio—who have been brought up separately as members of the opposite sex—Lucio raised by their mother Eugenia and Clara by

11 As I will briefly mention later, ballads and pornography more often portray women as the dominant and experienced participant, in keeping with their exploration and inversion of social norms. Dramas are the opposite: women in early modern drama tend to be delicate tabulae rasae.

their father Alvarez. Twenty years later, the family is reunited, and the siblings are commanded to conform to their expected gender behaviors. This play offers a divergent narrative in its construction of the relationship between its male lead Lucio and his love interest Genevora, a noblewoman. The pedagogical dynamic between the lovers skews toward the woman: Genevora appears to be simultaneously an experienced woman showing a naïve man the “sexual ABCs” and a mother teaching her child the tenets of (wo)manhood (Traub 295).

These two possibilities interweave closely, as is evident from the ambiguous diction in

Genevora’s speech at the double duel. In this final scene, Vitelli and his second Lamorall prepare to duel against Alvarez and his son Lucio to resolve their long-running feud. When the time for combat comes, the intended duelists are interrupted by Clara (Alvarez’s daughter and Vitelli’s lover), Genevora (Vitelli’s sister and Lucio’s lover), and Eugenia (Alvarez’s wife), who plead with them not to fight. Genevora declaims:

Oh Lucio! Be thou more mercifull: thou bear’st fewer yeers, Art lately wean’d from soft effeminacy, A maidens manners, and a maidens heart Are neighbours still to thee: be then more milde, Proceed not to this combat; bee’s thou desperate Of thine own life? yet (deerest) pitty mine: Thy valour’s not thine owne, I gave it thee, These eyes begot it, this tongue bred it up, This breast would lodge it: doe not use my gifts To mine own ruine: I have made these rich, Be not so thanklesse, to undoe me for’t. (V.3.110-121, emphasis mine)

The Oxford English Dictionary defines “wean” as the act of “accustom[ing] (a child or young animal) to the loss of its mother’s milk” (OED, “wean” v., 1). This word immediately recalls a mother-and-child dynamic in the interactions between the lovers. In fact, Genevora’s speech is littered with language of parenting, italicized in the quotation above: “to beget” means to bring (a child) into existence (OED, “beget” v., 2.a), while “to breed” not only implies the environment in which one grows up but also connotes the education of young persons (OED, “breed” v., I.10.b).

By employing these verbs, Genevora firmly establishes her position as a mother without whom there will be no masculine Lucio. In other words, she imagines Lucio as the feminized infant who comes to be through her parturition and requires her parenting.

Genevora is not the first theatrical character to acknowledge the necessity of women in the formation of masculinity, however. In fact, her speech harks back to a moment in

Shakespeare’s Love’s Labor’s Lost, when Lord Biron (or Berowne) declares:

[For] women’s sake—by whom we men are men— Let us once lose our oaths to find ourselves, Or else we lose ourselves to keep our oaths. (IV.3.334-6)

Here, Biron relinquishes the definition of masculinity as an exclusive single-sex academy and acknowledges that “masculinity is expressed only in relationship” (Moncrief 123). That is, men 12 do not gain masculine honor and self-enhancement through isolated study but through interactions with and positioning relative to women, for whose sake (and by whose maternal offices) “men are men.” Of course, Biron might just be referring to the fact that we are all born of women—an interpretation that Love’s Cure certainly takes advantage of. But Biron does not claim that “people are people” or “babies are babies” or “boys are boys,” but specifically “men are men,” insisting that women play a role in boys’ maturation into men, not just their existence as human beings. Love’s Cure is essentially making the same claim, but the play takes its

“transgressive reinscription” a step further by having Genevora proclaim her own significance.

As opposed to Love’s Labor’s Lost, what we witness in Love’s Cure is not a reflection by the man

12 For an excellent analysis of this speech, see Moncrief, “‘Teach Us, Sweet Madam’.

but an explicit assertion of authority by the woman: Genevora knows herself to be the master and claims her role: “Thy valour’s not thine owne, I gave it thee.”

Interestingly, Love’s Cure proposes more than one way “we men are men” by women.

The first, as we have identified in the use of “wean,” is through the narrative of motherhood, which signals that Lucio’s manhood results from the entire process of Genevora’s gestation, parturition, and parenting. Another route interprets “to breed” not as parenting but as copulation and reproduction: not only has Genevora birthed and raised Lucio, but she also breeds with him, thus conflating the parental and erotic dynamics between the two. This word, along with previous scenes in the play, explicitly spells out sexual education as the catalyst for Lucio’s gender transformation. For the first half of the play, Lucio presents as a young, innocent boy/girl so ignorant of the “sexual ABC’s” that he expresses surprise at the prospect of desire beyond a kiss. He is not exceptional in his cluelessness. Valerie Traub makes a case that “Renaissance texts are populated with women and men who simply do not know what other people seem to know; and more often than not, this lack of knowledge consistently evokes a pedagogical imperative that is elided or refused or fails” (295). In the case of Love’s Cure, the “pedagogical imperative” that springs from Lucio’s lack of knowledge, his initiation into the arts of love, officially begins with Genevora’s erotic instructions. Their kiss in Act 4, Scene 4 communicates new sexual knowledge that leads to “strange new motions” and “alteration,” which serve as a turning point for Lucio’s gender formation (IV.4.12-14). Shortly after this kiss, in response to

Genevora’s chiding for not protecting her love token, Lucio exclaims:

My womanish soul, which hitherto hath govern’d This coward flesh, I feel departing from me; And in me by her beauty is inspir’d A new, and masculine one: instructing me What’s fit to do or suffer; powerful love

That hast with loud, and yet a pleasing thunder Rous’d sleeping manhood in me, thy new creature, Perfect thy work so that I may make known Nature (though long kept back) will have her own. (IV.4.54-62, emphasis mine)

This monologue details Lucio’s most conscious utterance of his gender transformation from a

“womanish soul” into a “masculine one.” Crucially, this transformation relies heavily on

Genevora’s beauty, which Lucio claims to have “inspir’d” a new soul into him. Etymologically derived from the Latin prefix “in–” and the verb “spīrāre,” which means to breathe, “inspire” imagines the couple’s kiss as the literal act of Genevora breathing out and Lucio breathing in.13

This literalization signifies that Lucio’s soul, be it “womanish” or “masculine,” is not an inherent element within his natural body but rather a property obtained through and gendered by his participation in an erotic act. Intriguingly, Lucio’s sexual socialization, particularly his description of the kiss as Genevora “instructing [him]/ What’s fit to do or suffer,” bears a striking resemblance to that of the hapless male lover, Tomalin, in Thomas Nashe’s narrative poem “The

Choise of Valentines.” Tomalin, just like Lucio, is “clueless about the mechanics of sex, specifically about how to pleasure a woman” (Traub 114-15). On the whole, their experiences fit into the larger sexual narrative, which employs the compelling trope of naiveté that invites tutelage from the more experienced woman who performs the role of instructor. In Love’s Cure,

Lucio and Genevora’s sexual encounter inaugurates a pedagogical process, or at least a pedagogical dynamic, that Lucio identifies in this soliloquy and that conforms to Genevora’s speech in the dueling scene cited above. In this fashion, Lucio’s gender transformation is

“revealed to be the result of a particular social production, a process of knowledge construction,”

This parallelism solidifies Genevora’s position of power, possibly at the expense of the erotic dimension of the relationship.

What these two scenes illuminate is that whether she plays the role of a mother or a romantic partner, Genevora undeniably activates Lucio’s integration into masculinity through her

(sexual) tutelage. This proposition stands in contrast with Walter Ong’s influential observation that the departure from domestic life into Latin training was a kind of male “puberty rite” (Ong

103). In fact, Lucio has never fully entered the exclusively male society and remains entirely foreign to it, until Genevora’s interposition. We see this in Alvarez and Bobadilla’s futile attempt to redeem Lucio’s manliness:

Alvarez. Thou hast made me mad: and I will beat thee dead Then bray the in a morter, and new mold thee But I wil alter thee. Bobadilla. ‘Twill never be: He has bin three days practicing to drink, Yet still he sips, like to a waiting woman, And looks as he were murdering of a fart Among wild Irish swaggerers. (IV.3.25-31)

Bobadilla highlights Lucio’s status as an outcast who fails to enter the male world by comparing him to “a waiting woman,” a sneer at not only Lucio’s womanly behavior, but also the accompanying threat of downward social mobility. Furthermore, while the play is set in Spain, it is performed to an English audience well aware of English colonialism in Ireland. Ireland, like many others colonized countries, was often feminized, “increasingly imaged in wifely terms” in direct contrast with England, her masculine imperial master (Valente 190). In positioning Lucio 14

“among wild Irish swaggerers,” Bobadilla relegates him to the world of uncultured, unlearned

(wild) women (Irish) who lack proper, courtly behaviors (swaggerers). All three layers of otherness—in terms of gender, class, and race and ethnicity—simultaneously pronounce the
