danger of Lucio’s wanting manliness and confirm the men’s desperation and inability to transform him. When all their efforts prove to no avail, they resort to rage, carnality, and violence:

Ther’s only one course left, that may redeem thee, Which is, to strike the next man that you meet, And if we chance to light upon a woman, Take her away, and use her like a man, Or I wil cut thy hamstrings. (IV.3.37-41, emphasis mine)

While Anne Duncan cites this passage as an example of “the connection between rage and the performance of masculinity,” I am more concerned with the implication that sexual knowledge is an agent or catalyst of manly honor (399). We have seen in Lucio’s soliloquy above that it is not rage that “rous’d sleeping manhood” in him; it is his kiss with Genevora. In other words, sexual experience, rather than violence, triggers this process of masculinization. However, as Valerie

Traub makes clear, “eroticism isn’t just something that people do (…); it is something that people learn; it requires initiation, experimentation, education, [and] practice” (119). In that case,

Alvarez’s appeal to a final “course,” a term with forceful pedagogical connotations, does not terminate where he imagines it would: at a single lewd act of “[using] her like a man.” Instead, it

(unintentionally) marks the beginning of Lucio’s courtship with Genevora and thus occasions an erotic educational process. Ironically, this educational process at once echoes and fundamentally differs from the one implemented by the men themselves. As a pedagogue, Genevora chides as the men have chided: “Nay you are rude; pray you forbeare; you offer now/ More then the breeding of a Gentleman/ Can give you warrant for.” (IV.4.1-3). She instructs as the men have instructed: both parties adopt the learning-by-doing approach, Genevora with desire and kissing and Alverez with fighting and violence. Finally, when Lucio’s indecisiveness causes him to lose her “favour”—that is, her gloves, which were given as a love token—to another suitor, she resorts to “torment” in the same manner as Alvarez has threatened to “bray [Lucio] in the morter”:

For thy torment, If my poore beauty be of any power, Mayst thou doat on it desperately: but never Presume to hope for grace, till thou recover And weare the favour that was ravish’d from thee. (IV.4.45-52, emphasis mine)

In other words, Genevora employs similar pedagogical techniques as Alvarez and Bobadilla.

And yet, she yields the desired outcome as the men could not. Lucio’s successful education in masculinity, then, results not from the method of instruction but the instructor and the content.

Instead of drinking and “strik[ing]” with men, Lucio thrives under the sexual tutelage of a woman. More broadly speaking, he moves from one domestic scene—where he finds in his mother Eugenia a model for imitation—into another—where he learns from his mother-like fiancée. Contrary to Walter Ong’s argument, what the men fail miserably to do can be achieved rather seamlessly by two women: Eugenia teaches him to be a woman, and Genevora allegedly turns him into a man.

What exactly renders Genevora a more proficient educator than Alvarez and Bobadilla? I contend that Genevora’s success is attributable to her disinterest in the binary caricature of masculinity; on the contrary, she acknowledges that Lucio has the wisdom of all the different gender roles that he has played and employs her various roles to capitalize on this fluidity and capaciousness. A salient manifestation of this practice is in her speech at the double duel where

Genevora at once establishes her position as the mother and reasserts her power as the instructor.

“[B]e then more milde,” she commands her lover, asking him to temporarily reassume his “soft effeminacy,” which Lucio has practiced in his feminized infancy. Her directive encourages us to read “effeminacy” and by extension “masculinity” as a performance that one dials up and down rather than something that can be wholly eradicated and superseded. Her use of “soft effeminacy” in conjunction with “wean’d” also reinforces this idea of gender performativity, for the definition of “wean” as the act of “accustoming to” anticipates Butler’s language of acculturation and a “contingent construction of meaning” (Butler, Gender Trouble 139). In other words, gender in Love’s Cure is neither innate nor constant, but a series of possibilities to be performed as convenience and/or ethics dictate. To Genevora, Lucio’s earlier childhood femininity is not something shameful; instead, it contains useful information for him to draw on to become more expansive, more compassionate, and an altogether better partner for her. Thus, what makes Genevora stand out from Lucio’s other instructors is her cognizance of what we might now call the performativity of gender, her appreciation of Lucio’s various qualities of different genders, and her awareness of the significance of her presence. As a result, Lucio’s change of gender depends not on his will but hers: when she is upset that he cannot protect her love, he assumes masculinity; when she is upset that he is about to harm her family, he is compelled to revert to softness. Ultimately, Lucio’s gender is not only a performance; it is a series of performances cultivated and authorized by a female director and pedagogue.

In looking at Lucio’s gender transformation, which results from his accumulation of sexual knowledge, I have illustrated not only that, and how, a woman can occupy the role of an educator, but also the efficacy of her tutelage. Throughout Love’s Cure, Genevora weaves together motherhood and professorship, and in so doing, successfully trains Lucio to become a man—a considerable feat that other male figures in the play fail to do. What is remarkable is that

Genevora adopts a similar approach to teaching as Alvarez and Bobadilla do, with an emphasis on instruction, punishment, and practice, but yields vastly different results. Her favorable outcome, then, must be attributable to her ability to perceive Lucio as both the feminized, helpless infant and the masculine partner who has adult sexuality and can relate to her with desire. By understanding this simultaneity and by imagining her authority as both motherly and teacherly, Genevora asserts her claim to the result—Lucio’s honorable manliness/ manly honor—in both familial and academic terms: she simultaneously begets his outstanding qualities and trains him to develop a full consciousness of and mastery over those qualities. Consequently, she also reserves the right to revoke those characteristics and skillfully manipulates Lucio’s gender performance, calling on him to privilege his masculinity or femininity as she sees fit.

Read this way, the play is as invested in recording Genevora’s growth as a pedagogue as it is keen on the notion of gender as a performance, or the actual erotic content and training that contributes to Lucio’s increasing masculinity. Whatever the case, Love’s Cure undeniably compels its audience to interrogate and dismiss patriarchal assumptions about who can be a teacher, and what it means to be, become, or perform a gender.

Chapter 2: Doctor Rosalind Dismantles Patriarchal Authority in As You Like It

In December 2020, Joseph Epstein wrote an op-ed for the Wall Street Journal, calling for

First Lady Jill Biden to drop her honorific. “‘Dr. Jill Biden’ sounds and feels fraudulent, not to say a touch comic,” writes Epstein, suggesting that only physicians with M.D. are entitled to, well, the title. Dr. Biden only earned an Ed.D., a Doctor of Education, “through a dissertation with [an] unpromising title,” so she should think again and “forthwith drop the doc.” Never mind that it reeks of misogyny and sarcastic condescension; the piece leaves me questioning whether

Epstein fully comprehends what the doctorate signifies. The term “doctor” was originally a linguistic derivative of the Latin verb docēre, meaning “to teach.” Over time, it gained use as an academic title when the first doctorates were conferred in Europe, for those who have obtained a doctorate were qualified to teach or express an authoritative opinion. A physician, who had gone through a long university education, would therefore also be referred to as a “Doctour of 15

Phisyk” (documented in Chaucer, Canterbury Tales Prol. l. 413) or “doctour of deth”

(documented in Langland, Piers Plowman B. xviii. 362), to distinguish from their colleagues in church (Doctor of the Church) and law (Doctor of Law). Throughout its history, the term

“doctor” has accumulated nuances, each becoming more or less salient depending on the context in which the term appears. These nuances are not mutually exclusive—on the contrary, they are closely connected, and the activation of one does not inhibit or negate the (linguistic) validity of others. So, Mr. Epstein, the answer to your question is yes, not only is there a doctor in the White

House, but women have also presumed upon the title and role of doctor for centuries.

15 Not every medical practitioner in early modern England earned the title of doctor. In fact, only physicians, who had received extensive training and schooling in universities, were singled out for the appellation. This was because university education not only transmitted knowledge about healing but also trained students in cultivating and exercising their good judgment and advice, two crucial concepts in establishing professional authority. For further discussion, see Cook.

The inquiry into these varying resonances of the term “doctor” and their interplay is not merely a twenty-first century phenomenon: we can also see manifestations of it in early modern literature. The present chapter concentrates, in particular, on the maneuvering of the role and its various forms of authority in Shakespeare’s pastoral comedy As You Like It. In this play, the main character Rosalind is a witty woman with a delightful tongue-in-cheek sense of humor. When she meets her love interest, Orlando, in the forest, she pointedly performs—literally so, for she remains in disguise as the young, male Ganymede during the majority of her interactions with

Orlando—as both a teacher and a physician to shape him into the lover she desires. Throughout the play, she uses the two most prevalent resonances of “doctor”—physician and teacher—in parallel as roles to mutually bolster her authority and to infiltrate the patriarchal order. By doing so, Rosalind effectively ridicules and destabilizes the existing epistemological paradigm.

One salient moment in this pattern appears as soon as Rosalind sees Orlando in the forest, when she asks about the time and then demands to “tell” him about how time functions

(III.2.314). Rosalind unapologetically rejects the Renaissance trope of “the swift foot of time,” which is often cited in early modern literature, especially in Shakespeare’s sonnets, and 16 proceeds to explain that time moves at different speeds for different people. Her seemingly trivial question becomes highly productive when considered in conjunction with Jaques’s earlier musings on time and the different stages of maturation:

All the world’s a stage, And all the men and women merely players. They have their exits and entrances, And one man in his time plays many parts, His acts being seven ages. At first the infant, …

16 Two examples: Shakespeare’s Sonnet 19: “Make glad and sorry seasons as thou fleet,/ And do whate’er thou wilt, swift-footed Time”; and Sonnet 65: “O fearful meditation! where, alack,/ Shall time’s best jewel from time’s chest lie hid?/ Or what strong hand can hold his swift foot back?” (emphasis mine).

Then the whining schoolboy …

And then the lover, Sighing like furnace, with a woeful ballad Made to his mistress’ eyebrow. (II.7.146-156, emphasis mine)

In this passage, “time” refers to one’s lifetime, which can be divided into seven stages: infant, schoolboy, lover, soldier, justice, pantaloon (or foolish old man in pantaloons), and finally,

“second childishness and mere oblivion” (II.7.172). Thus, the concept of time in Jaques’s model refers to not only a point of existence measured in hours or minutes, but also to the broad idea of time as the continued progression of existence and events. This progression is not linear but circular; humans ultimately return to a second iteration of “childishness” and then finally quietus.

Subsequently, Rosalind’s question can be understood as partially a query about where Orlando is in the stages of men: it is not just “what is ’t o’clock?” but “what is ’t o’clock with him?” The phrase “o’clock” is also apt to evoke the cyclicity of time: etymologically an abbreviated form of

“of the clock,” both the letter “o” and the image of the physical clock suggest a circular contour and movement. Read this way, Rosalind is feeling out what her role is going to be in making the clock move forward, essentially giving Orlando a placement test before writing a curriculum.

This curriculum, it is hinted, is not going to be straightforward, for time itself is not linear, nor will Orlando’s progress be. Furthermore, if we use Jaques’s multi-stage model of time to assess

Orlando’s level and progress, then Rosalind’s proposition to “give him some good counsel” is appropriate. Jaques’s description of a lover here aligns with what Rosalind later cites as cues to

“know a man in love” (III.2.376-377). By dismissing Orlando’s claim to “loverness”—I offer my detailed analysis of this dismissal below—she positions him as a “whining schoolboy,” the stage immediately preceding lover (for it is clear he is no longer an infant “mewling and puking in the nurse’s arms” [II.7.151]). If this is so, Orlando’s earlier poetic declarations of love can be regarded as “whining,” and he the schoolboy “unwillingly to school.” This taxonomy provides the pedagogical imperative for Rosalind to rise to the role of the doctor (teacher) who can mentor

Orlando to the next stage: lover.

At the same time, this opening motif of time initiates Rosalind’s process of “transgressive reinscription,” the term Jonathan Dollimore coined to the subversive inversion or reversal of ideological categories. In rejecting the conventional understanding of time as swift-footed and 17 constant, and in providing humorously realistic evidence for her argument, Rosalind inaugurates her own system of knowledge independent of masculine poetics and courtly parameters. In this system, the foundation of Renaissance humanist education—that is, Latin language learning—is not the “puberty rite,” the required condition for young boys to be inducted into an exclusive male tribe, as Ong would have it. Instead, Latin training is degraded into “the burden of lean and wasteful learning”—something that offers little reward for abundant effort (III.2.329). This trivialization of Latin also serves as a vicarious critique of institutionalized masculine learning 18 and its various pedagogical methods as impractical and ineffectual in imparting transferable knowledge and skills.

In Rosalind’s system of understanding, the “natural” categories of male and female are also problematized, curiously, through the establishment of the categories of “lover” vs.

non-lover (or “loving yourself”). As I explained in the introduction, the Galenic model of anatomy proposes that men and women share the same anatomical structures, the only difference

18 Isn’t it ironic that I’m using this Latinate word to describe Rosalind’s disapproving attitude toward Latin? Perhaps the more profound point lurking in this playful question is that although Rosalind can play with and partially subvert the patriarchal structures in which Latin reigns supreme, there is no way to entirely get around it. In fact, as I have repeatedly demonstrated, it is not her goal to escape or transcend the system; she is more concerned with revealing the loopholes that can pervert it.

17 For a more detailed definition of this term, refer to page 9 above in the introduction.

being that female embryos lack the heat during gestation to extrude their sexual organs. This

“one-sex model” contends that maleness is the telos of gestation, while femaleness is a form of incompletion. A sloppy or lay interpretation of this model, which disregards anything invisible or intangible as irrelevant, is the (in)famous use of “nothing,” such as in Much Ado About Nothing, as a slang for a woman’s private part, for she has “no thing” or lacks a penis. This phallocentric discourse perpetually confines women within a negative space: always lacking, always 19 needing. In her conversation with Orlando, Rosalind sets out to invert this use of the negative: 20

ROSALIND, as Ganymede There is none of my uncle’s marks upon you. He taught me how to know a man in love, in which cage of rushes I am sure you are not prisoner.

ORLANDO What were his marks?

ROSALIND, as Ganymede A lean cheek, which you have not; a blue eye and sunken, which you have not; an unquestionable spirit, which you have not; a beard neglected, which you have not … Then your hose should be ungartered, your bonnet unbanded, your sleeve unbuttoned, your shoe untied, and everything about you demonstrating a careless desolation. But you are no such man. You are rather point-device in your accouterments, as loving yourself than seeming the lover of any other. (III.2.380-391, emphasis mine)

Here, instead of repudiating this patriarchal theory of women, Rosalind delegates the negative space to Orlando. In describing his not-a-lover mien, she reiterates the phrase “which you have not” four times and attaches the negative prefix un- to almost every adjective, emphasizing the lack that is, ironically, glaringly present in his accouterments. In the same way that Galen and other prominent early modern anatomists define the female body strictly in relation to its male

20 This phallocentric paradigm continues to reverberate through time. In the 20th century, Freud reports “that the feminine occurs only within models and laws devised by male subjects” (quoted in Irigaray 86). He notes a sociolinguistic discourse that defines females in the negative, that is, as Elizabeth Grosz notes, “[the] sociolinguistic inscription of women’s bodies [as castrated] must be seen as the unspoken condition of the attribution of men’s phallic status: it is only if women’s bodies lack that men’s bodies can be seen to have.”

19 Throughout this section, I will primarily be using the OED definition of “negative” as “consisting in, characterized by, or expressing the absence rather than the presence of distinguishing features; devoid of or lacking distinctly positive attributes” (adj., 4.a).

counterpart, Orlando is interpellated in Rosalind’s epistemological framework as “no such man,” a non-lover who exists wholly in the un-s and the have-nots. Most interestingly, Rosalind’s standards for a proper lover, according to which she is critiquing Orlando, is a list of stereotypical images. After all, early modern English literature “abounds with examples of melancholy lovers, who burn with passion, die of breaking hearts, or simply waste away”

(Dawson 12). Rosalind mocks both the (non-)lover (here, Orlando) and the trite depictions of a lover in their “careless desolation.” In the time of Shakespeare, Lesel Dawson explains, “while the clothing and bearing of the lovesick individual suggest that the symptoms of erotic melancholy were privately felt, the fact that this inwardness is expressed through recognizable conventions of posture, dress, and behaviour indicates the way in which lovesickness was a role performed as well as an emotion experienced” (34). That is to say, one must look and dress the 21 part if one wishes to be considered as a serious lover. By using the popular lovesick tropes curated and often employed by male poets, Rosalind is not only ridiculing the superficiality of early modern expressions of love, but she is also using the master’s tool to dismantle the master’s house—that is, using the rhetorical devices of the male lovers against one of its own representatives (Lorde 110). This subversion of power is even more impressive when we recall that Rosalind is dressed as a man in this scene. While it comes at the (temporary) expense of her feminine expression, this male costume enables her to enter the male society and effectively manipulates masculine authority in her favor. As the plot progresses, Rosalind becomes even

21 Melancholy also became increasingly fashionable for men in England, partly in an attempt to manipulate and rearrange the climatological mapping of the humors to make northern (Anglo-European) people more balanced and sensible than the southern (African) people. For further discussion of ethnological humoralism and the fashionability of melancholy, see Mary Floyd-Wilson, Chapter 3.

more explicit in her criticism of the tropes of lovesickness and the poetic rhetoric of attributing men’s demise to women, a point I will return to momentarily.

Eventually, Rosalind concludes that Orlando appears to be “loving yourself than seeming the lover of any other,” condemning his expressions as rooted in narcissistic infatuation rather than love. One may note that the few characters whom Orlando speaks of and/or interacts with in the first act are all men: his father, brothers, their servant Adam, Charles the wrestler, Duke

Frederick, and Le Beau. There is no mention of a mother or any female figure before his acquaintance with Rosalind and Celia in Scene 2. Thus, as far as we can observe from the text, 22

Orlando has always been contained within a male circle; and yet, he was never truly a part of that exclusive community, for he lacks “all gentlemanlike qualities” (I.1.68). Already, even as a man in this “man’s man’s man’s world” (in the words of singer James Brown), Orlando is a liminal figure who fails to be positively defined: though he tries to assert himself as the son of a Sir

Rowland de Bois, others—including the audience—know him as a man who lacks gentlemanlike behaviors and therefore a social position. Rosalind’s suggestion about his narcissism might therefore be underscoring Orlando’s confinement within the masculine homosocial circuit, thereby implying that the socially constructed wall of masculinity is accountable for his

“negativeness.”23

At the same time, Rosalind’s conclusion about Orlando’s neat appearance also hints at her reason for remaining cross-dressed even in the safety of the forest. As Marjorie Garber suggests,

23 I have decided against using “negativity” as the noun for negative here, since I do not want it to connote an attitude, emotion, or expression of criticism, pessimism, or unpleasantness. Throughout the paper, I will instead be using “negativeness” as the noun for “negative,” strictly in the definition that I have provided in footnote 19 (OED adj., 4.a).

22 For a more in-depth discussion of how motherhood is, or pointedly is not represented in Shakespearean dramas, see Rose.

“As the lessons she gives to Orlando immediately testify, Rosalind does not have to learn much, if anything, about love, or the quality and depth of her own feelings” (Garber 104). In fact, it is

Orlando who needs an education, who must learn “what ‘tis to love” (V.2.87). By electing to be

“caparisoned like a man,” Rosalind upends the expected patriarchal pattern of a father or husband educating his wife and daughter and offers a reverse paradigm of the female schoolmaster and male pupil. She dresses in male attire so that she can be liberal with her criticism and fashion Orlando into the lover that she desires, rather than a “point-device” man primarily concerned with “loving [him]self.” The phrase “point-device,” which appears most frequently in relatively staid texts of the period, such as chronicles of monarchs or discourses on scripture, connotes the quality of being “perfectly correct or precise, esp. in matters of dress or appearance; scrupulous, neat, fastidious” (OED, “point-device” adj.). Nevertheless, there seems to be significant support for reading “point-device” as a double entendre: “point” being a possible euphemism for the phallus and “device” meaning “will, pleasure, inclination, fancy, desire”—as in “leave one at one’s own device” (OED, “device” n., 3.a). Combined, this phrase could mean punctilious, neat, and meticulous, but it could also be interpreted as “at the pleasure of your penis.” The disconcerting implication that follows is the association of perfection and correctness with phallic desire: the receiving partner in a sexual act is somehow deficient, and her “no-thing” can only be made perfect through the presence of the phallus. By this logic, we may understand Rosalind’s mockery of Orlando’s appearance as, indirectly, a double critique of phallocentricism and narcissism. Once again, we see how Rosalind wields her new masculine power to undo the inveterate mindset of male prerogatives for her benefit.

Through their conversation in Act 3, Scene 2, Rosalind also makes clear her intention to draw on the medical connotation of “doctor” and perform as a physician in their relationship.

When asked to recount some of the “principal evils that [God] laid to the charge of women,” she immediately refuses: “No, I will not cast away my physic but on those that are sick.” However, she also opens up an opportunity for Orlando to enlist her help: “If I could meet that fancy monger [who worships Rosalind], I would give him some good counsel, for he seems to have the quotidian of love upon him” (III.2.364-372). Here, not only is Rosalind claiming to possess some

“physic” that she will bestow upon the “sick,” she is also diagnosing Orlando with the “quotidian of love,” in which “quotidian” is short for the quotidian fever or quotidian malaria. Figuratively,

“quotidian” also denotes a state of emotional or nervous agitation (OED), a fitting understanding of love in physiological terms. Then she goes on to validate her diagnosis and qualifications as a physician by listing the symptoms of love in the passage cited above. The seeming medical check-up concludes with her naming the disease (“Love is merely a madness” [III.2.407]) and offering a treatment plan (“Yet I profess curing it by counsel” [III.2.412]). This entire exchange follows an almost methodical process of medical examination, further highlighting Rosalind and

Orlando’s dynamic as doctor and patient.

Importantly, Rosalind also invokes Galenic physiology later when detailing her proposed cure: “… and this way will I take upon me to wash your liver as clean as a sound sheep’s heart, that there shall not be one spot of love in ’t” (III.2.429-431, emphasis mine). Her reference to the liver recalls humoral theory, which “assumed connections among bodily fluids, the four elements, and the seasons, leading to a theory of temperaments or bodily dispositions and psychosomatic phenomena” (Baltussen). During the Renaissance, lovesickness was considered a serious physiological affliction. Galen himself treated love as a disease. Lovesickness was said to have resulted from an imbalance of the humors, especially excessive heat and blood. In the scene in question, Rosalind’s invokes the Galenic understanding that blood was produced exclusively by the liver. Shakespeare could also have been influenced by Marsilio Ficino’s model of lovesickness as a pathological form of desire. According to Ficino, lovesickness is the result of an “enchantment” or “bewitchment,” a pathological sequence of erotic melancholy in which the eye, wide open and fixed upon someone, shoots the darts of its own rays into the eyes of the bystander, and along with those darts, which are the vehicles of the spirits, aims that sanguine vapor which we call spirit[.] Hence the poisoned dart pierces through the eyes, and since it is shot from the heart of the shooter, it seeks again the heart of the man being shot, as its proper home; it wounds the heart, but in the heart’s hard back wall it is blunted and turns back into blood. This foreign blood, being somewhat foreign to nature of the wounded man, infects his blood. (Ficino 160) 24

Thus, the lover becomes sick with alien blood, which must be cleansed through the liver. What we learn from Galenic humoralism and Ficino’s explanation of the origin of lovesickness is that the liver is a key organ in the understanding and cure of the malady, and that by promising to

“wash your liver as clean as a sound sheep’s heart,” Rosalind simultaneously demonstrates her in-depth knowledge of Galen and consolidates her prestige and authority as an erudite doctor

(physician) fluent in the medical language of the time.

Having successfully asserted her position, Rosalind takes advantage of her medical authority as leverage for her role as an educator: she proposes to cure “by counsel,” which is to say, by instruction. This recommended remedy appears to run counter to Galen and the 25 humoralists. During the early modern period, there were four prominent ways to redress

25 “Counsel” here can also be understood as advice, which sets Rosalind apart as a physician in the medical profession from other medical practitioners (such as apothecaries or surgeons). Harold J. Cook elaborates, in early modern England, “[the physicians] linked their professional authority to two key concepts, judgment and advice… Good judgment and advice were considered to be attributes of character at least as much as knowledge” (4).

24 For further commentary on Ficino and others’ theories of the etiology of lovesickness, see Dawson 19-27.

lovesickness: “two physical treatments—phlebotomy (or bloodletting) and sexual intercourse—and two mental or psychological cures—trickery (or performative healing) and humiliation” (Dawson 163). Out of these four, Rosalind’s suggestion that Orlando pretends to woo Ganymede as Rosalind appears to align most closely with trickery, “which is aimed at dislodging the sufferer’s mental fixation [and which] suggests how the lover is enraptured not by the actual beloved, but by an internal vision.” In trickery, early modern physicians would

“collude with the patients’ aberrant imagination to effect a therapy” (Dawson 177). As a result, the patients who undergo trickery may be relieved of their greater afflictions (such as lovesickness), but they never fully overcome their own mental fixation. Rosalind’s “counsel,” too, relies on this idea of imaginative therapy as she offers a subtle mockery of Orlando for not recognizing his beloved in disguise, even after her rather frequent hints. However, Rosalind’s 26 trickeryis innovative (and perhaps even poses a counterargument to Galen) for three reasons.

Firstly, Rosalind’s proposal to help Orlando is anything but altruistic, nor is her goal necessarily to cure him. It is for her sake that she sets out to arm Orlando with knowledge of herself and her preferences in love, thereby training him to become lovelorn in the particular way that will suit her. Secondly, Rosalind requests that Orlando view her (posing as Ganymede) as his beloved so that he can practice wooing her (Rosalind), and she can teach and give feedback on the spot.

Their play-acting courtship serves as exercise in the art of love; it adds an experiential component, which Jeff Dolven has illustrated to be potentially powerful. Thirdly and most 27 importantly, Rosalind’s cure by instruction brings in the pedagogical overtone of “doctor” in conjunction with the present medical connotation of the term. In this manner, Rosalind appeals to

27 For a discussion of Experience, see Dolven, Chapter 4.

26 Marjorie Garber also hints at Orlando’s psychological state of self-absorption and inability to recognize Rosalind, though Garber never uses the terms “trickery” or “mental fixation.” all the available resonances and authorities accrued to the title in order to achieve her goal: she must cure by teaching in order to reconfigure Orlando and revolutionize his whole understanding of love.

These two resonances of doctor prove to be mutually reinforcing and conducive to

Rosalind’s transformation of Orlando. In the popular scene of instruction in Act 4, Scene 1, she returns to the topic of lovesickness in her lesson:

ROSALIND, as Ganymede No, faith, die by attorney. The poor world is almost six thousand years old, and in all this time there was not any man died in his own person, videlicet, in a love cause. Troilus had his brains dashed out with a Grecian club, yet he did what we could to die before, and he is one of the patterns of love. Leander, he would have lived many a fair year though Hero had turned nun, if it had not been for a hot midsummer night, for, good youth, he went but forth to wash him in the Hellespont and, being taken with the cramp, was drowned; and the foolish chroniclers of the age found it was Hero of Sestos. But these are all lies. Men have died from time to time and worms have eaten them, but not for love. (IV.1.99-113, original emphasis)

As part of her lecture on love, Rosalind debunks the myth that love can lead to death, as poets and medical practitioners of the time contended. In her system of knowledge, men die because of love only by proxy—that is, lovesickness might instigate actions that lead to death, such as

“[having one’s] brains dashed out with a Grecian club” or “being taken with the cramp and … drowned” when swimming. Ironically, she exploits her title as a doctor in the Galenic tradition to debunk the Galenic myth about the fatal power of lovesickness. Simultaneously, this comment reinforces her expertise as a teacher and extends her earlier criticism of the overused lovesick tropes. Now going beyond merely listing clichéd representations of the lover, Rosalind employs her knowledge of the poetics and calls out the histrionic romance heroes by name: Troilus of

Shakespeare’s Troilus and Cressida (and/or of Chaucer’s Troilus and Criseyde) and Leander of

Christopher Marlowe’s Hero and Leander. It’s especially tempting to understand Rosalind to be including Shakespeare among the male poets whose exaggerated rhetoric she mocks: an authentic moment of master’s tools dismantling the master’s house!

Rosalind also goes so far as to label the “chroniclers of the age” foolish and their depictions of lovelorn men as “all lies.” There might also be a sexual double entendre in the word “die,” for orgasm is also termed la petite mort, or “the little death.” With this definition,

Rosalind’s concluding remark could be interpreted as a lampoon of men’s carnal desire: they have attained sexual release from time to time, but they have never done so for love (rather than for pure pleasure). Moreover, I identify in her speech a subtle commentary on gender discourse:

women would be blamed for the tragedies of men, even if they “had turned nun.” Speaking as a woman, Rosalind might be dismissed as transgressive, defensive, or even hysterical. Speaking as a man, however, she can meaningfully exercise the prerogatives exclusive to the male society to push back on gender discrimination. Her successful masquerade as Ganymede attests not only to the gender-specific nature of early modern pedagogy but also to Rosalind’s mastery over what she teaches and to her strategic understanding of when different gender performances are conducive to her aims. Once again, she employs the master’s tools to dismantle the master’s house; however, this time, the employment is threefold: a Galenic doctor refuting a Galenic doctrine, a schoolmaster mocking poetic banality, and a man ridiculing masculine clichés.

In dressing up and performing as a man, in assuming the varying postures of professional authority subsumed under the umbrella term doctor, all of which were exclusively male prerogatives, Rosalind fashions a new pedagogical and epistemological system that works to overturn existing patriarchal beliefs through transgressive reinscription. In the same way

Genevora performs multiple roles in Love’s Cure, so too does Rosalind perform multiple genders and positions. Her characterization foregrounds the contingency of performance: she chooses to be a man or a woman, a teacher or a physician, depending on context. Through her arrogation of the multiple roles of “doctor,” Rosalind exerts a subtle but meaningful shift in the power dynamics of romantic and pedagogical interactions, and invites us to question our normative assumptions about power and authority in early modern relationships, both erotic and instructional.

Coda

When I first started this project, I wanted to study female education. What kind of pedagogy did women receive? How did education shape understanding of femininity and female gender and sexualities, undermine or support female agency, and challenge or perpetuate patriarchal orders? I had imagined writing about women as astute pupils, transgressively educated to know and to become. Yet, as I dug deeper into Love’s Cure, it dawned upon me that

Clara the student was not the only female character who deserved the spotlight; Genevora the teacher did, too.

Thus began my journey into the world of female pedagogues, where I learned that female education does not consign women to the role of passive students. The Genevora and Rosalind that I have come to know are so much more than that: they are witty, they are compassionate, they are powerful. But most of all, they offer diverse (re)presentations of women as teachers—while both assume at least one other role, each takes a markedly different pedagogical approach: Rosalind cross-dresses and plays the physician while Genevora remains overtly feminine and performs as a mother as well as a lover. Naturally, their “transgressive reinscription” also carries markedly different implications. Rosalind temporarily relinquishes her femininity, establishes her credentials in two quintessentially masculine fields, and exacts her subversion from within. She dismantles—or at least, destabilizes—the master’s house using the master’s tools. This is a conscious decision on her part: she chooses to cross-dress as much as she chooses to teach. In fact, the success of her entire pedagogical agenda hinges on the fact that she is performing a masculine role, for Orlando has always been confined within an exclusively male world, and therefore only knows the principles perpetuated by men. Her transgression, then, lies in her endeavor to erode the epistemological system of gender from within.

On the other hand, I suspect that Genevora does not initially intend to teach, but when the occasion arises, she embraces the challenge beautifully and confidently. Unlike Rosalind, she loves as a woman and teaches as a woman. The question then becomes: what licenses

Genevora’s educational authority if not transvestism? The answer lies in another intriguing distinction between the two plays. In As You Like It, the characters’ genders are always clearly defined: Orlando performs the man, Rosalind the woman. Even when Rosalind is deceiving

Orlando, the audience can identify, at any given moment, all the layers of her gender performances: she is a boy actor playing a woman playing a man playing a woman. In Love’s

Cure, we deal with a much more complicated ambiguity: Lucio’s gender is entirely unintelligible to his contemporaries because the gender he is socialized into is incongruent with the gender associated with his sex at birth. Based on this premise, Love’s Cure probes into how this unreadability might challenge or transform teacherly authority and offers Genevora as a potential answer. She urges Lucio to embrace both his feminine and masculine sides and selectively to perform the gender that would be most suitable for each situation. This tutelage is in itself a

Butler-style manifestation of transgressive reinscription, for it destabilizes the idea of gender dimorphism and divulges how limited our set of gender categories has been.

In this regard, I find that As You Like It and Love’s Cure both offer wisdom to modern educators: whether they employ transvestism or celebrate gender fluidity, Rosalind and Genevora always have their students in mind; they tailor their approach to connect meaningfully with their students. In other words, our female pedagogues meet the students where they are. In them, we see a model for effective education: educators must be able to recognize, acknowledge, and encourage all the qualities that students possess (Genevora) and identify potential room for improvement (Rosalind).

title: Geospatial Evidence for Diversification Effects in Branch Banking Deposit Stability: A Case Study in Fracking
abstract: The heterogeneity of regional economies in the United States provides branch banks with plentiful opportunities to mitigate risk through geographic diversification. This paper introduces natural geography to the discussion of diversification in branch banking to examine the dynamics of deposit stability in the context of an economic shock. By developing a microeconomic index of geographic diversity by county, I assess how the emergence of hydraulic fracturing, or “fracking,” in the early 2010s impacted industry concentrations across five distinct regions. A regression discontinuity framework is applied to counties who concurrently began fracking operations and, as a counterfactual, the counties with which they share a border. Positive spatial autocorrelation of deposit variances between proximate branches is estimated to quantify the degree to which deposit stability is derived by location. Given the exogeneity of natural gas shale play discoveries, I construct a difference-in-differences model that identifies the directionality in which geographic diversity augmented the effect of fracking on deposit stability. My analysis reveals that geographically diverse branches mitigated the shock’s impact on deposits and in some cases even became more stable. I conclude that geographic diversification is positively associated with deposit stability, and that both interstate bank consolidations and online banking services are uniquely positioned to leverage this diversification advantage.
text:
Northwestern University March 17, 2021

Geospatial Evidence for Diversification Effects in Branch Banking Deposit Stability:

A Case Study in Fracking

JACOB WIESENTHAL

Abstract

The heterogeneity of regional economies in the United States provides branch banks with plentiful opportunities to mitigate risk through geographic diversification. This paper introduces natural geography to the discussion of diversification in branch banking in order to examine the dynamics of deposit stability in the context of an economic shock. By developing a microeconomic index of geographic diversity by county, I assess how the emergence of hydraulic fracturing or “fracking” in the early 2010s impacted industry concentrations across five distinct regions. A regression discontinuity framework is applied to counties who concurrently began fracking operations and, as a counterfactual, the counties with which they share a border. Positive spatial autocorrelation of deposit variances between proximate branches is estimated to quantify the degree to which deposit stability is derived by location. Given the exogeneity of natural gas shale play discoveries, I construct a difference-in-differences model that identifies the directionality in which geographic diversity augmented the effect of fracking on deposit stability. My analysis reveals that geographically diverse branches mitigated the shock’s impact on deposits and in some cases even became more stable. I conclude that geographic diversification is positively associated with deposit stability, and that both interstate bank consolidations and online banking services are uniquely positioned to leverage this diversification advantage.

Keywords: banks, geographic diversification, deposits, fracking

JEL Classification Codes: C3, C58, G11, G21, L71, Q33, R1

1 Introduction

Federally-insured banking in the United States is inherently shaped by the vastly diverse regional geographies of which it serves. Historically, intrastate branch banks have existed and adapted on a microeconomic level, optimizing each branch to synergize with the unique profiles of their local populations. With the passage of the Riegle-Neal Act in 1994, which enabled bank holding companies (BHCs) to acquire branches outside of their headquartered state, interstate banking was able to capitalize on this heterogeneity by inducing diversification through mergers and acquisitions. Hughes et al. (1999) examine the mass interstate consolidation of banks following the Riegle-Neal Act and identify significant gains in performance attributable to these mergers.1 Akhigbe and Whyte (2003) build on this theory and provide evidence that these gains are derived from a decrease in risk due to larger and more diversified branch portfolios.2

It is well understood that lending risk can be mitigated through the diversification of industries represented in a portfolio, and that doing so generally increases profitability. Demsetz and Strahan (1997) suggest that large BHCs are able to increase their leverage and charter more profitable loans because of a “diversification advantage” in which the heightened risk of such operations is counterbalanced by the stabilizing effect of diversified portfolios.3 However, there may also be diseconomies to interstate expansion in lending. Acharya, Hasan, and Saunders (2006) find evidence that a lack of localized lending experience, an inability to specialize, and potential complications in monitoring distant branches can offset the risk-based advantages

3 Demsetz, R. S., & Strahan, P. E. (1997). Diversification, size, and risk at bank holding companies. Journal of Money, Credit and

Banking, 29(3), 300.

2 Akhigbe, A., & Whyte, A. M. (2003). Changes in Market assessments of bank risk following the Riegle–Neal act of 1994.

Journal of Banking & Finance, 27(1), 87-102.

1References

Hughes, J. P., Lang, W. W., Mester, L. J., & Moon, C. (1999). The dollars and sense of bank consolidation. Journal of Banking &

Finance, 23(2-4), 291-324.

of lending diversification.4 Thus the effect on lending profitability through diversification-enabled leverage is understood to be contingent on the idiosyncratic management of BHCs.

However, unlike lending, geographic diversification as it pertains to branch deposits has not been the subject of sizable research following the rise of interstate banking in the United States. This paper seeks to reconcile the insights of previous literature on lending diversification with evidence concerning deposit stability as it relates to the geography of branch banks. In particular, I assess whether the geographic diversity of a regional economy is negatively associated with deposit variability in local branches, and by extension, whether geographically diversifying a portfolio of branches induces aggregate deposit stability for a bank.

Ascertaining an answer to these inquiries will complement our lending-based understanding of how diversification impacts bank performance. This is because the financial leverage of which diversification is found to enable may be the result of either increased stability in loan earnings or increased stability in the deposit bases on which leverage is measured. Maintaining a stable deposit base is critical to justifying enhanced leverage and is thus equally worthy of inspection.

Identifying the effects of geographic diversification on deposit stability is a more unidirectional problem than that of lending because, unlike loans, soliciting deposits from a more diverse clientele does not introduce significant diseconomies of expansion. Whereas information asymmetry and poor management may destabilize loan earnings, their effects are less profound in disrupting the stability of a branch’s deposit base. For this reason, evidence of diversification effects in deposit stability would, in combination with our lending-based understanding of interstate banking, suggest that geographically diversifying may be advantageous to branch banks in both lowering risk and increasing profitability.

Two key contributions to the econometric evaluation of this dynamic are made in this paper. First, geographic diversity is measured at a more microeconomic scope than in previous studies, adding precision to its description of regional economies. Second, deposit stability is assessed in the context of an economic shock (the emergence of hydraulic fracturing) in order to

4 Acharya, V., Hasan, I., & Saunders, A. (2006). Should banks be diversified? Evidence from individual bank loan portfolios. The

Journal of Business, 79(3), 1355-1412.

empirically test whether the effect of geographic diversity on stability is causal and significant.

1.1 Literature Review

Previous literature attempting to measure the implications of geographic diversification in banking has procedurally become more microeconomic but is generally limited to metrics of distance and quantity. Rivard and Thomas (1997) conducted one of the earliest studies to segment interstate banking presence by Federal Reserve Bank district in addition to a dummy variable representing whether a bank operates across states.5 Their results suggest that the advantages of geographic diversification in lowering risk are not only derived from an interstate presence, but also differ depending on which particular regions the bank’s branches are located in. This approach was expanded by Berger and DeYoung (2006) in estimating the efficiency of BHC branches by controlling for individual state fixed effects, as well as introducing a measurement of distance between each branch and the BHC’s headquarters.6 Deng and Elyasiani (2008) measure geographic diversification with an emphasis on this relationship between branch and headquarters, employing a Cobb-Douglas function of both distance and geographic dispersion.7 It should be noted, however, that while distance is a sensible predictor of difference, their connection is far from absolute. In a human geography as dispersed as that of the United States, it is not uncommon for greater distance from one city to, at some inflection, begin approaching another city more similar than any rural areas between the two. Therefore, there is an argument to be made that distance should not be relied on as a strict indicator of diversity.

Following Deng et al. (2007), a Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI) is constructed to represent the state and Metropolitan

7 Deng, S., & Elyasiani, E. (2008). Geographic diversification, bank holding company value, and risk. Journal of Money, Credit and

Banking, 40(6), 1217-1238.

6 Berger, A. N., & DeYoung, R. (2006). Technological progress and the geographic expansion of the banking industry. Journal of

Money, Credit, and Banking, 38(6), 1483-1513.

5 Rivard, R. J., & Thomas, C. R. (1997). The effect of interstate banking on large bank holding company profitability and risk.

Journal of Economics and Business, 49(1), 61-76.

Statistical Area (MSA) level concentration of a bank’s branches.8

A key development in Deng and Elyasiani’s second iteration of the measurement is the accounting of deposit dispersion, in which the HHI is weighted by the deposits held by each branch. This method calibrates the measure of geographic diversification to reflect the relative importance of each branch to the bank, assigning less weight to small branches and more weight to branches which represent a majority of the bank’s deposit base. They find that the relationship between geographic diversification and enhanced firm value is most significant for expansion to more remote MSAs, suggesting that the inclusion of rural regions in this body of analysis may elicit critical results which are currently unattainable from the mostly urban context of the literature.

In addition to the inability of these studies to extrapolate their results to rural banking, they are also limited in scope by the geographically broad indices of states and MSAs. Subregional economic differences within these geographies may lend inaccuracy to considering all states or MSAs as aggregately comparable exposures to risk, a condition which is generally assumed by these studies. However, as a more meticulous inspection of what it means to be geographically diverse, this paper does not make this assumption and instead allows for each subregion to contribute differently towards a measurement of a bank’s geographic diversification. This can be accomplished first by examining geography at a county level. Magnifying my measurement of geographic diversification by the 3,143 counties in the non-territory United States and the District of Columbia as opposed to its 384 MSAs grants larger sample sizes and enables proper analysis of rural banking. Further, the marginal contribution of each county to a bank’s measure of geographic diversification is, unlike previous studies, nonlinear and a function of the county’s risk profile as it differs from the rest of the counties where the bank has a presence.

Following the analysis of Hughes et al. (1999), which posits that macroeconomic diversification can be assessed as the standard deviation of the deposit-weighted average of unemployment rates across states, my measurement for geographic diversification is derived from the unique employment compositions of each county.1 In specific, the HHI is adapted to index all industries in a county as defined by the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) 2-digit code stratification. The contribution of each industry to the HHI is

8 Deng, S., Elyasiani, E., & Mao, C. X. (2007). Diversification and the cost of debt of bank holding companies. Journal of Banking &

Finance, 31(8), 2453-2473.

weighted by its share of total employment in the county as reported by the United States Census Bureau. As a result, this HHI not only describes the concentration of branches within geographical units, but also their concentration within subregional industries, hereafter referred to as “local industry exposures.”

This is an advantageous distinction when modeling deposit stability if assuming that the frequency and magnitude of client deposits and withdrawals are highly correlated with the frequency and magnitude of the client’s employment. That is, the more stable that employment is within a county, the more stable that the deposits in that county’s branches will be. Moreover, if diversification is to be interpreted as a mitigation of microeconomic shocks that affect particular locations or industries, then a county with a low concentration of employment by industry could be said to be diversified from potential microeconomic shocks to any one of them. By accounting for a county’s concentration of local industry exposures, my measurement of geographic diversification is closer linked to the fundamental roots by which deposit stability is inherited. Additionally, this methodology is applicable both to an analysis by branch and by bank, such that at either scope an appropriate measurement of geographic diversity is calculable. By this approach, a branch is geographically diverse if its respective county has a low concentration of employment by industry, and a bank is geographically diverse if its total deposits are dispersed among branches who are thusly diversified, both independently and as an aggregate.

1.2 Assessing Diversification in the Context of an Economic Shock

As previously mentioned, the inspection of geographic diversification in the context of economic shocks closer resembles the true dynamic by which diversity interacts with volatility. While simple measures of distance and quantity can approximate the risk mitigation of local industry exposures, the geography of banking is clustered, human-dependent, and ever-changing. Because deposit stability is a product of time, it can be thought of in terms of temporal changes in deposit bases as a result of economic growth and decline. The distinction of a stable deposit base is therefore most pronounced in the face of a transitional economic shock. Yet strictly financial analysis of economic shocks in banking typically either restricts implications of causality (due to endogeneity of the shock) or requires an instrument that limits predictive accuracy.9

Fortunately, the study of geography is uniquely disposed to present us with an abundance of natural experiments in which the resulting shocks can be understood as exogenous. Interpreting a shift in geographic diversification as an exogenous product of a natural, geographical event allows for its predicted effect on deposit stability to be causally attributed. This paper introduces insights from natural geography to the discussion of diversification in banking by examining the emergence of hydraulic fracturing or “fracking” in the early 2010s. During this period, banks were unable to proactively account for the rapid growth of the fracking industry, given the discovery of new technology, natural gas shale plays, and estimates suggesting unforeseen volumes of productivity.10 As such, the disruption to regional employment caused by the fracking industry can be translated into shifts in geographic diversity for proximate branches. Likewise, the degree to which our diversification measure was affected by fracking can be causally linked to patterns observed in these branches’ deposit stability.

2 A Case Study in Fracking

While the technique of hydraulic fracturing as a method of extracting shale gas has been known since first experimented with in 1947, high-volume horizontal fracking was not considered commercially viable until the late 1980s when an operation in the Austin Chalk formation of southeastern Texas began employing slickwater to increase fluid flow rates.11

Applying this slickwater treatment to natural gas shales proved highly effective and became exponentially adopted by energy firms in Texas leading up to the turn of the 21st century. Industrial-scale fracking spread within a matter of years from the

11 Bell, C., Holmes, B., & Rickards, A. (1993). Effective diverting on horizontal wells in the Austin Chalk. SPE Annual Technical

Conference and Exhibition, Houston, Texas.

10 Engelder, T., & Lash, G. G. (2008, May). Marcellus Shale Play’s

Vast Resource Potential Creating Stir In Appalachia. The American

Oil & Gas Reporter, 1(5).

9 Cai, W., Xu, F., & Zeng, C. (2016). Geographical diversification and bank performance: Evidence from China. Economics Letters,

147, 96-98.

Barnett Shale of central Texas to the Bakken, Eagle Ford, and Woodford shales, stretching the entire vertical length of the Great Plains.

When a series of studies released in 2008 proposed that the Appalachian Basin held far more potential for natural gas production than previously thought, with some estimates of the Marcellus shale rising over 250 times the volumes proposed by the U.S. Geological Survey, economic interest in the industry skyrocketed.10 An Environment Protection Agency (EPA) study on the proximity of fracking sites to drinking water resources found that 14,560 new wells commenced fracking operations in 2012 as compared to just 1,809 in 2005,12 a majority of the new locations targeting the Marcellus and Utica shales of the upper Appalachians and the Niobrara-Mowry shales of the Rocky Mountains.

2.1 Stratifying Counties by the Presence of Fracking

To identify the effects that these new wells had on their regional economies in the context of geographic diversity, I transform the data collected by the EPA into a collection of counties which saw at least one new well begin fracking operations within their borders during 2012. This group of counties includes both those which had fracking activities take place within their borders prior to 2012 and those for which the observed wells were the county’s first instance of fracking. Because our analysis isolates the consequences of the operations in 2012 in particular, this distinction is negligible. Counties included within this group are hereafter referred to as “fracking counties” to simply denote their classification.

12 U.S. EPA. Hydraulic Fracturing for Oil and Gas: Impacts from the Hydraulic Fracturing Water Cycle on Drinking Water

Resources in the United States (Final Report). U.S. Environmental

Protection Agency, Washington, DC, EPA/600/R-16/236F, 2016.

Figure 1. Map of hydraulic fracturing well locations that began operating in 2012. From U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. (2016). Hydraulic Fracturing for Oil and Gas [Map].

In obtaining a control group against which the fracking counties can be compared, I employ a geographically discontinuous treatment methodology in which I sample counties which did not have any fracking operations begin within their borders in 2012, but share a border of any length or coordinate with one or more fracking counties. These counties are hereafter referred to as “bordering counties” to indicate their relationship to the fracking counties. The use of these bordering counties as a control for the fracking counties takes advantage of the core insight behind the geographic regression discontinuity framework and benefits from its weak assumptions. Keele and Titiunik (2015) describe these as a natural spatial correlation between attributes of bordering locations, where the absence of their respective border would not significantly alter their aggregate demographics, markets, and other fixed effects.13 Fracking counties and bordering counties are assumed to be geographically similar where proximate, and therefore exhibit analogous trends in banking before the treatment of fracking.

13 Keele, L. J., & Titiunik, R. (2015). Geographic boundaries as regression discontinuities. Political Analysis, 23(1), 127-155.

While the number of wells in each county is not uniformly distributed across regions, this disparity is reflected instead in the varying increases in fracking employment and their corresponding effects on our measurements of geographic diversity following the year 2012. Of notable mention, there appear to be five defining formations that constitute a majority of the counties depicted. These clusters, from west to east, coincide with the Bakken, Woodford, Barnett, Eagle Ford, and Marcellus shales, respectively. Counties in the center of these clusters, despite having wells begin fracking in 2012, are dropped from the following analysis because they do not share a border with any non-fracking county and thus cannot be evaluated within the outlined geographically discontinuous treatment methodology.

As mentioned earlier, pursuing a county-level scope greatly standardizes the size of each observation in contrast to MSAs, whose erratic sizes are difficult to compare spatially. Apart from the more expansive observed counties of the Rocky Mountains, which are still generally comparable between neighbors, the 250 fracking counties and 393 bordering counties are consistent in size and representative of both urban and rural environments. Therefore, my modeling of these counties can account for the natural differences between urban and rural economies and prove applicable in either case.

3 Hypothesis Development

Given the literature on geographic diversification as it pertains to lending risk and the mechanisms by which industry diversity may be tied to deposit stability, it would intuitively follow that there is some relationship between the geographic diversification of a bank’s branches and the stability of their deposits. Namely, a low concentration of industries in a county is likely to mitigate the effect of any industry-dependent microeconomic shock on the deposits in proximate banks. This dynamic necessitates that deposit stability be at least partially derived from its geography, and therefore I expect to observe spatial autocorrelation in

Figure 2. Map of fracking counties and bordering counties as defined by the presence of hydraulic fracturing wells that began operating in 2012.

deposit stability across all counties. As such, I will test the following hypothesis:

H1: Deposit stability is positively spatially autocorrelated between branches.

If, in fact, spatial autocorrelation is observed in the deposit stability between counties, then it would be appropriate to regress deposit stability on a geographically-based index such as my modified HHI. More specifically, in the context of fracking, I expect the emergence of fracking to have variable effects on the measured diversity of fracking counties, depending on whether a county was previously concentrated in the energy sector. The dynamic effects on deposit stability of the treatment of fracking can then be translated into bank-level insights. Based on the arguments given above, I expect this relationship to be positive and causal. In other words:

H2: Geographic diversification is positively associated with deposit stabilization.

Not only this, but by taking the economic shock of fracking as exogenous, this relationship can be inferred as causal, proposing geographic diversification as a tool by which banks can intentionally mitigate variability and potentially increase their leverage of deposits.

4 Data and Methodology

Industry and employment data by county are obtained from the United States Census Bureau’s County Business Patterns (CBP) series across the 7-year period of 2009 to 2015.14 The CBP provides information on total employment by county as well as the employment of each NAICS 2-digit industry present in the county. Information on the location of fracking operations commencing in 2012 is given by the EPA’s 2016 report on Hydraulic Fracturing for Oil and Gas,12 and this data is consolidated with the CBP series to categorize fracking counties and bordering counties by the dummy variable fracking. Deposit data by branch is acquired from the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) Summary of Deposits (SOD) for all

14 United States Census Bureau County Business Patterns (CBP).

(2021, February 9). Retrieved from https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/cbp.html.

FDIC-insured banking institutions.15 The SOD database is used to segment banks by organizational structure using the categorical variable bhc, which denotes the type of holding company associated with each branch (a one bank holding company, a multi-bank holding company, or neither). I also use the SOD annual deposit balance variable deposits to calculate a three-year moving coefficient of variation as an inverse measure of the stability of deposits in each branch, deposits_cv. Because the coefficient of variation, unlike a standard deviation, is normalized for all branches irrespective of the magnitude of deposits, the estimated effect of the diversification variable on deposit stability will not be directly influenced by branch size.

My sample procedure draws only FDIC-insured branches belonging to a non-unit bank and therefore being a member of a branch portfolio. These branches are then sorted by the FDIC’s branch service type classification (brsertyp), from which I only select those which accept on-site client deposits as a brick and mortar, retail, or drive-through office (codes 11, 12, and 23). I obtain 21,542 branches meeting this criteria belonging to 1,590 distinct banking institutions. The panel format of the data is balanced by year with each year’s observations representing between 13.40% and 14.84% of the total observations. Lastly, the SOD data is matched with the CBP industry and employment data to assign county-level statistics to each branch’s observations.

4.3 Identifying Geographic Diversification Effects on Deposit Stability

To empirically test H2, I construct a quasi-experimental difference-in-differences model which estimates the causal effect of a change in geographic diversity on deposit stability. The temporal trend in deposit stability among the bordering counties which did not receive the treatment of new fracking operations in 2012 serves as a counterfactual to the fracking counties which did experience this exogenous shock. Subject to the validity of the parallel trend assumption, which in this case would necessitate that annual changes in deposit stability pre-2012 were symmetric in both fracking counties and bordering counties, this model will identify the causal treatment effect of being located within a fracking county in 2012 on a branch’s subsequent change in deposit stability. Using the natural log of deposits_cv to interpret percentage changes in deposit stability as a log-linear function of the treatment and its covariates, I estimate the following model:

𝑙𝑛_𝑑𝑒𝑝𝑜𝑠𝑖𝑡𝑠_𝑐𝑣𝑖𝑡= β0 + β1 * 𝑝𝑜𝑠𝑡𝑖𝑡+ β2 * 𝑓𝑟𝑎𝑐𝑘𝑖𝑛𝑔𝑖𝑡+ β3 * 𝑏𝑟𝑎𝑛𝑐ℎ_𝑑𝑖𝑣𝑖𝑡+ where αi is the branch fixed effect and μt is the year fixed effect. Of most importance are the coefficients of β4 and β7, which can be interpreted as the treatment effect of fracking in 2012 on a branch’s deposit stability and the degree to which this effect differed by the geographic diversity of that branch’s county, respectively. In particular, the coefficient of the triple interaction term postit*frackingit*branch_divit will indicate the directionality in which geographic diversity impacts deposit stability for branches and, by proxy, for their parent banks.

5.2 Difference-in-Differences Model

Annualized trends in deposit stability by geography can be visualized in Figure 5, which plots the median deposit variance for both fracking counties and bordering counties by year. The parallel trend assumption is assessed for the years 2010 to 2015, as banking diagnostics in 2009 were exogenously impacted by the global financial crisis of that year. As illustrated in the line plot, deposit stability in both fracking counties and bordering counties experienced parallel shifts across all years except 2012, in which fracking counties became more stable while bordering counties became less stable. This inequality was sustained for all years following 2012, as the median deposits_cv in fracking counties remained roughly 3% less than that of bordering counties.

At a glance, the magnitude of diversification effects in the context of the economic shock of fracking is estimated to be roughly eight times greater (and far more statistically discernible) than its magnitude as estimable without considering the shock.

To assess the robustness of the model, I first test the null hypotheses that the covariates bhc and brsertyp are equal to 0 and calculate the two leftmost results of Table 3. The covariates bhc and brsertyp are determined to be different than 0 and statistically significant at the 5% and 0.1% levels, respectively. The year fixed effects are determined to be different than 0 and statistically significant at the 0.1% level. Thus, the model is justified in including these covariates and fixed effects.

Noteworthy is the strongly positive coefficient corresponding to branches with the FDIC branch service type of 23, representing drive-through offices. The estimate suggests that, as compared to typical brick and mortar offices, branches offering drive-through depositing services are much more prone to deposit instability, especially in the face of an economic shock such as fracking. This makes intuitive sense given the relatively low opportunity costs to clients of making drive-through deposits and withdrawals without having to physically enter the branch.

As an additional robustness assessment, a second model is estimated with random effects in place of branch fixed effects and compared against the original model in accordance with the Hausman (1978) econometric model specification test.17 The results of the specification test are given in Table 4, which rejects the null hypothesis that there is no systematic difference in the estimated coefficients given either fixed or random effects. Therefore, the inclusion of branch fixed effects in my model is justified. An important intuition as to why branch fixed effects are key covariates in modeling geographic diversity lies in their derivation. Since a branch will be located within the same county for all years observed in the dataset, the fixed effects of its county are inherited within the branch fixed effects when absorbed. By including branch fixed effects, the model not only controls for static characteristics of each branch such as locational advantages and management style, but also controls for static characteristics of each branch’s county such as demographics and, to an extent, its competitive landscape of banking.

Together, the treatment effect and its triple interaction with geographic diversity are substantiated by the above statistical robustness analysis. More importantly, it tells a story consistent with both the proposed underlying mechanisms of diversification and the existing literature on branch banking, exogenous economic shocks, and the industry of fracking. As hypothesized, the introduction of fracking as an exogenous economic shock was an industry-specific destabilizing event whose effect on deposit stability was augmented by geographic
