title: The DMCA in Action: Copyright Law, Algorithmic Censorship, and Free Speech in The Internet Age
text:
The DMCA in Action: Copyright Law, Algorithmic Censorship, and Free Speech in the Internet Age

Brian Vogel

3/14/2022

INTRODUCTION

In 1998, during the infancy of the internet, Congress began holding legislative sessions and committee meetings to construct the legal mechanisms necessary to regulate this brave new technology. One of the largest questions posed to the legislature was related to the liability of copyright infringing content on online spaces mediated by a third party. Online content never exists purely independently – a content-hosting platform is required to broadcast content through the world wide web. This left an important question of legal responsibility: if someone illegally posts copyrighted material, who is to become liable? The individual user who illegally posted copyrighted intellectual property, or the third-party content hosting platform that disseminates the infringing material? To answer this question, Congress established the Digital Millennium

Copyright Act (DMCA), an act that established the modern interface of legal structures that governs legality in online spaces to this day.

The DMCA lays out a series of hoops that content hosting platforms and users are required to jump-through in order to discern liability. The user is liable for copyright infringing material, but rather than immediate litigation, the remedy is for third party platforms to de-platforming the infringing material. This de-platforming is carried out by the content-hosting platform on behalf of the copyright holder, but these platforms have not escaped liability. If they refuse to take down any claimed material, these platforms then take on the liability for any copyright infringement, should the justice system decide if such infringement occurred. This fear of liability has incentivized platforms to wield content-removing tools with absolute and unchecked restraint, using automated filtering algorithms to remove all content with even the prospect of copyright liability, often without the instruction of the Internet Protocol (I.P.). holder.

This has empowered some bad-faith actors to abuse this system. This abuse comes in two forms:

reporting copyrighted material for a purpose other than remedying the copyright misuse, or claiming legal material as copyrighted, knowing that platforms will remove the content without doing due-diligence. Indeed, no such requirement for due-diligence exists in the DMCA, giving content hosting platforms all-powerful control over what types of online speech are “legal” or

“illegal”.

In the Trump era, when concerns over the truth and validity of what is said online became a well-known concern, the phenomenon of DMCA abuse became somewhat mainstream. I aim to investigate how the DMCA differs in intention from execution with regards to freedom of speech online. The particular angle this investigation seeks to tackle is related to the mechanization of DMCA claim management through algorithms. Too much content is posted each and every day for a human to analyze and verify that it is copyright compliant, so platforms employ algorithms to automatically filter content based on broad, indiscriminate criteria. The use and effect of these algorithms were a total blindspot of the DMCA, and their use has radically altered what is allowed to be said on the internet. I therefore sought to examine: How were copyright-law algorithms for content-hosting platforms exploited to control speech online between 2016-2020?

ANALYSIS

SECTION I

[omitted from condensed version]

SECTION II

Between the years 2016 and 2020, when the political climate was ripe for mistrusting any information disseminated online, the ways in which the DMCA was used as a tool to silence internet-based content became thrust into the spotlight. Much has been written of the DMCA’s potential to economically harm online content creators, but comparatively little has been written about how the very same law can be exploited to politically harm an individual.

Algorithms are pieces of code that are used to carry out a specific function1. Their use is varied, but where the DMCA is concerned, algorithms are used to recognize patterns on a volume incapable of individual human examination2. These content hosting platforms see incalculable amounts of content uploaded each day, which raises a problem with regards to being

DMCA compliant. According to DMCA Section 512, a content hosting platform is liable to be sued for copyright infringement if they maintain the infringing content on their platform after a claim has been filed by the holder of the copyright. Because of the sheer volume of content, it is impossible for groups of people to comb through all of the content and manually identify copyrighted material3. The platforms therefore employ algorithms to flag copyrighted material and remove it in order to avoid liability4. This system has two main problems however: first, the pattern recognition of these algorithms cannot match human pattern recognition, which leads to

DMCA-compliant content being filtered out on account of overzealous algorithms protecting the platform. Second, in order to minimize red tape and liability and maximize efficiency, copyrighted content is removed without the consultation of the holder of the copyright.

One of the through-lines in the presented examples is overzealous claiming of material via algorithms with little to no human oversight. Three of the five examples below deal with copyright claims that removed content that would have been deemed acceptable if a nuanced and

4 Nighat Mir, “Copyright for Web Content Using Invisible Text Watermarking,” Computers in Human Behavior no. 30 (January 2014): 648–53.

3Joel D. Matteson, "Unfair Misuse: How Section 512 of the DMCA Allows Abuse of the Copyright Fair Use Doctrine and How to Fix It," Santa Clara High Technology Law Journal 35, no. 2 (November 2018): 1-22.

2 Niva Elkin-Koren, "Contesting Algorithms: Restoring the Public Interest in Content Filtering by Artificial Intelligence," Big Data & Society 7, no. 2 (2020).

1 Xiaoqiang Ma, Jiangchuan Liu, and Hongbo Jiang, “On the Design of Algorithms for Mobile Multimedia Systems: A Survey,” International Journal of Communication Systems 24, no. 10 (October 2011): 1330–39.

properly-discerning human actor was to have considered the validity of these claims instead of an algorithm, whose only job is to automatically protect corporate interests. The absence of the intervention of a copyright holder makes the actions of these algorithms all the more egregious – since an algorithm cannot manually prove the person filing the complaint is the valid copyright holder, any claim – no matter how spurious – is treated as a valid concern, even if that is not the case. Both examples one and three are valid and protected forms of speech whose objector was not the copyright holder for the material called into question, but an unrelated third party. The algorithm therefore empowers neither the copyright holder nor the consumer, but instead empowers any bad-faith actor unscrupulous enough to exploit this system.

This system is ripe for exploitation because the DMCA offers little to no consumer protections. Platforms are free to utilize algorithms to censor content without the interest of the content creator nor the copyright holder, only the interest of the platform. The ability for the

DMCA to create exploitable systems of algorithmic enforcement has undoubtedly exposed the

DMCA’s shortcomings, which can be interrogated through the following examples:

Example 1: Officer James Knoblauch, a police officer in Oglesby, Illinois, was attempting to make an arrest at an office in LaSalle County. A civilian began to record the officer on her phone, and when Knoblauch turned around and noticed he was being filmed, he immediately pulled out his phone and began to play a Blake Shelton song at full volume in an attempt to trigger copyright detecting algorithms to keep the video of the arrest from being uploaded online.5

The noteworthy aspects of this example include the degree of knowledge exhibited by the actors, the absence of the intervention of a copyright holder, and the hierarchies present in this

5Tim Cushing, "Officer Claims Sheriff's Office Told Him To Play Copyrighted Music To Shut Down Citizens' Recording,". Newstex Blogs Techdirt. September 13, 2021 situation. First, this case is noteworthy in that all parties involved (the person under arrest not included) were aware of how copyright-filtering algorithms currently operate. The officer knew how these algorithms could be exploited, and the person recording the officer vocally calls out this deliberate tactic in the video footage. This is indicative of how widespread this phenomenon actually is, and its media coverage is only giving more ammunition to those with similar jobs and incentives. Second, the copyright holder is not present anywhere in the incident. Blake Shelton and his publisher, Universal Music Group, never filed a copyright claim against the video, and yet it was claimed and taken down. There is a possibility that the use of his song as a tool of suppressing police accountability may be against the interest of the copyright holder, but those interests were never taken into account. The final noteworthy aspect is that this incident exposes how the DMCA and the algorithms that uphold it can be used to reinforce hierarchies. Law enforcement being held above the common citizen, the use of an internet copyright law to maintain such a hierarchy is a pointed example of how these systems are codified into law in unexpected ways.

Example 2: In 2017, famous YouTube star PewDiePie released a stream of himself playing video games wherein he made several racist insults and casual pro-Nazi jokes. Members of the audience who were offended by such comments attempted to get the video taken down on the grounds that it violated YouTube’s guidelines regarding harassment and hate speech. When no remedy to this complaint materialized, the same people reported the video for copyright misuse, which led to the video being taken down almost immediately, and landing PewDiePie in a lengthy YouTube suspension6

6 Mona Ibrahim, “Firewatch Creators can Target PewDiePie with DMCA Takedowns, and it’s Perfectly Legal” Polygon (Sep 17, 2017)

This example is interesting in that the relatively positive outcome of the story also serves as an example as to why the systems relied upon to achieve this outcome are worrying. The

DMCA was utilized in preventing the proliferation of hate speech – it is a clear example of those with less power (the audience) leveraging the legal system to hold a party with a considerable amount of power (the wealthy YouTube star) to account. What is troubling is that copyright liability was the only incentive taken into account by the platform. It is an unfortunate example about the priorities of content hosting spaces like YouTube: harassment, hate speech, and violations of community guidelines were met with apathy, while the only complaint these platforms are willing to take seriously are those revolving around copyright and the DMCA. It is a clear value-judgment on the part of the law and the platforms that copyright liability is a priority over the health and safety of their user base.

It’s also an example of algorithmic abuse. The copyright claim immediately triggered a takedown algorithm, but after a several month battle, the content was evaluated to fall within the

“fair use” guideline of the DMCA, denoting the copyright claim as having been made in bad faith7. Hate speech is something that is tied to moral and social values, a concept that is challenging for an algorithm to recognize. No such value judgment needs to be made for copyrighted material however, especially when the legal security of a company is on the line.

This example shows that human resources need only be employed when non-legal issues arise, such as those of harassment, but no human resources are needed in cases concerning the DMCA.

The implications for algorithms and algorithmic censorship online in relation to free speech are of foremost importance. As established in section one, the very existence of

7 The “Fair Use” determination is a process that requires human intervention, given that it relies on pattern recognition not currently available in modern algorithm technology. When evaluating a subject for fair use, the platform needs to determine if the alleged infringing material is suitably “transformative” in relation to the original work, common examples being parody, education, and criticism.

content-filtration algorithms was never imagined by the authors of the DMCA because their scope for internet use was so limited. But the question remains as to whether the implementation of these algorithms was inevitable, or if the constraints and expectations established by the

DMCA propelled their widespread adoption. This analysis concludes that it is the latter. This is because the DMCA elevates the power of the Section 512 “notice and takedown” feature of the law above protections for the content creator by legally mandating Section 512, but only legally suggesting consumer protections. There are a few key consumer protections built into the

DMCA, such as the “fair use” protection, which defends consumers from copyright infringement if their content is suitably transformative from the original material. However, the way the

DMCA allocates legal penalties in such a lopsided way makes this nearly irrelevant in the face of algorithmic content filtration. YouTube or Facebook face consequences for hosting copyright content, but do NOT face consequences for removing content, regardless of fair use or the established precedents surrounding freedom of speech. This incentivizes harsh censorship that can be carried out by unfeeling, uncaring machines.

Example 3: In 2020, a Black Lives Matter protest held in Douglas County, Nevada was being live-streamed as a way to drum up support for the ongoing movement. Protesters numbered approximately 30-40 people, but counter protesters numbered in the hundreds. As the protest march proceeded into the streets lined with counter protesters, members of the counterprotest began to blast country music, and within minutes the livestream was terminated prematurely due to copyright infringement8

This example is consistent with the hierarchical evaluation presented in example one, but also illustrates a clear divide between freedom of speech on and offline. In this scenario, both

8 Kelly Penrose, “BLM Protest in Douglas County Draws Hundreds of Counter-protestors, Militia” Sierra Nevada Ally, (Aug 9, 2020)

protestor and counter-protestor are entitled to a right to assemble and express their freedom of speech, but those rights are no longer represented when this speech becomes digitized into its online form. This is consistent with Marceau and Chen’s legal analysis of how the DMCA inconsistently holds freedom of speech to a different standard online than off.9 The algorithmic regulation is also noteworthy in this case because the ability of censorship to occur in real time.

The ability to enforce a DMCA copyright ban was immediately effectuated during a live stream

– this is not a case where a piece of content was removed following its completion and posting, it was censored mid-creation, giving platform filtration algorithms the power to immediately censor speech in a chilling way. A piece of speech cannot be challenged in its entirety, but can be challenged before the completion of the speech based on alleged copyright misuse that was determined by an inhuman mechanism

Example 4: In 2016, a London-based children’s charity posted a negative review of construction company BuildFirm on a review forum called Mumsnet. Several days after posting the negative review, Google sent Mumsnet a notice and takedown order that her negative comment had been removed for violating DMCA policy. No copyright infringement had occurred. Instead, the review was copied verbatim into a separate web page entirely, which then retroactively copyrighted the bad review’s exact language in order to trigger the review as being flaggable for copyright misuse. It would later come out that employees of Buildfirm had done this maneuver deliberately. Google rejected the counterclaim by Mumsnet, and the review thread was removed entirely.10

10 Alex Hern, “Revealed: How Copyright Law is Being Misused to Remove Material from the Internet” The Guardian (May 23, 2016)

9 Justin Marceau and Alan K. Chen, “Free Speech and Democracy in the Video Age,” Columbia Law Review 116, no. 4 (2016): 991–1062; Their analysis is a legal exercise by which they take court precedent for various free speech cases and apply the given precedent to an online space, exposing how speech online does not align with constitutional law set about by the First Amendment

The implications for this particular example are threefold. The first implication is one of internationality and the consequences of the DMCA on a global stage. Despite the United

Kingdom having entirely separate copyright jurisdiction than the United States, Google – the company who hosts Mumsnet – is an American company, and is thus subject to regulation by the

DMCA, and American law. This essentially makes a huge section of the internet the legal domain of the United States, giving the U.S. unprecedented authority to control the flow of information on a global scale. The second implications of this case-study concern corporate and economic sabotage. The DMCA was not only used to limit the free speech of the charity in question, but it was done so with an economic motivation in mind. The BuildFirm scheme to copyright a bad review and use that as the basis for a DMCA claim was directly motivated by

BuildFirm’s bottom line. In the internet age when a bad review carries weight for the future success of a business, the freedom of speech of the actors involved is no longer an abstract political idea, but an economic force that poses a threat to certain companies.

Another implication is centered on the lack of due-diligence on the part of Google, and the lack of consequences for this mistreatment of internet-users. The remedy for an illegitimate

DMCA takedown is known as a counterclaim – a feature whereby the injured party can protest against the filtration of their content by filing a complaint to the content-hosting platform11. The ways in which these claims are handled varies from platform to platform, but because each platform is a private company, the regulation of the counterclaim function is internal. There is no external force that mandates counterclaims be taken seriously12. This gives content-hosting

12 Wendy Setzer, "Free Speech Unmoored in Copyright’s Safe Harbor: Chilling Effects of the DMCA on the First Amendment," Harvard Journal of Law & Technology, 24, no. 171 (Fall, 2010).

11 Alan Gocha, "A Modern System for Resolving Online Copyright Infringement Disputes: Administrative Rulemaking and adjudication, a One-Stop Fix to The Digital Millennium Copyright Act," IDEA: The Journal of the Franklin Pierce Center for Intellectual Property, 58, no. 131 (2018).

companies no real incentive to take these claims seriously. If they accept the counterclaim as valid in error, the platform becomes liable for copyright infringement, and verifying the validity of a counterclaim can be a costly process because it cannot be easily managed by an algorithm.13

Therefore, the only incentive companies have to take counterclaims seriously is to ensure the trust of their user base, which is not a strong incentive given the fact that most users will not switch to a competing platform over this type of controversy. There is also a degree of intersection between the first and third implication. The international nature of the incident means that if an individual in a foreign country wanted to bring a platform to court over their lack of due-diligence processing DMCA counterclaims, that remedy would not be available because the DMCA would be a law in a completely separate country.

The nature of this exploitation is another key implication. The DMCA – not just its algorithmic enforcers - is an incredibly exploitable law in a way that was not intended. Its exploitability is partially due to the universality of the internet; the internet is a tool used by a majority of people every single day, and that volume of use allows its user-base to become familiar with its mechanisms fairly quickly and fairly intimately. Both officer Knobloch and

BuildFirm were so aware of the law’s driving Section 512 mechanism that they were able to bend that mechanism to their own ends. Likewise, this controversy demonstrates that internet users do not approach the DMCA with the same skepticism for the law as is ordinary. Law is often regarded by a majority of the public as an arcane set of rules outside the scope of knowledge for the average lay-person14, but this is not so with the DMCA. The governing

14 Justin Marceau and Alan K. Chen, “Free Speech and Democracy in the Video Age,” Columbia Law Review 116, no. 4 (2016):

13 Zoe Carpou, "Robots, Pirates, and the Rise of the Automated Takedown Regime: Using the DMCA to Fight Piracy and Protect End-Users," Columbia Journal of Law & the Arts 39, no. 4 (2016): 551-590 mechanisms for a tool as important as the internet have made the widespread understanding of the law ripe for exploitation.

The intent of the DMCA is also affirmed by the transnational influence of U.S copyright law. This topic was arguably the most central ideal underpinning the DMCA. Congress was looking for a way to make the U.S the dominant force in the new internet landscape, and the system they devised whereby content-hosting platforms are the nexus for the legal viability of online content made that ideal a reality. If anyone – regardless of location – wants to post content, they need to be mediated by a U.S-based content hosting platform, and because the

DMCA regulates these platforms, it also regulates users across the globe.

Example 5: The Nicaraguan election of 2020 saw large protests against reigning President Daniel

Ortega. The state sponsored news media being unwilling to cover such protests, protesters turned to independent and international journalism to spread the word about the protests. The Ortega regime filed several false DMCA claims against reporting unsympathetic to his rule, falsely claiming the reporting was copyright infringing, leading YouTube to remove all coverage of the protest.15

This example is profoundly chilling in the way in which it demonstrates the power transnational corporations have over international politics. This case demonstrates how the abstraction of information through multiple mediums can disrupt the flow of information. The message of the protest is communicated through journalists, who communicate their journalism through content-hosting corporations like YouTube, who then broadcast that journalism through telecommunications networks. If any link in this chain becomes disrupted, the availability of information becomes compromised, and the fact that corporations with monied interests hold

15 Danae Vilchez, “YouTube Censors Independent Nicarguan News Outlets after Copyright Complaint from Ortega-Owned Media,” Committee to Protect Journalists; (May 6, 2020)

these links establishes a system where information can only be disseminated if that information is deemed profitable. Other noteworthy elements of this case include its international scale and political implications. The example falls in line with the precedent set by Google v. Equustek, demonstrating the intentional international reach of the DMCA – here though, the sovereign law of one nation is being upheld by the sovereign law of the United States, rather than being challenged16. The DMCA is therefore a political impediment, given its sweeping censorship capabilities on a global scale.

The previous examples demonstrate the fulfillment of the DMCA’s intent in a somewhat sinister way. The pre-eminence of U.S. law is undeniable: these are definitive cases where the

DMCA’s global reach is explicitly shown, but the context of that global reach is controversial. In both cases, the international reach of the DMCA was wasn’t used to protect U.S. copyright holders, but was instead used to attack some outside party, be it Mumsnet or independent

Nicaraguan journalists. The DMCA is not acting as a shield for U.S. markets on a global stage, but is instead used as a weapon to control international internet use with laws that constrain non-U. S. online action. This is a tightrope has yet to collapse, but remains precarious:

company’s suffer damage to their reputation when bad-faith DMCA claims exploit their platforms, and because this is an international affair, the profit motivation to let this occur is much weaker than a similar domestic infraction. These platforms are currently exchanging international reputation for international control, but the future of this transaction is uncertain.

Finally, the implications with regards to the establishment of user rights are defined by what rights each respective algorithm permits. The section two examples highlight that content filtration platforms are highly sensitive to music and quoted text. User rights extend in so far as

16 Robert Diab, "Search Engines and Global Takedown Orders: Google v Equustek and the Future of Free Speech Online," Osgoode Hall Law Journal 56, no. 2 (Winter 2019): 231-270 they can avoid these easily flagged categories, which is extremely tenuous given that, in situations of live recording or text-based commenting, any actor can take away the user’s right to post, regardless of the legality of said post. User rights are therefore constrained, left to the mercy of platforms too large and complex to guarantee these rights in any legally-recognized way.

CONCLUSION

The modern internet is a necessity to most people in The United States. Millions of businesses, livelihoods, and creative projects rely on content hosting platforms to function, which is a precarious position given that a single bad-faith actor or algorithmic misfire can damage or destroy anyone’s online contributions. The legal landscape of such a necessary space invests all-powerful authority in machines who are incapable of filtering content using the nuance and sensitivity required to accurately weigh the merits of copyright. Going forward, the framework of the DMCA needs to change. The internet no longer exists in the halcyon days of

1998, before Google, Facebook, and YouTube even existed, and the internet’s seminal governing law must reflect this fact.

I advocate for a legal mechanism that requires content hosting platforms demonstrate a greater degree of due-diligence when investigating copyright claims. I also advocate for the regulation of copyright-filtration algorithms, and suggest that future research be conducted into the specificities of these algorithms. The code for these algorithms is guarded by the platforms that utilize them, but any in-depth analysis of these codes would be invaluable to advancing this field of inquiry. This field is also in need of more meta-analysis. How many claims are done in bad faith? How many are made in error by an algorithm? How many counterclaims get ignored or under-investigated? These types of raw data would be especially useful in a future policy proposal. While these algorithms are a necessary function for a large, complex internet, they ought not to be the final, unchallengeable arbiters of who is allowed to speak in online spaces.

title: ‘The End of All Things’ & Other Works
text:
‘The End of All Things’ & Other Works

AUDREY Clarendon

Email: audreyclarendon2026@u.northwestern.edu

BIO

My name is Audrey Clarendon and I’m a current sophomore from northwest Missouri studying Physics & Astronomy and Art Theory & Practice. I spent last summer researching how to capture the abstract feelings of those afflicted by the poorly understood Depersonalization/Derealization disorder, in which a person disconnects from their sense of self and/or their surroundings. I chose to investigate the condition through visual art, specifically oil painting, as it has a demonstrated ability to capture the intangible.

Table of Contents

The end of all things

Through the eyelids (Participant vs. Observer)

Abducted in plain sight (Le coup de vide)

As the veil lifts (What once was is no more)

title: A Pipeline Flows Both Ways: Contradictions of an Activist Trajectory
text:
A Pipeline Flows Both Ways: Contradictions of an Activist Trajectory

Lucy London

Senior Honors Thesis, Department of Performance Studies

April 2023

In the Beginning: Maple Syrup Spring

In the beginning there was sap. It was late March, just around Zisbawktoke Gises—the Maple Sugar Moon[1]—and spring was starting to warm the ground. I had traveled up to northern Minnesota for my spring break with two comrades from Chicago and Madison. We pulled up to the Welcome Water Protectors camp in Aitkin County. Signs along the road read “Water Is Life,” “Land Back,” and “Honor the Treaties.” Things were quiet as we entered camp. A kind woman explained that Enbridge was waiting to drill until the ice melted, the ice blanketing the Mississippi. Water protectors who usually kept up camp were using this hiatus as a time to rest or go home to family. We were eager to help out, and asked what needed to be done around the camp. She offered us the task of going down to the Mississippi River, just a short stroll from camp, to see if the ice had melted and if the river was flowing yet. She said it would be coming soon— any day now. As we walked there we passed another sign: “Down to the River to Pray.” I started humming the Allison Krause tune and my companions joined in. As we came upon the Great Mississippi, we saw movement. My stomach dropped.

Water was flowing. Never had I dreaded so much the end of winter. Pieces of ice floated away on ripples of water, and the river was coming alive with the turn of the season. The awakening of spring meant the hiatus was over; drilling was to begin.

We sat by the river for a while. It was the first time I had seen the Mississippi and I was surprised at how narrow it looked compared to the grandness of its reputation. We were near the northern tip of the Great River, the river of all rivers. The river that is the main freshwater source for 15 million people along its path,[2] the river that Enbridge drilled underneath, twice, to install a tar sands oil pipeline.

We walked solemnly along the river through the trees until we came to a streak of bald earth that signaled the impending path of the pipeline. Eerily straight, the trees along this chunk had been demolished, signs forbade trespassing and the site was marked off with orange tape. In its path, by the side of the river, a traditional Anishinaabe lodge stood ground, proclaiming the land rights of its people to this territory protected by treaty and opposing in sacred prayer the construction of this pipeline.

We returned to camp with the news of spring, and in accordance with the turn of the season, a group was huddled around a large, steaming pot smelling of smoke and maple. They were making maple syrup out of the freshly tapped sap! We stood by the boil down, taking turns stirring and flirting with the direction of the smoke.

An Anishinaabe elder exited the main cabin to have a smoke. I was told her name was Tania Aubid and that she had just broken a 38 day hunger strike in protest of the pipeline.[3] 38 days. Over a month of not eating. Seeing Tania and hearing her story moved me to feel the gravity of this fight, part of a chain of historical Indigenous resistance, environmental justice and manifestations proclaiming sovereignty. In this moment, Line 3 felt like more than just a strategic “campaign”—it represented a struggle for actual livelihood and survival. Tania’s hunger strike represented a moment of clarity for me in understanding the depth and seriousness of the movement. Little did I know that 5 months later Tania and I would be arrested together and briefly share a jail cell.

When we left that first day of spring, folks at the camp offered us the special gift of freshly boiled down maple syrup. We accepted the three jars with gratitude, knowing that they contained far more than just syrup.

Coming back home after this brief trip to Minnesota I wept: tears I didn’t know how to explain, tears that my roommates couldn’t understand. I didn’t know how to process the experience or who to process with. I wrote a letter to myself and decided to fast the next day, inspired by Tania’s hunger strike. As I reflected on why I was heavy with emotion, I realized that I had felt a sense of alignment being up north, a sense of the change and uncertainty of life that I had felt mostly removed from my whole life, and felt especially estranged from in the protective bubble of college. There was something vivid, connected, and directly affected by both the elements of nature and the real consequences of oil projects like Line 3. The activism I had been doing for years seemed distant and removed from the actual realities of the projects I was trying to stop, the realities these Indigenous people were living every day. My glimpse of this type of on-the-ground resistance work seemed to present a way to live into my values more deeply and led me to spend my summer up at Line 3 in different Indigenous-led resistance camps along the pipeline route. My commitment to the movement that followed unveiled some key alignments and contradictions of changework and fostered me through a variety of episodes in my ideology and theory of change. Recounting some of those episodes here, I will demonstrate how I’ve both grown through them and simultaneously continue to hold each one as true in my present understanding of dialectical, multiple truths.

My Whiteness Is a Cloud

My whiteness is a cloud I can’t always see. It extends beyond my skin into every interaction, into every relationship, into every footstep I take, have taken, and will take. It clouds my own vision of myself.

My whiteness is a cloud made of guilt, shame, taking and separating. It clouds my sense of spirit, my connection with all things.

My whiteness is a training, and a lifelong untraining, an aloneness, a “forgive me” from my most well-meaning ancestors and a “redeem me” from the more ignorant. My whiteness is a lost child, without story, without culture, forgotten somewhere overseas. My whiteness is blank, a white page, a canvas.

I am ruled by my whiteness, by the fear I’ve been trained to contain as a white femme. Fear of confrontation, of sounding stupid, of being ridiculed, of causing harm. In most situations I get by by remaining a quiet bystander, politically correct in the not-saying.

I have been taught as a woman to be quiet and demure. I tiptoe around difficult subjects for fear of offending. I don’t want to be called racist, even though I know that I am the expression of a racist system. I don’t want to hurt anyone, but sometimes by not addressing difficult subjects I cause more harm than good. I am conflict-avoidant, and that is a tenet of white supremacy.

As a principle of movement work I have learned to prioritize taking leadership from the most impacted. This often looks like striving to take everything a person of color says to be true, fact, and right. Although it is critical to listen to and trust those who have been historically oppressed, I believe there is a complexity to it that I don’t always see. People of color are not a monolith. Even within resistance spaces with the same goal of stopping a pipeline, Indigenous leaders have differing ideas of what needs to be done.

Looking back at my journals from my time living at camp Namewag, I am remembering how uncomfortable it felt much of the time. Distrust was the dominant attitude, fear of infiltration made relationships testy, and security culture meant to protect also sometimes was used to gate-keep. Leaders were often stressed, angry and demoralized, which led to some manipulative attitudes surrounding arrests and a lack of full consent regarding risk level during actions. With the dominant strategy being to “put our bodies on the line” to stop construction, actions began to feel self-sacrificing and bodies were being regarded as resources, with the full humanity of each subject not always fully acknowledged.

It can be difficult to strike a balance between showing up in full capacity to trust in whatever Indigenous leaders call for, and prioritizing, or at least accounting for, my own agency and wellbeing. On the one hand there is the decentering of the self, the regard for Indigenous futurity over settler futurity, and the understanding that this fight isn’t about me. And on the other hand there is the real acknowledgement that my stake in this movement only goes so far as I believe in the cause I am fighting for, knowing that I am fighting for the liberation of all beings and that that liberation includes me. Although I likely won’t live to see a completely liberated society, I strive to perform into existence the type of liberatory care and pleasure that I hope all beings can someday experience. I believe in a more joyful militancy, one that builds bridges rather than burns them. I believe in the success of a movement rooted in love, with a regard for the humanity and agency of everyone, even our enemies. I believe in the strategies of joy over guilt, learning and honest communication over shame, and repair and transformative justice over revenge. Grappling with my whiteness is full of contradictions that I will continue to struggle through and rehash, but for now I strive to embody a commitment to the liberation of all, understanding that this means trusting in my own body and agency while simultaneously decentering myself.

Things Have Come to Be the Way They Are Right Now

“Out beyond ideas of wrongdoing and rightdoing there is a field. I’ll meet you there.”

- Rumi[4]

I sat on the cushion, my legs stiff from the last 4 days of meditating 10 hours a day. I was trying to breathe through my physical discomfort, feeling a mix of impatience, sleepiness, melancholia, and wonder. I visualized these feelings in my body as colors and shapes, observing how they played with me. I was trying to practice acceptance, allowing my thoughts and feelings to pass through me, minimizing my suffering by letting go of my attachment.

Then one of the teachers said something that stuck with me, a phrase I used as a mantra throughout the rest of the retreat. In her Dharma talk, Bruni had reminded us of the historic fatefulness of all things: things have come to be the way they are right now, she said. Things have come to be the way they are.

History is intentional, fateful, created by the agency and choices of “things”. Things have not simply fallen into place like this—rather, they have come to be this way. This knowledge opens up in me an appreciation for how unique and specific and destined this moment is, and how each thing had agency in its path to get here, creating the current reality.

This, of course, doesn’t mean that it’s good, or that it can’t change. That’s just it; it’s always changing. It’s not good or bad, just the way it is. The negative brings in the positive and the positive gives rise to the negative. There’s always a struggle for balance.

This is the view of eternity I like to hold. Everything has come to be like this. Not fate or destiny in a way that robs us of our agency. Rather, we are God building Change, we create the reality in company with every being and force on this Earth. All is well in this universe. We must not be ruled by fear. And yet, there is an understanding of the ephemerality of this moment, the malleability of the future, the deconstruction of time and the force of every contradiction creating change.

Although some may think that the Buddhist way is training to accept the conditions of the moment as they are, I think there is a nuance, and perhaps a contradiction: Buddhist practice invites us to let go of our clinging in order to accept the force of change. Suffering comes from clinging: clinging to the past, to a relationship, to an idea. What if we let go of that attachment and accept the fluidity of everything? What would that do for movement spaces?

I think movement spaces tend to operate best when there is an idea that people can get behind and get excited about, but at the same time there must exist the wisdom of knowing when to let go, change paths, and let emerge another iteration or a different thing. “How we live and grow and stay purposeful in the face of constant change,” writes adrienne maree brown, “actually does determine both the quality of our lives, and the impact that we can have when we move into action together.”[5]

The Line 3 fight was successful in many ways: it radicalized hundreds of young people and trained them in frontline direct action. It forged connections and networks that are now showing the beginnings of a constellation of chained actions and campaigns, inspired and supported by one another.

But the Line 3 fight made a lot of mistakes. One of the main pitfalls was the attachment to the tactic of direct action before all else. There had been legal and legislative fights to stop the pipeline already, all of which had failed. Direct action was considered both the last resort and a physical representation of the movement’s strength and people power. As a tactic, direct action can be very impactful, but in the Movement to Stop Line 3 the same types of actions were overused, forfeiting the element of surprise and losing the attention of the media. Over and over people locked themselves to construction equipment, on almost a daily basis during the summer. And the result was maybe an hour or two of delayed construction and the water protector(s) being thrown in jail. In my opinion, clinging to the ideals of direct action—or at least the same type of action—as the worthiest tactic was part of what caused us to lose the fight.

In Joyful Militancy, carla bergman and Nick Montgomery coin the term “rigid radicalism” to describe this phenomenon in movements. Participants tend “towards mistrust and fixed ways of relating that destroy the capacity to be responsive, creative, and experimental.”[6] This dynamic is created on the relational level and creates rigidity in the flow of tactics and strategies at an organizational level. “It is the pleasure of feeling more radical than others and the worry about not being radical enough; the sad comfort of sorting unfolding events into dead categories; the vigilant perception of errors and complicities in oneself and others; the anxious posturing on social media and the highs of being liked and the lows of being ignored; the suspicion and resentment felt in the presence of something new; the way curiosity feels naïve and condescension feels right.”[7] These attitudes ring true to my experience, and, I’d propose, mostly stem from a common fear of change, the clinging to a certain idea of radicalism. It is also the human need to form packs, to corroborate our opinions, the need for certainty in the inevitably uncertain work of changemaking.

Upon acknowledging this root and its unfortunately prevalent consequences, how might we train ourselves to recognize and unlearn these attitudes? Joyful Militancy provides some helpful ideas: they suggest working non-ideologically, not privileging morality but instead listening to the milieu of different truths and experiences and using common understandings to guide decisions, accepting uncertainty, and holding ambivalence. I hope to continue to remind myself of these important nuances and ideas and embody them in my presence in movement spaces to come, as this is a major step to prefiguring the world we wish to create.

On the Hill in Santa Clara

“If everything has come to be the way it is right now, how can I justify my desire to make change?” I asked my friend Jeremy, an ardent Marxist. “Can I be both righteous and recognize that this is just one truth, one side of the whole, one small argument in the complex trajectory of the universe?”

We were climbing a hill overlooking Santa Clara, the city that housed the final historic battle of the Cuban Revolution. I was trying to make sense of the many contradictions of changemaking that had been nagging at me lately. Ever since I went full force planning an all-night Earth Day “teach-out” the past April, I had been extremely burnt out, unmotivated, and disillusioned with movement work. The added toll of the conflict in my defendant group left me feeling unsupported and unequipped to participate in the difficult work of rebuilding trust. I felt angry at the dogmatic righteousness that seemed to guide many leftists and alienate anyone who dared to disagree. I was also processing the Vipassana meditation retreat I had attended in the summer where I was reminded of the alignment of the universe and the synchronicity of each thing. Between disillusionment and encouragement of the broader picture, I was perplexed by the tension between my belief in change as a guiding force and my complicated relationship with movements and the motivation necessary to create that change. I brought these feelings and questions with me up this hill, and a formative dialogue helped me unwind them.

Jeremy queried my assertion of the inherent rightness of the universe. “Things are what we make them,” he asserted, “in accordance with the conditions at hand.” He doesn’t think we can believe in fate to the point of quelling our sense of agency, for our subjectivity is a part of the force of change, the flow of nature. Perhaps it's the feeling of control that we can let go of; we can’t control many things, and it doesn’t help us to worry about controlling them, but we can try to shape change in most situations. I accept this nuance. I go on:

I think it is not just that things are as they are meant to be, but that within every opinion, every experience, every human story there is a seed of influence for the building or destroying, creating or critiquing of the new world. Regardless of whether someone is conservative, liberal, progressive or leftist, regardless of whether they are ignorant or wise, well-read or out-of-touch, they have a place in the ecosystem of things. For example, I think of my friend who is a radical leftist, quite critical of almost everything, sometimes, I think, too critical, but with very original and well-argued critiques. I think he has a strong role to play in the making of a better world because, even if people don’t agree with him all the time, he stretches those around him into new ways of thinking; he pulls us further left because he stands his ground and is smart, loveable, and unapologetic in his views.

Then I think of my dad, a somewhat nutty man who lives alone in his RV and is deep into conspiracy theories. Some, like my mom, are apologetic of his behavior, or that I don’t have a more responsible father, but I wouldn’t have it any other way. He has shown me ways to live life outside of the constructs of society, taught me to challenge dominant culture and be skeptical about mainstream stories and news. My father has a role in the ecology of things as an outsider, a weirdo, an influencer of those related to him and those he interacts with to think a little differently.

There’s my Cuban grandfather, the republican Trump supporter who “disowned” me after I posted a blog post with the word “eco-socialist” in it. His views, coming from a place of unhealed trauma from his adolescence when his wealthy family fled the communist revolution, show me another side of how people experience change. My relationship with him has been a difficult one, but I see it as a rehearsal for dealing with conflict in the greater arena of societal changemaking. We can’t have a revolution unchallenged.

All these roles either stretch us in some direction or teach us to stand our ground. They serve to diversify us, for we can’t have a society where we all think homogeneously. But this can be a lot to grapple with for those of us trying to figure out what we believe (which, I think, is most of us). With influences and messaging coming at us from all angles, how are we to parse out what we think, what feels right to us as individuals coming into the movement or just trying to live life? How do we discern our truth in a world with multiple truths? How can we regard other beings with a radical understanding of their whole story that has led them to this point, with a compassion that bridges divides, while also holding true to our theory of change? How much should we accept the continued replication of counterproductive forces/people in society, and how much can we assert our ideologies and try to change people?

Jeremy responded to my rant with the brilliance of Marxist dialectics: of course, the view of the necessary ecology of things has its happy opposite, he noted. Contradicting the plurality and indiscernibility of truths is the other, equally true notion that if we are to make change, we must believe in some right way. We cannot make change by justifying everyone’s position. Rather changemakers must act to change circumstances that change people. Sometimes, they must get carried away in the righteousness of their own path and assert their opinions over others.

Jeremy’s point brought me to another, more personal question: why am I doing changework? Why do I feel like I can/should assert my righteousness and try to change others? If I can just as easily justify stepping away to “be in the rightness of eternity,” what is continually bringing me to this work?

I know that I am oppressed, as a subject of the American education system, as a young person, as a woman, as a consumer and a product of capitalism, and as a member of the oppressive white race (as Nelson Mandela writes, “the oppressor must be liberated just as surely as the oppressed”).[8] I know that my liberation is tied up with the liberation of all beings. I know I am a human in a historical moment and I have the ability to influence change. But I also know I could, and have the privilege to, accept things as they are. I often get a strong urge to escape or retreat, go live in a commune or a van, climb mountains and fulfill my adventure spirit. I could learn to live without actively shaping change in the world, in the sense of committed organizing. What is stopping me from retreating like that?

I have a sense of responsibility. A sense of faith in the idea of change as a divine force—“God is Change,” as Octavia Butler writes in Parable of the Sower.[9] A sense of the meaning I’ve created for myself in changework, a feeling of truth in the philosophies of dialectical materialism and the exciting opportunity present for change in the historical moment we are living in. An alignment with the prefigurative embodiment of recognizing ourselves within the ecology of things, the decentering of the self and of the human, the construction of practices to remember the inherent truths of change and interconnectedness.

I won’t kid myself by claiming that I need any of this to live. Depressingly, I think it does all boil down to something to stave off the chilling and stagnating force of boredom. But in alignment with the values I’ve been taught and what brings me joy and energy, changework is the meaning I’ve chosen to imbue my life with. In the words of a dear friend and lover, Emma Lohman, with regard to the Line 3 fight:

We who went back where we failed to stop construction can't say what it means. We don't even know what to ask. Maybe it's a better way than most to get older.[10]

We began to head down the hill. On our way down, Jeremy explained to me the laws of dialectics, the second of which proved to be particularly relevant to my questions. In his words (emphasis mine):

2) the unity and conflict of opposites means that in certain conditions seemingly "opposite" things in our world are interconnected and struggle together to produce change. for example, proletariat and bourgeoisie are "opposites" but are bound together within one total system (capitalism) and could not exist without the other as categories. their struggle (class struggle) produces change, the proletariat overthrows capitalism and therefore abolishes itself as "proletariat" along with all class distinctions. The point is that things that seem "opposite" to one another shouldn't be thought of as rigidly isolated from one another, but interpenetrate and struggle which produces change

This is intriguing. How do we hold both the necessity of contradictory, opposing, polarizing forces while also fighting for one side? What does our vision of an ideal society look like when we recognize that contradictions will inevitably persist? I think this principle of the unity and conflict of opposites calls on us to devise a new orientation towards changemaking: instead of aligning ourselves with “leftism” or with any vision of utopia, what if we align ourselves with the divine force of change itself that contains and challenges both political sides and negates any utopic endpoint? Perhaps some diversity is required: some of us must maintain this cosmic alignment, while some hold to the left and some to the right, some fight for a vision and some accept the conditions at hand. Together we change, through contradiction, systems and cultures and people.

title: Loopholes in the Fourth Amendment: Predictive Policing and the Threat of Data Brokers
abstract:
The rise of big data surveillance and predictive analytics has transformed the capabilities of law enforcement and created new forms of big data policing. Police departments (P.D.s) have increasingly used algorithms to analyze massive amounts of information in order to forecast and investigate potential criminal activity, such as Chicago P.D.’s Strategic Subject List (SSL). State governments have also adopted surveillance technologies such as facial recognition and acoustic sensors in their crime-reduction efforts. This has raised many concerns about individuals’ constitutional rights of privacy, as well as the adverse impacts on marginalized communities.

More alarming, however, is the role of data brokers in allowing law enforcement agencies to not be held liable for these violations. These for-profit companies aggregate individuals’ personal data and sell it to the largest bidders. This is not only concerning but also unconstitutional as these purchases bypass the Fourth Amendment through the third-party doctrine. Yet, Congress has still not passed a federal data privacy law addressing these loopholes.

As such, this paper explores the impacts of predictive policing programs and argues for the necessity of policy intervention on data brokers in three parts.
