Discussion

Unsurprisingly, our study findings suggest that fake news is a very nuanced subject. A part of our hypothesis was not supported: liberal extremism was not a significant predictor of fake news identification performance. We hypothesized that being more extremely liberal would decrease one’s ability to detect fake news, as they might be “blinded” by the actual facts an

PREDICTORS OF FAKE NEWS SUSCEPTIBILITY 23 article does or does not provide; however, this was not supported. No results for overall score, fake news identification score, or real news identification score were statistically significant. Nor did we find any correlation between extremism and ability to detect fake news. This is in line with trends across the general United States population; regardless of political affiliation, people generally overestimate their ability to detect fake news and are ultimately susceptible to fake news online (Guess et al., 2021). Additionally, Casino and Jenkins (2013) found that members of both political parties and ideologies can be susceptible to conspiracy theories and fake news.

Given their findings on susceptibility to conspiracy theories, it is possible that the headlines utilized in our study were not quite to the level of extremity as studied in the past, and that may be why political extremism did not seem to be a predictor for fake news identification.

Alternatively, it is possible that being more liberally extreme was not a large factor in fake news detection simply because there could be a “baseline” that most people are susceptible to in the first place (Casino & Jenkins, 2013).

Despite liberal extremism not being a significant predictor of fake news identification, we found that social media usage is a predictor of fake news identification. Social media usage and overall identification scores were found to be very statistically and practically significant, indicating that social media usage appears to have an effect on fake news detection, which supports our hypothesis. In fact, social media usage accounted for 8% of all variance in possible reasons for fake news identification, showing there is likely a strong relationship between the two. This was seen further when examining the real news identification scores: again, there was a relationship with social media usage, this time accounting for 9% of variance. Lastly, participants who reported Low social media usage for news scored better across all metrics, compared to those who had Medium and High social media usage, once again supporting our

PREDICTORS OF FAKE NEWS SUSCEPTIBILITY 24 hypothesis. This is supported by Allcott and Gentzkow (2017), who found that those who use more social media are more likely to believe ideology-aligned articles—since we were examining liberal participants, those who had High social media usage likely could have immediately believed any headlines from liberal news sources, while those with Low social media usage could have been more skeptical (Allcott & Gentzkow, 2017). Alternatively, this could be explained by confirmation bias, where liberal users with higher social media usage are more likely to be surrounded by liberal media. Thus, they are more likely to believe liberal headlines (Moravec et al., 2018).

Given the statistically insignificant relationship between liberal extremism and fake news detection capabilities, as well as the significant relationship between social media usage and fake news detection capabilities, we looked to identify any relationship between liberal extremism and social media usage. Social media usage is a significant predictor of liberal extremism, accounting for 14% of variance. Confirmation bias could explain this large effect. The more time a person spends on social media, the more likely their social network is to be aligned with their political ideologies (Allcott & Gentzkow, 2017).

Limitations and Future Directions

Limitations of our study include having exclusively liberal participants, underpowered samples, and the lack of consideration for misinformation vs disinformation of fake news.

Northwestern University is an institution known for its liberal student body, and our sample consisted of only Northwestern students. Thus, our sample was heavily concentrated with liberal extremes, as reflected in the average liberal extremism score of 4.95 out of 7. If our sample included more participants across the liberal extremism spectrum, we could have looked at differences between those with a more moderate liberal ideology and more extreme liberals.

PREDICTORS OF FAKE NEWS SUSCEPTIBILITY 25

Further, had our study included an equal number of liberal, moderate, and conservative participants, we would be able to examine fake news susceptibility predictors across all political affiliations. This could provide insight as to whether the same fake news susceptibility predictors are applicable to the entirety of the political spectrum.

Additionally, this study was underpowered. We estimated a minimum sample size of 82 participants was required to maintain a medium effect size. While there were initially 87 respondents to the survey, 25 participants were removed from our analysis after leaving the survey incomplete or having a conservative or moderate political affiliation. This means that despite significant findings regarding social media usage as a predictor of fake news identification, there is a chance of a false positive given that our sample size was not large enough.

As defined by the American Psychological Association (2023), misinformation is false information, whereas disinformation is information that was falsified with the intention of misleading individuals. The wording in our survey was intentionally ambiguous around the word

“fake” as we were interested in how various participants would respond. However, because it was not specified whether participants in our study were identifying fake news based on if they thought the information was false or false with the intentions of misleading, it is unclear whether participants identified fake news sources as fake due to misinformation, disinformation, or both.

It is possible participants would have scored differently on the overall score and fake news identification score had there been more specification between the two.

Due to the limited number of studies available regarding liberal extremism and mode of news consumption as potential predictors of fake news susceptibility, as well as the limitations of our own study, more research is necessary to provide evidence for a significant relationship

PREDICTORS OF FAKE NEWS SUSCEPTIBILITY 26 between fake news susceptibility and liberal extremism or mode of news consumption. Future researchers need to take into consideration the political affiliation of those sampled in order to provide an inclusive sample of individuals across the liberal extremism spectrum as well as an ample amount of individuals across the political spectrum, the power of the sample in order to avoid false positives, and detailed definitions of misinformation and disinformation along with specific instructions on which one is to be considered when answering questions about fake news.

Conclusion

In conclusion, we found that liberal extremism is not a significant predictor of fake news identification. However, social media usage is a large, significant predictor of liberal extremism.

This suggests that low social media usage predicts better performance, especially at identifying real news as real. Additionally, people are often far more confident at their abilities to detect fake news than they actually are. It could be easy for malicious actors to prey on this disjunction, creating disinformation that is intentionally difficult to detect. Possible warning signs or pre-viewing programs could be implemented on social media based news sites themselves to combat these findings, as investigated by Pennycook et al. (2020), who found that priming individuals to think about accuracy resulted in a tripled level of discernment between sharing real and fake news in relation to the control group who were not primed. With the continuous rise of both social media and fake news on social media, it is recommended that this study be used for educational purposes for not only politicians and voters, regardless of age, but the general public as well.

title: Evaluating Knowledge of Biotechnology and Attitudes Toward Genetically Modified (GM) Foods in Community School of Naples (CSN) High School Students
abstract: Agricultural and biotechnology research scientists have asserted genetically modified (GM) foods offer immense financial, health, and environmental benefits to society, but the implementa- tion of such benefits greatly depends on public acceptance of this genetic technology (Fernbach). Widespread opposition and concern towards GM foods raise questions about the public’s understanding of GM foods and biotechnology processes in general. Therefore, the complicated interrelation between the specific variables knowledge of biotechnology and attitudes towards GM foods demands evaluation. To better understand this relationship, a detailed survey containing two distinct sections measuring knowledge of biotechnology, both self-assessed and objective, and attitudes towards GM foods was distributed to a sample of 32 high school students at Community School of Naples (CSN) in Southwest Florida. Specifically, simple random sampling was completed with the use of an online random number generator. Responses from the distributed questionnaire were critically analyzed with MiniTab statistical software. Statistically significant results show that as CSN students’ opposition to GM foods increases, scores measuring objective knowledge of biotechnology linearly decrease (correlation coefficient (r)=-0.763). Within a real- life context, this research provides insight into a notable factor (lack of knowledge of biotechnology) not only driving CSN high school students’ widespread opposition to GM foods but also potentially the general public’s opposition. The results of this research could directly aid to implement change to increase high school students’ knowledge of biotechnology, such as through curriculum adjustments in biology courses, in order to consequently achieve lower opposition and greater acceptance of GM foods in society.
text:
Running head: EVALUATING KNOWLEDGE OF BIOTECHNOLOGY AND ATTITUDES TOWARD GM FOODS IN CSN HIGH SCHOOL STUDENTS 1

Evaluating Knowledge of Biotechnology and Attitudes Toward Genetically Modified (GM)

Foods in Community School of Naples (CSN) High School Students

Abstract

Agricultural and biotechnology research scientists have asserted genetically modified (GM) foods offer immense financial, health, and environmental benefits to society, but the implementa- tion of such benefits greatly depends on public acceptance of this genetic technology (Fernbach). Widespread opposition and concern towards GM foods raise questions about the public’s understanding of GM foods and biotechnology processes in general. Therefore, the complicated interrelation between the specific variables knowledge of biotechnology and attitudes towards GM foods demands evaluation. To better understand this relationship, a detailed survey containing two distinct sections measuring knowledge of biotechnology, both self-assessed and objective, and attitudes towards GM foods was distributed to a sample of 32 high school students at Community School of Naples (CSN) in Southwest Florida. Specifically, simple random sampling was completed with the use of an online random number generator. Responses from the distributed questionnaire were critically analyzed with MiniTab statistical software. Statistically significant results show that as CSN students’ opposition to GM foods increases, scores measuring objective knowledge of biotechnology linearly decrease (correlation coefficient (r)=-0.763). Within a real- life context, this research provides insight into a notable factor (lack of knowledge of biotechnology) not only driving CSN high school students’ widespread opposition to GM foods but also potentially the general public’s opposition. The results of this research could directly aid to implement change to increase high school students’ knowledge of biotechnology, such as through curriculum adjustments in biology courses, in order to consequently achieve lower opposition and greater acceptance of GM foods in society.

I. Introduction

Since their introduction in 1994, genetically modified foods have lacked public support and invoked outspoken responses due to their highly controversial nature (Klintman, 2002). According to the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), genetically modified (GM) foods are de- rived from organisms whose DNA, or genetic material, has been artificially altered through biotechnological processes (FDA, 2020). Biotechnology describes a relatively new and emerging scientific discipline characterized by the exploitation of biological processes for industrial pur- poses (Usak & Erdogan, 2009). While the American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS) has stated “GM foods, created through biotechnological procedures, are as safe to eat as conventionally grown crops” and offer numerous benefits, such as increased crop yields and re- duced use of pesticides, public contention persists (Bernheim, Berge, & Richroch, 2013). Such as, in 2016, a Pew Research Center (PRC) poll found that “about 90% of scientists thought GM foods were safe to eat, while only 37% of laypeople, people lacking specialized knowledge in scientific areas, shared this view” (“Public opinion”, 2016, para. 8). This 53 percentage point gap proves concerning as it demonstrated the “largest difference in opinion between scientists and the general public” for any scientific issue ever tested by the PRC (Funk & Kennedy, 2018).

Therefore, lack of knowledge of biotechnological topics seems to be a possible underly- ing factor contributing to the public’s widespread opposition and concern toward GM foods (Frewer, 2003). Moreover, as GM foods become increasingly prevalent in modern-day society, it is imperative that young people are “knowledgeable about biotechnological topics to contribute to public debate and make well-informed personal decisions” regarding purchasing and consum- ing GM foods (Dawson & Schibeci, 2003, p. 3).

To date, no published studies have specifically investigated the relationship between the two categorical variables: knowledge of the increasingly influential field of biotechnology and attitudes toward GM foods in US high school populations. Therefore, as a result of the sheer lack of published studies on this narrow topic, the overarching question driving the research presented in this paper is “How does knowledge about biotechnology correlate with attitudes toward genetically modified (GM) foods in high school students in Grades 9-12 at Community School of Naples?”.

II. Literature Review

Scientific Literacy and Attitudes Toward GM Foods

Although the research question aims to understand the relationship between knowledge of biotechnology and attitudes toward GM foods in a particular population of high school students, no current literature directly examines these two specific variables. Therefore, the best method to review existing literature is to analyze the relation between slightly different variables, such as scientific literacy and attitudes toward GM foods in populations of adults. The accepted definition of scientific literacy as published by the American Psychological Association (APA) is “public understanding of general science knowledge” (Macias, 2019). As explained by a Public Understanding of Science (PUS) comprehensive meta-analysis that critically reviewed the relationship between scientific literacy and attitudes toward GM foods across 40 countries, “empirical evidence from most studies points to a weak positive correlation” (Allum & Sturgis, 2002, p. 36).

The meta-analysis, published by Nick Allum and Patrick Sturgis in 2002, highlights the results of two individual studies. First, Martin Bauer and John Durant (1997), two public opinion researchers from the UK, explored the relationship between scientific literacy and attitudes toward GM foods across twelve European countries through the distribution of surveys to adult consumers in the late 1990s. As published in the International Journal of Public Opinion Research, Bauer and Durant (1997) found “overall there is a moderate positive correlation between scientific literacy and attitudes toward GM foods” (p. 167). Specifically, the survey research concluded adults from European countries with relatively high levels of scientific knowledge, such as the Netherlands and Denmark, showed the most positive attitudes and greatest acceptance of GM foods (Bauer & Durant, 1997). This conclusion aligns with the idea that individuals with greater scientific knowledge better understand the numerous benefits GM foods offer and thus, hold more positive attitudes.

The second study mentioned in-depth in Allum and Sturgis’s meta-analysis was published by Michael Grimson (1999), a Swiss psychology professor at the University of Zurich, in Nu- clear Europe Worldscan. Grimson (1999) found, like Bauer and Durant (1997), a weak positive correlation between scientific literacy and attitudes toward GM foods in a representative sample of over 1000 Swiss residents. This further supports the notion that greater understanding of sci- ence accompanies more positive attitudes toward GM foods.

In contrast to the weak positive correlation found between scientific literacy and attitudes toward GM foods by Allum and Sturgis (2002), more recent research published by Jon D. Miller and Ronald Paldo (2004), two professors at the University of Northern Illinois, has conversely shown the relationship between the two variables to be negative. Moreover, in 2005, a lengthy paper titled “Public Attitudes Towards Genetically Modified Foods” was published in the British Food Journal showing a moderately strong negative association between scientific literacy and attitudes toward GM foods in a sample of “participants recruited from Norway, Italy, and England” (Miles & Frewer, 2005, p. 251). Therefore, it is unclear whether with time the relationship between scientific literacy, or more simply general science knowledge, and attitudes toward GM foods has become negative.

Measuring Knowledge: Self-Assessed and Objective

Numerous previously published studies including works mentioned above by Bauer and Durant (1997), Grimson (1999), and Miller and Paldo (2004) have assessed general science knowledge and attitudes toward GM foods in adult populations. However, new literature published within the last three years exploring these two specific variables has interestingly taken a different approach and divided general science knowledge into two distinct sub-variables: self- assessed knowledge and objective knowledge. This division evidently has functioned to more thoroughly and accurately measure the variable general science knowledge (Fernbach, 2016). As published in Advances in Consumer Research, self-assessed knowledge can be defined as “how much an individual thinks he/she knows about a specific topic or idea” (Selnes & Gronhuang, 1986, p. 68). Moreover, self-assessments of knowledge are typically measured by asking individuals to rate their perceived levels of understanding of a topic or subject. In contrast to self-assessed knowledge, objective knowledge as defined by the Journal of Consumer Psychology refers to “actual knowledge of a topic or subject” (Raju, Lonial, & Mangold, 1995). Previous research has used true-false questions adapted from validated surveys to directly measure objective general science knowledge (Fernbach, 2016; McFadden, 2019).

While only two published psychological studies have evaluated the relationship between both types of general science knowledge (self-assessed and objective) and attitudes toward GM foods, the survey questions used and the results obtained from the two works were quite different (Fernbach, 2016; McFadden, 2019). The study published first titled “Extreme opponents of genetically modified foods know the least but think they know the most” was issued in the rep- utable Nature Human Behavior (NHB) by author Phillip M. Fernbach (2016), a professor at the University of Colorado Boulder. In this study, self-assessed knowledge was measured using an unbiased 7-point rating scale adapted from the U.S. National Library of Medicine (NIH) “cognitive science literature”. McFadden, a professor at the University of Florida’s Food and Resource Economic Department, published the second recent study evaluating both types of general science knowledge and attitudes toward GM foods in 2019. Unlike Fernbach, McFadden selected an alternative approach to measure self-assessed knowledge: three individual questions from the “Cognitive Reflection Test” (CRT), a test designed to measure reflections on perceived knowledge and cognition, were used (Frederick, 2005; Toplok & West, 2011). Despite differences in measurements of self-assessed knowledge, both Fernbach and McFadden used fourteen true- false questions with a unique scoring mechanism from the validated National Science and Engineering Indicators (NSEI) survey to measure objective general science knowledge (NSEI, 2016).

Following measurements of both types of general science knowledge, Fernbach and McFadden employed differing tactics to measure attitudes toward GM foods. Fernbach utilized two Likert-type rating scale items. A Likert-scale is a specific type of psychometric scale frequently used in psychological research to reliably measure attitudes or opinions (Joshi, Kale, & Chandel, 2015). Fernbach’s first Likert-type scale item asked participants to measure their extremity of opposition, or degree of opposition, to GM foods (1=no opposition; 7= extreme opposition), and the second item asked participants to rank their extremity of concern, or degree of concern, toward GM foods (1= no concern; 7=extreme concern). In contrast, McFadden (2019) only used one item that asked participants to state whether they viewed GM foods “favorably, neutrally, or unfavorably” (p. 3).

Although slightly different surveys were used, both Fernbach and McFadden’s research found participants with the greatest opposition to GM foods showed the lowest objective knowledge of general science topics. However, Fernbach found self-assessed knowledge increased linearly as objective knowledge decreased while McFadden found no statistically significant correlation between self-assessed knowledge and objective knowledge. Thus, the current literature examining both types of general science knowledge and attitudes toward GM foods has evidently yielded mixed and unclear results possibly due to the differing survey questions used to measure self-assessed knowledge.

Principle of Extremism and Illusory Knowledge

In order to most thoroughly understand the current body of literature evaluating the variables general science knowledge and attitudes toward GM foods, differing psychological perspectives on this relationship must be considered. According to Dr. Paul Rozin, a professor at the University of Pennsylvania’s Department of Psychology, the principle of extremism states “ex-treme opposition to scientific concepts, such as GM foods, often stems from lack of knowledge, or more formally an illusion of knowledge” (Berger, 2019, p. 1). An illusion of knowledge oc- curs when individuals believe they are particularly knowledgeable on a topic or subject when in reality they lack understanding altogether (Hall, 2007; Dunning, 2011).

The principle of extremism seems to be at work in both Fernbach and McFadden’s research as individuals with the lowest objective knowledge scores demonstrated the greatest opposition to GM foods. However, illusory knowledge seems to be present in only Fernbach’s research and not McFadden’s; this is because Fernbach specifically concluded self-assessed knowledge scores increased linearly while objective knowledge scores decreased. Therefore, participants in Fernbach’s research who showed the lowest objective knowledge scores greatly over- estimated their knowledge of GM foods in the self-assessed knowledge portion of the survey.

General Science Knowledge vs Biotechnology Knowledge

As explained earlier, while the research above analyzed correlations between general science knowledge and attitudes toward GM foods, the overarching research question aims to understand the relationship between a specific type of scientific knowledge, knowledge of biotechnology, and attitudes toward GM foods. Limited literature has examined knowledge of biotechnology as an explanatory variable. The few published studies evaluating knowledge of biotechnology have compared this variable to acceptance levels and attitudes toward biotechnology, rather than specifically attitudes toward GM foods. Although the relationship between knowledge and attitudes of biotechnology has hardly been investigated, the few studies prove important as they carefully examine variables similar to the two driving the empirical research present- ed in this paper (knowledge of biotechnology and attitudes toward GM foods).

Knowledge and Attitudes Toward Biotechnology

The literature evaluating knowledge and attitudes toward biotechnology has shown complex and unclear results. Pavol Prokop (2007), a behavioral ecology researcher at Comenius University in Bratislava, published a quantitative study in the International Journal of Science Education titled “Slovakian Students’ Knowledge of and Attitudes toward Biotechnology”. The quantitative study found a “statistically significant positive correlation” between knowledge of and attitudes toward biotechnology in a sample of 378 Slovakian high school students (p<.001) (Prokop, 2007, p. 897). Similarly, Usak and Erdogan (2009), two Turkish professors at the Department of Education at Dumlupınar University in Kutahya, Turkey, also found a strong positive correlation between knowledge of and attitudes toward biotechnology as published in the U.S. National Library of Medicine (NIH). Usak and Erdogan (2009) utilized the validated Biotechnology Knowledge Questionnaire (BKQ) with 14 items to measure students’ knowledge of biotechnology and Likert-type questions to measure attitudes toward biotechnology. Like Prokop (2007), Usak and Erdogan (2009) concluded as knowledge of biotechnology increased, attitudes toward biotechnology became more positive in the simple random sample (SRS) of 628 high school and university students.

However, unlike the research conducted in Slovakia and Turkey, other literature has shown no statistically significant correlation between knowledge of and attitudes toward biotechnology. Such as, Dawson and Schibeci (2003), two western Australian cognitive psychology researchers, and Sorgo and Dolinsek (2009), professors at the University of Maribor in Slovenia, both independently concluded no statistically significant relationship between knowledge of and attitudes toward biotechnology in populations of students (p=0.409 and p=0.523 re- spectively). The differing geographic locations of the four studies occurring in Slovakia, Turkey, Australia, and Slovenia might be a factor contributing to the obtained contradicting statistical conclusions. Such as, different political policies pertaining to the biotechnology industry across the four studied countries may have influenced participants’ attitudes; therefore, this could account for dissimilarity in statistical conclusions (Wohlers, 2010).

Gap

While previous research has investigated the relationship between the variables general science knowledge and attitudes toward GM foods and the relationship between knowledge of and attitudes toward biotechnology, no research has directly analyzed the specific relation between knowledge of biotechnology and attitudes toward GM foods. Moreover, the existing literature examining variables similar to those of interest has been conducted primarily outside of the United States (US), such as in the UK, Netherlands, Switzerland, Turkey, Slovakia, and Australia. As briefly stated above, the varying geographic locations can affect statistical conclusions due to the differing governmental policies of countries on the commercial sale of GM foods and other technologies related to the biotechnology industry (Veccochione, Feldman, & Wunderlich, 2015; Lynch & Vogel, 2001). It is also important to note prior research conducted outside of the US has not investigated specific subtypes of knowledge, such as self-assessed and objective.

Additionally, the only studies conducted in the US have used adult consumers as the population of interest (Fernbach, 2016; McFadden, 2019). Logically, US high school students may exhibit different knowledge levels than US adult consumers due to disparity in age and perspec- tive. Therefore, new understandings of US high school students’ knowledge of biotechnology, self-assessed and objective, and attitudes toward GM foods are needed to address a considerable gap in the current body of literature; furthermore, this quantitative research will function to directly explore how knowledge levels affect US high school students’ attitudes toward GM foods and may indicate curriculum changes are necessary to better “educate students in order to consequently increase acceptance of GM foods” (Lusk, 2004, p. 201; Scholderer, 2003).

III. Hypothesis

If objective knowledge of biotechnology increases, then attitudes toward GM foods will become more positive and self-assessed knowledge will accordingly decrease among high school students in Grades 9-12 at Community School of Naples (CSN). The rationale behind the first portion of the hypothesis is with greater knowledge of biotechnological topics, students will better understand the numerous potential benefits related to GM foods, such as increased crop yields and reduced use of pesticides (Bernheim et al., 2013; “Food from”, 2020). Therefore, this will lead to more positive attitudes toward GM foods overall. The reasoning behind the second part of the hypothesis is supported by the “illusion of knowledge”; previous research in adult populations has shown individuals with low objective scientific knowledge tend to have high self-assessed scientific knowledge (Fernbach, 2016; Hall, 2007).

IV. Methods

Sample Selection

The study was conducted during the first two weeks of February 2020. A simple random sample (SRS) of 32 students (17 females, 15 males; mean age= 16.3 years) in Grades 9-12 was obtained to ensure the sample would be representative of the population of Community School of Naples (CSN) high school students for gender and ethnicity (Moerbeek, 2005). To acquire the SRS, a list of all 326 CSN high school students was collected. Each student on the list was num- bered from 000 to 325. Using an online random number generator and the specified range (000 to 325), 32 numbers were randomly selected, which corresponded to the participants chosen for the data collection process. It is important to note a sample size of 32 was specifically used to abide by the 10% statistical condition, which states sample sizes should be no more than 10% of the population of interest (“10% Condition”, 2013).

Observational Study

To most directly address the research question and test the hypothesis, an observational study, rather than an experimental investigation, was employed to remain consistent with the general approach taken in prior research. The data collection process solely included a detailed questionnaire created with Google Forms, a free survey administration app, to effectively acquire responses (see Appendix A for the complete survey). All 32 sample members were first distributed the questionnaire through school email, rather than in person, to avoid difficulty locating the selected sample members across the 77 acre campus of CSN.

The questionnaire included an introductory statement explaining what is intended to be accomplished with the aid of the participants and the anonymity of responses. Additionally, a statement of consent explained the volunteerism of the participants and asked for a virtual signa- ture of agreement. The questionnaire asked four basic demographic questions and then was divided into two sections to measure each individual variable, knowledge of biotechnology and attitudes toward GM foods, stated within the research question and hypothesis.

Measuring Participants' Knowledge of Biotechnology

The first portion of the questionnaire aimed to explore the participants’ knowledge of biotechnology. To most thoroughly measure knowledge of biotechnology, both distinct subtypes of knowledge were measured: self-assessed and objective. Self-assessed knowledge was measured with one direct question for conciseness altered from Fernbach’s survey that asked participants to rate their current knowledge of biotechnology on a single-item rating scale (1= very poor understanding; 7= excellent understanding).

To accurately record participants’ objective knowledge of biotechnology, the validated Biotechnology Knowledge Questionnaire (BKQ) with 14 true-false questions was adapted from Usak and Erdogan’s published research. The BKQ was chosen due to its high Cronbach’s α value, which is a measure of questionnaire reliability (Usak & Erdogan, 2009). Responses to the 14 true-false BKQ questions were measured uniquely on a 7-point scale anchored by ‘definitely true’ and ‘definitely false’. Specifically, the 7-point scale and the corresponding scoring mechanism were adapted from McFadden and Fernbach’s research to greatly “reduce the probability of participants guessing the correct answer by chance” (McFadden, 2019). Participants were scored with -3 to 3 points depending on correctness. For example, “when a participant chose definitely true, they received 3 points if the correct answer was ‘true’, and −3 points if the correct answer was ‘false’” (Fernbach, 2016, p. 254).

Lastly, one question was inserted at the end of the objective knowledge section of the questionnaire to ensure participants were reading carefully: “Please select “definitely false” if you are reading carefully”. Questionnaires of respondents who did not select “definitely false” were discarded.

Measuring Participants’ Attitudes Toward GM Foods

The second portion of the questionnaire aimed to measure attitudes toward GM foods. Two items were adapted from Fernbach’s Nature Human Behavior study due to their thorough- ness. The first item tested “extremity of opposition”. This term, “extremity of opposition”, has previously been used to reliably rank research subjects’ opposition to controversial topics on a scale of 1 to 7 (1= no opposition; 7= extreme opposition). After participants ranked their opposition to GM foods, the second item measured “extremity of concern”; as explained earlier, this term refers to participants’ degree of concern toward controversial issues on a scale (1= no concern; 7= extreme concern). Consistent with previous research, “extremity of opposition” and “extremity of concern” can be used in conjunction or numerically averaged to accurately measure attitudes toward controversial topics (Fernbach, 2016).

V. Findings

Although all 32 responses to the online questionnaire were obtained, one response was discarded as the participant did not select “definitely false” for the question confirming careful reading. To best understand the relationship between knowledge of biotechnology and attitudes toward GM foods, both variables must first be analyzed independently due to their individual complexity. Additionally, since both distinct subtypes of knowledge of biotechnology were measured, self-assessed knowledge will be carefully considered prior to evaluating objective knowledge.

Sample Data Measuring Respondents’ Self- Assessed Knowledge of Biotechnology:

Table 1 below was created to visually display the 31 valid responses to the single question measuring self-assessed knowledge. Table 1 shows over 20% of the SRS indicated vague understanding of biotechnology (a score of 1), and 0% of the SRS indicated thorough understanding of biotechnology (a score of 7). Furthermore, the average reported self-assessed knowledge score (x̅ ) was calculated to be 3.48 on the single-item rating scale from 1 to 7. This indicates students within the sample rated their understanding of biotechnology as adequate on average.

6 | 5 | 16.1

Sample Data Measuring Respondents’ Objective Knowledge of Biotechnology:

After independently examining self-assessed knowledge of biotechnology, objective knowledge was analyzed. As explained earlier, the 14 true-false questions adapted from Usak and Erdogan’s validated BKQ were scored uniquely with McFadden and Fernbach’s procedure. Participants were awarded -3 to 3 points depending on correctness “to account for guessing” (McFadden, 2019; Fernbach, 2016, p. 252); therefore, the maximum possible score for this portion of the questionnaire was 42 points, and the minimum possible score was -42 points.

The mean objective knowledge score (x̅ ) was found to be 16.32 (see Appendix B for all objective knowledge scores). This reveals a need for potential curriculum changes at CSN to better educate high school students on the increasingly influential field of biotechnology in the modernizing world.

Relationship Between Respondents’ Self-Assessed and Objective Knowledge:

To best understand knowledge of biotechnology before comparing this variable to attitudes toward GM foods, self-assessed and objective knowledge were directly compared in the scatterplot shown below in Figure 1, which was created with MiniTab statistical software. Figure 1 shows a moderately strong positive linear association between self-assessed and objective knowledge of biotechnology. The calculated Pearson correlation coefficient (r) was found to be 0.567. This statistical value indicates as participants’ self-assessed knowledge scores increase, objective knowledge scores accordingly increase. In simpler terms, participants were able to somewhat accurately assess or predict their actual, or objective, understanding of biotechnology.Therefore, the “illusion of knowledge” previously shown in Fernbach’s research was unexpect-edly not seen in the sample of 31 CSN high school students.

Figure 1 Objective Knowledge vs Self-Assessed Knowledge of Biotechnology

Sample Data Measuring Participants’ Attitudes Toward GM Foods:

Figure 2 below was created to visually display responses to the two items measuring attitudes toward GM foods: extremity of opposition and extremity of concern. Both histograms shown in Figure 2 are clearly skewed right. Therefore, medians, rather than means, were calculated as the appropriate statistical measures of center. Both the calculated median extremity of opposition and extremity of concern values were found to be 2.0 on the Likert-type scale ranging from 1 (no opposition/concern) to 7 (extreme opposition/concern). This indicates CSN high school students demonstrated very low levels of opposition and concern toward GM foods in general.

Figure 2

Histograms of Extremity of Concern and Extremity of Opposition r = 0.567

Note: Frequencies for extremity of concern and extremity of opposition sum to 31.

Additionally, to most thoroughly evaluate participants’ attitudes toward GM foods, Figure 3 below was created to graphically display the relation between extremity of opposition and ex- tremity of concern values. Figure 3 depicts a strong positive linear association between these two items measuring attitudes. Furthermore, responses to the two questions were highly correlated (Pearson coefficient of correlation (r)=.854; p<.0001). Thus, this evinces as participants’ opposition to GM foods increases, concern about GM foods accordingly increases. Lastly, extremity of opposition and extremity of concern values were averaged for each individual respondent to create a singular reliable measure of attitude for main analyses; this new averaged value was concisely termed “overall opposition”.

Figure 3 Extremity of Opposition vs Extremity of Concern

Extremity of Concern

Extremity of Opposition

Sample Data Comparing Knowledge and Attitudes:

To directly address the overarching research question, both types of knowledge of biotechnology, self-assessed and objective, were compared to students’ calculated “overall opposition”, a measurement of attitude, as shown below in Figure 4 and 5. Figure 4 communicates as self-assessed knowledge increases, “overall opposition” does not linearly increase or decrease. Moreover, the Pearson coefficient of correlation (r) was calculated to be -0.228, which further indicates no correlation is present between self-assessed knowledge of biotechnology and attitudes toward GM foods.

Unlike Figure 4, Figure 5 comparing objective knowledge of biotechnology and “overall opposition” (to GM foods) reveals a strong linear negative association between the two variables. As objective knowledge scores increase, overall opposition values decrease correspondingly. This apparent negative relationship evidently supports Rozin’s principle of extremism. There seems to be one noticeable outlier occurring at (-12, 3.5). For statistical calculations, this specific data point was discarded. The calculated Pearson coefficient of correlation (r) was found to be -0.763; this value statistically supports the negative association seen in Figure 5.

Figure 4 r = 0.854

Figure 6

Statistical Tests:

Although Figure 5 relating objective knowledge of biotechnology and overall opposition from the sample of 31 participants shows a clear negative association, the researcher aimed to understand the relationship between these variables in the population of CSN high school students in Grades 9-12. Thus, a significance test for the true slope (β) of the population regression line relating objective knowledge and overall opposition was conducted. At the standard significance level α=.05, the following hypotheses were tested.

Scatterplot of Overall Opposition vs Self-Assessed Knowledge

Scatterplot of Overall Opposition vs Objective Knowledge

Null (H0): β= 0, There is no linear relationship between objective knowledge of biotechnology and overall opposition to GM foods in the population of CSN high school students. Alternative (Ha): β<0, There is a negative linear relationship between objective knowledge of biotechnology and overall opposition to GM foods in the population of CSN high school students.

All four statistical conditions for inference were checked. 1. The scatterplot shown in Figure 5 shows a linear form. 2. Since sampling was done without replacement, the 10% condition was checked. The population of CSN high school students (326) is greater than ten times the SRS. 3. The scatter of the residuals above and below the “residual=0” line is roughly the same from the smallest to the largest x-value (see Appendix C). 4. Random sampling took place.

After checking the necessary conditions and completing the standard calculations with n- 2 degrees of freedom, the obtained p-value was 4.694 x 10−7 . Since the p-value of 4.694 x 10−7 is less than the α=.05 significance level, there is convincing evidence to reject H0 in favor of Ha. Thus, I can conclude there is a statistically significant negative linear relationship between objec- tive knowledge of biotechnology and overall opposition to GM foods in the population of CSN high school students. Therefore, as CSN high school students’ knowledge of biotechnology in- creases, overall opposition to GM foods decreases linearly or, more simply put, attitudes become more positive. This finding supports the first portion of the initial hypothesis, which stated “if knowledge of biotechnology increases, then attitudes toward GM foods will become more positive”.

VI. Results

While Fernbach and McFadden’s research examining general science knowledge and attitudes toward GM foods showed Rozin’s principle of extremism (2019), this research is the first to convey this psychological principle holds true for specifically the comparison between knowledge of biotechnology and attitudes toward GM foods in a particular population of high school students (Berger, 2019; Fernbach, 2016; McFadden, 2019). This finding proves significant as schools across the US are currently taking action to implement biotechnological topics into high school curricula; the analysis of this research directly shows the current educational action being taken could possibly lead to students developing more positive attitudes toward GM foods (Wahono, Utomo, & Narulita, 2018).

Although this quantitative study showed Rozin’s principle of extremism held true, the collected data regarding self-assessed and objective knowledge of biotechnology did not show the “illusion of knowledge” seen in Fernbach’s survey research. Instead, unexpectedly, CSN high school students somewhat accurately predicted their knowledge of biotechnology (see Figure 1). This unexpected result, which does not align with conclusions from previous research using adult populations, could be explained by the frequent testing high school students undergo. Since students, unlike adults, are constantly tested on a variety of topics in school, perhaps they are able to better self-assess their true knowledge of school-related topics, such as biotechnology.

VII. Limitations

To most thoroughly understand the complex relationship between knowledge of biotechnology, both self-assessed and objective, and attitudes toward GM foods, all potential limitations must be considered. Although this observational study provides insight into the interrelation between knowledge and attitudes at a singular Southwest Florida (SWFL) high school, the obtained statistical results cannot be generalized to a larger population. Generalizing to a larger population, such as all US high school students, would require future research with a different and sub- stantially larger selected SRS.

Another notable limitation stems from the possibility of students accessing and using external resources to answer true-false questions presented on the portion of the questionnaire measuring objective knowledge of biotechnology. While a sentence above this specific section of the questionnaire stated “Please answer the following questions to the best of your ability. Do not use external resources for assistance”, it is still possible participants could have searched online or utilized school science textbooks to glean answers. As a result, participants’ objective knowledge scores may not be accurate representations of their actual knowledge of biotechnology.

Finally, the time of day participants completed the Google Forms survey could have altered results. Since the survey was distributed online, participants were given the option to re- spond at any convenient time of the day. Google Forms releases the times that responses were submitted; interestingly, six participants submitted the online survey after 11 p.m. Logically, participants completing the survey late at night may have been less focused due to fatigue (Blatter & Cajochen, 2007). Overall, this could have negatively affected the care with which the survey was completed in general and thus, specifically altered participants’ objective knowledge scores as this section required great mental clarity.

VIII. Conclusion

This research is the first to directly compare knowledge of biotechnology to attitudes toward GM foods in a specific population of high school students. The results of this observational study show Rozin’s principle of extremism, which states extreme opposition often stems from lack of knowledge, held true for CSN high school students. Furthermore, as mentioned above, the data also show, unlike previous studies, the psychological phenomenon termed an “illusion of knowledge” did not hold true for participants at CSN (Berger, 2019; Fernbach, 2016). As a result of this unexpected finding, the relationship between frequent school testing and students’ ability to self-assess knowledge should be further investigated.

Additionally, because of the outcomes of this study, future qualitative research should center around evaluating the effects of educational interventions that explain biotechnological topics on students’ attitudes toward GM foods. This future research would improve the current understanding of the relationship between knowledge of biotechnology and attitudes toward GM foods, which would prove immensely beneficial in potentially identifying lack of knowledge of biotechnology as a statistically significant factor contributing to widespread public opposition to genetically modified (GM) foods.

title: Why Work When You Can Play: A Literature Review on Theatre-based Interventions for Autism Spectrum Disorder
text:
Why Work When You Can Play:

A Literature Review on Theatre-based Interventions for Autism Spectrum Disorder

Few disorders are as complicated or as debated as autism spectrum disorder (ASD). It has a broad and heterogenous disorder; it has multiple etiologies with a combination of polygenetic and environmental factors; it’s very nature as a diagnostic category has changed within the last iteration of the DSM-V (Beauchaine & Hinshaw, 2017). The one fact that everyone seems to agree on is that ASD manifests largely through social communication impairments. These impairments often manifest in toddlerhood, during a developmental period in which typically developing children begin to display signs of joint attention (shared focus with another person on a stimulus), self-concept, and emotion regulation (Siegler et al., 2020). Any developmental deficit in these areas leads to cascading effects throughout childhood and adolescence, often adversely affecting one’s adult life. Early intervention is therefore vital; but it isn’t always possible due to resource limitations. Also, given the chimeral nature of the disorder, choosing and implementing an intervention can be daunting.

The National Clearinghouse on Autism Evidence & Practice currently cites 27 different evidence-based practices and hundreds of non-evidence-based interventions being practiced at this time (Steinbrenner et al., 2020). Many interventions that have yet to be determined as evidence-based are not necessarily ineffective interventions but lack rigorous scientific studies to support their claims of efficacy. Again, this comes down to resources. However, it also has to do with the difficulty in operationalizing experiments for treatments that are often as heterogenous as the disorder they hope to help. One such intervention is theatre-based or socio-dramatic play.

This paper will illuminate some of the successes and struggles of theatre-based interventions.

First, I will provide further background on the components of autism spectrum disorder that many interventions hope to address. I will briefly discuss the approach taken by some of the more well-known interventions, before explaining how theatre-based interventions have the potential to improve upon previous methods. I will then discuss the few experimental studies of theatre-based interventions, underlining their respective strengths and weaknesses. Finally, I will discuss future directions for both the research and treatment opportunities in a promising, if complicated, intervention.

ASD as a Series of Social Skills Deficits

To be diagnosed with ASD according to the DSM-V, one must display at least two restricted and repetitive behaviors, while also showing evidence of deficits in socio-emotional reciprocity, nonverbal communication, and relationship development/maintenance (American

Psychiatric Association, 2013). These impairments often appear through a child’s struggles with joint attention (JA), play behavior, and facial/emotional recognition (Siegler et al., 2020). While the outward manifestations of such deficits are often obvious through an inability to understand and respond appropriately to other people’s emotions and actions, the underlying causes can be less straightforward. Typically, the disorder is seen as a combination of affective and cognitive deficits.

Prevailing theories tie these communication deficits together under a banner of Theory of

Mind (ToM), meaning the ability to take on the perspective of another person (Baron-Cohen,

1995). A classic measurement of ToM is the false-belief task in which a person must recognize that another person can believe something even if it is counterfactual. Children with ASD find this task especially difficult (Siegler et al. 2020). A nativist viewpoint is that an individual with

ASD struggles with ToM tasks due to atypical brain size and activity in areas such as the prefrontal and temporal cortices, amygdala, and temporoparietal junction; these brain regions relate to selective attention, face-recognition, empathy, and interpersonal information processing

(Beauchaine & Hinshaw, 2017). While this theory finds support through brain scans and post- mortems of individuals with ASD (Arioli et al., 2021; Kennedy & Adolphs, 2012), the question of whether the differences in brain volume etc. come from genetics or environmental impact remains unclear. Empiricists argue that ToM deficits come from a dearth of learning opportunities through interactive experience with other people (Seigler et al., 2020). In reality, the ToM deficits experienced by children with ASD are probably a combination of both nature and nurture. Early disruptions in brain activity lead to struggles with social interactions which, in turn, discourage children from honing social skills through interpersonal interactions. Many therapies (especially early interventions) aim to disrupt this cycle. Because of the complicated etiology of ASD as well as its heterogenous nature, most interventions attempt to help through addressing behavioral issues.

ASD Interventions: How They Can Hurt and Help

The most well-known ASD intervention is Applied Behavioral Analysis (ABA), a predecessor to the many behavioral therapies on today’s evidence-based practice list. ABA targets specific skills such as making eye contact or repetitive behaviors such as hand-flapping to either enforce or extinguish through operant conditioning. The intervention involves long sessions of exposing a subject to a repeated stimulus, traditionally using both reinforcement and punishment to train the behavior of children with ASD. The use of punishment is less popular now, but adults with ASD who received ABA in childhood intervention claim that it was not only ultimately unhelpful, but abusive. ABA is seen by many in the ASD community as compliance conditioning or obedience training (Devita-Raeburn, 2020). By targeting an individual’s behavior alone, ABA often misses an opportunity to address underlying cognitive aspects of ASD, making it difficult for the individual to translate progress they made in therapy to other people or environments. While ABA has been shown to be effective in eliminating or encouraging certain behaviors, the intervention often struggles to generalize effects outside of intervention conditions (Sandbank et al., 2020).

Failing to be able to generalize to real-world situations is a problem that many psychosocial interventions for ASD encounter (Smith et al., 2007). However, a number of interventions have found ways to overcome this methodological hurdle. In a meta-analysis of

ASD interventions for young children, Sandbank et al. (2020) found the largest positive effect sizes for Developmental Interventions and Naturalistic Developmental Behavioral Interventions.

While only the latter employs the less punitive social skills training techniques of ABA, both approaches emphasize Vygotsky’s principle of social interaction as a mechanism for learning and development (Siegler, 2020). Setting the session in naturalistic contexts and using real life relationships such as parent-child or child-peer, the interventions produce positive effects for children with ASD that generalize to people and contexts in every-day life. The two interventions are also administered almost exclusively through play.

The use of play as intervention technique is not only proven to be effective, but importantly, creates conditions that allow for more agency on the part of the child. One of the first points of entry in treating children with ASD is JA. In a systematic review of studies on JA literature, White et al. (2011) found that the most effective interventions involved play as primary component. Teaching JA through play provides a naturalistic environment with natural consequences in which to learn, two key components of generalization. Moreover, White et al.

(2011) point out, the use of play is especially advantageous for children with ASD as play is a critical part of one’s development of communication skills beyond JA. Finally, play provides the opportunity for the child to lead her own treatment, creating intrinsic motivation to learn and practice social skills (Gupta, 2009). Putting more control in the hands of the child with ASD also supports a growing need voiced by the ASD community for a neurodiversity conceptualization of ASD (Sandbank et al., 2020). In accepting that ASD is simply a naturally occurring difference of how to exist in the world, a play intervention provides opportunities for the child to learn skills as they choose, rather than training them to comply with specific societal standards.

A study by Kasari et al. (2006) on JA and Symbolic Play (SP) found evidence to support the integration of symbolic (in addition to functional) play in ASD interventions. Using a sample of 58 children with ASD, the study randomly assigned participants to either a control group, a JA behavioral training session, or an intervention involving SP. The researchers found that the SP intervention was just as effective in teaching the children to initiate and be receptive towards efforts of JA. Even more exciting, however, was the finding that the SP group improved significantly more than the JA group in functional play (such as brushing a doll’s hair) and SP

(such as using a block in place of a brush) as well as sophistication of play (mastery level overall). The study also found that the children were able to generalize treatment outcomes to interactive play with their mothers at home. These results have encouraged further studies on the effects of SP in interventions for children with ASD.

Socio-dramatic Play & Theatre-based Interventions

SP may be divided into three subtypes: substitution (eg. a child uses a block as a brush), agent-directed (eg. a child has a doll brush its own hair), and imaginary (eg. a child brushes the hair of an imaginary friend). Socio-dramatic play encompasses all three of these play behaviors with the added component of interpersonal interaction (Siegler et al., 2020; So et al, 2020).

Children with ASD typically struggle with all three forms of SP and rarely participate in, let alone initiate socio-dramatic play. This play deficit has shown to be predictive of further deficits in ToM, language development, social communication, and interpersonal relationships (Baron-

Cohen, 1995). Theatre, by naturally addressing aspects of these issues, seems to contain all the components for an effective ASD intervention. Theatre encourages interpersonal communication on a verbal and nonverbal level. It requires rehearsal of such skills in a controlled, but naturalistic environment. Theatre exercises an individual’s empathy and understanding of multiple perspectives.  It also revolves around imaginary circumstances (while clearly delineating the difference between reality and fiction). Importantly, theatre puts ownership of the process in the hands of the participants and creates intrinsic motivation through its reliance on play. Finally, theatre requires the formation of relationships through creation of ensemble (Gallo-

Lopez, 2012; Gupta, 2009). It’s no surprise, then, that several researchers have begun to investigate the effect of socio-dramatic or theatre-based interventions on the ASD population.

Research on theatre-based interventions for ASD, while small in number, takes many forms. From single case studies to random controlled trials (RCTs), from qualitative to quantitative measures, from a focus on specific skills-training to the performance of a full play, the ways in which researchers choose to operationalize theatre-based intervention research is heterogenous to say the least. In the following section, I will first discuss the studies addressing cognitive aspects of ASD. Next, I will examine the studies that measured behavioral indicators of social comprehension. Finally, I will mention a third category of measurement loosely defined as emotional well-being of child and family.

Social Knowledge: Cognitive Effects of Theatre-based Interventions

Development of ToM, which encompasses the cognitive aspects of social communication, in a child typically follows in this order: 1) the ability to initiate, receive, and maintain joint attention, 2) the understanding that other people act on what they want, 3) the understanding that other people have diverse beliefs, 4) the understanding that those beliefs may be counter to reality, and 5) the understanding that a person’s desires and beliefs may not always be readily perceivable through what they say or do (Baron-Cohen, 1995). Conceptually, this is a very clear break-down of the growth of social comprehension; however, measuring such concepts is not nearly as straightforward. Because of ToM’s many components, there are many ways to measure it, some of which are discussed below.

A study by Goldstein & Winner (2012) on neurotypical populations has shown a clear connection between acting experience and improved empathy and Theory of Mind. Though the study does not focus on an intervention for the ASD population, it indicates the potential effectiveness of theatre as intervention for cognitive-perceptual aspects of social deficits. In two studies of different age groups (9 year-olds and 14 year-olds, respectively), the study examined effects of a year-long acting program (involving improv games, character analysis, scene studies, and physical activities) on children’s empathy and ToM. At the completion of the program, researchers measured ToM and empathy through a series of established and novel tasks. The study found significant improvement in empathy, but not ToM for the 9 year-old group; however, it found significant improvement in both empathy and ToM for the 14 year-old group.

These results indicate potential age-related differences in a neurotypical individual’s ability to improve empathy and ToM through acting. Moreover, they imply a potential for individuals at a lower social-developmental level to increase empathic abilities, if not also ToM. It’s important to note that the study was analyzing effects of a preexisting school program and not an intervention of their own design. To compensate, researchers observed and coded the classes for content material. They found ToM was addressed more explicitly than empathy in classes for the 14 year-old group, suggesting that ToM may need to be more explicitly taught for younger (or less socially-developed) populations.

While empathy and ToM are important components of social comprehension, they are difficult to measure. This poses a clear hurdle for researchers hoping to assess the validity of interventions for ASD. One established measure that has demonstrated sensitivity with children with ASD is the DANVA2, a computer-based objective measure of nonverbal cue reading. Two studies that have made use of this measure are Lerner, Mikami, Levine (2011) and Guli et al.

(2012). Lerner, Mikami & Levine tested a performance-based social skills curriculum that utilized improv games and dramatic exercises against a waitlisted control group. While not randomized, the study did ensure the control group was demographically matched. The study found a significant difference between groups in the intervention group’s ability to detect emotional cues in adult voices, but not in other measures of nonverbal cue reading. Guli et al.

(2012) also used the DANVA2 to measure effects of a similar theatre-based intervention on a mixed population of children diagnosed with ASD, NLD, and/or ADHD. This study did not find a significant difference in the intervention group’s ability to recognize nonverbal cues; however, it did find significant effects across a number of behavioral measures, discussed in detail in the following section. The discrepancy between significant effects in behavioral versus cognitive measures may indicate the inability of certain cognitive measures to accurately capture change in a child’s cognition. For instance, a computer-based test employing static pictures of faces is a poor approximation of the flurry of emotional cues one receives from a person actively communicating in real time.

A perhaps more easily measured component of social comprehension is face and emotion recognition. These are commonly measured in ASD interventions through NEPSY subtests called Memory of Faces and ToM, respectively (Corbett et al., 2019). These two tests were used in Corbett et al. (2016) and Corbett et al. (2019). Both studies were of the same peer-mediated theatre-based intervention for children with ASD and both found a significant positive effect for the face and emotion recognition tasks in the intervention versus the control group. The studies also supported their findings through EEG scans of participants during a separate face- recognition activity. The studies found heightened neural activity in children from the intervention group during the activity compared to the control. Baseline EEG’s indicated quantifiable deficits in children with ASD for face recognition and posttest EEG’s illustrated the interventions ability to improve said deficits.

Social Performance: Behavioral Effects of Theatre-based Interventions

While arguably less quantifiable than cognitive measures due to their reliance on self and parent-reports, behavioral analyses of theatre-based interventions show robust treatment effects.

Most of the studies previously mentioned employed measures of behavioral outcomes to some degree. For instance, Lerner, Mikami & Levine (2011) relied on both a parent report on their child’s nonverbal communication skills as well as a parent report on their child’s social impairment. Using these measures, the study found that the children in the intervention improved significantly in increased social assertion as well as decreased social problems. In a follow-up analysis 6 weeks post-treatment, those effects were maintained. Using post-hoc analyses, the study was able to confirm the observed maintenance was associated with change during the intervention. It should be noted, however, that this intervention was a part of an established summer program and, as such, was not provided for free to participants. Positive parental reports, therefore, may reflect their desire to see a return on investment as much as indicate true behavioral changes.

Lerner & Mikami (2012) conducted a follow up study comparing the effects of the aforementioned summer program to a more didactic skills-training program. The use of a comparison intervention in addition to a control group is useful for beginning to establish specific mechanisms of change in an intervention (Smith et al., 2007). This study used exclusively behavioral measures and improved upon the previous study’s methods by measuring behavior throughout the intervention and by enlisting feedback from the children’s teachers. The study found that both the theatre-based and direct skills-training interventions led to significantly improved social skills. However, the theatre-based intervention produced effects almost immediately, whereas the social skills group took longer to warm up. In terms of time and financial resources allocated to interventions, this study indicates increased feasibility for the theatre-based intervention as it appears to work faster (Smith et al., 2007).

Another study that employed both cognitive and behavioral measures is Guli et al.

(2012). While the study did not find significant results according to the DANVA2 cognitive measures, it found significant effects in social functioning that generalized to other environments and people. Interestingly, the behavioral assessments that were measured on a scale did not produce significant effects, whereas the observed and coded behavioral reports did. This may indicate that the scaled measures of cognitive and behavioral change lack sensitivity to social behavioral nuances that are more readily caught by observers in situ. This study involved children with social difficulties not limited to just a diagnosis of ASD. However, the majority of participants in the study had received a prior ASD diagnosis and the study’s inclusion criteria required proof of social competence difficulties through scores on the SSRS (a widely used parent-report measure employed by many ASD interventions). Also, the inclusion of participants with comorbidity diagnoses may actually get closer to generalizability, as real-world ASD and

ADHD populations overlap considerably (Beauchaine & Hinshaw, 2017; Guli et al., 2012).

Of the many studies mentioned already, the most comprehensive in terms of number and variability of measures are those of Corbett et al. (2016) and Corbett et al. (2019). Not only did the studies assess cognitive and neural outcomes of their theatre-based intervention, but they also included a battery of behavioral measures, including multiple parent reports and coded observations. Combined findings included significantly increased social communication

(especially in cooperative play and verbal interactions) for the intervention versus control group that generalized to other environments and were maintained 2 months post-treatment. These findings are especially exciting as the 2019 study was the largest sample size of any study found yet. Also, the parents did not pay for the theatre-based intervention and, thus, were less likely to inflate perceived effectiveness.

Another study that builds on the findings of Corbett et al. (2016), is that of Ioannou et al.

(2020). Using the same theatre-based intervention, the study found a significant increase compared to a control group in group play behavior as observed through a natural play paradigm that innovatively uses age-matched peers as confederates. This finding is indicates theatre-based interventions’ ability to generalize to peers outside of the intervention program and illustrates the potential effectiveness of a trained peer-mediated program in heightening reading and response to nonverbal cues coming from individuals other than adults. This study also measured comorbid conditions that will be elaborated on in the following section.

Perhaps the most innovative and certainly most interesting study on theatre-based interventions has come out of Hong Kong. So et al. (2020) also measured intervention effects on play behaviors but took a page from Kasari et al. (2006) in juxtaposing play behavior with measure of JA. The most unique aspect of the study, however, lies in the method of administering the intervention. They used robots. Specifically, the study employed two NAO

(Aldebaran Robotics Company) robots that are widely used in autism interventions (So et al.,

2020) to perform 3 scripted short dramas of varying realism and familiarity for participants. In using robots, So et al. (2020) were able to sidestep the often confounding factor of human variability in administering interventions. Whereas other interventions and studies must rely on human (and thus variable) researchers to model and respond to children during theatre activities, robots provide a consistent and reliable series of performances and interactions. This may sound disconcerting on the outside (and certainly has implications for generalizability to human-human interactions), but studies have found that children with ASD often prefer the lower stimulus level afforded by robots. The study also used human experimenters to take part in role-play scenarios related to the 3 previous dramas enacted by robots. So et al. (2020) found that children receiving the intervention as opposed to the control group increased significantly in functional play and SP as well as JA. Interestingly, when comparing the roleplay with robots to the roleplay with human experimenters, researchers found a significant increase in gestures used and decrease in prompts required for the human experimenters. Effects also seemed to generalize as the differences in play behavior and join attention were measured 1 month post treatment and involved human experimenters. This indicates that the use of robot-based interventions may increase social behaviors, if not necessarily affect underlying cognitive processes.

Social Feelings & Impressions: Emotional Effects of Theatre-based Interventions

Ironically, many studies of ASD -a disorder based in the struggle to understand others’ emotions- do not study the emotional states of their participants. While this seems like an obvious oversight, it is understandable, as reading the emotions of a child with ASD can be particularly difficult. Some studies, however, have attempted to get at this important question through parent and child questionnaires and interviews.

Perhaps because of theatre’s immediate emphasis on emotion and empathy, many of the theatre-based interventions have endeavored to measure the emotional well-being of participants.

Lerner, Mikami & Levine (2011), Lerner & Mikami (2012), Guli et al. (2019), and So et al.

(2020) all employed post-treatment parent and child-reports in an attempt to elicit such information. All studies found enthusiastic and positive responses to the interventions, indicating that parents not only observed post-treatment effects on social comprehension, but also on overall positive mood changes in their children mid and post-treatment. Participants, themselves, reported positive change in emotional well-being with comments like the following from Guli et al. (2012): “I’m a bit calmer. I can understand people now. I have a social life now,” and “I learned that I could handle myself a lot better than I thought I could” (p. 42). Two studies

(Lerner, Mikami & Levine, 2011; Ioannou et al., 2020) directly addressed depression and anxiety through CBCL and STAIC self-reports. While Lerner, Mikami & Levine found no significant change in depressive symptoms post-intervention, Ioannou et al. (2020) reported significant decreases in trait anxiety post-treatment. These improvements in emotional well-being and self- esteem may seem insignificant in comparison to the more targeted behavioral changes, however they are important indicators of protective factors that could improve outcomes for these children later in life (Beauchaine & Hinshaw, 2017). Also, participants who enjoy the intervention are much more likely to continue it, thus preventing against recidivism, a common problem for intervention studies (Smith et al., 2007; Sandbank et al., 2020). Participants are more likely to form the motivation to practice acquired skills outside intervention conditions when the form of learning is fun (Gupta, 2009). Finally, struggles with mood and internalizing behaviors are exceedingly common for children with ASD (Beauchaine & Hinshaw, 2017). Therefore, any intervention that can address comorbid conditions such as depression or anxiety in the participants is worth a second look.

Future Directions

While many of the results from the aforementioned studies are promising, they must be taken with a grain of salt. Most studies addressed in this literature review had very small sample sizes (the largest being 77 children) as well as homogonous participant pools (primarily

Caucasian males). Also, many studies differed in administration of the interventions both in terms of duration of treatment as well as content covered. Next, as shown above, there are many different forms of measurement used, not all of which have established validity. Finally, the study designs often lacked a comparable intervention and, if they did have a control group, were typically unable to randomize participants. These are all significant blows to the integrity of the results. However, the potential benefits of an intervention that may be administered over a relatively short period of time by practitioners aside from certified therapists and that show promise for generalizability and maintenance through their use of naturalistic play are difficult to ignore.

Aside from addressing the clear research-related issues in theatre-based interventions, there are also several factors to consider in formulating future interventions. The majority of the studies on socio-dramatic play were on high-functioning children in ages ranging from middle to high school. It will be important moving forward to assess if and how interventions may help younger and lower-functioning children with ASD. The Vygotskyian concept of scaffolding may be especially important in this regard (Siegler et al, 2020).

Overall, theatre-based interventions are a promising new approach to helping children with ASD develop skills that they may apply as they choose to everyday social interaction.

Rather than directly training children in set behaviors, theatre-based interventions provide children with opportunities to experiment, and practice set skills in a variety of circumstances, all the while allowing and encouraging children to play.
