title: The Idea of Tibet: Forms and Functions of Narrative Storytelling in Exile
text:
Zhou 1

​

​

​

​

The Idea of Tibet:

Forms and Functions of Narrative Storytelling in Exile

Audrey Zhou

Professors Arthur McKeown and Sarah Jacoby

December 7th, 2024

​

​

​

​

Zhou 2

Our Shared Stories

The air was crisp that Wednesday morning, but I was uncomfortably sweaty. A few wrong turns and Google Maps misreadings resulted in an unexpected morning spent scaling a neighboring hillside in a fruitless attempt at finding an easy shortcut. Pushing past tall pine trees and prickly underbrush, I prayed that I was heading in the direction of Jampaling Elder’s Home, known by locals as ‘Old People Home.’ It was here that I met Sonam Lhundup, an 82-year-old former cowherd for the Dalai Lama. Sitting on a small green bench outside his simple room, exhausted by my unexpected climb, I asked him to tell me his story.

With a slight reluctance, Sonam-la1 began. Originally from a small village at the foothills of Mount Kailash —  the mountain of Milarepa legend —  Sonam-la crossed the Himalayas in

1959 when he was only fifteen years old, step-in-step with approximately one hundred thousand other Tibetans and His Holiness, the Dalai Lama.2 The story of this treacherous crossing is one shared by many of the Tibetans I met and interviewed during my time in Dharamshala, a small town in the north Indian state of Himachal Pradesh and home to the Tibetan

Government-in-Exile. Dhondup Gyalpo —  now Headmaster of the Junior School at the Tibetan

Children’s Village school —  made the crossing when he was six years old;3 Bhuchung D.

Sonam, poet, writer, and founder of TibetWrites — a publishing house for Tibetan writing — at eleven years old;4 Kunsang Tenzin-la, creator of the Stories of Tibetans project and Tibet Hope

4  Bhuchung D. Sonam quoted by Tenzin D. Tsagong, “An Exiled Publisher Creates a ‘Brotherhood across Tibetans.’” The New York Times, The New York Times, 12 July 2023.

3 Personal interview with Dhondup Gyalpo. Headmaster of the Junior School at Upper Tibetan Children’s Village. Mcleodganj, India. November 30th, 2024.

2 Personal interview with Sonam Lhundup, Elder residing at Jampaling Elder’s Home and former cowboy for the Dalai Lama, Mcleodganj, India. Personal Interview. November 27th, 2024.

1 -la is a common Tibetan honorific added to the end of names to convey respect.

Zhou 3

Center, at six years old.5 In Dharamshala and its neighboring suburb of Mcleodganj, nearly every

Tibetan I met spoke of their relationship to their homeland, speaking of either a longing to return or a dream to see a place they have never been before. It is clear that this shared story of the exile experience is central to the Tibetan-in-Exile community, a narrative which holds, bridges, crosses, contains, and colors each individual’s life narrative.

The purpose of my inquiry is to further understand how the creation of this shared narrative occurs through storytelling. In asking the very broad and open question, “How does storytelling function within the Tibetan-in-Exile community?,” I have found a diversity of rejoinders unique to the political context and history of this community. Separated from the lands of Tibet, the Tibetan diaspora in Dharamshala and Mcleodganj must instead actively construct a rich and complex idea of Tibet, one that becomes real in the active process of storytelling. It is through the vehicle of narrative that diasporic Tibetans unlock full potential for creative transformation. In an interview for the New York Times, Bhuchung D. Sonam sums it up best:

“Until we find a political solution, we have to hold and build this idea of Tibet — whether you call it a home or an idea, . . . and art does that.”6 The voice of writer and editor Tenzin Dickie echoes this sentiment, succinctly expounding on the power of Tibetan prose: “It’s not like I can live my life on Tibetan land . . . but I can live it in Tibetan literature.”7

In this paper, I synthesize my observations from three weeks in the field. By weaving together fresh art, literature, and stories directly from people themselves, I aim to show how storytelling in exile functions cohesively in three broadly construed ways — as reclamation, protestation, and creation — to construct a real ‘idea of Tibet.’

7 Tsagong.

6 Tsagong.

5 Personal interview with Kunsang Tenzin, Founder of Tibet Hope Center and Stories for Tibetans. Mcleodganj, India. December 2nd, 2024.

Zhou 4

Theory and Praxis

Initially, I had approached this assignment with a much simpler hypothesis, one rooted in my practice and study of chaplaincy last summer, which posits that storytelling is the key to grief processing and psychological healing. Through storytelling, actors gain both the critical distance and the necessary empowerment to fully claim their narrative in an act of radical transformation from passivity toward activity. In the words of Arthur Frank in The Wounded Storyteller: “The ill person who turns illness into story transforms fate into experience.”8 Further, storytelling requires at least two parties — one to tell and one to hear. Chaplaincy capitalizes on the dialectical nature of this dynamic, often using the mere presence of a ‘story-hearer’ to prompt the patient to embody the role of storyteller. In psychologist Honey Oberoi Vahali’s book Lives in

Exile: Exploring the Inner World of Tibetan Refugees, she expounds on the therapeutic nature of these forms of encounters, explaining how a “dialogical aperture enables a person to articulate certain aspects of her inner experience in the presence of an empathetic ‘other’ . . . [thus]

creati[ng an] inter-subjective, intermediary ‘third’ space [that] makes it possible . . . to gain fresh understandings about the past.”9 Though her argument refers to the relationship between researcher and research-participant, I believe that it applies to any encounter between a storyteller and empathetic listener — especially when that ‘third space’ of healing is intentionally contrived, as is between chaplain and patient.

And thus, it is with therapeutic aims that narrative theory and the practice of chaplaincy encourages the ill to reframe their life story in a way that is both communicable and palatable to themselves and to their audience. Scholar Anne Hansen explored this practice in her work in

9 Honey Oberoi Vahali, Lives in Exile: Exploring the Inner World of Tibetan Refugees. (Routledge India, 2023), xx-xxi

8 Arthur W. Frank, The Wounded Storyteller: Body, Illness, and Ethics. (The University of Chicago Press, 2013), Prologue, xi.

Zhou 5 narrative therapy with Khmer refugees and trauma victims, explaining in her article “Narrative,

Sub-Ethics, and the Moral Life: Some Evidence from Theravāda Buddhism,” co-authored with

Charles Hallisey, that a key ‘refiguration’ may be achieved through narrative “insofar as it enables us to cultivate a crucial distance from our own circumstances and gives us a way of seeing our lives with a degree of detachment.”10 Hansen reflects further, noting how at times when reflecting on one’s own life may be too painful, Khmer refugees often found solace in the telling of well-known Buddhist stories of grief and loss (e.g. the story of Patacara11 or Kisa

Gotami), stories they found their own life narratives reflected in.12

Additionally, once the story has been heard and told, psychiatrist and anthropologist

Arthur Kleinman’s narrative theory expounds, the chaplain is able to respond with their own interpretation. Together, the dyad can begin to build a collaborative retelling of the person’s lived experiences.13 With proper training and skill, these critical revisions can disrupt cycles of grief, working to liberate patients from many of illness’s trappings.

The potential of the dynamic, dialectical act of storytelling is one propounded not only in the Western psychological cannon but also reflected in some of Buddhism’s oldest tales. Kisa

Gotami’s mustard seed story is one famous for its universal resonance. A young mother, Kisa

Gotami’s story begins with the deeply grieved loss of her son. Unable to process this personal tragedy, she goes mad with anguish. An ‘empathetic story-hearer,’ the Buddha witnesses and guides, offering her a simple instruction: Bring me a pinch of mustard seeds from a house which

13 Daniel H. Grossoehme, “Chaplaincy and narrative theory: A response to risk’s case study.” Journal of Health Care Chaplaincy, vol. 19, no. 3, July 2013, pp. 101

12 Hallisey and Hansen, pp. 323.

11 Suffering the loss of her husband, two sons, her parents, and brother, Patacara falls mad with grief. It is only through the kindness and wisdom of the Buddha that she is redeemed and attains arhathood.

10 Charles Hallisey and Anne Hansen. “Narrative, Sub-Ethics, and the Moral Life: Some Evidence from Theravāda Buddhism.” The Journal of Religious Ethics, vol. 24, no. 2, 1996, pp. 323.

Zhou 6 has not experienced grief, and I’ll bring back your son. And thus, Kisa begins her journey knocking door to door in an attempt to find such a household. Gradually, as each house tells her their own stories of loss, Kisa begins to see outside her own grief, realizes the suffering of others, and moves forward. In her essay, “Searching for Mustard Seeds and Flickering Flames: A Guide to Reading as a Mode of Care,” Harvard Divinity School student Sarah Fleming explains that “it is not just the content of the teaching that enables her to move on — it is also the process, the relationships that her impossible quest draws her into, . . . [and the] sustained attention required in moving through the narrative of another, that allows [Kisa Gotami] to move through her grief.”14 Fleming argues that in this story, Kisa herself holds a chaplain-like role, illustrating a more overlooked process: one in which in the receiving of grief stories, the chaplain herself is transformed.

When presented with the opportunity to spend three weeks traveling on the other side of the world to investigate any topic I might be interested in, I jumped at the opportunity to continue my investigation of spiritual care and grief processing. I had heard of an opportunity to shadow at Delek Hospital, a small allopathic hospital founded in 1971 with the blessing of His

Holiness the 14th Dalai Lama, and the support of the Central Tibetan Administration.15 Delek is a Buddhist hospital by and for the Tibetan community, with an emphasis on equity and compassion. I was curious how staff attitudes and behaviors, institutional policy differences, and its specific patient population would affect the flavor of care provided here.

However, arriving in Dharamshala with these questions, an attitude of openness, and a just-show-up mentality, I was able to discover far more than I had initially imagined— though I

15“About Us - Who We Are.” Delek Hospital, delekhospital.org/about-us/. Accessed 7 Dec. 2024.

14Sarah Fleming, "Searching for Mustard Seeds and Flickering Flames: A Guide to Reading as a Mode of Care." Harvard Divinity School. 2021.

Zhou 7 found some evidence for my original thesis of storytelling as a vehicle for transformative healing

— such as Bhuchung D. Sonam’s reflections on why he writes:

Left in a foreign country without kin . . . everything was new. Writing and literature became a salve to help survive the loss of homeland and family. The writing seals the pain. It’s a process of negotiating this really harsh and endless barrage of obstacles and challenges that exile throws at you.16

And the words in poet Ten Phun’s introduction to his collection Sweet Butter Tea: “The truth is that a mere exercise of putting pen to paper creates necessary values through which the mental void and trauma of dislocation can get streamed out.”17 What truly struck me was the sense of joyful unity, determination, and collective protest embodied by the Tibetan-in-Exile community I met in my time at Dharamshala.

In the remainder of this paper, I strive to accurately capture the current lived attitudes and movements of this group, along with distilling a sense of the ‘idea of Tibet’ that is created in

Vahali’s ‘third space’ of narrative storytelling. Though with the scope of this project it would be impossible to make wide and sweeping generalizations, I hope to have captured a semi-realistic snapshot informed by a diversity of voice. In the last three weeks, I conducted nine formal interviews and countless informal conversations with students, monastics, business owners, teachers, doctors, nurses, artists, and storytellers. My interviewees range from ages 30–82. The stories I have collected span generations. I read widely, seeking out the voices of Tibetan authors, poets, and activists. I participated in both the second annual Dharamshala Khadhok Art

Exhibition: Unsettled, and the inaugural Tibetan Artists Festival. Visiting historic institutions such as the Central Tibetan Administration, upper Tibetan Children’s Village (TCV), the Tibet

17 Ten Phun. Sweet Butter Tea. Square One Classic, 2017.

16 Tsagong.

Zhou 8

Museum, and the Dalai Lama’s Temple, I attempted to receive the rich stories and harrowing history of this community with openness and clarity.

In this abridged version of my thesis, I hope to introduce and discuss how narrative is an important vehicle for reclamation, allowing actors not only to transition from passivity toward activity in an Arthur Frank-ian sense of the idea, but creating the space necessary for them to re-define and tell their own complex stories, refuting the predominant and reductive stereotype.

Further, returning to the specific context and history of Tibet and the ongoing conflict with

China, I explore how the mere circulation and preservation of Tibetan literature and language is an act of protestation, actively challenging oppressive powers. Finally, I explore these ideas in the context of Tibetan children, those of whom were born in exile and have never stepped foot in

Tibet. For them, narrative functions as creation, constructing an ‘idea of Tibet’ from the stories they learn from their families and schools.

Reclamation

In one of the first conversations I had in Mcleodganj, I spoke with artist and founder of

Khadhok Art Collective Tashi Nyima about the symbolism and story behind his painting Lost in

Searching, the only piece he decided to showcase at Unsettled, a two-week gallery showcasing

Tibetan Contemporary Art. A massive painting, Lost in Searching depicts a young Tibetan man meditating under the Bodhi Tree (where the Buddha himself sat when he attained enlightenment), with a rainbow and map of a Buddhist pilgrimage circuit behind him. Next to and below him are painted a naked woman, a box of pizza, scattered cash, and a boombox.

Compositionally inspired by traditional thangka paintings, Lost in Searching contrasts the highest, most spiritual subjects near the top of the painting with the realities of desire and attachment as a young person near the bottom. Nyima-la explained how this painting was a

Zhou 9 reaction to frustratingly one-dimensional stereotypes of Tibetans as highly spiritual and untouched people he has encountered. “You don’t know me,” I recall Nyima-la explaining with a laugh, “I may have more temptations and desires than even you!”18 In completing this painting and organizing the large gallery space it was displayed at, Nyima-la expresses a complex lived experience, directly challenging popular conceptions. With one painting, Nyima-la deconstructs an abstract and nebulous stereotype to a real and personal level.

The many writings of Tenzin Tsundue, red-bandana-ed activist and co-founder of

TibetWrites and Blackneck Books, echo a similar sentiment. In his February 2005 article

“Celebrating Exile II: Our religion and the struggle,” Tsundue-la speaks about the disappointment he has noticed in his non-Tibetan friends when they realize that he does not pray, prostrate, or do other rituals19 — and yet he proudly claims to be Buddhist: “That’s why the reality disappoints them: Tibetans in jeans, enjoying discos, monks on motorbikes, doing the things they do in their lives. Their imagined glass idol is broken. For me kindness and sincerity are guiding principles of Buddhism in life. One’s service in action for society is true worship.”20

As new young voices strive to elevate themselves and be heard, they work directly to dispel old stereotypes. In many ways, these individual stories humanize this community, impelling readers to relate to the authors themselves instead of focusing on larger historical and cultural contexts.

Individual stories, however, are often overlooked or overshadowed by competing narratives. One of my interviewees, Kunsang Tenzin—  the producer, director, and interviewer behind Stories for Tibetans—  spoke about the importance of a platform to highlight the voices

20 Tsundue.

19 Tenzin Tsundue. “Celebrating Exile II: Our Religion and the Struggle.” Tenzin Tsundue, Tibetbridges, 1 Feb. 2005. Accessed 9 Dec. 2024.

18 Personal interview with Tashi Nyima. Artist and founder of Khadhok Arts Collective. Mcleodganj, India. November 27th, 2024.

Zhou 10 of Tibetans-in-Exile as a collective.21 Having made the crossing to India when he was only six years old, Tenzin-la went to the Tibetan Children’s Village (TCV) for education, an environment he claims spoiled him — failing to instill in him the drive to take responsibility to do his part for the Tibetan cause. It was only in university, after a fight with Indian peers and a sharp jab of

“you refugees don’t have anything” that everything changed for Tenzin-la. Initially planning to immigrate to America with his family at 23, Tenzin-la decided instead to stay and invest all his energy into building something for his community.

Tenzin-la began by teaching English classes of 10–15 students. Over the years, these classes grew and grew, until eventually, Tenzin-la founded the Tibet Hope Center in 2000, a volunteer-powered NGO which works to further education, aid, and cultural exchange. Almost twenty years later, inspired by Humans of New York, an American storytelling project, Tenzin-la started the Humans of Dharamshala project, and then Stories of Tibetans — a platform designed to give people the flexibility to share however they want. Tenzin-la explained how traditional interviewees are always those who have already accomplished something. Stories of Tibetans, on the other hand, hopes to capture raw stories of people wherever they are, real people whose work-in-progress projects and goals could use the help and connections this exposure might bring, in real time. Tenzin-la is humble, explaining how though his weekly hour-long videos may not currently receive much attention or money, their true importance will shine twenty, fifty years in the future — as an important record of how people live now. In these stories, he explains, there is the power to dispel the judgements that people in small communities inevitably have of each other, and act as an important force in “uniting our own people.” In the now over

200 videos up on the Stories of Tibetans YouTube channel, it is clear that Tenzin-la not only

21 Personal interview with Kunsang Tenzin.

Zhou 11 believes in the philosophy at the center of his work but has put in countless hours toward working toward its realization: “All stories should be documented; all stories matter.”22

Protestation

In every interview I have conducted as part of this project, politics has inevitably come up. And how could it not? With the urgency, continuation, and every-present nature of the ongoing political situation in Tibet, every attempt to preserve Tibetan language and culture becomes an inherently political act. Burning the Sun’s Braids: New Poetry from Tibet, is a slim volume of poetry translated by Bhuchung D. Sonam and published by Blackneck Books in 2017.

To protect writers that may face detention if the People’s Republic of China (PCR) suspected them of collaborating with Tibetans-in-Exile, Sonam-la chose not to seek any copyright permissions from the poets of the original works. The translator’s note at the beginning of the book reads, “None of the poets featured in this collection knows his/her work is rendered into

English and published in exile. I decided not to get in touch with or relay to anyone of them about this translation project for reasons that Beijing knows best.”23

While this book strongly alludes to the political implications of its existence, I believe that it could also be argued that, in the context of Chinese occupation, every production and circulation of Tibetan language and literature is an act of protest. The afterword featured in

Burning expounds on the reality of being an artist or writer in Tibet. Tenzin Dorjee — lecturer at

Columbia University and former executive director for Students for a Free Tibet — explains how

“for anyone living in a political tinderbox like Tibet, where every attempt to live . . . is choked by

23 Bhuchung D. Sonam, Burning the Sun’s Braids: New Poetry from Tibet. Blackneck Books, 2017.

22 Personal interview with Kunsang Tenzin.

Zhou 12 an inescapable web of rules, restrictions and penalties . . . even nonpolitical matters like love, friendship and leisure are never truly free from the tentacles of politics.”24

While this reality paints a bleak picture, conversely, it also means that Burning can be read as a triumph, “evidence that the Chinese state has not won the battle for Tibetans’ hearts and minds.”25 In a very real way, these poems challenge “Chinese colonial power by naming the poverty of life under its rule and in refusing the colonized present,” while also providing a rallying impetus for action. I have noticed that in the narratives I have engaged with, actors are always careful not to paint an entirely discouraging picture, always coupling the honest, and at times bleak, picture of Tibet’s reality with encouraging calls to continue fighting for a Free Tibet.

In the words of Tsering Wangmo Dhompa, the first female Tibetan poet published in English, “It is through reminders of a shared history that the poets speak as though to be with the people and to rouse the people to consciousness . . . The present is the space and place in which a national community and a collective consciousness is generated by Tibetian people about Tibetan struggles.”26

Creation

Dreaming Tibet, one of Khadhok Art Collective’s new projects this year, asked 200 hundred students across five different schools to create an artwork in response to the prompt, ‘If I were in Tibet . . .’ For these children, artist Tashi Nyima-la explained, though they have never stepped foot into Tibet, they share a common longing for this place they have learned about through the stories of their parents and cultures. For them, Tibet exists only as an intangible

26 Dhompa, pp. 18.

25 Tsering Wangmo Dhompa.“Revolutionary Literature: Writing from Tibet.” Burning the Sun’s Braids: New Poetry from Tibet, Blackneck Books, Gamru Village Dharamsala, HP India, 2017, pp. 16.

24 Tenzin (Tendor) Dorjee. “Rain, Fire and Freedom.” Burning the Sun’s Braids: New Poetry from Tibet, Blackneck Books, an Imprint of TibetWrites, Gamru Village Dharamsala, HP India , 2017, pp. 119–128.

Zhou 13

‘idea,’ one constructed through the narratives of others. A grassroots project, Dreaming Tibet selected fifty artworks from all that was submitted to be showcased at the Gangra Art Museum.

Inviting the Tibetan community, press media, and local Indians (Nyima-la emphasized the importance of sharing Tibetan stories outside of the community), Dreaming Tibet was an exhibition that celebrated the pure expression of these children’s work. For Nyima-la, after struggling himself to resist societal and familial academic pressures and find the courage to pursue artistry, being able to give these children a real exhibition and, for some, opportunities to interview with the press, has been immeasurably rewarding.27

Inspired by Dreaming Tibet, I found myself suddenly curious about how Sonam-la’s ‘idea of Tibet’ functions differently among children born in exile who have never entered Tibet compared to older folks who may still retain faint memories of Tibet. Unsure of what I would find, I decided to make a trip up to upper Tibetan Children’s Village, a place where so many of the Tibetans I had interviewed or spoke with had personally attended school. On my first day,

Mr. Tsultrim Dorjee-la gave me a personal tour of the TCV campus and a brief overview of the history of this unique place. Founded in 1960 when the Dalai Lama crossed the Himalayas with

51 young students, TCV’s initial operations were headed by the Dalai Lama’s elder sister,

Tsering Dolma Takla, and Diki Tsering, his mother. A charitable school created to provide a

Tibetan education for exiled Tibetan orphans and destitutes, TCV strives to preserve Tibetan language and culture through education. Now, upper TCV serves over 1000 students with most of them boarding in 32 homes, each with 24 children and an ‘ama-la,’ a Tibetan word for mother, who, living in housing quarters in the home and on call 24 hours, helps enforce the daily schedule and teaches life skills including cooking and cleaning.28

28 Tsultrim, Dorjee. Director of Upper Tibetan Children’s Village. Mcleodganj, India. Personal interview. November 29th, 2024.

27 Personal interview with Tashi Nyima.

Zhou 14

The next day, I returned to spend the morning with Mrs. Jampa Palmo-la’s Montessori class. From 8:45–11:00 a.m. every weekday and every Saturday (except every second Saturday), these twelve three-to-five-year-olds spend most of their morning reading, either aloud to each other or listening to Palmo-la’s expressive and patient narration. Palmo-la said she recently counted and found that the kids and her have already gotten through 80 books together this year.

All the books available in her classroom were printed in Tibetan. Some featured classic fairy tales, one that I had similarly grown up with, while others were familiar contemporary titles. But a curious subsection was entirely new to me. As it turns out, there is a rich library of children's books written, illustrated, and published by the Department of Education of the Central Tibetan

Administration in partnership with The Tibet Fund. Since 2014, these two organizations, along with Manjushri Educational Services, Tibetan Children’s Village, the Library of Tibetan Works and Archives, Shasta, and USAID have together supported more than 200 volumes of original and translated children’s books. Determined to increase access to “high quality, age-appropriate, culturally relevant books in Tibetan language . . . critical for Tibetan children to achieve literacy and reading proficiency in their mother tongue,”29 570,000 copies have been distributed to schools and families in India and Nepal. These books cover a wide range of topics from original works explicitly about Tibetan culture — Green Chupa and His Holiness the Dalai Lama’s

Birthday and Making Gyathuk — to translations of other children's literature including Fat Cat:

A Danish Folktale and The Very Wiggly Tooth.

In conversation with Mrs. Tsering Dolkar-la, I learned that much of TCV’s philosophy in preservation of culture is linked explicitly to the Tibetan language. Children here are raised with

Tibetan first. English is only introduced in grade four, and Hindi in grade six. Concepts and

29 “Children’s Literature.” The Tibet Fund, tibetfund.org/what-we-do/publications/childrens-literature/.

Zhou 15 ideas, she explains, are better learned in one’s own native tongue.30 Though TCV is still bound by many Indian education requirements, a recent project is translating textbooks of subjects such as social studies for older students into Tibetan, to continue the emphasis on Tibetan first.

Beyond language, TCV also incorporates cultural immersion and study in many other ways. For example, Wednesdays are Lhakar, His Holiness the Dalai Lama’s auspicious day, and children are required to attend class on Wednesdays dressed in traditional dress. Cultural songs and dances are also taught, morning Buddhist prayers are part of the daily routine, and the food cooked and served is Tibetan-ized Indian food — think rice and dal, but also tingmo’s and thukpa.

But beyond the beautiful celebration of Tibetan language and culture practiced here, there is a sense of complexity. In 2008, China began cracking down on borders, leading to much fewer influx of Tibetan immigrants and Tibetan children coming into the exile community. Now, TCV is faced with a growing lack of students, a problem which threatens to shut down other schools in this district permanently. The demographic of the children here has now changed, with more children coming from other Himalayan regions to take advantage of the cheap and quality education offered here. “Earlier this was a school for Tibetan children,” Dolkar-la explained,

“and we had a strong sense about doing something for our culture and language.”31 Now, there is a diversity of children who still don traditional Tibetan clothing every Wednesday, and there is a shared sense that “maybe this does not make sense.” But generally, Dolkar-la is careful to explain, these are not things that come to mind often and certainly are not something that affects her teaching. It will be an ongoing curiosity to see how things in this community continue to

31 Personal interview with Tsering Dolkar.

30 Tsering Dolkar. English teacher at Upper Tibetan Children's Village. Mcleodganj, India. Personal Interview. November 30th, 2024.

Zhou 16 change — how much rests on an assumed homogeneity of the community here, and how much it will adapt and transform to the ever-changing nature of our conventional realities.

Conclusion

Initially inspired by my long-time academic interests, it was only when I got out into the field, spoke with all the people I met there, and cultivated an openness to receiving what was presented to me, that this project revealed itself as a much larger, more nebulous endeavor. It is unclear to me whether I have been able to synthesize my findings in a clear and linear fashion. It has, however, been an illuminating process. In writing this essay, I myself have embodied a role like Kisa Gotami, and garnered a front-row seat to observe the playing-outs of the abstract theories I have studied. I feel incredibly grateful to have been so welcomed into the

Tibetan-in-Exile community in Dharamsala. This project rests squarely on the shoulders of all those willing to share their lives and stories with me — I know it is not always an easy task.

In my original outline, I had more space dedicated to exploring the identity and responsibility of being on the receiving end of storytelling, questioning what it means to be a listener outside of the illness narrative context. It is an interesting question, one I wish to continue to explore, of what it means to be a complete outsider to this community receiving these stories. And what it means, specifically in my case, to be a Chinese-American student traveling next to visit my distant family in China. How can I, now knowing so much more about Tibet's history, still make the crossing across that impossible border, in a journey I now know so many can only dream of. What is my place — our collective places — in the fight for a free Tibet? In the liberatory fight for all oppressed people? I suppose these are questions the poets know we will ask ourselves. The ending of Dhompa-la’s article, positioned as the introduction to

Sonam-la’s Burning, ends with a haunting warning: “The poems in this collection are

Zhou 17 heartbreaking, groundbreaking and revolutionary; readers need courage.”32 So have courage, dear readers! And continue to question your place in the order of things. If any insights arise, do let me know. I would love to hear your story.

32 Dhompa, pp. 20.

Zhou 18

title: Manufactured Color: An Analysis of the Euro-American Historic Decorated Ceramics of the Montgomery Site
text:
Manufactured Color: An Analysis of the Euro-American Historic Decorated Ceramics of the Montgomery Site

Laurel Anderson

Introduction

Industrially produced European and American ceramics produced throughout the 18th and 19th century are an invaluable resource for the dating of historic sites, as the extensive records left by their increasingly standardized production provide known dates that can be used to situate the site from which these artifacts are recovered in a broader temporal context.

Figure 1. Areas of the Montgomery Site: (1) 1836 Log House, (2) Parsonage Northwest Midden, (3) Parsonage, (4) Cabin 1, (5) Cabin 1 Southwest Midden, (6) Trails and General, (7) Cabin 2.

The Montgomery Site

The Montgomery cabin, reported to be the earliest documented Euro-American structure in Kenosha County, is located within Petrifying Springs County Park in the township of Somers, Wisconsin. Initial excavations of the site were conducted by the Kenosha County Archaeological Society (KCAS) between 1975 and 1977. From 2013 to 2023, the University of Wisconsin-Parkside has worked in conjunction with the Kenosha Public Museum to reconstruct the methods and findings of the prior group, as well as conducting further investigations across the site. These periods of work have generated a collection of 1,342 earthenware historic ceramic sherds, which form the basis for this analysis.

The investigations of the Montgomery site have yielded artifacts from seven main areas, which are laid out in Figure 1. Cabin 1 is the eponymous Montgomery family’s residence, which was occupied from approximately 1834 to 1839. This structure was likely razed before 1855 and has a midden nearby. Cabin 2 was built around 1855, occupied for a year by John Soutour. Following this, Edward Cooley then occupied the building for around 15 years. The 1836 Log House is recorded on an 1836 survey map; however, investigations have currently yielded no signs of foundations. Building materials and household items have been recovered from the area. The parsonage was built in 1855 and eventually served as a private residence until it was razed in 2014 (Sasso 2023). North of the parsonage, there is a structure shown on two maps from 1861 and 1873 respectively. Survey of the area has yielded domestic refuse and construction materials. The category “Trails and General” refers to any material found during survey outside of these specified areas, or objects whose provenience was not recorded.

Elements of Nineteenth Century Ceramics

Ware Types

The primary terms for non-vitreous, white-bodied wares (creamware, pearlware, and whiteware) do not possess mutually exclusive definitions within literature concerning historical ceramics and are often used interchangeably. Part of the reason for this discrepancy is the differences in language used by those who are primarily interested in ceramics from a collector’s perspective and those who approach this form of classification from an archaeological background.

Figure 2. An illustration of the difference in surface appearance among white-bodied wares.

Majewski and O’Brian (1984) outline the historical developments in the creation of white-bodied ceramics, as well as the contemporaneous ambiguity with which terms describe this style of ware. Roughly, what has been termed creamware was typically manufactured prior to the late eighteenth century. Pearlware introduced ca. 1780, is considered by some to be only a subtype of creamware, the primary difference in manufacturing being the addition of cobalt oxide to the glaze used on a very similar clay body. This created the illusion of a whiter appearance compared to the coloration of creamware, as well as creating the primary visual characteristic associated with pearlware: a noted pooling of blue pigment in areas of heavy glaze, which is noticeable around the foot or base of a vessel. This can also present as a greenish cast to the surface of the vessel. Further refinement in the early nineteenth century led to what is referred to as whiteware, which may have been a result of the addition of cobalt to the body of the vessel in tandem with a lesser amount in the glaze. The body of this type is much closer to a “paper white” color, rather than the yellow or blue leaning hues of the wares that preceded it.

The ceramics outlined in these categories comprise a large portion of the white-bodied decorated ceramics of the Montgomery site. Type distinction is also of less use when attempting to distinguish between whitewares produced after the 1820s, as whiteware dominated the ceramics produced after this point. The relative similarity of the visual appearance of these ware types, in addition to the fact that they were not distinct lines of production, but rather broad areas in a temporal continuum representing advances in commercial manufacturing, lead to the conclusion that a categorization based on these factors would be of relatively little use within this analysis.

Application of Color

Beginning in the early nineteenth century, commercial ceramic production likely would have relied upon color preparations manufactured by specialists (Majewski and O’Brian 1984: 139). The various metallic oxides used as the basis for color application all have differing levels of volatility and stability, meaning that not all colors were equally suitable to being subjected to high firing temperatures.

The application of these colors could be done before the application of a layer of clear glaze or after the addition of a glaze. Underglaze coloration would have to withstand the full firing temperature of the finished vessel. Overglaze coloration, though less durable, could be hardened in several steps at potentially lower temperatures, greatly increasing the range of colors that could be reliably used. The use of overglaze enamel decoration was particularly common in the production of porcelain. The firing temperatures to which underglaze colors could be reliably subjected allowed the decoration of non-vitreous and semi vitreous whitewares to utilize a larger palette of colors compared to the few colors that could be used in the decoration of vitrified wares such as porcelain.

The main components of the ceramic stains used in both these methods are colorants, diluents, and fluxes. The properties of a given coloring agent could be modified by changing the composition of the flux to suit the application that was intended. The most common color used for both hand painting and transfer printing prior to 1820 was cobalt blue, due to its high stability in both underglaze and overglaze decoration. This dominance was partially disrupted in the late 1820s, with the expansion of available underglaze colors from classic blue to include black, red, green, and yellow. Majewski and O’Brian (1987:139) attribute the explosion of colors available that took place from 1820 to 1830 to a rapidly increasing understanding of the properties of the flux and color used in decoration rather than the introduction of lead-free glaze, as proposed by Lofstrom et al. (1982). The market demand for more exclusive table wares distinct from the blue transfer print motif that had become commonplace by the 1820s may also have contributed to the motivation for applying these new chemical developments (Samford 1997).

Methods

The scope of this analysis encompasses all non-vitreous or semi-vitreous decorated earthenware recovered from the Montgomery Site over the course of the 1975-1977 KCAS excavation and the field school sessions held from 2013 to 2023 by U.W.-Parkside in conjunction with the Kenosha Public Museum. All sherds had been washed, broadly sorted, and assigned catalogue numbers prior to the beginning of this examination. The initial stage of the study involved sorting the sherds into broad types of decoration, as well as verifying previous assessment of decoration type. Multiple decorative techniques could be used on a single surface, but the size of sherds recovered from the Montgomery site makes reconstruction of individual vessels impractical, and thus sherds were sorted by their individual characteristics.  These groupings were then further separated by the location from which they were recovered. For the purposes of this study the Montgomery site was divided into seven major areas: Cabin 1, Cabin 1-Southwest Midden, Cabin 2, Parsonage House, Parsonage-Northwest Midden/Structure, 1836 Log House, and Trails & General Areas. The catalogue number of each sherd was then recorded under its decoration type and general location.

Though there are many ways to go about the classification of historic ceramics, and merits to forgoing the system of taxonomy entirely, this study focused on decoration type almost exclusively, with some allowance for wares of a different ceramic body entirely. The classification system used within this analysis is a modified version of that outlined in the DAACS Ceramic Genre Appendix, with further specification added to groups within categories which have established documentation.

Median dates were drawn from established literature regarding the general manufacturing period for any given type of ceramic. For types whose manufacture continues until the present, end production dates were taken from the end of the period of popularity. In order to complete the Mean Ceramic Dating process, a tally was taken of the number of sherds of each decoration type that was found in each area. This was then multiplied by the mean (average) production date and added to the sum for each site area, which was then divided by the total number of sherds in that location, yielding an approximate mean ceramic date for each area. Although vessel counts provide a more accurate estimation of the occupation date of a site (Lofstrom et. al. 1982), no complete ceramic objects were found at the Montgomery site, and very few could be absolutely confirmed to be from the same vessel. Using mass of sherd rather than count is also potentially problematic, as it would be disproportionately informed by those decoration types that covered the whole of a vessel and thus are likely to have more sherds attributed to them when categorizing by decoration type.

Differential breakage is also not a particularly relevant source of error, as the sample of sherds analyzed is composed of similar paste types and shares roughly the same physical properties. Porcelain, though represented at the Montgomery site, was not accounted for. This is because of the size of the sample it represents, as well as the fact that its vitrification would mean that vessels are more likely to fracture into several large pieces rather than many smaller ones. This difference would artificially inflate the weight of any non-vitreous or semi-vitreous ceramics in the averaging process, hence porcelain’s exclusion.

Figure 3. A Taxonomic tree representing the process of how decorative types were assigned. For more information on the characteristics of each type, see Appendix.

Figure 4. Timeline of Production Ranges for Nineteenth Century Ceramics.

Results

Table 1. Mean Ceramic Dates Generated by Area.

Area | Mean Ceramic Date (Sample Size)

1836 Log House | 1836.522 (n = 23)

Parsonage NW Midden | 1843.502 (n = 203)

Parsonage | 1863.333 (n = 6)

Cabin 1 | 1849.408 (n = 448)

Cabin 1 SW Midden | 1841.422 (n = 457)

Trails and General | 1839.600 (n = 10)

Cabin 2 | 1847.195 (n = 192)

All | 1845.242 (n = 1342)

Overall, the mean ceramic dates generated align with the known occupations of the Montgomery site. Though the first recorded structure in the Cabin 1 area was built ca. 1834, and occupied for about five years, the mean ceramic date for that location reflects an estimated occupation of 1849. This discrepancy may be explained by the limits of mean ceramic dating as an analytical tool. The formula applied relies on initial dates of manufacture, which are not necessarily reflective of when an object was used or discarded. Particularly with ceramics of this era, the lifespan of a piece could easily extend to ten or more years past the date that it was initially made.

Furthermore, the pattern in the ceramics found at the Montgomery site represents the disposal of sherds, not necessarily how objects were used as the site was occupied. These potential errors in blanket application of mean ceramic dating are also documented within existing archaeological literature (Majewski and O’Brian 1987). It is also known that the Parsonage House’s residents used the abandoned Montgomery Cabin’s cellar (Cabin 1) as a place to discard refuse during the mid to late 1800s. Applying these considerations to an analysis of the mean ceramic dates produced reveals the more likely reconstruction of the temporal trends in disposal of ceramics within the Montgomery site.

The later date indicated by the ceramics, in conjunction with analysis of other artifacts found in Cabin 1 indicates that it was likely used as a rubbish dump by later inhabitants of the site after its original occupants had left the area and it had ceased to be used as a home. The fact that the proposed date of 1847 for Cabin 2 also predates any recorded building in this area of the site by almost ten years is also reflective of the lag between the dates of manufacture and the period during which ceramic objects were used and discarded. Bearing in mind that mean ceramic dating commonly generates a period of at least ten years before the actual occupation of the site, the dates produced by this analysis are consistent with both the historically documented occupation of the Montgomery site and archaeological analyses previously conducted.

An additional consideration for the results of this study is that most sherds recovered are also of a relatively small size. More sizable fragments are usually associated with the breakage of this type of ceramic. Their absence strongly indicates that larger pieces were disposed of in a privy whose location has not yet been identified during archaeological surveys of the area.

The completion of this aspect of ceramic analysis for the Montgomery Site excavations not only provides further insight into both the past of the area and potential avenues for future work but may also serve as a case study in the application and modification of the technique of mean ceramic dating.

Figure 7. Montgomery site ceramic assemblage by location and decoration type.

Appendix: Guide to Decorated Ceramic Types

Transferware

Standard

Based on the description given by Majewski and O’Brian (1987:141-146): In general terms, the process of transfer printing involved the application of ink or paste to an engraved plate, which then fills all of the indentations in the pattern. Excess ink is then removed, and a piece of paper or glue bat is used to take an impression of the inked pattern and then pressed onto an unfired ceramic surface. The transfer medium is then removed, leaving the color pattern behind, which is hardened through a preliminary firing. In the case of underglaze ceramic, the piece is then dipped in the final coat of glaze and fired once again. Changes in value within transferware are produced through the use of cross hatching or stippling, details which often appear less distinct on earlier examples of transfer printing. In the early 1800s, the industry had largely moved to the use of line and stipple engraving. Other technical improvements from the same period made the use of bats for transferring impression of engravings the most common mode of production, as it allowed the use of even finer detail (Samford 1997). Polychrome, or decoration with multiple colors within the same pattern, may have been applied through multiple steps of transfer printing, or by the application of color by hand to specific areas of a transfer printed outline, though the latter is more common. Transferware in the following colors was identified from the Montgomery Site collection: red, green, black, brown, blue, purple, and polychrome. Figure . Blue transferware sherdFigure . Example of early transferwareFigure . Polychrome TransferwareFigure . Black transferware with handpainted color detailsFigure . Flow blue and flow mulberry sherds

Flow

This variation of transferware was introduced in the mid-1830s. The effect of flow decoration was produced “by firing vessels in an atmosphere into which Figure . Slip decorated sherdsvolatile chlorides were introduced” (Majewski and O’Brian 1987). Though other colors of flown transferware have been produced, the two colors featured in the Montgomery site assemblage are blue and mulberry. Within the subcategory of flow blue, denser and darker motifs are associated with earlier examples, ca. 1835-1860, while lighter patterning is more common in the later decades of the nineteenth century (Peterson 2015).

Slipped Wares

General

Rather than being a distinct type of decoration outlined by previous work on ceramic analysis, this label was used as a category for sherds exhibiting a marbled or swirled pattern of slip not consistent with any other subgroup identified below.

Annular

Refers to a technique through which colored slip is used to apply stripes to the body of a vessel, the results of which are often slightly raised or otherwise distinguishable from flat or hand painted stripes (Majewski and O’Brian 1984:45). Within analysis of the Montgomery site, sherds that exhibited uniform bands or striping associated with this method, as well as those that contained solid colors only otherwise observed in annular wares, were placed within this group.Figure . Slip decorated sherds, annular

Rouletted

An additional decorative technique used on some annular ware in which a shaped instrument is pressed into damp slip, thus lifting the color and exposing the body below (Majewski and O’Brian 1984:45).  Only one sherd of this type is known within the existing Montgomery site ceramic assemblage.Figure . Slipped Sherds, Annular (Left and Right), Rouletted (Center)

Mocha

A variation of annular ware in which “decoration is created when an acidic mixture (consisting of various combinations of tobacco juice, hops, urine, dry printer's black, turpentine, citric acid, and water) is dripped on an area of colored slip, where it spreads into dendritic forms resembling trees, seaweed, fronds, etc.” (Majewski and O’Brian 1984:45).Figure . Slip sherds, mocha

Sponge

Figure . Sponge decorated sherds, assortedWhat is most often termed “spatter ware” was achieved by tapping a brush full of paint against the side of a vessel, creating a dotted effect (Majewski and O’Brian 1984:44). Sponge ware refers to the application of glaze by use of a sponge, which typically resulted in a pattern like that of spattering, though more densely packed. Both methods were also used in combination with stencils in order to create a desired result.” (Majewski and O’Brian 1984:44). These patterns could both be either monochrome or have multiple colors applied to the same vessel, as with the striping on the characteristic tricolor spongeware, which typically features bands of red, green, and blue around a central hand painted motif (Majewski and O’Brian 1984:44). Though some authors make a distinction between the groups of “sponged”, “spattered”, and “splattered” wares, the terms do not have distinct definitions within ceramic literature, and so the general category of sponge decorated wares was not subdivided further, except for one very specific and well-defined pattern.Figure . Sponge decorated sherds, red

Open Sponge

Figure . Open sponge patterned sherdsA subset of sponge decorated wares within the Montgomery assemblage fit the characteristics of what has at times been referred to as “flowing spatter”, “kitchen”, or “cottage spatter” ware, which was likely manufactured by both British and American companies from 1860 to 1935 (Majewski and O’Brian 1987:162). The term open sponge is taken from the Diagnostic Artifacts in Maryland database, which uses that label to describe several vessels with very similar patterns to the sherds from the Montgomery site (Samford and Miller 2015).

Edge Decorated

The term “edge decorated ware” refers to all sherds that have distinct patterning or glaze decoration that is consistent with application exclusively to the rim or edge of a vessel. A large portion of these fall under the “shell edge” pattern described by Majewski and O’Brian (1987:148). This motif is comprised of short, perpendicular, impressed lines along the edge of a vessel, to which the characteristic stripe of colored glaze is applied by hand. Edge decorated shreds from the Montgomery assemblage all feature blue glaze, although green coloration was utilized during the same era.Figure . Edge decorated sherds

Hand PaintedFigure . Hand painted sherds

Hand painted ware is a category with a large amount of internal variety, including broad and narrow brushstrokes, and possibly also exhibiting stenciled designs. Motifs could be large or small, and applied Figure . Hand painted sherds, spriggedFigure . Hand painted sherd to the entire body of a piece or only a small portion. The most common pattern observed in the Montgomery Site assemblage are sherds with what is referred to as a “sprig” pattern often “composed of a black hairline stem with small green leaves and stylized red and blue flowers and berries” (Majewski and O’Brian 1987). Vessels with hand painted features may also include border stripes along the rim of a vessel, which may cause some to identify them as annular, even though they share most of the traits attributed to the general hand painted category. In these cases, the characteristic pigments used in hand painted ceramics were used as the distinguishing factor of categorization. When cataloging the Montgomery Site ceramics, those sherds only exhibiting a stripe in chrome red, a color rarely observed in true annular ware, were determined to be hand painted. Lofstrom et al. (1982) remark that the colors observed in sprig decoration are exceedingly similar in appearance to those used in tricolor sponge or splatter ware.Figure . Hand painted sherds

Victorian Majolica

Named for its imitation of 15th century Italian maiolica, Victorian Majolica is characterized by its unusually vivid colors applied to a molded base. The decorative motifs with which a piece was embossed are frequently floral or botanical in nature. All sherds under the Majolica category from the Montgomery Site are consistent with a specific pattern of vessel produced by Simon Fielding’s Railway Pottery company from ca. 1880-1890 (Majolica International Society 2014). This specific pattern had a larger counterpart used to produce decorative umbrella stands, but the specific placement of design elements on the more complete sherd that were recovered indicates that what was found at the Montgomery Site was likely the remains of a smaller object used in table service, such as the hexagonal kettle or pitcher produced with the same motif.Figure . Majolica sherds, exteriorFigure . Majolica sherds, interior and exterior

Decalcomania

Decal decoration differs from transfer printing in how the decoration is prepared before being applied to the surface of the ware. For decal wares, a pattern is transferred to the ceramic body in some sort of adhesive, and color is then brushed or dusted over it. The visual signifiers of decalcomania are clearer lines, the presence of shading rather than stippling or hatching, and the use of colors that differ dramatically from those observed in transferware (Majewski and O’Brian 1987). Though decal decoration had existed for some time prior, the style gained popularity at the end of the nineteenth century, which Majewski and O’Brian (1984) attribute to its use as an alternative to hand painted motifs which were more costly to produce. Decalcomania refers to the period of intense popularity experienced by decal decoration.Figure . Decal decorated sherds

Yellow Ware

Yellow ware is a broad category that encompasses all ceramics found that display a distinctly yellow past color, both unrefined and decorated (Majewski and O’Brian 1984). Yellow ware was produced in England during the Figure . Yellow ware sherdseighteenth century but was not introduced to America until ca. 1820 (Majewski and O’Brian 1984). Yellow ware was produced in the United States, beginning ca. 1830, and was used for heavy-duty utilitarian wares in addition to more specialized vessels. When categorizing the Montgomery assemblage, all sherds with a yellow paste body (that did not otherwise possess a decorative characteristic belonging to another type) were labeled as yellow ware. It is to be noted that styles such as annular decoration were practiced on yellow ware, and that yellow ware sherds that bore these styles were categorized as annular for the purposes of quantification.

Rockingham Ware

Rockingham is the name given to a particular type of slip-glaze finish, most often practiced on yellow ware, that results in mottled brown coloration. A brown glaze was applied to a vessel with a light-colored paste by spattering or dripping, causing the glaze to streak, and resulting in a distinctive tortoise shell finish (Majewski and O’Brian 1984). Rockingham glaze is notable for its application to body molded vessels, on which the thin glaze pools in low-lying areas and accentuates the embossed detail. Figure . Rockingham ware sherds

Redware

Redware refers to unrefined earthenware with a red coloration to the ceramic body. It is the softest category of unrefined earthenware and was produced in America beginning in the seventeenth century, though the majority was produced in the nineteenth century (Majewski and O’Brian 1984:21). If it is glazed, the coating is typically lead-based, with manganese pigments, which can include “shades of brown and yellow, copper-green, and brownish black” (Majewski and O’Brian 1984:21).

title: A Nonparametric Approach to Market Sentiment and M&A Deal Premiums in the United States
text:
A Nonparametric Approach to Market Sentiment and

M&A Deal Premiums in the United States

Mergers and acquisitions (M&A) are among the most strategically significant transactions in corporate finance, often involving substantial premiums paid by acquiring firms over the market value of target companies. Conceptually, M&A premiums are the differences between the M&A prices and the fair values of the companies. These premiums are influenced by a variety of factors, including firm fundamentals, strategic synergies, and broader macroeconomic conditions. Amongst the latter, market sentiment

— often proxied by measures of volatility or risk aversion — plays a potentially important but difficult-to-model role.

Prior research has extensively examined determinants of M&A premiums. For instance, Rhodes-Kropf, Robinson, and Viswanathan (2005) explore how market misvaluations influence merger activity, suggesting that periods of overvaluation can lead to increased M&A activity with resulting higher premiums.1 Moeller, Schlingemann, and

Stulz (2004) analyze the impact of firm size on acquisition premiums, finding that larger acquirers tend to pay lower premiums.2

However, the relationship between market sentiment and M&A premiums remains less clear. While some might suggest that heightened market volatility may deter

M&A activity due to increased uncertainty, others might propose that such periods may present opportunities for acquirers to negotiate lower premiums. The CBOE Volatility

2 Sreedhar T. Bharath and Guojun Wu, “Long-run Volatility and Risk Around Mergers and Acquisitions,” University of Michigan, Department of Finance (2005): 1–43.

1 Matthew Rhodes-Kropf, David T. Robinson, and S. Viswanathan, “Valuation Waves and Merger Activity: The Empirical Evidence,” Journal of Financial Economics 77, no. 3 (2005): 561–603.

Index (VIX), commonly referred to as the "fear index," serves as a widely recognized proxy for market sentiment, capturing expected market volatility. Yet, empirical analyses directly linking VIX levels to M&A premiums are limited.

This study aims to fill this gap by investigating the relationship between market sentiment, as measured by the VIX, and M&A deal premiums using nonparametric regression methods. Unlike linear regression models, nonparametric techniques allow for flexible estimation of the conditional expectation of deal premiums without imposing a specific functional form, accommodating potential nonlinearities and threshold effects.

The objective is to estimate the regression function:

𝑚𝑥 ( ) = 𝐸𝑃𝑟𝑒𝑚𝑖𝑢𝑚|𝑉𝐼𝑋= 𝑥 [ ]

and to assess the shape and properties of this function in order to understand how acquirers adjust their bidding behavior in response to changing market sentiment. While this primary analysis relies on nonparametric regression of deal premiums in VIX, the investigation is further extended by incorporating robustness checks and complementary analyses — including a percentage-based normalization of premiums and distributional comparisons across different VIX regimes — to evaluate the statistical and behavioral underpinnings of the observed patterns.

I.​ DATA

To investigate the relationship between market sentiment and M&A deal premiums, a dataset is first constructed by combining manually-retrieved transaction-level M&A data from S&P Capital IQ with market-level volatility data from

Yahoo Finance. The analysis focuses on completed U.S.-based acquisitions of whole companies, announced between 1993 and 2025, with a reported deal premium.

The M&A data is then obtained using Capital IQ’s transaction screening tool, restricted to deals with the following criteria:

●​ Geography: United States.

●​ Deal type: acquisition of the whole company (including majority stakes).

●​ Deal status: completed.

●​ Deal size: greater than $5 million.

●​ Premium paid: not N/A.

The extracted dataset includes the announcement date, premium paid (in millions

USD), transaction value, and parties involved in the transaction. For each deal, the variables announcement_date and premium_paid are retained to serve as the basis for the analysis. After cleaning and filtering for extreme outliers and incomplete entries, the resulting sample consists of 3,662 M&A transactions from 1993 through early 2025.

Specifically, 30 deals that reported premium values below -100% are removed, as these likely reflect data errors, highly distressed scenarios where the acquirer paid far below the target’s pre-announcement market value, or possibly intra-group transactions used to transfer assets within related entities, making them unsuitable for comparative analysis.

To measure market sentiment, the VIX is utilized, which serves as a widely used proxy for market fear or uncertainty. Historical VIX data is primarily downloaded from

Yahoo Finance using the get.hist.quote() function in the software R. Because M&A deals are typically negotiated prior to their announcement, each deal is matched with the VIX level on the day prior to the announcement date. Missing values in the VIX series due to holidays or weekends are imputed using the last observation carried forward.

The merged dataset provides a time-aligned panel of deal premiums and corresponding pre-announcement market volatility, enabling nonparametric analysis of how premiums vary with investor sentiment.

II.​ METHODOLOGY

To estimate the relationship between market sentiment and deal premiums, kernel-based local linear regression is utilized. This nonparametric technique estimates the conditional expectation function without assuming a 𝑚𝑥 ( ) = 𝐸𝑃𝑟𝑒𝑚𝑖𝑢𝑚|𝑉𝐼𝑋= 𝑥 [ ]

specific functional form. This is crucial within this context, as prior literature and intuition suggest that the relationship between market volatility and buyer behavior may be nonlinear, exhibiting potential threshold effects or regime shifts. Although deal premium is often expressed as a percentage of transaction value to normalize for deal size, focus primarily lies on the raw premium (in USD) to capture the absolute dollar magnitude of acquirer aggressiveness; robustness checks using percentage premiums are included in subsequent analyses and yield consistent patterns.

Because deal premiums are highly right-skewed and include extreme outliers, a log transformation of the form is applied prior to estimating the 𝑙𝑜𝑔 𝑃𝑟𝑒𝑚𝑖𝑢𝑚+ 1 ( )

regression function. This transformation is a common statistical approach that serves to stabilize variance, reduce the influence of unusually large observations, and improve the performance of local regression estimators in the presence of heteroscedasticity. In nonparametric settings, such transformations are particularly useful when the response variable exhibits heavy tails or nonconstant variance, as they help satisfy the conditions under which kernel estimators perform most effectively. After estimating the regression function in the transformed space, a back-transformation is applied to recover predicted deal premiums on the original scale, thereby enhancing interpretability without sacrificing estimation robustness.

Bandwidth selection is conducted via least-squares cross-validation to balance bias and variance in the regression estimates. The final fit is then plotted over the scatter of observed deals, using zoomed and transformed views to enhance interpretability.

III.​ REGRESSION RESULT: DEAL PREMIUM ON VIX

The estimated regression function reveals a non-monotonic relationship between market sentiment and M&A deal premiums. In general, premiums are higher when VIX is low, suggesting that acquirers are more willing to pay a premium during calm, confident market conditions. As VIX rises above 30, the expected premium declines significantly, consistent with the hypothesis that uncertainty depresses acquisition valuations or limits buyer aggressiveness.

Figure 01. Back-Transformed Kernel Regression of Deal Premium on VIX, Zoomed In.​

Interestingly, the relationship is not strictly decreasing. Two local upward bumps are observed in the estimated premium function — one near and another near 𝑉𝐼𝑋≈22

. These deviations could reflect opportunistic acquisitions during transitory 𝑉𝐼𝑋≈38 dislocations, where confident buyers perceive mispriced targets and are willing to pay a premium to preempt competition. Alternatively, they may signal shifts in buyer composition or strategic objectives that become more salient under certain market conditions. To assess the robustness of these features and better understand their drivers, additional regression-based diagnostics are conducted, focusing on premium normalization and volatility-regime-specific bidding distributions.

Back-Transformed Kernel Regression (Zoomed)

IV.​ FURTHER REGRESSION ANALYSES

To explore the causes behind the two observed upward deviations in the premium-VIX relationship (around and ), two complementary 𝑉𝐼𝑋≈22 𝑉𝐼𝑋≈38 regression-based investigations are conducted: (1) a bootstrapped kernel regression using percentage premiums to evaluate robustness and statistical uncertainty, and (2) a kernel density comparison across volatility regimes to examine distributional shifts in bidding behavior.

Figure 02. Kernel Density Estimates of Log-Transformed Premium Percentage by VIX Regime.

In the first analysis, nonparametric regression is then re-estimated using premiums expressed as a percentage of total transaction value, rather than in raw dollar terms. This adjustment controls for heterogeneity in deal size and provides a more normalized measure of acquirer willingness to pay. The resulting curve, plotted with 95% bootstrap confidence bands, confirms the overall negative relationship between VIX and premium percentage: buyers are generally less aggressive during high-volatility periods.

Yet, crucially, the shape of the curve remains non-monotonic. The same two local spikes near and persist, now appearing as modest but statistically discernible 𝑉𝐼𝑋≈22 𝑉𝐼𝑋≈38 deviations above the baseline downward trend. These findings suggest that the pattern is not driven by outliers or scale effects and is instead a genuine feature of the underlying relationship.

Figure 03. Kernel Regression of Premium Percentage on VIX with 95% Bootstrap Confidence Bands,

Zoomed In.

To better understand the behavior of buyers during these volatility zones, deals are classified into three groups based on VIX at announcement: , , and 𝑉𝐼𝑋≈22 𝑉𝐼𝑋≈38 all other periods. The kernel density of log-transformed premium percentages across these groups are then estimated and compared. The densities for the and 𝑉𝐼𝑋≈22

Kernel Regression with 95% Bootstrap Bands (Zoomed)

bands both exhibit a subtle rightward shift relative to the baseline group, 𝑉𝐼𝑋≈38 indicating that the distribution of premiums is tilted toward higher values during these periods. In particular, the group shows a pronounced peak in the upper range of 𝑉𝐼𝑋≈22 premium intensity, while the group displays a more dispersed but still elevated 𝑉𝐼𝑋≈38 tail. This supports the interpretation that the observed spikes are driven by a subset of opportunistic or strategic buyers who maintain aggressiveness even during market turbulence.

Taken together, these analyses suggest that the two local increases in the premium-VIX regression are not statistical artifacts but reflect real behavioral dynamics.

While most acquirers become more conservative under uncertainty, there appear to be windows of moderate dislocation where certain buyers act countercyclically, offering higher premiums either to secure undervalued targets or to preempt competition. These insights underscore the value of a flexible, nonparametric approach in uncovering subtle nonlinear patterns that standard linear models might overlook.

V.​ CONCLUSION

This project applies nonparametric regression techniques to examine the relationship between market sentiment and M&A deal premiums, using the VIX as a proxy for investor uncertainty. The results confirm an intuitive baseline finding: as market volatility increases, acquirers generally offer lower premiums, likely due to greater perceived risk and caution. However, the nonparametric framework reveals a more complex pattern. Instead of a smooth decline, the estimated premium function features two local upward deviations — around and — indicating that 𝑉𝐼𝑋≈22 𝑉𝐼𝑋≈38 in specific volatility regimes, certain buyers remain active and willing to pay higher premiums.

To further investigate the underlying mechanisms behind the observed spikes in premium behavior, additional analyses were conducted using percentage-based premium normalization and kernel density comparisons across VIX regimes. These robustness checks confirmed that the local bumps were not driven by extreme deal sizes or scale artifacts but instead reflect meaningful shifts in buyer behavior under specific volatility conditions. Future research could build on this work by examining acquirer characteristics — such as whether the buyer is private equity or strategic, or whether financing conditions differ across regimes — to better understand who drives these deviations. Additionally, incorporating time-varying models or splitting the sample by macroeconomic cycles (e.g., pre- vs. post-crisis periods) could provide deeper insight into how market sentiment influences deal-making over time.

References

Bharath, Sreedhar T. and Guojun Wu, “Long-run Volatility and Risk Around Mergers and

Acquisitions,” University of Michigan, Department of Finance (2005): 1–43.

Rhodes-Kropf, Matthew, David T. Robinson, and S. Viswanathan. “Valuation Waves and

Merger Activity: The Empirical Evidence.” Journal of Financial Economics 77, no. 3 (2005): 561–603.
