title: Probing the properties in Local Bubble by linking three-dimensional dust data and HI absorption
abstract: The Local Bubble (LB) contains significant internal structure, including many partially ionized interstellar clouds. Some of the clouds in the vicinity of the Local Bubble have extreme properties as traced by neutral hydrogen (HI) absorption measurements towards pulsars. By observing time variability of HI absorption profiles it was suggested that some of the HI structures have high density and pressures, data representative of the tiny scale atomic structure (TSAS). However, the exact location of these structures are unknown and understanding their origin in the framework of LB formation and evolution has been impossible. We use three-dimensional dust maps (Edenhofer et al. 2023) to extract density profiles of the hydrogen volume density along the line-of-sight (LOS) to four selected pulsars. High correlation of the density profile ”peaks” to the Gaussian components of the absorption spectra as measured by Stanimirovi´c et al. (2010) reveal potential 3D ”structures” that may correspond to warm neutral medium and/or cold netural medium. Column density images and analysis of dusty structures along the LOS using Glue reveal the structural and intrinsic properties of interstellar matter (ISM). Using the calculations of mean and maximum density along the LOS, we derive the ionization fraction and thermal pressure to characterize the properties of the ISM as traced by the pulsars. Our method of using absorption data in conjunction with three-dimensional dust data holds potential for broader applications, especially to validate the structures and properties of dust clouds in the LB and beyond.
text:
Draft version June 7, 2026 Typeset using LATEX twocolumn style in AASTeX631

Probing the properties in Local Bubble by linking three-dimensional dust data and HI absorption

Aishani Das-Ghosh,1 Nickolas M. Pingel

,2, 3 and Sneˇzana Stanimirovi´c

1Department of Engineering Sciences and Applied Mathematics, Northwestern University, 2145 Sheridan Rd, Evanston, IL 60208, USA 2Department of Astronomy, Indiana University, 727 East Third Street, Bloomington, IN 47405, USA 3Department of Astronomy, University of Wisconsin–Madison, 475 N. Charter Street, Madison, WI 53706, USA

ABSTRACT

The Local Bubble (LB) contains significant internal structure, including many partially ionized interstellar clouds. Some of the clouds in the vicinity of the Local Bubble have extreme properties as traced by neutral hydrogen (HI) absorption measurements towards pulsars. By observing time variability of HI absorption profiles it was suggested that some of the HI structures have high density and pressures, data representative of the tiny scale atomic structure (TSAS). However, the exact location of these structures are unknown and understanding their origin in the framework of LB formation and evolution has been impossible. We use three-dimensional dust maps (Edenhofer et al. 2023) to extract density profiles of the hydrogen volume density along the line-of-sight (LOS) to four selected pulsars. High correlation of the density profile ”peaks” to the Gaussian components of the absorption spectra as measured by Stanimirovi´c et al. (2010) reveal potential 3D ”structures” that may correspond to warm neutral medium and/or cold netural medium. Column density images and analysis of dusty structures along the LOS using Glue reveal the structural and intrinsic properties of interstellar matter (ISM). Using the calculations of mean and maximum density along the LOS, we derive the ionization fraction and thermal pressure to characterize the properties of the ISM as traced by the pulsars. Our method of using absorption data in conjunction with three-dimensional dust data holds potential for broader applications, especially to validate the structures and properties of dust clouds in the LB and beyond.

1. INTRODUCTION

The local diffuse interstellar medium (ISM), made up of mostly gas and dust, is characterized by ionization state, temperature and density. A multiphase model establishes that most of the ISM consists of hot low- density medium (HIM), and within it are warm neutral medium (WNM) and cold neutral medium (CNM). (Field, Goldsmith & Habing 1969; McKee & Ostriker 1977; Wolfire et al. 2003). Traditionally, the CNM and WNM are understood as being two thermal equilibrium states of the neutral medium. The theoretically expected properties of the CNM and WNM, based on the heating and cooling balance, are: a kinetic temperature Tk ∼60 −260 K and a volume density of nH ∼7 −70 cm−3 for the CNM , and Tk = 5000 −8300 K and nH ∼0.2−0.9 cm−3 for the WNM (Wolfire et al. 2003, Table 3 for the Solar neighborhood). The diffuse ISM phases have a roughly comparable thermal pressure (Ferri`ere 1998). These gases have been observed through 21 cm emissions and absorptions (e.g. Dickey et al. 2003; Heiles & Troland 2003; Fukui et al. 2014).

The Local Bubble (LB) has been widely studied for its interesting properties of the ISM. Thought to be the result of several supernova explosions taking place over the past 10 −15 Myrs, the LB has pushed out the evac- uated matter into a dense shell of cold atomic neutral hydrogen (HI) gas and dust. Early investigation of the properties of neutral hydrogen in the LB revealed the ex- istence of considerably large diffuse clouds (nH = 0.01 cm−3) with high temperatures (about 106 K) (Cox & Reynolds 1987).

While warm, low-density clouds have been extensively studied inside the LB, cold dense HI clouds have been found widespread in the Solar neighborhood (e.g. Be- gum et al. 2010) but their exact location in relation to the LB have been hard to constrain. The Local Leo Cloud (LLC) is a spectacular example of a cold HI cloud located 45 pc from the Sun, with a mean temperature of 20 K and mean Hi column density of 2.5 · 1019 cm −2

(Meyer et al. 2006). While cold, the diffuse structure of the LLC raises questions on the formation of cold yet diffuse molecular clouds in the seemingly (mostly) hot LB. Assuming that the cloud is in thermal equilibrium,

2 Das-Ghosh et al.

the temperature and column density imply an extremely thin (< 0.1 pc), sheet-like geometry (Meyer et al. 2012).

A recent comprehensive analysis into the structure of the LB from Zucker et al. (2022) furthers the investigation of ISM properties. In addition to finding that all major molecular clouds about 200 pc from the cen- ter lie on the surface of the LB, most clouds on the LB wall show either sheet-like or filamentary structure. In modeling the expansion of the LB as a function of time, the ambient density of the ISM found to be n0 = 2.7 cm−3 with uncertainty +1.57 cm−3, −1.02 cm−3, using estimates made with previous iterations of a three- dimensional dust map from (Leike et al. 2020). These estimates are representative of the denser shell of neutral gas and dust where uncertainties in dust extinction are lesser, and thus do not account for the very hot dense interior closest to the Sun. Thus, the structure and walls of the LB make for interesting interactions between different temperatures and phases of ISM that lead to the formation of molecular clouds.

With interactions between WNM and CNM in the LB that lead to a “survival of the fittest” of molecular clouds, tiny scale atomic structure (TSAS) is a phenom- ena that may potentially lead to the fragmentation of the wall of the Local Bubble. Stanimirovi´c et al. (2010) investigated HI absorption towards five pulsars with the aim of capturing signatures of TSAS that manifest as fluctuations in the optical depth spectrum and provide a probe of the overall kinetic energy cascade from the fragmentation of the LB wall. In the direction of one pulsar, B1929+10, the authors found repeated changes in the depth of the HI optical depth, suggesting the ex- istence of cold HI structures on spatial scales 5-45 AU with a temperature of 50-200 K and an inferred density of few × 104 cm−3. However, since HI absorption spectra provide only a one-dimensional probe, obtain- ing an understanding of the origin, morphology, and exact position of these absorbing structures was diffi- cult until recent advances in 3D mapping of nearby dust structures. Also, while HI column densities are measured from obtained spectra, H density calculations need an assumed line-of-sight (LOS) structure/cloud length. Structures elongated along the line-of-sight would result in a much lower H volume density, and thermal pressure (e.g. (Heiles 1997)). Therefore, observational constraints of the TSAS spatial extent is of high interest.

Previous probes of the ISM have made use of direct telescope observations of the absorption and emission spectra of elements of interest. The advent of large sky surveys such as 2MASS (Skrutskie et al. 2006), PanSTARRS, (Kaiser et al. 2002) and SDSS/APOGEE (Albareti et al. 2017), and WISE (Wright et al. 2010)

have paved the way for several reconstructions of the local three dimensional (3D) dust within ∼0.5 kpc that may allow for greater analysis of the structure and properties of the neutral hydrogen. They utilize photometric measurements and spectra from thousands of stars, from which the calculation of photometric distances is possible. In particular, a dust map that sourced reddening data from 71000 sources was used to perform a 3D reconstruction via Gaussian process regression. The resulting dust map covers a 4kpc square of the galactic plane and 600pc in the perpendicular direction with a voxel size of 5 pc (Lallement et al. 2018) . In Green et al. (2018) a 3D dust map is produced by combining the star data of Pan-STARRS and 2MASS, binning it in angular and distance bins, and performing independent Bayesian reconstructions per angular bin. The result is a dust map that covers three quarters of the sky to a distance up to 2kpc. Leike et al. (2020) combined observational data of Gaia DR2, ALLWISE, PANSTARRS, and 2MASS to yield one consistent catalog with stellar parameters by (Anders et al. 2019). Edenhofer et al. (2023) created a new, expanded three-dimensional dust map based on the updated extinction catalog from Zhang et al. (2023), citing improved methodologies from Leike et al. (2020) that increased the distance resolution to 1 pc with lower uncertainties in the distances from stars, while the dust reconstruction has a resolution of 2 pc. Based on the map from (Edenhofer et al. 2023), (O’Neill et al. 2024) create an improved model of the LB accurate to the ir- regular structure and densities of the LB walls. The resulting maps show tendrils and filaments of dust on scales that range as small as 2 pc up to scales of several hundred parsecs.

Due to the higher densities (n ∼10−100 cm−3) of the CNM phase of Hi , collisions are sufficient to completely thermalize the Hi 21 cm hyperfine transition, mean- ing that the spin temperature (Ts)—which is measured unambiguously from Hi absorption detections and de- scribes the relative level population between the two hyperfine levels—is equal to the kinetic temperature (Tk). For the first time, we can utilize the 3D rep- resentation of the total hydrogen (atomic+molecular) distribution inferred from the 3D dust maps of Edenhofer et al. (2023) in conjunction with the temperatures provided by the Hi absorption measurements of Stanimirovi´c et al. (2010) as a novel probe of important local ISM properties. Specifically, we use the density and temperature information towards four of the five pulsars: B0823+26, B1133+16, B1929+10, and B2016+28, as they fall within the captured distance range (1.25 kpc) of the (Edenhofer et al. 2023) map (2. The primary goals of this project are to attempt to localize the

LB properties using 3D dust and absorption 3 absorbing CNM structure seen against these pulsars to investigate their relation to the LB and provide innova- tive and independent measurements of thermal pressure and ionization fraction in the direction of these pulsars.

2. DATA

2.1. 3D Dust Maps

We use the three-dimensional dust maps of Edenhofer et al. (2023) that are sampled at 516 distance bins spanning 69 pc to 1.25 kpc radially from the position of the Sun. The distance resolution ranges from 0.4 pc at a distance of 69 pc to 7 pc at 1.25 kpc. These maps were constructed by leveraging the stellar distances from parallax measurements with BP/RP spectral data from Gaia DR3 (Zhang et al. 2023) and the dust optical extinction towards approximately 54 million sample stars. Due to artificially high dust extinction values from the positivity prior from Zhang et al. (2023), the inner 69 pc were removed from the maps provided by Edenhofer et al. (2023). The posterior inference from Edenhofer et al. (2023) results in 12 realizations of the dust extinction discretized to HEALPix spheres at logarithmi- cally spaced distances. We utilize these 12 realizations to estimate our uncertainties in the derived line-of-sight (LOS) properties (see Section 3.1). We emphasize here that estimated H number densities (ntot) from the 3D dust maps are strict lower-limits since the small-scale fluctuations are averaged over 1 pc3 voxels when inter- polating the discretized HEALPix spheres to Cartesian grids.

2.2. Hi Emission/Absorption & Pulsar Properties

The 3D dust maps are used in conjunction with multi-epoch Hi absorption measurements made with the Arecibo radio telescope by Stanimirovi´c et al. (2010) and Hi emission data from the The Galactic Arecibo L- band Feed Array HI (GALFA-HI) Survey (Peek et al. 2011, 2018) measured towards several pulsars—see Stanimirovi´c et al. (2010) for specific details on how these spectra were constructed. The Hi absorption spectra were decomposed into individual cloud components employing the Gaussian decomposition method from Heiles & Troland (2003a) to derive spin temperatures (Ts), the CNM Hi column density (NHi,CNM), WNM Hi column density (NHi,WNM), and the total Hi column density (NHi,tot = NHi,CNM + NHi,WNM) along each LOS.

We study the sightlines towards four pulsars that are within the volume of the dust maps: B0823+26, B1133+16, B1929+10, and B2016+28. Stanimirovi´c et al. (2010) showed the Hi absorption and emission towards several pulsars have multiple Gaussian components, indicating there are multiple CNM clouds along the line of sight moving with different velocities, B1133+16 has two, B1929+10 has three, and B2016+28 has five; B0823+26 is determined to have only a single component in Hi absorption. In the direction of B1929+10, Stanimirovi´c et al. (2010) noted that the deepest velocity component centered at a velocity of 4.8 km s−1 shows variability across four epochs, indicating the presence of TSAS on the scale of ∼10s of AU when accounting for the proper motion of this pulsar in this specific LOS.

The pulsar properties are obtained from the Australia Telescope National Facility (ATNF) pulsar database (Manchester et al. 2005) and summarized along with the derived properties for each Hi absorption/emission component in Table 1.

2.3. Model of the Local Bubble

O’Neill et al. (2024) constructed a model of the Local Bubble by applying a custom peak-finding algorithm to identify inner and outer edges within the larger 3D dust volume of Edenhofer et al. (2023). They found that the Local Bubble (LB) is irregularly shaped and highly porous, indicating it is supernovae-driven superbubble structure that burst to create a local chimney that fun- nels ISM material to the Galactic Halo. They found that several well-known molecular clouds and dust features lie on the surface of the Local Bubble. We use the mean shell differential extinction interpolated onto a heliocentric Cartesian grid1 to investigate whether the CNM traced by the Hi absorption detections from Stanimirovi´c et al. (2010) towards our four pulsars is associated with any structures on the wall of the Local Bubble.

Figure 5 shows the projected total hydrogen column density structure from the extracted subvolumes. 3.3. Isolating Absorbing Structures

We aim to characterize the structure associated with the CNM that causes Hi absorption. Determining the mean nH of the absorbing structure enables us to put constraints on important ISM properties, such as the thermal pressure and ionization fraction. To isolate the 3D structures within the Edenhofer et al. (2023) data cube, we use the subset selection features within the visualization software Glue (Robitaille et al. 2017).

We probe the clumpy structures along the LOS observed as peaks in the density profile and dusty structures in the column density images. We generate cat- alogs in the sub-volumes extracted in Section 3.2 con- taining Cartesian coordinates, galactic coordinates, the distance in parsecs, and the density value for each voxel. We load the catalog file in Glue and generate a 2D scatter plot correlating the ntot of each voxel with its distance. We then select a rectangular subset of the distance values that enclose the full-width half-maximum (FWHM) of the density peaks (see red profiles in Figure 2 and the range of ntot for the primary component along the LOS.) In Figure 3, we map the subset onto the EF24 cube to visualize the location of the absorbing CNM relative to the Earth and structure associated with the Local Bubble.

This analysis increases our understanding of the position and distribution of density of the absorbing structures, which we hypothesize to be correlated with the peaks in the density profiles. With this, we can conclude whether or not the absorbing structures are within or outside of the LB and contribute to the further char- acterization of the WNM/CNM makeup of the LB.

The kinematic distance ambiguity (KDA) within the Sun’s orbit, where a given local standard of rest velocity could correspond to a near or far distance, results in kinematic distances that are highly uncertain. The KDA, when coupled with deviations from circular motion drives our uncertainties to range between 50−100%. Nevertheless, the ntot density profile in the direction of B1929+10 shows three peaks at distances of 89 pc, 213 pc, and 278 pc, respectively, and tentatively agrees with the re- turned kinematic distance estimates for the absorbing structures in the Hi absorption profile. For example, component two with the velocity centroid at 4.8 km s−1 has the highest optical depth (0.120), while the most prominent dust feature in the ntot density profile has the highest density (1.8 cm−3). While we cannot unequiv- ocally associate the density peaks with specific CNM components due to the large uncertainties in kinematic distances, it is likely that CNM Components one, two, and three, are associated with the peaks at distances of 89 pc, 213 pc, and 278 pc, respectively, when also con- sidering the peak optical depth. Furthermore, we find that the LB structure identified by O’Neill et al. (2024) is associated with the nearest density peak whose kinematic distance is most consistent with the wall of the LB. It is therefore likely that the other two CNM components are located beyond the LB.

The total hydrogen column density images of the most distant dust structures towards B1929+10 show very diffuse structures, while the middle (strongest) one in Figure 6 shows interesting an sub-structure with several higher-density clumps around the pulsar position. The Hi column density images for all three components do not show a clear correlation between the dust structures, likely stemming from the complicated sightlines near the Galactic Plane and the components centered around LSR velocities of 0 km s−1.

The Hi absorption and emission spectra of B2016+28 contain multiple velocity structures that have significant velocity overlap, complicating the decomposition of individual components and radiative transfer calculations and resulting in large uncertainties for the spin temperatures of individual components. We conclude that this pulsar is probing a direction that is too complex to disentangle and match to dusty structures. This is consistent with the large uncertainties in spin temperature estimates that stem from fitting Gaussians to blended CNM and WNM components. Finally, we find that the closest dusty structure is located at the wall of the LB, according to the O’Neill et al. (2024) model. The large optical depth of this CNM feature suggests that the structure of the LB wall appre- ciably contributes to the Hi absorption in this direction.

4.3. Lower Limits on the Thermal Pressure

Using our connections between individual Hi absorption components and density structures established in Section 4.2 and summarized in Tables 3, along with the 4 the DM values in Table 1, we calculate lower and upper limits on the thermal pressure and ionization fraction. For the thermal pressure, we use two methods. Firstly, we assume the CNM is an ideal gas and use the ⟨npeak⟩ density as an estimate of the particle volume density within the structure. For each density component, we multiply this density by the corresponding Ts, which at the densities of the CNM we assume is fully thermalized by collisions and thus a proxy for kinetic temperature, to obtain an estimate for the thermal pressure in units of cm−3 K. The uncertainties are statistically propagated from the systematic errors on ⟨npeak⟩and Ts. We note that since the dust data are interpolated and smoothed onto a 1 pc−3 voxel, the peak density values we report are effectively lower limits on the true density in any given LOS and, thus, our thermal pressure estimates are also strictly lower limits. We call this approach the “direct” thermal pressure.

Our second method for estimating the thermal pressure takes advantage of the 3D dust data constraining the LOS extent of the absorbing structures. From ntot density profiles shown in Figures 4, we measure the FWHM of the LOS extent for each of nine structures and show these values in Table 4. These range between 10–40 pc. Just as Stanimirovi´c et al. (2010) measured the CNM column density for each absorption component, as well as the ratio of the CNM mass fraction (the ratio of the CNM column density to the CNM+WNM Hi column density along each LOS, we estimate the total volume density of Hi (⟨nHI⟩) for each structure by dividing the CNM column density by the mass fraction. The result is then divided by the LOS extent to obtain an estimate of the average Hi volume density, ⟨nHI⟩. Our primary assumptions are that our connections between the CNM components in velocity and dust structures are correct, which is more uncertain for the complex sightlines near the Galactic Plane, and the Hi and dust are sufficiently well-mixed to trace similar 3D depths. We estimate the thermal pressure in the Hi by multiply- ing ⟨nHI⟩with the associated Ts values. As these estimates considers the neutral hydrogen only, this is again a lower limit. We call this second method the “geometric” thermal pressure. Here, the lower bounds are primarily limited by high uncertainties in the Ts values. We list these estimates of the neutral hydrogen density and resulting thermal pressure in Table 4. The uncertainties are statistically propagated from the systemic errors on NHI,CNM and the FWHM span.

Figure 7 makes a comparison between the equilibrium curve in the Solar neighborhood from Wolfire et al. (2003) and our lower limits on the thermal pressure (we distinguish between structures inside and outside of the LB). Using this direct approach, most of the structures have a thermal pressure in the 20–300 K cm−3 range. This is a factor of a few to ∼100 times lower than what is expected for thermal equilibrium based on Wolfire et al. (2003). Only the dusty structure located at ∼760 pc in the direction of B2016+28 has a thermal pressure of ∼700 K cm−3, which is a few factors lower than what is expected for the Solar neighborhood thermal equilibrium conditions. 4.4. Upper Limits on the Ionization Fraction

The ionization fraction can be used to categorize the Hi structures as either WNM, CNM, or perhaps a combination of both. Due to a combination of embedded and external sources of extreme ultraviolet, X-ray, and cosmic ray radiation, the WNM near the solar neighborhood is expected to have a ionization fraction of ∼1.7 × 10−2, while the CNM is expected to be less ionized at ∼4 × 10−4 (Draine 2011). The ionization fraction is defined as

⟨xe⟩= ⟨ne⟩/⟨ntot⟩, (7)

where ⟨ne⟩is the mean electron density along the LOS. We first estimate ⟨ne⟩by dividing the D.M. values listed in Table 1 by the distance to each pulsar. We note again that structures within the 3D dust maps are interpolated to 1 pc−3 voxels, effectively washing out sub- parsec density fluctuations, resulting in a lower limit on the true ⟨ntot⟩for a given LOS; thus, our estimates for ⟨xe⟩should be taken as an upper limit.

Table 2 summarizes our upper limit on the mean ionization fraction along the LOS towards each pulsar. Both of our ⟨ne⟩and ⟨ntot⟩values are consistent with the implied electron densities from Jenkins (2013) at Hi volume densities of ∼0.5 cm−3 within a few hundred parsecs of the Sun. We note two points: (1) that ⟨ne⟩values from DMs, as they preferentially intersect highly ionized regions around pulsars, can be inflated relative to sightlines not directed towards pulsars; and (2) that a direct comparison with the observations of Jenkins (2013) is tenuous since the ratio of neutral species Ar i and O i column densities was used as a proxy for the fractional ionization of Hi only. Nevertheless, our upper limits are consistent with these measurements. Unfortunately, the limited physical resolution of the 3D maps prevents us from robustly testing the ultimate conclu- sion of Jenkins (2013)—that the systematic deficiency of Ar iresults from ionization caused by supernova explosions, whose effects on the WNM persist long after the remnants are visible in the X-rays.

Table 2 shows that upper limits on the fractional ionization of ∼2% are associated with the lowest latitude Galactic pulsars, indicating sightlines through the Galactic Plane can provide better constraints; though, one also needs to account for the bias introduced by fo- cusing on sightlines that inherently intersect regions of high ionization towards pulsars. Nevertheless, our upper limits towards low Galactic latitudes are consistent with ⟨xe⟩∼0.003 values measured for diffuse clouds (Welty et al. 2003) in the Galactic Plane. This is higher than what would be expected from photoionization from carbon and other heavy elements, suggesting the ⟨xe⟩is overestimated. Our upper limits are in better agreement with the theoretical predictions for ⟨xe⟩from using Paris-Durham shock code from Godard et al. (2024), which range between 0.01 and 0.03 when a ∼200 km s−1

5. DISCUSSION

5.1. TSAS towards B1929+10 is not associated with the Local Bubble

Stanimirovi´c et al. (2010) found persistent variations in the Hi absorption profiles towards B1929+10 over four epochs. The presence of Na I absorption from G´enova et al. (1997) towards two nearby (< 3◦from the pulsar sightline) stars—HD 178125 at a distance of 173 pc and HD 180555 at a distance of 106 pc with central velocities at 5.9±1.0 km s−1 and 5.6±1.0 km s−1, respectively suggests that an interstellar cloud either within or on the LB wall is responsible for these absorption features, indicating the Hi absorption variability is linked to TSAS on AU scales. However, the most pronounced variation was seen in our Component two centered at 4.8 km s−1, which we associate with a dusty structure along the LOS located at a distance of ∼215 pc. This is more than 100 pc more distant than the LB structure identified by O’Neill et al. (2024) (see Figure 2). Interestingly, this LB structure is located within the upper bound of 106 pc distance suggested by the Na I absorption towards HD 180555. However, the prominence of the more distant density feature, the offset between the stellar and pulsar sightlines, and the absence of a corresponding structure in an independent LB model based on the same dust map all suggest that most of the TSAS fluctuations observed by Stanimirovi´c et al. (2010) are not associated with a cloud within or on the LB wall, but rather with another structure along the same LOS. We do not see any indication of small-scale structure corresponding to TSAS, though this could be due to the low resolution of the dust maps. Ultimately, the limita- tions of physical resolution and lack of data within the inner 69 pc of the Sun preclude us from definitively con- cluding that the cloud causing the TSAS is located outside the LB. Nevertheless, our comparison demonstrates promise for identifying structures within 3D dust maps along sightlines with observed TSAS to better under- stand the properties of the LB wall and the multi-phase ISM that lies beyond.

5.2. Hi Absorption Inside and Outside the LB

Our analysis shows that three CNM features seen in Hi absorption are feasibly associated with the LB wall when compared with the O’Neill et al. (2024) model: the primary component towards B1133+16, Component one towards B1929+10, and Component one towards B2016+28. The lower limit on < npeak > from the 3D dust maps reveal systematically lower values than those made outside the LB, consistent with the notion that the Local Bubble is occupied by a warm/hot ionized medium traced in X-rays that easily evaporates cloud atomic clouds (Snowden et al. 1998). Regardless of the method used, our lower limits on the thermal pressure do not show any systematic differences between components we associate as being inside and outside the Local Bubble.

While there are detections of CNM clouds associated with the Local Bubble Wall (Rybarczyk et al. 2024), the majority of the CNM structures seen in Hi absorption towards these pulsars are seemingly associated with dusty structures at distances of 200 pc to 500 pc. Our < ntot > profiles demonstrate that this is especially true for sightlines near the Galactic Plane. However, we note that the direct association between CNM detected through Hi absorption and distant dusty structures de- pends on the uniqueness of the kinematic distance estimates, making the matching process highly uncertain for the lower latitude sightlines. Nevertheless, the most prominent density features along these LOS do not correspond to the structure of the Local Bubble Wall, again aligning with the view that the Local Bubble is gener- ally devoid of CNM clouds—with some notable excep- tions like the Leo Cold Cloud (Verschuur 1969; Heiles & Troland 2003b)

The sightline towards B0823+26 demonstrates that the association between Hi absorption and dust structures is relatively unique and reasonable towards higher Galactic Latitudes. Complex structures in the sightlines and the distance ambiguity inherent to kinematic distance estimates make it extremely challenging to match CNM clouds to 3D dust structures. Similarly, the velocity crowding in Hi emission makes it complex to match Hi structures traced by emission spectra with 3D dust structures. Our study establishes that future work look- ing to correlate the atomic ISM with the 3D structures in dust maps should focus on correlating simple (< 3 components) absorption spectra towards intermediate to high (|b| ≳10◦) Galactic latitudes.

LB properties using 3D dust and absorption 17 ing an effective upper limit on the thermal pressure in the atomic gas within the solar neighborhood. The high- pressure regions, found close to massive stars and likely due to shocks and stellar winds, have been confirmed recently by Jenkins & Tripp (2021). In regards to Hi specifically, numerical and analytical work (e.g., Wolfire et al. 2003; Bialy & Sternberg 2019) predict a minimum pressure of 3000 K cm−3 for CNM, with the WNM able to exist in pressure equilibrium up to ∼6500 K cm−3 for the solar neighborhood. The presence of Hi emission in our sightlines, which predominately traces the WNM due to low Ts for the CNM, indicates the thermal pressure in the Hi must lie within this range. Thus, the lower constraints on the thermal pressure in Hi suggest our sightlines nearest to the Galactic Plane intersect environments typical of the Solar neighborhood.

On the other hand, the lower limits on the thermal pressure towards pulsars at high Galactic latitudes are systematically offset from the those towards pulsars that reside within the Galactic Plane, with no clear difference between the direct and geometric approaches to constraining the thermal pressure. The distance to the density peaks towards B0823+26 and B1133+16 and b values imply vertical extents of ∼175 pc and ∼130 pc for these isolated CNM clouds, or 3.5 times and 2.5 times the thickness of the CNM disk for clouds with τ > 0.1 (Rybarczyk et al. 2024). The systematically reduced lower limits for sightlines outside of the Galactic Plane are consistent with the picture that, outside of the thin CNM disk, the total pressure decreases due to the reduced weight of the ISM.

While our sightlines seemingly probe typical conditions in the local ISM, clouds with extremely high pressures do exist within the Local Bubble, likely resulting from the warm cloud collisions. For example, the Leo Cold Cloud at a distance of 11 pc–24 pc (Meyer et al. 2006; Peek et al. 2011) is located inside the Local Bubble. Heiles & Troland (2003b) estimate its kinetic temperature to be 20 K based on Hi absorption detections. Its total hydrogen column density of 3×1019 cm−2 suggests it has a sheet-like geometry and a LOS thickness of < 0.1 pc. Analysis of UV spectra towards two background stars by Meyer et al. (2012) imply a striking mean thermal pressure of 60000 cm−3K at an inferred Hi volume density of 3000 cm−3, potentially caused by the colliding flows of warm gas. Unfortunately, the Leo Cold Cloud falls within the inner 69 pc that is not available in the Edenhofer et al. (2023) maps. Future work will focus on systematically applying our geometric approach for placing a lower bound on the thermal pressure to a large sample of nearby molecular clouds with Hi absorption (Stanimirovi´c et al. 2014; Nguyen et al. 2019), constraining the geometry—e.g. filament vs. sheet-like—and comparing their environments to diagnose the mecha- nisms producing structures with remarkable pressures like the Leo Cold Cloud.

6. CONCLUSIONS & FUTURE WORK

We present total hydrogen density profiles along the LOS to four local pulsars– B0823+26, B1133+16, B1929+10, and B2016+28– and draw correlations to the corresponding absorption and emission spectra previously measured by (Stanimirovi´c et al. 2010). We investigate each pulsar’s local column density images of neutral hydrogen and total hydrogen density to make preliminary connections with the physical surrounding gaseous structure to the absorption and emission spectra. Then, we extend our analysis to three dimen- sions by modeling each pulsar’s LOS in the (Edenhofer et al. 2023) three-dimensional dust maps in conjunction with the Local Bubble model of O’Neill et al. (2024). Through our measurement of neutral hydrogen density along the line of sight to each pulsar, we place lower and upper limits on the thermal pressure and lower limits on ionization fraction to work towards a quantitative char- acterization of the gas as either CNM or WNM. Our main findings are summarized below:

• The density profile of B0823+26 has a single high- density (10 cm−3) peak near 350 pc, matching the sole Gaussian velocity component (4.91 km/s) in the associated absorption spectra. The total hydrogen column density image taken over the FWHM distance reveals a well-defined clump of gas near the LOS, providing confidence that the density peak and velocity component correspond to a small CNM gas cloud located beyond the LB. Similarly, the density profile of B1133+16 has a single low-density (0.5 cm−3) peak near 150 pc. The associated absorbing structure is a diffuse cloud is located in the wall of the LB, and is correlated with the two CNM components (-2, -3.5 km/s respectively) of the absorption spectra as well as the single H1 component of the emission spectra.

• Given their proximity to the Galactic plane, B1929+29 and B2016+28 have multiple density peaks along their respective lines of sight. We roughly correlate the first three peaks of the density profile of B1929+10 located at 89, 213, and 278 pc with the first 3 components of the absorption spectra with mean velocities of -0.7, 4.8, and 8.4 km/s. However, the total hydrogen column density taken along the FWHM for each peak

Meanwhile, the first density peak in the density profile of B2016+28 proba- bly corresponds to an absorbing structure in the LB wall, but the four other peaks are not well- correlated with the four other Gaussian components in the absorption spectra.

• We calculate lower and upper limits of the thermal pressure by using the ideal gas law, employing two different method to measure the H1 volume density: (a) directly measuring the peak density and (b) dividing the FWHM density value of each peak by the CNM fraction as measured by Stanimirovi´c et al. (2010). The geometric approach (b) yields lower limits closer to the thermal equilibrium curve as set by Wolfire et al. (2003) since the absorption spectra are more sensitive to variations in the density on a smaller scale than the three-dimensional dust maps. The upper limits of the ionization fraction along the line of sight to each pulsar are consistent with the WNM calculations of Jenkins (2013), demonstrating that diffuse adding using the mean H1 volume density along the line of sight to each pulsar. Also, our measurements are in agreement with theoretical predictions from Godard et al. (2024), signifying the possibility of when an approx. 200 km/s shock interacts with the surrounding ISM.

Our study shows promise in physically correlating dusty structures via density profiles to their absorption spectra along the line of sight to pulsars with higher Galactic Latitudes. Furthermore, our analysis of line of sight properties shows while both diffuse and clumpy structures are correlated with absorption, the LB is made up mostly of diffuse WNM and CNM structures lie outside of the LB. A larger survey of the lines of sight to local pulsars will place important constraints on its thermal properties of the LB and elucidate its overall evolution.

title: Doula Care and the Role of Maternal Age in Reducing Maternal Morbidity Rates in the United States
abstract:
Background: Maternal morbidity rates and high rates of risky obstetric interventions remain a problem in the United States. Birth doulas are a suggested solution to mitigate obstetric interventions. Despite women of different maternal ages facing different risks during pregnancy, research is not yet conclusive on whether the benefits of doulas may vary for different age groups.

Methods: A literature review was conducted through PubMed and CINAHL with the inclusion criteria that the article be published in English between 2000-2025, be about doula care and its impact on cesarean sections and/or forceps-assisted deliveries, and include age as a measured demographic. Articles must be from peer-reviewed journals. Literature regarding forceps-assisted deliveries were parsed out.

Findings: Doulas likely reduce the risk of cesarean sections for adolescents (<20) by connecting adolescents with needed resources and reducing stress. Stronger evidence exists showing doulas reduce cesarean section rates for adults (20-34) by screening for maternal mental health, assisting mothers in accessing needed resources, and providing culturally competent care. Inconclusive literature was identified for pregnant people in the advanced age group (35+).

Conclusion: Existing literature has the strongest evidence that doulas reduce cesarean section rates for pregnant women in the adult age category. More research must be conducted to confirm the differences in degree of benefit between the age groups.
text:
Doula Care and the Role of Maternal Age in Reducing​

Maternal Morbidity Rates in the United States

Zora S. Warren

Global Health Studies Department, Northwestern University

Advised by Professor Sarah B. Rodriguez, Global Health Studies

Abstract

Background: Maternal morbidity rates and high rates of risky obstetric interventions remain a problem in the United States. Birth doulas are a suggested solution to mitigate obstetric interventions. Despite women of different maternal ages facing different risks during pregnancy, research is not yet conclusive on whether the benefits of doulas may vary for different age groups.

Methods: A literature review was conducted through PubMed and CINAHL with the inclusion criteria that the article be published in English between 2000-2025, be about doula care and its impact on cesarean sections and/or forceps-assisted deliveries, and include age as a measured demographic. Articles must be from peer-reviewed journals. Literature regarding forceps-assisted deliveries were parsed out.

Findings: Doulas likely reduce the risk of cesarean sections for adolescents (<20) by connecting adolescents with needed resources and reducing stress. Stronger evidence exists showing doulas reduce cesarean section rates for adults (20-34) by screening for maternal mental health, assisting mothers in accessing needed resources, and providing culturally competent care. Inconclusive literature was identified for pregnant people in the advanced age group (35+).

Conclusion: Existing literature has the strongest evidence that doulas reduce cesarean section rates for pregnant women in the adult age category. More research must be conducted to confirm the differences in degree of benefit between the age groups.

Introduction​

Maternal morbidity rates are a crisis in the United States, and studies suggest that increased rates of medical interventions, such as cesarean sections and forceps-assisted births, may be partially due to their associations with postoperational conditions such as hemorrhaging and infection. To reduce the risk of maternal morbidity, researchers have suggested birth doulas as a non-medical intervention to reduce the use of these obstetric interventions. Pregnancy risks differ greatly between maternal age groups, and published research is inconclusive about the benefits of a doula based on the age of the mother. This literature review seeks to determine to what degree working with a doula during labor increases or decreases the risk of a cesarean section or forceps-assisted delivery for women of different age groups in the 21st century.

Background

Doula Care

Birth doulas are trained professionals who provide emotional, physical, and informational support during labor and the antepartum and postpartum periods (Mottl-Santiago et al., 2023, p.

467). Doulas are not clinicians, but nonetheless play a vital supportive role for pregnant people.

While hospital staff are typically able to spend about 21% of a person’s labor with the patients, doulas provide continuous support throughout labor, as well as during prepartum and postpartum visits (Kennell et al., 1991, p. 3). Doulas can assist in explaining procedures in terms that pregnant people can easily understand, and they can facilitate communication between the patient and their provider by encouraging the patient to speak up when they have questions or concerns (Futch Thurston et al., 2019). Doulas provide both emotional and physical comfort during birth via techniques such as counter pressure, position changes, and encouragement throughout labor (Papagni K & Buckner E, 2006, p. 15). During the postpartum period, doulas can assist with breastfeeding, household chores, and safe practices like proper car seat use (Hans et al., 2018, p. S105).

​ There are three models of doula care. The first is private practice: doulas who are hired directly by the family, visit pre- and postpartum, and attend the labor (Thomas et al., 2017, p.

S61). The second is the hospital-based model, in which doulas are employed by the hospital and are offered to families at a subsidized rate or no fee. Hospital-based doulas may not offer the full breadth of services in the pre- and postpartum periods, and instead, their practice typically centers around labor and delivery support (Lesser et al., 2005, p. 28). Finally, community-based doulas serve primarily low-income families in their own neighborhoods and often share an aspect of their identity with the mothers they serve; their services are typically offered to families at no charge. In addition to providing home visits pre- and postpartum and during labor, community-based doulas emphasize screening for social determinants of health such as access to food, safe housing, and exposure to violence. Community-based doulas receive additional training to help connect pregnant people whose needs are not being met to resources in the community (Futch Thurston et al., 2019). Doulas are increasingly recognized as important members of the healthcare team in labor, but according to the 2013 Listening to Mothers III survey, the most recent survey available, only 6% of mothers in the United States used doula care during labor (Declercq et al., 2013, p. 16). However, studies have found that doulas may be a key to reducing maternal morbidity.

Maternal Morbidity in the United States

Maternal morbidities are the adverse consequences of pregnancy that affect a pregnant person’s health and may include hemorrhaging, eclampsia, gestational diabetes, hypertension, and puerperal fever. Severe maternal morbidity has increased over the past two decades, rising from a rate of 146.8 per 10,000 births in 2008 to 179.8 per 10,000 births in 2021 (Fink et al.,

2023, p. 1). There are numerous risk factors for maternal morbidity: young maternal age or old maternal age; being a person of color (largely specific to the U.S.); Medicaid enrollment; and cesarean section (Fink et al., 2023, p. 14). Cesarean section in particular is associated with triple the odds of severe maternal morbidity compared to vaginal delivery (Fink et al., 2023, p. 11).

Despite this statistic, there is an attitude in the US that vaginal delivery is inherently risky, while cesarean sections can protect women from the risk of morbidity (Wolf, 2018, p. 134).

Misinformed attitudes have caused cesarean section rates to skyrocket in the United States.

While the World Health Organization recommends a cesarean section rate of 10-15% for optimal benefit with minimized morbidity, in 2022, the U.S. cesarean section delivery rate was 32.1%

(Osterman et al., 2024, p. 40; WHO Statement on Caesarean Section Rates, 2015). Of particular concern, severe maternal morbidity (morbidities with significant health impacts) rates associated with cesarean section have increased during the 21st century, increasing from 252.4 cases of severe maternal morbidity per 10,000 discharges in Q1 of 2008 to 312.1 per 10,000 discharges in

Q4 of 2021 (Fink et al., 2023, pp. 1–5). Many surgical morbidities are associated with cesarean section, including sepsis, wound infection, bladder injury, hemorrhage, blood clots, and increased risk of post-delivery complications such as wound separation, uterine tract infections, gastrointestinal problems, and septic thrombophlebitis (Klaus & Klaus, 2010, p. 6; Quinlan &

Murphy, 2015, p. 178). Doulas reduce the chance of obstetric interventions during labor, including cesarean section. In one study, women with doula care had a cesarean section rate of only 13.9% compared to a 26.9% overall rate (Lesser et al., 2005, p. 30).

Forceps-assisted births are another intervention technique associated with maternal morbidity. While less common than cesarean sections, they still pose a potential complication for pregnant women. Forceps use is associated with severe birth trauma, including severe injury to the peripheral nervous system and higher rates of severe postpartum hemorrhaging (Muraca et al., 2019). Research suggests that continuous doula support during labor is associated with lower rates of forceps assisted delivery; one study found forceps usage in patients with doula care was

8.2% compared to the control rate of 26.3% (p=0.0006) (Kennell et al., 1991, p. 4). The finding that doulas may reduce the risk of cesarean sections and forceps-assisted births is significant, especially considering heightened morbidity risks associated with maternal age.

Typically, when comparing risk between age groups, 25–29 years of age is used as a comparison. Compared to 25–29 year olds,women under twenty years of age have a heightened risk of endometritis, preterm delivery, and mild preeclampsia. Women ages 15–19, specifically, have higher risks for severe preeclampsia, postpartum hemorrhage, and fetal distress. Women of advanced maternal age (35+) are more likely to suffer from severe preeclampsia, preterm birth, fetal distress, and hypertension (Cavazos-Rehg et al., 2015, p. 5). Older maternal age has also been associated with higher risk of cesarean section. In 2022, women ages 40 and older had a

47.7% cesarean section rate compared to women ages 25-29 who had a 29.7% rate and women under 20 with a rate of only 18.9% (Osterman et al., 2024, p. 40).

Doula Care to Reduce Maternal Morbidity

Doulas may help lower morbidities associated with cesarean sections and forceps assisted deliveries. Continuous support from doulas has been hypothesized to reduce maternal anxiety and thus reduce catecholamine levels, a class of molecules that can negatively impact delivery outcomes by lowering the ability of the uterus to contract and decreasing blood flow to the uterus and placenta  (Kennell et al., 1991, p. 5; Papagni K & Buckner E, 2006, p. 13). Doulas may help women communicate their preferences for labor interference, avoiding unnecessary interventions that may increase their risk of morbidity (Lesser et al., 2005, p. 31). Importantly,  the beneficial findings of continuous doula care have not been replicated with the continuous labor support of nurses or a patient’s partner, suggesting the doula’s care and training have unique and powerful effects (Hodnett et al., 2002, p. 1373; McGrath & Kennell, 2008, p. 96).

Research has not yet been conducted on the degree of benefit of doula care for women of different age groups, despite the different risks they face. Understanding the extent to which doula care positively affects different age groups  would allow for more effective and timely education of mothers on doula support and more effective referrals for mothers who may glean the most benefit. It may also mitigate increased maternal morbidity risk associated with age.

Methods

To identify literature related to a doula’s differing effect on women of different age groups, I searched PubMed and CINAHL (Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health

Literature) because of their emphasis on quantitative, peer-reviewed medical literature.

Beginning with the concepts of doulas, cesarean sections, forceps-assisted births, and age, I used

PubMed MeSH (Medical Subject Headings) terms to identify other potential key terminology to account for all variations. These terms, along with the appropriate Boolean terms (i.e. AND,

OR), were combined into searches. At times when two MeSH variations were quite similar (i.e.

“cesarean delivery” and “cesarean section”), only the common part of the phrase was used in the final search (“cesarean”), so it would identify results for both MeSH terms. Search terms can be found in Table 1 in Appendix I. At times, I deployed different age group filters, since the databases differed in their age-group filter options.

I then copied The searches into PubMed and CINAHL to gain a total of 3082 articles.

The articles were then filtered to exclude articles published before the year 2000, leaving a total of 2955 articles. Articles were then de-duplicated, and articles were eliminated if they were not written in English, or if they were clearly not related to pregnancy, doulas, or birth interventions

(i.e. articles about heart surgery). Articles I found manually through searching bibliographies of previous articles were combined with the articles found in databases. After this stage, 346 articles remained. I then screened the articles by title and abstract; articles were eliminated if they were not related to cesarean sections or forceps, if the study was done outside of the U.S., or if the article was a recount of the author’s personal stories, rather than a formal research study or review. I also eliminated Articles if they were not explicitly about professional doulas. 112 articles remained after this step. I then performed a full-text screening, eliminating articles if the study was completed in another country, if the article was a review of literature that was already collected for this review, if the article was not related to cesarean section or forceps rates and doula care, if the data was theoretical, if the article was not from a peer-reviewed journal, or if the full-text was not in English (1 article). This left 16 articles that I deemed eligible for analysis.

Included articles are detailed in Table 2 in Appendix I.

Originally, rates of forceps-assisted delivery were intended to be a measured variable in this review. During screening, incredibly few articles were identified that included forceps-assisted birth as an outcome. Due to this outcome, I broadened the search from

“forceps-assisted births” to all “assisted vaginal births,” which includes a vacuum assisted delivery. A new round of searches was conducted, as listed in Table 3 in Appendix I. This new search retrieved 201 articles. After removing duplicates, publication date check, and title screening, 15 articles remained. After abstract screening, 8 articles moved on to full-text screening. When this step was completed, one article did include data on assisted vaginal deliveries, but was only applicable to women in the adult age group. Because of this, no analysis based on age groups could be drawn, and data on assisted vaginal births with doulas has been excluded from the body of this review.

Findings

The three age groups examined in this study are adolescent (pregnant people <20 years old), adult (20-34), and advanced (35+).

Adolescents

Doulas, especially community-based doulas, may be particularly beneficial for pregnant adolescents due to their ability to mitigate the heightened social determinants of health risks that put adolescents  at greater risk for maternal morbidities (Cavazos-Rehg et al., 2015, p. 7). A study showed that in a population of teen parents in Washington D.C., 37% did not access any resources to assist with their food security, housing, or finances, pointing to barriers specific to teens that keep them from essential  assistance (Smiley et al., 2025). Adolescents may also delay or not seek prenatal care at all in an effort to avoid revealing their pregnancy, which could potentially result in backlash from their vital support systems, negative stereotypes about their sexuality, and tension with healthcare providers (Gentry et al., 2010, p. 25; Smiley et al., 2025).

Doula programs, especially those focused on serving a younger demographic , can bridge the gap in resources for pregnant adolescents and refer them to necessary services/programs  (Smiley et al., 2025). . For example, doulas can attend medical appointments with pregnant women and assist them in enrolling in public support systems to ensure they have access to food, housing, and financial support (Smiley et al., 2025).

Doulas can also attend to  adolescent parents’ mental health. The stress and trauma of parenthood at a young age can result in an elevated risk for clinical depression (Gentry et al.,

2010, p. 25; Smiley et al., 2025). In one community-based doula program in Georgia, doulas took baseline assessments of adolescents’ mental health and attempted to provide mental health support and encouragement to help them cope and thrive in their pregnancy (Gentry et al., 2010, p. 36). While this was perceived as beneficial by the participants, they also noted that doulas are not mental health providers, and thus may be more impactful in  screening adolescent parents’ mental health  and referring them to professional mental health services rather than providing direct support themselves (Gentry et al., 2010, pp. 36–37). Mental health screening and support may play a role in reducing cesarean section rates, as perinatal mood disorders have been associated with higher rates of primary cesarean sections (Zochowski et al., 2021, p. 6).

Separate from mental health services, adolescents in the Washington D.C. doula program noted that childbirth education, access to social support systems, and encouragement to advocate for themselves in clinical settings eased their stress around maternity (Smiley et al., 2025).

Advocacy is especially important, as some adolescents mentioned that they felt manipulated by their obstetric providers to accept more medical interventions (Gentry et al., 2010, p. 34). A doula’s stress-reducing support and encouragement to communicate desires and concerns likely mitigates the risk of a cesarean section, per the outcomes of four studies. In a 2013 study of the birth outcomes of 1,892 adolescents who were supported by doulas during labor, only 12.6% of participants had a cesarean section, and only 2.5% of these cesarean sections were elective

(Everson et al., 2018, p. 140). According to the National Vital Statistics Report (NVSR) detailing birth outcomes of adolescents without doula support from the same year, 21.8% of these births were cesarean sections, a difference of 9.2% (Curtin et al., 2015, p. 4). The number of elective deliveries is also important, as elective repeat cesarean sections make up 30% of the indications of cesarean sections in North America (Quinlan & Murphy, 2015, p. 178). The Washington, D.C.

doula program found a cesarean rate of only 8% (1/12 participants), and community-based program in Georgia found a cesarean rate of only 17% (53/314 participants), both of which were lower than the national rate of 21.8% (Gentry et al., 2010, p. 29; Smiley et al., 2025). These findings suggest that doula care can lower adolescent cesarean section rates.

The significance of doulas’ effects on adolescent cesarean section rates may also be dependent on whether the adolescent parent is supported during labor, rather than only during prenatal visits, and whether they are low risk and nulliparous . In one study of participants under the age of 26 (with a mean age of 18.4 years old), no significant difference was found between the doula care arm and the non-doula care arm (Hans et al., 2018, pp. S105–S107). The authors of this study  hypothesized these results may have been because their population of young and low-income mothers may have presented as more medically complex than expected/than the program could support?? and only 75% of the doula treatment group actually received doula support during labor (Hans et al., 2018, pp. S108–S110). In future studies, it may be helpful to include a larger sample of pregnant adolescents who were randomized into doula and control care groups and exclude samples in which the doula was not present during labor. It may also be enlightening to compare doulas that provide care before, during, and after delivery  to labor-only or prenatal-only doulas.

Adults

Unlike the adolescent age group, existing literature rarely reflected sample groups in which every participant was within the adult age group of 20-34 years old. However, many studies were concerned with populations whose means and standard deviations fell within the adult age parameters. These studies, along with a study that had results distinct to the 20-34 age group demographic, were used to investigate the adult age group. A total of 10 studies were used.

Adults appeared to face some similar struggles to adolescents. Multiple studies noted that doula programs specifically screened patients, sometimes more than once, for food insecurity, intimate partner violence, and housing insecurity, three important social determinants of health

(Mottl-Santiago et al., 2023, p. 469; Thomas et al., 2023, p. S61). Doulas also screened patients for depression and provided referrals to necessary mental health services, a factor that adolescent-specific doula care was missing (Thomas et al., 2017, p. S61). Doulas worked with pregnant women to identify their desires for their birth and educate them on how best to advocate for themselves with their medical providers (Thomas et al., 2017, p. S61). This may help women feel more confident in their decision if they intend to have a vaginal birth, reducing the rate of elective cesarean sections. Discussing a comprehensive birth plan may also encourage the pregnant person to speak up and continue to attempt labor if a cesarean section is suggested by a medical provider during delivery l.

These doula interventions may be particularly effective for  women on Medicaid, many of whom are also women of color. These women face the additional stressors of systemic and interpersonal racism and poverty, and their communities bear disproportionate rates of chronic health issues (Thomas et al., 2017, p. S60). Doulas are able to provide culturally specific care, which may mitigate the impact of some of these stressors (Futch Thurston et al., 2019).

However, because Medicaid rarely covers doula services and private doula fees can range from hundreds of dollars to around $2,000 (Futch Thurston et al., 2019; Kozhimannil et al., 2013, p.

118, 2016, p. 25), many pregnant women cannot afford doula care (Futch Thurston et al., 2019).

Several studies suggest doula support is effective at lowering cesarean rates for adult patients in labor. Out of the 10 studies used for the adult age group analysis, four studies did not return statistically significant results. However, all relevant studies showed a direct trend of doula care reducing cesarean section rates (See Figure 1 in Appendix II). In the only study that separated results for the adult age group, the study found that women with doula care had a

21.6% rate of cesarean section compared to women without doula support who had a rate of

29.3% (Gruber et al., 2013, p. 54). While this difference was not found to be statistically significant to a p-value of 0.05, it does show a positive trend. The difference may have not been significant because of the low power of the relatively small sample size (n=92) (Gruber et al.,

2013, p. 54). This trend was found in another study without exact adult age constraints, where non-doula supported patients had a cesarean section rate of 33.3% and supported patients had a rate of 31.9%, though the difference was not found to be statistically significant (Lemon et al.,

2025, p. 387.e5).

Other studies without a specific/explicit adult age sample group but with mean ages and standard deviations within ages 20-34 showed a substantial decrease in risk for cesarean sections when doulas were part of their healthcare team. For cesarean sections, adjusted odds ratios

(AORs) for a cesarean section with doula care were reported at 0.44 (95% confidence interval

0.39-0.49) (Kozhimannil et al., 2016, p. 23) and 0.41 (95% CI 0.18-0.96) (Kozhimannil et al.,

2014, p. 6), 0.59 (95% CI 0.51-0.68) (Kozhimannil et al., 2013, p. 116). Another study reported a relative risk of 0.53 (95% CI 0.43-0.66) (Falconi et al., 2024, p. 1280) between patients with and without doulas. For non-medically indicated cesarean sections, an even stronger association was found with an AOR of 0.17 (95% CI 0.07-0.39) (Kozhimannil et al., 2014, p. 6).

Another finding was the ability of doula care to increase rates of VBACs (vaginal birth after cesarean). In one study, the rate of VBACs for non-doula supported births was 18.8%, while doula-supported births had a VBAC rate of 34.4% (p=0.002) (Lemon et al., 2025, p.

387.e5). Another study also reported that when doulas supported patients during delivery, they were 116% more likely to have a VBAC delivery than their non-doula-supported counterparts

(Falconi et al., 2024, p. 1280). VBACs have been shown to result in fewer maternal morbidities such as ruptured uteri, unplanned hysterectomies, and ICU admissions than repeat cesarean sections, (Curtin et al., 2015, p. 1; Lemon et al., 2025, p. 387.e6). These studies suggest doula care may play a substantial role in reducing rates of cesarean sections for adults.

Advanced Age

Women of advanced maternal age face significantly higher rates of cesarean section than younger women? in the United States. While the overall cesarean section rate in 2022 was

32.1%, for women ages 35-39 years old, that number jumped to 40.0%, and for women 40 and older, it jumped again to 47.7% (Osterman et al., 2024, p. 40). Women 35 and older have a higher risk of developing maternal morbidities such as severe preeclampsia, superimposed preeclampsia, and hypertension. Because of their elevated risk levels,  mothers of advanced maternal age may benefit greatly from  doula care. However, women in the advanced age group were less likely to have doula support compared to mothers ages 18-24 (Kozhimannil et al.,

2014, p. 5).  Unfortunately, no studies were identified for this review that considered the benefits of doula care on advanced maternal age.

Comparing Benefits Between Age Groups

When examining AORs of cesarean section for women of different ages, it appears that doula care may have a more significant benefit for adolescent and adult women than for women in the advanced age category. According to a study published containing data from 2010-2014, the AOR of cesarean sections, among all women with full term births in the study who had a doula compared to those who did not, was 0.44 (95% CI 0.39-0.49)—showing clear benefit

(Kozhimannil et al., 2016, p. 26). When comparing between age groups, with ages 26-30 being the reference age group (1.00), the AORs of women with full term deliveries having a cesarean section (and 95% CIs) were as follows: ages 20 and under, 1.46 (1.38-1.53); ages 21-25, 0.90

(0.86-0.94); ages 26-30, 1.00; ages 31-35, 1.29 (1.22-1.37); ages 36 and up, 4.67 (4.35-5.01)

(Kozhimannil et al., 2016, p. 26). If the degree of benefit of doula care for women of different age groups was the same, it would be expected that the AORs between age groups would remain the same when comparing doula care to doula care and non-doula care to non-doula care.

However, the data does not suggest this.

In order to compare data with as few confounding variables as possible, the control data for this review was taken from the National Vital Statistics Report (NVSR) from 2012 so as to stay within the timeframe of Kozhimannil’s study (2010-2014) reviewed above: the most recent comparison between benefits to age groups. According to the National Vital Statistics Report from 2012, the cesarean rates for the different age groups were as follows: ages 19 and under,

22.3%; ages 20-24-,27.9%; ages 25-29, 31.5%; ages 30-34, 35.8%; ages 35-39, 42.1%; ages

40-54, 49.7% (Martin et al., 2013, p. 51). While the NVSR does not provide AORs, a few conclusions may still be made from the comparisons of the data.

Firstly, while the 19-and-under age group in the NVSR was 9.2% less likely to have a cesarean section compared to women ages 25-29, Kozhimannil et al.’s study found that with doula care, women under 20 have a higher risk of cesarean section compared to women ages

26-30. This suggests that, while doula care has been found to have a positive effect on birth outcomes for adolescents, it is likely a smaller magnitude of benefit. There also appears to be a smaller magnitude of benefit for women of advanced maternal age. The NVSR reported that women ages 35-39 were 10.6% more likely, and women 40-54 were 18.2% more likely, to have a cesarean section than women ages 25-29. However, that is a much smaller difference than AOR presented in the study, which suggests that women ages 35+ are 4.67 times more likely to have a cesarean section. This suggests that doula care has a much smaller impact (if both impacts are positive) on the cesarean section rates of women of advanced maternal age.

This comparison is not ideal, given that it necessitates comparing data from different sources and conditions. More research should be conducted that directly compares doula care to a lack of doula care and age to limit cross-data set analysis and provide valid conclusions.

Strengths and Limitations

​ A strength of this review is that it specifically focuses on trained birth doulas. Lay doulas, partners, and nursing staff who provide labor and prenatal support were excluded from analysis to specifically identify  the impact of doula training. Another strength of this review is the variety of studies that were analyzed, including both large quantitative studies using national data, as well as smaller, interview-based qualitative studies—which allowed for closer examination of how doulas cater their care to mothers of different age groups.

A major limitation of this review is the paucity of published literature on the effect of doula care, maternal age, and forceps use, as well as a general lack of specific information on advanced age pregnancies. There are no articles that break down cesarean section rates by age group and compare them to the non-doula-care-control condition. This gap in the research led to my need for comparing different data sets, which is not ideal. Another limitation of the studies used in this review is the potential for selection bias, for most did not randomly separate participants, but rather, they used data where pregnant women may have been referred to doula care because of risk factors they faced or sought it out themselves (Falconi et al., 2024, p. 1276;

Kozhimannil et al., 2016, p. 26). This may have led to confounding factors such as the populations in the study being at higher risk compared to non-study populations.

Conclusion

Published literature suggests that doula care has varying degrees of benefit to pregnant people in reducing cesarean sections based on their age. This may be due to specific obstetric risk factors that come with age, social determinants of health, or whether a specific age group tends to have medically-indicated or non-indicated cesarean sections.

Future research, in addition to filling in the gaps identified in the Strengths and

Limitations section, may take a few different paths. One is to separate delivery outcomes into medically-indicated and non-indicated cesarean sections to pinpoint whether doulas play a larger role in medically indicated outcomes or elective delivery choices. Medical indications include issues with the placenta, the baby being in the wrong position, fetal distress, and maternal health conditions that make vaginal birth dangerous (Kozhimannil et al., 2014, p. 4). Further research may also compare results between the different models of doula care.

Finally, more research should be conducted on insurance status and the impacts of doula care. Many studies read for this review looked only at Medicaid-insured populations. Cost has been shown to be a significant barrier to doula care access for all women, not just women on

Medicaid— and in one study, nearly three fourths of women reported that, if their health insurance covered doula care, they would take advantage of this benefit (Mitchell et al., 2023, p.

187). This comes in stark contrast to the mere 6% of women who reported, in the most recent data available, actually using doula care in the United States (Declercq et al., 2013, p. XI).

Studying, more specifically, the impacts of both private and public insurance covering doula care may lead to significant policy action that can expand doula access for all women in the United

States.
