title: Belief Formation in the Age of Misinformation: Evaluating the Role of Perceived Expertise in Health Content
text:
Belief Formation in the Age of Misinformation: Evaluating the Role of Perceived Expertise in Health Content

Asha S. Henry

Northwestern University

Advisor: David Rapp, Ph.D.

Second Reader: Galen Bodenhausen Ph.D.

Department of Cognitive Science, Northwestern University

School of Education and Social Policy, Northwestern University

Introduction

Since its inception in the early 2000s, social media has become a cornerstone of everyday life for many people around the world, with 5.24 billion people estimated to have used social media as of February 2025 (Statista). Sites such as Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, X (formerly

Twitter), and Reddit have become international hubs for sharing news, art, and music, connecting with friends, and building communities based on shared interests and hobbies. Exposure to health and wellness content is frequent when a user spends any length of time on social media, often with a near-immediate crossover to real-world impacts. Exposure can occur via influencers, friends, news sources, sponsored content, and advertisements. Many social media users even seek out sources of specific wellness content by following accounts that focus on niche health topics (Lim & Molenaar et al., 2022).

The practice of sourcing information via social media is particularly prevalent in the case of the app TikTok, a short-form video-sharing platform originally released in 2016. The app is particularly popular among teens and young adults, with more than half of adolescents reporting using the platform (Leppert & Matsa, 2024). The hope for social media to share information and build community is nearly limitless; however, with an increase in digital consumption, the simultaneous proliferation of health misinformation is visible and concerning.

The risk to public health has risen as social media increasingly has become a pathway through which people consume health information. Many people, particularly youth, are generally unfamiliar with how to identify trusted health sources online, making the credibility of those accounts sharing health and wellness information particularly pertinent (Eysenbach, 2008).

Credibility checks of accounts sharing health and wellness information ensure that misinformation does not spread as people are less likely to interact with sources they deem not credible (Eysenbach, 2008). As social media has expanded, it has become a hotbed for misinformation that can harm community health. Balancing the growth of social media alongside the urgent need to combat misinformation will remain a life-and-death public health concern for the healthcare industry, nations, and the global community.

Cognitive Consequences of Misinformation

Researchers have outlined the harmful effects of misinformation in the online context and have explored how it impacts decision making. Misinformation is defined as “inaccuracies generally conveyed through discourse, whether intentional or accidental” (Jia, 2020). Regardless of intentionality, misinformation can cause people to retain falsehoods, and the resulting confusion can contribute to misunderstandings of events (e.g., Butler et al., 2009; O’Sullivan et al., 2022; Schiff et al., 2024; Umanath et al., 2012). Exposure to misinformation can cast doubt on the credibility of outside sources (news media, podcasts, etc.), information dissemination systems, and knowledge-based communities (Brashier & Schacter, 2020; Marwick & Partin,

2024; Westbrook et al., 2023). Even following minimal exposure to these inaccuracies, people are more likely to be influenced by misinformation, rather than to spontaneously generate the same ideas after accurate or unrelated information exposure (e.g., Appel & Richter, 2007; Butler et al., 2009; Fazio et al., 2015; Gerrig & Prentice, 1991; Marsh et al., 2003; Marsh & Fazio,

2007; Rapp, 2016; Salovich et al., 2022; Salovich, Mason, et al., 2023). In cases wherein participants previously held accurate understandings of information, exposure to inaccuracies appeared to suspend and supersede the prior knowledge that participants previously held, with falsehoods taking precedence (Hinze et al., 2014; Marsh et al., 2003; Salovich et al., 2022;

Salovich, Mason, et al., 2023;  Salovich & Rapp, 2023). Previous knowledge should have allowed participants to rationally doubt and internally refute the inaccurate information presented in the stimuli (Brashier & Schacter, 2020; Marwick & Partin, 2024). The fact that misinformation can so easily dislodge prior accurate information among users portends a worrisome future for public health, marked by both unintentional and malicious efforts that spread misinformation.

Moreover, in the online environment, misinformation has exploited social media algorithms, spreading misinformation to an ever-widening audience more rapidly than truths.

Vosoughi et al. (2018) investigated the spread of false information on the social media site

Twitter (now X), and found that falsehoods diffused faster than the truth. Falsehoods were found to reach between 1,000 and 100,000 people, while the truth seldom reached more than 1,000 individuals. Furthermore, exposure to inaccuracies can result in confusion about what is the truth and can foster doubt in previously held accurate beliefs, which causes additional reliance on misinformation, (Rapp & Salovich 2018). The perceived credibility of the sources offering information has also been proven to further impact the spread of misinformation. When information is shared via sources that are perceived to be credible, such as an immigration attorney speaking on common visa issues, people are more likely to learn and depend on the misinformation presented to make decisions (Andrews & Rapp, 2014; Appel & Mara, 2013;

Ecker & Antonio, 2021; Heinbach et al., 2018; Nadarevic et al., 2020; Walter & Tukachinsky,

2020).

Health misinformation is defined as ‘health-related statements that are anecdotal evidence, factually incorrect, or misleading due to a lack of scientific evidence’ (Suarez-Lledo &

Alvarez-Galvez 2021). Current work has found that engagement with videos—including clicks, shares, views, comments and retweets—that include inaccurate information is higher than the engagement with videos containing accurate information (Goobie et al., 2019; Selvi &

Baydilli, 2022; Xu et al., 2021). General online users, such as those who have lay knowledge of health and healthcare, claim to receive health and wellness information from both credentialed healthcare professionals and non-credentialed general users regularly (Kirkpatrick & Lawrie,

2024). However, the process of ascertaining expertise in online space is often based on surface-level visual cues such as account username, number of followers, presence of a verification check, profile photos, biography and other superficial details (Kirkpatrick & Lawrie,

2024). Although these sources may appear to be valid forms of account credibility verification, visual cues can easily be changed, manipulated, or intentionally misrepresented to deceive audiences. Experimental research has shown that exposure to videos that contain health inaccuracies can result in changes in both behaviors and beliefs (Vraga et al., 2021). Given the effectiveness of online media to influence thought and behavior, content creators can manipulate users by projecting an image of credibility, which then increases the existence and impact of health misinformation online.

In the online environment, much of the health and wellness information being disseminated is through Social Media Influencers (SMIs), online creators with large followings gained from the narration of their daily lives (Thompson, 2022). Health and wellness SMIs often focus on niche topics such as reproductive health, dermatology, fitness training, or

Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), and they often present on topics of interest to their cultivated audience—including income-generating efforts to promote products and services.

These SMIs have a wide range of claimed expertise, from board-certified surgeons, specialty nurses, and health researchers to naturopaths, and to those who may simply suffer from a condition.

In general, Americans tend to have a high degree of trust in medical doctors and other healthcare professionals, with 74% of Americans having a mostly positive view of doctors, and

68% having a mostly-favorable opinion of medical research scientists (Funk & Gramlich 2020).

Real-world trust overlaps with the online environment:the materials shared on social media via influential users with expertise (i.e. the username @Dr.Smith) are proven to be more likely to be shared and re-processed by other users than informational materials shared by general users

(Thompson, 2022). However, there has been a significant increase in anti-expertise rhetoric and accompanying health misinformation by SMIs and a resulting proliferation of health-related inaccuracies and myths online. Media theorist Mark Davis has critiqued that anti-vaccination and other anti-expertise groups have fabricated and weaponized the ‘politicized’ agendas of healthcare professionals to create an “us versus them” mentality between those with health knowledge and those without. Under this framework, groups can conflate expertise with political or ideological bias as a rationale for the promotion of supposedly harmful vaccines by healthcare professionals (Davis, 2018). This process of demonizing healthcare professionals as supporters of ideological bias encourages users to doubt those with traditional forms of expertise (education, professional experience, board certifications) and to trust those that are perceived to be ideologically pure and anti-expertise, even if their own authority on a topic is unfounded.

Short-form videos, typically less than one-minute long, have become one of the most popular forms of media on apps such as TikTok (For You Page), Instagram (Reels), Facebook

(Shorts), and YouTube (Shorts), with each app creating their own version of short-form media feeds within the larger app platform. Misinformation in these short form video feeds has not been investigated in the field of cognitive psychology under experimental conditions. However, observational studies of TikTok videos covering the Covid-19 pandemic found moderate misinformation to be present in 22% of videos studied, which were viewed a median of 6.8 million times, and a high-level of misinformation to be present in 7% of of videos, viewed, on average, 9.4 million times (Baghdadi & Coffey, 2023). Inaccuracies present in short-form videos can be viewed in several modalities, including through speech, text, imagery, out-of-context visuals or verbalizations, or artificial intelligence-generated images or videos (Rapp, Holohan, &

Withall, in press). In the present study, we have created experimentally controlled videos modeled after those that one would find on social media containing speech misinformation.

Social Media and Misinformation

Unlike other models of communication, which utilize a vertical approach—those at the top of the information hierarchy spreading knowledge down to the base—social media utilizes a horizontal model, with anyone, regardless of positionality on the information hierarchy, sharing knowledge equally with everyone (Fisher, 2022). Social media’s  transformation of the communication model allows misinformation to be shared by anyone and to be viewed by any number of users, with or without claims of expertise, or proof of knowledge. Social media apps that utilize short-form videos are designed to capture the attention of the audience, with videos that have garnered significant audience interactions (likes, comments, views, shares, etc.) being boosted by the app’s algorithmic presentation, which then promotes high-engagement videos to increasingly broader audiences, thus creating an exponential reach and potentially resulting in the harmful spread of misinformation online. Furthermore, this algorithmic process means that users sharing videos including misinformation out of alarm or dismay actually boost the reach and impact of that misinformation.

Real-World Application of Research

Currently, there are significant gaps in the literature regarding misinformation in the format of short-form videos in the cognitive psychology realm; however; this is an area that should not be overlooked, for many hundreds of thousands of social media users are exposed to health and wellness information daily, a significant proportion of which has been proven to be misinformation. This misinformation is of critical concern because, as of early 2025, there is a spreading outbreak of measles in many parts of the United States. The spread of measles likely a result of current efforts by anti-vaccination groups, who incorrectly claim online that vaccinations cause autism in children and who further question the efficacy of vaccines and their long-term effects. The spread of vaccine misinformation in the digital age has resulted in the eradication of prior national immunity due to widespread vaccination efforts, which resulted in the elimination of measles from within the country in 2000 (CNN, 2025). As of October 2025, the current outbreak has already caused the death of three unvaccinated children in, along with hundreds of hospitalizations (U.S. Centers for Disease Control). Despite this, the National

Institutes of Health has terminated dozens of scientific grants for projects on the topic of vaccine use and hesitancy, since this research has been considered to be unaligned with the Trump administration’s priorities (PBS).

Current Study

The current study seeks to determine if the claimed expertise of the content creator has an impact on the reproduction of health and wellness misinformation in the social media realm.

Participants viewed 12 short-form videos that shared both correct and incorrect health and wellness information. Each video was presented along with an account username, which was presented as either an expert (e.g., @Derm_Dr.Reith) or non-expert (e.g.,. @user124085). After viewing the videos and completing a distractor task, participants answered questions about the validity of the statements presented in the videos, along with several filler statements. Previous work has shown that response accuracy decreases after exposure to inaccurate information as compared to response accuracy after exposure to correct information, and we expect this typical misinformation exposure effect to be replicated in the current study (Holohan & Rapp, in prep).

Furthermore, we expect that participants will be more likely to reproduce incorrect health and wellness inaccuracies shared by a user with claimed expertise, as compared to non-expert users.

Method Participants—We recruited one hundred and six (n = 106) undergraduate students via

Northwestern’s psychology subject pool. We excluded participants who had not completed the survey, and we continued recruitment until the goal sample size of 100 was reached. This sample size was chosen to roughly match the sample size in Salovich et al., (2022), which utilized a series of three experiments to investigate if evaluative mindsets reduce the likelihood of the use and influence of inaccurate statements. Salovich et al. (2022) included 80 participants per within-subject condition, with a total of 160 participants to reach adequate power. Since all of our variables were manipulated within-subjects, we determined that a sample of 100 participants would be sufficient to achieve adequate power.

Design—This experiment used a 2 (exposure idea accuracy: accurate or inaccurate) x 2 (test item accuracy: accurate or inaccurate) x 2 (username expertise: expert or non-expert) design with all variables manipulated within-subjects.

Materials—24 videos were adapted from text vignettes created by Salovich et al. 2023 and videos created by Holohan & Rapp, in prep. The vignettes contained information on various topics that were considered to be true or false based on an accumulation of evidence, and the health and wellness vignettes were selected to be made into short-form videos. A screenshot from one of the videos can be found in Appendix A. The vital information in each vignette was normed for the baseline rates, at which participants were able to correctly identify the accuracy of each statement. Results from the norming study showed that the accurate assertions were more likely to be determined to be as correct as compared to the inaccurate assertions. The script dialogues were used to develop and record short-form videos, including a single individual speaking about a topic (e. g., Vitamin C efficacy as a treatment for a cold) in a neutral setting.

Each video was between 29 and 46 seconds (M = 30.9 sec) in length. Two versions of each video were created with the same actor discussing the accurate version of the stimuli (e.g. “Vitamin C is an effective treatment for a cold”) and the inaccurate version of the stimuli (e.g. “Vitamin C is not an effective treatment for a cold”). Each video contained a simple caption to model those seen on short-form video platforms (“Vitamin C & Alleviating Cold Symptoms”).

Procedure

After providing consent, participants began the exposure phase of the study. Participants viewed 12 videos, one at a time, presented in a different random order for each participant. Half of the videos each participant viewed contained accurate information about various health and wellness topics, and half contained inaccurate information about the same topics. Half of the videos offered a tag that highlighted a source’s ostensible expertise in their username (e.g.,.

@Derm_Dr.Reith), and half of the videos included a non-expert username (e.g.,. @user124085).

Participants were required to watch each video in its entirety before a blue arrow popped up and allowed the participant to click and view the next video. After watching the videos, participants completed a mandatory 8-minute distractor task that consisted of simple math problems.

Participants were unable to advance until the eight minutes had passed, and they were automatically advanced regardless of their degree of completion of the task once eight minutes concluded/passed. Following the distractor task, participants began the judgement phase of the task. Participants read 18 statements, 12 of which were related to the content of the videos, while

6 filler statements were also presented. Statements were presented in random order to each participant. Participants were then asked to determine whether the statements provided were

“True” or “False,” then required to answer each statement before continuing onto the next statement. After the competition of the judgement task, participants were asked to complete a brief demographic questionnaire and were subsequently thanked and debriefed.

Results

Data analyses were run using logistic regression using generalized linear mixed effect models (GLMER) with the statistics R package (R Core Team, 2025). All factors were contrast coded. The model included the factors of Expertise (contrast coded: expert = -.5, non-expert =

.5), Exposure Accuracy (contrast coded: accurate = -.5, inaccurate = .5), and Test Condition

(contrast coded: accurate = -.5, inaccurate = .5), along with their interactions as fixed effects. The model also takes into account the random effect of the participants. Accuracy analyses were determined via the proportion of incorrect judgements yielded by each participant as a function of accuracy of the content at exposure and test. Incorrect judgements (contrast coded: correct =

0, incorrect = 1) included cases in which participants identified inaccurate test statements as true, and accurate statements as false. All means and standard deviations can be found in Figure 1.

We observed a main effect of exposure condition, b = 1.74, SE = .14, z = 11.92, p < .001.

In line with predictions, participants made more incorrect judgments after having been exposed to inaccurate information (M = .45, SD = .49 ), than after having been exposed to accurate information (M = .13, SD =.34).

We did not observe a main effect of the test condition, b = .08, SE = 0.14, z = 0.62, p =

0.53. This indicates that participants did not make a significantly different amount of incorrect judgments in the inaccurate test condition (M = .30, SD = .45) as compared to the accurate test condition (M =. 29, SD = . 45). Further, we found no significant main effect of expertise, b =

-.01, SE = .14, z = -.07, p = 0.94. This indicates that there was no difference in incorrect judgments after exposures to low expertise (M = .29 , SD=. 45) as compared to high expertise

(M = .30, SD = .45) usernames.

The analyses also revealed a marginal, three-way interaction between expertise, exposure condition, and test condition, b = 1.12, SE = 0.57, z = 1.95, p = .05. Follow-up analyses revealed that the interaction between exposure condition and test condition was reduced and inverted in the expertise condition, b = -0.96, SE = 0.44, z = -2.18, p = 0.02, as compared to in the no expertise condition, b = 1.72, SE = 0.20, z = 8.28, p < 0.001. These results indicate that, in the expertise condition, after participants were exposed to inaccurate information, they made more incorrect judgments when reading accurate test statements (M = .53, SD = .50) as compared to inaccurate test statements (M = .39, SD = .49). However, in the no expertise condition, after participants were exposed to inaccurate information, they made fewer incorrect judgments when reading accurate test statements (M = .40, SD = .49) as compared to inaccurate test statements

(M =.51, SD =.50). No other interactions were significant (All ps > .05).

Results from this study replicate previous work, that exposure to inaccurate information results in an increase in post exposure errors. Regardless of username expertise, participants were equally as likely to replicate inaccurate information from an expert (e.g.,.

@Derm_Dr.Reith) as the non-expert (e.g.,. @user124085). A marginal three-way interaction was found between expertise, exposure condition, and test condition, indicating that a combination of these factors result in increased participant’s replication of inaccurate information.

General Discussion ​ When participants were exposed to inaccurate health and wellness statements, they are more likely to produce errors at test. Expertise was a negligible factor in participants'

performance on judgement tasks, as participants replicated inaccuracies when shared by expert users (e.g.,. @Derm_Dr.Reith) and non-experts (e.g.,. @user124085) at similar rates. However, after exposure to inaccurate information, an engaging trend emerges. After viewing videos shared by an expert user, participants made more errors when judging accurate test statements as compared to inaccurate test statements, but after viewing videos with a non-expert username, participants made more errors when judging inaccurate test statements as compared to accurate test statements.

The proportion of errors after exposure to falsehoods in short-form videos replicated the typical misinformation exposure effect found in previous studies (Appel & Richter, 2007; Gerrig

& Prentice, 1991; Rapp, Hinze, Kohlhepp, et al., 2014; Salovich & Rapp, 2021, Loftus et al.,

1992;). This indicates that when participants are exposed to incorrect stimuli via short-form videos, they make more errors as compared to if they had been exposed to correct stimuli in the videos. Exposure to inaccuracies can cause confusion and foster doubts about previous knowledge, causing further reliance on inaccuracies (Rapp & Salovich, 2018). For example, when participants are exposed to a video stating that “microwave radiation causes cancer,” they may refer back to previously acquired knowledge and question if they have mis-remembered the previous knowledge or the knowledge’s utility (Rapp & Salovich, 2018). The assertions used to create the short-form videos in the current project were normed to ensure that participants had some prior knowledge of the claims. Despite this, participants continued to make errors after exposure to inaccuracies. These results are in line with previously reported literature, which indicates that, even when people have accurate prior knowledge to disregard inaccurate stimuli and respond with correct judgments, they still often continue to make errors (Ecker & Antonio,

2021, Anderson, J. R., 1981, Fazio, L. K., Barber, S. J., Rajaram, S., Ornstein, P. A., & Marsh, E.

J. 2013).

Previous work on the perceived credibility and expertise of sources suggested that source credibility has a significant impact on the extent to which information is encoded and relied upon. Information shared by sources deemed to be unreliable is less likely to be encoded and utilized to make decisions and solve problems than information deemed to be reliable (Andrews

& Rapp, 2014; Appel & Mara, 2013; Ecker & Antonio, 2021; Heinbach et al., 2018; Nadarevic et al., 2020; Walter & Tukachinsky, 2020). However, the results of the current project indicate that expertise had no effect on incorrect responses after exposure to inaccuracies in short-form videos. This indicates that inaccurate information was relied on similarly across sources of high-expertise and low-expertise. The results of the current study suggest that, unlike other forms of social media, credibility determined via username expertise for short-form videos may have little impact on the replication of misinformation. However, when further comparing the proportions of incorrect judgements by condition, an interesting pattern emerges. Within the expertise condition, when isolating solely for inaccurate exposure, we find that the proportion of incorrect judgements was higher when judging accurate test statements, as compared to inaccurate test statements. In the non-expertise condition, the proportion of incorrect judgments was higher when judging inaccurate test statements compared to accurate test statements. This reversal of trends may be a result of participants' willingness to use that information to combat accurate claims when expert knowledge is assumed, but when the information comes from a non-expert, they are more likely to only use the inaccuracies to support the same, inaccurate idea.

This pattern may be due to the exposure effect, where participants are unduly influenced by the inaccurate knowledge at exposure (Appel & Richter, 2007; Calvillo & Smelter, 2020; Rapp &

Salovich, 2018). It is also possible that in the non-expert condition, participants are more likely to defer to their own judgment and utilize prior knowledge rather than blindly believing the knowledge shared by non-expert online users (Toth et. al, 2011). Another potential explanation for this discrepancy is a lack of attention given to the username and source expertise by participants, which can be a source for future research.

There are several factors that could have influenced the results observed. The sample size

(n = 106) was used to replicate that of Salovich et al., (2022), which used similar methods to discover methods to reduce the influence of inaccurate statements; however, the limited sample size can influence results. Future research related to this study includes how expertise was represented in the videos. The claimed expertise of the short-form videos was presented in the version of a username (e.g.,. @Derm_Dr.Reith or e.g.,. @user124085) located directly above the video. Participants were instructed to pay attention to the username along with the content of the videos, however it is possible that participants did not pay attention to the username, and as a result, were unable to aptly encode the username along with the video. Future research could include the modulation of the font size and placement of the username, which may draw participants to place additional attention onto the expertise or lack thereof of the account’s user.

Under these conditions, it is possible that participants will pay increased attention to the usernames in relation to the videos, possibly resulting in an increased effect of expertise.

Further research can seek to understand expertise as expressed through visual cues other than username. Expertise can further be represented by the physical description of the person speaking (e.g. wearing a white coat) as well as the setting and background of the video (e.g.

framed degrees or bookshelves). Will these forms of visual expertise result in similar rates of inaccuracies as does the username? Further research can focus on understanding expertise through cues other than username as potentially fueling misinformation. These cues can take the form of the physical appearance of the individual speaking, an informational “bio” of the account and user, overall content themes (e.g. an account solely posting content about adolescent diabetes), or verbal claims of expertise. Alternative forms of expertise may impact the spread of health and wellness misinformation online and can be an area of future research.

Results from this study replicated the misinformation effects from previous research in the novel format of short-form videos commonly found on social media sites. A marginal three-way interaction was found between expertise, test condition, and exposure, indicating that a combination of these factors cause participants to produce errors. This is particularly alarming as users online are not required by the sites to verify any form of credibility (education, professional expertise, scientific basis for assertions, etc.), and it is the onus of the viewer to determine the credibility of those sharing health and wellness information online.

When isolating within the expertise condition and inaccurate exposure, we found that, when participants are exposed to inaccurate information shared by expert users, the proportion of incorrect judgements was higher when judging accurate test statements, as compared to inaccurate test statements. This may indicate that, after exposure to inaccurate expert statements, users online may use that information to deny accurate information shared later on. However, when exposed to non-expert inaccurate information, participants are more likely to replicate inaccurate information, as opposed to the accurate test statements.

title: Parenting with ADHD Symptoms: Investigating Warmth, Discipline, and Their Impact on Children with ADHD Symptoms
abstract:
Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by persistent inattention and/or hyperactivity, often emerging in early childhood and impacting social, emotional, and academic development. Given the high heritability of ADHD, many parents – particularly mothers – of affected children also exhibit symptoms that may, in turn, influence their parenting behaviors. This study examined associations between maternal ADHD symptoms, parenting behaviors, and child behavioral outcomes. Eighty-eight mothers of children aged 4-6 were recruited via Prolific and completed the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS), the Comprehensive Early Childhood Parenting Questionnaire (CECPAQ), and the Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL). Results indicated that although more boys (67.5%) than girls (44.7%) were diagnosed with ADHD, symptom severity did not significantly differ by gender. Children diagnosed with ADHD showed significantly higher internalizing behaviors, t(87)=2.22, p=.029, but not externalizing behaviors. Maternal inattention was significantly associated with greater use of negative discipline, r(87)=.29, p=.01, though no meaningful associations emerged with warmth or positive discipline. Additionally, positive discipline was negatively correlated with children’s internalizing behaviors, r(87)=-.27, p=.01.

Findings suggest that maternal ADHD symptoms, particularly inattention, are linked to greater use of negative discipline, which may contribute to child behavioral difficulties. The gender gap in diagnoses, despite comparable symptom severity, further highlights potential diagnostic biases. The use of a community, rather than clinical, sample may have influenced parent-reported data and should be considered in future research.
text:
Parenting with ADHD Symptoms:​

Investigating Warmth, Discipline, and Their Impact on Children with ADHD Symptoms

Samantha Hesekiel

Northwestern University, Department of Psychology

Advisor: Alissa Levy Chung, Ph.D., Department of Psychology

Abstract

Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by persistent inattention and/or hyperactivity, often emerging in early childhood and impacting social, emotional, and academic development. Given the high heritability of

ADHD, many parents – particularly mothers – of affected children also exhibit symptoms that may, in turn, influence their parenting behaviors. This study examined associations between maternal ADHD symptoms, parenting behaviors, and child behavioral outcomes. Eighty-eight mothers of children aged 4-6 were recruited via Prolific and completed the Adult ADHD

Self-Report Scale (ASRS), the Comprehensive Early Childhood Parenting Questionnaire

(CECPAQ), and the Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL). Results indicated that although more boys (67.5%) than girls (44.7%) were diagnosed with ADHD, symptom severity did not significantly differ by gender. Children diagnosed with ADHD showed significantly higher internalizing behaviors, t(87)=2.22, p=.029, but not externalizing behaviors. Maternal inattention was significantly associated with greater use of negative discipline, r(87)=.29, p=.01, though no meaningful associations emerged with warmth or positive discipline. Additionally, positive discipline was negatively correlated with children’s internalizing behaviors, r(87)=-.27, p=.01.

Findings suggest that maternal ADHD symptoms, particularly inattention, are linked to greater use of negative discipline, which may contribute to child behavioral difficulties. The gender gap in diagnoses, despite comparable symptom severity, further highlights potential diagnostic biases. The use of a community, rather than clinical, sample may have influenced parent-reported data and should be considered in future research.

Hesekiel, 1

Introduction

In 2022, an estimated seven million U.S. children aged 3-17 were diagnosed with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), marking an increase of one million diagnoses since 2016.1 ADHD is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by persistent patterns of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity that interfere with daily functioning.2

While many children outgrow some symptoms, untreated ADHD often persists into adolescence and adulthood, making early recognition and intervention crucial.3 However, diagnosing ADHD in young children is challenging because behaviors like high activity levels are often typical for this age.4 This overlap requires a careful, nuanced approach to diagnosis.

Parenting Children with ADHD

Raising a child with ADHD presents unique challenges related to emotion regulation, attention, and behavioral control. Managing these behaviors can be overwhelming for parents, often draining their emotional resources5 and causing elevated stress. 6 In many cases, this elevated stress increases the likelihood of harsher and more reactive disciplinary practices as well, which not only fail to improve behavior but also weaken parent-child relations.7

7 Alizadeh, H., Applequist, K. F., & Coolidge, F. L. (2007). Parental self-confidence, parenting styles, and corporal punishment in families of ADHD children in Iran. Child Abuse & Neglect, 31(5), 567–572. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chiabu.2006.12.005

6 Lunkenheimer, E., Lichtwarck-Aschoff, A., Hollenstein, T., Kemp, C. J., & Granic, I. (2016). Breaking down the coercive cycle: How parent and child risk factors influence real-time variability in parental responses to child misbehavior. Parenting, Science and Practice, 16(4), 237. https://doi.org/10.1080/15295192.2016.1184925

5 Alizadeh, H., Applequist, K. F., & Coolidge, F. L. (2007). Parental self-confidence, parenting styles, and corporal punishment in families of ADHD children in Iran. Child Abuse & Neglect, 31(5), 567–572. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chiabu.2006.12.005

4 Egger, H. L., Kondo, D., & Angold, A. (2006). The epidemiology and diagnostic issues in preschool attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: A review. Infants & Young Children, 19(2), 109–122. https://doi.org/10.1097/00001163-200604000-00004

3 Lahey, B. B., Lee, S. S., Sibley, M. H., Applegate, B., Molina, B. S. G., & Pelham, W. E. (2016). Predictors of adolescent outcomes among 4–6-year-old children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. Journal of Abnormal Psychology, 125(2), 168–181. https://doi.org/10.1037/abn0000086

2 National Institute of Mental Health (n.d.). Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder. https://www.nimh.nih.gov/health/topics/attention-deficit-hyperactivity-disorder-adhd

1 Center for Disease Control and Prevention. (2024b, October 23). Data and Statistics on ADHD. https://www.cdc.gov/adhd/data/index.html

Hesekiel, 2

It is important to identify effective ways to support children with ADHD and co-occurring conditions. This requires a deep understanding of parenting strategies that combine emotional support with appropriate behavioral guidance. Evidence-based approaches tailored to the child’s unique needs are essential for fostering healthier parent-child interactions and improving long-term behavioral outcomes.

Warmth and Discipline in Parenting

Parenting research highlights two key dimensions linked to child development:  warmth

(referred to as support in this study) and discipline. Warmth involves acceptance, nurturance, and positive reinforcement, while discipline encompasses strategies parents use to guide and manage their child’s behavior.8 Though distinct, both techniques can coexist within an authoritative parenting style that balances emotional security with behavioral control.9

This balance is particularly important for children with ADHD, who often struggle with self-regulation and attention control. However, the stress of managing ADHD-related behaviors makes it difficult for parents to sustain this warmth and consistency.10 As a result, parenting may tilt toward a more controlling approach, often at the expense of support.

Impact of Parental Discipline

​ Not all forms of discipline affect children equally. Harsh or punitive approaches often intensify behavioral problems rather than reduce them. Patterson’s research demonstrated that coercive parent–child interactions can reinforce externalizing behaviors such as aggression and

10 Alizadeh, H., Applequist, K. F., & Coolidge, F. L. (2007). Parental self-confidence, parenting styles, and corporal punishment in families of ADHD children in Iran. Child Abuse & Neglect, 31(5), 567–572. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chiabu.2006.12.005

9 Garcia, O. F., Fuentes, M. C., Gracia, E., Serra, E., & Garcia, F. (2020). Parenting warmth and strictness across three generations: Parenting styles and psychosocial adjustment. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, 17(20), Article 20. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph17207487

8 Parmar, P., & Nathans, L. (2022). Parental warmth and parent involvement: Their relationships to academic achievement and behavior problems in school and related gender effects. Societies, 12(6), Article 6. https://doi.org/10.3390/soc12060161

Hesekiel, 3 defiance.11 When a child stops misbehaving after harsh discipline, the parent’s response is inadvertently reinforced, perpetuating a negative cycle.

Children with behavioral or emotional challenges are especially vulnerable to these dynamics. Those with ADHD, who already struggle with emotion regulation, may react more strongly to harsh discipline and escalate conflict instead of learning self-control.12 Consequently, punitive discipline can worsen defiance and strain relationships.

Impact of Warmth

While discipline supports behavior management, it must be balanced with emotional support to be effective. Discipline without warmth often neglects children’s emotional needs, which are central to healthy family dynamics.13 Research indicates that parental warmth, more than discipline alone, has a stronger effect on improving behavioral outcomes.14

For children with ADHD, warmth plays a critical role. Research shows that higher parental warmth at age five predicted fewer ADHD symptoms at age nine.15 Additionally, early symptoms predicted reduced parental warmth later on. This bidirectional relationship shows how warmth can buffer symptoms but may also decline as behaviors worsen. Overall, emotional support addresses both immediate behavioral challenges and fosters improved well-being.

Parental Mental Health

15 Shelleby, E. C., & Ogg, J. (2020). Longitudinal relationships between parent involvement, parental warmth, ADHD symptoms, and reading achievement. Journal of Attention Disorders, 24(5), 737–749. https://doi.org/10.1177/1087054719859075

14 Neppl, T. K., Conger, R. D., Schofield, T. J., & Donnellan, M. B. (2021). The influence of parental warmth and harsh discipline on child behavior: A longitudinal study. Journal of Family Psychology, 35(4), 450–460. https://doi.org/10.1037/fam0000812

13 Kirby, J. N. (2017). Compassion-focused parenting. In E. M. Seppälä, E. Simon-Thomas, S. L. Brown, M. C. Worline, C. D. Cameron, & J. R. Doty (Eds.), The Oxford handbook of compassion science (pp. 129–140). Oxford University Press. https://doi.org/10.1093/oxfordhb/9780190464684.013.8

12 Barkley, R. A., & Murphy, K. R. (2006). Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder: A clinical workbook (3rd ed.). The Guilford Press.

11 Patterson, G. R. (1982). A social learning approach: Volume 3 coercive family process. Multivariate Experimental Clinical Research, 3(3).

Hesekiel, 4

As previously discussed, parenting a child with ADHD often leads to elevated stress levels, disrupting a parent’s ability to remain consistent and emotionally available. These challenges are often compounded when parents themselves experience ADHD symptoms, which is common given the disorder’s high heritability. Approximately one-third to one-fourth of parents of children with ADHD meet diagnostic criteria themselves.16 Parental ADHD symptoms—particularly inattention, impulsivity, and emotional dysregulation—can impair executive functioning, leading to inconsistent discipline and reduced warmth toward the child.17

Parental ADHD Symptoms and Parenting

Parental ADHD symptoms can further complicate the balance between support and discipline. Maternal hyperactivity has been linked to lower levels of emotional support, as impulsive and emotionally reactive behaviors can interfere with maintaining a nurturing attitude.

18 In contrast, maternal inattention is more closely associated with difficulties in enforcing structured discipline.19 Challenges with focus, organization, and inhibitory control make it harder to plan and apply consistent rules, leading to inconsistent parenting.

Current Study

19 Friedman, L. M., Dvorsky, M. R., McBurnett, K., & Pfiffner, L. J. (2020). Do parents’ ADHD symptoms affect treatment for their children? The impact of parental ADHD on adherence to behavioral parent training for childhood ADHD. Journal of Abnormal Child Psychology, 48(11), 1425–1437. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10802-020-00672-1

18 Miklósi, M., Kovács, B., Janovicz, J., Lelki, F., & Kassai, R. (2024). Adult attention-deficit/hyperactivity symptoms and parental cognitions: A meta-analysis. Frontiers in Psychiatry, 14. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyt.2023.1321078

17 Breaux, R. P., Brown, H. R., & Harvey, E. A. (2017). Mediators and moderators of the relation between parental ADHD symptomatology and the early development of child ADHD and ODD symptoms. Journal of Abnormal Child Psychology, 45(3), 443–456. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10802-016-0213-1

16 Chronis-Tuscano, A., Wang, C. H., Woods, K. E., Strickland, J., & Stein, M. A. (2017). Parent ADHD and evidence-based treatment for their children: Review and directions for future research. Journal of Abnormal Child Psychology, 45(3), 501–517. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10802-016-0238-5

Hesekiel, 5

This study focused on primary caregivers, recognizing that mothers are most often in this role.20 Therefore, mothers of preschool-aged children were recruited to examine how maternal

ADHD symptoms relate to parenting behaviors. Additionally, parental ADHD symptoms were measured dimensionally rather than categorically to capture subclinical traits that are undiagnosed but may still affect parenting. This approach also accounts for the underdiagnosis of women.21

Overall, the study explored links between maternal impulsivity and parental support, and between maternal inattention and parental discipline, both in relation to children’s ADHD symptoms. These focuses contributed to my primary research question: How do parental ADHD symptoms (impulsivity vs. inattention) relate to both parenting behaviors and behavioral outcomes in children with ADHD?

​ After investigating past research, I established three main hypotheses regarding the relationship between parental ADHD symptoms, parenting styles, and child behavior outcomes.

1.​ Higher maternal impulsivity will be associated with lower parental support scores.

2.​ Higher maternal inattention will be associated with lower positive discipline scores and higher negative discipline scores.

3.​ Children of more impulsive mothers will display more behavioral difficulties, as impulsivity is tied to lower parental warmth, a key factor in positive outcomes.

Methods

Participants

21 Attoe, D. E., & Climie, E. A. (2023). Miss. diagnosis: A systematic review of ADHD in adult women. Journal of Attention Disorders, 27(7), 645–657. https://doi.org/10.1177/10870547231161533

20 Zimmermann, P., Mühling, L. E., Lichtenstein, L., & Iwanski, A. (2022). Still mother after all these years: Infants still prefer mothers over fathers (if they have the choice). Social Sciences, 11(2), Article 2. https://doi.org/10.3390/socsci11020051

Hesekiel, 6

Eligibility was described to participating mothers as those who had “a child between the ages of 4 and 6 years old who presents with behaviors consistent with ADHD.” The study focused on parent-reported symptoms rather than clinical diagnoses, given that these young children likely have not yet received an official diagnosis. Prolific was used to recruit individuals who met the specific eligibility criteria for this study.

Demographics

I recruited 88 participants, with an average age of 36.7 (SD = 10.5) and an age range of

22 to 77. It is important to note that the older participants, aged 73 and 77, may have been biological mothers, but rather assumed the maternal role in the lives of the children. Additional maternal demographics are included in Table 1.

The average age of children in the study was 5.0 years (SD = 0.72). The gender breakdown was 53.4% female (n=57) and 45.5% male (n=40), with one participant missing gender data. Regarding ADHD diagnoses, 54.5% (n=48) of the children were diagnosed with

ADHD, 44.3% (n=39) were not diagnosed, and one data point was missing.

Measures

Child Behavior Checklist

The Child Behavior Checklist is a caregiver-report tool designed to assess behavioral and emotional problems in children aged 1.5 to 5 years.22 It includes 99 items across subscales grouped into internalizing, externalizing, and other problem domains, with T-scores indicating borderline (65-69) and clinical (≥70) levels (see Table 2). The CBCL demonstrates strong reliability, with all subscales showing internal consistency alphas above 0.70 and good test-retest reliability over one week.

22 Naar-King, S., Ellis, D. A., & Frey, M. A. (2004). Child behavior. In S. Naar-King, D. A. Ellis, & M. A. Frey (Eds.), Assessing children’s well-being: A handbook of measures (pp. 123–145). Lawrence Erlbaum Associates Publishers.

Hesekiel, 7

Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale

Parental ADHD symptoms were self-reported using the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale

(ASRS v1.1), a validated 18-item screening tool developed by the WHO.23 The ASRS has two subscales—inattention (10 items) and hyperactivity (8 items)—with questions rated on a 5-point

Likert scale from “Never” to “Very Often.” The inattention subscale assesses difficulties with organization and focus, while the hyperactivity subscale addresses restlessness and impulsivity.

Scores range up to 36 per subscale, with scores above 24 generally considered clinically elevated.24 The ASRS also demonstrates high test-retest reliability among adults.

Comprehensive Early Childhood Parenting Questionnaire (CECPAQ)

The Comprehensive Early Childhood Parenting Questionnaire (CECPAQ) assesses parenting behaviors focusing on five domains: support, stimulation, structure, positive discipline, and harsh discipline. This study used 29 items covering support, positive discipline, and negative discipline, rated on a 6-point Likert scale. The subscales measure warmth and nurturing

(support), proactive strategies (positive discipline), and punitive responses(negative discipline).

The CECPAQ demonstrated good reliability, with Cronbach’s alphas of .88, .76, and .79 for support, positive discipline, and negative discipline, respectively.25

Procedures

Qualtrics Survey

25 Verhoeven, M., Deković, M., Bodden, D., & Van Baar, A. L. (2017). Development and initial validation of the comprehensive early childhood parenting questionnaire (CECPAQ) for parents of 1–4 year-olds. European Journal of Developmental Psychology, 14(2), 233–247. https://doi.org/10.1080/17405629.2016.1182017

24 Corbisiero, S., Hartmann-Schorro, R. M., Riecher-Rössler, A., & Stieglitz, R.-D. (2017). Screening for adult attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder in a psychiatric outpatient population with specific focus on sex differences. Frontiers in Psychiatry, 8, 115. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyt.2017.00115

23 Silverstein, M. J., Alperin, S., Faraone, S. V., Kessler, R. C., & Adler, L. A. (2018). Test–retest reliability of the adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS) v1.1 screener in non-ADHD controls from a primary care physician practice. Family Practice, 35(3), 336–341. https://doi.org/10.1093/fampra/cmx115

Hesekiel, 8

The survey on Prolific was distributed via Qualtrics, another online survey tool. To ensure consistency and reduce response biases, the survey was designed to prevent participants from skipping questions or moving backward to previous sections. On average, it took approximately 15 to 20 minutes to complete the survey. The structure of the survey began with a demographics section, followed by the CBCL, ASRS, and CECPAQ. Informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to their involvement in the study.

Results

Child ADHD Data

Gender and ADHD Diagnoses

A chi-squared test of independence revealed a significant association between gender and

ADHD diagnosis status (breakdown provided in Table 3). The analysis yielded a statistically significant result: χ²(1, N=47)=4.55, p = .033. This suggests a significant association between gender and ADHD diagnosis status, with a greater proportion of male children diagnosed

(67.5%) compared to female children (44.7%). However, female and male children did not differ significantly in the severity of symptoms they exhibited. For internalizing behaviors, t(87)=-1.72, p=.089, and for externalizing behaviors, t(87)=-0.58, p=.564 (breakdown provided in Table 4).

Internalizing vs. Externalizing Across Diagnoses

​ I also examined the differences in internalizing and externalizing behaviors across diagnostic groups, shown in Table 5. Independent samples t-tests revealed that children diagnosed with ADHD had significantly higher levels of internalizing behaviors than children who were not diagnosed, t(87)=2.22, p=.029. There was no significant difference in externalizing behaviors, t(87)=-0.06, p=.952. It is interesting to note that there was no significant difference in attention problems between the two groups, t(87)=-1.38, p= .170, despite being a core symptom.

Hesekiel, 9

Interaction with Maternal Diagnoses

I also conducted a chi-squared test of independence to explore the relationship between maternal and child ADHD diagnoses (breakdown shown in Table 6). The analysis did not yield a statistically significant result: χ²(1, N=86)=1.01, p = .315, suggesting that there was no meaningful association between parental ADHD diagnosis and their children’s diagnosis.

Maternal Data

​ After analyzing the children’s data, I examined the mothers’ characteristics. Table 7 shows descriptive statistics for mothers’ ADHD symptoms and parenting styles. Mothers exhibited clinically significant inattention but subclinical hyperactivity. Parenting styles, measured by CECPAQ (max score 6), revealed high warmth and positive discipline scores, with relatively low negative discipline scores.

ADHD Symptoms

​ Before exploring the links between ADHD symptoms and parenting, it’s important to note that hyperactivity and inattention were strongly positively correlated (Table 8). This means mothers with higher hyperactivity also tended to report higher inattention, explaining that parenting behaviors may not be fully independent.

Parental Hyperactivity. Contrary to my hypothesis, hyperactivity was not significantly related to parental warmth but was positively correlated with negative discipline. However, hyperactivity was positively correlated with negative discipline.

Parental Inattention. I expected a negative relationship between discipline and inattention overall, assuming that greater levels of inattention would be associated with lower levels of effective discipline. This was correct in the sense that there was a positive correlation

Hesekiel, 10 between inattention and negative discipline. However, there was no association between inattention and positive discipline or warmth.

Associations Between Parenting Style Dimensions. Parental support was negatively correlated with negative discipline. In contrast, parental warmth was positively correlated with positive discipline.

Child Behavior Outcomes

​ I also conducted Pearson correlations between parenting strategies and child behavior outcomes (Table 9), which suggested that maternal ADHD symptoms of inattention and hyperactivity are positively related to externalizing behaviors, including sleep problems and attention problems, but excluding aggressive behavior. However, they are not correlated with internalizing problems.

Parenting Style

After linking parental ADHD symptoms to parenting strategies, the next set of analyses explored how specific parenting strategies were linked to child behavioral outcomes. There was a negative relationship between positive discipline in parents and internalizing behaviors in children (displayed in Table 10), meaning higher use of positive discipline was related to fewer internalizing symptoms. Interestingly, positive discipline was only negatively correlated with some facets of internalizing behavior but not others (displayed in Table 11).

Discussion

Overview of Findings

​ This study examined associations among maternal ADHD symptoms, parenting styles, and preschool-aged children’s behavioral outcomes. Maternal inattention and hyperactivity were linked to greater use of negative discipline, but not to warmth or positive discipline. Positive

Hesekiel, 11 discipline was negatively related to children’s internalizing behaviors, suggesting that parenting approaches may shape emotional adjustment—or that parents may respond more positively to children with internalizing symptoms.

Children with ADHD showed higher internalizing symptoms than those without a diagnosis, though no differences emerged in externalizing behaviors or attention problems.

Males were more likely than females to be diagnosed with ADHD despite similar symptom severity, indicating possible gender-related diagnostic differences. Although many mothers reported ADHD diagnoses or elevated symptoms, maternal and child diagnoses were not significantly related.

Child ADHD Symptoms

​ Gender Discrepancy. Although existing literature suggests that boys are diagnosed with

ADHD more frequently than girls, I found that there were no significant gender differences in actual behavior scores.26 Interestingly, despite this sample including more female children than males, males still had a significantly higher rate of diagnoses. This difference highlights a potential gender bias in diagnostic practices, in that both genders displayed the same levels of behavioral difficulties, yet boys were still more frequently diagnosed.

​ Another important factor to consider is the age of the children in this sample. Many preschool-aged children may not have received a formal diagnosis yet, despite the potential to receive one later in life. Some children, especially girls, may be diagnosed later in life, which could contribute to the lower rate of diagnoses observed among females at this stage. Literature supports this, suggesting that the males are, on average, 1.7 years younger than females when

26 Center for Disease Control and Prevention. (2024b, October 23). Data and Statistics on ADHD. https://www.cdc.gov/adhd/data/index.html

Hesekiel, 12 they receive their ADHD diagnosis.27 This later diagnosis in females can result in later treatment and, as a result, more severe outcomes.

These findings highlight that ADHD symptoms may be more similar across genders than previously assumed, yet diagnostic patterns suggest a gender bias in identification and referral.

Greater awareness of how ADHD presents in girls is essential to reduce underdiagnosis and ensure timely support.

Diagnosed vs. Undiagnosed Children. In line with previous studies, children diagnosed with ADHD in this study exhibited high levels of internalizing behaviors, such as anxiety, depression, and somatic complaints.28 These align with the expectation that emotional dysregulation often occurs alongside ADHD. Interestingly, however, children diagnosed with

ADHD did not differ from their undiagnosed peers in terms of externalizing behaviors, which are core symptoms of ADHD as well.29 This result contrasts with the widely accepted view that

ADHD is primarily characterized by externalizing behaviors. Instead, the findings propose the idea that emotional and internal struggles may play a larger role in how ADHD is experienced early on.

Heritability. Another surprising finding was the lack of a significant relationship between parental and child ADHD diagnoses. Children of diagnosed parents were not more likely to have ADHD, though this measure reflects only diagnosed cases and may overlook undiagnosed symptoms. This limitation, along with the children’s young age and the use of

29 Center for Disease Control and Prevention. (2024a, October 7). Diagnosing ADHD. https://www.cdc.gov/adhd/diagnosis/index.html

28 Lahey, B. B., Lee, S. S., Sibley, M. H., Applegate, B., Molina, B. S. G., & Pelham, W. E. (2016). Predictors of adolescent outcomes among 4–6-year-old children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. Journal of Abnormal Psychology, 125(2), 168–181. https://doi.org/10.1037/abn0000086

27 Martin, J., Langley, K., Cooper, M., Rouquette, O. Y., John, A., Sayal, K., Ford, T., & Thapar, A. (2023). Sex Differences in ADHD Diagnosis and Clinical Care: A National Study of Population Healthcare Records in Wales. https://doi.org/10.1101/2023.10.20.23297324

Hesekiel, 13 maternal data only, may explain the discrepancy from prior research highlighting the genetic transmission of ADHD.

Maternal Data

​ ADHD Symptoms. The parent self-report data provided further insight into both ADHD symptoms and parenting styles within this sample. Notably, mothers in this group reported average inattention scores that exceeded the clinical cutoff, suggesting that these participants did experience deficits in attention. However, the same was not true for hyperactivity, being that this number did not exceed the clinical cutoff. Even so, both parental inattention and hyperactivity interacted significantly with parenting style and child behavior outcomes in various ways.

​ It is important to first highlight the correlation observed between the inattention and hyperactivity subscales of ADHD in this sample. Mothers who scored high in hyperactivity also tended to score high in inattention. This relationship between inattention and hyperactivity in adults might actually be causal, with inattention potentially driving hyperactive behaviors.30 This perspective is particularly relevant to the current study, as it suggests that the observed parenting challenges may be more strongly linked to the overall ADHD symptom profile.

​ An alternative explanation points to the progression of ADHD across the lifespan.31 Their research outlines how hyperactivity is common in children with ADHD but tends to decrease significantly as they grow older. However, while hyperactivity decreases, inattention often persists into adulthood, manifesting in various ways. These symptoms, especially those relating to executive functioning, can have a significant impact on parenting techniques and child outcomes, as pointed out in this study.

31 Barkley, R. A., & Murphy, K. R. (2006). Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder: A clinical workbook (3rd ed.). The Guilford Press.

30 Sokolova, E., Groot, P., Claassen, T., Van Hulzen, K. J., Glennon, J. C., Franke, B., Heskes, T., & Buitelaar, J. (2016). Statistical evidence suggests that inattention drives hyperactivity/impulsivity in attention deficit-hyperactivity disorder. PLOS ONE, 11(10), e0165120. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0165120

Hesekiel, 14

​ Parenting Style. In terms of parenting styles, warmth and positive discipline were commonly reported, whereas negative discipline appeared less frequently. These findings were somewhat surprising given the high inattention scores, which previous research has linked to increased parenting stress and less consistent parenting behaviors.32

Interaction Between Parental ADHD Symptoms and Parenting Style

​ A negative association was hypothesized between maternal hyperactivity and parental warmth, but this was not supported. Similarly, although maternal inattention was not related to positive discipline, it was significantly associated with greater use of negative discipline. This suggests that mothers with higher inattention may engage in harsher or more reactive parenting, possibly due to emotional regulation or planning difficulties.

​ Maternal hyperactivity was also correlated with negative discipline. Given the strong correlation between inattention and hyperactivity, it is possible that the presence of ADHD symptoms more broadly – rather than any single subtype – contributes to increased use of negative discipline. This larger pattern suggests that negative discipline may be a common behavioral outcome among parents experiencing elevated ADHD symptoms.

​ Further supporting these findings, associations between the two parenting style dimensions revealed that parental support was negatively correlated with negative discipline and positively correlated with positive discipline. These results suggest that parenting behaviors tend to cluster in predictable ways: parents who are warmer and more supportive tend to use constructive discipline strategies. In contrast, parents experiencing greater challenges, such as

32 Chronis, A. M., Chacko, A., Fabiano, G. A., Wymbs, B. T., & Pelham, Jr., W. E. (2004). Enhancements to the behavioral parent training paradigm for families of children with ADHD: review and future directions. Clinical Child and Family Psychology Review, 7(1), 1–27. https://doi.org/10.1023/B:CCFP.0000020190.60808.a4

Hesekiel, 15 those associated with ADHD, may find it more challenging to sustain this support and instead rely heavily on negative discipline and other, less constructive strategies.

Interaction Between Parental ADHD Symptoms and Child Behavior Outcome

My final hypothesis predicted a relationship between maternal hyperactivity and behavioral deficits in the sample of children. However, because inattention and hyperactivity ended up being correlated with one another, this hypothesis was more challenging to test.

Instead, it may be more informative to consider the broader impact of elevated parental ADHD symptoms on child outcomes.

​ Across the board, both inattention and hyperactivity were significantly associated with child externalizing behaviors but not internalizing behaviors. These findings suggest that elevated ADHD symptoms in parents—regardless of the subtype—may contribute to increased overt behaviors in children. Although the correlation with aggressive behavior did not reach statistical significance, sleep problems and attention difficulties showed significant relationships, indicating that these issues are still meaningfully associated with parental ADHD symptoms.

​ Research indicates that internalizing disorders like anxiety and depression show lower heritability than externalizing disorders, which may explain the stronger link between parental

ADHD symptoms and children’s externalizing behaviors. Specifically, heritability is estimated at

49% for anxiety and 53% for major depression.33 These differences suggest that genetic factors may play a larger role in externalizing outcomes, underscoring the importance of targeted interventions for children of parents with ADHD.

Interaction Between Parenting Style and Child Behavior Outcome

33 Guffanti, G., Gameroff, M. J., Warner, V., Talati, A., Glatt, C. E., Wickramaratne, P., & Weissman, M. M. (2016). Heritability of major depressive and comorbid anxiety disorders in multi‐generational families at high risk for depression. American Journal of Medical Genetics Part B: Neuropsychiatric Genetics, 171(8), 1072–1079. https://doi.org/10.1002/ajmg.b.32477

Hesekiel, 16

Unlike the correlations with parental ADHD symptoms – which were strongly linked to externalizing behaviors – the associations with parenting style were more related to internalizing behaviors. Specifically, there was a negative relationship between parents who reported higher levels of positive discipline and internalizing behaviors in children. This suggests that supportive, nurturing discipline strategies may serve as a protective factor against internal emotional difficulties in children.

Further analysis showed that positive discipline was negatively correlated with certain internalizing subscales, including somatic complaints and withdrawn behaviors, but not with emotional reactivity or anxious/depressed behaviors. This is noteworthy given that emotional reactivity is often viewed as a core feature of ADHD, reflecting impulsive or intense emotional responses. Its lack of association with positive discipline may indicate that emotional reactivity is less influenced by parenting practices alone and may require more structured interventions.

Moreover, emotional reactivity may be more heavily influenced by genetic factors than other internalizing symptoms. Some children may be more biologically sensitive to stress and other emotional challenges.34 These children might exhibit more intense emotional responses even in relatively mild situations, explaining why the positive discipline strategies used by the parents in this study did not significantly correlate. Similarly, the lack of significant correlation between positive discipline and anxious/depressed behaviors suggests that these symptoms also may not be as easily mitigated through parenting practices alone.

​ This finding also highlights the nuanced ways that child behavior interacts with parenting practices. While positive discipline may effectively fight against certain internalizing symptoms, it may not be sufficient to address others. Alternatively, there may be a bidirectional relationship

34 Barzman, D. (2015). Review of the genetic basis of emotion dysregulation in children and adolescents. World Journal of Psychiatry, 5(1), 112. https://doi.org/10.5498/wjp.v5.i1.112

Hesekiel, 17 here, with parents using gentler discipline with children who present in more vulnerable ways.

Understanding these distinctions is critical for targeting interventions for these children.

Limitations

​ While this study provides valuable insight into the links between maternal ADHD symptoms, parenting styles, and child outcomes, several limitations should be noted. First, the reliance on self-report measures may have introduced response bias. Additionally, the use of a community rather than a clinical sample means that not all children had formal diagnoses, and some symptoms may not have reached clinical levels. Nonetheless, many mothers reported elevated internalizing symptoms, suggesting that community-based parents can still be highly attuned to their children’s difficulties—though this may reflect the characteristics of parents who chose to participate in the study. Future studies would benefit from using more observational methods and potentially recruiting clinical samples to better understand the complex interactions between parents and children experiencing ADHD.

Conclusion ​

Overall, this study aims to deepen our understanding of the complex effects that maternal

ADHD symptoms may have on parenting behaviors, particularly regarding warmth and discipline in mothers of preschool-aged children diagnosed with ADHD. The findings revealed that maternal ADHD symptoms, especially inattention and hyperactivity, are significantly linked to negative parenting practices such as increased use of negative discipline. However, positive parenting strategies, particularly positive discipline, were found to be protective against internalizing behaviors in children, highlighting the potential benefits of supportive parenting.

Hesekiel, 18

In light of these findings, the study calls for more tailored interventions to address the specific needs of children with ADHD and their families. Understanding the distinct ways that parental ADHD symptoms and parenting styles interact with child behavior outcomes can provide critical insights for clinical practices in the future.

title: The Kids Are Alright: College Environments, Student Wellbeing, and the Role of Institutional Selectivity
abstract:
According to previous research, Generation Z undergraduate students, or students born between 1997 and 2012, are experiencing unprecedented high levels of anxiety. Another study investigated whether anxiety is more strongly predicted by undergraduate students’ cognition and thought processes (internal factors) or the university environment (external factors), and whether these factors play an equal role. Defined as highly ranked universities with low acceptance rates, elite institutions may bolster anxiety levels due to the perceived environment, as suggested by Role Strain Theory. Alternatively, anxious students may be self-selecting into elite universities, as those with a high need for achievement and high avoidance goals experience more anxiety.

Participants within this study were undergraduate students who attended a wide range of institutions, each with varying degrees of selectivity. They completed measures of anxiety (state-trait, general), internal factors (goal orientation, fear of failure, and achievement motivation), and external factors (class and professor perceptions). Results suggested that internal factors, specifically fear of failure, were the strongest predictor of anxiety compared to external factors. There were no significant differences between selective, moderately selective, and less selective schools in overall anxiety when compared across three groups, but students at the most selective schools were surprisingly less anxious than students enrolled in moderate and less selective schools when those groups were combined. Altogether, the findings suggested that internal factors – goal orientation, fear of failure, and achievement motivation – are the largest determinants of undergraduate anxiety, compared to institutional selectivity and environmental perceptions.
text:
The Kids Are Alright:

College Environments, Student Wellbeing, and the Role of Institutional Selectivity

Olivia Lauri

Northwestern University, Department of Psychology

Alissa Levy Chung

Primary Advisor

Ben Gorvine

Second Reader

Final Honors Thesis

May 5, 2025

Abstract

According to previous research, Generation Z undergraduate students, or students born between 1997 and 2012, are experiencing unprecedented high levels of anxiety. Another study investigated whether anxiety is more strongly predicted by undergraduate students’ cognition and thought processes (internal factors) or the university environment (external factors), and whether these factors play an equal role. Defined as highly ranked universities with low acceptance rates, elite institutions may bolster anxiety levels due to the perceived environment, as suggested by

Role Strain Theory. Alternatively, anxious students may be self-selecting into elite universities, as those with a high need for achievement and high avoidance goals experience more anxiety.

Participants within this study were undergraduate students who attended a wide range of institutions, each with varying degrees of selectivity. They completed measures of anxiety

(state-trait, general), internal factors (goal orientation, fear of failure, and achievement motivation), and external factors (class and professor perceptions). Results suggested that internal factors, specifically fear of failure, were the strongest predictor of anxiety compared to external factors. There were no significant differences between selective, moderately selective, and less selective schools in overall anxiety when compared across three groups, but students at the most selective schools were surprisingly less anxious than students enrolled in moderate and less selective schools when those groups were combined. Altogether, the findings suggested that internal factors – goal orientation, fear of failure, and achievement motivation – are the largest determinants of undergraduate anxiety, compared to institutional selectivity and environmental perceptions.

The Rise of Anxiety in Generation Z Undergraduates

For Generation Z, born between 1997 and 2012, anxiety is rising in prevalence, especially in comparison to older generations, but why? Is the current generation of undergraduate students innately more prone to anxiety? Is higher education causing higher levels of mental distress? As prestigious universities become more selective and sought after,1 is there a difference in the impact between elite and non-elite institutions on student anxiety? Existing research postulates that the rise in anxiety could be due to a myriad of factors, such as

COVID-19, increased screen usage, or an overall generational difference due to more judgment and societal expectations.2,3,4 As the current socioeconomic environment presents new challenges that were not prevalent or even present before, Generation Z has been forced to grapple with contemporary stressors that shape their current world, increasing anxiety levels overall.

Similarly, today’s undergraduate students are widely known as being the most anxious to date, raising concern on a global scale. Recent mental health studies revealed that one-third of undergraduate students are suffering from a possible anxiety disorder, with 10% of students in the United States alone diagnosed with or treated for an anxiety disorder.5 The majority of

3 Kumari, C. S. R. (2024). Self-Esteem, Coping Strategies, and Anxiety Among Generation Z: A correlational study. Global Research Journal of Social Sciences and Management, 02(01), 01–12. https://doi.org/10.55306/GRJSSM.2024.2101.

2 Goodwin, R. D., Weinberger, A. H., Kim, J. H., Wu, M., & Galea, S. (2020). Trends in anxiety among adults in the United States, 2008–2018: Rapid increases among young adults. Journal of Psychiatric Research, 130, 441. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jpsychires.2020.08.014.

Types of Anxiety

While reflecting contemporary cultural and social factors, the surge in anxiety among

Generation Z undergraduates also reveals important distinctions between the expression of anxiety in individuals. State and trait anxiety, respectively, distinguish between situational anxiety and baseline personality anxiety, while general anxiety is all-encompassing. Trait anxiety is a measure of the personality trait that determines how people react to stress and difficulties.

High-trait anxiety describes a high level of baseline anxiety as one moves through daily life.12 If an individual experiences high levels of trait anxiety, they operate through daily tasks and situations with increased worry and unease, making smaller issues feel more threatening and increasing the frequency of anxious feelings. As it is not driven by anxiety-provoking situations, trait anxiety is largely stable and tends to be associated with the personality trait of neuroticism.13

On the other hand, state anxiety is a more acute, transitory form of anxiety and produces elevated bodily arousal and mental distress, varying in intensity and complexity based on the catalyst event. Situational and trait anxiety are both important factors in determining state anxiety.14

While trait and state anxiety are not the same, they are intertwined, contributing to an individual’s overall general anxiety levels together. Since high-trait anxiety is typically linked to high-state anxiety, stress leads to more severe anxiety reactions for those with elevated trait anxiety.15 Finally, general anxiety is a state of worry and panic due to the anticipation of a stressful or threatening event.16 General anxiety merges the experiences of trait and state anxiety in both individuals’ daily lives and in specific instances.

All three of these anxiety types help characterize the complexities in how anxiety manifests for undergraduate students. Trait anxiety could be crucial to identifying self-selection effects, as those with higher levels of innate stress may be more driven to attend a selective institution and pursue higher achievement depending on factors like academic motivation and personal standards. State anxiety relates more to the perceived environment, as the university environment could influence levels of worry and stress through various factors. Both state and trait anxiety paired with general anxiety provide a holistic representation of anxiety for undergraduate students, exposing the possible contrasts between high-pressure environments influencing anxiety versus high-anxiety students being drawn to such institutions. The distinctions between anxiety types exhibit how differences between internal predispositions and external drivers are important for understanding undergraduate anxiety.
