Competition

The interaction between social situations and academic pressures are key components to how a student experiences their classrooms, professors, and overall college climate, propagating viewpoints surrounding difficult classroom structure and negative impressions of professors.

Students’ perceptions of their social and academic surroundings are crucial for how external factors may shape their anxiety. A competitive environment where students feel more like rivals can be harmful, especially in a learning situation where collaboration is vital for mental growth.

Within undergraduate programs, there are a myriad of settings in which students may feel pressure to compete, including class performance, clubs and student groups, and job placement.

Since cooperation is more effective for learning than a competitive environment, undergraduate programs with more peer competition cause negative habits and feelings surrounding learning and classes.20 According to Posselt and Lipson’s findings, perceived peer competition not only fails to foster a strong learning environment, but also leads to increased predicted levels of anxiety and depression among students. Along with promoting divisive conflict in the classroom, perceptions of competition within the institutional environment are linked to weakened motivation, increased procrastination, and increased incidence of academic dishonesty.21, 22 These findings suggest that peer competition may be a crucial contributor to an anxiety-inducing environment.

Social Support vs. Loneliness

The pressure to compete also cultivates isolation, as students attempt to meet heightened expectations with less social support and more demands to prove to both themselves and others.

When perceived competition is prevalent on campus, social support becomes limited as peers are seen as rivals and not as possible friends, breeding isolation and amplifying mental health risks.23

Social support is key for life satisfaction, especially for college students who are going through a life transition; as a result, less robust support networks can increase loneliness on campuses.

Perceived social support is linked to a decreased likelihood of depression and anxiety, especially in times of high stress.24 If students experience a less welcoming undergraduate culture where students are pitted against each other rather than inspired to work together, perceived social support decreases and loneliness increases. Competitive curve grading, weed-out classes, limited campus opportunities, and overemphasis on academic prestige all contribute to conditions of competition and isolation that act as breeding grounds for anxiety.

While higher levels of social support, better self-esteem, and lower perceived levels of stress lead to better adjustment to college,25 loneliness predicts the opposite, inspiring negative perceptions of the social environment. These perceptions then influence negative cognitions, including maladaptive coping, which are linked to student anxiety as well as the negative

Academic Pressures

While loneliness and competition are crucial to the broader culture of all societies, academic coursework is the main aspect of any college environment. Therefore, exams, presentations, and papers may be the most obvious driver of stress and worry in students.

Academic pressures vary based on rigor, previous education, and institutional expectations, but existing empirical findings illustrate that elite institutions often have undergraduate courses with higher levels of cognitive complexity, increasing both academic pressures and anxiety.27 If courses are more difficult due to the university environment and standard of achievement, overall stress regarding completing assignments and performance increases. Regardless of national ranking, environment and academic pressures have similar effects on anxiety in both public and private institutions. For instance, community college students are more likely to struggle with academics in a four year undergraduate program due to the new environments and expectations.28

Goal Orientation

Goal orientation is an internal factor that describes how students’ internal motivation affects their behavior and initiative in goal approach efforts.31 Achievement goal orientation defines how people respond and react to achievement situations, rendering it a key internal process behind undergraduate anxiety levels. Within the main achievement goal framework, there are two constructs — performance and mastery goals — that are differentiated by conceptions of success, reasons for approaching achievement goals, and self-definition.32

Mastery goals focus on the value of learning and posit that effort leads to individually defined mastery, which then defines success. In contrast, performance goals define success by outperforming others; as a result, self-worth becomes linked to one’s ability to demonstrate

Fear of Failure

Fear of failure is defined as the dispositional tendency to avoid failure in achievement settings because of the shame associated with possible defeat, identifying how individuals define failure and behave in related settings.43 It is an internal psychological factor, linked to a similar dimension of the individual as goal orientation and the need for achievement. All three are tied to individual differences in how students focus on outcomes and equate success with self-worth and competency. For those high in fear of failure, a misstep carries more weight and impacts the individual’s self-worth more compared to success, so tasks that risk possible failure increase anxiety.44 While it stems from internal orientation, fear of failure also interacts with environmental factors. The learning environment has an important influence on fear of failure, interactions between internal goals and perceptions of external circumstances can increase such fears. Institutions that emphasize receiving the highest score and encourage competition can make students define personal success in comparison to others, which can increase performance-orientation which is positively related to fear of failure.45 Therefore, certain higher

While some schools prioritize a diverse student body and teaching methods, some elite, private institutions have increased focus on maintaining selectivity and placing focus on students to participate in acquiring resources.47 The expectations promoted by prestigious universities focus more on undergraduate students’ educational outcomes like GPAs, putting students under more pressure to fulfill their roles in perpetuating the schools’ high-end reputation. Conclusion

My study delved into the anxiety levels of undergraduate students through the lens of external factors, internal factors, and selectivity of institutions. I explored if consistently-increasing anxiety could be due to the perceived environment — as some climates have a culture of loneliness, academic pressure, competition, and perfectionism — which influences classroom and professor perceptions,50 or if anxious students could be self-selecting into universities, as those with a high need for achievement, high avoidance goals, and other internal predispositions tend to experience more anxiety.51 I hypothesized that perceived environments would be a stronger predictor of anxiety compared to internal factors, regardless of school selectivity. In addition, I hypothesized that individuals with a performance-approach goal orientation would be less anxious than those with a performance-avoidance goal orientation.

When accounting for selectivity, I hypothesized that elite institutions would influence higher levels of anxiety in undergraduate students over less elite institutions. There were key correlations between anxiety and both internal factors and external factors, specifically fear of failure and classroom avoidance. Fear of failure was found to be the strongest predictor of anxiety, supporting the conclusion that internal factors are driving up anxiety for college students. Finally, selectivity did not have the expected relationship with anxiety. The results

title: Spelling to Communicate for Minimally Speaking Autistic Individuals: An Assessment of Current Evidence
abstract: Spelling to Communicate (S2C) is an increasingly visible motor-based communication method for minimally speaking autistic individuals, yet its scientific status remains unsettled. This review evaluates S2C’s theoretical claims, instructional framework, and empirical evidence within the broader context of motor function, language comprehension, and assessment limitations in minimally speaking autism. Research across fine motor skills, oromotor control, neural organization, and electrophysiological responses shows that motor differences can influence expressive behavior and that standard speech and motor dependent assessments often underestimate ability. These findings create plausible conditions for S2C’s rationale that expressive limitations may mask underlying competence. At the same time, current S2C-specific studies, which rely on small samples and unblinded observational designs, do not establish independent authorship or demonstrate that motor training yields reliable, self-generated communication. Anecdotal reports and media examples illustrate a wide range of real-world experiences but do not provide controlled evidence. This review integrates these domains to clarify where S2C’s assumptions align with existing research, where claims remain untested, and what methodological advances are needed. Establishing independent authorship, improving outcome measures, and defining appropriate target populations are essential steps toward determining whether S2C is a valid communication approach for minimally speaking individuals.
text:
Spelling to Communicate for Minimally Speaking Autistic Individuals: An Assessment of

Current Evidence

Kaimei Gescuk Abstract Spelling to Communicate (S2C) is an increasingly visible motor-based communication method for minimally speaking autistic individuals, yet its scientific status remains unsettled. This review evaluates S2C’s theoretical claims, instructional framework, and empirical evidence within the broader context of motor function, language comprehension, and assessment limitations in minimally speaking autism. Research across fine motor skills, oromotor control, neural organization, and electrophysiological responses shows that motor differences can influence expressive behavior and that standard speech and motor dependent assessments often underestimate ability. These findings create plausible conditions for S2C’s rationale that expressive limitations may mask underlying competence. At the same time, current S2C-specific studies, which rely on small samples and unblinded observational designs, do not establish independent authorship or demonstrate that motor training yields reliable, self-generated communication. Anecdotal reports and media examples illustrate a wide range of real-world experiences but do not provide controlled evidence. This review integrates these domains to clarify where S2C’s assumptions align with existing research, where claims remain untested, and what methodological advances are needed. Establishing independent authorship, improving outcome measures, and defining appropriate target populations are essential steps toward determining whether S2C is a valid communication approach for minimally speaking individuals.

1. Introduction

1.1 Origins and Overview of S2C Spelling to Communicate (S2C) was created in 2015 by speech-language pathologist Elizabeth Vosseller, founder of the International Association for Spelling as Communication (I-ASC), which promotes and trains practitioners in the method. S2C is designed to help minimally speaking individuals, meaning they produce few or no words, communicate by developing purposeful motor skills to point to letters on a letterboard. According to I-ASC, it can take a year or more of consistent sessions to reach “open communication,” the stage at which an individual independently spells original thoughts rather than responding to structured lessons (International Association for Spelling as Communication [I-ASC], n.d.). Early sessions emphasize co-regulation, motor control, and trust before focusing on language output. Learners begin with three small letterboards (A–I, J–R, S–Z), then progress to a full alphabet board and eventually to typing independently on a stationary keyboard, which is the method’s ultimate goal. Supports are systematically reduced and learners are expected to spell with multiple communication partners to demonstrate generalization and independence. Vosseller reported that S2C included practitioners in 43 U.S. states and 25 countries (Vosseller, 2025, 37:35).

1.2 Theoretical Foundation​ S2C is grounded in the claim that many minimally speaking autistic individuals have intact cognitive and linguistic capacities, but experience disruptions in motor planning and execution which interfere with speech (I-ASC, n.d.; Vosseller, 2018). Vosseller draws on research identifying high co-occurrence between autism and childhood apraxia of speech and on studies suggesting motor coordination differences as a potential core feature of autism (Fournier et al., 2010; Tierney et al., 2015). She distinguishes between language as a cognitive process and speech as a motor act, proposing that nonspeaking individuals may “know what they want to say” but lack the motor control to produce speech reliably. From this perspective, communication difficulties reflect motor control impairments rather than language deficits.

The claim is further influenced by research on sensory and movement differences in autism (Leary & Donnellan, 2012; Robledo et al., 2012), which describe challenges in initiating, sequencing, and regulating physical movement. Within this framework, S2C aims to strengthen the neural pathways connecting intention and action through repetitive, structured motor practice. Lessons are designed to train motor consistency while assuming that comprehension and reasoning are already present. This assumption reflects what Jorgensen (2005) termed the “least dangerous assumption”—that it is safer to presume competence and risk overestimating ability than to assume a lack of capacity.

1.3 Instructional Process​ The instructional process of S2C focuses on developing large-muscle control, particularly in the shoulder and elbow, to establish purposeful pointing. Repeated practice is intended to strengthen the brain-body connection so that movements become more automatic. Dr. Dana Johnson, owner of Interplay Therapy Center and a non-profit private school for students with sensory-motor differences, compares the process to coaching a child to ride a bike: “We do not just say, ‘Go ride a bike.’ We have to coach them,” providing step-by-step motor guidance until the skill becomes automatic (Villegas, 2022). Early sessions involve repetitive forward and backward arm movements to stabilize motor patterns while maintaining regulation. As motor fluency increases, cognitive load is gradually introduced through academic lessons such as reading about historical topics like “Benjamin Franklin” or “the history of pyramids” to build attention and reasoning while continuing motor training. Proponents contend that synchronizing motor control and cognition enhances regulation, communication access, and participation in education, work, and community life (I-ASC, n.d.; Vosseller, 2018, 2025).

1.4 Ethical and Procedural Framework

According to Vosseller, S2C is structured around four guiding principles that define its procedural fidelity and ethical boundaries: replicability, reliability, responsibility, and researchability (Vosseller, 2025). Replicability ensures that practitioners worldwide use the same pacing, prompts, and supports, allowing comparability across settings. Reliability focuses on authorship by requiring practitioners to avoid any verbal, physical, or gestural influence. Responsibility defines professional limits. S2C practitioners are not therapists and must refer clients to other professionals for emotional or clinical support. Researchability emphasizes consistency as a prerequisite for empirical validation. Together, these principles are intended to position S2C as a standardized, ethically bounded, and research-oriented intervention (Vosseller, 2025).

These principles reflect Vosseller’s description of the intended procedural and ethical framework, but have not been independently validated or widely endorsed in scientific literature. Current evidence for S2C’s effectiveness and authorship remains limited, and skepticism among researchers persists. This issue will be examined later in this review.

1.5 Comparison with FC and RPM

Because S2C is often discussed alongside older assisted-communication methods, it is important to clarify how it differs from Facilitated Communication (FC) and the Rapid Prompting Method (RPM). All three involve minimally speaking individuals selecting letters with some level of partner support, but the type of support, theoretical rationale, and goals for independence differ.

Skepticism toward S2C is shaped by the legacy of the FC controversies of the 1990s, when controlled studies revealed that facilitators, not users, authored messages once they were blinded to correct answers (Wheeler et al., 1993; Eberlin et al., 1993). These findings led professional bodies such as the American Speech-Language-Hearing Association (ASHA) to deem FC invalid and unethical (Jacobson et al., 1995). Ethical reviews, including one published by The Hastings Center (2024), continue to advise strong caution or opposition to FC and, by extension, to methods that resemble it. This history contributes to a default bias against S2C, often shaping evaluation even though empirical testing has yet to occur.

RPM, developed later, removed physical touch, but relied on rapid verbal and gestural cueing while an aide held a letterboard. ASHA (2018) concluded that RPM “lacks supporting scientific evidence and is potentially harmful in its similarities to the long-discredited technique known as Facilitated Communication.” Because the aide controls both the board and the timing, authorship in RPM also remains unverified.

S2C distinguishes itself by framing communication as a motor-learning process rather than a facilitation technique. In early sessions, practitioners hold the board stationary while providing neutral rhythmic pacing, such as “keep going” or “next letter,” to assist timing and regulation rather than directing content (Villegas, 2022). Proponents of S2C explain that, as motor accuracy improves, these prompts are systematically reduced. Physical touch and board movement are explicitly prohibited. The goal is for the individual to eventually type independently on a stationary keyboard. Reports from practitioners describe individuals who have reached this level of independence, although these outcomes have not been validated in controlled research.

1.6 Ongoing Debate Some clinicians and scholars support S2C’s rationale. Barry Prizant, Ph.D., CCC-SLP, co-developer of the SCERTS model and author of Uniquely Human: A Different Way of Seeing Autism, has reported observing minimally speaking individuals who initially required motor support later communicate independently through typing (Prizant, 2023). He argues that these cases demonstrate that speech and communication are distinct functions and that linguistic competence may be underestimated when motor challenges are overlooked.

Other professionals remain skeptical. They argue that because a communication partner continues to hold the board and provide rhythmic pacing, even if only in beginning stages, S2C constitutes a form of “facilitator-dependent communication” (ASHA, 2018; Novella, 2018). Until controlled, blinded message-passing studies verify independent authorship, these critics maintain that S2C lacks scientific validation.

Supporters counter that standard message-passing tests are ill-suited to individuals with motor and sensory regulation difficulties. They propose that authorship should be evaluated through longitudinal observation and progressive independence rather than single-session accuracy tests. Thus, the debate remains unresolved.

1.7 Scope of Review S2C’s theoretical rationale and procedural design distinguish it from earlier assisted-communication methods such as FC and RPM, yet its empirical foundation remains limited. Few peer-reviewed studies have directly tested S2C and much of the criticism continues to rely on findings from the FC literature rather than data specific to the method. This review therefore examines whether S2C’s framework and observed outcomes provide sufficient evidence to consider it a valid approach to communication for minimally speaking autistic individuals.

To assess this question, the review analyzes four core areas: (1) the theoretical foundations of S2C, including claims that minimally speaking individuals experience motor planning impairments alongside intact cognitive and linguistic abilities; (2) existing empirical research on S2C and the question of authorship; (3) media and public representations of S2C; and (4) the current gaps that limit empirical validation.

By synthesizing these domains, the review aims to clarify what existing evidence supports S2C’s underlying assumptions, where claims remain untested, and what research is necessary to determine its scientific validity. The goal is to move discussion beyond anecdote and controversy toward replicable, data-driven evaluation.

2. Methodology

This literature review integrates academic research and publicly available media to examine the scientific, clinical, and sociocultural claims surrounding S2C. I surveyed peer-reviewed studies across domains relevant to minimally speaking autism. This included motor control, receptive and expressive language, literacy, semantic processing, and authorship verification. I used broad search terms like minimally verbal autism, nonspeaking autism, motor planning, Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC), facilitated communication, and S2C. I included sources that addressed communication, motor ability, language assessment, and authorship in minimally speaking autism. To capture viewpoints and practices not represented in academic literature, I also reviewed news coverage, podcasts, opinion articles, YouTube videos, documentaries, and social media posts produced by practitioners, critics, autistic individuals, and family members. Exclusion criteria removed materials that lacked basic methodological transparency or provided no substantive information about communication processes. All selected sources were analyzed for their claims, evidence base, and limitations.

3. Population: The Minimally Speaking Subgroup

Before investigating the theoretical foundation of S2C for minimally speaking individuals with autism, it is important to define this population. The prevalence of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is increasing, with current U.S. estimates at approximately one in 36 children and a significant subset of this population remains minimally speaking (Pereira et al., 2025). Approximately 25–30% of autistic children never develop functional speech (Posar & Visconti, 2021) and 20–30% remain minimally speaking past kindergarten age despite having received early intervention (Pizzano et al., 2024). This group is often termed the "neglected end of the spectrum" because progress in intervention outcomes for them has been rare (Posar & Visconti, 2021; Tager-Flusberg, 2013). Though some gain limited speech after age five, often producing only single words or short, rote phrases, broad expressive language development after early childhood is uncommon, and few randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have directly examined interventions for this older group (Tager-Flusberg, 2013).

3.1 The Lack of a Consistent Definition One challenge that hinders progress is the lack of a consistent definition for "minimally speaking" or "minimally verbal" or “nonspeaking” individuals (Posar & Visconti, 2021; Tager-Flusberg, 2013). Definitions vary widely in the literature, ranging from producing 0–2 functional words to fewer than 20–30 words, or simply meeting the criteria for ADOS Module 1 (Pizzano et al., 2024; Posar & Visconti, 2021). This inconsistency causes prevalence estimates to range from 13% to 28% and makes it difficult to compare research, conduct meta-analyses, or effectively evaluate communication methods (Posar & Visconti, 2021). Tager-Flusberg (2013) differentiates between preverbal children, who are expected to gain speech, and minimally verbal children, whose speech remains persistently limited. To maintain clarity in this review, I use the term minimally speaking to describe autistic individuals who produce few or no functional words, including those whose speech consists primarily of isolated words, echolalic phrases, or scripted lines that are not used for spontaneous social communication.

3.2 Profound Heterogeneity The minimally speaking population is extremely heterogeneous (Pizzano et al., 2024; Posar & Visconti, 2021). This group does not reflect a single developmental profile, but rather, encompasses individuals with differing underlying abilities and support needs (Pizzano et al., 2024). For example, some individuals have global developmental delays that affect both language comprehension and expression, while others have strong receptive language, cognition, and symbolic play skills despite minimal or absent speech (Pizzano et al., 2024; Posar & Visconti, 2021). The latter group is theorized to have intact cognitive and linguistic capacities that are disrupted by challenges in motor planning and execution (Pizzano et al., 2024). Recognizing this variability, specifically the distinction between individuals whose minimal speech is due to broader developmental delays versus those whose minimal speech may be motor-based, is important as we interpret research and evaluate the applicability of S2C. S2C only fits individuals who have intact comprehension, nonverbal reasoning, and symbolic understanding but marked difficulty with motor planning for speech. For minimally speaking individuals whose limited speech stems from global cognitive delay or significantly reduced receptive language, the method’s assumption of intact linguistic competence would not hold.

3.3. The Research Gap Despite representing up to one-third of the autistic population, minimally speaking individuals are significantly under-represented in intervention studies (Posar & Visconti, 2021). Research disproportionately focuses on speaking participants because standardized language tests can more easily measure their progress (Tager-Flusberg, 2013). The scarcity of controlled research for this subgroup is striking: one systematic review identified only two randomized controlled trials specifically targeting minimally speaking children, compared to hundreds involving speaking participants (Posar & Visconti, 2021). This methodological gap limits the development of valid outcome measures for minimally speaking populations, making it difficult to reliably assess independent authorship or genuine progress in methods such as S2C (Pereira et al., 2025).

In sum, for the purpose of this review, the minimally speaking population refers to autistic individuals who produce little to no functional speech and whose expressive limitations arise from multiple, heterogeneous pathways rather than a single developmental profile. Some have broad cognitive and language delays, while others show intact receptive language and nonverbal reasoning but remain unable to translate those abilities into speech, in part because of motor-planning and speech-motor constraints. This subgroup remains poorly defined, insufficiently measured, and under-researched. To determine whether S2C is a valid communication approach, the field must first progress in establishing clearer definitions, reliable outcome measures, and inclusive research practices for minimally speaking individuals.

4. Motor Function and Speech Coordination in Autism

The central claim behind S2C is that many minimally speaking autistic individuals possess intact cognitive and linguistic abilities, but cannot express them because of motor execution difficulties. The research reviewed in this section does document motor patterns that could interfere with speech in some of these individuals. The evidence therefore creates a context for evaluating whether S2C’s emphasis on motor training aligns with known motor profiles in autism. At the same time, the findings show clear limits and do not establish that motor impairments are the primary or universal barrier to communication.

4.1 Fine Motor Skills and Expressive Language Research on fine motor performance shows associations between motor coordination and expressive language. Importantly, however, it does not demonstrate that motor impairments alone suppress speech. Simarro Gonzalez et al. (2024) found that most autistic youth in their sample performed below expectations on at least one fine motor task. They also reported significant correlations between fine motor scores and several verbal communication measures, including expressive language, receptive vocabulary, articulation accuracy, oromotor sequencing, and parent-reported everyday communication. In practical terms, children with stronger fine motor control also tended to show stronger verbal communication skills on standardized tests. The study does not explain why these skills move together. It cannot determine whether fine motor difficulties directly limit a child’s ability to speak, or whether both motor and communication differences reflect a broader developmental pattern.

Pecukonis et al. (2025) examined minimally speaking autistic adults and found that fine motor ability predicted expressive language scores but did not predict receptive language scores. Adults with weaker motor skills produced less expressive output even when they showed typical-range receptive vocabulary. This pattern illustrates how someone may understand far more than they can physically express when motor output is difficult. The study does not establish how common this pattern is across the wider minimally speaking population, and it does not show that motor training changes expressive outcomes.

Together, these findings show measurable links between motor ability and expressive language but do not identify motor impairment as the sole barrier to speech.

4.2 Large Scale Evidence Large sample analyses contribute additional context. Chen, Siles, and Tager Flusberg (2024) examined 1,579 minimally speaking autistic children and adolescents. Their analysis identified a subgroup of participants with stronger receptive language than expressive language. Motor coordination predicted membership in this subgroup. Children with stronger motor skills were more likely to display higher receptive than expressive scores. Those with weaker motor abilities generally performed poorly across both domains. The authors interpreted these findings as evidence that motor demands influence observed communication performance.

This outcome is partially consistent with the logic of S2C, which assumes that expressive limitations may mask underlying capacity. However, the study did not evaluate S2C or motor-based interventions, and it did not determine whether motor difficulties explain the expressive receptive gap for all minimally speaking children. The results therefore provide context for S2C’s assumptions, but do not validate them.

4.3 Oromotor Control and Speech Production Findings from physiological studies show measurable differences in speech motor execution. Zulfikar et al. (2024) used surface electromyography to record facial and neck muscle activation during simple syllables and short-word tasks. Minimally speaking autistic adults produced stronger muscle activation, higher synchrony across muscle groups, and lower coordination complexity than neurotypical adults. Their speech muscles worked harder, moved in less differentiated patterns, and showed reduced flexibility. These results point to challenges in the motor execution of speech. However, the study did not examine language comprehension or determine whether these motor patterns directly limit communication.

Maffei et al. (2024) documented similar difficulties in oromotor control. Their sample showed impaired articulation, slowed mouth movements, vowel distortions, consonant distortions, reduced intelligibility, and difficulty with nonspeech oral gestures. These patterns resemble features described in oral apraxia. The study reported associations between oromotor deficits and both expressive and receptive language skills. These findings support the possibility that motor execution influences expressive output, which aligns with S2C’s emphasis on motor planning. The results do not show whether motor impairment fully accounts for limited speech or whether motor training improves authorship.

Overall, these studies describe motor features that could restrict speech but do not demonstrate a direct causal link between motor impairment and the absence of functional communication.

4.4 Neural Overlap Between Motor and Speech Systems Structural MRI findings provide another perspective. Conti et al. (2020) compared children with autism and children with childhood apraxia of speech. Both groups showed enlarged regional brain volumes relative to typically developing children. The autistic group displayed widespread differences across frontal and temporal regions, basal ganglia, and cerebellum. The CAS group showed more localized differences in frontal motor planning regions. Machine learning models distinguished autism from typically developing children but did not reliably distinguish autism from CAS. This overlap indicates that some motor-related neural characteristics may occur in both groups.

These results are relevant to S2C’s theoretical foundation because S2C draws heavily on parallels between autism and apraxia. However, the study did not assess language level, did not evaluate speech performance within groups, and did not test any motor-based interventions. The small sample size and retrospective nature of the MRI data further limit interpretation. The findings therefore do show neural overlap, but do not establish that speech limitations in autism arise from the same mechanisms that produce apraxia.

4.5 Broader Motor Coordination and Expressive Behavior

Broader research on motor behavior shows additional movement differences across autistic samples. De Silva et al. (2025) reported impairments in fine motor skills, gross motor skills, balance, gait, strength, manual dexterity, imitation, gesture, and eye orientation. These areas describe how a person moves, coordinates their body, copies actions, or orients their attention. Mosconi and Sweeney (2015) described difficulties with praxis and movement sequencing, meaning that planning and carrying out a series of actions can be harder, and also noted differences in oculomotor control, which affects how the eyes move to guide attention and action. An et al. (2021), cited in the review, reported atypical motor oscillatory coupling, indicating that the brain rhythms that normally coordinate movement may not synchronize in a typical way. Together, these findings map out a broad pattern: many autistic individuals show differences not just in one type of movement but across several motor systems.

These studies do not evaluate speech production or language comprehension, and they do not link any specific motor feature to communication abilities. In other words, they show that motor differences are present, but they do not establish whether these differences affect how a person understands language or how much they can express.

The presence of wide-ranging motor differences is consistent with S2C’s rationale that some autistic individuals have difficulty initiating or sequencing movement. This means S2C’s starting assumption (that movement can be hard to organize for some people) fits within what these motor studies describe. However, the motor findings do not show that these difficulties limit spoken or written language expression, and they do not demonstrate that motor training can create or unlock new communication abilities

4.6 Implications for S2C and Assessment Across the research provided, motor control appears to influence expressive performance in some autistic individuals. Fine motor coordination, oromotor execution, and neural patterns all show associations with aspects of communication. These results support the possibility that motor demands contribute to expressive limitations. They also help explain why S2C positions motor planning as a central focus.

At the same time, the evidence is incomplete. None of the studies in this set evaluate S2C directly. None demonstrate that motor difficulties fully account for limited speech. None show that motor training produces independent, self-generated communication. Motor impairment appears to play a role for some individuals, but the extent of that role remains unclear. These gaps constrain how strongly S2C’s theoretical assumptions can be supported with current evidence.

Overall, the research reviewed here provides partial context for S2C’s rationale, but does not offer empirical validation. Motor differences exist, and some correlate with expressive outcomes, but the scientific record does not yet show that motor impairment is the primary barrier to communication or that motor-based intervention leads to independent authorship. Further controlled studies are required before S2C’s core claims can be confirmed.

5. Cognitive Ability and Measurement Limitations in Minimally Verbal Autism

If motor and expressive challenges constrain how minimally verbal (MV) autistic individuals communicate, then an equally important question is how accurately current assessments capture what they know and understand. A growing body of research shows that traditional measures of language, intelligence, and social ability often underestimate competence in this population. These measurement limitations have direct implications for evaluating S2C which assumes that nonspeaking individuals possess intact cognition and language comprehension that remain hidden by tools ill-suited to their motor and expressive profiles.

5.1 The Floor Effect and the Limits of Standardized Testing Standard language and intelligence tests rely heavily on speech, pointing, imitation, and sustained cooperation. Many minimally speaking autistic individuals cannot produce these behaviors consistently. As a result, their test scores frequently collapse to the lowest measurable values.

Chen et al. (2024) demonstrated the scale of this limitation. In a sample of 1,579 autistic participants, 89 percent of minimally speaking individuals scored at the floor of the Preschool Language Scale (PLS-5). When a test bottoms out this way, it cannot differentiate levels of understanding or track progress. A single “floor score” obscures the possibility that individuals differ widely in what they comprehend.

Researchers have attempted to bypass these limitations with eye-tracking, EEG/ERP, and MEG methods that measure comprehension without requiring speech or pointing. These tools can reveal covert processing, yet they also demand stillness and sensory tolerance that many individuals cannot sustain. The result is a measurement landscape in which behavioral tests underestimate ability and physiological tools are difficult to use consistently.

5.2 Nonverbal IQ Tests and the Motor-Language Confound When speech is limited, clinicians often use nonverbal IQ tests. These instruments, however, still depend on receptive comprehension and motor execution. CTONI-2 uses spoken directions. The UNIT-2 and Leiter-3 rely on pantomimed or pictorial instructions. All require interpreting gestures, manipulating materials, or coordinating fine-motor actions.

Short (2021) found that receptive vocabulary predicted Leiter-3 scores, while expressive language and executive-function measures did not. This pattern shows that even “nonverbal” reasoning tasks are not free from language demands. Neuroimaging findings reviewed in Short 2021 also indicate that nonverbal reasoning activates motor-related brain regions. Many minimally speaking autistic individuals experience dyspraxia or fine-motor delays. Their low scores may therefore reflect difficulty executing responses rather than difficulty solving the problems.

The implication for S2C is significant. Claims that minimally speaking individuals “score low on IQ tests” cannot be interpreted as evidence of limited cognitive ability when the tests themselves require motor skills that this population may not have.

5.3 Evidence of Understanding Beyond Speech Studies that measure neural responses offer a distinct perspective on comprehension in minimally speaking autistic individuals. DiStefano et al. (2019) used ERP methods to examine whether participants detected semantic mismatches between pictures and spoken words. All groups, including the minimally speaking group, produced a reliable N400 mismatch effect. In cognitive neuroscience, the N400 is a well-established electrophysiological marker of semantic processing. Its presence indicates that the brain differentiated between congruent and incongruent picture-word pairs.

This result demonstrates one specific point: minimally speaking autistic participants showed a neural response pattern associated with semantic processing despite producing little or no expressive behavior. The finding does not determine the breadth or depth of their comprehension, the stability of this processing across contexts, or their ability to use this understanding to generate independent communication. It also does not validate any particular communication method, including S2C. It does however show that the neural systems involved in detecting basic meaning relationships are functioning even when outward communication is minimal.

The study also reported that the minimally speaking group showed slower and more spatially localized neural activation and that response patterns varied across individuals. These features indicate that semantic processing is present but atypically organized. The heterogeneity also cautions against assuming uniform cognitive profiles within this population.

Taken together, these results contribute to the overall evaluation of S2C by showing that the absence of overt expressive behavior cannot be taken as evidence of absent semantic understanding. This does not confirm S2C’s claims about authorship or motor-based communication, but it does clarify why expressive limitations alone cannot be used to infer cognitive limitations.

5.4 Cognitive Variability in Minimally Speaking Autism Research that reduces the need for speech and fine-motor output shows that many minimally speaking autistic individuals have stronger reasoning skills than standard tests suggest. Courchesne et al. (2015) found that autistic children who could not complete the WISC-IV often performed in the average range on Raven’s Progressive Matrices, a test that involves visual reasoning rather than speech. Some also solved visual pattern-finding tasks faster than non-autistic peers with similar reasoning abilities. These results make clear that limited speech does not automatically signal limited reasoning.

Guerrera et al. (2025) reported a similar pattern in a large clinical sample. Although minimally speaking participants scored lower on average than verbal peers, more than one quarter scored at or above 70 on nonverbal IQ, placing them within the broad normal range. After controlling for nonverbal IQ, the minimally speaking and verbal groups did not differ on social-communication severity. This suggests that poor performance on expressive tests can give an incomplete or misleading view of overall cognitive functioning.

Peristeri and Andreou (2025) added an important clarification: nonverbal IQ did not predict receptive or expressive language among their minimally speaking participants. Individuals with higher reasoning scores did not necessarily have stronger language skills and those with lower reasoning scores did not necessarily have weaker language skills. The study does not claim that reasoning and language are unrelated. It simply shows that nonverbal IQ was not a reliable indicator of linguistic ability in this group. Together, these findings show considerable cognitive variation that standardized, speech-based assessments usually fail to capture.

5.5 Measurement and Diagnostic Bias Several studies show that assessment tools themselves can distort how ability appears when speech is limited. Zheng et al. (2022) found that ADOS scores varied in predictable ways based on spoken language level and nonverbal mental age, even when controlling for underlying autistic traits. Minimally speaking individuals consistently received higher severity scores than more verbal peers, which indicates that the scoring system is partly influenced by expressive ability rather than only by core symptoms.

Outcome measures create a different problem. Pereira et al. (2025) reviewed common pragmatic-language assessment tools used in autism intervention studies and found no evidence that any of them reported responsiveness. Without this information, researchers cannot tell whether the tools can detect small or gradual improvements. This limitation is significant because many minimally speaking individuals make progress slowly or inconsistently, which means insensitive tools may fail to record meaningful change.

Test performance is also shaped by contextual factors. According to the UNIT-2 manual, individuals with long histories of communication failure may show reduced persistence or engagement during testing. Attention, temperament, and medication can further influence behavior. When these situational factors are interpreted as evidence of low ability, they create a misleading picture of the individual’s skills.

5.6 Interpreting Behavior and Implications for S2C The results from the earlier sections show that many minimally speaking autistic individuals understand more than their test scores suggest. They also show that standard tests often underestimate ability because they depend on speech, motor skills, and cooperation. A final issue that contributes to this gap is how adults interpret behavior during testing and everyday interactions. People often assume that what someone does on the outside tells us what they understand on the inside, but this is not always true.

Jaswal and Akhtar (2019) explain that certain behaviors often seen in autism (such as looking away, repeating words, or moving in repetitive ways) are easy to misread. These behaviors may happen because of motor or sensory challenges, not because the person lacks interest or understanding. Their point is this: some autistic individuals may understand what is being said even if their behavior does not show it clearly. This idea fits with the earlier findings that expressive behavior and test performance do not always match actual ability.

When all of the studies in this section are considered together, a consistent pattern appears. Many minimally speaking autistic people show stronger reasoning, better receptive language, or clearer signs of understanding than their limited speech would suggest. At the same time, test design, motor demands, sensory factors, and past experiences with communication failure can all make performance look weaker than it truly is.

These findings do not show that S2C works or that it produces independent communication. They also do not prove that most minimally speaking autistic individuals have advanced cognitive skills. What they do show is that relying only on speech or motor-based tasks to judge ability is not reliable for this group. This helps explain why S2C’s basic idea that expressive difficulties can hide real understanding appears plausible to some families and clinicians.

However, whether S2C actually allows minimally speaking individuals to communicate independently is a separate question. That issue requires direct testing of authorship and reliability, which the next section examines.

6. Literacy, Authorship, and Independent Communication in S2C

The previous section showed that some minimally speaking autistic individuals may understand more than their test scores or behavior suggest. This raises a natural next question: can those abilities be expressed through S2C?

Only a small number of peer-reviewed studies have investigated this directly and almost all come from the same research group led by Vikram Jaswal. These studies examine two issues:

1.​ whether nonspeaking autistic people show signs of literacy, and​ 2.​ whether their letterboard responses are produced independently rather than shaped by a communication partner.

The evidence is limited, but it offers useful starting points for evaluating S2C’s claims.

6.1 Literacy in Minimally Speaking Autism Jaswal, Lampi, and Stockwell (2024) conducted the first preregistered experiment designed to test literacy without relying on speech, pointing accuracy, or partner support. Thirty-one nonspeaking autistic adolescents and adults completed an iPad tapping task in which letters flashed rapidly on the screen. Some sequences formed real English sentences; others were random strings.

Participants tapped significantly faster when the sequences formed meaningful sentences. They also responded more quickly to common letter pairs in English (such as th or er) and naturally paused before new words. These timing patterns are typical of literate readers and suggest that many participants recognized written structure.

The study tested several possible alternative explanations. Pattern-learning could not explain the results because the “bigram advantage” disappeared when letters were scrambled. The researchers also ruled out simple motor effects by adjusting for tap distance and fatigue. Although the study did not test comprehension directly, the timing data indicate that many participants had some level of orthographic knowledge.

This finding does not prove that all nonspeaking autistic individuals are literate. It does show, however, that the ability to read and process written language can exist even when a person produces little or no speech, and that relying on speech alone would misclassify some individuals’ true literacy skills.

6.2 Gaze-Hand Coordination and Signs of Agency A second study by Jaswal, Wayne, and Golino (2020) examined whether nonspeaking autistic adults who spell on letterboards show signs of choosing letters intentionally. Nine adults with at least two years of S2C experience wore eye-tracking glasses while answering comprehension questions in their usual sessions with familiar assistants.

Across trials, participants typically looked at a letter about half a second before touching it. They produced letters at a steady pace and spelled correct answers on most items. The “look-before-point” pattern is often seen when people type voluntarily on a keyboard and is generally interpreted as a sign of intentional motor planning.

However, the study had several limits. The sample was small, all participants had long-term experience with the same communication partner, and assistants were not blinded to the answers. For these reasons, the study cannot rule out the possibility that subtle cues contributed to performance. The researchers did not include message-passing tests either which is the standard method for determining authorship. They claim to have made this choice because they believed it might disrupt participants’ emotional and motor regulation.

Overall, the eye-tracking results are consistent with intentional spelling, but they do not provide conclusive evidence of independent communication.

6.3 Ongoing Debate About Authorship The decision not to use message-passing is a major point of debate. Critics, such as Beals (2023), argue that without blinded conditions, it is impossible to determine whether the typed or spelled messages come from the individual or from influences, conscious or unconscious, by the assistant. Research on Facilitated Communication, which is not the same method as S2C but does involve a partner holding the communication surface, shows that accuracy drops sharply when facilitators do not know the answers. Because S2C shares some structural similarities with FC, critics contend that it must undergo controlled testing in the same way. From this perspective, message-passing or other blinded procedures are necessary to rule out facilitator influence and to confirm that the communication being produced is genuinely independent.

Supporters of Jaswal’s approach argue that message-passing may not be fair for individuals who rely on familiar sensory or motor supports while communicating. They view the eye-tracking results (anticipatory gaze, stable pacing, and pauses at word boundaries) as behaviors that are difficult to reconcile with externally driven responses. From this perspective, the eye-tracking methods represent an early effort to develop more appropriate tests of agency.

In all, current studies offer promising indicators but do not yet meet the standard needed to confirm authorship.

6.4 Integrative Interpretation Together, the tapping task and eye-tracking study provide initial evidence relevant to S2C’s core ideas. The tapping task suggests that some nonspeaking autistic individuals have knowledge of written English despite limited speech. The eye-tracking study shows gaze-hand patterns that are consistent with self-directed spelling.

However, both studies come from a single research group, involve small samples, and omit the blinded methods typically used to rule out facilitator influence. For these reasons, the findings should be interpreted as suggestive, not definitive.

They show that written language understanding and goal-directed motor planning may be present in some nonspeaking autistic people. They do not show that S2C reliably enables independent communication.

As it stands, S2C remains plausible in theory, but not empirically verified as an independent communication method. The next section examines anecdotal reports and case descriptions to understand how families and practitioners describe S2C in practice.

7. Anecdotal Examples

Public interest in S2C and related letterboard methods is fueled in part by widely circulated videos and personal stories. These examples do not provide controlled scientific evidence, and they cannot determine authorship. However, they are relevant to understanding the public conversation around S2C and why many families view it as credible.

7.1 Why Online Videos Create Confusion For anyone searching online for “Spelling to Communicate,” the available video material varies widely in quality and method. Some older videos, often misidentified as S2C, show communication partners clearly prompting, guiding, or physically influencing a nonspeaking autistic person. These reflect earlier methods such as Facilitated Communication (FC) or early-stage Rapid Prompting Method (RPM), not S2C as currently taught.

There are also videos that are labeled as S2C, but show the method being used incorrectly. In these cases, a partner may prompt the person spelling or hold the board in a way that allows influence. In addition, beginners learning S2C typically need someone to hold the board steady at first. Videos of this early stage can easily give the impression that board-holding is the final goal of S2C, when in fact many individuals move past this stage and later type on a stationary board or keyboard without anyone touching them. These early-stage and improperly performed videos often become the basis for skepticism because they make it difficult to distinguish between genuine S2C practice, outdated methods, and situations where influence cannot be ruled out.

At the same time, there are multiple publicly available examples of independent typing, where the nonspeaking individual types or spells on a fixed, unmoving surface, with the partner not touching the person or the device. These examples cannot determine authorship scientifically, but they show what families and practitioners point to when arguing that independent communication is possible.

The sections below describe the most widely referenced examples.

7.2 Independent Typing Depicted in Spellers (2023) The documentary Spellers (2023) presents several nonspeaking autistic individuals using letterboards or keyboards. The term “Speller” is used to refer to those individuals with minimally speaking autism who use S2C. During a scene that occurs around 1:14:14, Jamie Handley, an individual with minimally speaking autism, types on a table-mounted keyboard, using a single finger to press each key. His communication partner sits nearby but does not touch him or the keyboard and gives no verbal prompts during the typing. This moment in the film is an example of what appears to be intentional, self-generated S2C communication.

Another scene shows a Speller named Vincent typing, “I am a rudderless ship in the sea of thought” (44:12–45:03). The filmmakers use this line to highlight the idea of a disconnect between internal cognition and motor control, which is a central theme in the film.

These scenes are compelling, however, they are still documentary footage, not controlled scientific tests.

7.3 J.B. Handley, Father of Jamie Handley The example of Jamie typing independently in Spellers continues into a YouTube interview titled “Underestimated — An Autism Miracle with Ride or Die Dad J” (2023). In this interview, Jamie’s father, J.B. Handley, expands on what viewers saw in the film.

Handley responds to the claim that facilitators guide the typing. He argues that skepticism comes from long-standing assumptions that “nonspeaking means non-thinking,” and that many professionals resist the idea that motor challenges, rather than cognitive limitations, prevent speech. He says, “Every movement that changes the world starts with people being mocked. Galileo was mocked.” Handley challenges critics to observe independent typing in person: “Go watch an independent typer. Sit in a room and see it happen. Then tell me with a straight face that it’s not them communicating.”

These statements reflect the perspective of families who see progress in their own children. They do not substitute for blinded or controlled testing, but they partly explain why many families support S2C and view independent typing as authentic.

7.4 News Coverage of Independent Typing: UC Berkeley Examples A 2022 news segment from ABC7 highlights David Teplitz, a minimally speaking autistic UC Berkeley graduate. The footage shows Teplitz typing slowly on a speech-generating laptop while his communication partner is present but does not touch him or the device (ABC7 News, 2022). Teplitz states: “I want people to know that we can achieve a lot if we are allowed to participate.”

His friend Hari Srinivasan, also minimally speaking, graduated from Berkeley with a 4.0 GPA and is now pursuing a PhD in neuroscience. Both credit communicating via typing for giving them access to academics and self-advocacy.

These cases are cited in public discussions as examples suggesting that strong cognitive skills can exist despite limited speech. As with all anecdotal material, they describe individual outcomes rather than controlled evidence of authorship.

7.5 The Case of Naoki Higashida Naoki Higashida, a minimally speaking autistic writer from Japan, uses a stationary letterboard to communicate independently, without anyone holding or touching the board. Video recordings show him pointing to letters on his own to spell meaningful sentences. Although Higashida does not use S2C, his method is built on the same underlying idea (speech may break down because of motor-control challenges, while language and thought remain intact) and end-goal (independent communication on a stationary board).

Higashida’s communication shows that some minimally speaking autistic individuals can produce written language through independent letterboard use. It does not validate S2C, but it helps clarify why some people believe written communication can reflect genuine thought despite severe speech challenges.

7.6 Summary These anecdotal examples do not answer the scientific question of authorship. They do, however, show why S2C and related methods have gained attention. Some videos online clearly show prompting or potential influence, while others show fully independent typing. This mixture contributes both to skepticism and to strong support among families.

In the context of this review, these stories illustrate the range of real-world experiences but do not provide controlled evidence.

8. Future Directions

The earlier sections of this paper showed that (1) many minimally speaking autistic individuals may have stronger receptive and cognitive abilities than their expressive behavior suggests, (2) standard assessments often underestimate ability because they rely on speech and fine-motor output, (3) motor differences may contribute to expressive challenges but have not been shown to cause minimally speaking status on their own, and (4) current studies on S2C provide only preliminary evidence about literacy and agency. Building on those findings, the next step is to define a research agenda capable of determining whether S2C allows truly independent communication and for whom it may be appropriate.

8.1 Establishing Independent Authorship This direction follows directly from Section 6, which reviewed the limited empirical work on literacy and agency in S2C. The studies by Jaswal and colleagues show promising indicators, such as anticipatory gaze and timing patterns, but do not include blinded procedures capable of ruling out communication partner influence.

Future work should:

●​ Implement blinded message-passing or other controlled authorship tests in which the communication partner does not know the correct answers.​ ●​ Use preregistered protocols with objective scoring rules, so interpretation does not shift after data collection.​

●​ Compare performance across assisted vs. independent conditions (partner-held board versus stationary keyboard).​ ●​ Test whether individuals can communicate with multiple unfamiliar partners, which is necessary to rule out practiced coordination.

These studies should be designed so that S2C can be rigorously evaluated for success. Without such tests, authorship cannot be established.

8.2 Clarifying the Target Population Section three of this paper detailed the extreme heterogeneity of the minimally speaking population. That section explained that some individuals have strong receptive language and nonverbal reasoning alongside motor planning challenges, while others have global developmental delays. Because S2C assumes intact comprehension, it is unlikely to fit all minimally speaking individuals.

Future research must:

●​ Use consistent definitions of “minimally speaking,” building on the definitional problems described in Section 3.​ ●​ Stratify participants based on receptive language, nonverbal reasoning, and motor profiles before analyzing outcomes.​ ●​ Determine whether individuals with certain profiles, specifically those with strong comprehension but significant motor challenges, benefit more from S2C than others.

These studies would make it possible to evaluate S2C within the correct subgroup rather than treating “minimally speaking autism” as a homogeneous category.

8.3 Improving Outcome Measures Section five reviewed major limitations in current assessment tools, including floor effects, motor demands built into testing, contextual influences on performance, and the absence of responsiveness data for pragmatic-language measures. These problems make it difficult to evaluate any communication method for minimally speaking individuals, including S2C.

Future work should develop or validate:

●​ Low-motor, low-speech outcome measures for tracking change.​

●​ Instruments with demonstrated responsiveness​ ●​ Measures that reflect a broader range of outcomes, including receptive language, participation, and quality of life, not just spelling accuracy.

Improving measurement tools is essential before S2C can be evaluated rigorously in intervention studies.

8.4 Comparative and Longitudinal Study Designs Earlier sections of this paper showed that most evidence for S2C comes from anecdotal descriptions (Section 7) or short observational studies that do not track learners over time (Section 6). These designs cannot determine whether individuals actually progress from partner-held boards to fully independent typing, nor can they show which learners benefit, plateau, or discontinue the method. Because S2C is described as a gradual motor-learning approach, long-term data are essential.

Future research should:

●​ Track learners across months or years, documenting how they move from early-stage board holding to full independence on a stationary keyboard.​ ●​ Record each participant’s starting profile, including baseline motor ability, receptive language, and nonverbal reasoning, to determine which characteristics predict progress.​ ●​ Document non-responders and attrition, including individuals who do not advance beyond early stages or who discontinue instruction, so that success rates are not based only on visible or publicized cases.​ ●​ Measure changes in motor planning, accuracy, fluency, and communication complexity using outcome tools that minimize speech and fine-motor demands, building on the measurement issues identified in Section 5.​ ●​ Examine stability and generalization by tracking whether skills transfer across communication partners, environments, and communication tasks over time.

Longitudinal data cannot resolve authorship on their own, but they are essential for determining whether S2C produces meaningful, reproducible progress, which individuals benefit, and how the method functions across extended instructional periods.

8.5 Ethics, Transparency, and Safeguards

The section comparing S2C with FC and RPM emphasized why ethical safeguards are necessary given the long history of unintentional facilitator influence. To build public trust and scientific credibility, S2C research must adopt transparent practices.

Future work should:

●​ Provide detailed procedural manuals and fidelity checklists that clarify acceptable vs. unacceptable forms of support, which is important given the variability described in Section 7.​ ●​ Include video documentation (with consent) in research settings so that board handling, prompting, and partner behavior can be independently reviewed.​ ●​ Establish ethical guidelines stating that unverified S2C output should not be used in legal, medical, or high-stakes decision contexts until authorship is confirmed.​ ●​ Involve minimally speaking autistic individuals and their families as research partners to ensure that studies measure meaningful outcomes.

These steps would help differentiate responsible S2C practice from misapplied or high-risk versions seen online.

8.6 Integrating Neuroscience and Motor Research Section four summarized research on motor function and neural organization in autism. Section five discussed electrophysiological evidence showing semantic processing despite limited speech. Integrating these findings with S2C research could clarify which components of the method, if any, have a motor-learning effect.

Future studies should:

●​ Use combined eye-tracking, EMG, ERP/EEG, and behavioral measures to examine how motor planning and language comprehension interact during S2C sessions.​ ●​ Investigate whether progress in S2C correlates with changes in neural or motor patterns over time.​ ●​ Determine whether motor improvements are specific to S2C

This work would clarify whether S2C’s focus on gross-motor pointing is scientifically grounded.

9. Conclusion

This review examined the scientific, clinical, and public evidence surrounding S2C and evaluated its claims within the broader context of minimally speaking autism. The earlier sections of the paper established several key points that shape how S2C should be interpreted.

First, research on motor function and neural organization (Section 4) shows that many autistic individuals experience differences in fine motor control, oromotor coordination, and motor planning. These differences can influence expressive performance, but the available data do not support the conclusion that motor impairment alone causes minimally speaking status for most individuals. Motor challenges may be one factor among many, and their contribution varies across people.

Second, evidence on measurement limitations (Section 5) demonstrates that standard assessments often underestimate ability in minimally speaking autistic individuals. Floor effects, motor demands built into testing, diagnostic bias, and contextual factors all contribute to artificially low scores. Electrophysiological findings show that some individuals process language meaningfully even when they cannot express it through speech. These results create plausible conditions under which expressive behavior may not reflect underlying comprehension, a premise that S2C relies on. They do not, however, confirm that motor-based interventions can grant access to language.

Third, the empirical work directly related to S2C (Section 6) remains limited. The literacy and gaze-hand coordination studies by Jaswal and colleagues provide valuable insights, including evidence of orthographic knowledge and anticipatory gaze patterns that could reflect intentional letter selection. Still, these studies involve small samples, do not include blinded authorship tests, and cannot rule out partner influence. They offer suggestive signals, not confirmation of independent communication.

Fourth, the anecdotal material reviewed in Section seven illustrates the range of real-world experiences: some videos show prompting or potential influence, while others show fully independent typing on stationary keyboards or letterboards. These examples explain why families view S2C as meaningful, but they do not constitute scientific evidence.

Considering these findings together, S2C occupies an intermediate position. Its central assumptions that expressive behavior may underestimate cognitive ability and that motor challenges may interfere with speech are supported by broader research on minimally speaking autism. Its specific claims about independent, self-generated communication, however, remain unverified. No controlled, blinded studies have yet demonstrated that S2C reliably produces independent authorship and without such evidence, scientific validation is not possible.

The future directions outlined in Section eight describe a path forward. Controlled authorship studies, improved outcome measures, clearer population definitions, comparative trials, and transparent ethical safeguards are essential for establishing whether S2C is effective, for whom it is suitable, and under what conditions it should be used. Integrating neuroscience and motor research may clarify which parts of S2C align with established motor-learning processes and which elements require revision.

At present, S2C remains a method with theoretical plausibility, strong anecdotal support from families, and early but inconclusive empirical indicators. Its validity as an independent communication system cannot be assumed, and meaningful progress will require rigorous, transparent, and falsifiable research. The stakes are high: minimally speaking autistic individuals are among the most overlooked groups in autism research. Developing reliable methods for assessing and supporting their communication is an urgent scientific and ethical priority. S2C may eventually contribute to that goal, but its claims must be tested directly before it can be considered a validated communication approach.

title: Preschoolers’ Creativity During STEM Play
abstract: In the past few years, educators have been pushing for an integration of the arts into science, technology, engineering and math (STEM) learning to promote innovation and creativity in these fields. The present study explores the relation between creativity and STEM learning among young children in digital and non-digital contexts, and how creativity affects STEM engagement. Parent-child dyads consisting of one parent and one child aged 4-and-a-half to 5-years old participated in a repeated measures experiment during which they played with magnetic tiles, similar to blocks, and then with a coding application on a tablet. Levels of creativity during non-digital play, performance on the coding application and parent report of children’s STEM engagement are measured to better understand their relation. Results show that there may be a connection between creativity and STEM learning, but this relation is still unclear. This study will contribute to the development of STEM curriculum and its incorporation of creative activities in the preschool years.

title: Moroccan Female Entrepreneurship
abstract: Morocco is a fairly stable country, with parliamentary elections and limited political instability. When compared to neighbors such as Egypt and Tunisia, Morocco came out of the Arab Spring relatively unscathed. However, the Moroccan people remain unhappy with the economic state of their country. In a country of 34.9 million people, unemployment is at 10% and youth unemployment is at a staggering 27.5%, with female unemployment surpassing that number. The 42% of urban Moroccans who are unemployed have been protesting and voicing their discontent at the economic situation; experts call this a “ticking time bomb.” ³ This structural unemployment can be accredited to the education system’s rigid and increasingly obsolete curriculum, a rising population and the lack of private-sector job creation. Additionally, the unemployment rate is leading to an increase in inequality and is putting a strain on government social programs. Morocco is facing a great economic challenge, one that requires robust job creation and innovative solutions. However, the high unemployment rates and rising inequality cannot be overcome unless the government harnesses the talent and potential of Moroccan women.

title: Locating previously unmapped water-filled cave passages feeding the Echo River Accessory Spring using electrical resistivity tomography at Mammoth Cave
abstract: What we know about the Mammoth Cave system stems from the 833 km of explored cave, but it is hypothesized that this represents only half of the total cave system. Many caves passages within this complex system are extremely hard and, in some cases, impossible to physically access. The independent water source feeding the Echo River Accessory Spring can be classified as one of these “impossible” caves to access. Mammoth Cave scientists have attempted to use a variety of different methods, such as dye-tracing, scuba diving, and even remotely operated vehicles, to access this water-filled cave passage, with no success. Difficulty in locating the water-filled cave passage feeding the Echo River Accessory Spring suggests that another approach is necessary. Electrical resistivity tomography allows us to model and “explore” caves tens of meters below the Earth’s surface without stepping foot inside. Using this technique, we imaged low-resistivity anomalies interpreted to be water-filled cave passages, which likely supply the Echo River Accessory Spring water. This result characterizes a previously undiscovered Mammoth Cave passage and could potentially extend the known extent of the total cave system. These findings will ultimately open up the possibility for further scientific advancements regarding the cave. We also anticipate that this result will allow for a better understanding of how water flows through the Mammoth Cave system and out through springs into the Green River, while also demonstrating the utility of ERT in subsurface karst terrain exploration.

title: Determining the Toxicity of Natural Products on Caenorhabditis elegans in the Search for New Anthelmintic Drug Leads
abstract:
This project aims to discover new molecules from microbial extracts that prove toxic to C. elegans yet harmless to mammals...

One promising compound has been screened against C. elegans, and while the results seem to illustrate a sensitivity to the compound in traits such as mean time of flight (animal length), this may be an artifact of the assay because the brood size (animal fertility) seemed to increase with increasing drug concentration.

title: Picturing Java (Wo)Man: Visual Reconstruction of Colonial Paleoanthropology
abstract:
The question of man’s origin has plagued philosophers, scientists, and intellectuals alike for centuries. After Charles Darwin’s revolutionary Origin of Species (1859) and The Descent of Man (1871) were published, fossil discoveries became paramount in establishing the connection between humans and earlier life forms...

However, despite decades of progress, the absence of the ‘missing link’ between apes and humans confounded scientists. In 1891 Dutch paleoanthropologist and geologist Eugene Dubois discovered what was claimed to be the missing link in the Dutch East Indies. He dubbed the fossil he discovered in Trinil, Java “Java Man” (Pithecanthropus erectus). Java Man was later found to be a subspecies of Homo Erectus, but for a time debate raged regarding its place in human ancestry.

title: “When did the depictions become worse than the reality?”: Black Trauma Porn and The Black Horror Genre in Television and Film
abstract: The American film industry is inextricably tied to the history of racism in the United States; thus, Black representation in film and T.V. has been a topic of rigorous academic and public debate. Most recently, that debate has circulated around the topic of “Black Trauma Porn” (BTP). Emerging on social media in 2016 during the Black Lives Matter movement, Black thinkers used the phrase “Black Trauma Porn” to articulate the nuanced complexities of the phenomenon, specifically sharing police brutality videos and the production of films and T.V. series with similar themes. Many pieces have received extreme backlash, and BTP became loaded with negative connotations, labeling the pieces as exploitative and harmful. However, as the phrase gained popularity, the analysis of these movies and T.V. shows became derivative and uncritical, instigating the need to investigate if the phrase properly articulates what authors were utilizing it for. To interrogate BTP, it is necessary to explain the impact of film on the spectator and engage the history of race in Hollywood in order to conclude that BTP is actually a modernist subgenre of Black horror. This conclusion is supported through an analysis of white versus Black horror as well as a deep-dive into what “trauma” and “porn” mean individually and within this context. Reframing and usurping the phrase BTP provides the beginning to a new framework for analyzing Black historical horror films and answering larger questions about Black representation in film and T.V.
