title: Unashamed: Exploring A South Korean Female Tattoo Artist’s Negotation of Identity
text:
Unashamed: Exploring A South Korean Female Tattoo Artist’s Negotation of Identity by Kiana Staples

Department of Asian Languages and Culture

Faculty Adviser: Jeong Eun Annabel We

Introduction Like many other countries across the globe, South Korea’s tattoo culture con­ tinues to grow rapidly, with its tattooed population reaching three million in 2021.1,2 Walking down the streets of Seoul in areas like Sinchon and Hongdae, it is not uncommon to see both Korean and foreign young adults marked with tattoos of various sizes, styles, and subject matter. As an exchange student studying abroad at Ewha Womans University during the Fall 2021 semester, I observed Korea’s booming tattoo scene firsthand, seeing tattooed Korean youths on a daily basis. I also visited five different tattoo studios while in Korea, getting a total of six tattoos. My foreign body, adorned with patchwork old-school American tattoo designs, attracted only a small fraction of the stares I had expected.3 Rather, I encountered tattooed Ko­ reans serving me at restaurants or walking past me down the street, and even heard whispers behind me from Koreans who, after noticing my inked skin, started discussing their own pos­ sible first tattoo designs.

1 Friedman, The World Atlas of Tattoo. 2 Yonhapnews, “T’at’u 300man.” 4:58. 3 The term “patchwork” refers to tattoos that exist together as separate, individual pieces rather than tattoos combined into a single cohesive “sleeve” design. 4 Yonhapnews, “T’at’u 300man.”2:14. 5 Kukka—bŏpnyŏng—jŏngbo—sent’ŏ (National Legal Information Center), “Pogŏnbŏmjoe—Dansoge—Gwanhan—t’ŭk­ byŏlchoch’i—Wiban (Violation of the Act on Special Measures for the Control of Health Crimes).”

As opposed to other countries, however, Korea currently criminaliz­ es the practice of tattooing for those without medical degrees. Yonhap News, a major South Korean news agency, refers to Korea as the “only nation in the world” where tattoos are still ille­ gal.4 In 1992, South Korea’s Supreme Court decided that due to risks such as infection, tattooing would only be legal when performed by those with certified medical training.5 Even nurses who can give patients injections do not meet the qualifications to legally tattoo others.6 Those caught tattooing without the proper medical license could be fined as much as $40,000 USD and sentenced to anywhere between two years and life in prison.7 De­ spite the growth of Korea’s tattoo scene as well as the demands of tattoo artists, in March 2022, the Constitutional Court in Seoul upheld the current laws making tattooing illegal.8 Many tattoo artists and enthusiasts continue to protest against these laws, and the perception of tattoos in Korea is shifting from a potentially harm­ ful medical practice to a legitimate form of artistic expression.9,10

Under current tattoo-related legisla­ tion, the majority of Korean tattoo artists are working illegally in an underground scene. Combined with their other identi­ ties, such as nationality, gender, and class, Korean tattoo artists’ profession shapes their existence in Korean society. Despite the abundance of tattooed bodies in Korea, there are historical associations between tattoos and crime dating back to Korea’s Koryŏ dynasty (918—1392 CE), informing perceptions of tattoos that Korean tattoo artists cannot fully escape. The Korean state has continued to criminalize the tat­ too artist profession long after the end of penal tattooing, creating a lasting negative stigma against tattoos in South Korea.

6 Yonhapnews, “T’at’u 300man.”2:51 7 Chung, “Tattoos, Still Illegal in South Korea, Thrive Underground — The New York Times”; Kukka—bŏpnyŏng—jŏngbo—sent’ŏ (National Legal Information Center), “Pogŏnbŏmjoe—dansoge—gwanhan—t’ŭkbyŏlchoch’i—bŏb, je—5—jo (Act on Special Mea­ sures for the Control of Health Crimes, Article 5).” 8 Chung, “Tattoos, Still Illegal in South Korea, Thrive Underground — The New York Times.” 9 Tattoo Artist “H”, Oral History. H noted in her interview that among tattoo artists in the industry, there are differing opinions on the positive and negative aspects of current legislation on tattoos. There is also a Tattoo Artists’ 10 Yonhapnews, “T’at’u 300man.” 11 Kim, “Han’guk Hyŏngbŏl Munsin—Ŭi Paljŏnsa—Wa Hyŏndaejŏk Ŭimi—e Taehan Sogo (A Study on the History of the Develop­ ment and Modern Meaning of the Korean Punishment Tattoo)”; Mun, Munshinyuhŭi: chigŭm, han’gugŭi t’at’u munhwa (Tattoo Game: Now, Korea’s Tattoo Culture); Namgung, Han’gugŭi munshin: t’at’uisŭt’ŭga chŏnhanŭn iyagi (Korean Tattoos: A Story Told by Tattoo Artists). 12 Namgung, Han’gugŭi munshin: t’at’uisŭt’ŭga chŏnhanŭn iyagi (Korean Tattoos: A Story Told by Tattoo Artists). Although pictures and accounts of men are more prevalent in this text, there are several instances in which Namgung describes tattoo practices that were adopted by both men and women in Korea, such as jŏmsangmunsin, or dot—like tattoos that symbolized tight bonds between friends (see pages 163—76). 13 Due to the illegal nature of the tattoo artist profession, I refer to each tattoo artist using a single initial.

While there is an existing scholarship dedicated to Korean tattoo culture and his­ tory, the majority of it is published in Kore­ an and centers on male experiences, wheth­ er it be the punishment of male criminals, the tattoos of war veterans, or the lives of men working in South Korea’s current tat­ too scene.11 However, historical accounts of tattooed women in Korea do exist, and female tattoo artists contribute to South Korea’s contemporary tattoo culture.12 Due to the absence of both English and Korean language scholarship on tattoos in Korea in general, especially that which significantly addresses the role of women in Korean tat­ too culture and history, I designed a research project which emphasizes the narratives of individual South Korean women — tattoo artists “C,” “H,” and “Y.”13 Though this single thesis is far from comprehensive, my hope is that the role of women in shaping Korean tattoo culture will continue to be recorded over time, expanding the current scholar­ ship on tattoos in Korea.

This paper serves as my exploration of the South Korean female tattoo artist iden­ tity through an analysis of oral history nar­ ratives. While I interviewed three artists, the following pages will focus on the oral history of Tattoo Artist “C.” By analyzing her responses, I aim to demonstrate what her individual narrative reveals about dif­ ferent experiences of South Korean female tattoo artists. Focusing on the experiences and knowledge of C, I argue that South Korean female tattoo artists negotiate their understanding and display of their bodies in the context of Korean tattoo history and culture, which continues to associate tat­ toos and tattooing with crime.

Oral History: Tattoo Artist “C” C was the first tattoo artist I decided to interview for my project. I first discovered C while searching Instagram for Korean tattoo artists who specialize in an tradi­ tional American-inspired tattoo style. As soon as I found C’s account, I admired her use of bold colors as well as her distinct designs. She not only tattooed old-school motifs such as eagles or panthers, but also custom designs. After months of admiring C’s online portfolio, I decided to book an appointment with her during my time studying abroad in Seoul and got a small tattoo of one of my household cats. Al­ though I could not complete our interview in person while I was in Korea, C was en­ thusiastic when hearing about my project and was more than happy to participate in a remote interview.

C covered an array of topics while answering my questions; many of her re­ sponses subverted my expectations regard­ ing the gender dynamics of Korea’s tattoo culture and industry. I prepared multiple questions that directly addressed how C’s female gender identity might relate to her craft as a tattoo artist — if she experiences discrimination that her male counterparts do not, how she is perceived differently than tattooed men in Korea, and how marginalized communities and activism are related to South Korean tattoo history and culture. To my surprise, however, C would often respond by telling me that there was no such clear difference between men and women in many cases, and she incorporat­ ed gender into her responses in ways that I had not anticipated. Instead, I found that many of C’s responses reflected her own negotiations of identity as a female South Korean tattoo artist — how she perceived tattoos in relation to Korea’s tattoo history and the way that Koreans negatively view heavily tattooed women. I focus on two themes present in her responses: historical associations between tattoos and crime in Korea, and C’s negotiation of her own body and identity in relation to shame (or lack thereof).

14 Tattoo Artist “C,” Oral History. 15 The corresponding Sino characters in this instance are 文身. However, to specifically indicate the practice of criminal punish­ ment through tattooing and not tattoos more generally, 黥 is used (as in ‘黥刑/경형’).

I began by asking C about the sto­ ries she has heard about Korea’s tattoo history. C started by recalling the practice of penal tattooing in the Chosŏn dynasty (1392—1897 CE), noting that tattoos were used to punish criminals. According to C, the wounding of one’s skin by engraving these letters was “the most shameful insult” that one could receive at the time.14 The Korean word for tattoos, munshin, could be translated as letters engraved onto the body (mun meaning letters or writing and shin meaning body).15 Korean scholar Kim Hyŏng-jung traces such punishment back to Korea’s Koryŏ period, in which penal tat­ toos became legalized. These tattoos would permanently mark a criminal’s face or body with letters indicating the type of crime committed.16 Particularly due to the grow­ ing influence of Confucianism in Korea at the time, wounding of the body received from one’s parents was viewed as a betray­ al of filial piety.17 Chosŏn dynasty rulers favored harsh tattoo punishments, deliber­ ately marking criminals’ faces to make their past crimes visible to the public.18

When recalling Korea’s tattoo his­ tory, C immediately began with the cruel practice of penal tattooing, focusing on strong associations between tattoos and crime; however, she was not specifically prompted to do so by my questions. In fact, when I conducted my second oral history interview a month later with artist “H,” I got a response comparing pre- and post-social media tattoo culture, centering on technological development rather than criminality.19 However, it cannot be denied that since the end of the penal Chosŏn dy­ nasty tattoo punishments, tattoos continue to be associated with the illegal activities of gangsters and prostitutes, which C also mentioned in her personal timeline of Ko­ rean tattoo history.

The image of tattooed gangsters in South Korea, while considered outdated by some, does not come from a place of mere speculation.20 i-D’s mini-documen­ tary features Grace Neutral speaking to a self-identified current gang member, Mr. Kim, who has just received a large back tat­ too. Mr. Kim estimates that “if 100 [gang­ sters] have tattoos, then only one would not have one.”21 Associations between tattoos and gang activity in Korea became preva­ lent in the 20th century due to Japan’s col­ onization of the peninsula. Tattoos received by Korean gang members were heavily inspired by the tattoos of Japanese Yakuza gang members.22 While, as Mr. Kim men­ tions, gangsters do not intentionally expose their tattooed flesh to the public as a form of intimidation, South Koreans continue to associate tattoos with gangsters’ criminal activity in the 21st century.23 Although C did not directly express a connection be­ tween the historical associations of tattoos, shame, and crime with the criminalization of her own career, she recognizes that the practice of marking the body that is central to her profession was once used by the state as a form of corporal punishment.

16 Kim, “Han’guk Hyŏngbŏl Munsin—Ŭi Paljŏnsa—Wa Hyŏndaejŏk Ŭimi—e Taehan Sogo (A Study on the History of the Develop­ ment and Modern Meaning of the Korean Punishment Tattoo),” 31–32. 17 Kim, 31. 18 Kim, 37. 19 Tattoo Artist “H,” Oral History. 20 Yoon, “[T’at’u 300man Shidae]①.” 21 i—D, “Grace Neutral Explores Korea’s Illegal Beauty Scene [FULL FILM].” 27:59. 22 Glietsch, “The Korean Tattoo Culture,” 20. 23 Glietsch, 20–21. 24 Pitts, In the Flesh: The Cultural Politics of Body Modification.

C also related the shameful practice of wounding the body through tattooing to the current tattoo legislation in South Korea. Intentional damage to the physi­ cal body was viewed as shameful, causing tattoos to continue to be illegal in South Korea and viewed by the government as a dangerous medical procedure rather than an art form. This notion of purposefully “damaging” one’s own skin through body modification is similar to beliefs in North American cultures. Body modifications like tattoos which involve voluntarily hurting one’s own skin have often been compared to forms of self-harm or addiction, making heavily modified bodies taboo.24 Through her own retelling of the origins of Korean tattoo history, C continued to draw con­ nections between tattoos and criminality in pre-modern and modern Korea.

At some point in the middle of our interview, I decided to ask C about the tat­ toos on her own body, and whether or not she felt the need to cover up her tattooed skin in South Korea. Knowing that C is a visibly tattooed Korean woman, and also considering associations between both tattoos and crime and tattooed women and prostitution, I was curious about C’s per­ ceptions of her own body.25 When I asked C if she ever hides her tattoos, however, she expressed that she felt it was unneces­ sary as they were not shameful to her.

STAPLES: So, when you go home [to your family], do you usually show a lot of your tattoos? Or do you prefer to hide them?

C: Oh not at all, I don’t want to hide them. [Having tattoos] isn’t a shameful thing, so I don’t want to hide them … but even so, if I go to a place where there’s a lot of older people, if I end up going [to a place like that], then I might try to hide them a bit. Not in public, but in a place with lots of older people, when I go somewhere like a wedding, I hide them, but [otherwise] I generally don’t hide them.26

What struck me in C’s response was the immediate connection she made between hiding one’s tattooed body and the concept of tattoos being shameful, or pukkŭrŏpta. Though there are multiple words that can be translated as “shameful,” pukkŭrŏpta is the same Korean word that C used to describe penal tattooing prac­ tices in pre-modern Korea. When writing this question, I perceived it as more of a question of deciding whether to respect or subvert normative expectations depending on the context of a situation. C, however, partially understood my question as asking whether or not she is ashamed of display­ ing her own tattooed body in public. A few weeks after the interview, I decided to message her privately and ask if she had ever experienced feelings of shame show­ ing her tattoos or if she ever felt it was inappropriate to have them uncovered. C confirmed that she has never felt ashamed of showing her tattoos in public settings and only opts to cover them when she is around large numbers of elders.27

25 During our interview, C made a couple references to prostitution (sŏngmaemae). See i—D, “Grace Neutral Explores Korea’s Illegal Beauty Scene [FULL FILM]” and Yonhapnews “T’at’u 300man” for other mentions of prostitution in relation to tattooed Korean women. None of the three women I interviewed knew the origin of associations between prostitution and tattoos in Korea. 26 Tattoo Artist “C”, Oral History. 27 Tattoo Artist “C”, Instagram direct message to author.

Despite the historical association between tattoos and shame, and the South Korean government’s continued refusal to reform tattoo legislation and stop requiring medical licenses in order to tattoo, C has not consequently understood her own skin and body to be shameful.

“

”

C’s responses did not contain infor­ mation about how Korean society’s per­ ceptions of tattoos were communicated to her personally. Compared to the other artists I contacted for interviews, C is much more heavily tattooed, with colorful, old-school inspired designs covering her arms down to her wrists; I would expect that C herself may face criticism for having less delicate, small tattoos. However, C answered me with general observations of Korean society and history for most of the interview. As I reflect on my interview with her, I am left wondering how C might understand her own identity as a South Korean female tattoo artist in relation to her narration of Korean tattoo history and culture. How could C’s understanding of the criminalization of her career, as well as the historical role of tattooing as a form of corporal punishment in Korea, shape how she views herself? As a female tattoo artist in South Korea, C faces complex obstacles in Korean society and must interpret her own identity and body within a particular cultural and historical context.

I find it most encouraging that de­ spite the historical association between tattoos and shame, and the South Korean government’s continued refusal to reform tattoo legislation and stop requiring med­ ical licenses in order to tattoo, C has not consequently understood her own skin and body to be shameful. Rather, even in the historical and current context of South Korea’s tattoo history and culture, C views her tattoos as something that does not need to be hidden in the public eye and rarely chooses to censor or police her own tattoos. Although C’s experiences are nuanced and her identity negotiated, I find it significant to recognize her view of her own tattooed body, separate from historical and contemporary perceptions of tattoos and tattooing in Korea.

28 Tattoo Artist “C,” Oral History; Tattoo Artist “H,” Oral History; Tattoo Artist “Y,” Oral History. 29 Tattoo Artist “C,” Oral History; Tattoo Artist “Y,” Oral History.

Identity Negotiation: C’s Understanding and Display of Her Tattooed Body All three women I interviewed reported some instance of covering their tattoos in certain settings. However, each artist qual­ ified these statements, expressing that they do not “hide” (sumgida) or want to hide their tattoos from family or the public, but that they might “cover” (karida) them up or choose to not show them in certain contexts.28 C particularly emphasized that this covering of tattooed flesh is not an act of shame, for having tattoos is nothing shameful to her.29 While I find it encour­ aging that C does not view her tattoos as shameful, it cannot be ignored that she makes a conscious choice to cover her tat­ toos in certain social contexts. If C is un­ ashamed of her tattoos, why cover them in any situation? Certainly, C’s choice to limit the display of her tattoos around elders alone does not necessarily indicate that she feels a sense of shame as a heavily tattooed South Korean woman. How, then, could we (or should we) interpret the negoti­ ation of identity through the covering of tattoos? How is this different from “hiding” one’s flesh? And, finally, considering that this covering is not done out of shame, what are some other emotions that may be driving this action? Although all of these questions cannot be fully answered, I do think they are significant in understand­ ing the unique identities and experiences of each artist. I find that in these social situations, C does not hide her tattoos in shame but rather practices an intentional negotiation of identity that relates to her own understanding of tattoo history and culture in Korea.

This concept of negotiation is dis­ cussed by scholars who interviewed North American women with tattoos using oral history methods similar to mine. Scholars Michael Atkinson and Victoria L. Pitts both express that their interviewees’ bodies should be understood not as sites of agency or conformity alone but rather as sites of an ongoing negotiation.30 As Victoria L. Pitts notes, “Women’s marked bodies ex­ emplify both the praxis of culturally mar­ ginal body projects and the limits of that praxis. As I see it, they highlight the female body as a site of negotiation between pow­ er and powerlessness, neither of which are likely to win fully.”31 Considering this defi­ nition, I suggest that C’s body is also a site of negotiation, being displayed or covered according to context rather than sites of complete subversion of or submission to Korean societal norms.

Moreover, through examining all three oral history narratives, I find that the negotiation of one’s tattooed body and flesh is incredibly nuanced and varies on an individual level. Each negotiation is per­ sonal and is not only based on larger social hierarchies or norms but also on personal identities, relationships, and interactions. In addition to the works of Atkinson and Pitts, I also frame my understanding of identity negotiation around Deaux and Ethier’s defi­ nition: “agentic identity work carried out in response to contextual demands.”32 Essential to this definition is the agency of the identity negotiator, as well as the demands which ne­ cessitate a negotiation of identity. Given C’s responses, it is clear to me that her covering of tattoos is a conscious choice that depends heavily on contextual elements; thus, I would like to frame her as an agent rather than an object of discrimination.

30 Atkinson, “Pretty in Ink”; Pitts, In the Flesh: The Cultural Politics of Body Modification. 31 Pitts, In the Flesh: The Cultural Politics of Body Modification, 81. 32 Deaux and Ethier, “Negotiating Social Identity,” 301. 33 Atkinson, “Pretty in Ink,” 229.

”

However, I find that covering or even hiding parts of the body, whether influenced by shame or some other emotion, can also function as an exercise of agency.

To some, exercising agency exclusively looks like uncovering one’s flesh and show­ ing it at all times for the world to see. As scholar Michael Atkinson notes in his own oral history interviews with tattooed Ca­ nadian women, several believe “that tattoo body projects intended for social resistance must be visible to be effective”; otherwise, if the tattooed body remains concealed in certain circumstances, “no discernable challenge to established understandings of the body can be established.”33 However, I find that covering or even hiding parts of the body, whether influenced by shame or some other emotion, can also function as an exercise of agency. While the act of cov­ ering one’s own body is not total resistance against forces of gender and legal oppression faced by South Korean female tattoo artists, it should also not be characterized simply “ as an act of conforming to societal norms. Rather, the different ways in which each woman I interviewed intentionally covers or uncovers her tattoos can be understood as acts of agency negotiated to fit within current social and legal boundaries.

One of my most interesting findings was that the three women I interviewed chose to negotiate their identities in very specific, distinct social contexts. Contrary to what I had expected, there was no clear distinction between the artists’ negotiation of identity in public versus private spaces, around young versus old people, inside or outside of the family, etc., that was con­ sistent across all three narratives. Rather, each woman negotiates the display of her tattooed flesh, as well as her identity as a tattoo artist, in relation to specific individ­ uals or groups with whom they interact. In other words, they negotiate differently depending on the relationship between their individual, intersecting identities, and their own everyday social interactions.

As stated previously, C said that she does not cover up her tattoos in front of family or in public but will sometimes cov­ er them if she is suddenly around elders at an event like a wedding. The social and cul­ tural contexts which inform C’s negotiation are not broadly defined such as public or private, or between friends versus in front of strangers. Instead, C specifically identi­ fied elders as the group of people in front of whom she conceals her tattooed body. Moreover, C stated that she covers her tat­ toos when she ends up going to places with many older people and gives a wedding as an example of a setting in which she may encounter elders and negotiate the display of her tattoos accordingly. This suggests that C generally does not cover her tattoos in circumstances where she might encoun­ ter smaller, sporadic numbers of older people, such as when she is simply walking outside or going to the store. The formality of a large gathering and ceremony such as a wedding also seems to influence C’s nego­ tiation of her tattoos. C asserted that when she chooses to refrain from showing her tattoos, she does not do so out of shame. Combined with her consideration of her relation to others’ ages, it is possible that C instead negotiates her display of tattoos as a way to show respect for elders.

Looking at all three cases of identity negotiation together highlights how de­ cisions to negotiate identity vary across individuals. While the method of covering up tattoos and the language used to describe this act are similar throughout all three oral history narratives, the contexts which each woman feels demand this negotiation are very different. The differences in contexts — the nuances of the spaces and people which necessitate a distinct display or covering of one’s tattooed body in Korean society — also suggest that motivations behind identity ne­ gotiation can differ from person to person. Covering one’s tattoos in certain contexts becomes a conscious negotiation influenced by care, respect, and/or the consideration of others’ gaze. Care and concern for family, respect for elders, and a consciousness of what is expected of mothers in particular settings — practiced by artists Y, C, and H, respectively — shape South Korean female tattoo artists’ daily existence within the Korean tattoo industry and Korean tattoo culture more broadly.

Conclusion Ultimately, the three oral history narra­ tives told by South Korean female tattoo artists C, H, and Y inform current un­ derstandings of women’s roles in Korean tattoo history and culture by providing nuanced accounts of the evolution of Ko­ rea’s tattoo scene as well as the gendered dynamics within it. Moreover, these nar­ ratives demonstrate how each individual’s understanding of Korean tattoo culture is distinct. The timelines, social perceptions, and gender dynamics connected to Korean tattoo culture are presented differently by each artist. Together, these unique narra­ tives also suggest that each artist negoti­ ates her own tattooed identity in specific contexts related to her own understanding of Korean tattoo history and culture.

The full version of my thesis aims to answer questions relating to both the in­ terpretation of oral history more broadly and what each individual narrative reveals about different experiences of South Ko­ rean female tattoo artists. When looking at the oral history process itself, how does each woman narrate Korean tattoo culture and history in relation to her own personal identities and experiences? How can we read their narratives in a way that values what they chose to say but also acknowl­ edges and carefully considers what was left out of their accounts? When considering the specific content in each narrative and how all three narratives are distinct yet connected, what can we discover about the different roles and experiences of fe­ male South Korean tattoo artists? How do these artists make sense of their own iden­ tities as women in South Korea working in an 	 illegal industry, and how could their perceptions of Korean tattoo culture inform how they present themselves to Korean society?

34 Exploring the differences between the body and flesh and how they relate to gender ended up being outside of the scope of this

Interviewing C gave me a sense of direction for the rest of my senior thesis project, leading me to the concept of iden­ tity negotiation and shaping the questions that I would later ask artists Y and H. Af­ ter completing all three narratives, I found that each woman not only narrates her own understanding of Korean tattoo history and culture as well as how they shift over time; she also situates herself within contempo­ rary Korean society and reveals how gender dynamics do or do not exist in Korea’s tat­ too scene. Ultimately, each artist tells a story not only of the evolution of Korea’s tattoo culture but also how historical and cultural context shape the display of their tattooed bodies and flesh in Korean society.34

“The differences in contexts — the nuances of the spaces and people which necessitate a distinct display or covering of one’s tattooed body in Korean society — also suggest that motivations behind identity negotiation can differ from person to person. Covering one’s tattoos in certain contexts becomes a conscious negotiation influenced by care, respect, and/or the consideration of others’ gaze.”

Given the small scale of this project and the depth of information available from only three oral history narrators, I imagine there is great potential for success in using oral history to record more wom­ en’s perspectives of tattoo history and cul­ ture in Korea. As Namgung Ho-sŏk notes in his retelling of Korean tattoo history, current archives privilege particular narra­ tives, such as that of penal tattooing prac­ tices in the Koryŏ and Chosŏn dynasties, while leaving out other possible functions of tattoos over time.35 While our ability to make up for the missing pieces of written records is limited, making an effort to col­ lect narratives from current tattoo artists and tattooed people in South Korea will diversify future historical records. Con­ sidering the absence of women’s voices in particular, I hope to continue communi­ cating with other South Korean women about Korean tattoo culture in the future. Through oral history projects such as this thesis, the roles of marginalized people’s roles in Korean tattoo culture can be ex­ plored and recorded in depth.

In present-day Korea, tattooing is still a criminalized act; yet it has become a marker of individuality and agency. Since the Koryŏ dynasty, tattooing has trans­ formed from a form of state control of the body and flesh to an underground indus­ try operating against the law. In his own research on tattoos, Korean scholar Kim Hyŏng-jung characterizes the state’s crimi­ nalization of tattoo artists, as well as differ­ ent forms of discrimination tattooed Ko­ reans face from the government and older generations, as a method of modern tattoo punishment that evolved from the penal tattoos executed in the Koryŏ and Chosŏn dynasties.36 With this in mind, what does it mean for South Korean female tattoo artists to strategically negotiate the display of their tattooed flesh? To wear the marks that have marked slaves, criminals, gang­ sters, and prostitutes throughout Korean history? To mark their flesh and the flesh of others through a criminalized practice? To enjoy the freedom of a freelance career despite the constant danger of a fine and prison sentence?

paper; however, it is an important consideration that I plan to incorporate into future research. 35 Namgung, Han’gugŭi munshin: t’at’uisŭt’ŭga chŏnhanŭn iyagi (Korean Tattoos: A Story Told by Tattoo Artists). 36 Kim, “Han’guk Hyŏngbŏl Munsin—Ŭi Paljŏnsa—Wa Hyŏndaejŏk Ŭimi—e Taehan Sogo (A Study on the History of the Develop­ ment and Modern Meaning of the Korean Punishment Tattoo),” 44.

Through this thesis, I have at­ tempted to partially answer the first of these questions, but the rest require fur­ ther research. As I contemplate what fu­ ture research on this topic will look like, I return to the ways in which these three artists’ responses to my questions subvert­ ed many of my expectations, particularly in relation to gender dynamics. Although I expected that one or possibly even all of the artists would find ways in which their female identities shaped their work as tat­ too artists, none of them had reflected on how their work might connect to their Ko­ rean womanhood. This makes me wonder if my focus on gendered differences — such as varying perceptions of men and women with tattoos, different challenges faced by male versus female tattoo artists, etc. — was an effective way to frame my oral his­ tory questions. If these gender dichotomies of male/female and masculine/feminine experiences within Korea’s tattoo culture are not the most helpful aspect of Korean tattoo culture to analyze, what questions would be more productive? The difficulty of centering women’s voices and a gendered analysis while also capturing the significant elements shaping Korean tattoo culture be­ came very apparent through this research.

Acknowledgments First and foremost, I would like to ac­ knowledge and thank C, Y, and H for sharing their stories with me and allowing me to make them the centerpiece of this paper and my larger honors thesis project. I am so thankful that they gave me their time and were open and honest while answering my questions, and I am even more grateful that they were patient as I undoubtedly made mistakes speaking Korean. As my project continues to trans­ form and at times face setbacks, I thank every tattoo artist who responded to my requests for interviews, even if they were unable to accept the offer.

I would also like to thank my peers Sydney Smith and Joyce Giboom Park for helping me translate these interviews live while they were busy with their own work. As fellow seniors at Northwestern Univer­ sity, I know they were struggling to com­ plete their own important deadlines when they agreed to work with me. I absolutely could not have completed these interviews and this paper without their help.

Finally, I would like to thank all of my advisors at Northwestern University, inside and outside of my department. Pro­ fessors Jeong Eun Annabel We and Pat­ rick Noonan in the Department of Asian Languages and Cultures were both instru­ mental in the different stages of develop­ ing this thesis project and paper. I cannot express enough how appreciative I am of their compassion and guidance at all times while working on this project. My advisors working at the Mellon Mays Undergrad­ uate Fellowship Program at Northwest­ ern University were also there to support me whenever I felt myself losing focus. Professor Geraldo Cadava, Senior Project Coordinator Stephanie Marin, and Ph.D. students and fellows Oscar Ruben Cornejo Casares and Alexandria Keith — thank you all for everything. ◆

title: Monstrous Masculinities, Male Angst, and Adolescent Development in the Twilight Saga
text:
Monstrous Masculinities, Male Angst, and Adolescent Development in the Twilight Saga by Juliet Jacques

Department of English Faculty Adviser: Nick Davis

Introduction Over the past two decades, the Twilight series has become a staple of popular culture, with an enormous and dedicated fanbase. The “vampire versus werewolf” or “Edward versus Jacob” debate is almost universally recognizable, especially among fans of 2010s Young Adult (Y.A.) media. However, fans and critics alike miss a crucial element of analysis (or obsession) in Twilight. Inseparable from this study of masculinity is the related issue of ra­ cialization, which is especially salient for werewolf and love interest Jacob Black — Edward’s chief rival in the franchise from both a romantic and species (coded as racial) standpoint.

1 See Melissa Click’s Bitten by Twilight for a comprehensive collection of essays on Twilight’s influence on fandom culture, Holly­ wood teenage idols, and the commodification of literature.

Twilight may at first appear as an un­ usual object of literary analysis. The saga has attracted no lack of criticism, ranging all the way from its depiction of unhealthy teenage relationships to the quality of its writing. However, the series has had a profound impact on the entire Y.A. genre of popular culture. Many scholars cred­ it Twilight as paving the way for other popular franchises such as Fifty Shades of Grey, which originated as Twilight fanfic­ tion, and other teenage romances such as The Hunger Games, which has continued Twilight’s revival of the Y.A. genre’s in­ terest in tropes such as love triangles and strong, independent, teenage heroines.1 It is clear that the series has had an enduring effect on popular culture, cementing it as a cornerstone of Y.A. literature. Due to the immeasurable impact of both the original novels and the multimedia phenomenon they launched, Twilight deserves its own field of scholarship. Millions of readers and viewers have seen and internalized the saga’s surprisingly new themes surround­ ing gender roles and masculinity. Literary analysis of Twilight’s language, character construction, recurring metaphors, and Gothic antecedents can uncover the spe­ cific themes and messaging that have made Twilight such an enduring, influential, and beloved series. Furthermore, it can help us to understand the way that Y.A. literature engages with and reshapes representations of adolescent masculinity.

Analysis of the Current State of Twilight Scholarship The field of Twilight scholarship is quite young, with scholarship beginning around 2010 after the first of the novels were published in 2006 and the first film was released in 2008. Even so, in the decade since the start of the field, there has been enormous growth in scholarship and perspectives surrounding Twilight, with a growing confidence in approaching this series through various modes of literary analysis. Thus far, Twilight scholarship has followed two main avenues: close-reading analyses that examine the language and rhetoric of the texts independently as well as more sociological approaches that think about elements of the series in conversa­ tion with the success and reception of the franchise. The field is, in general, con­ flicted about how much these approaches should overlap or rely on each other. It appears as if the inclination to analyze the Twilight novels as literary texts separately from their corresponding cultural impact only came later in the 2010s. After all, it takes courage to admit to studying this series as literature.

2 It is interesting that many of the first books on Twilight were published by McFarland, including a third book, Wilson’s Seduced by Twilight. The publisher is especially known for its books on popular culture and media.

The first books and essays written on Twilight focus heavily on the sociological and cultural aspects of the series. For ex­ ample, Amy Clarke’s The Twilight Mystique (2010) and Parke and Wilson’s Theorizing Twilight: Critical Essays on What’s at Stake in a Post-Vampire World (2011) explore the overall series through the lens of its recent success.2 The essays in these books are often reflexive in that they think both about how Twilight is influenced by popu­ lar culture norms and stereotypes as well as how it influences them in return. Thus, in these earlier books, it is harder to separate literary analysis from sociological analysis. These articles act almost as primary sourc­ es because they differ so much from the intricate, detailed analyses of language and theme that come later. In fact, early authors such as Benning (2011) acknowledge that they are writing at the very beginning of the field and suggest many potential topics for later authors. These older articles often cover both a sociological analysis of the readers and culture surrounding Twilight as well as more literary elements of the text itself, particularly genre tropes and influ­ ential literary predecessors. However, this seemingly comprehensive approach actu­ ally weakens the literary analysis because scholars are unwilling to look at Twilight’s language and themes for their own merit, separately from the ensuing reception and sociological aspects. To better understand the success and appeal of the series and its legacy in Y.A. fiction, we should also view the textual elements themselves as insight­ ful and intentional.

Indeed, as more articles were writ­ ten and published, the field became more varied and more accommodating of close-reading methodologies. For exam­ ple, Anne Morey’s collection Genre, Recep­ tion, and Adaptation in the ‘Twilight’ Series (2012) looks and reads much differently from earlier collections in its willingness to analyze the literary aspects of the series separately from the sociological. Claudia Bucciferro’s collection The Twilight Saga: Exploring the Global Phenomenon (2014) also demonstrates this growth, though it is no­ table that studies of Twilight remain con­ fined to para-academic publishers and not major university presses. Overall, these later books divide the two types of analysis more than previous collections — a trend that only grows throughout the rest of the decade. Morey’s introduction separates the articles by subject matter: first looking at genre and narrative within Twilight, then turning to the reception of Twilight as a cultural phenomenon, and finally study­ ing adaptation and film. Significantly, Morey emphasizes the importance of studying novels in the romance genre — a well-established practice within literary and cultural studies, especially in the wake of Janice Radway’s foundational text Reading the Romance (1991), but not previously applied to Twilight, at least in print. As with Morey’s, Bucciferro’s book is divided into sections for articles on spe­ cific areas of study, such as fandom and reception, gender in Twilight, and looking beyond the franchise. This last section is particularly interesting, as it recognizes Y.A. novels as their own genre that de­ serves analysis by examining common themes and tropes across a varied section of series and franchises.

3  Examples of this common tendency include Torkelson’s Violence, Agency, and the Women of Twilight (2011), Rocha’s Wife, Mother, Vampire: The Female Role in the Twilight Series (2014), Durham’s Blood, Lust and Love: Interrogating Gender Violence in the Twilight Phenomenon (2011), and similar critiques cited later in this thesis. 4 Ashley Benning’s “How Old are You?” Representations of Age in the Saga (2011) argues that the lack and ineffectiveness of parental figures in Twilight allows Bella the independence to come of age.

Other clear patterns emerge as schol­ arship on Twilight evolves. Early literature focused on critiquing antifeminist and mi­ sogynist aspects of the series, arguing that Bella was forced to submit to a dominant patriarchal culture.3 After this initial ap­ proach, and likely in response to the cul­ tural backlash and hatred for the series, an opposing, postfeminist movement arose, wherein scholars began to look at the ways in which Bella could still represent a progressive, autonomous character. These two reactions formed the basis for the field of scholarship, but authors then quickly moved beyond these “good” and “bad” bi­ naries, and scholarship began to be more detailed, intricate, and creative. Twilight scholarship became more diversified as authors looked beyond the more obvious aspects of the series, such as the portrayal of unhealthy teenage relationships, to take a more nuanced look at gender roles and relationships, albeit with a predominant interest in the female gender. Scholarship also began looking at Twilight as a coming- of-age series or bildungsroman in which Bella finds her place and identity in the world.4 Whereas earlier authors wrote broadly about the series, later authors began filling in the gaps, finding more intricacies and subtleties. For example, Nicole Willms, writing in Bucciferro’s collection, discusses race, masculinity, and rivalry in the series, and Sara Day, as a contributor to Morey’s anthology, argues that Bella’s increasing passivity can be un­ derstood through the lens of what she calls “narrative intimacy” and her weakening relationship with the reader as the series progresses. Both of these articles lay the key groundwork for readings I pursue later in this thesis.

The Limits of Current Approaches to the Study of Gender and Masculinity Within this emerging field of Twilight literary scholarship, one subfield looks at portrayals of gender and masculinity using two common approaches. The first refer­ ences Gothic tropes and historical charac­ teristics in relation to gender and sexuality. For example, Budruweit (2016) argues that Twilight sanitizes Gothic monsters, instead making women’s uncontrolled bodies into the primary sites of the “mon­ strous.” In contrast, Moruzi (2012) gives a postfeminist reading of Bella, arguing that the incorporation of Gothic characteristics intensifies the romance, adding danger and allowing Bella to explore her desires and identity, which can be messy without being monstrous. Moruzi argues that as­ pects of Edward such as self-discipline, in­ experience, and “vegetarianism” (Twilight’s language for vampires who refuse to feed off humans) shift the power dynamics of their relationship, obligating the male part­ ner to the stereotypically feminine task of relentless self-monitoring, and by contrast allowing Bella more control and autonomy.

5 There is a large, in-depth body of literature on this Gothic tradition, especially for Twilight’s 19th century vampiric counterparts as Stoker’s Dracula (1897) and Le Fanu’s Carmilla (1872). Just a few of the essays on this topic include Craft’s “Kiss Me with those Red Lips”: Gender and Inversion in Bram Stoker’s Dracula (1984), Signoretti’s Repossessing the Body – Transgressive Desire in “Carmilla” and “Dracula” (1996), and Schaffer’s “A Wilde Desire Took Me”: The Homoerotic History of Dracula (1994).

Beyond short-changing the texts under review, these Bella-centric approaches to the series lead scholars to ignore masculine characters’ questions and anxieties about their own performance of masculinity and the way male identity relates to the supernatural. “

“

These two examples demonstrate the common elements scholars often de­ fer to when talking about the Gothic in conjunction with Twilight. These generic tropes, whether physical (blood), moral or behavioral (self-control), affective (desire), or specifically sexual (including queerness, or an alleged lack of queerness) can be cat­ egorized as disparate yet closely connected aspects of the Gothic, all of which center the body in some way. Desire for blood and desire for sex always go hand in hand in this tradition: The act of desiring and drinking blood is often erotic, representing other sexual desires, usually those deemed devi­ ant.5 For example, scholars such as Moruzi (2012) and Lindén (2013) argue that the desire for blood is replaced or subordinated by the desire for sex in these more recent, Y.A.-style reinterpretations of vampirism. However, this approach again fails to look at major, masculine characters such as Ed­ ward as individuals who confront other conflicts and wrestle with their own stages of development, separate from their ro­ mantic relationships. Thus, critical lenses such as postfeminism and others that pre­ vail in Twilight scholarship may not do full analytical justice to these characters.

Within this Gothic approach, schol­ ars also look at Twilight in terms of its po­ tential historical influences from 19th-cen­ tury British novels and their often Byronic heroes. Common comparisons in studies such as Nancy Reagin’s Twilight and Histo­ ry (2010) include the love interests from Pride and Prejudice (1813), Jane Eyre (1847), and Wuthering Heights (1847).6 These texts are often chosen because of overt refer­ ences in the Twilight novels. However, scholarship too often conflates Twilight’s themes and internal dynamics with those of its famous predecessors without paying enough attention to their differences or, once more, thinking more forwardly about masculinity and male characters. In other words, while literary-historical analysis foregrounding 19th-century antecedents of Twilight is an interesting and fruitful approach, there is a gap in that literature connecting these historical perspectives with how Edward thinks of himself, his masculinity, and his quasi-filial relation to his vampire “creator,” Carlisle. In addition, there is a dearth of scholarship that reads Twilight with its more monstrous, Gothic predecessors, an issue that will be discussed more in Chapter 2. Because Bella is the pri­ mary narrator, scholars are more likely to think critically about her actions and moti­ vations while taking Edward’s at face val­ ue, even if he is Twilight’s clearest anchor within the Gothic tradition specifically and perhaps in 19th-century character tropes more broadly.

6 For a variety of articles on this topic, see Parke and Wilson’s Theorizing Twilight (2010), specifically the second part of the col­ lection titled: Once Upon a Twilight: Fairy Tales, Byronic (Anti) Heroes, Post-Feminist Romance, and Growing Up in a Twilight World.

The other common approach to looking at gender and masculinity moves away from literary and cultural paths to argue that characters such as Edward are most interesting for how they embody the characteristics and desires of current soci­ ety. This approach, whether or not it re­ flects the sociological and reception-based tendencies in early Twilight criticism, also considers the way Twilight both influences and is influenced by societal values. For example, Christensen’s article Blood Absti­ nent Vampires and the Women Who Consume Them (2013) argues that these 21st-century vampires represent a desirable Other, an antiseptic epitome of consumer culture in explicit contrast to Gothic messiness. In Twilight, the Cullen family is inhumanly beautiful and perfect: a collective para­ gon, to which other characters, as well as readers, aspire. In Mukherjea’s My Vampire Boyfriend: Postfeminism, “Perfect” Masculini­ ty, and the Contemporary Appeal of Paranor­ mal Romance (2011) she argues that these vampire boyfriends present a “perfect” mix of masculinity, embodying white, old-fash­ ioned, gentlemanly, and protective values without crossing a line into patriarchal creepiness or overtly controlling behavior (in Twilight alone, Bella describes Edward as “perfect” over 30 times). Characters such as Edward also juggle values from multiple eras and classes. This combination allows female characters to perform patriarchal norms of femininity while also gaining freedom from societal values and explor­ ing their own independence. Once again, articles like these omit any focus on mas­ culinity or male angst, instead centering anxieties around postfeminism and how to be feminist. The two examples I have cited, though seemingly very different, get close to the issue of men’s anxiety around mas­ culinity and growth, specifically Edward’s, but never actually address it. Christensen focuses only on the 21st-century aspects of vampires, without thinking about their influences from previous eras. Mukherjea acknowledges that characters like Edward are juggling values from multiple eras but focuses only on how that confusion affects their romantic partners. They argue that Edward and other male characters always portray masculinity “perfectly” without considering how this pressure to perform may affect them internally, even though the original novels clearly indicate that struggle.

Midnight Sun further confirms that there are more elements at play in the series than Ed­ ward’s relationship with Bella.

Beyond short-changing the texts un­ der review, these Bella-centric approaches to the series lead scholars to ignore mas­ culine characters’ questions and anxieties about their own performance of mascu­ linity and the way male identity relates to the supernatural. More broadly, these interpretive angles perpetuate patriarchal assumptions and norms around the in­ fallibility and confidence of cis-heterosex­ ual men. Much of Edward’s inner conflict centers around his own relationship with vampirism, aging, and eternal adolescence, rather than being focused solely on Bella. Distancing our analysis of Edward from Bel­ la’s perspective will reveal his own deep dis­ comfort and insecurity, foregrounding his intense self-scrutiny rather than Bella’s sec­ ond-hand and often idealized observations.

“

”

As a subject of analysis, masculinity regularly receives less focus than women and feminism, with particular gaps around cis, straight, masculine characters. By paying attention to these gaps and studying these types of masculinities, we can gain a better understanding of how these characters internalize and perpetuate toxic patriarchal norms, but also offer alternative masculinities that already exist.

In reality, as a very old vampire, Ed­ ward is navigating both these historical values and current ones. The messiness of these past and present pressures reveals how some forms of masculine and patriar­ chal anxieties have not changed completely for men over this long historical timespan. The past and present often unstably coexist for Edward, although Twilight criticism of­ ten does try to partition the past from the present. We need to look at how maturity is portrayed within an unchanging but eter­ nal vampire body and how Edward views his maturation in relation to both humans, such as Bella, and other vampires, like Carlisle. Edward’s relationship to growth is fraught because his expected character development and societal pressure contrast with his allegedly “perfect,” unchangeable, and impermeable exterior. In other words, as Edward’s life changes and society chang­ es around him, his appearance cannot also change in parallel. The mythology around vampires as unchanging and set in stone both physically and psychologically at the age they are “turned” (when they are bitten) contributes to his general anxiety and insecurity about his inhumanness and inability to change. Because scholarship focuses on Bella’s relationships and char­ acter growth, we are currently missing an understanding of how Edward has his own anxieties around morality and masculinity and how being a vampire not only “freez­ es” his development, but also prompts his constant uneasiness and self-questioning. This pattern within Twilight scholarship also points to a broader gap in masculinity scholarship within the field of gender stud­ ies as a whole, including its engagement with literature. As a subject of analysis, masculinity regularly receives less focus than women and feminism, with particular gaps around cis, straight, masculine char­ acters. By paying attention to these gaps and studying these types of masculinities, we can gain a better understanding of how these characters internalize and perpetuate toxic patriarchal norms, but also offer al­ ternative masculinities that already exist.

To gain a fuller understanding of Ed­ ward and the diverse — and perhaps con­ tradictory — ways masculinity is presented within the series, we need to think of him as an independent and fallible character rather than only as an ideal romantic inter­ est for Bella. This, of course, is inherently difficult because Bella’s voice offers our only direct access to Edward’s headspace until Midnight Sun directly engages his per­ spective. But even before that point, when we consciously step back from Bella’s nar­ ration and cast doubt on her omniscience, the first Twilight novel does offer ways to take stock of Edward’s feelings and conflicts in ways that are not solely about Bella. By decentering Bella, even in the texts she nar­ rates, we can glean suggestive information about Edward’s other relationships, such as the father-son or perhaps creator-creature relationship with Carlisle, whom he often looks to as a role model.

In tandem with this new approach, we need to turn to other, often ignored Gothic aspects to understand Edward as an independent, three-dimensional character. As mentioned earlier, Twilight scholarship always reverts to Gothic vampiric tropes associated with sex and desire. Instead, we should also look at Gothic elements such as the interior versus the exterior, the du­ ality of identity, and the monster within. Midnight Sun’s emphasis on the monstrous Gothic solidifies Twilight’s connections to foundational novels like Dracula, as well as revealing its nods to other kinds of Gothic novels, such as Robert Louis Stevenson’s Strange Case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde (1886) and Oscar Wilde’s The Picture of Dorian Gray (1890).

Twilight’s complex masculine love interests and characters are at odds with the traditional heroes of romance novels by even being allowed to grow and change, rather than offering a fantastical, uniform, and “perfect” symbol of masculinity. Twi­ light’s massive, global readership means that the themes and characters within the series have an incalculable influence on fans, pop culture, and the genre of Y.A. fiction. Studying Edward well outside the terms of his romantic relationship with Bella serves not just to help us better un­ derstand his character, but to provide a whole new lens through which to under­ stand all masculine characters in the series.

“Twilight’s complex masculine love interests and characters are at odds with the traditional heroes of romance novels by even being allowed to grow and change, rather than offering a fantastical, uniform, and ‘perfect’ symbol of masculinity.”

Although it is easy to see Edward and Jacob as the pop cultural movement tends to por­ tray them, and which is exacerbated by the films, particularly New Moon and Eclipse, they are so much more than two dimen­ sional, hypersexualized, and idolized love interests.7 As the franchise has emphasized and commercialized the love triangle, the characters themselves are forced into stereotypical roles to portray hegemonic, toxic representations of masculinity. In parallel, the seemingly equal competition and dislike between the werewolves and the vampires is unbalanced and entirely due to the actions of the Cullens. When we take a closer look at the novels, we see a much more complex version of these char­ acters, many of whom do not fit into the masculine tropes that critics often assume the series to be arguing for, as well as a more nuanced portrayal of race.

Ultimately, all the masculine char­ acters in Twilight, both supernatural and human, are part of a complex system of social dynamics, each navigating their own relationship to masculinity and patriarchal norms, and each invites and deserves more attention and investigation than we often are willing to give characters credit for in a seemingly banal, generic teenage romance novel. As Nina Auerbach argues in her foundational book Our Vampires, Ourselves (1995), “every age embraces the vampire it needs” (145).8 Edward is certainly one of the most prominent vampires of this generation and so analyzing his own trials and tribulations with adolescence, matu­ ration, and the performance of masculin­ ity will perhaps help us understand why so many people gravitate toward Twilight, and what about the teenage experience in the 2000s has made it such an influential and beloved series.◆

7 See Cunningham (2012) for a thoughtful analysis of the changes between the novels and their adaptations. Beyond the ways the movies alter the narratives, even the promotional campaigns rewrite the modes and relations of different masculinities as I have outlined them in this project. For example, the hugely prevalent posters advertising the films feature Edward and Jacob looking brooding and dark, with Bella posed in between, directly in the spirit of the patterns Radway set forth but which Meyer compli­ cates. 8 Auerbach is an omnipresent, influential authority in the field of vampire studies. Her detailed and wide-ranging book documents and analyzes literary vampires from the 19th and 20th centuries, using the varied representations of vampires throughout the decades as a lens to study cultural history. This quote in particular is cited ubiquitously in vampire scholarship, and so this thesis would not be complete without following in this tradition.
