title: Structural Characterization via X-Ray Crystallography of III-Nitrides for APDs
text:
Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering

Structural Characterization via X-Ray Crystallography of

III-Nitrides for APDs by Michael Richards

Faculty Adviser: Dr. Manijeh Razeghi

Motivation

Research and development of III-Nitride semiconductors have led to promising, and increasingly important, optoelectronic applications ranging from light-emitting diodes (LEDs) to photodetectors (PDs). Previous developments in the III-Nitride material system have given rise to blue and green LEDs, while future advancement will allow for ultraviolet (U.V.) LEDs. Perhaps the most promising application is solar-blind deep- U.V. avalanche photodiodes (APDs) in Geiger mode for single photon detection, with high quantum efficiency (QE) and gain and low dark current. P.D.s in the U.V. range allow for precise control of furnaces via monitoring U.V. heat signatures within the civilian market [1]. The U.S. military has also conveyed its desire for solar-blind deep- U.V. APDs, operating between 200 and 250 nm for the detection of bio-chemical weap­ ons, explosive signatures, and missiles, as well as for covert space communications [2].

Due to the nature by which organic material characteristically fluoresces under U.V. light, PDs have also lent themselves to the detection of pathogens, bacteria, and chemicals such as Anthrax, Smallpox, Marburg, Ebola, Plague, and Tular [3]. With the advent of COVID-19, the focus of deep-U.V. APD-based detection is shifting to a new, more prominent threat in a pandemic-stricken society, and it is believed that these APDs will allow for the detection of this virus’ U.V. fluorescence with high-accuracy. Ulti­ mately, this technology will allow for the simultaneous fluorescence and detection of COVID-19 through portable U.V. LEDs and APDs.

Background

The III-Nitride semiconductor material system — formed from the combina­ tion of group III elements with group V Nitrogen — consists of AlN, GaN, InN, and their alloys. The most important property of III-Nitride semiconductors is their wide and direct bandgap energy. The wide bandgap allows for short, high energy wavelengths in the green, blue, and U.V. regions of the electromagnetic spectrum; the direct bandgap is ideal for optoelectronic applications as energy tran­ sitions do not require a momentum shift in k-space, which translates to stronger absorption and emission as optical transi­ tions will more readily occur [1]. AlN has a particularly large bandgap energy of 6.2 eV, which allows for bandgap engineering of solar-blind AlxGa1-xN epilayers accord­ ing to Vegard’s Law (Equation 1).

(1)

Within the U.V. range of the electromagnetic spectrum exist three sub- bands: long-wavelength U.V.-A (315-400 nm), medium-wavelength U.V.-B (280- 315 nm), and short-wavelength U.V.-C (100-280 nm), of which only U.V.-C is solar-blind [4]. The solar-blind region is critical for photodetection as it is the range at which the Earth’s ozone layer com­ pletely absorbs all solar radiation, leaving only artificially generated electromagnetic radiation. The solar-blind nature of III- Nitride-based deep-U.V. APDs is crucial to detection due to their single-photon sensitivity, as extraneous sun-originated radiation would detrimentally impact the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR).

Preceding the sophistication and development of the APD, the industry has relied on P.D.s such as the Schottky Metal-Semiconductor-Metal (MSM) pho­ todiode and the p-i-n photodiode. The MSM photodiode consists of two Schottky contacts on an intrinsic (undoped) semi­ conductor layer. These contacts operate through the rectification of a difference in work functions between metal and semiconductor through an electrostatic barrier, and carrier transport is fueled by thermionic emission [5]. This photodiode is easy to fabricate and is fast and efficient; however, it requires a high absorption co­ efficient, does not have a sharp cutoff or band-pass response, and may only operate via front-illumination. The p-i-n photodi­ ode, instead, makes use of doping to create n- and p-type regions separated by an in­ trinsic region, which has a low free-carrier density and high resistivity [5]. For this reason, it is capable of high-speed opera­ tion with low noise and low dark current. The main drawback of the p-i-n junction is its poor sensitivity under low reverse-bias conditions.

“The focus of deep-U.V. APD-based detection is shifting to a new, more prominent threat in a pandemic- stricken society, and it is believed that these APDs will allow for the detection of this virus’ U.V. fluorescence with high-accuracy.”

Design

Despite the merits of other photodiodes, the APD is optimal for applications in deep-U.V. single-photon detection for its high speed and extremely high gain, which benefits sensitivity. Unfortunate­ ly, there are many difficulties associated with the APD, including high sensitivity to defects and dislocations, high doping requirements, and leakage paths, which reduce the noise equivalent power (NEP) and therefore detectivity. The crux of APD design is to achieve high external quantum efficiency (EQE) and internal gain (M) while maintaining low dark current.

The APD is essentially a strongly re­ verse-biased p-i-n junction. This bias has the effect of causing an avalanche effect via impact ionization, wherein released charge carriers are accelerated and collide to gen­ erate additional electron-hole pairs (EHPs) in the active region resulting in a cascade (avalanche) of EHPs due to a single photon [5]. The carrier type that dominates the ionization is given by the ionization ratio (k) and dictates the performance of the device, with k>>1 being hole-dominant and k<<1 being electron-dominant [5]. An ionization ratio of approximately 1, mean­ ing that both carriers ionize effectively, is undesirable as the excess noise factor (F) increases linearly with internal gain (M), demonstrated in Figure 1. For the APDs designed at the Center for Quantum De­ vices (CQD), an ionization ratio of k<<1 is desired for its electron-dominance.

A III-Nitride ternary alloy, AlxGa1-xN, is selected for the p-i-n heterostructure of the APD due to its tunable bandgap be­ tween 3.4 eV and 6.2 eV, allowing for so­ lar-blind detection. Pertaining to the doped region of the p-i-n, p-AlxGa1-xN is doped with Mg while n-AlxGa1-xN is doped with Si. The p-i-n is grown on highly doped n+- AlxGa1-xN, which itself is grown on pulsed atomic layer epitaxy (PALE) AlN on a low-temperature (LT) AlN buffer [6]. GaN is used as a capping layer. These epitaxial layers are grown on a wurtzite/sapphire (Al2O3) substrate on the (00.2) plane. The APD structure is shown in Figure 2. The AlxGa1-xN epilayers have high dislocation densities due to the large lattice mismatch with the sapphire substrate and the high Al-content AlxGa1-xN, which comprise the APD, has low doping efficiencies. Both act to the detriment of the necessary high gain and sharp avalanche breakdown.

Growth

The epitaxial growth of APDs is per­ formed using CQD’s AXITRON metalor­ ganic-chemical-vapor-deposition (MOC­ VD) system. This growth technique is used for its capability for high-quality, thin-film deposition with atomic layer precision and abrupt interfaces [5]. The MOCVD system consists of a gas handling system, reactor chamber, exhaust system, and safety apparatus for toxic gas moni­ toring, the schematic of which is shown in Figure 3 [5]. Necessary for high-qual­ ity, low-defect, and single crystalline epilayers is precise control of the growth pressure, temperature, and III/V ratio. The group III sources are trimethylalumi­ num (TMAl) for Al and trimethylgallium (TMGa) for Ga, while the group V source is NH3 [7]. The Ga dopants are silane (SiH4) for n-doping with Si and DCpMg for p-doping with Mg [7].

Structural Characterization

X-Ray Diffractometry

X-ray crystallography is the experimen­ tal field wherein the molecular structure of crystalline materials is determined by the diffraction pattern of incident X-ray beams. Since X-ray electromagnetic ra­ diation is on the same order as the lattice spacing of the crystal structure (on the order of 1 Å), the resulting interference pattern from the incident beams is unique to the crystal and can reveal information regarding its structure and properties [8].

At CQD, X-ray crystallography is performed using the X-ray diffractometer (XRD). X-rays of approximately 1.54 Å are created by bombarding a water-cooled cop­ per target with electrons, introduced with a current of about 40 mA and accelerated to 20-50 keV [8]. This process, known as the Bremsstrahlung effect, is responsible for the generation of X-rays via electron-neg­ ative acceleration upon interaction with the copper nucleus’ Coulomb field. The X-rays are then filtered and collimated into a coherent, monochromatic beam. The co­ herent X-ray beam is diffracted through the crystalline sample and the interference pattern, dictated by Bragg’s Law (Equation 2), is recorded as the angle of incidence is varied [8].

(2)

Characterization of many of the III-Nitride semiconductors’ structural properties can be determined by XRD. Bragg’s Law is used to determine the lat­ tice constant of the crystal. If the rocking curve is narrow and the wavelength of the X-ray is known, the lattice constant may be determined by measuring the epilayer omega peak position relative to the sub­ strate reference peak [1]. Lattice mismatch between epilayers or substrate is indicative of the strain or relaxation present in the crystal [8]. The size of the rocking curve’s full-width at half-maximum(FWHM), which can be easily obtained from a sym­ metric XRD scan, is inversely related to the number of dislocations in the epilayer and therefore an indicator of film quality [3]. The composition of alloy III-Nitrides can be determined from Vegard’s Law using the lattice constants calculated from the XRD. Though traditionally achieved through more destructive or involved characterization techniques, XRD has even been shown to provide an accurate estimate of mosaicity and defect densities within crystalline materials using a tech­ nique known as Williamson-Hall plots. The thickness of epilayers and superlattice periods can be determined by the distance between satellite peaks on either side of the principal peak, known as Pendellösung os­ cillations, while the intensity and number of satellites are indicative of film quality.

CQD uses a Philips HR-XRD system for structural characterization. The X-ray half-beam intensity is kept at 30,000 steps for III-Nitride scans. For sample adjust­ ment, the X-ray is left in standby mode, 5 mA and -35 kV, and the shutters are closed; however, for performing scans of the sam­ ple, this is increased to 35 mA and the shut­ ters are opened. Important parameters, which must be controlled by the system, include the angle the sample stage makes with the incident beam (ω), the angle the detector axis makes with the incident beam (2θ), the tilt about the intersection of the plane of scattering vectors with the plane of the sample holder (φ), and the rotation about the surface normal (χ). In symmetric diffractometry, the angle of incidence, ω, is equal to the angle of detection, θ, which allows for probing of the sample normal, yielding information such as the c-plane family (00.1) in wurtzite crystalline struc­ tures; whereas in asymmetric diffractom­ etry, the angle of incidence, ω, is not the same as the angle of detection, θ, allowing for probing of a multitude of planes, unob­ tainable through symmetric geometry such as the (10-15) plane.

Williamson-Hall

Williamson-Hall (W-H) plots allow for an estimated analysis of the mosaicity of epitaxial layers — including tilt angle (αtilt), heterogeneous strain (ε┴), lateral coherence length (L║), and perpendicular coherence length (L┴) — via symmetric X-ray crystallography of three orders of the (00.1) plane: (00.2), (00.4), and (00.6) [9]. W-H plots take the form of in-plane or perpendicular, with the former being the plot of βω-2θ(sinθ)/λ vs. (sinθ)/λ and the latter being βω-2θ(cosθ)/λ vs. (cosθ)/λ, where βω-2θ is the full-width at half-max­ imum (FWHM), θ is the diffraction peak angle, and λ is the wavelength of the X-ray [9]. The (00.2), (00.4), and (00.6) values are plotted according to these axes and a linearly fit line is drawn. For the in-plane W-H plot, the lateral coherence length takes the form of the y-intercept of the linearly fit line, in angstroms, while the tilt angle takes the form of the slope of this linearly fit line, in degrees. For the perpendicular W-H plot, the perpendic­ ular coherence length takes the form of the y-intercept of the linearly fit line, in angstroms, while the heterogeneous strain takes the form of the slope of this linearly fit line.

The above four parameters, which describe the mosaicity of epitaxial layers, are essential to understanding the crys­ talline structure and quality of the III-Ni­ trides used at CQD for the development of APDs. Due to a large mismatch in lattice constants between the sapphire substrate and epitaxial layers, as well as a difference in thermal expansion coefficients, III-Ni­ trides take on a mosaic structure of discrete wurtzite grains due to the breaking of crys­ talline periodicity [10]. Figure 4 models the III-Nitride mosaicity, described by the four parameters estimated by W-H plots. The lateral and perpendicular coherence lengths describe the average mosaic grain size, which is dictated by epilayer thickness [9]. The tilt angle describes the angular distribution of mosaic grains normal to the c-plane, while the heterogeneous strain describes the strain along the c-plane (growth plane) due to mismatch between differing epitaxial materials [9].

W-H plots may also be used to es­ timate the screw (threading) dislocation density of epitaxial layers. Screw disloca­ tions occur when one side of the crystal undergoes shear stress and is displaced at least one lattice plane, while the other side is held fixed, modeled in Figure 5 [8]. Using the tilt angle, in radians, determined by the slope of the linear fit of the in-plane W-H plot, Equation 3 may be used to determine the screw dislocation density, where αΩ is

(3)

the tilt angle in radians and bc is the screw dislocation Burgers vector, particular to each epitaxial material [11]. The screw dis­ location Burgers vector (b = [00.1]) for AlN is 20.1 Å and 10.7 Å for GaN. The Burgers vector for AlxGa1-xN can be determined for its mole concentration using Vegard’s law (Equation 1). III-Nitride reference screw dislocation densities are readily available in the literature, with AlN on the order of 107 cm-2 and AlGaN on the order of 108 cm-2. The magnitude of increase between epilayers is inversely proportional to the quality of growth, wherein a small change in dislocation density from one epilayer to the next is preferable.

Thickness & Pendellösung Oscillation

In the case of high-quality epitaxial growths, X-ray crystallography may be used to calculate epilayer thicknesses. This is done via measurement of the Pendellösung oscillations which may be observed on one shoulder of an XRD epitaxial diffraction peak. These oscilla­ tions originate from the sharp interfaces between epilayers of high-quality growth, often the interface between the epilayer and substrate [12]. The epilayer thickness may be calculated according to Equation 4, where λ is the X-ray wavelength (~1.54 Å), Δθ is the Pendellösung period of oscil­ lation (the angular distribution between Pendellösung peaks), and θ is the diffrac­ tion peak [12].

(4)

Mismatch

Sapphire (Al2O3), used as a substrate, and the III-Nitrides used in the APD design have wurtzite crystal structure. This, cou­ pled with sapphire’s transparency to the deep-U.V., makes sapphire an ideal choice of substrate. The only major drawback of sapphire is its large lattice mismatch with III-Nitrides - an approximately 13% mismatch with AlN, which is shown in Figure 6 [3]. Large mismatches can result in semi-coherent or incoherent interphase boundaries, subject to strain-induced cracks, edge dislocations, and other defect structures. A III-Nitride substrate such as AlN would significantly reduce the mis­ match present; however, AlN is not prac­ tical due to its high cost and defect-related luminescence [13].

The relative difference in the in-plane lattice parameters of an interface boundary is used to determine the mismatch. In the case of wurtzite grown in the (00.1) ori­ entation, the a-planar family is in-plane. The hexagonal lattice parameter equation (Equation 5) is used to first determine the c-plane lattice parameter from the (00.2) diffraction peak angle and then the a-plane lattice parameter from the (10-15) peak [13].

(5)

XRD Findings

AlN on Sapphire (Al2O3) Substrate

W-H plots are used to determine the mosaicity and screw dislocation density of AlN samples grown on sapphire sub­ strates. The W-H plots calculated for one sample (R6-13036) are shown in Figure 7(a), for in-plane, and Figure 7(b), for perpendicular. This growth has a tilt, αtilt, of 0.1301° and a heterogeneous strain, ε┴, of 0.0176. The growth has a lateral coher­ ence length, L║, of approximately 222 nm and a perpendicular coherence length, L┴, of approximately 445 nm. Using the tilt angle and the AlN screw Burger’s vector, the screw dislocation density could be determined according to Equation 3. The screw dislocation density was found to be 2.9328×107 cm-2, which agrees with the expected value for AlN on sapphire.

The epilayer thicknesses of partic­ ularly high-quality AlN samples grown on sapphire (00.1) can be determined by measuring the period of the Pendellösung oscillations observed on ω scans of the (00.2) diffraction peak. The AlN epilayer thickness is calculated according to Equa­ tion 4 and then compared to more direct measurements of the epitaxial cross-sec­ tion using scanning electron microscopy (SEM). The Pendellösung oscillations (top) and SEM imaging (bottom) are shown for two samples in Figure 8. A discrepancy of 8-9% relative to the average of multiple measurements taken from SEM imaging is reported. This represents a difference of tens of nanometers on calculated thick­ nesses of 186 nm for sample R6-13024 in Figure 8(a), an 8.4% discrepancy, and 244 nm for sample R6-13025 in Figure 8(b), a 9% discrepancy. The mismatch between the AlN epitaxial growth and the sapphire sub­ strate can be determined by the in-plane (a-plane) lattice parameters. To measure this, the difference between mismatched (AlN on sapphire) and no lattice mismatch (AlN on AlN) samples are compared. No mismatch AlN has an a-plane lattice parameter of 2.94 Å (5.5% error), while mismatched AlN has an a-plane lattice parameter of 3.37 Å (8.1% error). This rep­ resents a mismatch of 14.5% with the AlN epilayer under strain, which is higher than expected. The large error of the a-plane lattice parameters is assumed to be a result of the Philips HR-XRD system, and more steps will have to be taken to optimize θ to improve accuracy.

AlN on AlN Substrate

W-H plots are used to determine the mosaicity and screw dislocation density of an AlN sample grown on an AlN substrate

(R6-12731), shown in Figure 9(a), for in- plane, and Figure 9(b), for perpendicular. This growth has a tilt, θtilt, of 0.0144° and a negligible strain, ε┴, of 0.0011, due to the nature of the homoepitaxial growth. The growth has a lateral coherence length, L║, of approximately 2.1 μm and a perpendic­ ular coherence length, L┴, of approximate­ ly 2.9 μm, owing to a thick AlN growth. The screw dislocation density was found to be 3.607×105 cm-2, which is two orders of magnitude less than that for AlN on a sapphire substrate indicating a substantial­ ly lower-defect growth.

AlxGa1-xN/AlN/Al2O3 W-H plots are used to determine the mosaicity and screw dislocation density of an AlxGa1-xN/AlN/Al2O3 growth (R6- 13056), shown in Figure 10: (a) and (b) are the in-plane and perpendicular plots for AlN, respectively, and (c) and (d) are the in-plane and perpendicular plots for AlxGa1-xN, respectively. This growth has a tilt, θtilt, of 0.1547° for AlN and 0.4034° for AlxGa1-xN. It has a heterogeneous strain, ε┴, of 0.0114 for AlN and 0.0282 for AlxGa1-xN. The lateral coherence length, L║, is approximately 195 nm for AlN and 83 nm for AlxGa1-xN. The perpendicular coherence length, L┴, is approximately 268 nm for AlN and 83 nm for AlxGa1-xN. The screw dislocation density was found to be 4.15×107 cm-2 for AlN and 4.86×108 cm-2 for AlxGa1-xN, which aligns with the expected values.

XRD mapping is performed on Alx­ Ga1-xN/AlN/Al2O3 to assess sample unifor­ mity. W-H plots are used to calculate the dislocation density, tilt, strain, and lateral and perpendicular coherence lengths of each epitaxial material at each point on the wafer. Additionally, bandgap energies, lattice parameters, and mole compositions of AlxGa1-xN are mapped across each lo­ cation. Figure 11 shows the aerial (a) and cross-section views (b) of an AlxGa1-xN sample (R6-13039), on which four loca­ tions, each 1 mm apart, were selected in uniformity mapping.

The AlxGa1-xN and AlN epilayers show good uniformity across the wafer for each measured parameter. Figure 12(a) shows the screw dislocation densities of each material at each of the four mapped locations; the mapping reveals a change in dislocation density of only about one order of magnitude between the AlN and AlxGa1-xNepilayers, which is highly desir­ able. Figure 12(b) shows the tilt angle and Figure 12(c) the heterogeneous strain at each mapped location, which were extrap­ olated from the slopes of the in-plane and perpendicular W-H plots, respectively. It should be noted that the tilt angle and het­ erogeneous strains are both slightly larger for the AlxGa1-xN epilayer, owing to the na­ ture of the epitaxial layering. Figure 12(d) shows the lateral coherence lengths and Figure 12(e) the perpendicular coherence lengths at each mapped location, which were extrapolated from the y-intercepts of the in-plane and perpendicular W-H plots, respectively. Since the coherence lengths represent the average grain size and are indicative of the growth thickness, it is ex­ pected that the thicker AlN epilayer should have a larger coherence length.

APD

XRD mapping is performed on the final APD epitaxial structure to assess sample uniformity. W-H plots are used to cal­ culate the dislocation density, tilt, strain, and lateral and perpendicular coherence lengths of each epitaxial material at each point on the wafer. Additionally, bandgap energies, lattice parameters, and mole compositions of AlN, AlxGa1-xN, and GaN epilayers are mapped across each loca­ tion. Figure 14 shows the aerial (a) and cross-section views (b) of the APD struc­ ture (R6-12164C), on which four loca­ tions, each 5 mm apart, are selected in the investigation into uniformity.

Each epitaxial layer shows good uni­ formity across the wafer for each measured parameter. Figure 15(a) shows the screw dislocation densities at each of the four mapped locations; the mapping reveals a change in dislocation density of only about one order of magnitude between the AlN and AlxGa1-xN epilayers and less than one order of magnitude between the AlxGa1-xN and GaN, which is highly desirable. Figure 15(b) shows the tilt angle and Figure 15(c) the heterogeneous strain at each mapped location, which were extrapolated from the slopes of the in-plane and perpendic­ ular W-H plots, respectively. It should be noted that the tilt angle and heterogeneous strains are both slightly smaller for the AlN epilayer, while those for AlxGa1-xN and GaN epilayers are similar, again ow­ ing to the epitaxial structure wherein AlN is on the sapphire substrate. Figure 15(d) shows the lateral coherence lengths and Figure 15(e) the perpendicular coherence lengths at each mapped location, which were extrapolated from the y-intercepts of the in-plane and perpendicular W-H plots, respectively. Since the coherence lengths represent the average grain size and are in­ dicative of the growth thickness, it makes sense that the thicker AlN epilayer should have a larger coherence length than the AlxGa1-xN and GaN epilayers.

Mapping also allows for analysis of the variation of the bandgap energy, lattice constant (c-plane), and mole composition of the epilayer materials at each location. Figure 16(a) shows the bandgap energy (in both eV and nm) vs. the lattice constant for the III-Nitride epilayers of the APD struc­ ture at each of the four mapped locations. Figure 16(b) shows the variation of the four AlxGa1-xN epilayers as well as the AlN and GaN bandgap energy and lattice pa­ rameter, with the center point represent­ ing the average of the four locations and the error bars indicating the minimum and maximum extrema. The findings unilater­ ally point to a high degree of uniformity within each epitaxial layer, while also con­ firming values consistent with those found in the literature for each material and the expectations from the MOCVD growth parameters. Particularly with regards to the four AlxGa1-xN epilayers, the observed high-Al concentrations are highly desir­ able for the deep-U.V. APD application. This successful material characterization of the APD structure predicts the capability of high-quality diodes with a high level of uniformity in performance from one diode to the next, across the device – important to the efficacy of APD development and device yields.

Conclusion

The ultimate objective of the research conducted is to achieve solar-blind deep- U.V. APDs in Geiger mode for single pho­ ton detection, with high QE and gain and low dark current. Most important to un­ derstanding the performance of the APD devices is a deep understanding of the foundational materials used in their fabri­ cation. Due to the highly reversed nature of APDs, they are inherently extremely sensitive to defects. Material character­ ization of high-quality heteroepitaxial growths is a crucial precursor to the fabri­ cation of high-performance APD devices. The result of the XRD investigation into the structural properties of III-Nitrides is significant: using a non-destructive char­ acterization method, information about the quality, composition, and uniformity of growths used for the fabrication of real, tested APDs are obtained.

Acknowledgements

I would like to extend my deepest grat­ itude to Professor Manijeh Razeghi for taking me into her lab my sophomore year and imparting her endless wisdom, both in and out of the lab. I would also like to thank Lakshay Gautam, to whom I owe all my understanding of III-Nitrides and who was an invaluable resource in preparing this thesis. Finally, I would like to acknowledge CQD for its world-class facility and amazing people — my research experience over the last two years has been both an honor and a pleasure. ◆

title: Baby got Bac: Associations Between Maternal Psychosocial Stress and Infant Gut Microbiotaa in Cebu, Philippines
text:
Department of Anthropology

Baby got Bac: Associations Between Maternal Psychosocial Stress and Infant Gut Microbiotaa in Cebu, Philippines by Rebecca C. Wu

Faculty Adviser: Katherine Amato

Introduction

Health is affected by a variety of both biological and sociocultural factors. While previous research has focused largely on biological factors, sociocultural determinants of health have also gained attention in recent years. These sociocultural components are related to structural disparities in health, including access to quality healthcare (Saluja & Bryant, 2021; Shavers, 2007), stress induced by socioeconomic status (SES) (Baum et al., 1999; Kapuku et al., 2002), and quality of physical environment (Evans, 2006; Wil­ son et al., 2004). While these factors can affect health through the course of one’s life, an important point of focus lies in the early-life environment, which includes both the prenatal environment experienced by a mother and fetus and an infant’s postnatal envi­ ronment. Specifically, maternal experiences, including energetic deprivation (Wu et al., 2004), climatic stress (Rylander et al., 2013), and psychosocial stress (Davis & Sandman, 2010) can have physiological consequences that are passed on to an infant in utero and during birth.

Maternal psychosocial stressors can impact maternal and infant immune responses (Ruiz & Avant, 2005), epigenetic activity (DeSocio, 2018; Thayer & Kuzawa, 2011), and microbiome composition and diversity (Jašarević et al., 2015, 2017). Infant cognitive development has been associated with stressors through changes in composition of the microbiota (Vogel et al., 2020). However, despite known links between maternal stress and infant gut microbiota composition (Jahnke et al., 2021), as well as the gut microbiota and physical health (Thursby & Juge, 2017), infant physical health out­ comes related to the microbiota remain understudied. In order to better understand pathways between maternal psychosocial stress, the microbiota, and infant health outcomes, the relationships between these variables were studied in Cebu, Philippines in a subset of 43 mother/infant dyads from the Cebu Longitudinal Health and Nutri­ tion Survey. Results shed light on potential connections between maternal psychoso­ cial stress, the infant gut microbiota, and infant health outcomes.

Background

Allostasis and Stress

Allostasis is a term used to describe the efficient regulation of physiolog­ ical processes through the biological “anticipation” of needs in an environment (McEwen & Gianaros, 2011; Sterling, 2004) and represents a shift from the traditional homeostatic model (Cannon, 1929). Importantly, allostatic processes occur in response to neurological predic­ tion, and thus, this concept can be used in better understanding stress. Stress is a broad term that encompasses a variety of physiological and psychosocial factors affecting allostasis, including nutrition, environment, and sociocultural factors. An accumulation of stress, sometimes termed allostatic load (McEwen & Stellar, 1993), can have negative effects on physiological systems, eventually resulting in disease. Psychosocial stress, which arises from stressors relating to sociocultural variables, as opposed to those that arise from physi­ cal phenomena (Elder Jr. et al., 1996), has gained increasing attention in recent years.

It can stem from a wide variety of factors across cultures, including SES, interper­ sonal relationships, and identity-based expectations (Taylor & Aspinwall, 1996). In particular, identity-based marginaliza­ tion, including racioethnic discrimination, can increase psychosocial stress for indi­ viduals in marginalized groups (Collier et al., 2013; Spruill, 2010). These stressors disproportionately affect individuals in underprivileged groups; thus, stress is often further exacerbated through a com­ pounding of several interrelated physical and social factors.

Developmental Origins of Health and Disease and the Human Gut Microbiota

Research shows that early-life differ­ ences in nutrition, environment, and stress can contribute to variable health later in life. This field of research is related to the Developmental Origins of Health and Dis­ ease (DOHaD) hypothesis, which posits that factors contributing to infant mor­ tality could also lead to morbidity later in life (Barker & Osmond, 1986). Research on mechanisms of DOHaD has largely focused on epigenetic effects (Bianco-Miotto et al., 2017; Kuzawa & Sweet, 2009), but the gut microbiota has received increasing atten­ tion as a potential pathway through which early environments can affect health.

The human gut microbiota refers to the collection of microorganisms, or microbes, that inhabit the human gastro­ intestinal tract (Ursell et al., 2012). The microbiome, by contrast, refers not only to the microbes themselves, but the genetic information possessed by the microor­ ganisms in a particular community. These microorganisms are integral to bodily functions, including provision of nutri­ ents, support of the immune system, and protection against pathogens (Thursby

& Juge, 2017). Changes in microbiota composition, termed dysbiosis, have been associated with a variety of morbidities, in­ cluding but not limited to Type 2 diabetes (Sharma & Tripathi, 2019), obesity (Ley, 2010), and Crohn’s disease (Wright et al., 2015). The microbiota is initially acquired at birth, either through the vaginal tract and maternal fecal during vaginal birth, or from the mother’s skin and environment in the case of Cesarean section (C-section) (Dominguez-Bello et al., 2010). It is re­ sponsive to changes in the environment, especially in the first two to three years of life (Rodríguez et al., 2015). Dysbiosis of the gut microbiota in infants, including changes resulting from C-section, anti­ biotic use, and environmental exposures, have implications for early life, as these al­ terations have been associated with future disease risk (Tamburini et al., 2016).

The Gut Microbiota and Stress

In addition to its environmental sen­ sitivity, the gut microbiota sits at the inter­ face between stress and physiology, as it is sensitive to both physical and psychosocial stressors. Gut microbiota composition is associated with neurocognitive develop­ ment in infants (Carlson et al., 2018; Vogel et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2016). Neurode­ velopmental disorders often coexist with physical health problems like gastrointes­ tinal issues, headaches, and asthma (Alabaf et al., 2019), suggesting that stressors per­ turbing the infant microbiota can impact physical health later in life.

Recent research has combined analy­ ses of maternal stress, the maternal micro­ biota, and infant health outcomes. Increas­ es in potentially pathogenic bacteria in the maternal gut have been correlated with high stress that alters the immune system

(Jahnke et al., 2021). Infant gut microbial composition is also associated with levels of maternal psychosocial stress (Hechler et al., 2019). Despite this, research on the spe­ cific pathways connecting these variables in human populations has been limited. Studies have focused on similar topics, but have centered on pregnancy-related stress (Dunlop et al., 2015) or utilized mouse models (Jašarević et al., 2017).

While mouse studies have provided strong evidence for pathways between maternal stress and the infant gut micro­ biota (Bowers & Yehuda, 2016; Jašarević et al., 2015), the physiologies of mice and humans, as well as the diversity of psy­ chosocial stressors that are experienced by each, differ greatly. Additionally, despite known connections between lower SES and higher levels of chronic stress resulting from social and environmental conditions (Baum et al., 1999), little work in this area has included robust information on SES and its related factors. Thus, while these studies provide valuable insight, studies in socioeconomically diverse human pop­ ulations are an important future step in understanding these pathways.

Health Disparities and Broader Impacts

While issues of stress and health are ubiquitous across populations, these effects are particularly significant in underprivi­ leged groups. Differences in ability to ac­ cess resources and prevalence of psychoso­ cial stressors can contribute to disparities in health outcomes across populations. In­ dividuals in socioeconomically underpriv­ ileged groups not only experience poorer access to healthcare and food (Kapral et al., 2002; Zhu et al., 2020), but also must cope with the compounded psychosocial stress resulting from these factors and discrim­ ination (Saluja & Bryant, 2021). It is im­ portant in scientific research, particularly when attempting to understand health inequities, to contextualize these within social environments and lived experiences. Studying differences in stress experience and their potential impacts on the mi­ crobiota, stress, and inflammation allows research to contribute to the broader body of race-conscious literature to improve understanding of health in minoritized groups.

Research Questions and Hypotheses

1. How is stress associated with the mater­ nal and infant gut microbiota?

Hypothesis One: It was hypothesized that higher levels of perceived maternal stress, as determined by validated stress surveys, would be associated with lowered microbial diversity in mothers and their infants at two weeks and six months. It was also hypothesized that different microbial taxa would be enriched or decreased de­ pending on levels of maternal stress.

2. How is composition of the infant gut microbiota associated with infant health outcomes?

Hypothesis Two: It was predicted that higher levels of maternal stress would correspond with a higher prevalence  of adverse health outcomes at both two weeks and six months, and that higher infant mi­ crobial diversity would be associated with a lower incidence of adverse health out­ comes. Additionally, it was hypothesized that the abundances of different microbial taxa would be enriched or decreased with the prevalence of illness outcomes at two weeks and six months.

Materials and Methods

Surveys

Data for this project were collected as part of the Cebu Longitudinal Health and Nutrition Survey (CLHNS), a cohort study based in Metro Cebu, Philippines since 1983. Data for the CLHNS were originally collected from 3,327 mother/infant dyads in 1983 and 1984 (Adair et al., 2011). Spe­ cific data for this study were collected from a subset of the original study. The moth­ ers in this study, who were infants in the original 1983/1984 study, were contacted for follow-up in 2017 and 2018 to gauge interest in this sub-study. Interviews were conducted in Cebuano with 51 pregnant mothers from the cohort during their third trimester of pregnancy. Answers to interview questions were coded in English. Follow-up to these original interviews oc­ curred at two weeks and six months post­ partum and included surveys of birth and infant health.

Survey questions included topics on diet, stress, medication, and other lifestyle factors. Stress was quantified using modi­ fied versions of the Perceived Stress Scale (PSS) and Center for Epidemiologic Stud­ ies Depression Scale (CES-D). The PSS is the most widely used validated survey for measuring stress in individuals (Cohen et al., 1983). The CES-D, another widely used scale, typically consists of 20 questions re­ lating to potential depressive symptoms (Radloff, 1977). The modified questions and frequencies of responses are recorded in Tables 1 and 2.

Using data from both scales, stress levels were indexed as follows: questions relating to positive emotions were re­ versed, as is typically done in both surveys, and numbers were summed both separate­ ly for the PSS and CES-D and together across both scales. Larger numbers indi­ cated higher levels of perceived stress or depressive symptoms. The possible range of PSS scores was 0 to 40, while the range of CES-D scores was 16 to 48. These scores were also divided into low, medium, and high tertiles (Figure 1) for analysis.

Additionally, data on income and SES were collected and analyzed to better understand stress in relation to SES. Av­ erage monthly income over the past three months was directly reported in 15 out of 43 households, with a range of 450 to 34,000 pesos per month (8 to 614 USD). An index of SES was generated using rel­ evant measures of social class previously used in Cebu (Desantis et al., 2015). Pos­ sible scores in this index ranged from 1 to 12, with higher values representing higher SES. Actual scores ranged from 1 to 10, with a mean score of 5.42 and a median of 5.

Microbiome Analysis

Fecal samples were collected as a proxy for the gut microbial community of mothers and infants in the community. Mothers were instructed to collect a fe­ cal sample from their most recent bowel movement before the time of the inter­ view. Infant fecal samples were collected by mothers at two weeks and six months of age from soiled diapers. Samples were stored in ethanol and containers were stored away from direct sunlight and warm temperatures until they were picked up by researchers between six and 12 hours after sample collection. The samples were stored at 4 °C until shipment to the Amato Lab­ oratory in Evanston, Illinois, where they were stored at -80 °C until DNA extraction.

Microbial DNA was extracted from fecal samples using the QIAGEN Powersoil Kit following manufacturer instructions, with some modifications to incubation times and centrifuge speeds and times. Af­ ter extraction, the V4-V5 region of the 16S rRNA gene was amplified using polymerase chain reaction and the 515Fa/926R primer set (Mallott & Amato, 2018; Walters et al., 2015) and following the Earth Microbiome Project protocol (Thompson et al., 2017). Each set of extractions and each PCR plate was run using a negative control to pro­ tect against contamination of samples by foreign DNA. Grouped amplicons were sequenced on the Illumina MiSeq V2 plat­ form at the DNA Services Facility at the University of Illinois Chicago.

”Studying differences in stress experience and their potential impacts ... allows research to contribute to the broader body of race-conscious literature to improve understanding of health in minoritized groups.”

Paired-end sequences were processed in QIIME2 v2020.2 (Bolyen et al., 2019). For each set of samples (maternal, two week, and six months), sequences from mitochondria and chloroplasts were re­ moved. Maternal samples resulted in a dataset with 11,916,665 reads and a mean of 18,790 reads per sample (minimum = 3,125, maximum = 42,154). Infant sam­ ples obtained at two weeks resulted in a dataset of 1,147,808 reads and a mean of 26,693 reads per sample (minimum = 95, maximum = 53,407). Infant samples at six months resulted in a dataset of 1,048,441 reads and a mean of 26,211 reads per sample (minimum = 1,928, maximum = 44,686). Using the dada2 plug-in, amplicon sequence variants (ASVs) were obtained and clustered.

Statistical Analysis

After processing in QIIME2, micro­ biome data were further analyzed in R us­ ing the phyloseq, ANCOM-BC, and vegan packages, which are designed for use with microbiome data. Using the vegan pack­ age, permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) tests were run for two week, six month, and mater­ nal microbiome data and the following variables: maternal PSS indexed scores, maternal CES-D indexed scores, maternal total stress score, infant health outcomes, and SES scores. Health outcomes were tested both as individual symptoms (fever, diarrhea, runny nose, sore throat, ear dis­ charge, nasal discharge, or other illness) and total illness frequency. Antibiotic use was included as a covariate in the two-week model. Maternal antibiotics, antibiotics at six months, breastfeeding, and delivery mode — all previously shown to impact microbial composition (Kurilshikov et al., 2021) —  were not significantly associated with microbial composition in this sample and were therefore not included in any models.

Microbial alpha diversity, or diver­ sity within each community of microbes, was measured at two weeks, six months, and the maternal third trimester using the Shannon Diversity Index (Kim et al., 2017). These values were tested for cor­ relations with the following: maternal PSS indexed scores, maternal CES-D indexed scores, maternal total stress, infant health outcomes, quantified as above, and SES scores. Similar to the PERMANOVAs, antibiotic use was included as a covariate at two weeks, while no covariates were in­ cluded at six months or with maternal data.

Finally, differential abundances of microbial taxa were tested using Analysis of Compositions of Microbiomes with Bias Correction (ANCOM-BC) (Lin & Peddada, 2020) at the phylum, class, order, family, genus, and species levels. The significance of aforementioned covariates was tested at each level, and only infant antibiotic use at two weeks at the phylum level and delivery mode at the species level at two weeks were found to be significant. Maternal PSS and CES-D levels were divided based on pre­ viously mentioned tertiles. Frequency of infant illness symptoms, individual symp­ toms, and presence or absence of illness were also tested. Results were interpreted based on q-values — measures of statistical significance controlled for the false dis­ covery rate — and log-fold change (LFC) values, where positive values indicate an increase in abundance, while negative val­ ues indicate a decrease in abundance in a condition.

Results

Maternal Stress and the Microbiota

PERMANOVA tests were run be­ tween maternal stress scores (PSS, CES-D, and combined) and weighted unifrac dis­ tances for mothers and for infants at two weeks and six months. Neither the mod­ els that controlled for covariates nor the unadjusted models showed any statistical significance in associations with microbial composition. However, pseudo-F values for maternal stress on all three scales and maternal microbiota composition were all lower than values for maternal stress and infant microbiota composition, suggesting that maternal stress may be more strongly related to infant than maternal microbiota composition (Figure 2).

Maternal alpha diversity was signifi­ cantly negatively associated with CES-D scores (p = 0.044), and higher total stress levels showed trends toward lower di­ versity (p = 0.055), but diversity was not significantly associated with PSS scores (p = 0.188). At two weeks, infant microbial diversity was significantly correlated with maternal CES-D (p = 0.030), maternal PSS (p = 0.037), and maternal total stress (p = 0.017). This association was not evident with the CES-D score (p = 0.475), PSS score (p = 0.299), or total stress (p =  0.288) (Figure 3).

ANCOM-BC analysis showed that at the phylum and class levels, medium CES-D level was associated with an increase in Spirochaetes abundance when compared with low CES-D level. Medium CES-D level was associated with an increase in abundance of Bacillales, Staphylococcace­ ae, and Staphylococcus at six months of in­ fant age. Medium PSS levels corresponded with a decrease in abundance of the family Ruminococcaceae at six months of age and showed trends toward a lower abundance of the genus Faecalibacterium and species Faecalibacterium prausnitzii. Results are displayed in Table 3.

Maternal Stress, SES, and Infant Health Outcomes

PERMANOVA testing showed that SES levels were correlated with maternal microbiota composition (p = 0.025), but not composition at two weeks (p = 0.0564) or six months (p = 0.499). SES levels were associated with income (p = 0.004), but not with maternal or infant microbial diversity. At two weeks, sore throat was significantly associated with infant microbiota compo­ sition (p = 0.025). Other symptoms and total frequency of illness symptoms were not associated with microbiota composi­ tion at two weeks. At six months, neither individual health outcomes nor total illness symptoms were associated with microbio­ ta composition.

Most health outcomes were not as­ sociated with infant microbial diversity, but notably, “other illness” at two weeks was associated with microbial diversity (p = 0.031) at two weeks. ANCOM testing of microbial taxa showed no significant asso­ ciations at any taxonomic levels, though the genus Megamonas trended toward dif­ ferential abundance between ill and non- ill infants at 6 months (q = 0.094). Health outcomes results are found in Table 4 and Table 5.

Discussion

Maternal Stress, Maternal Microbiota Com­ position, and Infant Microbiota Composition

Despite previous research pointing to associations between maternal perceived stress, maternal and infant gut microbiota composition, and infant health outcomes, few results were significant using PER­ MANOVA testing in our sample. Mater­ nal stress was associated with  infant gut microbial diversity at two weeks of age, while maternal gut microbial composition was associated with infant gut microbial diversity at six months of age. It was pre­ dicted that high maternal stress would be associated with low alpha diversity. How­ ever, it was only strongly associated with microbial diversity in infants at two weeks and showed trends towards lower diversity in maternal samples. It is therefore possible that, while maternal stress is an early pre­ dictor of microbial diversity, as an infant is exposed to more environmental fac­ tors and spends more time outside of the womb, other variables confound this rela­ tionship. Maternal stress, while associated with diversity, was not associated with composition at any time points, suggesting that these differences in diversity may be small compared to overall composition.

Another explanation that is consis­ tent with concepts in DOHaD is that ma­ ternal stress is “passed down” to the infant through a mechanism that is not the mi­ crobiota; that is, epigenetic modifications or changes in hormonal levels are passed to the infant in utero, signaling to the infant that high stress should be expected after birth. The infant may then need to adapt to the corresponding immunolog­ ical challenges predicted in utero, leading to a quicker increase in diversity at two weeks that is less evident at six months. Furthermore, at two weeks, the infant im­ mune system has not yet developed, while a functioning immune system exists at six months (West 2002). The microbiota plays a role in the development of the immune system, which influences composition of the microbiota (Martin et al., 2010), sug­ gesting that the connection between these factors in intergenerational effects of stress and health has not been fully explored.

ANCOM-BC results also support the hypothesis that increased maternal stress affects the immune system of the in­ fant. Enrichment of Staphylococcus at six months in infants of mothers experiencing higher stress suggests differences in im­ mune function. Staphylococcus has been implicated in immunological challenges (Pietrocola et al., 2017), and colonization by Staphylococcus in early life is associ­ ated with risk for atopic disease (Vael & Desager, 2009) and allergy (Björkstén et al., 1999), supporting its potential impacts on innate immunity.

”At six months, neither individual health outcomes nor total illness symptoms were associated with microbiota composition.”

”While maternal stress is an early predictor of microbial diversity, as an infant is exposed to more environmental factors ... other variables confound this relationship.”

Similarly, bacterial species Faecali­ bacterium prausnitzii, which is in the fam­ ily Ruminococcaceae, was decreased at six months in infants of mothers with higher

PSS levels. F. prausnitzii is a characteristi­ cally abundant species in the gut microbio­ ta, composing 1% to 6% of the gut microbi­ ota (Hold et al., 2003), and has been shown to be reduced in intestinal disorders (Lo­ pez-Siles et al., 2017). It is suggested that a reduction of F. prausnitzii decreases one’s ability to defend against inflammation (Parsaei et al., 2021). These results, in con­ junction with the enrichment of Staphylo­ coccus, which can increase inflammation, suggest that infants of more highly stressed mothers may experience immunological challenges as they age.

Importantly, differences in enrich­ ment and depletion of microbial taxa were most significant in infants at six months. Given that diversity measures are less strongly associated with maternal stress at six months than two weeks, this suggests that changes to the immune system be­ tween two weeks and six months contrib­ ute to specific selection of microbial taxa at six months, while a different physiolog­ ical pathway may contribute to decreased diversity of the infant microbiota at two weeks.

Health Outcomes

Health outcomes at two weeks, mea­ sured as a variety of physical health symp­ toms in the 14 days prior to survey, were only somewhat related to maternal stress at microbiota diversity at two weeks. Despite statistical significance, only one infant had a sore throat at two weeks, and only three infants exhibited a fever. It is therefore possible that neither maternal stress nor infant microbial diversity was truly predic­ tive of infant illness at two weeks.

The only significant associations were found between sore throat and fever and microbial diversity at two weeks, and these associations were notably absent in infants at six months. This is likely explained by the timing of survey data. At both two weeks and six months of infant age, moth­ ers were asked about the symptoms of their infants in the 14 days prior to the survey, which excluded approximately five months of health data between two weeks and five and a half months. Given this missing time frame, data on illness at six months were not indicative of overall infant health up to the point of the survey.

Furthermore, most health outcomes that have been associated with gut micro­ biota composition in the past have been later-life morbidities like diabetes, obesity, and heart disease, few of which are found in infants. Previous studies of the microbi­ ota and DOHaD have shown that early-life environments can predict later-life risk for non-infectious disease, but work on in­ fectious disease susceptibility is lacking in the intersection of microbiota and DOHaD research. The early immunological func­ tions of the gut microbiota must therefore be explored to better understand how differences in colonization can modulate susceptibility to infectious disease in early life before the establishment of the infant immune system.

”Early life environments can predict later-life risk for non-infectious disease.”

Future Directions

An increased timespan of this lon­ gitudinal study could shed more light on the later health outcomes of infants in this cohort. Given that data collection occurred in 2017 and 2018, follow-up in the present (five to six years later) could provide insight on the neurodevelopmen­ tal and physical health outcomes previ­ ously shown to be present in children of highly stressed mothers. It would also be beneficial to collect data on blood pressure, cholesterol levels, and other future predic­ tors of non-infectious disease. Given the likely role of the immune system in mod­ ulating — and being modulated by — the gut microbiota between two weeks and six months of age, valuable insight could be gained through longitudinal measures of immune activation and inflammation. These data from mothers and infants, in conjunction with microbiome data and data on frequency of infectious illness, could shed light on potential immune con­ sequences of intergenerational effects of stress.

Conclusions

This project supports ongoing research on the intergenerational effects of maternal stress on infant health. Importantly, it was discovered that mater­ nal stress was associated with microbiome diversity at two weeks and microbiome composition at six months, though it was not associated with diversity at six months or composition at two weeks. These seemingly contradictory results point to the timing of immune development as a critical point from which to further study the impacts of maternal stress on the microbiome and infant health. While few significant results were found with infant health outcomes in relation to microbiota diversity or composition, this may be due to the timing of survey data. Future work should have more comprehensive data on health outcomes — including pathogenic and non-pathogenic disease — and should incorporate markers of inflammation and immune activation to improve under­ standing of specific pathways to the inter­ generational transmission of stress. ◆
