title: The Impact of School Security on Student Wellbeing
abstract: Over the last decade, public schools have seen a dramatic rise in the use of visible school security measures, including metal detectors, security cameras, and security personnel (Tanner-Smith & Fisher, 2015). Although several studies have examined the impact of a school security presence on students’ academic outcomes, only a few studies have looked at how a security presence impacts school climate and student wellbeing, largely focusing on quantitative analyses. The lack of more qualitative approaches that offer in-depth descriptions of students’ lived experiences limits the scope of assessments examining school security presences. The present study seeks to fill these gaps by examining the relationship between school security and school climate through the lens of student wellbeing. A survey was completed by 97 Northwestern first-year students, assessing their high school’s climate with or without a school security presence. Afterward, 10 students were selected for follow-up interviews. The semi-structured interviews consisted of items related to dimensions of school climate and adolescent wellbeing, and all selected interviewees graduated from a high school with a security presence. Findings of the study included the impact of school violence on a student’s relationship with their school’s security and administration and its consequences for school climate and student wellbeing; direct impacts of school security on student wellbeing; how different security types elicit different perceptions in students; how student identity impacts the relationship between a student and their school’s security presence; and how a lack of adequate support affects student perception of school climate and student wellbeing.
text:
School of Education & Social Policy

The Impact of School Security on Student Wellbeing by Jacob Geil

Faculty Advisers: Dr. Timothy Dohrer and Dr. Regina Logan

Abstract Over the last decade, public schools have seen a dramatic rise in the use of visible school security measures, including metal detectors, security cameras, and security personnel (Tanner-Smith & Fisher, 2015). Although several studies have examined the impact of a school security presence on students’ academic outcomes, only a few studies have looked at how a security presence impacts school climate and student wellbeing, largely focus­ ing on quantitative analyses. The lack of more qualitative approaches that offer in-depth descriptions of students’ lived experiences limits the scope of assessments examining school security presences. The present study seeks to fill these gaps by examining the relationship between school security and school climate through the lens of student wellbeing. A survey was completed by 97 Northwestern first-year students, assessing their high school’s climate with or without a school security presence. Afterward, 10 students were selected for follow-up interviews. The semi-structured interviews con­ sisted of items related to dimensions of school climate and adolescent wellbeing, and all selected interviewees graduated from a high school with a security presence. Findings of the study included the impact of school violence on a student’s relationship with their school’s security and administration and its consequences for school climate and student wellbeing; direct impacts of school security on student wellbeing; how different security types elicit different perceptions in students; how student identity impacts the relation­ ship between a student and their school’s security presence; and how a lack of adequate support affects student perception of school climate and student wellbeing.

Introduction Public schools over the last decade have seen a dramatic rise in the use of visible school security measures, including metal detectors, security cameras, and security personnel (Tanner-Smith & Fisher, 2015). In response to several high-profile school shootings in the 1990s, federal and state legislation began establishing a security presence in schools that continues to grow.

This has prompted a fierce debate. Supporters argue that a security presence protects against school violence and helps to improve relationships between young people and security personnel. Opponents rebut that security in schools is disruptive and criminalizes student behavior with disproportionate damage done to minority students and students with disabilities.

Several studies have examined the impact of school security on student out­ comes. However, only a few studies have looked at how a security presence impacts school climate and student wellbeing, largely focusing on quantitative analyses. This leaves gaps in what to date has been observed and reported. The lack of more qualitative approaches that offer in-depth descriptions of students’ lived experiences limits the scope of assessments examining school security presences.

School climate plays a critical role in a school’s efforts toward meeting goals and resolving problems, as students ex­ periencing a positive school climate show stronger academic performance and lower rates of absenteeism, truancy, and drop out than that of students experiencing a nega­ tive school climate (Norton, 1984; Payne, 2018). Furthermore, schools have an enor­ mous impact on a student’s development, especially during adolescence, which is an important and complex period of the lifes­ pan, characterized by significant physical, psychological, and social transitions (PRB, 2014). Considering this importance, a thorough understanding of the elements of school climate and the factors that might be negatively impacting perceived school climate is essential to achieving academ­ ic goals, as well as promoting positive emotional and behavioral outcomes for students.

Additionally, this research, in exam­ ining school security through the lens of school climate and student experience, will help to establish a better understanding of how previously researched inequities related to school security and punishment manifest in student experiences and out­ comes, and what their consequences are for students of color. These findings could be informative to educators and adminis­ trators as they contemplate equity-based changes to their school security and school climate procedures.

This study examined the relationship between school security and school climate through the lens of its extended conse­ quences for student wellbeing. Through its methodology, it collected and examined student experiences of stress, safety, fear, and discomfort, assessed how they mani­ fested in anxiety, depression, and other mental health challenges among students, and explored their connection with the se­ curity presence at the student’s high school.

Review of Literature

Violence Within Schools School violence can encompass a mul­ titude of behaviors, including bullying, fighting, verbal threats, weapon posses­ sion, physical aggression, and acts of sexual violence, including harassment and assault (Turanovic & Siennick, 2022). Regardless of its form, school violence has been found to have a traumatic impact on everyone within a school community, most of all students, who are especially vulnerable to many of its consequences, including lone­ liness, low self-esteem, depression, anx­ iety, suicidality, self-harm, and fear (NIJ, 2022). Furthermore, due to the sensitivity of adolescence, experiencing violence in school during this period of development can have long-term effects on a student’s health, such as reactive attachment dis­ order, obesity, diabetes, heavy alcohol or substance use, and other poor health outcomes, in addition to the emotional consequences listed above (Ferrara et al., 2019).

Increase in School Security Presence In an attempt to mitigate threats of school violence, public schools over the last de­ cade have seen a rise in the use of visible school security measures (Tanner-Smith & Fisher, 2015). From 2005-2006, 26.2% of public primary schools and 75.2% of public high schools had a regular security presence. By 2017-2018, these numbers had inflated to 51.4% for public primary schools and 84.3% for public high schools. School Resource Officer (SRO) programs refer to the permanent placement of law enforcement officers within schools, and as a response to increasing rates of school shootings, SRO programs have grown in both size and mission over the last two decades (Ryan et al., 2017). As of 2017- 2018, 36% of public primary schools and 72% of public high schools had armed law enforcement stationed on campus (NCES, 2020). Nonetheless, evidence has shown that a school security presence does not neces­ sarily prevent school-based violence nor lead to increased school safety (Kupchik & Farina, 2016). Although some researchers have reported positive impacts of an SRO presence in schools (Johnson, 2016), based on a report by the National Center for Education Statistics (2022), the 2020-2021 school year saw the highest number of school shootings in two decades, despite a rise in the use of school security.

Impact of School Security on Student Outcomes Several studies have critically examined the impact of a school security presence on students’ academic outcomes and educa­ tional futures, finding that the presence of school security can lead to increased rates of student suspension and arrest (Finn & Servoss, 2014). The consequences of in­ creased suspension, expulsion, and arrest rates of students are severe, as any policy that removes a student who misbehaves from the classroom creates an “educational disruption” that prevents that student from receiving the protective effects of education on misbehavior or crime, there­ by predisposing that student to further misbehavior, disciplinary infractions, or incarceration (Passero, 2022).

Furthermore, researchers have found that race and gender play a large role in the frequency and severity of punishment received in schools (Pentek & Eisenberg, 2018). Research has shown a severe discrep­ ancy in who is punished, how frequently they are punished, to what severity they are punished, and the lasting consequences they might face. Black students, and Black female students in particular, experience dispro­ portionately high suspension and expulsion rates (Morris & Perry, 2017). Considering how law enforcement, other security mea­ sures, and punitive policies have created an avenue for student incarceration, the conse­ quences of these disparities and the implicit bias they affirm are severe.

School Climate School climate refers to the combination of beliefs, attitudes, and values that shape interactions between students, teachers, and administrators (Mitchell et al., 2010). It is the atmosphere and personality of a school, including its norms, values, expectations, and social characteristics (Brookover et al., 1978; Anderson, 1982). School climate has been linked to many student outcomes, such as academic achievement, discipline problems, and rates of absenteeism, truancy, and student dropout (Mitchell et al., 2010; Norton, 1984; Payne, 2018). Furthermore, the per­ ceived quality of school climate has been associated with behavioral and emotional adjustment in adolescents, with a negative perception contributing to declines in aca­ demic performance, self-image, perceived social support, and perceived quality of school life (Kuperminc et al., 1997).

School Security, School Climate, and Adolescent Wellbeing The use of certain visible security mea­ sures has been found to lead to a signifi­ cant decrease in students feeling safe while in school (Perumean-Chaney & Sutton, 2013). Even after controlling for the school’s level of violence, the use of metal detectors, security guards, or locked doors in a school is highly correlated with height­ ened levels of student fear (Gastic, 2011; Bachman et al., 2011). Particularly among students who have previously experienced victimization, research shows that visible security measures may magnify fear, promote distrust, and serve as a reminder of the threat of violence (Bachman et al., 2011). The stress, fear, and discomfort that may result from the use of certain visible security measures all impact dimensions of school climate.

There are five proposed domains of adolescent wellbeing: good health and op­ timum nutrition; connectedness, positive values, and contribution to society; safety and a supportive environment; learn­ ing, competence, education, skills, and employability; and agency and resilience (Ross et al., 2020). These five domains are meant to encompass both subjective and objective constructs of wellbeing, which include personal experiences and individual fulfillment, as well as quality of life indicators, such as material resources and social attributes (Ross et al., 2020). As we consider the impact a school security presence might have on school climate, in­ cluding increased levels of perceived fear, discomfort, or lack of safety, as well as the behavioral and emotional repercussions for a negatively perceived school climate, the extended consequences for student wellbeing are clear.

“Research has shown a severe discrepancy in who is punished, how frequently they are punished, to what severity they are punished, and the lasting consequences they might face.”

Methodology For data collection, this study incorporated a mixed methods approach. I collected quantitative data from a Qualtrics survey, distributed to students at Northwestern

University. These data were then sorted to only include responses from first-year col­ lege students who graduated in the last year from high school. Additionally, I collected qualitative data from interviews conducted with first-year students at Northwestern University who graduated the previous year from a high school with a security presence. “Security presence” was defined as a school’s use of police, security guards, security cameras, metal detectors, or any combination of the four. The quantitative method allowed me to identify potential trends in the relationship between school security and school climate, which I then built upon with personalized and detailed participant perspectives through the quali­ tative method.

Quantitative data was collected first, via the Qualtrics survey. I obtained 97 via­ ble responses to use in my analysis, which provided a sample size of about 5.7% of Northwestern University first-year stu­ dents. From the 2,039-person class of 2026, I subtracted an approximate number of Northwestern first-year students who took a gap year (based on national trends), as well as students who transferred from another university, as these students, despite being in their first year at North­ western, graduated from high school more than one year prior (Northwestern Admis­ sions; Hadden & Kaplan, 2020). See Table 1 for demographic details of the 97 total participants, including race, gender, type of high school attended, how many of the students’ schools had a security presence, and various types of security utilized by the students’ schools.

The survey began with demographic questions, questions about the school from which the student graduated, and questions about the security presence (or lack thereof) in said high school. From there, students were presented with 11 questions assessing school climate and wellbeing. A Likert-type scale ranging from one (Strongly Disagree) to five (Strongly Agree) was used to as­ sess students’ emotional reactions to these prompts, which included themes such as safety and comfort at school, instances of harassment or abuse, and experiences of mental health challenges. At the end of the survey, participants were asked if they were willing to be contacted in the future for an interview. See Appendix A for a full list of survey questions.

The quantitative data were analyzed using linear regressions, frequency tests, and one-way ANOVA tests through the program JASP. These analyses allowed me to identify potential relationships between school security and elements of school cli­ mate that negatively impact student well­ being, such as stress, discomfort, fear, and lack of safety, as well as ensure statistical validity and control for confounds. The trends established through these analyses informed the questions I asked in my in­ terview protocol and were used as support for themes that emerged in the interviews.

“Black students, and Black female students in particular, experience disproportionately high suspension and expulsion rates.”

Interview participants were selected based on their indicated willingness from the survey. I interviewed 10 individuals, which ensured that proper data saturation was reached (Guest et al., 2006), and in­ terviews took place over Zoom, due to the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic. Although there were no specific demographic re­ quirements for interviewees, I recruited a target population that was diverse in terms of personal and high school demographics based on the survey responses. The final sample of interviewees was Elizabeth, Alice, Emily, Jack, Elise, Deva, Marianna, Abby, Landon, and Maya. Nine were public school graduates, and one, Elizabeth, was a private school graduate. Alice, Elise, Jack, and Abby are white, Elizabeth is Black, Emily is East Asian, Deva is South Asian, Marianna is Hispanic/Latine, and two stu­ dents were multiracial: Maya is Black and white, and Landon is Hispanic/Latine and white. Alice, Elise, Abby, Elizabeth, Emily, Marianna, and Maya are female-identify­ ing, Jack and Landon are male-identifying, and Deva is non-binary/non-conforming. Among the 10 interviewees, every possible response to the student’s assessment of their school climate on the survey was rep­ resented, ensuring a diverse sample both in terms of student identity, as well as student perception of their school and its security.

The interview protocol consisted of 10 questions and followed a semi-struc­ tured approach. By using semi-structured interviews, I was able to introduce new concepts based on an interviewee’s re­ sponse. The semi-structured interview protocol consisted of original questions, drawn from previously researched mea­ sures of school climate, and informed by trends established via the quantitative sur­ vey (Bernhardt, 1998). It began with ques­ tions regarding the student’s high school and its security presence, including the type of security present, its visibility to stu­ dents, and the systems of support the high school offered in conjunction with the security presence. From there, questions pertained to interactions with and emo­ tional reactions and feelings as they related to the security presence. See Appendix B for a copy of the semi-structured interview protocol.

Qualitative data were organized and analyzed following a grounded theory framework. As a methodology designed to uncover explanatory theories grounded in data, utilizing this framework not only al­ lowed for a potential relationship between a student’s wellbeing and their school’s se­ curity presence to emerge, but also helped create a buffer for the biases that could oth­ erwise influence my interpretation (Chun Tie et al., 2019).

Findings In assessing each student’s impression of their school’s security, the level of school violence experienced or witnessed by the student emerged as a predictor. Students such as Alice, Maya, Deva, and Marianna, who reported the most negative percep­ tions of their school’s security, were also the students who reported experiencing or witnessing the most violence on a reg­ ular basis within their school. This finding stands out, as Maya, Alice, Deva, and Marianna would theoretically have the most to gain from the presence of school security, considering the intention behind security measures is to protect students from the violence that these students were experiencing and witnessing. However, Maya, Alice, Deva, and Marianna spoke of a gap between the intention of the school security, the funding that it required, and the actual effect, or lack thereof, on the school climate and their feelings of safety as a main reason behind their negative perceptions of their school’s security. They witnessed the violence that contributed to the hiring of their school’s security pres­ ence; they experienced the security, took notice of the resources it consumed, and in some cases, experienced harm as a result; and they failed to see its promised changes in either mitigated acts or threats of vio­ lence or positive effects to their wellbeing.

Similarly, the students who had the most positive reactions toward their school’s security, as well as the students who were mostly indifferent toward their school’s security, all reported low levels of violence within their schools and con­ sistent feelings of safety. Two students remarked that their school’s security offi­ cer felt like a member of the school com­ munity. Although there were a number of characteristics of the officer contributing to this perception that these students list­ ed, such as frequent, positive interactions and conversations with students, as well as active involvement in school events, the fact that none of these students had to encounter violence presents an alternative explanation as to why the security presence could exist purely as a community mem­ ber; neither student had to experience the security presence outside of that context. Their interactions could entirely consist of greetings and friendly questions, and the interactions they had to witness only revolved around standard school rules, which both students thought were fair. Furthermore, neither student had to ex­ perience a situation of violence by which to assess the security’s effectiveness at its intended protection, in the way that the students with negative reactions did.

For some students, the type of securi­ ty that was present proved a big distinction in the student’s perception of said security. Different types of security include passive measures, such as cameras, and active mea­ sures, such as bag checks, security guards or paraprofessionals, and SROs or police. When asked about their school security presence, regardless of which types were present within the school, students more often brought up active measures than passive measures. Similarly, when asked about various consequences of the secu­ rity presence, either positive or negative, students more often defaulted toward commenting on security personnel, such as security guards/paraprofessionals or SROs/police. It may be the case that stu­ dents think of passive security measures either differently than active measures or not at all, due to differences in frequency and type of encounter between the two types of measures.

Many students reported having posi­ tive impressions of and relationships with the security guards or paraprofessionals at their school, regardless of their gener­ al reaction toward security. For students who reported negative feelings related to features of the security, such as them be­ ing armed, or to harm committed by the security presence, such as instances of racial profiling and targeting or especially forceful or punitive protocols, the students differentiated between SROs/police and security guards/paraprofessionals when the two contrasted in these features or behaviors. This was amplified when, as it was in many of these cases, the security guard or paraprofessional did not resemble what one might imagine a typical security presence to be, such as one student de­ scribing her school’s paraprofessionals as “old ladies”.

Every male-identifying interviewee reported a positive or neutral percep­ tion of their school security, and only female-identifying and non-binary in­ terviewees reported negative reactions. Additionally, only interviewees of color discussed instances of racism when an­ swering questions about the impact of their school’s security on the school cli­ mate. Thus, it may be the case that cer­ tain kinds of violence are only included in assessments of school security when the assessment is being conducted by stu­ dents of certain identities, emphasizing the need for diverse perspectives on the matter. Furthermore, as only students of certain identities can speak firsthand to the emotional, mental, and physical impact of instances of discrimination or prejudice, it is critical that we include diverse voices in our conversations, if we hope to get a complete picture of the impact of school security.

Several students described witnessing or experiencing acts of racism from their school’s security. These included racial profiling, targeting, microaggressions, and acts of violence against Black and brown students. For these students, all of whom are students of color, these observed and experienced acts of racism shaped the student’s view of and relationship with security, as well as greatly impacted their wellbeing as a student within the school.

When describing their high school experience, many students mentioned the necessity of mental health support, speaking on behalf of both themselves and their peers. However, despite this stated significance of mental health challenges in a student’s experience at and perception of their school, the majority of the students describing mental health challenges faced by themselves or their peers followed those sentiments with reports of inadequate re­ sources and care. Several of the students remarked on how this lack of support amplified their frustration toward their school and its security. They saw the se­ curity presence growing, absorbing more and more of their school’s resources and funding, and they continued experienc­ ing and witnessing violence, all the while seeing students suffer without adequate support. Several students also mentioned that they saw mental health support as key to addressing the violence and conflicts they witnessed or experienced within their school. Especially for the students who saw security measures as punitive, reactionary, and ultimately ineffective, they described mental health support as an opportunity to address school-based conflicts and violence at their source before they turned more severe.

“. . . as only students of certain identites can speak firsthand to the emotional, mental, and physical impact of instances of discrimination or prejudice, it is critical that we include diverse voices in our conversations, if we hope to get a complete picture of the impact of school security.”

Discussion and Analysis As we consider the relationship between security, school climate, and student well­ being, the greatest reported impact from the interviewed students came from the security’s perceived ineffectiveness. The students that encountered regular violence experienced a negative impact on their school climate caused by said violence that had ramifications for their wellbe­ ing. Additionally, when acts of violence disproportionately affected Black and brown students, as was the case in some schools, we see an even greater disruption in the school’s climate for these (Black and brown) students. These disruptions had an emotional and mental toll on these students, as they navigated intense feelings of fear and lack of safety.

With the addition of school security, the impact was amplified. In some cases, this came from acts of violence and racism committed by security officers. However, for many of these students, it came from the security’s perceived ineffectiveness at addressing the violence in the schools: the safety it failed to ensure, the emotion­ al and mental stress it failed to remedy, and the frustration toward the school, its administration, and the security presence that it prompted. Many students explained that they saw security as a failure on their school’s part to protect them from the threats, both internal and external, that they were experiencing. It communicat­ ed a lack of care and support on behalf of the school, regardless of whether this was the school’s intention. Furthermore, these students were already experiencing intense anxiety and fear related to actual and perceived threats to their safety, and this added an additional layer, where these anxieties and fears were not eased, and students now felt as though they could not trust their school to support them. In con­ junction with inadequate systems of men­ tal health support, students described situ­ ations spiraling, feelings of frustration and lack of trust in the school, and a collective hopelessness at the idea of receiving help or support from the school, all of which contributed to a negative perception of the school’s climate and thus, facilitated the negative consequences of a poor percep­ tion of school climate for these students.

“They saw the security presence growing, absorbing more and more of their school’s resources and funding, and they continued experiencing and witnessing violence, all the while seeing students suffer without adequate support.”

For many students, there was a dis­ tinction made between different types of security, particularly security guards or paraprofessionals and SROs or police. This finding is somewhat supported by current research but also presents an opportunity for future research. Some studies differ­ entiate between school security measures through characteristics such as visibility, in­ trusiveness, and rigidity, which aligns with the distinction between active and passive measures found in this study (NCES, 2012; NASP, 2018). However, most research assessing the impact of school security categorizes all security measures within the same definition of security or only focuses on the measures often associated with most people’s conception of school security, such as metal detectors, security guards, and police. There have been few studies examining how different types of security may affect students differently, but based on this study, this could be an area of research worth exploring, particularly for schools that wish to maintain a security presence.

Throughout the study, students of different gender and racial identities de­ scribed varying perceptions and impacts of their school’s security, revealing how students of different identities can have different experiences within the same school climate and, thus, will form unique impressions and bear unique consequences of their school’s security and climate. This is supported by current research, which has found that race and gender play a large role in the frequency and severity of pun­ ishment for subjective infractions in school (Pentek & Eisenberg, 2018; Morris & Per­ ry, 2017), and presents an area for future research. A thorough understanding of the role of intersecting identities in school punishment and discipline is critical for a complete assessment of school security and its impact: on students, their perception of their school’s climate, and their wellbeing.

Conclusion This study attempted to fill in the gaps in current school security literature by exam­ ining the impact of a school security pres­ ence on school climate through the lens of student wellbeing. In this study, student wellbeing was assessed through student experiences with stress, perceived safety, fear, and discomfort, as well as how these emotional outcomes manifested in student experiences with depression, anxiety, and other mental health challenges. Findings of the study included the impact of school violence on a student’s relationship with their school’s security and administration, and its consequences for school climate and student wellbeing; direct impacts of school security on student wellbeing; how different security types elicit different per­ ceptions in students; how student identity impacts the relationship between a student and their school’s security presence; and how lack of adequate support affects student perception of climate and student wellbeing.

Hopefully, these findings will pave the way for future research on the matter, as well as meaningfully contribute to the current literature. As threats and acts of violence within schools continue to affect student learning and wellbeing, and as an unprecedented number of schools resort to security measures and security personnel, it is critical that we continue to study the best ways to support our students, protect them from threats, and promote their long-term wellbeing. Furthermore, it is imperative that we acknowledge that these answers will only emerge once we begin to not only include but center student voices and experiences in this conversation.◆

title: Are People “Real” on BeReal? Perception and Authenticity in Utilization of Social Media App
abstract: BeReal grew rapidly in popularity throughout 2022. Created as a response to social media platforms where idealized images and higher usage are encouraged, BeReal takes a different approach. Valuing authenticity, BeReal asks users to post a daily front and back-facing picture within a random two-minute time slot and provides a short daily feed of BeReals from friends. In an online survey, U.S. college students 18-23 years old were studied in two groups: BeReal users (n = 100) and non-BeReal users (n =100). Both groups completed questions on perception and usage of different social media platforms and anxiety, public self-consciousness, fear of missing out, and authenticity scales. BeReal users were asked additional questions to observe trends in how people use and perceive BeReal, determine the extent to which BeReal usage moderates the relationship between total time spent on social media and anxiety, and examine whether inauthentic BeReal behaviors are correlated with greater anxiety, self-consciousness, fear of missing out, and inauthenticity. Results show that BeReal usage did not significantly mitigate the link between time spent on social media and anxiety, fear of missing out, public self-consciousness, and authenticity. The average user posted 78% of the time, posted late 52% of the time, and retook their BeReal at least once 37% of the time before posting. While the app was designed to promote authenticity by keeping users accountable, actual users were more forgiving with these inauthentic behaviors, with the median accepted late post of 10 hours late and the median accepted number of retakes being three. We also found that the percentage of late posts had a negative public correlation with anxiety, and the percentage of skipped posts had a positive correlation with public self-consciousness.
text:
Department of Psychology

Are People “Real” on BeReal?

Perception and Authenticity in Utilization of Social Media App by Amy Fan

Faculty Adviser: Alissa Chung, Ph.D. Second Reader: William Horton, Ph.D.

Author Note This research was supported by the Academic Undergraduate Research Grant through Northwestern’s Office of Undergraduate Research. Conclusions, opinions, and other statements of the author are not necessarily representative of Northwestern University. This project would not have been possible without the support of my adviser, Dr. Alissa Chung; my senior thesis seminar instructor, Dr. Sandra Waxman; and teaching assis­ tant, Kayla Garner.

Abstract BeReal grew rapidly in popularity throughout 2022. Created as a response to social media platforms where idealized images and higher usage are encouraged, BeReal takes a different approach. Valuing authenticity, BeReal asks users to post a daily front and back-facing picture within a random two-minute time slot and provides a short daily feed of BeReals from friends. In an online survey, U.S. college students 18-23 years old were studied in two groups: BeReal users (n = 100) and non-BeReal users (n =100). Both groups completed questions on perception and usage of different social media platforms and anxiety, public self-consciousness, fear of missing out, and authenticity scales. BeReal users were asked additional questions to observe trends in how people use and perceive BeReal, determine the extent to which BeReal usage moderates the relationship between total time spent on social media and anxiety, and examine whether inauthentic BeReal behaviors are correlated with greater anxiety, self-consciousness, fear of missing out, and inauthenticity. Results show that BeReal usage did not significantly mitigate the link between time spent on social media and anxiety, fear of missing out, public self-conscious­ ness, and authenticity. The average user posted 78% of the time, posted late 52% of the time, and retook their BeReal at least once 37% of the time before posting. While the app was designed to promote authenticity by keeping users accountable, actual users were more forgiving with these inauthentic behaviors, with the median accepted late post of 10 hours late and the median accepted number of retakes being three. We also found that the percentage of late posts had a negative public correlation with anxiety, and the percentage of skipped posts had a positive correlation with public self-consciousness. Keywords: BeReal, social media, authentic­ ity, anxiety, public self-consciousness, fear of missing out

Are People “Real” on BeReal? Perception and Authenticity in Utilization of Social Media App

With over 10 million daily users and 53 million downloads, BeReal claims to be “a new and unique way to discover who your friends really are in their daily life” (BeReal). Created as a response to social media platforms like Instagram, where us­ ers tend to post picture-perfect images on a never-ending feed, BeReal takes a different approach. The app shows a limited daily feed of friends’ BeReals, taking up only a small part of the day.

The overall objective of this app is to “be real.” A BeReal user gets a notification at any point during the day and has two minutes to take a front and back-facing camera picture. If they do not post within that time frame, the delayed time is shown; for example, “10 minutes late” or “8 hours late.” Users are discouraged from posting later when they may be doing something that is more appealing to their audience. Users cannot see their friends’ BeReals for the day until they post one themselves. BeReal does not show the feature of likes or followers but instead has “reacts” where users can respond to a BeReal with a pic­ ture, emoji, or comment. Users can only see friends’ BeReals from that day and not from past days to keep users’ feeds short and up to date. All these aspects combined could potentially eliminate the popularity aspect of other social media platforms, such as comparing numbers of followers, likes, and other interactions. The main goal of the app is for users to see what their friends are up to while mitigating the neg­ ative effects of other social media platforms such as Instagram and Facebook. Due to the novel popularity of BeReal, there is no current literature studying this platform.

“While the app was designed to promote authenticity by keeping users accountable, actual users were more forgiving with these inauthentic behaviors.”

Given its widespread usage among college students and younger adolescents, looking into how people use and perceive BeReal could reveal unintended negative conse­ quences to using the app and/or show that it is a social media app that connects people in a positive manner.

Existing Authenticity in Social Media Platforms

Before BeReal’s prominence, authen­ ticity on social media platforms was en­ couraged in other ways. For example, on Instagram, users often have a main account and a “finsta” or a “fake Instagram.” The main account is where users post their best pictures for a more general audience, while the finsta is where users post less polished photos, emotional photos, archival photos, funny moments (Kang & Wei, 2020), and unfiltered thoughts to a small group of friends (Huang & Vitak, 2022). Despite this push for authenticity by using Instagram in this manner, young adults and children still may face certain pressures to “perform” on these finstas since there are a set of norms as to what content is posted and how often (Dewar et al., 2019).

Looking even further into the past, blogging in a personal journal or diary form on platforms like MySpace and Tumblr has allowed users to vent and seek feedback on difficult situations or everyday life situations by giving users an online platform where it is appropriate and encouraged to share personal experi­ ences and seek support from a community (Baker et al., 2008). Certain social con­ straints hinder people from bringing these situations up in face-to-face conversations. When comparing bloggers on MySpace to nonbloggers, bloggers’ social integration, reliable alliance, and friendship satisfaction all increased compared to nonbloggers’, suggesting that blogging may have benefits in perceived social support (Baker et al., 2008). Blogging could even be used as a form of self-therapy (Tan et al., 2018).

Despite the push for authenticity in previously existing social media using these two methods, BeReal remains dis­ tinct. BeReal is a photo & caption-based platform with authenticity as a focus throughout the design process. Finstas and blogging on MySpace are features embed­ ded in the larger overall platform. People use Instagram and MySpace for purposes other than finstas and blogging on those respective platforms, so there could still be several other features on the platform that could negatively affect how authentic users are.

“Despite this push for authenticity by using Instagram in this manner, young adults and children still may face certain pressures to ‘perform.’”

Authenticity, despite its nuances, is important to study because past research has shown that authenticity is related to a lower risk of developing social media addiction (Monacis et al., 2021). In addi­ tion, authentic self-expression is associated with greater reported life satisfaction compared to self-idealized self-expression (Bailey et al., 2020).

Self-Presentation & Authenticity

False or adapted self-presentation and inauthenticity in portraying one’s life and emotions is a frequent problem with certain social media platforms (Gil- Or et al., 2015). Even with the measures against false self-presentation and push for showing the true self on BeReal, like the two-minute time limit and the randomized time a user gets a notification to post for the day, there is still an opportunity for inauthenticity through retakes, not post­ ing on time, and not posting at all. If the first photo is bad, the user might retake the photo to get a better angle of themselves. If the user feels like they are not doing some­ thing interesting enough, they could wait to post until later. And there is always the option of not posting at all if they do not want to show themselves for that day.

The number of friends a user has on social media could push users to in­ crease positive self-presentation regardless of whether the user is doing well or not (Kim & Lee, 2011). BeReal shows friend counts in increments after a certain point. For example, if a person has 68 friends on BeReal, it is displayed as 50+ instead of that specific number. It is possible that the relationship between audience and false self-presentation is hindered by the lack of specificity in BeReal of how many friends a person has added. However, there are lim­ itations to studying the effect of this spe­ cific feature due to other factors affecting false self-presentation like the presence of photos (Gil-Or et al., 2015) and the makeup of the audience (Rui, 2013). And it is still possible that those with more friends may still display more false self-presentation behaviors than those with fewer friends on BeReal.

Despite research showing that authentic self-expression can be positive, it is also important to note that there could be moments where authenticity can be negative. For instance, “vague-booking” is defined as when people go on Facebook to post a true but vague message about their current feelings that elicits a response from other users (Astleitner et al., 2023). Vague-booking may mediate the rela­ tionship between personality and mental health and is linked to suicidal ideation (Berryman et al., 2017). It is possible that sometimes going to social media to com­ municate and seek support may not be the best form of action, and it may be better to reach out to personal networks instead.

Social Media & Fear of Missing Out

Past studies suggest that an increase in social media usage is correlated with lower self-esteem (Jan et al., 2017; Hawi & Samaha, 2016). Lower self-esteem is associated with lower life satisfaction (Hawi & Samaha, 2016). A phenomenon where social media users feel left out of specific social events is known as the Fear of Missing Out (FoMO). Studies have shown that the negative impacts of social media sites leading to lower self-esteem are mediated by FoMO (Salim et al., 2017). Higher levels of FoMO were also related to increased social media presence through behaviors like updating their status more often or posting more pictures. BeReal aims to avoid FoMO by showing when users post late as an accountability fea­ ture. That way, people cannot only post their most interesting social interactions because they need to post when prompted to avoid “being late.” However, FoMO may still be prominent since users will likely see if they were left out of a social gathering on BeReal.

Social Media & Psychopathology

Several studies have implicated more time spent on social media as a risk factor for developing an anxiety disorder (Keles et al., 2020; Vannucci et al., 2017). Increased social media use has been linked to depression and anxiety, particularly when there is greater emotional invest­ ment in social media (Woods & Scott, 2016). Since BeReal is designed to take up a relatively short amount of time per day (~10 minutes), it is possible that users who primarily use BeReal and no other social media platforms have a reduced risk of developing psychopathology due to the minimal time spent on the app. In addi­ tion, if users utilize BeReal in an authentic manner, it is possible BeReal use mitigates the relationship between social media use and negative outcomes.

Research Questions

This study will explore the ques­ tions: (1) Does BeReal usage mitigate the link between time spent on social media and anxiety, fear of missing out (FoMO), public self-consciousness (PSC), and au­ thenticity? (2) How do people use BeReal, and what do they think BeReal’s intended purpose is compared to other social media apps? (3) Are inauthentic BeReal behaviors such as retakes, posting late, and skipping related to greater anxiety, PSC, FoMO, and inauthenticity?

Main Hypotheses

My hypothesis is that BeReal use moderates the link between total time spent on social media and anxiety, PSC, FoMO, and authenticity. Past research has shown a link between total time spent on social media and increasing anxiety, FoMO, and self-consciousness and decreasing self-esteem and authenticity (Monacis et al., 2021). BeReal’s push for authentic use could potentially mitigate these negative outcomes.

In open-ended questions about BeRe­ al, participants are expected to report ben­ efits like functionality (which limits time spent on the app), the encouraged lower friend count, the refreshed daily feed, and the spontaneity of posting. Some disadvan­ tages participants may bring up are FoMO, opportunities for inauthenticity often re­ ferred to as “being fake,” and the random notification during the day being at an inconvenient time. I expect there to be a greater positive attitude toward BeReal compared to other social media platforms.

Those who have more BeReal friends and exhibit more inauthentic behaviors such as greater average number of retakes, posting late, and skipping posts despite seeing the notification on time may have greater anxiety, PSC, FoMO, and less au­ thenticity. Those who have greater anxi­ ety, PSC, and FoMO, and less authenticity may care more about how they look during the two-minute window than remaining authentic, so they may retake their BeReal more often and skip or post late instead of showing what they are doing at the time of notification. A greater percentage of time spent scrolling through feeds may be correlated with higher levels of anxiety and FoMO due to a greater likelihood that a user may see other friends spending time with each other, while a greater percent­ age of time spent interacting with friends’ BeReals may be correlated with greater authenticity and lower FoMO.

Methods

Participants

Undergraduate college students of all genders, races, and ethnicities who are En­ glish speakers (n = 650) aged 18-23 years old across the United States were surveyed about their TikTok, Instagram, and BeRe­ al usage on the research platform Prolific. This screening on Prolific was used to sep­ arate participants into two groups. Group 1 participants (n = 100) did not use BeReal (less than once every two weeks for one month). Group 2 participants (n = 100) did use BeReal (at least once every two weeks for one month). Additional participants for the BeReal survey were sought out from the Northwestern University under­ graduate community due to the low num­ ber of qualifying BeReal users (n = 158). Participants in Group 2 (n = 100) were a mix of Prolific users (n = 75) who were compensated and Northwestern students (n = 25) who were not. Participants were only asked what college they go to in the demographics section since Prolific pro­ vides data on age, race, ethnicity, gender identity, year in school, and region.

Questionnaires

The survey included a question on college attended, questions on general so­ cial media usage across different platforms, questions about their perception of each social media platform (purpose, affect, etc.), questions specific to BeReal, the Gen­ eral Anxiety Disorder-7 Scale (Spitzer et al., 2006), Public Self-Consciousness Scale (Scheier and Carver, 1985), the Fear of Missing Out Scale (Przybylski et al., 2013), and Authenticity Scale (Wood et al., 2008).

General Anxiety Disorder Scale

The General Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7) was used to measure anxiety in the current state (Spitzer et al., 2006). This short questionnaire utilized a Likert scale of 0-3 (not at all, several days, more than half the days, and nearly every day) with prompts like “Feeling nervous, anxious, or on edge” and “Worrying too much about different things.” Scores were calculated by summing the numerical score of each item for a final score. For this study, scores were treated as a continuous variable. A greater score is indicative of greater anx­ iety. Cronbach’s α for the GAD-7 scale in this sample is 0.938 (n = 191). The GAD-7 Scale is widely used in clinical settings and was shown to be reliable and valid (Spitzer et al., 2006).

Public Self-Consciousness Scale

Public Self-Consciousness (PSC) re­ fers to the tendency to think about aspects of self in the matter of public display. Only the PSC Scale from the overall Self-Con­ sciousness Scale (Scheier and Carver, 1985) was utilized as this form of self-conscious­ ness may be particularly relevant to BeReal usage. The seven-item questionnaire gave prompts like “I am concerned with my style of doing things” and “I usually worry about making a good impression,” which are an­ swered on a 0-3 Likert scale (not like me at all, a little like me, somewhat like me, a lot like me). Scores were averaged to obtain an overall score. A higher score is indicative of greater PSC. The PSC Scale was shown to be reliable and valid (Scheier and Carv­ er, 1985). Cronbach’s α for the PSC Scale in this sample is 0.846 (n = 191).

Fearing of Missing Out Scale

The 10-item FoMO Scale was used to measure the degree to which someone fears missing out on social events and uses social media to remain hyper-connected using a 5-point Likert scale (not at all true of me, slightly true of me, moderately true of me, very true of me, and extremely true of me) with prompts like “I get worried when I find out my friends are having fun with­ out me” and “I fear my friends have more rewarding experiences than me.” Each item’s score from 1-5 points was summed to a total score, and an average between all answers provided a final score. A greater score is indicative of a greater fear of miss­ ing out. The FoMO Scale was shown to be reliable and valid (Przybylski et al., 2013). Cronbach’s α for the FoMO Scale in this sample is 0.897 (n = 191).

Authenticity Scale

The 12-item Authenticity Scale mea­ sured authenticity in knowing oneself, expressing emotions in a way that is con­ gruent with values and beliefs, and staying true to personal beliefs despite external influences (Wood et al., 2008). There were four items for each of the three subscales: Self-Alienation (AS), Authentic Living (AL), and Accepting of External Influences (AE). Participants were given prompts like “I feel as if I don’t know myself very well,” “I live in accordance to my values and be­ liefs,” and “I am strongly influenced by the opinions of others,” which were answered on a Likert scale of 1-7 (does not describe me at all to describes me very well). The AS and AE Subscales were reverse-scored. The final authenticity score was the sum of the reverse-scored subscale items and AL Subscale items. In the overall Authenticity Scale and AL Subscale, a greater score was indicative of greater authenticity. For the AS and AE Subscales, a lower score was indicative of greater authenticity. The Au­ thenticity Scale and Subscales were shown to be reliable and valid (Wood et al., 2008). The Authenticity Scale Cronbach’s α is 0.832. The AS Subscale (α = 0.958), AL Subscale (α = 0.855), and AE Subscale (α

= 0.852) were also internally reliable (n =191).

General Social Media Questions

This nine-item section was repeated for every social media platform partic­ ipants indicated they use. Participants were asked which social media platforms they used, percentage breakdowns of the amount of time spent on each platform, how often they used each platform (daily or almost daily, 2-3 times per week, 1 time per week, 1-2 times per month, <1 per month), average amount of time spent per day, how they used each platform (catch up with friends, scroll through feed for en­ tertainment, scroll through feed for news, post about own life, make entertaining content, other) and percentage breakdown of time spent on those options. They were also asked open-ended questions about what they thought the intended purpose of this platform was and whether the benefits outweigh the disadvantages.

BeReal Questions

Group 2 participants (n = 100) who were active users of BeReal (at least once every two weeks for a month) were asked a separate set of questions (28 items). They were asked how many friends they have on BeReal, the percentage of time they post, the percentage of time they are on time when they post, the percentage of time they retake their BeReal before posting, the percentage of time they retake 1, 2, 3, or 4 times, the motivation behind retak­ ing BeReals, what percentage of time they scroll through the feed after they post, the percentage of time they skip the BeReal despite seeing the notification on time, the percentage of time they skip the Be­ Real after seeing the notification late, the percentage of time they interact with their friends’ BeReals, and when they do inter­ act with friends’ BeReals, the percentage of time they utilize face react compared to emoji compared to comment. The last two questions gauged when users thought the latest someone could post and the maxi­ mum number of retakes that they would consider to be socially acceptable to them.

Plan of Analysis

We ran a linear regression to com­ pare total time spent on social media and the four numerical dependent variable scores. BeReal use is expected to moderate the correlation between total time spent on social media and the four DVs, so hours spent on social media per week and BeReal use acted as independent variables and an interaction term between hours spent on social media per week and BeReal use was included in the model. Pearson correlations were run between separate IVs (number of friends, percent of times posted, percentage of late posts, percentage of retakes, average number of retakes per BeReal, percentage of skips despite seeing BeReal on time, per­ centage of skips after seeing notification on time, percentage of time spent scrolling through feed after post, percentage of time they interact with friends’ BeReals) and the four DVs to determine further correla­ tions. Qualitative data was coded for the top five occurrences.

Results

Data Cleaning & Scoring

Participants were removed from the data if they did not meet certain criteria (n = 9). For both the General Survey and the BeReal Survey, those who did not complete the questionnaires about anxiety, PSC, FoMO, and authenticity were re­ moved (n = 3). Those who took the BeReal survey and did not post at least twice in the last 30 days were removed (n = 5). Partic­ ipants who had given out-of-range data (e.g., over 24 hours of social media use per day) were also removed (n = 1). 191 par­ ticipants remained: 93 BeReal users and 98 non-BeReal users.

Social Media Usage

Results are based on hours spent on social media per day and on what specific apps are shown (Table 1). On average, par­ ticipants used apps like TikTok, Instagram, and YouTube for a greater amount of time. For the BeReal group, the mean time spent on social media was 4.0 hours (SD = 2.3) per day. The BeReal use percentage mean was 4.96 (SD = 5.86), ~12 minutes a day.

TikTok and Instagram percentages were higher for the BeReal group, with a slightly lower YouTube percentage (Table 2). We see that Facebook percentages are low across the board for college students. Many participants thought the intended purpose of Facebook is to connect with friends and family of the older generation or for event invites and notifications.

How social media was used greatly differed depending on the platform. Par­ ticipants generally used BeReal to scroll through their feed or stories to see what people in their network were up to (M = 51.7%, SD = 35.5%) and post or create con­ tent (M = 27.8%, SD = 32.9%). Participants primarily scrolled through their feed for entertainment on TikTok (M = 72.4%, SD = 26.6%)) and YouTube (M = 72.0%, SD = 35.3%), while Instagram was used in a greater variety of ways: scrolling through the feed to keep up with network (M = 36.8%, SD = 27.3%), scrolling through the feed for entertainment (M = 31.0%, SD = 25.8%), and directly interacting with friends (M = 21.9%, SD = 22.6%). Face­ book’s main usage was scrolling through the feed to keep up with their network (M

= 48.4%, SD = 35.6%).

BeReal Results

In the BeReal data set, participants posted a BeReal 78% of the time. Of our 93 participants, 55 provided insight as to why they skipped posts (Table 3). Participants posted late on average 53.8% of the time (SD = 29.3%). The most occurring reasons for posting late were inconvenient times, perceived interest, and apathy (Table 4). Out of our 93 participants, 84 participants provided qualitative data on reasons for posting late. The mean percentage they re­ took their BeReal before posting was 37.5% (SD = 30.8%). When participants retook their BeReal, they tended to retake it only once (M = 74.2%, SD = 24.6%) or twice (M = 19.4%, SD = 18.9%). Most users retook BeReals for unclear photos, appearance of self, and because it did not include desired content (Table 5). Out of our 93 partici­ pants, 90 participants provided qualitative data on reasons for retaking BeReals.

The mean percentage of participants interacting with friends’ BeReals was 56.5% (SD = 38.1%). The methods participants used to interact with friends on BeReal were Face React (M = 60.3%, SD = 37.0%), Comment (M = 19.4%, SD = 25.1%), and Emoji React (M = 12.6%, SD = 25.8%). Face React, or taking a selfie response, was the most popular. The median number of friends users had on BeReal was 47 (SD = 15). In users’ opinion, the mean max hours a user should post late is 11.9 with a me­ dian of 10 hours (SD = 8.8), and the mean max number of retakes a user should take is 3.7 with a median of 3 retakes (SD = 2.6).

Primary Analyses

We ran Pearson correlations be­ tween time spent on social media and anxiety, PSC, FoMO, and authenticity and found a positive correlation between time on social media and anxiety (Table 6). Cor­ relations between the four scales were all significant. Anxiety, PSC, and FoMO all had moderate positive correlations with each other, while anxiety, PDC, and FoMo had moderate negative correlations with authenticity (Table 6).

To test if BeReal use moderated the relationship between total time spent on social media and anxiety, PSC, FoMO, and authenticity, four linear regression models were run with those four variables as the DVs. Hours spent on social media per week and BeReal use acted as independent vari­ ables, with an interaction term between hours spent on social media per week and BeReal use included in the model. There is no evidence that BeReal use mitigates the relationship between total time spent on social media and the DVs (Table 1A-4A).

Analyses were also run to test the BeReal group and see if authentic vs. in­ authentic BeReal use moderates the rela­ tionship between total time spent on social media and anxiety. Authentic BeReal use was defined as practical reasons for not us­ ing BeReal as intended. If a participant said that they could not take the BeReal on time because they were in the shower or in class, that reasoning would be coded “authentic.” If a participant said they could not take the BeReal because they were doing something boring and would do something more in­ teresting later, then their reason was coded “inauthentic.” Similar reasoning was ap­ plied to reasons for retakes and skipping the BeReal. Authentic usage did not mod­ erate the relationship between total time spent on social media per week and the four DVs (Table 5A-7A).

Secondary Analyses

Percentage of late posts had a positive correlation with the authenticity scores (r

= 0.279, p < 0.003) and a moderate negative correlation with the self-alienation authen­ ticity score (r = -0.429, p < 0.001). In this subscale, the higher the score, the greater self-alienation and decreased authenticity in that aspect. The percentage of late posts also had a slight negative correlation with the GAD-7 anxiety score (r = -0.306, p < 0.003). Percentage of skips had a positive correlation with the PSC score (r = 0.208, p < 0.046). See Table 8A for full results.

Discussion

Summary & Interpretation of Results

In terms of general social media use, we found that apps that have an entertain­ ment aspect, like TikTok, Instagram, and YouTube, were used for a greater duration. Time spent on BeReal is generally low (Ta­ ble 2). BeReal was mainly used to keep up with people in users’ networks and post or create content that has a greater social or community aspect.

We found that BeReal use does not mitigate the link between time spent on social media and anxiety, PSC, FoMO, and authenticity. In addition, out of the four possible correlations between time spent on social media and the four DVs, only time spent on social media and anx­ iety had a significant positive correlation. Descriptive statistics showed that among those who use BeReal, the average user posted 78% of the time. When users post­ ed, they tended to post late 52% of the time and retake their BeReal at least once 37% of the time before posting. It is possible that because users did not always adhere to the intended use of BeReal, no moderating effects were observed, as users only spent 12 minutes on BeReal every day. A shared understanding that it is okay to post late or retake your BeReal despite the counter­ measures built into BeReal shows that it was not being used in the intended way.

“We found that BeReal use does not mitigate the link between time spent on social media and anxiety, public self- consciousness (PSC), fear of missing out

(FoMO), and authenticity.”

Anxiety, PSC, and FoMO all had moderately positive correlations with each other, while anxiety, PSC, and FoMO had moderate negative correlations with authenticity. This result showed those with either high anxiety, PSC, or FoMO may have higher scores in the other two variables as well. The percentage of late posts has a positive correlation with the Authenticity Scale and a moderate neg­ ative correlation with the self-alienation authenticity scores, which differed from the hypothesis. We expected that those who exhibited more inauthentic behavior would show lower authenticity scores. Those who posted late may be more likely to be engaging in in-person activities in­ volving others, which suggests authentic living outside of the app. The percentage of late posts also had a negative correla­ tion with anxiety, which could possibly be explained by the idea that those with less anxiety may not be as vigilant about post­ ing on time. If a user cares a lot about how they are seen by the public, then they may have opted to skip BeReal altogether even when they are available to post late, which explains the positive relationship between percentage of skips with PSC score.

Limitations

In the data collection process for au­ thentic usage in retakes, posting late, and skipping, participants were asked for rea­ sons why they retake, post late, and skip, which we coded as authentic or inauthen­ tic. While the number of participants who listed each reason was obtained, data were not collected longitudinally to see the fre­ quency of each reason in specific instances. Although some may have listed authentic or inauthentic reasons, we still do not know how often they are engaging these behav­ iors for authentic or inauthentic reasons and whether some users fall somewhere in the middle in terms of authentic use. More detailed studies on BeReal use with a great­ er sample size are necessary to gain a better understanding of this relationship.

Future Direction

The predicted mitigation effect of BeReal was hypothesized under the as­ sumption that BeReal would largely be used in the intended manner. We found that this was not the case. However, since we collected a great deal of data on how BeReal is used, that can be helpful in cre­ ating and designing further BeReal studies.

The most recent update on BeReal showed a significant change in design. Now, users can post up to three BeReals if they post their first BeReal on time. They likely made this decision because, as this study shows, adherence to BeReal rules is low. However, this does defeat the original purpose of the app, which was for users to show what they are doing at any given time during the day. This new update makes BeReal more of a mix between the original app and Instagram, where you post your highlights. Although some may argue that the new BeReal update is still better than Instagram since users must post on time to unlock the extra posts, there is a possi­ bility that this could lead to more FoMO since BeReal is already an intimate view into one’s life as a daily task. Now, with the added option of posting up to three times a day, there is even greater visibility. Re­ searchers must adapt to these changes to fully understand the relationship between social media and psychopathology. ◆
