title: Illustrating Indigeneity: Xie Sui’s Huang Qing zhigong tu and the critical reevaluation of its depictions of aboriginal Taiwanese peoples, 1751–1775 and 2006–2022
text:
Department of Art History

Illustrating Indigeneity: Xie Sui’s Huang Qing zhigong tu and the critical reevaluation of its depictions of aboriginal

Taiwanese peoples, 1751–1775 and 2006–2022 by Grace A. Wu

Faculty Advisers: Dr. Yuthika Sharma and Dr. Peter J. Carroll

Visualizing Empire After decades of battle, the Aisin-Gioro clan from Manchuria officially became the sovereigns of Imperial China after conquering Beijing in 1644, establishing the Qing 清 dynasty. Among the 10 rulers of the dynasty, the Qianlong 乾隆 emperor (r. 1736–95) reigned the second-longest and oversaw China at its geographic peak. During his 60- year tenure, the ruler immersed himself in administrative and artisanal affairs, serving “as conqueror and empire builder, aesthete and sponsor of culture, poet and artist, grand ruler over the world’s largest society.”1 A series of military campaigns from the 1740s to 1790s doubled the geographic size of the Qing empire, extending from Mongolia to Myanmar and Xinjiang to Tai­ wan (Figure 1). This expansion also brought numerous ethnic groups into the empire’s domain. To celebrate this success, the Qianlong emperor instructed his court to create the Huang Qing zhigong tu 皇清職貢圖 [Qing Imperial Illustration of Tributaries], which historian Laura Hostetler describes as a “cultural cartography of empire.”2 The Huang Qing zhigong tu contains image likenesses and textual descriptions of over 300 groups of people within the mid- to late-18th century Qing domain. Upon imperial behest, court artists made several versions, leading to the circulation of ethnographic tropes, including nakedness, animalistic qualities, and ‘uncultured’ mannerisms.

1 Mote, Imperial China, 900-1800, 912. 2 Hostetler and Wu, Qing Imperial Illustrations.

Although the genre of zhigong tu histori­ cally depicts people who paid tribute to the Chinese court, the large number of figures—who did not all pay tribute—in the Huang Qing zhigong tu reflects the scope of the Qing domain. Empire is as much of a visual project as a material one, and the Qing utilized cultural cartography to supplement topographical maps they created. The National Palace Museum’s il­ luminated handscroll version of the Huang Qing zhigong tu, attributed to court artist Xie Sui 謝遂 (hereinafter “Xie Sui scrolls” or “NPM scrolls”), has distinct formal attributes, such as its brilliant illumination (Figure 2). The four Xie Sui scrolls are unique out of surviving editions of the Huang Qing zhigong tu (Appendix A) due to their frequent public display in Tai­ wan’s National Palace Museum (Appendix C). Curators’ decision to regularly exhibit these scrolls highlights their curatorial and educational importance in 21st centu­ ry Taiwan, which I discuss further in the conclusion.

The Qing-Imagined World The genre of zhigong tu 職貢圖 first emerged during the Liang 梁 (502–57) dynasty. Zhi 職 is used in phrases relating to duty and responsibility; gong 貢 is shorthand for gongfu 貢賦, or tribute. Together, zhigong expresses the obligation to respectfully submit, obey, and present things to someone higher in the hierar­ chy. Tu 圖 describes an image, illustration, or map. Zhigong tu, or illustrated tributary documents, is unique from textual docu­ mentation of tribute because it contains the supposed visual likeness of the indi­ vidual or group.

Throughout Chinese history, the imperial court leveraged zhigong tu to celebrate the dynasty’s influence within and outside of its domain. Their high-quality materiality and careful documentation suggest only the highest-ranking officials viewed them, celebrating their political and diplomatic successes. The earliest-known zhigong tu, Tribute Bearers to the Liang Court (c. sixth century), depicts full-length portraits of the actual ambassadors who paid tribute to the Chinese court (Figure 3). Despite the envoys’ formalized stiff poses, each of the over two dozen illustrated figures ex­ hibits individualized characters with emo­ tions and personalities. An accompanying textual description of their respective polity details its topography, customs, re­ lationship with the Liang, and the tributes presented to the court.3

3 Zheng, “Tribute Bearers to the Liang Court,” 36. 4 Zhigong manifested in three types of relationships: “from tributary states to the Qing empire, from regional governments to the court, and from individual officials above a certain rank to the emperor.” The Qing tributary system was complex and flexible to changing conditions. In this thesis, I focus on the foreign relations aspect of this system. Ko, The Social Life of Inkstones, 45.

“Despite the claims of faithful representation, the provincial and court artists inevitably generalized millions of people into 300 male-female paradigmatic types.”

Zhigong tu supplemented chaogong tixi 朝貢體系 [the tributary system].4 With rudimentary origins during the Han 漢 dynasty (206 BCE-220 CE), the Chinese tributary system reinforced imperial suzerainty by organizing people by their perceived civility. The frequency of tribute paid to the center vaguely determined the groups’ positionality.5 The Qing codified the tributary system, conducting foreign relations through this “abstract creed of loy­ alty.”6 Although not all polities interpreted the practice of zhigong as demonstrating loyalty to the Chinese emperor, the Qing perceived their submission as such; the in­ clusion of European countries in the Huang Qing zhigong tu serves as a prime example of this difference in understanding.

The Qing viewed the tributary system as a method for foreigners and ethnic mi­ norities to gravitate towards the court out of admiration of the political, military, and cultural supremacy of the Chinese state. As a visual reflection of these beliefs, the Huang Qing zhigong tu exhibits the dynas­ ty’s narrative of its superiority within and beyond its borders. Content evolved from individu­ alized portraiture to ethnographic repre­ sentations that delineated the dress and habits of the other 12 centuries after the first known zhigong tu’s creation. Instead of documenting male ambassadors who physically were at court, the Huang Qing zhigong tu depicts male-female stock pairs who lived far from the imperial center. This shift to male-female pairs reflects an attempt to know ‘all’ people of a group. As the distance widens between the Qing court and their subjects, the illustrations in the Huang Qing zhigong tu become more exaggerated and archetypal. Terminologies in the Huang Qing zhigong tu also emerged to convey ideas of cultural difference and inferiority, such as referring to Indigenous Taiwanese as fan 番. Though its meaning is nuanced, fan translated as “savage” or “barbarian.”7 The Qing’s usage of fan enables its superiority by accentuating Taiwanese’s relative and cultural distance from the inner court.

5 Tribute could be paid daily, monthly, quarterly, annually, or occasionally. Stuart-Fox, A Short History of China and Southeast Asia, 20. 6 For example, legal international trade could only occur when envoys paid tribute to the emperor. Ko, The Social Life of Inkstones, 45. 7 For the purposes of my thesis, I use “fan,” “savage,” and “barbarian” interchangeably. An in-depth investigation into this term can be a whole thesis on its own.

The handscroll versions of Huang Qing zhigong tu offers a unique viewing experience for the audience. The viewer would first lay the scroll flat on a table; then, they would unroll about a shoul­ der-width section of the tributary scroll to simultaneously view one to three entries. To progress further along the handscroll, the viewer would roll the right roller end while unrolling the left, bringing more figures into his gaze. This interactive na­ ture of a constant progression brings the viewer on a journey throughout the Qing domain without leaving Beijing.

Creation and Layout of the Huang Qing zhigong tu In 1751, the Qianlong emperor issued edicts to governor-generals within the empire detailing the imperial ethnographic and encyclopedic project that later became known as the Huang Qing zhigong tu:

My dynasty has united the vast expanses. Of all various peoples from within and beyond [neiwai miaoyi 內外 苗夷] our domains, there are none who have not sincerely turned toward Us and been transformed. As for their clothing, caps, appearance, and bearing, each has its differences. Now although we have likenesses from several places, they are not yet uniform and complete. Gather together the several models that we now have, and deliver them to each of the gov­ ernors and governors-general near the borders. Order them to take the Miao, Yao, Li, and Zhuang within their jurisdictions, as well as the myriad Yi and Fan beyond, and according to these examples copy their appearance, bearing, clothing, and ornaments, make illustrations and send them to the Grand Council for classification and arrangement for presentation and inspection.8

Incumbent government officers across China mobilized upon receiving this decree. As the governor-general of Fujian and Zhejiang, Karjišan 喀爾吉 善 quickly instructed his subordinates to create detailed visual likenesses of “all various peoples” with whom they crossed paths with, such as during trade.9 Other Fujian provincial officials sent the sketches to Karjišan’s office, where workers created final drawings. After an official envoy approved them upon detailed inspection, workers decorated the compiled album for presentation to the Qianlong emperor.10 To accompany the drawings sent to Bei­ jing in 1752, provincial officials included a written addendum presenting the illus­ trations to the emperor, describing the people’s clothing, accessories, facial char­ acteristics, culture, preferences, and geo­ graphic jurisdiction. The Grand Council in Beijing received and finished compiling the submissions from across the empire in

1758; the Council then likely presented the drawings to the emperor for inspection before handing them to court artists.11 This process of creating and approving the illustrated likenesses at different levels of the government reflects how deeply the Qing administration involved itself in every step of the Huang Qing zhigong tu’s creation.

8 The Miao, Yao, et al. are different derogatory categorization terms for ethnic minorities. See Da Qing Gaozong Chun Huangdi Shilu, 8: 5834–35 for edict in Chinese. Hostetler and Wu, Qing Imperial Illustrations, 3 (emphasis added). 9 Song, Luzong, 23; Hostetler and Wu, Qing Imperial Illustrations, 3. 10 Song, Luzong, 23. 11 Wei, “‘Huang Qing zhigong tu’ chuangzhi shimo,” 10. 12 Wei, 10. 13 Deal and Hostetler, The Art of Ethnography, xx–xxii; Wei, “‘Huang Qing zhigong tu’ chuangzhi shimo,” 10. 14 The scrolls’ dimensions, respectively, are: (I) 33.9 x 1462.2 cm, (II) 33.8 x 1402.2 cm, (III) 33.4 x 1822.8 cm, and (IV) 33.8 x 1694 cm. Liu and Cheng, Si fang lai chao, xiv–xv. 15 See Hostetler and Wu, Qing Imperial Illustrations, 27.

The Qianlong emperor personally appointed a master court painter to work on each of the four scrolls: Ding Guan­ peng 丁觀鵬, Jin Tingbiao 金廷標, Yao Wenhan 姚文瀚, and Cheng Liang 程梁, respectively.12 As part of their roles, these painters analyzed the provincial albums and finalized the colored likenesses. To fulfill the Qianlong emperor’s wish to have his empire recorded for posterity, other court artists—including Xie Sui—triplicat­ ed each scroll and created a polished album folio of each figure (Appendix A).13

Each of the NPM handscrolls is roughly one-foot tall, and their lengths vary from 46- to almost 60-feet long.14 The expressive title of each scroll written on the orange frontispiece celebrates the power of the Qing court through its col­ lection of tributary subjects (Appendix B). Poems appear at the beginning and end of each scroll, praising the prosperity of the multi-ethnic Qing-ruled society and claim­ ing the information in the scrolls—spe­ cifically the illustrations—as accurate and trustworthy.15 Despite the claims of faith­ ful representation, the provincial and court artists inevitably generalized millions of people into 300 male-female paradigmatic types. However, the Qianlong emperor’s approval signals these drawings were good enough for the Qing’s self-admiration. Hundreds of vertical sections, with varying widths between six- and 12-inch­ es, lie between the bookend colophon poems. Each section, or entry, depicts a group of people associated with a foreign polity or Qing administrative region. In the upper register of the scroll, text in the Qing’s official languages, Chinese and Manchu, identifies the group and describes their social customs. Sometimes the text explicitly mentions tribute being made to the Qing court, which would have been performed by ambassadors or carefully se­ lected representatives.

Illustrated figures that correspond to the text occupy the lower register. In al­ most all the entries, an archetypal male and female pair in generalized local dress rep­ resents the group. The figures are roughly five- to six-inches tall and interact with a quotidian object, local crop, or animal mentioned in the text. Some figures stand erect, and others contort their bodies while engaged in an activity or turn away from the viewer. The figures seemingly float on the paper with no painted background; clearly, the focus of the object is on people’s visual likeness, dress, and other local cus­ toms. In a compendium of over 300 entries and 100,000 words,16 the diversity of dress, pose, and color visually displays the cultur­ al heterogeneity and geographic span of the Qing empire. The Qianlong emperor then viewed the final product, claiming all of these subjects in his domain by stamping important personal seals onto the scroll.

16 Wei, “‘Huang Qing zhigong tu’ chuangzhi shimo,” 11. 17 See “Balebu Headman with Servant” entry in the first scroll. Olivova, “Tobacco Smoking in Qing China,” 236. 18 Skoggard, The Indigenous Dynamic in Taiwan’s Postwar Development, 10.

Xie Sui worked on the scrolls between 1751 and 1775, though sections were add­ ed up to 1790—likely not by the same artist due to differences of artistic rendering and male-male pairs. 17

Taiwan in the Huang Qing zhigong tu: A Case Study From the founding of the Qing dynasty in the seventeenth century until the early 19th century, Taiwan had “an uprising each three years, a rebellion every five” largely due to both Ming loyalists attempting to subvert the Qing dynasty and inter-ethnic conflicts between Han Chinese settlers and Indigenous Taiwanese communities.18 In 1684, the Qing annexed Taiwan into Fujian Province—naming it “Taiwan Prefecture”—in hopes of directly combatting future threats emerging from the island (Figure 4).

“The entries’ text and image mutually reinforce Qing notions of savagery yet sometimes diverge on their extent, creating conflicting portrayals of fan.”

Documents like the Huang Qing zhi­ gong tu demonstrate the Qing continued to view Taiwan as liminal and savage a centu­ ry after the annexation through their ter­ minology, text, and illustrations. Although fan became a general term for unaccultur­ ated people, three specific subdivisions of fan became closely associated with Taiwan: shoufan 熟番, guihua shengfan 歸化生番, and shengfan 生番. The terms sheng 生 and shou 熟 literally translate to “raw” and “cooked,” respectively, with connotations of “wild” and “tame” or “unacculturated” and “acculturated.”19A third term, guihua shengfan 歸化生番 [naturalized raw fan], or huafan 化番 for short, refers to a middle designation where wild fan affirm their al­ legiance to the Qing court through tribute and taxes. The representation of the sub­ divisions fan in the Xie Sui scrolls demon­ strates tension between the arguments that the Taiwanese aboriginals can become assimilated into Chinese society but also have less developed ways of living, such as a reliance on hunting and eating raw food.

In the second NPM scroll, 13 Tai­ wanese male-female pairs appear in the Fujian Province section, and their titles all contain the “fan” label.20 The entries’ order is organized by a perceived decline in cul­ tural refinement; there are eight shoufan followed by three huafan and two shengfan (Appendix D). Savagery is most visually apparent through the male figure’s pose, dress, and facial expression while the fe­ male figures are more passive, have fairer skin, and dressed more modestly than their male companion.21 The details in the text and illustrations complement and refer­ ence one another, though some differences are apparent upon closer inspection.

By 1747, Qing records included 299 aboriginal villages by name. The consol­ idation of the almost-300 villages into 13 male-female pairs in the Xie Sui scrolls is a deliberate one; the title of each entry sug­ gests that the information generalizes the living practices of the fan living in a partic­ ular Qing administrative region (Appendix D).22 The Huang Qing zhigong tu reflects an ethnographic framework by documenting Taiwanese society through specific cate­ gories—such as housing, food, costume, marriages, burials, and tools—though the depth of detail varies depending on the Qing’s familiarity with that group.23 This structure, organization, and emphasis re­ flect Qing administrative and cultural log­ ics rather than how the Taiwanese identi­ fied themselves.

The seventh Taiwanese entry doc­ uments the shoufan of Dehua and other communities in Danshui Subprefecture in northwest Taiwan (Figure 5). These shou­ fan are among the most modestly dressed, and their upright pose and direct gaze fur­ ther connotes their civility and humanity. An excerpt of the accompanying text de­ scribes the terrain and people:

Their lands are very swampy be­ cause they are close to the ocean. They therefore use thatch or wooden boards to make their dwellings. They eat mil­ let together with a mixture of fish and shrimp prepared in a spicy broth. Both men and women wear short upper gar­ ments bound at the waist with a strip of cloth. They work hard at farming and they also fish and hunt. They play flutes and zithers made of bamboo for enter­ tainment in their spare time.24

The text portrays the shoufan as adaptable and resourceful, with the con­ junction “therefore” to explain the logic of using construction materials suitable for the swampy environment. The sho­ ufan also utilize local natural resources, catching fish and shrimp from the ocean to sustain themselves. Reflecting their shou [“cooked”] and acculturated nature, their food involves cooking with fire. The text also notes that these fan have gustatory re­ finement: they add spices to this dish and mix different flavors and textures together in their food.

The pair’s illustrated costume departs from the text. Instead of wearing “short upper garments bound at the waist,” both figures wear embroidered and woven cloth shirts that loosely extend beyond their hips and cover their arms. Though the text does not mention leg garments, the pair wears long flowy skirts that cover the entirety of their legs. This length of skirt would be highly impractical while farming and fishing in swampy surroundings; this dis­ connect shows the artist’s creative liberty in rendering costumes without seriously contemplating the textual description. The man holds a bamboo flute in his hands and eagerly offers it in the direction of his female companion, who gazes to her right towards the next entry while hold­ ing a hoe and basket. The text notes that the shoufan sustain themselves through farming, fishing, and hunting, but the artist only included agricultural tools. The deliberate exclusion of weaponry elevates the shoufan’s perceived civility through their non-threatening appearance. Thus, the textual description and illustrations work together to portray this group as hardworking, yet also engaging in cultural entertainment during their spare time.

19 Hostetler and Wu, Qing Imperial Illustrations, 195. 20 In the entries’ titles, fan is written as 畨. The modern way of writing fan is 番. This section also includes a dog and two children. 21 As a predominantly patriarchal society, China has long-standing cultural values of female demurity. This emphasis of women’s modesty likely influenced the artist’s decision to render gendered difference of propriety. 22 This is a continued practice of the Dutch and Spanish, who previously occupied parts of Taiwan, to group Indigenous Taiwanese by geographic regions rather than ethnolinguistic characteristics. Ye, The Colonisation and Settlement of Taiwan, 1684-1945, 22. 23 In 1722, Qing inspector Huang Shujing 黃叔璥 recorded 151 Taiwanese villages that paid taxes to the Qing. In each cluster, he described its culture through housing, food, costume, marriage, burial, and tools. The text in the Huang Qing zhigong tu generally follows these categories. Ye, 22. 24 Hostetler and Wu, Qing Imperial Illustrations, 207 (emphasis added). 25 Hostetler and Wu, 213 (emphasis added).

The second case study pair, the huafan in Zhuluo County (Figure 6) have customs that situate them in the Qing imaginary as unacculturated fan. The figures’ concentric bracelets and leg wrappings highlight their exoticness and distance from the Manchu Qing. A portion of the accompanying text documents their living habits:

They dwell in mountainous earth­ en caves. Their dress and diet are similar to those of Shanzhumao and other com­ munities. They are not well versed in farming, only raising sweet potatoes and taro in cracks in the rock. They use bow and arrow to hunt river deer for food. Their feet are like chicken claws, allowing them to climb steep surfaces as if they were flat. They annually submit a head tax of more than 30 silver taels.25

In contrast to the more resourceful shoufan who build their residences, the text says the huafan live in “earthen caves” in the mountains. The huafan’s practice of growing food “in cracks in the rock” fur­ ther signals the group’s liminal position between developed civilization and the wilderness placing themselves on a lower register in the Qing imagination.

In the bottom half of the entry, the man and woman face one another, stand­ ing upright. They both wear sleeved deer­ skin jackets and patterned woven skirts with fabric belts. The man holds a barbed spear in his right hand, and he carries a bow, quiver, and basket filled with flowers on his back. The text does not discuss hunting spears; the addition of this weap­ on in the image depicts these people as potentially threatening. The combination of collected flowers and weaponry simulta­ neously asserts the huafan as primitive yet potentially hostile. In line with the text, the male figure has long, claw-like nails on his feet. In contrast, the female figure has nor­ mal-length toenails, and she displays the group’s craftsmanship by holding a beaded circle and wearing a beaded necklace. This artistic insistence of expressing savagery through the male figure while simultane­ ously refining the female reflects the Qing perception of wild fan and Chinese values of the demure woman. This visual repre­ sentation demonstrates the nuanced Qing understanding of fan as having the poten­ tial to assimilate into Chinese society yet perpetually far from civilization.

The last Taiwanese entry in the sec­ ond scroll, the shengfan of Youwunai and other wild communities in Danshui (Fig­ ure 7), contains the most-nude figures out of the 13 pairs. In Chinese visual culture, women are rarely portrayed bare-chested; the Qing perceived these people to be so savage that the artist broke cultural norms to illustrate an exposed female chest. The accompanying text purportedly reports the shengfan’s untamed living habits:

The Shengfan live in the moun­ tains. Men and women both bare their bodies. Some wear deerskins or use leaves for clothing. They eat raw food. Their nature is strong and fierce. They kill for a living. In winter when the grass and streams dry up they shoot deer. They can climb tall trees and run as if they are flying.26

The text’s tone differs greatly from the shoufan and huafan in the scrolls. The mentions of mountains, nakedness, un­ cooked food, and physical agility support the claim that the shengfan’s “nature is strong and fierce.” The “bare…bodies” of both male and female shengfan accentuate their separation from civilization. Though “some” shengfan wear clothing, deerskin and foliage are closer to nature than woven fabric. The ambiguity of the type of “raw food” the shengfan “kill” and eat contributes to a feeling of distance and unfamiliarity. Lastly, the text associates the shengfan with animals, describing their running “as if they are flying”; this detail works with the phrase “they kill for a living” to create an image of a group of fierce and threatening people.

26 Hostetler and Wu, 219 (emphasis added).

“People residing in the 21st century, myself included, boldly “write back” to the Qing empire that its view of Taiwanese fan does not have the last say in our collective history and understanding of Taiwan’s original peoples.”

Both the male and female figures wear deerskin cloaks that cover their shoulders and upper backs, exposing their torso. A contradiction between artistic expression and the textual description is the female’s fabric skirt despite its noninclusion in the text; the artist attempted to give some level of civility to the female through a woven skirt rather than a full animal hide cos­ tume. The male wears a deerskin skirt, and he raises a downwards-facing barbed spear with his right hand and holds a sheathed sword-like object in his left. He raises his right foot as if he is about to spear an an­ imal. The exaggerated lines on his face, limbs, and chest accentuate his grotesque­ ness and muscular strength. Compared to her fierce male companion, the female’s gaze is blank. Her pose suggests she cau­ tiously walks in the presence of her fero­ cious companion. These shengfan are the only Taiwanese fan who have a “raw” diet, and this detail’s artistic exclusion is glaring because sheng literally translates to “raw.” Working with—yet sometimes departing from—the text, the artist created a literal image of Indigenous Taiwanese who are wild and hostile.

Throughout the three case studies of Taiwanese fan, image and text collaborate to create a supposed authoritative record of those who are refined versus barbaric. The representations of savagery are most explicit through the males’ costumes, asso­ ciation with weaponry, corporal pose, and grotesque facial features. The males’ cloth­ ing encapsulates the progression of barba­ rism from tame fan to wild fan: the shoufan of Danshui wears layers of woven textiles, the huafan of Zhuluo dons a deerskin jack­ et and a woven patterned skirt, and the shengfan of Danshui is the least-clothed in his deerskin costume. The male figures’ object-interactions become increasingly threatening, from the shoufan presenting a musical instrument to the huafan carrying weapons to the shengfan actively spearing an unspecified target. All three men have untied, freely flowing hair in sharp contrast to the braided Manchu queue hairstyles required in the empire, highlighting their cultural distance from the Qing. None of the Taiwanese figures wear hats nor shoes, further indicating their primitiveness. The diet of these three groups literally reflects the categories of “cooked” fan and “raw” fan: the acculturated “cooked” fan makes broth for himself, and the wild “raw” fan eats raw food. The entries’ text and image mutually reinforce Qing notions of savage­ ry yet sometimes diverge on their extent, creating conflicting portrayals of fan. The Huang Qing zhigong tu emphasizes this framework of tiered savagery through the Taiwanese entries’ visual representations, reflecting Taiwan’s liminal position in the Qing empire.

27 The Republic of China Yearbook, 48–49.

The Twenty-first Century Afterlife of Xie Sui’s Huang Qing zhigong tu Chinese settler-colonialism of Taiwan continued to grow through the Qing era and into the present; people of aboriginal descent comprise 2.28% of present-day Taiwan’s 23-million population.27 Despite their small proportion in society, Indige­ nous Taiwanese have been the subject of growing public interest in recent decades. This increased respect towards and signif­ icance of Indigenous culture and history stems from a desire to distinguish Taiwan­ ese identity and nationality from China, including the modern-day Communist state and the Chinese imperial past. Xie Sui’s Huang Qing zhigong tu resided in the imperial Qing collection upon its completion in the eighteenth cen­ tury.28 After the fall of the Qing dynasty in 1911, portions of the imperial collections formed the collection of the newly estab­ lished, state-operated Palace Museum in Beijing. To safeguard the museum’s most culturally valuable objects from military threats—from the Japanese in the 1930s and from the Chinese Communists in the 1940s—the Chinese Nationalist govern­ ment evacuated thousands of crates filled with these objects around the country and then to Taiwan, respectively. Alongside the Nationalist government’s retreat to Taiwan, these select portions of the Qing imperial collections found their new home in the National Palace Museum in Taipei’s Shilin District in 1965. Today, the museum is internationally acclaimed for its extensive collection of imperial Chinese artifacts, and the Xie Sui scrolls serve as strong visual references for postcolonial discussions of Taiwanese Indigeneity.

In the early 2000s, aboriginal national legislator Kung Wen-chi 孔文吉 urged the NPM to develop more programming rele­ vant to Taiwan’s Indigenous communities; the public echoed his sentiment, as former NPM Director Wu Mi-cha 吳密察 said in an interview.29 Wu Mi-cha elaborated on the museum’s best efforts to meet pub­ lic interest, saying, “it is difficult to make interesting exhibitions” that highlight ab­ original Taiwanese society from the muse­ um’s Qing archives because the collection contains mostly text manuscripts.30 Thus, the exhibitions discussing Taiwanese Indi­ geneity often incorporate the second Xie

Sui scroll due to its visual representations of aboriginal Taiwanese figures.

28 The imperial city of Beijing held most of the imperial collection. The Qianqing Palace in the Forbidden City housed the original four scrolls, and it is unclear if the Xie Sui version would have been stored in one of the imperial auxiliary collections or with the originals. Chang, “The National Palace Museum: A History of the Collection,” 3.; Wei, “‘Huang Qing zhigong tu’ chuangzhi shimo,” 12. 29 Song, Luzong, 4; What is “Fandz”? curatorial team, “Chongxinrenshi Qingdiguowenxian Lide Taiwan Yuanzhuminzu,” 10. 30  What is “Fandz”? curatorial team, “Chongxinrenshi Qingdiguowenxian Lide Taiwan Yuanzhuminzu,” 15. 31 What is “Fandz”? curatorial team, “Chongxinrenshi Qingdiguowenxian Lide Taiwan Yuanzhuminzu,” 10. 32 “Fandz” is a romanization of fanzi 番子, another way the Qing referred to fan. 33 What is “Fandz”? curatorial team, “Sheme Shi ‘Fandz’? Qingdaiguo,” 27.

Wu Mi-cha noted a crucial step in facilitating present-day people’s compre­ hension of Qing archives: clarifying Qing terminology.31 “Fan” carries a derogatory connotation in modern-day Taiwanese society, and the 2022 exhibition What is “Fandz”? Taiwanese Indigenous Peoples in Historical Documents of the Qing Empire32 not only gave museumgoers an opportunity to understand the Taiwanese aboriginals’ liminal positionality in the Qing empire, but also encouraged them to recenter Indigenous perspectives in imperialist archives through “write back” exercises.33 The Xie Sui scrolls served as an education­ al tool, providing visual references for each Qing-imagined category of fan: shoufan (tame fan), guihua shengfan (wild fan who pay taxes), and shengfan (wild fan).

Museum staff utilized the Taiwanese figures in several aspects of the exhibi­ tion to not only highlight the association between the Qing-imagined savage and Taiwanese fan, but also call attention to the imperial prejudice and ethnographic oversimplification within the displayed documents. The main decal in the 2022 exhibition hall (Figure 8) features some of Xie Sui’s aboriginal figures—including the male-female shengfan from Danshui (Figure 7)—transposed on a Qing map of Taiwan. The original figures in the Huang Qing zhigong tu sit on a blank background, so giving them an illustrated backdrop modifies their meaning. This addition affirms Indigenous presence in Taiwan; they inhabited real spaces on the island and did not aimlessly float in ethnographic documents.

To accompany the Fandz exhibition, the curatorial staff created a website titled “Nixie Qingdiguo 逆寫清帝國” [“Write back the Qing Empire”] (Figure 9). Nixie 逆寫 [“write back”] encourages the public to share new interpretations of Xie Sui’s fan figures through postcolonial interven­ tions, such as summoning collective mem­ ory and rejecting the language of the colo­ nizer.34 This method draws upon the work of several British, Indian, African, and ab­ original Taiwanese postcolonial theorists, which encourage the reconstruction of the (historically marginalized) subject through embracing Indigenous theory and replac­ ing imperialist terminologies and ste­ reotyped motifs.35 The website currently features seven “write back” pieces by high school and graduate students in Taiwan, along with an aboriginal author. These short historical fiction essays draw inspi­ ration from Xie Sui’s Taiwanese figures, offering imagined interactions between the Indigenous Taiwanese and the Qing scribes who recorded their likenesses.36 The first-person narratives include: diary entries of a court painter in Beijing during the production of the Huang Qing zhigong tu, the dog accompanying the shoufan of Dadu witnessing a Qing official command his subordinates to sketch the dog’s owner, and an aboriginal individual criticizing the Qing’s failure to depict her culture’s shawl correctly. This last essay, written by a stu­ dent of one of Taiwan’s best all-girls high schools, calls attention to the ambiguous state of the images’ accuracy as Qing impe­ rial preconceptions of Manchu superiority hung over the project.

34 The NPM translates nixie as “write back,” so I use this phrase to be consistent with how the museum presents this methodology. This phrasing draws upon the work of Ashcroft, Griffiths, and Tiffin, The Empire Writes Back. What is “Fandz”? curatorial team, “Sheme Shi ‘Fandz’? Nixie,” 77. 35 See What is “Fandz”? curatorial team, “Sheme Shi ‘Fandz’? Nixie”, especially 70-73, 77. 36 While these alternative perspectives provide valuable postcolonial critiques, they contain some factual errors because they are written by non-subject matter experts. For example, “Excerpts from the ‘“Huian Diary’” says that “poor old Xie [Sui] was assigned to the minorities in Gansu.” However, we know that Xie Sui was an artist in the imperial atelier in Beijing who worked on illuminated figures across the four scrolls; the localized workers were the ones who drew these ethnic minorities within the provinces. Huang, “‘Huian rizhi’ jielu.”

Public engagement with “write back” also extends to this thesis: in this academ­ ic project, I chose to consider the Xie Sui scrolls in not only their historical context, but also of the present. I critically studied the textual description and formal repre­ sentation of three paradigmatic Taiwanese fan types in Xie Sui’s Huang Qing zhigong tu, noting discrepancies and how they visually assert the Qing-imagined savageness of Taiwanese aboriginals. While understand­ ing Qing imperialist ideologies shines valuable light on why the Taiwanese rep­ resentations take the form they do, study­ ing them without considering their pres­ ent-day impact can perpetuate or diminish the weight of these harmful narratives. Thus, this conclusion embraces the post­ colonial “write back” methodology by also analyzing how people in the present-day think about these objects, emancipating the scrolls from solely holding historical significance. People residing in the 21st century, myself included, boldly “write back” to the Qing empire that its view of Taiwanese fan does not have the last say in our collective history and understanding of Taiwan’s original peoples. ◆

title: The Health Identities of Northwestern Students with Chronic Physical Health Conditions
text:
Department of Sociology

The Health Identities of Northwestern Students with Chronic Physical Health Conditions by Sierra Erdman-Luntz

Faculty Advisers: Dr. Bruce Carruthers and Dr. Steven Epstein

Introduction “How do Northwestern undergraduate students with chronic physical conditions inte­ grate their health status into their identities?”

I interviewed Northwestern undergraduates who have been physically ill for the past six or more months to understand how they have or have not integrated their health status into their identities.1 In this sense, “identity” refers to a part of someone’s sense of self that they either disclose or choose not to disclose in different settings. My interview guide covered a wide array of situations, from intimate, private conversations between friends or family to very public settings such as at work, on medical forms, in govern­ mental surveys, and so on.

Part of making an accessible world is first studying how disabled individuals and communities understand themselves and relate to society. However, there is a gap in the literature regarding the intersection of disability studies and identity formation when it comes to ill young adults. Identities are impactful and important: they help dictate who is excluded or included in a group, help build a sense of community and alliance, and help people publicly express their internal experiences. Since the 1980s, the queer community has experienced a proliferation of labeling, including the reclamation of some words and the rejection of others, which sociologists have studied to better understand the queer community and its needs on a social policy level. My study aims to do parallel work within disabled spaces.

1 Note: 6+ months of illnesses is an accepted distinction between acute and chronic illnesses in the medical community.

Literature Review My study investigates how Northwestern undergraduate students with long-term illness(es) form an identity around their health and how they think about, express, and label their health during that process. There is an abundance of sociological research on identity formation, and many studies empirically apply this theory to chronically ill communities. My study specifically aims to understand the unique experiences of young adults in college.

Identity Formation

Psychologist and psycho-analyst Erik Erikson popularized identity formation as a social science subcategory in the mid- to-late 20th century. Heavily influenced by Freudian thought, Erikson developed a “psychosocial construct of identity for­ mation” (Herman 2011) that he labeled the theory of ego (Erikson 1950). This theory proposed that young adulthood was a time of self-reflection and individualization where young adults either developed a unique, individual identity or failed to do so and then struggled to become full adults.

Even before Erikson, Charles Cooley was the first to specifically discuss identity formation in the context of sociol­ ogy (1902). He proposed the looking-glass self theory, which argued that individuals create a sense of self and identity by con­ sidering how they are perceived by others and by society writ large. In other words, people use how they think others think about themselves to determine how they view themselves.

George Herbert Mead and Charles W. Morris furthered sociological thought with their symbolic interactionism theory (1934). Symbolic interactionism proposed that conversations, interactions, and expe­ riences with other people informed how someone built their identity and how they viewed themselves. Thus, it constructed the individual from a sociological per­ spective by studying “how the individual internalizes the self and its roles from in­ teractions with others” (Brekus 2020).

Erving Goffman added to identity formation theory by coining the term “social identities,” which suggested that an individual’s identities might change based on social context (1959). Goffman specif­ ically employed a drama allegory to relate different social contexts to different acts in a play. Just like actors might change their behavior or comportment for different scenes, people might act differently and even think about themselves differently depending on their current social context.

Anthony Giddens critically built upon identity formation by conceptualizing it as a reflexive process between the individual and their social environment. He argued that society shifted from low to high with the advent of mass-mediated communica­ tion via the internet, late-stage capitalism, and globalization. As a result, identity for­ mation became both active and political: individuals taking up or refusing certain identities shifted larger social institutions’ perception of those identities, which could influence social processes such as individ­ uals’ future identification, social relations between people with different identities, politics, and so on (Giddens 1991). In re­ sponse to their changing worlds, individu­ als increasingly and repeatedly reconstruct their identities to match their environment and create a stable life story.

Most studies that consider identity formation theory’s specific application to physical health conditions are interviews and surveys that researched how respon­ dents felt their illness impacted their life or how they manage their illness in academic, medical, personal, and other settings. The most influential thinker on this topic is Michael Bury (1982; 1911), whose early work on chronic illness as “biographical disruption” provided the foundations for an identity-based approach within med­ ical sociology. Biographical disruption is the idea that becoming chronically ill is so life-changing that it can alter or disrupt the ill individual’s other identities and sense of self.

Sociological interrogation of Bury’s theories can be found in recent studies, like the Oris et al. study that investigated how chronically ill adults had or had not integrated their illness into their identities, using four potential stages: engulfment, rejection, acceptance, and enrichment (2018). The study did not ask how labels inform or intersect with the four stages. However, the four stages have been em­ ployed in other studies, such as one on how youth handled their Type 1 Diabetes diagnoses (Raymaekers 2019).

A few leading studies consider illness identity formation specifically in the con­ text of young adulthood. Ceri Wilson and Jennifer Stock’s research noted that phys­ ically ill young adults reported experienc­ ing a mixture of emotions related to their health, including personal empowerment, depression, anxiety, and “being different” (2019). Spencer et al. studied the experi­ ence of chronically ill college students, in particular how each participant felt their illness impacted their daily life, how they explained their illnesses to both them­ selves and to their peers, and how they tried to manage their health alongside all of the other pressures of university (2021). My study aims to build upon this body of knowledge.

Motivation The motivation behind this project is threefold: sociological, current relevance, and personal. On the sociological level, outlined above in the literature review, there are few studies that specifically con­ sider young adults with long-term illness and how their health might impact their identity, making my research topic both interesting and significant.

Secondly, this topic is timely and increasingly relevant in the context of COVID-19, the looming threat of another pandemic, climate change, and other so­ cial health hazards that disproportionately impact and create chronically ill people. These social and medical catastrophes pushed conversations about disability and disabled people to the forefront of national discourse, albeit temporarily. One conver­ sation focused on how hospitals should triage COVID-19 patients when they had limited ventilators: disabled people were often the first to be deprioritized (Chen and McNamara 2020). Another discussed who should qualify to receive a COVID-19 vaccine in the first few waves of distribu­ tion: people with very specific diagnosed conditions were prioritized, but many other disabled people were not. Largely missing from both of these conversations were the voices of disabled people. Thus, re­ search on how this population understands their health and how they choose to frame it in different engagements with society is incredibly pressing and necessary. I believe my research will positively impact the so­ ciological and chronically ill communities.

Finally, my interest in this topic is also deeply personal. As a person with chronic physical health conditions, my own experience reflects a roughly linear trajectory from engulfment to enrich­ ment. Throughout my thesis, I was aware that my personal experiences might skew my interpretation of data collected in the interviews, mistakenly and erroneously pushing my data closer to my hypotheses. I implemented a couple of mechanisms in place to counteract my bias. First, I was aware enough of my bias to be able to name and recognize it, making it easier to identi­ fy moments where my assumptions might have overridden the data directly collected through the interviews. Second, I worked with two faculty members and a cohort of other seniors writing theses whose feed­ back and review helped me identify and counterbalance my biases. Third, I was a competitive debater in high school and now coach debate, so I have ample practice divorcing my personal feelings and attach­ ments to my professional work. Further­ more, I believe my personal experience with my research material also benefited my project: I strategically and succinctly self-disclosed my health status at times during interviews, allowing me to relate to respondents on a level that encouraged more fruitful and lush answers.

Methods I collected data through one-time, semi-structured interviews with a small sample size of Northwestern students. I was primarily interested in the thought processes and experiences that shaped and influenced each participant’s health identi­ ty, so my study was qualitative rather than quantitative.

My interview guide started with a short introduction about myself and my study, a reminder that participants can skip questions or stop the interview at any time, and a couple of easier, get-to- know-you questions to build rapport, such as their major at Northwestern and their favorite place to study. The main body of my interview had two distinct parts.2 The first phase included a series of closed-end­ ed statements adapted from the survey in Oris et al’s study. I asked respondents to rank each statement on a Likert scale from one to five (one meaning strongly disagree, three neither disagree nor agree, and five strongly agree).3 Like the Oris et al. study, each statement corresponded to a different stage of identity development: engulfment, rejection, acceptance, and enrichment. Af­ ter the interview, I tallied how many points a respondent accrued in each of the four categories, placing them into the category in which they had the most points. I spe­ cifically compared a participant’s average score in each category during this process (raw score divided by number of questions for that stage) because each category had a different number of questions.

2 Note: please find a complete copy of the interview guide in appendix one. 3 Oris, L., Luyckx, K., Rassart, J. et al. Illness Identity in Adults with a Chronic Illness. J Clin Psychol Med Settings 25, 429–440 (2018). https://doi.org/10.1007/s10880-018-9552-0

The interview’s second phase consist­ ed of open-ended questions to understand the thought processes and experiences that influenced and shaped the participant’s responses to phase one. The open-end­ ed questions started with their internal health identity, progressed to more private expressions of their health identity, and ended on more public displays. While I could not guarantee my participants told me the truth, I made it clear throughout the interview that participants were free to skip questions if they found them too pri­ vate and also tried to read the participants’ body language. If they seemed too uncom­ fortable with a line of questioning, I would switch to a different topic that would hope­ fully make them feel more comfortable and more likely to tell me their truth.

For recruitment, AccessibleNU shared my study via email with all North­ western students currently receiving ac­ ademic accommodations who might be eligible for my study, which helped me reach students on campus who held other marginalized identities. Although my sam­ ple size was still too small to make defin­ itive statements or generalizations about how holding other marginalized identities might impact someone’s health identity, I identified a few preliminary trends.

Interviews lasted anywhere from 30 minutes to two hours, with most inter­ views falling between 40 and 60 minutes. On average, I spoke for 10% of the inter­ view time and the interviewee spoke for 90% of the time. I interviewed 13 people for my study.

Initial Empirical Analysis As an inductive study, its purpose was to identify key emergent themes in how Northwestern students with long-term health conditions understood and labeled their health. Thus, analysis throughout the data collection period was critical because it informed how I guided future interviews to gather data relevant to the emerging themes. My intended sample size was 10-20 participants, so I conducted my first round of preliminary analysis after the first 4 interviews. I uploaded the transcripts to ATLAS.ti, a software for analyzing and coding qualitative data. It was advantageous because I could input my codes and easily apply them to quotes, search all transcripts by codes or key­ words, and highlight critical passages for later review. It also provided small-scale quantitative data, such as how often I used each code, that helped me quickly identify patterns.

My analysis section had two parts that corresponded with the interview’s two parts. First, I turned to the data collected in the interview’s statement section. I tallied the participant’s points in each category and then computed each category’s aver­ age score: average scores above three in any category indicated that the participant identified with that stage of identity forma­ tion, and scores below three denoted a lack of identification with the respective stage. Scores close to three indicated ambivalence while scores notably higher or lower than three indicated a stronger feeling.

Second, I analyzed the respondents’ answers to the open-ended questions, tak­ ing note of patterns and creating relevant codes in my codebook. The first major codes I imputed into ATLAS.ti were still the four health identity integration phases from the Oris et al. study: engulfment (coded 76 times), rejection (34), acceptance (218), and enrichment (66). As I started coding and potential themes emerged, I then added other codes: accommodations and school (85), interactions with others (72), managing health/treatment/coping mechanisms (88), interactions with med­ ical institutes (48), explicit mentions of label preferences (74), explicit or implicit mentions of perceived illness validity (55), and mentions of illness’s visibility or in­ viibility (58).

See Appendix II for details about each participant.

Findings The analysis revealed some of the shared experiences of Northwestern students with chronic physical health conditions. It supported the theory of four stages of health integration but complicated my hypothesis that students would prog­ ress linearly through the stages. While participants did report a roughly linear progression in terms of how they thought about and mentally understood their health, their actual health symptoms did not always improve linearly. As a result, some participants reported being mentally in the acceptance or enrichment stages while also scoring highly in the engulfment stage due to their burdensome daily symptoms.

It is noteworthy but not surprising that none of my participants scored in the “rejection” stage as their primary catego­ ry: students who were actively rejecting their health conditions were least likely to self-select to participate in a study explic­ itly about their health status. Most partic­ ipants scored primarily in the acceptance stage, which would explain their willing­ ness and comfort in participating in an interview about their health. Participants mentally and physically in the engulfment stages tended to be diagnosed the lon­ gest, suggesting that time since diagnosis increased their comfortability in talking about their health despite their persistent and pronounced challenges. Supporting my secondary hypothesis, I did find a cor­ relation between the participants’ mental integration stage and their preferred labels. Finally, I also identified other emergent themes, social identities, and experiences that directly influenced participants’ health identities and can inform future research.

Four Stages & Linear(ish) Progression

My findings support the validity of the four stages of identity integration: par­ ticipants who scored highly in engulfment spoke about feeling overwhelmed by their health during the open-ended questions, participants in acceptance affirmed their peace with their illness, and so on. Par­ ticipants who scored highly in the engulf­ ment stage most often reported a lack of social support and all-encompassing daily symptoms:

On feeling engulfed as a child: I was so used to pain…so all of that was going on for years and…my dad refused to take me to a doctor and my dad is a doctor, but he couldn’t fathom the idea of something being wrong with his kid…so he did not take me to a doctor, even when I literally couldn’t move my hands very much for years…it finally got really, really bad and then my dad agreed to take me. (Participant 4)

“While participants did report a roughly linear progression in terms of how they thought about and mentally understood their health, their actual health symptoms did not always improve linearly.”

As explained above, none of my par­ ticipants scored highest in the rejection stage, which makes sense given that peo­ ple rejecting their health probably would not self-select to participate in a study on chronic illness. On the other end of the spectrum, people who scored highly in the acceptance or enrichment categories talked about their health and its impact on their life in less emotionally charged or negative ways, often citing more manageable daily symptoms, coping mechanisms that en­ abled them to continue living their lives, and a strong support system:

I can deal with the pain…I’ve learned to just get through it…If I don’t eat in a very specific way then it’s GI symptoms [that impact her life the most] but I have learned the way to manage it. So most of the time I’m good, but that’s only through very specific decisions. (Participant 1, acceptance = 4)

I have ill days, like one to two days a month now, which is great. It used to be much more than that where I, physically, I’m stuck in bed, physically ill, cannot walk….I have gotten much better, thankfully. (Participant 6, acceptance = 4.6)

I’m definitely better now at setting boundaries and listening to myself… my friends now and my two roommates, they know everything and they’re always so respectful and my boyfriend is really understanding. He helps me a lot and my family, of course, is very understanding. (Participant 5, enrichment = 3.7)

Participants who scored highly spe­ cifically in the enrichment stage often identified one or more ways that their life was improved or positively impacted by their health:

I’ve had a lot of positive [medical interactions], like such a positive impact that they had in my life and how supportive medical professionals were really inspired me to want to do something in healthcare. (Participant 1, enrichment = 3.6)

I make [TikTok] videos because I

[think] a lot of content on chronic illness and autoimmune disease is really negative on social media. (Participant 5, enrichment = 3.7)

I specifically work with a lot of disabled populations now because I love it and I’m really passionate about it, and it’s something that I do so much advocacy work for…I am able to empathize so much with their situation. (Participant 6, enrichment = 4.9)

Participants in the acceptance and enrichment stages also spoke about their lived experiences, acting as a social re­ minder that anyone can become disabled at any time or point in their life:

Prior to developing [gastroparesis], I was an otherwise able-bodied person. I am sort of proof of the really uncomfortable truth, that able- bodied people don’t like to listen and hear, that you can become disabled at any time. You can develop a chronic illness at any time…The scary thing is that there’s still a lot of people who have this internalized ableism. (Participant 9, acceptance = 3.8)

It’s this idea of like, trying to be like “Hey, no, [disability] can happen to young people. Young people can have non- sports related injuries. Or non-sports related, like physical health problems. (Participant 12, enrichment = 3.3)

I like to inform people that I used to know not be this disabled, and it just happened all of a sudden. And that can happen for anybody. You know, I also like to remind people that COVID has caused so many illnesses for people who were completely healthy before they got COVID. You know, just as a warning? (Participant 8, acceptance = 4.4)

Suggesting an approximately linear progression through the health identity stages, participants in the engulfment stage reported working towards acceptance and participants in acceptance or enrichment often retroactively reported starting in a place of engulfment:

I feel like the past three years have been consumed by dealing with these sorts of issues. I feel like I’ve just tried to find ways to adjust and not make that the center of my life, even though it takes up a lot of time and energy. (Participant 7, acceptance = 3.8)

I would never have used the word… ”disability” when I was that young, right?... I was in middle school, I would pretty much just be like, “Oh, I have joint issues.” Like, that was kind of the extent of it. (Participant 10, acceptance = 4.2)

I don’t see it as a moral failing of myself [that] I can’t get a job right now. Or that I’ve had to take time off of school. Like I don’t. When I was younger, I used to definitely feel that way about myself. But by now I’ve been able to…hear like, you know, disability, acceptance and awareness. (Participant 8, acceptance = 4.4)

“I don’t see it as a moral failing of myself [that] I can’t get a job right now.

Or that I’ve had to take time off school.

Like I don’t.When

I was younger, I used to definitely feel that way about myself. But by now

I’ve been able to…hear like, you know, disability, acceptance and awareness.”

While my data supports a linear pro­ gression in terms of mental models around participants’ health identities, I also discov­ ered two different iterations of the engulf­ ment stage that complicated my results. One iteration was the mental engulfment depicted in the above analysis. The second was physical rather than mental engulfment. Participants who were physically engulfed had such severe daily symptoms that they scored highly in the engulfment stage. Still, they also scored highly in the acceptance or enrichment stage as they more accurately reflected their current mental model:

I love Northwestern other than accessibility issues and dorm lifestyle. I like Northwestern and I really do, I like my teachers, my friends, I love the area. And I love what I’m learning. I would like to continue progress… I’ve enjoyed [college]. But it definitely got harder, the more that my collection of illnesses hit me. And it was harder to keep up with assignments… It was hard to stay awake because of the physical effects of my illness, like I couldn’t…. I was struggling to do schoolwork.

I was you know, I’ve been getting extensions all the time… I was getting accommodations. Unfortunately, it wasn’t as many as I probably needed… I was still struggling with my migraines all the time, which made it so I couldn’t read. I couldn’t walk around the house. (Participant 8, engulfment = 3.75, acceptance = 4.4)

Thus, my data supports the four- stage theory of identity formation, com­ plicated slightly by the two different forms of engulfment. This formation process also proved to be approximately linear, encour­ aged by factors such as manageable daily symptoms and a strong social support net­ work. I will next analyze how label prefer­ ence intersects and reflects a participant’s current stage of identity formation.

Discussion Aside from its small size, a few other factors potentially made my sample more biased and less representative. First is self-selection bias. My participants con­ centrated more on the acceptance and enrichment end of the identity formation spectrum, and none identified with “rejec­ tion” as their primary stage. Second, my main recruitment method for this study was an informational email sent from AccessibleNU to students who currently receive accommodations due to a physical illness they have experienced over the past 6 or more months. Thus, my recruitment methods themselves limited my potential participants to people who have already disclosed their health conditions to the school and their professors.

“Identifying, labeling, and proving social problems and barriers faced by marginalized populations such as the disabled community is a critical first step to creating institutional and social policy that would make both Northwestern’s campus and the rest of the world a more accessible and safer place.”

As an inductive study, it created more questions than answers, such as the poten­ tial relationship between perceived visibil­ ity and feelings of validity. Hopefully, larg­ er and more resourced studies in the future can help fill some of the gaps in my study. It would be helpful to more actively recruit participants who are less confident in their health, more recently ill, and who hold other marginalized identities to under­ stand how those variables impact one’s un­ derstanding of their health and their health identity. It would also be advantageous to conduct studies with larger sample sizes that might be generalizable and to examine how populations other than young adults in prestigious academic environments re­ flect or do not reflect the themes identified in this study. My study underscores the im­ portance of researching disabled people to gain knowledge about their thoughts and social engagements. Identifying, labeling, and proving social problems and barriers faced by marginalized populations such as the disabled community is a critical first step to creating institutional and social pol­ icy that would make both Northwestern’s campus and the rest of the world a more accessible and safer place. ◆

Appendix: Interview Guide

Note

Please note that because this study is inductive and seeks to identify emerging themes, questions are meant to shift, becoming more specific and focused during the interview process. The following interview guide is a sample of likely questions and their poten­ tial order. Interview Guide

Building Rapport: Major and minors at Northwestern? Clubs or other campus interests? Favorite place to study on or off campus? If one of your friends were to describe you to a stranger, what do you think they would say?

Great! This information really helps me start to get to know you as a person. There are now two main sections to this interview: closed-ended questions and then open-ended ones. Great! Thank you for this information. Now that I know a little about how you think about your health, I would like to ask some open-ended questions about your health situation a little bit more.

Health history + internal/personal health identity: 1. I know from your answers to the pre-screening questions that you have been experiencing physical health troubles over at least the past 6 months. Can you tell me a little bit about what’s going on? a. Okay, great: this information is really helpful for me to get to know you more as a person and about the health struggles you’ve been dealing with. I’d now like to transition to talking more about how you conceptualize your illness in your relationships and interactions with others.

title: Black-Owned Small Businesses in Englewood, Chicago: Documenting the Effects of COVID-19 and the Black Lives Matter Movement in 2020
abstract: Media accounts report that the COVID-19 pandemic and 2020 Black Lives Matter (BLM) movement disproportionately affected Black communities and businesses, amplifying already- existing racial health and economic disparities. Black-owned small businesses experienced significant indirect and direct economic damages in Chicago, Illinois, and research literature is now striving to provide analyses of Black business owners’ experiences in 2020. The present study uses quantitative and qualitative data analyses to discern the impact of 2020 crises on small businesses in Englewood, Chicago. The study examined foot traffic data from cell-phone records to identify business visitation patterns relative to the March 21 Illinois stay-at-home order and the commencement of BLM protests after the murder of George Floyd on May 25. After both March 21 and May 25, there were statistically significant changes in foot traffic in majority-Black neighborhoods as compared to majority-non-Black neighborhoods. The research elucidated the complexity of the mechanisms by which COVID-19 and BLM activities disproportionately influenced Black communities through semi-structured interviews with Black-identifying small business owners (n=8) in Englewood. The study participants detailed their evolving perceptions of policing in Englewood after looting in June, concern for employee well-being in the pandemic, and complex grant application processes throughout 2020. Business owners were motivated to keep their firms open to support their families, promote values benefitting Englewood residents, and refute stereotypes about Englewood itself. This project provides insight into the range of experiences Black entrepreneurs in Englewood have faced in 2020 and suggests ways that policy responses might usefully support their survival and success.
text:
Black-Owned Small Businesses in Englewood, Chicago:

Documenting the Effects of COVID-19 and the Black Lives Matter Movement in 2020 by Sophie Boorstein

School of Education and Social Policy

& Department of Statistics Faculty Advisers: Prof. Jonathan Guryan, Ph.D., Prof. Reuel Rogers, Ph.D., & Prof. Elizabeth Tipton, Ph.D.

Background

The year 2020 was characterized by insurmountable losses for communities around the world. Amid the global COVID-19 pandemic and the largest recession since the mid-20th century in the U.S., the Black Lives Matter (BLM) movement rose to a global scale and brought the epidemic of police brutality to the public eye. All aforementioned events in the United States disproportionately impacted Black communities, amplifying pre-existing racial health, income, and social disparities.

News media reported that Black- owned businesses were severely financially impacted by 2020’s crisis events. From

February to April 2020, the number of all active business owners in the United States dropped by 22%. During the same period, the number of active Black business owners dropped 41% (Leatherby, 2020). When BLM protests erupted in all 50 American states in response to George Floyd’s murder and the unjust murders of countless other Black victims, a minority of protesters, including individuals not associated with the protests, looted local businesses in several cities across the country.

Englewood, a neighborhood on the South Side of Chicago, was identified as one of the areas severely damaged by looting and the COVID-19 pandemic (Bayne,

2020). The area of Englewood, for the purposes of this paper, contains two adjacent neighborhoods: West Englewood and Englewood. Of Englewood’s 75,000 residents, approximately 90% are Black (“Household Income in Englewood,” 2020). The median household income in Englewood is $28,000, which is half of Chicago’s overall median household income, and at least 30% of its residents live below the poverty line. According to Englewood activists’ testimonies, COVID-19 restrictions and looting activity exacerbated many hardships that Englewood community members already faced.

Yet, policy responses inadequately addressed Black-owned businesses’ heightened vulnerability in 2020. The federal government attempted to remedy the effects of the recession on all small businesses through the Paycheck Protection Program (PPP), a $669 billion loan program from the Small Business Administration (SBA). However, structural characteristics of the PPP disadvantaged Black-owned small businesses’ access to loans (Abramson, 2020; Selvam, 2020). Even prior to the contingencies and concerns exacerbated by COVID-19, Black- owned small businesses were at higher risk of financial hardship compared to white- owned small businesses. Although 32% of Chicago residents are Black, in 2017, Chicago had only 1,875 Black-owned businesses, comprising only 3.7% of all Chicago businesses (Marotti & Elejalde-Ruiz, 2020). Systemic racism in financial institutions, which have become systems that maintain white supremacy, is one cause of racial financial inequities. Historically, non-white business owners have had disproportionately low access to bank credit, and lower-income, minority neighborhoods have suffered from lower lending rates than higher-income, white neighborhoods (Blanchard et al., 2008). Due to racial disparities in credit access, the majority of small businesses in Chicago that have fewer than two weeks of cash reserves are in majority-Black neighborhoods (Leatherby, 2020).

Historical crisis events reveal potential direct and indirect effects of the 2020 crises on Black-owned small businesses in Englewood. After the riots in Ferguson, Missouri, following the 2014 murder of Michael Brown, businesses in Ferguson suffered up to 50% in profit losses, regardless of whether they were physically damaged (Hackman, 2014). Literature has documented indirect damages of riots during the Civil Rights Movement, and the effects were particularly significant for Black-owned properties because the majority of cities’ Black populations resided in riot-affected areas. Further, economic recessions disproportionately affect minority and low-income communities due to predatory lending and low cash reserves among family units and local businesses (Williams et al., 2013).

Despite the significant challenges that Black business owners face, scholars have found that Black-owned business development is an effective strategy to create job opportunities in urban areas, and Black business owners exhibit higher political activity and a stronger commitment to community development than white business owners. Black-owned small businesses can politically and financially support their community amid crisis events, as Black-identifying businesspeople have leadership abilities that can influence local political institutions and strengthen human capital in disadvantaged neighborhoods (Ferleger & Lavallee, 2018).

To better understand how Black- owned businesses can succeed and positively impact their communities, the present research aims to understand the effects of combined 2020 crisis events on Chicago’s minority-owned small businesses, using Englewood as a case study. The work builds upon topics covered by scholars examining natural disasters, riots, and recessions, which have to date significantly impacted low-income and non- white communities like Englewood. Using a mixed-methods approach, I address the research question: how were Black-owned businesses in Englewood economically impacted by COVID-19 and the BLM movement in the spring and summer of 2020? More specifically, I examine two secondary research questions:

1. How was Englewood economically impacted according to foot traffic data records? 2. How was Englewood economically impacted according to business owners’ accounts?

Methods

Quantitative Methods For quantitative analyses, I employed mobile phone data from SafeGraph, Inc., a commercial entity that offered free datasets in 2020 to aid scholarly research on the COVID-19 pandemic. SafeGraph’s compiled mobility datasets used ano- nymized cell phone location records and governmental open data to capture weekly population movements at the census block group (CBG) level. Two datasets provided foot traffic data on visitations to respective points of interest (POI), defined as locations at which a consumer spends money or time.

Quantitative analyses focused on two events of interest in Chicago: (1) the Illinois stay-at-home order declared on March 21, 2020, and (2) the murder of George Floyd on May 25, 2020. I aimed to determine if there existed significant differences in business visitation following the two events of interest between (1) majority-Black Chicago neighborhoods as compared to majority-non-Black Chicago neighborhoods and (2) Englewood as compared to other majority-Black Chicago neighborhoods. Because majority-Black neighborhoods have higher rates of Black business ownership, examining foot traffic on the CBG-level provided information on foot traffic at Black-owned businesses, and demographic variables served as a proxy to examine the research questions (Frey, 2018; Safegraph, 2020). A difference in difference analysis with two

S Figure 1. Silhouette plot of (x= pamx$clustering, dist = dist)

outcome variables, raw visit counts and raw visitor counts, was determined as the appropriate tool to determine potentially disproportionate changes in the foot traffic among multiple neighborhoods in the data.

Before analyses began, significant data cleaning occurred. I added a total of 218,343 new data points with unique week and POI combinations to include visit counts of zero. I then assigned POI to Chicago neighborhoods, or Chicago Community Areas (CCA), through their CBG identification. I matched each data- point with demographic variables corresponding to its CCA, using data from the City of Chicago and a Tract to Community Area Equivalency File (Chicago Data Guy, n.d.; Community Snapshots Raw Data). Finally, for each data point, I added the average COVID-19 positivity rate by week for each neighborhood.

I used Gower’s distance calculations to establish comparison groups. I first created a dissimilarity matrix to analyze dissimilarity between the 77 Chicago neighborhoods, including all 14 variables in the final dataset.1 I used R’s Partition Around Medoids algo- rithm for clustering. The silhouette plots indicated that two clusters were ideal, with an average silhouette width of 0.2, as shown in Figure 1. Cluster 1 contained 49 neighborhoods while Cluster 2 contained 28 neighborhoods. Appendix B displays the average characteristics for Cluster 1 and Cluster 2 neighborhoods. After establishing comparison groups, I assessed the parallel trends assumption using a sandwich estimator of linear regression with the two outcome variables. I assessed covariate balances using a coefficient test on the regression of the

As seen in Equation (1), I estimated the impact of the two events of interest on business visitation outcome in neighborhood n on calendar day d. I indexed neighborhoods’ demographic compositions by c ∈ C, with C = {1, 2}, and indexed weeks relative to events by k. Dnkc is a dummy variable equal to 1 when neighborhood n with neighborhood demographic composition c is k days away from being “treated” by the policy or event. There was a dummy variable for days before the event window: k =-3- for three weeks pre-event and k = 3+ for three weeks post-event. I accounted for the COVID-19 positivity rate in each neighborhood with Xnd. Finally, εnd is an error term for neighborhood and day. I clustered standard errors at a neighborhood level (Weill et al., 2020).

Table 1 presents descriptions of each of the 10 difference-in-difference analyses conducted. For each respective event of interest, the first research question was examined with four comparison group combinations. For example, in Analysis 1, the difference in difference analysis would be conducted with C = 1 for neighborhoods with racial compositions 0-33% Black and C = 2 for neighborhoods with racial compositions 66-100% Black. Neighborhoods with racial compositions of 33-66% Black would be excluded from this analysis. The dummy k = -3- would represent three weeks before March 21, and k = 3+ would represent three weeks after March 21.

Qualitative Methods Qualitative data and quantitative data were collected separately, but the two methods took place simultaneously and informed each other. I chose one-on-one interviews for the qualitative methodology due to their potential to yield contextualized findings on business owners’ perceptions of the policy and events, supplementing the quantitative data that offered aggre- gate insights into foot traffic patterns and indicated potential policy and event effects on transactions.

There were three primary methods for recruitment: contacting business owners directly, referrals from participants, and referrals from local organizations. There were a total of eight participants, seven of whom identify as Black and/or African American and own a small business in Englewood. I additionally interviewed the manager of a non-profit cafe, owned and run by an executive board with a majority of members who identify as Black or African American. Table 2 presents the participants and descriptions of their businesses’ characteristics.

During the interviews, I aimed to
