Open-ended questions throughout the interview allowed for the participant to lead this discussion (see Appendix A for interview protocol). Additionally, I edited the protocol as needed throughout the interview stage. To reduce the influence of any a priori expectations I brought to analyses and to remain open to multiple possibilities of meaning from the data, I enacted a grounded theory approach and drew from Weiss’s (1994) four-phase method for coding and analysis.

I would like to address the specific limitations, risks, and biases in the project. Some participants may have been coping with the psychological costs from the 2020 crises, and they may have experienced discomfort during interviews when asked to reflect on personal experiences. Further, differences between the participants and myself existed on the levels of race, age, religion, socioeconomic status, education, and overall social location, or some combination of them. Due to my positionality as a white woman, participants may have been reluctant to reveal vulnerability during interviews. Concerns or discomfort from participants were considered seriously, and throughout the research, it was imperative that I elevated participants’ voices, centering their experiences rather than my own perceptions. Engaging with the data with high awareness of the strengths and limits of my subjectivity was my highest priority in this process.

Results

Quantitative Results Covariate balance and parallel trend tests maintained that difference in differences was an appropriate tool for the research question. The subsequent analyses assessing the influence of Event 1, the stay-at- home order, on foot traffic found that businesses in neighborhoods with higher proportions of Black residents experienced a smaller decline in visitors and visits per week after the stay-at-home order was enforced than did businesses in neighborhoods with lower proportions of Black residents. This finding is visualized in the sharper decrease in the line representing majority-non-Black neighborhoods in Figure 2. This was true when comparing (1) neighborhoods indexed as 0-33% Black with neighborhoods indexed as 66-100% Black, (2) neighborhoods 33-66% Black with neighborhoods 66-100% Black, and (3) neighborhoods in Cluster 1 with those in Cluster 2. The significant findings align

The higher foot traffic in majority-Black neighborhoods after the stay-at- home order may seem to contradict news media reports that Black businesses have been influenced most negatively by the pandemic. However, essential workers traveling to their workplace within majority-Black neighborhoods could explain the statistically significant higher visitor counts. There are a disproportionate number of Black workers who work in “essential industries” and who are less likely to work from their own homes as an alternative to in-person work during the pandemic (Gould & Wilson, 2020).

Meanwhile, there was no significant difference in visit or visitor count in Englewood as compared to other majority-Black neighborhoods or other neighborhoods in Cluster 2. This finding suggests that the impact of the stay-at-home order on foot traffic was similar in Englewood as in other majority-Black neighborhoods. During interviews, Englewood small business owners reported that customer visitation dropped significantly in the spring and summer of 2020, confirming that business visitation declined in Englewood. Furthermore, participants’ descriptions of decreased business visitation and the effects of these drops on profit are likely consistent with the experiences of business owners in other majority-Black neighborhoods in Chicago.

Analyses for Event 2, the murder of George Floyd, showed that after May 25, 2020, majority-Black neighborhoods experienced a smaller increase in visit count and visitor count as compared to majority-non-Black neighborhoods. This was true when comparing (1) neighborhoods 0-33% Black with neighborhoods 66-100% Black and (2) neighborhoods in Cluster 1 with those in Cluster 2. Figure 3 shows that business visitation increased disproportionately in majority-non-Black neighborhoods as compared to majority-Black neighborhoods after May 25, 2020, and that total visitor counts in neighborhoods indexed as 0-33% Black rises at a higher rate around and after May 25, 2020, as compared to neighborhoods indexed as 33- 66% Black. The significant findings align with analyses 6 and 9, and Table 3 displays the point estimates and significance levels.

While foot traffic increased disproportionately in majority-non-Black neighborhoods after George Floyd’s murder on May 25, 2020, there were no differences in visit or visitor count in Englewood as

S Figure 2. Visitor Count Pre- and Post-Lockdown compared to other majority-Black neighborhoods after May 25, 2020. Thus, Englewood is statistically similar to other majority-Black neighborhoods in terms of business visitation after the murder of George Floyd. Business owners in the present study’s sample explained that generally few protests occur in Englewood: “I think a lot of times protests come from groups that have a little bit more than what we have. We’re more in survival mode than we are in changing mode.” News media also confirms that thousands of individuals rallied in majority-non-Black Chicago neighborhoods to protest for causes associated with the BLM movement. Because quantitative data indicates that Englewood is comparable to other majority-Black neighborhoods after May 25, 2020, it can be reasonably concluded that the increase in total visit counts and visitor counts in majority-non-Black neighborhoods relative to majority-Black neighborhoods can be attributed to higher protest activity in majority-non-Black neighborhoods.

Qualitative Results Although quantitative data indicates a disproportionate decline in business visitation in Chicago’s majority-non-Black neighborhoods, interviews show that the majority of businesses in the Englewood sample experienced declines in business visitation after the March 2020 stay-at-home order, which participants attributed to customer fear of contracting COVID-19. At the time of the interviews, the majority of participants said that visitation was at 50-60% of the pre-pandemic volume. In fact, COVID-19 exacerbated the challenges of acquiring and retaining customers among the participants sam- pled. Customer health concerns about the virus were likely amplified by poor public health infrastructure and high COVID-19 positivity rates in Englewood compared to other neighborhoods in Chicago (“COVID-19 Community Mobility Report,” 2020). Participant 7 stated that before the pandemic, most of his customers lived in majority-white, north-side Chicago neighborhoods. After the stay-at-home order, Participant 7 noticed that these customers “haven’t been calling.” Participants said that even prior to COVID-19, “acquiring a customer was much harder than in a different neighborhood” in Chicago due to public perception of Englewood as dangerous, and customers from outside of the neighborhood were less likely to patronize businesses in Englewood.

COVID-19 precautions also increased business costs and decreased revenue through modes other than business visitation. For

S Figure 3. Visitor Count Pre- and Post-May 25 example, Participant 3 stopped making food for delivery services like DoorDash due to “problems where delivery people didn’t want to wear masks.” Sanitation supplies to address COVID-19 were costly, and shortages early in the pandemic contributed to high expenditures on the sanitation supplies. Participant 5 explained, “Say you made about five or six hundred dollars for the week. Now, you have to take $100 of that just for sanitation. That’s not including your lights, your gas, your product.” The majority of participants were forced to balance cost and revenue streams by decreasing the number of days their business was in operation, lowering service prices, or let- ting go of employees. It is important to note that business success after the stay-at-home order varied by industry; the funeral home and hardware store had higher customer visitation than before 2020. However, such improved business performance was due at least in part to implications of the stay- at-home order, including increases in bike riding and home repairs. And, even with unharmed revenue streams, the COVID-19 pandemic affected these businesses’ interactions with customers due to mask mandates and storefront capacity limits. Participant 2, whose profit was not affected by the stay- at-home order, recounted his concern with employee and customer health: “We talked with employees about the importance of not only keeping them safe and healthy, but also keeping the public safe. And that we were concerned about them as our staff. We were concerned about their family.”

All participants’ businesses were at least partially re-opened by June 2021 after the initial economic shock from COVID-19 restrictions. However, Participant 5 explained that just after her business re-opened in June, looting occurred in Englewood. She said, “It was very heartbreaking for that damage of all breaking in and stealing stuff and destroying stuff. It was really tough. Especially mixed in with this pandemic.” The two participants whose storefronts experienced looting damage assumed additional financial obligations for repairs. Participant 5’s costs amounted to over $25,000, with

90% of products and “countless” pieces of equipment stolen. Looters broke Participant 3’s doors and windows in an attempt to steal the ATM machine. Business owners who did not experience direct effects of looting reckoned with the destruction of their community. Participant 4 explained that looters “burnt down a lot of stores and bust out windows around the Englewood area.” Participant 3 told me that she “watched someone’s business being destroyed for eight hours” and that at the liquor store across the street from her business, looters took “about $6 or $7 million worth of alcohol.”

Business owners were unable to control

“Clearly, political protests — and police presence — are more salient in Chicago’s majority-non-Black neighborhoods, while majority-Black neighborhoods like

Englewood are deprived of the political infrastructure to manage or prevent looting.” looting activity themselves, and police failed to protect their storefronts during the looting. While participants stayed in their businesses as long as possible, sometimes the entire night, many returned home to sleep, at which point the looting occurred. Unpro- tected and vulnerable to the physical damage of their storefronts, the consequences of looting in Englewood amid pre-existing financial hardship represent the racial and socioeconomic discrimination inhibiting the success of Black-owned small businesses.

Physical damage from looting associated with the BLM movement after the murder of George Floyd negatively affected participants’ businesses and emotional well-being, but participants reported some positive consequences of the BLM movement itself, which helped counteract the negative effects of the pandemic. After losing customers in majority-white neighborhoods, Participant 7 began posting ad- vertisement flyers in the Englewood area to attract new customers. Now, the majority of Participant 7’s customers live in Englewood, and he has a higher proportion of Black customers. He said, “Ever since COVID, a lot of Black people have been trying to look for a Black computer repairman.” BLM affected Black customers’ patronization of Black-owned businesses, demonstrating intra-community asset-building. Therefore, participants revealed BLM as an avenue to bolster economic capital in addition to political capital.

As expected from the accounts of decreased profit and increased costs, participants in the sample demonstrated considerable financial need in 2020. Some business owners in Englewood, explained Participant 4, were not “able to pay the landlord their rent” due to “losing their business” in 2020. Participant 3 explained that what she needed most right now was “financial aid,” and half of the participants reported using out-of-pocket or personal funds to support their businesses in this “time of need.” Additionally, rather than discussing expansion or business strategy, most participants explained that their most important “business goal for 2020” was “to stay open.” This data indicates that positive effects of the BLM movement on patronization of Black-owned businesses did not remedy the financial crises that participants faced in 2020. Ultimately, Englewood’s Black-owned businesses faced immense socioeconomic and emotional hardship throughout the crisis events in 2020.

Discussion Numerous circumstances in 2020 interacted to affect the experiences of Black-identifying business owners in Englewood. In sum, their experiences, hardships, and perspectives are not quantifiable. While the effect of the stay-at-home order was more statistically significant in majority-non-Black neighborhoods, business owners in Englewood reported significant economic dam-

[T]he consequences of looting in Englewood amid pre-existing financial hardship represent the racial and socioeconomic discrimination inhibiting the success of Black- owned small businesses. “

” ages from COVID-19. Statistical analyses suggested that participants’ descriptions of decreased business visitation and the effects of these drops on profit are consistent with the experiences of business owners in other majority-Black neighborhoods in Chicago.

After the murder of George Floyd, foot traffic increased disproportionately in majority-white neighborhoods, reflecting participants’ accounts of low protest activity, at least in part due to political and economic disinvestment in majority-Black neighborhoods like Englewood. At the same time, interviews revealed that looting activity after the murder of George Floyd injured Englewood’s physical storefronts and further inhibited financial security for participants in the sample. Clearly, political protests — and police presence — are more salient in Chicago’s majority-non-Black neighborhoods, while majority-Black neighborhoods like Englewood are deprived of the political infrastructure to manage or prevent looting.

Although some business owners experienced increased patronage from customers in Englewood due to increased awareness of BLM — and one participant noticed that Englewood residents displayed an increased propensity for patronizing his business because it is Black-owned — the movement was an insufficient force for substantially increasing business visitation at Black-owned businesses in Englewood. Customers from majority-white neighborhoods stopped using another participant’s services due to COVID-19 safety concerns. This aligns with some media accounts that support for Black-owned businesses because of the 2020 BLM movement most benefited majority-white, north-side neighborhoods. Future research and media reports should clarify the effects of the BLM movement on patronization by delineating interactions among Black customers, white customers, businesses in majority-white neighborhoods, and businesses in majority-non-white neighborhoods.

The present discussion is limited due to the range of businesses represented in the study. This is especially true in analyses of looting effects; according to participants, liquor stores and corner stores were frequently looted, but they were not included in the sample due to outreach constraints. I interviewed only two business owners among the dozens of looted stores in Englewood. Additionally, a limitation to the quantitative methods is my ability to differentiate between protest foot traffic and business visitation foot traffic due to the inaccuracy of SafeGraph geospatial data. However, the mixed-methods nature of this research remedies some potential limitations in that interview findings on protest activity and business visitation suggest that the quantitative results are accurate.

Fortunately, scholars will likely continue to document the impacts of 2020’s crisis events on small businesses in Chicago. However, the effects of these crises will last for decades to come, especially in minority and low-income communities, as has been observed after recessions in the 20th century and after Civil Rights-Era riots (Collins & Margo, 2007; Williams et al., 2013). While this paper demonstrates that business owners’ experiences amid crises are highly complex, it also forms a foundation on which researchers can examine the potentially enduring damages of 2020 crises in majority-Black and low-income communities in Chicago. Equally as important, the research provides information for future policy- making so that, as Participant 8 expressed, policymakers, NGOs, and private firms can “take action and be held accountable to bring resources to the Englewood community.” ◆

Appendices (A-B)

Appendix A: Interview Protocol

Introduction

My name is Sophie Boorstein, and I am a senior at Northwestern University. As you know, I am conducting a research study on the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic and 2020 Black Lives Matter Protests on Black-owned small businesses in Englewood. The research is for my senior thesis that culminates my academic coursework as a Social Policy major. I am working with professors in the School of Education and Social Policy and the Department of Political Science at Northwestern. We are focusing our research on businesses in Englewood due to its rich culture of community organizing, as well as the significant impacts of COVID-19 and BLM on the community in 2020.

I want to preface the interview by telling you that I’m new to researching small businesses, as well as researching Chicago in general. You are the expert. I’m first and foremost here to learn from you, and afterwards, to document your story as accurately as possible. I’ve reached out to just a handful of other business owners in the area and value this opportunity to listen to your perspective. Talking with you will really help me understand what’s been happening in the Englewood area.

After our research is completed, we want to present our findings to you personally. We will give you the information we learned in this entire year-long research project in a way that may be able to benefit your business.

Background / Business History. This first section will help me understand your business and its operations before the pandemic. [Note: questions will be based on answers to the screening questions.]

1. If you started your business, why did you start it, and had you owned a business before?

a. If you did not start the business, why did you decide to buy it?

b. What do you feel the strengths of your business have been since you founded the business or joined it?

2. I’m new to learning about the Englewood area. Can you give me an idea of what the area is like by comparing it to another neighborhood or other neighborhoods in a. Which neighborhood is Englewood most similar to? Why?

b. Why did you choose Englewood as the site for your business? Did you consider other neighborhoods?

General Questions. [Note: I will begin with this section of general questions. I will ask questions from subsequent sections, “BLM Questions” and “COVID-19 Questions,” if and when appropriate.]

1. Tell me about how your business performed in spring and summer 2020. Here I’m referring to the months of March through August, but your answer can include other months as well.

2. Tell me about your best quarter of 2020. Tell me about your worst quarter of 2020.

a. Can you think of any specific examples or stories about how COVID-19 affected your business?

4. I want to talk about the inflow of customers to your business. Have you noticed any changes throughout the year?

5. Among the damages that you have described to me so far, which one is your primary concern?

a. What do you need most right now? What does your business need most right now?

6. Are there any policies or initiatives that you would have liked to have seen enacted in 2020?

a. If yes, when and how did these policies/initiatives help?

i. What was this process like?

c. Were there differences in those that came due to COVID-19 versus those that came due to the BLM movement?

7. Have other Black-owned businesses in Englewood been affected by BLM protests and the COVID-19 pandemic?

8. Have other Black-owned businesses in Englewood been affected by BLM protests and the COVID-19 pandemic?

a. Have you interacted with other business owners during any crises? During the process of recovery?

b. Have any community organizations and/or community organizers interacted with affected businesses?

COVID-19 Questions. I’d like to ask about what’s happened in your business in the time of the COVID-19 pandemic. I’m not sure if it’s affected your business a lot, but I want to ask.

1. How have business costs and revenue evolved throughout 2020?

a. Has there been an increase or decrease in business costs due to COVID-19?

b. Has there been an increase or decrease in business revenue due to COVID-19?

2. Is there anything else you want to say about COVID-19 related to your business?

BLM Questions. Based on what I’ve read and heard, there have been protests in the Englewood area after the tragic murder of George Floyd in May.

1. I first want to ask how aware you are of the Black Lives Matter movement?

a. Do you see yourself as part of the movement?

2. Is there anything else you want to say about COVID-19 related to your business?

3. Can you explain what the BLM protests looked like in Englewood?

a. Has your business suffered any damages due to the BLM protests?If no, did you seek out governmental or community support?

i. Did protests cause direct damages? Direct damages may include property destruction, loss of store contents, etc.

ii. Did protests cause indirect damages? Indirect damages may include loss of cash flow, staff, previous investments, temporary closure, etc.

b. What, if any, good has come from the BLM movement in 2020?

i. Have you noticed an increased interest for shopping at Black-owned businesses in Englewood overall? At your business in particular?

4. If your store or community area did experience looting, did the police intervene? How do you feel about police stepping in during looting incidents?

5. I have read that on August 10, police shot Latrell Allen in Englewood, and he was hospitalized with multiple gunshot wounds. The shooting prompted protests and looting in various neighborhoods in Chicago. Are you aware of this incident?

a. Are you aware of anything that happened in Englewood after this incident?

b. What additional effects, if any, did this shooting or these protests have on you? Your community? Your business? How so?

6. Is there anything else you want to say about the Black Lives Matter movement?

title: Framing and Youth Participation in the Sunrise Movement
text:
The Green Dream:

Framing and Youth Participation in the Sunrise Movement by Keerti Gopal

Department of American Studies Faculty Adviser: Prof. Chloe Thurston, Ph.D.

Introduction

On Nov. 13, 2018, a group called the Sunrise Movement (hereafter referred to as “Sunrise”) made national headlines for taking over Speaker Nancy Pelosi’s office, staging a sit-in to demand immediate federal action to address the climate crisis. The sit-in was led by 200 teenagers and young adults wearing matching black and yellow t-shirts and holding signs with slogans like “12 years”1 and “we have a right to good jobs and a livable future.” Singing, chant- ing, and giving speeches, they were soon joined by newly elected Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who would later co-introduce the Green New Deal resolution — a proposed set of guidelines for federal action to combat the climate crisis while tackling economic inequality. The resolution posits that it is the federal government’s duty to “achieve net-zero greenhouse gas emissions through a fair and just transition for all communities and workers” by investing in infrastructure, creating “millions of good, high-wage jobs” in clean energy industries, and focusing on the communities that will bear the brunt of devastation from climate change: poor, Indigenous, Black and brown communities, young people, and unhoused populations, among others.2

“The green dream or whatever they call it, nobody knows what that is,” said Pelosi in 2019, responding to the resolution’s

1 This number refers to a special report published in 2018 by the United Nations’ Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) that stated if global warming is worsened by any more than 1.5 degrees Celsius before 2030, the planet will experience climate devastation past the point of repair. 2 Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, “Text - H.Res.109 - 116th Congress (2019–2020): Recognizing the Duty of the Federal Government to Create a Green New Deal.” Congress.gov. February 12, 2019. Accessed March 02, 2021. https://www.congress.gov/bill/116th-congress/house-resolution/109/text.

introduction.3 Pelosi’s words set a tone for establishment backlash labeling the Green New Deal as too radical or unrealistic,4 but over the next two years, the Green New Deal became a fixture in national Democratic politics; it infiltrated local, state, and federal elections and legislation, getting adopted by 16 presidential candidates and appearing in national headlines and debate stages. Meanwhile, Sunrise grew to operate as a key player in the national mobilization around climate justice.5

In this project, I explore Sunrise’s communication strategies and operations,6 focusing on the organization’s tactics around framing from its founding in 2016 through 2020. Through 21 semi-structured interviews with young people currently involved with Sunrise, I explore how the young (defined as under 35) organizers who make up the group conceptualize and disseminate their strategic messaging. Looking at these interviews alongside selected social media outputs and drawing from existing social movement research in the fields of sociology, political science, and media studies, I argue that Sunrise’s strategy of using movement rhetoric and outsider framing to work within the electoral process provides an example of how organizations can bridge the gap between movements and electoral politics to mobilize young people to take civic action. I also argue that the exploration of Sunrise’s framing and social media communication illustrates the possibility that the United States (U.S.) is in the process of an economic and political paradigm shift, characterized by a renewed understanding of who has a stake in the political process.

Bridging the Youth Movement-Electoral Divide In recent years, it has been well documented that young people in the U.S. are less involved in formal politics than older people. According to the U.S. Census Bureau, 18–29-year-olds are consistently the least reliable voting bloc in the U.S.,7 and a 2017 study found that trends of low youth participation extended to other political activities like writing to representatives, attending town halls and public legislative meetings, and campaigning or working for political parties.8 A 2000 survey by Heather Bastedo found that young people were less likely than any other age group to express interest in traditional politics, follow political news, or participate as a member in an advocacy organization, but the young people in this study were not apathetic; instead of voting, subjects identified protest and community volunteering

Sunrise’s theory of change calls for both “people power” (an active base of public support) and “political power” (enthusiastic involvement from public officials) as essential components of winning progress,17 demonstrating a narrative framing that brings outsider energy — the energy of a social movement — into formalized politics and questioning existing ideas of who has power in political processes and what political participation can look like. By combining movement rhetoric with political aims, Sunrise asserts that although politicians do not often seem to have the best interests of the youth (roughly defined as Gen Z and younger millennials) in mind, they should. Sunrise demands that those in political power listen to young people, or step aside.

Framing in the Sunrise Movement For Sunrise and other organizations like it, a crucial aspect of building both people power and political power is telling a convincing story, or in other words, political framing. In the social movement scholarship in the fields of sociology, political science, and communication and media studies, a frame is a way of looking at information.18 Framing describes the way that movement actors, like organizations or leaders, attempt to publicly explain the problems they are working to solve and the solutions that they propose. There is a prevalent idea in social psychology that people live in a perceived world, meaning that they respond to external events based on their built perceptions of what is happening around them. This suggests that, for social movements, framing has potential for real-world impact; if people’s perceptions shape their responses, then influencing those perceptions is a task with great potential power.19

Benford and Snow’s seminal 1988 sociological scholarship on social movement framing provides a blueprint for social movement organizations (SMOs) looking to develop effective framing. The authors write that frames for collective actions are “intended to mobilize potential adherents

According to Benford and Snow, there are three main stages for this kind of frame: diagnostic framing, or the identification and description of a problem; prognostic framing, or the proposal of a solution; and motivational framing, or the rationale for action.21

Sunrise’s framing falls clearly into Benford and Snow’s three stages. First, they diagnose the problem: the climate crisis is here, and we have (now) less than 10 years before our habitat is damaged beyond repair, but the fossil fuel execu- tives and corrupt politicians who brought about this crisis continue to enact their decades-long strategy of blocking action in protection of their profits. Meanwhile, the dominance of neoliberalism over the past several decades has cemented economic and racial hierarchies that ensure that poor communities of color are most immediately in danger of the devastating impacts of climate change.22

Next, the prognosis: we need the federal government to lead a complete transition away from fossil fuels, invest in green housing and infrastructure, concentrate aid to frontline communities, and enact a jobs guarantee to ensure good union jobs for any American in need during this transition. These changes need to be enacted immediately and comprehensively, and the cost of these investments is nothing compared to the devastating economic and societal dangers of allowing the climate crisis to continue unchecked.23

In order to achieve such a comprehensive transformation in society, we need to change the cultural understanding of what is politically possible and what needs to be accomplished in order to combat climate change. This calls for a paradigm shift — one that will prioritize people over profits and advocate for dignity, justice, equality, and the common good. Achieving such a shift will require a combination of people power (in the streets) and political power (in government).24 This is where Sunrise’s motivational framing comes in: young people must join the movement and take action because time is running out, and there is no path to winning a Green

Digital Dimensions: Disseminating the Frame Sunrise’s use of contemporary social media platforms — particularly Instagram, Twitter, and sometimes TikTok — has been essential in the organization’s dissemination of its messaging, exemplifying how digital tools create a more decentralized and participatory information society. This paves a way for new voices to be included in political idea generation and illustrates how the bounds of what constitutes a political stakeholder are being expanded.

At the time of this writing, Sunrise uses Twitter and Instagram, along with (to a lesser degree) TikTok and (even more decreasingly) Facebook, to disseminate its framing and communicate with the public.25 Sunrise also engages with more traditional media sources — members li- aise with the press and place op-eds and letters-to-the-editor in mainstream news sources — but a significant portion of the organization’s recruitment and communication efforts occur over social media platforms. “I think a lot of Sunrise’s success has been in … changing dominant cultural narratives around climate justice topics,” Sunrise’s Oregon-based video network lead Allyson Woodward said, discussing the way that the Green New Deal rhetoric has infiltrated mainstream media and politics. “I do think that we could not have done it without digital organizing,” she added, suggesting that social media was a key element of the organization’s strategy.

She went on to explain that the digital dimension of Sunrise’s strategy is about gaining narrative power:

How do we destroy the climate versus jobs narrative, and how do we get our own to be dominant, which is this idea of tying good jobs to climate action? We do that through effective organizing … but it can’t happen unless we are pulling organizing into smart digital campaigns that further our narrative.

Woodward went on to argue that in the current information landscape, social media platforms like Instagram and Twitter are essential to ensuring that people see an SMO’s organizing. “Digital comm[unica- tions] are the tools to gain cultural power,” she summarized.26 And this cultural power can manifest through the infiltration of mainstream narratives and rhetoric in both media and legislative spheres.

Digital Framing in Action: #YoungAndNaive Sunrise’s strategic use of digital communications as a tool for building power and infiltrating mainstream media discourse was emblemized when videos27 of Pennsylvania gubernatorial candidate Scott Wagner (who lost to Democrat Tom Wolf) calling Sunrise activist Rose Strauss “young and naive” went viral. Sunrise used Twitter in conjunction with traditional media outlets to cap- italize on the moment — which could otherwise have been seen as a blow to the movement’s credibility — and start a conversation about the moral authority of young people, claiming that the younger generation has a unique perspective on

The story began when, during a Q&A at a campaign event, Sunrise member Rose Strauss stood to ask Wagner a question.

“My name is Rose,” she began. “I’m 18, and I’m really concerned about the future of our country. Two-thirds of Pennsylva- nians think that climate change is an issue that needs to be addressed, but you’ve said that climate change is a result of people’s body heat and are refusing to take action on the issue. Does this have anything to do with the $200,000 that you have taken from the fossil fuel industry?”

Wagner paused for less than a full second before responding.

“Rose, I appreciate you being here,” he said. “And you’re 18 years old. You know, you’re a little young and naive. Let’s talk about something else.” Wagner turned away from Strauss and looked at the rest of the people at the event, many of whom were clapping and cheering, before continuing, “Are we here to elect a governor, or are we here to elect a scientist?” Multiple videos of the exchange began to circulate online — mostly on Twitter and YouTube — starting some buzz about the candidate’s attitude.29

This was an opportunity for Sunrise to take hold of the narrative, and the organization did just that. Sunrise took to Twitter, starting the hashtag “#youngandnaive” in order to weaponize Wagner’s words against him and elevate its own platform.

As the hashtag began gaining attention, Sunrise turned to traditional media. In an op-ed for Teen Vogue, Rose Strauss described the exchange as “one of the most embarrassing and frustrating moments of [her] life,” saying she felt “belittled” and “insignificant.”30 She then went on to reclaim and repurpose the candidate’s words. “If being ‘young and naive’ means I expect my politicians to reject contributions from the fossil fuel CEOs and lobbyists most responsible for burning our planet, then call me young and naive,” she wrote, addressing her response to Wagner and “all politicians like him.”31 By turning Wagner’s words against him, Strauss questioned the notion that her youth was a weakness and instead painted Wagner to be a symbol of the establishment — old and out of touch.

By reframing the narrative around Wagner’s words, Sunrise pushed back at the idea that an 18-year-old should keep her nose out of politics and instead asserted that being “young and naive” was a designation of moral authority: to be young and naive was to be uncorrupted by money and the fossil fuel industry, to be clear-eyed and strong. This narrative resonated in both traditional and participatory information spaces; the exchange was covered by local and national publications including the Philly Voice, The Guardian, and The New York Times, and the hashtag was used by organizations and public figures like NextGen America, 350 Action, Now This, and Al Gore. In this instance, social media allowed Sunrise to send a clear message. A 2018 New York Times article featuring an interview with Strauss introduced the exchange by noting that “it quickly went viral on social media,” using this as a justification for its newsworthiness. That Sunrise was able to begin spreading this story on Twitter, get noticed by press, public figures, and political actors, and then successfully transition to traditional media sources, shows how participatory media platforms can influence political discourse by giving voices that might ordinarily be discounted — like Strauss’ — the opportunity for greater reach. On Twitter, politicians, activists, and unofficial actors are using the same platform; participatory social media disrupts the previously entrenched dynamics of who has access to spheres of political idea-generation and persuasive messaging.

Participatory technologies also influence the ease with which the public consumes movement messaging. Although viral activism, sometimes known as “slacktivism” and defined as showing support for a social cause on social media alone, is often criticized for being low effort and lacking substance,34 Sunrise’s strategy exemplifies a different dimension of digital organizing. For Sunrise, the battle does not end with the virality of #youngandnaive, it begins there: social media is a vehicle for framing, which seeks to reach young people in order to politicize and, subsequently, mobilize.

Sunrise is just one example of how this potential paradigm shift is manifesting in robust social movement engagement and translating to electoral spheres. This shift is further evidenced in the recent influx of progressive politicians who cut their political teeth organizing with movements outside the system, not amongst the establishment. One example is Rep. Ocasio-Cortez, who in the past three years has rocketed to political superstardom and got her start through movement participation in the #NoDAPL movement at Standing Rock. Sunrise is part of this moment where shifting conceptions of what is politically possible abound. Its framing strategies and digital practices, along with its outsider infiltration of formalized electoral politics, provide an example of how progressive organizations can (and are) bridging the gap between youth movement energy and electoral action, while also illustrating the prevalence of shifting paradigms for economic and political thought and suggesting that maybe it is time for the establishment of a new common sense. For young people, Sunrise provides a blueprint for building political power and taking control of their country’s narrative. Reflecting on the way her involvement with Sunrise has impacted her personally, Woodward summed it up.

“Before Sunrise, I felt like I was screaming into the void and that I didn’t really have any impact or effect on larger world events or the political process, and I didn’t even see a pathway into how to get that,” she said. “I feel now that I understand how to shape [the] larger public understanding of issues, and that I can’t do it alone, but I also am connected with other people, and as a collective, we can, like, to- tally shift the dominant cultural narratives if we choose to.”45

Perhaps this is the true impact of framing: it provides people who have been left out of the political process and have had no faith in their ability to impact politics or their government’s interest in working for them with a new understanding of their own power and a new motivation to fight. As more people enter into political processes, staking their claim on the establishment, the realm of possibility expands until everyone sees themselves in their representatives, organizers, and changemakers. Ultimately, the paradigm shift becomes this: the realization of true democracy, where the power lies with the people. ◆

title: The Impact of Climate Change on Energy Poverty: Evidence from the European Union, 2004–2019
abstract: Energy poverty can be understood as the inability or difficulty of a household to meet their basic energy needs. While the condition is already widespread across Europe, it will likely worsen in the near future, as average temperatures increase due to climate change and there becomes a greater need for heating and/or cooling. The present study addresses the gap in research in this area by using Eurostat data on energy poverty and changes in heating degree-days (HDD) and cooling degree-days (CDD) across the 28 European Union (EU) Member States from 2004–2019. These metrics are then used to create a composite indicator of energy poverty based on a household’s inability to keep warm, pay utility bills on time, and the presence of damp, leakage, or rot in the home. The results indicate that an increase in the number of days in which air conditioning is needed to be comfortable significantly increases the share of energy-poor households, but there is no significant association with HDD. Additionally, a comprehensive analysis of temporal and macroeconomic trends shows that energy poverty is severely unevenly distributed across the Member States and that both climate change and the ongoing energy transition will likely exacerbate these inequalities. Thus, policy implications include increasing general awareness of the phenomenon and implementing country-specific policies that directly address energy poverty in the context of a changing climate, especially in Southern and Eastern European EU countries.
text:
The Impact of Climate Change on Energy Poverty:

Evidence from the European Union, 2004–2019 by Ginny Ip

Department of Economics Faculty Advisers: Prof. Mar Reguant, Ph.D.

& Prof. Jeffrey Lewis, Ph.D.

Abstract Energy poverty can be understood as the inability or difficulty of a household to meet their basic energy needs. While the condition is already widespread across Europe, it will likely worsen in the near future, as average temperatures increase due to climate change and there becomes a greater need for heating and/or cooling. The present study addresses the gap in research in this area by using Eurostat data on energy poverty and changes in heating degree-days (HDD) and cooling degree-days (CDD) across the 28 European Union (EU) Member States from 2004–2019. These metrics are then used to create a composite indicator of energy poverty based on a household’s inability to keep warm, pay utility bills on time, and the presence of damp, leakage, or rot in the home. The results indicate that an increase in the number of days in which air conditioning is needed to be comfortable significantly increases the share of energy-poor households, but there is no significant association with HDD. Additionally, a comprehensive analysis of temporal and macroeconomic trends shows that energy poverty is severely unevenly distributed across the Member States and that both climate change and the ongoing energy transition will likely exacerbate these inequalities. Thus, policy implications include increasing general awareness of the phenomenon and implementing country-specific policies that directly address energy poverty in the context of a changing climate, especially in Southern and Eastern European EU countries.

I. Introduction and Background Awareness of energy poverty has been rapidly growing in recent years and is increasingly being recognized as a critical social policy issue. Importantly, energy poverty not only affects those living in the poorest countries without any access to power but also those in some of the wealthiest countries in the world. While the term “energy poverty” does not have a universal definition, it is generally understood as a distinct form of poverty associated with households who have a hard time meeting their basic energy needs or spend a very high proportion of their income to do so. For example, the United Kingdom officially declares a household energy-poor if it “needs to spend more than 10 per cent of its income on fuel to maintain a satisfactory heating regime” (DTI, 2007). However, this definition of energy poverty may be overly simplistic, as the causes of energy poverty are often multidimensional, stemming from a combination of low household incomes, high energy expenditures, and energy inefficient buildings and appliances (EU Energy Poverty Observatory, 2016).

As a result, energy poverty is not only a development issue but also involves public health, environmental, and national security issues, as its prevalence is often associated with adverse consequences ranging from respiratory and cardiac illnesses, exacerbated mental health problems, increased air pollution, and higher levels of social unrest and instability (EU Energy Poverty Observatory, 2016; Yumkella & Bazilian, 2015). Additionally, energy poverty often coincides with food poverty, as energy-poor, income-constrained households are forced to choose between prioritizing their energy needs or food needs (Omic, 2019). Thus, addressing energy poverty has the potential to bring many benefits, including healthier citizens, a healthier environment, improved social security, and higher levels of economic productivity overall.

Energy Poverty & Climate Change Recent decades have seen increasing average temperatures and extreme temperature days due to the onset of climate change. For instance, a group of climate scientists found that each of six European heat waves since 2010 was significantly more likely and intense because of climate change (Schiermeier, 2019). This may elicit an increase in household energy demand, particularly for cooling purposes, causing a positive feedback loop that further perpetuates climate change and puts a strain on existing energy services (Jessel et al., 2019). However, most of the current literature on household energy to date have not sufficiently considered climate change and its impact on vulnerable populations (Jessel et al., 2019).

Moreover, subsequent global efforts to undertake an energy transition, which involves moving away from conventional sources of energy such as oil and gas and “towards a more sustainable energy system characterised by universal access to energy services … and security and reliability of supply from efficient, low-carbon sources,” are also having a significant impact on household energy bills (Bridge et al., 2013). McGee and Greiner (2019) have found that attempts to address climate change through subsidies and other in- centives for carbon mitigation, including transitioning away from fossil fuels, have disproportionately increased the percentage of household income spent on energy by marginalized groups. Bouzarovski & Herrero (2017) would agree, arguing that European energy transitions in particular have deepened existing regional inequalities and energy poverty.

Acknowledging this gap, the present study uses panel data to examine how changing average temperatures as a result of global climate change have impacted energy poverty levels in European Union (EU) Member States over the last few decades. The principal finding is that an increase in the number of CDD significantly increases the share of energy-poor households, but there is no significant association with HDD. Moreover, energy poverty is indeed very unevenly distributed across the Member States, and both climate change and the ongoing energy transition will likely exacerbate these inequalities.

Energy Poverty in the EU I focused on the EU for three reasons. First, an estimated 30 million people were living in energy poverty as of 2019, with the highest rates in Southern and Central-Eastern European countries (Omic, 2019). Many countries are still suffering the repercussions of the economic crisis of 2008/9, with high unemployment and inequality rates having serious consequences on the living conditions of EU citizens (Kyprianou et al., 2019). Second, there is a high degree of geographic, social, and economic variation across the Member States, which means that climate change will likely have very different effects on energy poverty levels across the EU. Bouzarovski and Herrero (2017) note that the “classic economic development distinction between the core and periphery also holds true in the case of energy poverty,” where the Southern and Eastern European countries are simultaneously milder in climate and poorer compared to the frigid but wealthy Northern countries. At the same time, the EU Member States share both a common currency and an interconnected power grid, which makes it easier to compare and control for trends in energy costs and prices. This unique combination is particularly useful in understanding the macro-scale spatial patterns of energy poverty and how they relate to wider economic and geographic disparities within the EU, an area that is also currently under-researched (Petrakos et al., 2011). Finally, the Eurostat provides a rich body of publicly available, highly reliable data on energy poverty that is currently un- matched in other regions of the world.

II. Data & Descriptive Statistics The main data source was the EU Energy Poverty Observatory (EPOV), launched in 2018 by the European Commission with the goal of better monitoring and addressing energy poverty across member countries (EU Energy Poverty Observatory, 2019). It recognizes the multidimensional nature of energy poverty and thus includes a portfolio of indicators that I used collectively. Specifically, I combined three primary indicators to create an Energy Poverty Index using the following formula:

(1) EP = 0.4 · % W + 0.4 · % A + 0.2 · % HP

EP – Energy Poverty

W – Warm A – Arrears H – Housing Problems

The variables warm, arrears, and housing problems measure the population percentages of people who reported (1) not being able to keep their homes adequately warm, (2) having trouble paying their utility bills on time, and (3) the presence of damp, rot, or a leaking roof in the home, respectively.1 This approach is based on Bouzarovski & Herrero’s (2017) energy poverty index and previously developed efforts to capture the multidimensional nature of energy poverty. However, while Bouzarovski & Herrero’s index gives warm a weight of 0.5 and gives arrears and housing problems a weight of 0.25 each, I gave the same weight to warm and arrears and gave housing problems a lower weight. This was because the latter is not necessarily a direct indicator of energy poverty, while the former two are. For instance, a household might have a leaking roof but have no problem meeting its energy needs. Likewise, a household might have a perfectly functioning home but can barely afford to pay the heating bills in the winter. Additionally, I did not weigh warm higher than arrears because the former does not take into account the inability of households to keep cool in the summer, which is highly relevant in the context of a predominantly warming climate, while the latter keeps track of late payment in energy bills pertaining to both heating and cooling.

Other secondary indicators that were included as controls are household electricity prices and household gas prices, both of which include taxes and levies and are measured in cents per kilowatt hour (ct/kWh); the percentage of the population living in an area with intermediate urbanisation; the percentage of the population who are paying tenure market rent; and the percentage of the population with access to air conditioning and heating in the home, respectively.

The other main dataset that tracks historical temperature patterns was supplied by the Eurostat (the Statistical Office of the

European Union). The annual data series covers the Member States of the EU and the EU aggregated from 1975 to 2019, except Cyprus, which only has data from 1978 to 2019. The two variables of interest were Heating Degree Days (HDD) and Cooling Degree Days (CDD). HDD measures the difference between the daily mean outdoor temperature (Ti) and 15°C, below which a building is assumed to need heating; CDD measures the difference between Ti and 24°C, above which a building is assumed to need cooling. Both estimates are based on daily observations from approximately 3,000 weather stations across Europe, which are then added up to make yearly °C temperature sums (Eurostat, 2019).

To control for differences in macroeconomic conditions across the EU countries, two additional datasets from the World Bank and World Inequality Data- base were included.

The former dataset includes information on national GDP per capita (in thousands of U.S. dollars) and the unemployment rate from 1960 to 2019, while the latter captures income inequality by measuring the bottom 50% share of total national income from 2004–2019.

A few weaknesses in the data sources need to be acknowledged. First, while most studies have used household-level microdata in their analysis of energy poverty, I used individual Member States as the unit of analysis, which means that the maximum yearly sample size is 28.2 Nevertheless, this approach is in line with the objective of the analysis to uncover patterns across Member States as a whole. I also supplemented my macroanalysis with a case study on Spanish

1 Note that data are available from 2004–2019 for the warm and arrears variables while only data from 2005–2016 are available for the housing problems variable. 2 The United Kingdom is excluded from the sample even though the period covered is pre-Brexit. This is because the U.K. oper- ated differently from the rest of the EU in many aspects even prior to Brexit, which may affect the reliability of the results. In its place, I’ve included average observations for the European Union in general, which is why the sample size is still 28 and not 27.

households using micro-level panel data, presented in Section V. Second, the EPOV energy poverty indicators are based on the consensual-based European Union Statistics on Income and Living Conditions (EU-SILC) survey microdata that rely on households’ self-reported assessments, which has received some criticism in the literature (Thomson et al., 2020). However, it is difficult to think of other ways to go about gathering the more qualitative data, such as a household’s inability to keep warm, that are not completely exempt of methodological problems either. Further, the EPOV has included a methodology guidebook on their website which details the measures they took to ensure full compliance with Eurostat rules (Thomson et al., 2020). Finally, since the main EPOV energy poverty indicators only cover the period from 2004–2019, the regression analysis was limited to this time period, even though there is temperature and macro data dating back to the 1970s. Data for the percentage of the population with access to heating and cooling were only available for the year 2007, which means that these two variables are time-invariant. For this reason, they were omitted from the regression models where fixed-effects were added.3

Table 1 presents summary statistics for the main variables used in the analysis. The table shows that the mean percentage of arrears, warm, and housing problems are 10.82%, 12.27%, and 16.89%, respectively (see Appendix). Those variables taken in combination, according to equation (1), find that the mean energy poverty is approximately 12.5% across all EU countries. Also, it is interesting to note that while more than 90% of the population are equipped with heating, only roughly

10% of the population are equipped with air conditioning, a problem which will be magnified with climate change and increasingly hot summers.

As an initial exploration of the differences in climate and characteristics of energy poverty across the EU, Table 2 reports average CDD and HDD statistics, the population percentage unable to keep warm, and energy poverty index by country. The means confirm the paradox involving EU members in the Mediterranean Basin: even though winters are milder in Southern Member States such as Cyprus, Portugal, and Greece, households in these countries consistently report higher percentages of people who are unable to stay warm in their home (Bouzarovski & Herrero, 2017). This phenomenon is shown more clearly in Figures 2A and 2B, where the number of HDD is highest in the Scandinavian and Northern European countries and lowest in the Southern and Eastern European countries, yet the opposite is true for the percentage of households unable to keep warm.

3 This is the reason for the different sample sizes in Tables 4, 5, and 6. Column 2 does not contain either the aircon or heating variable, or their interactions with energy poverty, which is why the sample size is slightly higher than that of columns 1, 3, and 4.

A country's level of income inequality seems to be a huge predictor of energy poverty prevalence. “ ”

Additionally, one can see that energy poverty levels are by far the highest in previously socialist states such as Bulgaria, Lat- via, and Lithuania. This can be attributed to the legacies of the centrally planned economy, including poor thermal insulation of the housing stock and historically low energy prices (Fig. 1; Bouzarovski & Herrero, 2017). When these countries transitioned to a market economy in the 1990s, energy tar- iffs increased without accompanying social welfare and energy-efficiency mechanisms, which further exacerbated the problem (Bouzarovski & Herrero, 2017).

Table 3 presents the correlation matrix for central macroeconomic indicators and energy poverty. As expected, GDP per capita is highly inversely related to both energy poverty and unemployment, meaning that richer Member States tend to have lower rates of both unemployment and energy poverty-related issues. Also, richer societies tend to have a more equal distribution of income, with a higher share of GDP going to the bottom 50% of the population. Subsequently, a country’s level of income inequality seems to be a huge predictor of energy poverty prevalence — the two are highly inversely related with a correlation coefficient of -0.511.

In plotting average yearly unemployment rates and energy poverty in 2004– 2019 (Fig. 3), there is also strong evidence for unemployment as a main driver of energy poverty. In line with the literature, the spike in unemployment following the 2008/9 economic recession drastically increased energy poverty prevalence in Europe, especially in Portugal, Italy, Ireland, Greece, and Spain (the PIIGS countries; Halkos & Gkampoura, 2021). The gradual drop in unemployment rate after peak- ing at over 11% in 2013 is accompanied by a similar drop in energy poverty rates, suggesting that the two go hand-in-hand. However, it seems that after the dramatic spike in energy poverty rate from 6% in 2004 to 9% in 2005, energy poverty rate did not decrease along with the unemployment rate in the years preceding the recession, suggesting that other factors might be causing energy poverty to be sticky.

III. Empirical Model I used a country-level approach and regressed the energy poverty index on cooling or heating degree days, macroeconomic factors, and other relevant controls. The general model was:

(2) yst = β0 + β1x(t-1)s + β2z2007s + β3x(t-1)z2007s +

Mst + Hst + βs + βt + βst The dependent variable, yst, denotes the energy poverty index as calculated by (1) in Member State s and year t. In some specifications, I also broke down the index into its component parts and used either inability to keep warm or arrears on utility bills as the dependent variable. x(t-1)s is the independent variable of interest, either HDD or CDD. I took degree days data from the year before under the assumption that respondents are thinking of their ability to pay bills or comfort experienced in the months leading to the survey, which could span the previous year. z2007j is either the fraction of the population with heating when the independent variable is HDD or the fraction of the population with air conditioning when the independent variable is CDD. Similarly, xt-1z2007s is the interaction term between either HDD and heating or CDD and air conditioning. Mst includes a vector of macroeconomic controls, including the bottom 50% share of total national income (income inequality), real GDP per capita, and unemployment rate. Hst is a vector of housing characteristics, including dwelling type and urbanisation level. The vectors γs and νt are country and year fixed effects, respectively. The former controls for unobservable variables that vary across countries but not over time, such as national energy resources and welfare policies, while the latter controls for unobservable variables that vary across time but not countries, such as oil shocks and global recessions.

Some specifications also include country-specific linear time trends, which allow trends over time to differ across countries. This is owing to the huge variation in development stage and economic and political climate across different Member States. For instance, we might expect a steeper decline in those unable to keep their houses warm for poorer Member States compared to richer ones because there is more potential for technological progress in poorer countries.

As I discuss later, not all of these controls are included in each specification. My preferred specification includes both country and year fixed effects but not time trends. This is because time trends absorb too much of the variation in the dependent variables, leading to imprecise estimates of the coefficients. For all of my models, I used robust standard errors that are clustered by country in order to eliminate the possibility of heteroscedasticity, and I assigned weights to countries based on their total population.

IV. Results The main results for HDD and CDD on energy poverty are presented in Tables 4 and 5, respectively. I provide four specifications to highlight the role played by the control variables and fixed effects. In the first column, neither interactions nor fixed effects are included in the regressions. The second column adds country fixed effects, and the third column has both country and year effects. The last column adds country-specific linear time trends.

The results show that the number of HDD is not statistically associated with energy poverty but that the number of CDD is consistently positively associated with energy poverty. The CDD coefficients are statistically significant below the 5% level in every specification presented in Table 5, except for specification 2. In my preferred specification, which includes both country and year effects (column 3), the results imply that for every 100 °C sum increase in CDD per year (which has a range of 0 to 812 °C/yr), mean energy poverty is expected to increase by an estimated 1.383%, all other factors held constant. This result is statistically significant at the 1% level.

Additionally, the increasing importance of household air conditioning is high- lighted in Table 5. In column 1, the aircon coefficient implies that a 1% increase in the share of the population with air conditioning leads to an estimated 0.132% reduction in energy poverty incidence. Moreover, the interaction term between CDD and aircon in column 3 suggests that for any given number of CDD, a 1% increase in household air conditioning reduces energy poverty by a further 0.056%. Both results are statistically significant at the 1% level. However, the results for heating seem to be less robust. Table 4 predicts that a 1% increase in the share of population with heating reduces energy poverty by 0.103% (column 1), but once fixed effects are added, the interaction term between HDD and heating is no longer significant (column 3).

As expected, controlling for country and year effects has a large impact on estimated degree day effects. These fixed effects control for unobserved differences across the Member States and across time. Without these controls, the estimated climate effect is biased upward; the HDD coefficients drop from positive to negative (albeit insignificantly), and the CDD coefficient drops from 2.414 (column 1) to 1.383 when both fixed effects are included (column 3). However, when country-specific time trends are added (column 4), the coefficients become imprecise, as they absorb too much of the variation in the dependent variable, which is reinforced by the extremely high adjusted R-squared value of 0.982 in both tables. With regard to the macroeconomic control variables, the results show that many of them are significantly associated with energy poverty (column 1) but have insignificant effects once fixed effects are added (column 3). Nevertheless, three variables in particular stand out: household gas prices and the unemployment rate are consistently positively associated with energy poverty, especially for CDD, and GDP per capita is significantly negatively associated with energy poverty.

The main results using the preferred specification (both country and time fixed effects but no linear time trends) are presented in Table 6. I also include the results when the composite energy poverty index is broken down into its components, with inability to keep warm (column 1) and arrears on utility bills (columns 2 and 3) as the dependent variables, respectively. The regression tables showing the results of the four different specifications for warm and arrears can be found in Tables 4, 5, and 6 in the Appendix.

The results in Table 6 are mostly robust across the three dependent variables. The exception is the negative association between HDD and both the inability to keep warm and arrears on utility bills (columns 1 and 2), which is significant at the 10% level. This seems counterintuitive, since an increase in the number of cold days should make it harder to stay warm, not easier. Additionally, the interaction term between HDD and heating is positively associated with both warm and arrears and is significant at the 5% level. Again, this is counterintuitive, as it suggests that conditioning on HDD, an increase in the share of households with access to heating actually increases their difficulty of keeping warm and paying their utility bills on time. It is possible that the Mediterranean Paradox is behind some of these counterintuitive estimates, but it is also likely that some important explanatory variables are missing from the model and are therefore limiting our ability to see the full picture.

The fact that the presence of damp, leakage, or rot is significantly associated with warm and arrears only when HDD, and not CDD, is concerned highlights the importance of the energy efficiency of the home during the cold winter months. Additionally, the larger association with warm than with arrears (where

“Households with inefficient, poorly insulated homes find it especially difficult to stay warm, even if they are able to afford heating, since cold air finds its way into the home regardless.” a 1% increase in the presence of housing problems is predicted to increase the share of households unable to keep warm by 0.274% compared to only 0.0458% for the share of households with arrears on utility bills) implies that households with inefficient, poorly insulated homes find it especially difficult to stay warm, even if they are able to afford heating, since cold air finds its way into the home regardless.

V. Conclusion This paper has sought to investigate the link between the climate crisis and energy poverty in the EU against a backdrop of existing regional spatial inequalities and the ongoing energy transition. My theoretical approach has identified some of the key dimensions that link climate change and energy poverty: the need to position increasing average temperatures and its effect on overall energy poverty within the context of existing patterns of uneven geographic and economic conditions, while keeping in mind the important role that renewable energy policies play in exacerbating existing or creating new disparities. The empirical model has involved regressing degree-days temperature data on a multidimensional energy poverty indicator and a vector of controls over time and states to (1) uncover the aggre- gate effect of a warming climate on energy poverty incidence and (2) understand the complex macro-scale spatial patterns of energy poverty and how they relate to wider disparities within the EU.

In relation to the first aim of the study, a cross-country and time series analysis of Eurostat data showed that higher average temperatures and more frequent heat waves have increased the overall share of energy-poor households across all EU Member States and that this trend will likely continue in the absence of targeted policy intervention.

Addressing the second aim of the study, the results support the findings of previous studies by showing that there is a clear regional and economic division between the Northern and Southern EU countries that is similarly reflected in terms of an energy divide. In the colder but well-off North, income inequality and unemployment rates are lower, a higher percentage of the population have access to heating and air conditioning, and as a result, energy poverty rates are much lower. On the other hand, the warmer but poorer South experiences a much higher rate of energy poverty and population percentage that is unable to keep warm in the winter; this is in part due to the legacies of socialism, the 2008/9 economic recession, and the low efficiency and quality of the housing stock.

The results do not indicate that the ongoing energy transition is having any

“

”

There is a need for greater general awareness of the phenomenon of energy poverty at both the national and international levels, as well as recognition of the importance of implementing policies that directly address energy poverty in the context of a changing climate.

significant effect on energy poverty levels in the EU as a whole, but there is reason to suggest that they have or will have important impacts on regional inequalities for individual Member States, given the speed and direction in which the EU is moving in this arena. This highlights a need for more research into how specific renewable energy policies and projects are impacting energy poverty and overall welfare levels in individual EU countries. This also shows a general necessity to acknowledge the energy poverty risks associated with a long-term transition towards a decarbonised future and the necessary steps needed to overcome them.

Nevertheless, this paper serves as a starting point in examining the relationship between climate change and energy poverty at the regional level. Further analysis could be done in other contexts, especially those in the global South that will be hardest hit by climate change, to inform a wider range of policy and development projects. To this end, there is a need for greater general awareness of the phenomenon of energy poverty at both the national and international levels, as well as recognition of the importance of implementing policies that directly address energy poverty in the context of a changing climate. ◆
