title: Transcending the Stage: Exploring the Applicability of an Actor’s Training to Other Vocations and Our Everyday Lives
abstract: The following paper seeks to explore and discover how the tools and resources that actors gain throughout their training are applicable to vocations outside of just performing and in the process of everyday life. By conducting interviews with current Northwestern students, current and former Northwestern acting professors, as well as Northwestern alumni who are at the pinnacle of their fields in both the entertainment industry and professions outside of this particular industry, I use anecdotes and qualitative applications to dive into the substance, and not just the form, of acting — in short, this paper will share how techniques and skills related to the entertainment industry are crucial to more than just the actor. Furthermore, I argue that being an actor is akin to being a scientist and that the process an actor undergoes in preparing to play a role is a process one should try to implement in their own walk of life.
text:
Transcending the Stage: Exploring the Applicability of an Actor’s Training to Other Vocations and Our Everyday Lives by Nolan Fizoires Robinson II

Department of Theatre Faculty Adviser: Prof. Gail Shapiro, MFA

Abstract The following paper seeks to explore and discover how the tools and resources that actors gain throughout their training are applicable to vocations outside of just performing and in the process of everyday life. By conducting interviews with current Northwestern students, current and former Northwestern acting professors, as well as Northwestern alumni who are at the pinnacle of their fields in both the entertainment industry and professions outside of this particular industry, I use anecdotes and qualitative applications to dive into the substance, and not just the form, of acting — in short, this paper will share how techniques and skills related to the entertainment industry are crucial to more than just the actor. Furthermore, I argue that being an actor is akin to being a scientist and that the process an actor undergoes in preparing to play a role is a process one should try to implement in their own walk of life.

I. Introduction

“I like to say that if medical professionals get it right, we live longer and healthier lives. If economists get it right, we enjoy higher material standards of living. But without the arts — literature, dance, music, the visual arts, cinema, etc. — life loses its meaning. The arts inspire us, inform us, and help us understand differences. Nothing else comes close.”

— Northwestern University President Morton O. Schapiro

The impetus of this project began to grow from several places throughout my time at Northwestern University, the first of which was a class I registered for in the winter of my junior year: “Economics and the Humanities: Understanding Choice in the Past, Present, and Future.” The course — offered in the College of Arts and Sciences and taught by Morton O. Schapiro, American economist and University President, and Gary Saul Morson, American literary critic and internationally renowned scholar of Slavic studies — required its students to engage in conversations among various disciplines.

Throughout the quarter, I grew in the knowledge that in order to understand the world as I wish to and to connect with those around me, I must be willing to engage in conversations that encourage me to switch points of view and examine questions in perspectives and disciplines different from my own. This prospect fas- cinated me, as it pertained to my studies as an actor. I related this understanding of the world and attitude towards interactions to an essay written by Yale Professor Elinor Fuchs, “EF’s Visit to a Small Planet: Some Questions to Ask a Play,” that provides actors with the tools to analyze and understand the world of a play when discovering it for the first time, as well as what the play itself demands of the actor. She states:

The play asks us to focus upon a total awareness, to bring our attention and curiosity without the censorship of selective interpretation, “good taste,” or “correct form.” Before making judgments, we must ask questions. This is the deepest meaning of the idea, often repeated but little understood, that the study of art shows us how to live.1

This idea of “selective interpretation,” as Fuchs shares, can be akin to the refusal to integrate ideas other than our own in coming to the conclusions that we do in argu- ments — that, essentially, no other world exists but the one we have grown accus- tomed to through our studies, upbringing, and ways of living. The scholarship taken from my humanities class shares the same logic as that of Fuchs’: through breaking out of uncertainty, we cannot focus solely on what we already know, as this keeps us from asking questions — questions that “are intended to light up some of the dark matter in dramatic worlds,” or the worlds in which we live every day.2

As acting is a very specialized path, its power in connecting human beings to the world, to each other, and to their own humanity is seldom understood by those who are not in the craft and sometimes even forgotten by those who have received training, like me. Given this understanding, I followed my impulse to dive deeper into what an acting education truly teaches. The interviews integrated into this paper are conversations I have had with actors, writers, producers, doctors, managers,

1 Fuchs, EF’s Visit to a Small Planet (Some Questions to Ask a Play). 2 Ibid.

financial advisors, etc., who have all studied or taught acting at Northwestern University and discovered how their training has appeared throughout their daily lives. I hope to be in constant communication with the reader through the material that follows, and I hope readers will be able to discover themselves within this work and within these people.

II. Exploring What Acting Is

“We believe to study theatre is to seek to understand what it means to be human.”

— Lookingglass Theatre Founding Ensemble Member and Northwestern Head of Acting David Catlin

The process I developed in conducting this research first required me to step outside of what I already know about the art of acting. As this paper analyzes the tools of an actor, what they know, and how this work and knowledge continue to be present even outside of acting, I began to try to unlearn this craft as if I were discovering it for the first time. I desired for anyone reading this to do the same — to discover, or rediscover, the power and magic behind what acting is. With this, it became crucial that I presented this work for both the seasoned actor and one who has no idea what it is that actors actually do and learn, other than performing and how to perform. So, in examining the factors that propelled me into wanting to pursue acting professionally, the starting point of this thesis naturally gravitated towards acting teachers themselves and what they believe they are teaching their students from the study of acting.

The role of an acting teacher is to, obviously, teach acting. However, just as a mathematics professor strives to teach their students how to analyze the mathematical complexities that surround human beings in everyday life or how political science does more than just encourage students to understand politics and explains through analytical frameworks why political actions are conducted, acting, too, contains more than what many may believe it does. One of the teachers to whom I had the pleasure of speaking is an Emeritus Professor of Acting at Northwestern University, David Downs. Downs was an acting professor from 1973 to 2000 and, during his tenure, taught actors who would go on to become world-renowned artists, including David Schwimmer, Greg Berlanti, Harry Lennix, and Dennis O’Hare. To begin our conversation, I asked him to break down what his job was as an acting teacher, as this profession can have several meanings attached to it. He explained that there was always an impulse in him to be an acting teacher. The paths that “[spun] around in his life” included being an actor and writer, but teaching was the thing that he wanted to do the most. He credited Alvina Krause, former Northwestern University acting professor and the driving force behind the acting sequence still continued today at the university, for contributing to that choice:

“

”

“As acting is a very specialized path, its power in connecting human beings to the world, to each other, and to their own humanity is seldom understood by those who are not in the craft and sometimes even forgotten by those who have received training.”

I met [Alvina Krause] during her career in the 30s, 40s, and 50s, and early 60s. And suddenly, what she believed that acting was, and theater was, hit my heart deeper than anything else that I had done, even all the acting experiences that I’d had. And that’s what I wanted to teach and the reason why was just what you’ve articulated: that beyond the skills that are needed for a certain kind of profession, there was something that the art of theater and the art of acting dealt with [and] developed in people that was profoundly about what it means to be a human being in a culture, in a society. And teaching that in a liberal arts education environment, made great sense. I wouldn’t have wanted to teach in a professional studio in the city, where what acting is is much more specific than what I just described.3

An aspect of training that all actors experience is approaching the question “who am I?” In the process of being able to accurately portray the life of another person in a piece, it is of the utmost importance to know, to the greatest depths, who this person is. “Who am I?” encompasses all of the questions that we ask ourselves every day: who am I? How do I see myself? How does the world see me? How does my family see me? What do I want? How do I get it? How do I feel if I do or do not get it? The processes we use in discovering who we are as individuals are no different from the processes that trained actors use in discovering who they are within the worlds they inhabit. Acting, in a way, is a mode in which those who practice it are able to understand a person made real through the words of a playwright. While we maneuver through this process every single day of our lives, in one of my conversations with Tom Swift, an alumnus, it was fascinating to see just how the “who am I?” comes up in practice and how he uses it in his daily work life.

Swift is a graduate of Northwestern University’s School of Speech,4 where he earned a Bachelor of Science degree in theatre. He completed his studies under the instruction of David Downs. He is the co-founder of the Financial Avengers, a financial planning and investment management firm based in Oakland, CA, and has worked in this position for over 20 years. As of today, the Financial Avengers manage over $300 million in client assets. In our email interaction before our interview, Swift mentioned that without his training and background in acting, he would not have succeeded and that all he ever does and will ever do is framed by his acting degree and theatre education. This relates to Downs’ philosophy stated earlier about instilling acting into his students’ lives so that it may become a central part of who they are as educated human beings. Swift said this in relation to Downs’ point:

The work that we do with clients is literally based entirely on acting. So when we do financial planning, everyone thinks, “Oh it’s, you know, all this detailed shit,” and it is — I mean … you know, there’s mathematics and economics, and economics is incredibly fascinating and the numbers don’t lie. But it’s, you know, only ever about how people operate around money, how people operate around finance, how people operate in the world, how people operate relative to their relationship, how people operate based

3 Downs, David Downs Conversation. 4 Northwestern University’s current School of Communication was named the School of Speech from 1921 to 2002. A significant portion of the people I have spoken with attended or taught at the university before it was renamed. The school was renamed to reflect its ever growing catalog of academics, including: Communication Sciences & Disorders, Digital Media, and Health Communication, for example.

on, you know, what their parents told them they could and couldn’t do, what their parents made them, you know, become. Their fears are steeped in all of those human relationships and if you don’t untangle that, then you’ll never fundamentally create a financial plan that addresses their actual needs.5

Part of what Swift is describing lies in the “who am I?” How people operate around money is akin to how characters operate in the environments of their pieces. Questions such as “why does a character act this way towards their partner?” and “why do they think certain ideas about themselves and about the world?” all relate directly to questions about why a person may act the way that they do around money. The accompanying answers lie in the actors discovering their relationship to all the factors that make up their lives, and Swift’s comment argues that the aforementioned questions are continuously present even outside the art of acting.

III. Words, Subtext & Naturalism

“Death and life are in the power of the tongue,

And those who love it will eat its fruit.” -Proverbs 18:21

Words create the universe of a play — they breathe life. They build the foundations of civilizations and the flow of thoughts from one character to another. These words move the actors through a story and create images for both themselves and the audience to follow. To use this manifestation of power means to create.

With this, it is important to understand the unspoken words that actors are trained to understand in their studies, also known as the subtext. Defined by the Oxford Dictionary, subtext is the “hidden meaning or theme in a piece of writing or conversation.”6 Subtext, as per the definition, is the meaning that lies behind the mask that explicit words inherently put over themselves — they are what someone means to say but decides not to. One of the most prolific writers known for allowing actors the opportunity to dig into the meaning lying behind the words is Anton Chekhov. Throughout his career, Chekhov used a naturalistic view of the world in his writing. In a 2002 piece from The Atlantic, journalist Philip Hensher said this about his writing:

His stories, like life, have no beginnings, middles, or ends; they do not deal in crises and happy endings; they are simply glimpses of ordinary lives in their untidiness and irresolution.7

Having been a practicing physician before he became a writer, and drawing from his scientific training, Chekhov believed early on that literature should show life as it is. As a materialist, he believed that in exploring and creating new artistic worlds, he must employ the “concept of scientific objectivity in all of his writing” in order to “depict life as it actually is.”8

The challenge, though, that Chekhov faced throughout his quest of crafting his writing to depict life as it is — and where we may now cue the actors — came from needing to express life “as it ought to be, while avoiding being overtly judgemental

5 Swift. 6 “Subtext.” 7 Hensher, “Incomparable Naturalism: Only an Artificer of the Highest Skill Could Have Produced so Seamless an Illusion of Reality.” 8 Borny, Interpreting Chekhov.

or polemical.”9 This then encouraged him to integrate subtext in the characters’ speech.

Among the various ideas I discussed with Broadway actress Kate Baldwin, subtext was one of them. A graduate from Northwestern’s School of Speech, Kate Baldwin is a renowned actress noted for her work in musical theatre. Having made her Broadway debut in 2000 with the production of The Full Monty, she was featured in several shows following that, including Big Fish, the 2009 revival of Finian’s Rainbow, and the 2017 revival of Hello, Dolly!, the last two of which garnered her Tony Award nominations.

I asked her, “What have you learned about subtext, and how do you think the knowledge that not everything is seen as face value has shown up in your life?” Baldwin replied:

Hmm, that’s — mm-hmm — yeah.10 I find — I don’t know if you have experienced this too, but I find even with a close close friend, if they’re not an actor, I have to ask them three times how they are to get the truth. The first answer is always, “I’m fine.” Are you, though? You know, I mean like. Actually, a friend of mine talked about a phrase that he heard that was called “COVID good.” “How are you?” “Oh, I’m COVID good.”(laughs) Which is different from just, like, regular good. I mean, just as an observant human, you can see a person — their body can, like, revolt when they lie, you know? So you say, “Hey, how are you?” and they go, “Fine.” And then look to the side and you’re like, “You’re not fine; you just lied and your eyes are going — you’re darting to the left,” you know.11

This technique is all the more fascinating when it comes to discovering how all of these ideas continue to appear within another profession: clinical psychology. I had the privilege of speaking with Nina Uziel-Miller, a School of Speech class of ‘92 graduate who studied under Dawn Mora. Working primarily in private practice, Uziel-Miller currently has offices in Chicago and Evanston, IL. She is a faculty member at Northwestern’s Feinberg Medical School and has, for a number of years, taught a class in which she worked with students in navi- gating the transition to the medical profession, addressing topics like work-life balance and inequities in medicine and helping them understand themselves and their goals as they move into working with patients:12

You know, it reminds me of this incident with a woman and her husband, where she was just carrying on about apples he had bought, you know, and, and I said, “You know, I don’t think we’re talking about the apples. I don’t think it’s the apples that matter,” right? And so, being able to sort of hone in on that and articulate it is probably informed by my work as an actor.13

All of these ideas in regard to subtext connect to the theme of a TEDx Presentation by Ann Woodworth — kindly directed to me by Ms. Baldwin — titled “Acting for Your Life.” In it, Woodworth shares that social science studies indicate that “86% of what we communicate … is non-verbal.”14 She goes on to say that of the 14% remaining, 7% is the tone of voice, and only 7% is content. Just as Uziel-Miller was able to

9 Borny. 10 I wish one could hear the inflection she gave of this line. Read as if the subtext is “Oh boy, do I know how this has shown up in my life.” 11 Baldwin, Kate Baldwin Conversation. 12 As of the COVID-19 pandemic, and as of our interview, this class has been discontinued. Per Uziel-Miller, struggles ensued with figuring out how to conduct the class virtually, but “hopefully it will get replaced with something similar and maybe even better.” 13 Uziel-Miller. 14 Woodworth, “Acting for Your Life: Ann Woodworth at TEDxEducationCity.” deduce that her patient’s story about apples was truly not about apples, this awareness of subtext requires an understanding of what these statistics share. Human beings rarely ever say what they mean directly; what we truly mean lies in how we say it and how we show it — through our actions. Actors are keenly aware of this, for discovering words and how human beings present them are part of what they are trained to know.

IV. Acting as a Science For quite some time, I have related what actors do in their training and performance to what physicists learn in their own studies. In order for the following to make sense, it is necessary to understand that the process of performance and human life is the process of motion and that life is in constant motion: past with the present and the future, one person to another, etc. When a play begins, the plot does not end until the last line, and even then, the piece’s contents are still in constant motion with the audience. Theatre, in this sense, is always moving. Isaac Newton’s third law of motion states that:

For every action (force) in nature, there is an equal and opposite reaction. In other words, if object A exerts a force on object B, then Object B also exerts an equal and opposite force on object A.15

This idea can also be illustrated through a Newton’s cradle, which Northwestern University acting teacher Henry Godinez mentioned he has on his desk because it is the “simplest way to demonstrate what acting is.”16

I cannot remember the specific name of this particular acting game, but it was what allowed me to first discover this idea of Newton’s law of motion in motion. About five or so actors stand on the stage next to each other, spreading from stage left to stage right. The furthest stage left person begins with a slight sound, the tiniest idea of what a laugh could be, and once they find it they turn to the next actor and “pass the laugh” to them. The second actor must

15 “Newton’s Third Law.” 16 Godinez, Henry Godinez Interview. 17 Palermo, “How Does Newton’s Cradle Work?”

“[T]he process of performance and human life is the process of motion. [L]ife is in constant motion: past with the present and the future, one person to another, etc.” “

” then match the same level of “force” being exerted onto them, and once they have successfully emulated this, they then increase that “force” and exert it on the next person, and so on, until this one little bit of a sound explodes into the loudest idea of what a laugh can sound like. This same exercise can be explored through crying as well.

Furthermore, I got to speak about listening with the wonderful Kathryn Hahn. Another Northwestern University alum and world-renowned actress, Hahn has been recognized for her roles in the films We’re the Millers, Step Brothers, Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse, and Bad Moms. She is also known for her television work in Parks and Recreation and the new Disney Plus series WandaVision. When I asked her if she could recall any moments of her life in which the techniques she had learned in her classes have helped her outside of performing, she said that at the top for her would have to be the idea of stillness:

I had always had an impulse. It took me a long time to find stillness on stage and the power of stillness. … I have a very buzzy interior life, and I always felt like I had to be doing something rather than just being, and when I first found the power of just standing on stage and listening, I remember that being a very profound moment. … I feel that when you are authentically listening, onstage, and receiving and listening with all of your whole self, whether it’s on stage or on camera, that’s where the most magic is happening, even if the words are not yours. If you’re listening with your whole self, that’s where the most connection happens. And so, if you’re listening with your whole self, in your real life, you know, that’s where the deep — real deep — connection can happen as well.18

Hahn’s point about connecting with others, being still, and listening with one’s entire being relates to a tool that actors, throughout their training, are expected to understand and grow in: empathy. Per the Oxford dictionary, empathy is “the ability to understand and share the feelings of another.”19 Empathy can only happen through active listening, and listening happens when actors observe Newton’s third law of motion — exerting force on each other, constantly moving and being moved. Uziel-Miller spoke on this crucial idea in acting and how it relates to her profession as a psychologist:

I think to be a really good actor, you need to have the desire and the ability to understand other perspectives, right? You play roles of people that you at face value might not get, they’re not like you, they’re different, and you have to figure out how to play them in a way that is true and honest, and respectful of that person. I think that’s something that I was able to explore as an acting student. And certainly applies to my work. I can feel compassion for a serial killer, which, you know, might be

18 Hahn, Kathryn Hahn Conversation. 19 “Empathy.”

“[T]here is a true science to what acting is. Acting is a process of discovery, research, and observation that can then be repeated.” stretching it a tiny bit, but I’m always interested in like, what is it that made this, you know. Nobody wakes up in the morning thinking, “How can I do bad things and hurt people?”

As illustrated through my conversations, there is a true science to what acting is. Acting is a process of discovery, research, and observation that can then be repeated. No analysis of these ideas has been truer to what science is.

V. Conclusion When speaking to my acting teacher, who also served as my thesis advisor, about this research, she asked me to dig deeper into why I chose this particular subject — why am I exploring these questions and these ideas? From studying under her, I have learned that all actions have intentions, that I had intention behind this action — researching these ideas and writing this thesis — and that I needed to discover more of that. Truth- fully, I chose this topic out of annoyance and anger. Very often, in approaching the world as an artist, I often receive verbal or non-verbal responses of “why acting?” In the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic, I also asked myself this question. There was a part of me that felt selfish in exploring this art when I could be investing my time in what — at that moment — I had thought to be more “important” career paths. Needing to consistently justify to the world and to myself (albeit less frequently) that my studies and training as an actor carried with it just as much merit as other professions made me tired and also made me question, “Why is this profession viewed as it is?”

This thought made me think of Maslow’s hierarchy of needs, pictured below:

This pyramid is a motivational theory in psychology that comprises a five-tier model of human needs in order of their importance to a human being. Basic needs must be met in order to reach the self-fulfillment needs. These basic needs are those close to the bottom of the pyramid: physiological needs, such as food, water, shelter, etc. The self-fulfillment needs are closer to the top, involving the achieving of one’s full potential and including creative needs.

One theory that I have developed throughout this research relates to why some believe the study of acting needs to be justified: it just is not important enough. I argue that society is in a constant state of physiological and safety needs, especially during this pandemic. When one is starv- ing, everything that they do and everything they strive for becomes about finding food. They care about nothing else, and as long as it never truly becomes fulfilled, we never reach the top, where creativity lies. Once we as a society, hopefully after this pandemic, remember the pyramid has five tiers, we can remember that in order to be fulfilled as human beings, all of these needs must be met.

On the other hand, through this project, I found myself doing the very thing that I said I hated doing when explaining to others my career in acting: justifying it. In many ways, this paper was a justification for why acting is important and why it is more than what many think it is. It allows us to observe, to discover, to connect, to

20 McLeod, “Maslow’s Hierarchy of Needs.” feel, to research, to investigate, and to understand. I hope that through this thesis, one will be able to open their mind up to a world they may know nothing about, explore this environment and this walk of life, and try to learn something from it. In the last moments of most of my interviews, I asked if acting can make us better humans.

As one continues on in their daily lives, I hope this project has instilled in them an understanding that there is much to learn from what an actor knows and that it can be found if they find stillness, connect to the world, and observe the environment around them. ◆

title: The Rise of the Female Vernacular: Contemporary Indian Women Authors and the Subversion of the Heteropatriarchal Linguistic Establishment
text:
by Tara Shirvaikar

Department of Comparative Literary Studies

Faculty Adviser: Prof. Laura Brueck, Ph.D. The Rise of the Female Vernacular: Contemporary Indian Women Authors and the Subversion of the Heteropatriarchal Linguistic Establishment

Introduction

In Indian society, the social divides of caste, class, gender, and urban/rural groups fall along the same fault lines as linguistic divides. These linguistic divides largely fall into two categories: the elite and the vernacular. Language — both elite and vernacular — is always actively changing; the manner in which it is wielded defines it as much as the language itself. A primary example of elite language is the authoritative discourse found in places of heteropatriarchal dominance: education, state government, medical facilities, and even traditional marriages and households in India where literature shows agency and identity usually being wrested from the woman. In contrast, those not traditionally given power/authority in society

— lower castes, lower classes, women, and the rural populations — find themselves unable or unwilling to represent themselves with the elite languages and ideologies made available to them. Thus, they are driven to make themselves heard through a vernacular language instead (Gupta et al., 812). Though the vernacular is traditionally thought of as culturally substandard — in large part because any subjectivity not sanctioned by the societal elite is considered illegitimate — it nevertheless has become a way for voices in these margins to make themselves heard (Lemke 5). The vernacular emphasizes the everyday lived and spoken language of the masses and margins; it is “consistently anti-hierarchical and anti-exclusionary”

(Lemke 5). This thesis will further narrow this definition of vernacular to one of politically gendered identity. This gendered vernacular centralizes female subjectivity through the self-expression of embodied experience and the self-affirmation of the politics of womanhood and resistance. Working through a lens of feminist agency, the vernaculars analyzed in this thesis deconstruct and reappropriate the central social concept of female shame.

In English Heart, Hindi Heartland, Rashmi Sadana posits that “literature reflects and represents, but it is also produced and con- sumed under particular social and political conditions” (Sadana 27). Through examining these particular social and political conditions, this thesis will analyze the work of contemporary Indian women writers, all of whom explicitly engage with the gendered politics of language and the overlaps of (and distances between) their vernacular and the elite. We will consider an array of gendered vernaculars: tribal languages translated to Bengali and then to English, Tamil translated to English, Hindi translated to English, and then finally original works in both English and Hindi. All of the authors discussed in this thesis have deconstructed elite linguistic structures in some way — some by repopulating these structures with their own lived experience and others by communicating through an embodied vernacular instead. Through undercutting and mocking the ostensible cultural and sociopolitical authority denoted by elite languages like Sanskrit and English, these authors’ feminized vernacularization1 of the elite language critiques the language’s role in sustaining heteropatriarchal authority and colonial power structures, all while working to subvert these forms of dominance.

Further, Meenakshi Thapan points out that “oppression, in its psychological form, is then an experience of a disjunc- tion between a woman’s body image and the male constructions of it” (Thapan and Nehru Memorial Museum and Library 19). Essentially, female internalizations of the patriarchal constructions of the female body then inform their own understanding of their body, agency, and sexuality. The heteropatriarchal authority is not external but is an oppressive force that actually exerts its power from within the woman through social expectation. In India specifically, the discourse of shame is intricately tied with womanhood and honor; shame is the internalized punishment for transgressing moral codes imposed and policed by the dominant male social, cultural, and political ideology. As such, women are forced to define their identity within these purely male discourses of shame and purity/honor (Viswanath 318). Thus, this thesis locates shame within the framework of heteropatriarchal power and understands that these authors are part of the movement to challenge its political and social existence/validity.

1 The particularity and singularity of these literary texts work to ground this essay in a hyper-contextualized space, thus avoiding any harmful false generalities; as such, the feminine, female experience, woman’s body, or Indian feminisms discussed will always be that in literature.

Trigger warning: The following thesis includes mentions of violence against women, including forced abortion, sexual assault, and rape.

I. Revealing English Linguistic Oppression: “Draupadi” (1981) and “Neela Scarf” (2014) The original story of Draupadi from the Hindu epic The Mahabharata illustrates the type of female representation and patriarchal control that these writers are fighting to subvert. Indian epics and religious texts were partially responsible for the sanskri- tization of norms and cultural values that are a primary source of violence towards women even today. By creating female characters who are forced to uphold realistically impossible standards of purity, devotion, and compliance, violence is perpetrated in multiple ways. First, holding the female body to these heteropatriarchal standards snuffs out any possibility for female subjectivity because now the woman is forced to be the site upon which social and national ideology and politics are carried out. Second, by worshipping women as shakti, or goddess, society is able to justify putting them on a pedestal and then judge and punish them harshly when they fail to meet these standards of perfection. Thus, these works established — and continue to establish — unreasonable social expectations for the female body.

In The Mahabharata, Draupadi2 is forced to marry five brothers by her mother-in-law after a misunderstanding. After one of the brothers stakes everything — including his wealth, power, and finally, Draupadi — in a gambling game to a jeal- ous king and loses, the king demands that all of the brother’s possessions, including Draupadi, appear before him. The king tries to humiliate Draupadi further by publicly disrobing her in the court, but the

Hindu god Krishna responds to Draupadi’s desperate pleas, intervenes, and blesses her with a never-ending sari. Now, no matter how much the king pulls her sari off, Draupadi’s honor is preserved (“The Story of Draupadi”). This story sets the tone for the expectation of the treatment of a female body and character; Draupadi is never given any choice in husband, home, or fate, and as a character, she is given no emotional or sexual subjectivity/desire. Using Draupadi as an introduction to discuss the nexus of elite language, religious and cultural authority and the conventions of appropriate/pure womanhood, Mahasweta Devi reimagines Draupadi through a feminist lens in her story “Draupadi.”

Mahasweta Devi, a prominent Bengali author and tribal activist, wrote “Draupadi” originally in Bengali and a tribal dialect (Swaminathan). Later translated to English with a foreword written by Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak, “Draupadi” is situated against the Naxalite movement, the Bangladesh Liberation War in 1971, and the Hindu epic The Mahabharata. Written in the style of a military report about the ap- prehension of tribal rebels, the short story is about Draupadi (Dopdi) Mehjen, a fight- er who, along with her erstwhile husband Dulna, murders the wealthy landlord in the area to gain access to and democratize the well water during a seasonal drought. She is then apprehended by Officer Senanayak who demands that she be raped by his officers so he can break her resistive silence and find out more information about the rebel uprisings that the military is there to quell.

Dopdi Mehjen brings English closer to a lived language, not just a language of colonial and state domination. When Draupadi is captured and raped by multiple

By refusing the narrative of shame placed upon women’s bodies, Dopdi retools the language of rape, refusing the silence that often excuses that violent behavior, and as an ultimate subversion of power, she refuses to cover herself in the clothes they give her.

Dopdi finally goes to meet Officer Senanayak, unclothed, and Senanayak’s theoretical knowledge of the tribals col- lides with the reality of a wounded tribal woman, turning the tables, and leaving him afraid and ashamed:

The object of your search, Dopdi Mejhen. You asked them to make me up, don’t you want to see how they made me? Draupadi wipes the blood on her palm and says in a voice that is as terrifying, sky splitting, and sharp as her ululation, “What’s the use of clothes? This is the most powerful moment in the story where Dopdi has the last word, and Officer Senanayak is reduced to silence. Dopdi refuses to be shamed into being dominated by masculine subjectivity and instead asserts her own. She places blame on Senanayak and mocks him by referring to herself as “the object of [his] search.” The italicization and repetition of “counter” foregrounds Dopdi’s vernacularization of the word officially used by the army, “encounter.” A technical, passive term that obscures the actual violence that the army does to bodies, “encounter” is an example of exactly the way in which English is used to dominate a subjugated population through, in this instance, rape or sexual assault. Dopdi actively challenges this, and then by mirroring his violence with her body, she reverses the semiotics of shame and thrusts it back into the face of Senanayak. She refuses to be covered by that language and instead names the violence inscribed on her body, her land, and her people; she turns the verb from passive to active. “Draupadi” draws attention to the feminine vernacular of Dopdi and contrasts it with the masculine violence of English. Initially, the reader sees the officer’s desire to dominate or conquer the subaltern by dominating her linguistic meaning, and the story ends with Dopdi’s

By creating female characters who are forced to uphold realistically impossible standards of purity, devotion and compliance, violence is perpetrated in multiple ways. “

” refusal to succumb to violence at both a bodily level (indicated by her refusal to cover up) and a linguistic level (by sub- verting “encounter” with “counter”). Though she is unclothed in a camp of men, she subverts the physicality of her body from weakness and vulnerability to power by calling into question the masculinity and humanity of Senanayak’s actions and making him come face to face — literally — with his actions and the consequences of his theory of “knowledge” dominance through her appropriation of English. Describing her presence and power as “terrifying, sky splitting, and sharp as her ululation,” Devi is once more calling into mind the tribal connection to land and tight community as well as reminding the reader that the female power and naturalistic vernacular upon which Dopdi draws comes from there. Dopdi daring Senanayak to “counter” her is to dare him to counter all of those reserves of power and is her taking his agency into her own self. He is unable to even question her presence and assert his power because she is reappropriating his English as her vernacular and recreating her body as a space for feminine resistance by using it to assert her socio-political subjectivity. Thus, the link between the vernacularization of language and a woman’s embodied experience is made clear: she refuses both with her words and with her body to submit to the violent appropriation that both the English language and a rape/ assault demand from her, and her refusal and reimagination of that conventional script causes fear.

Whereas English plays an active, mil- itaristic role in “Draupadi” to perpetuate physical violence, the medicalized English in the Hindi-language short story “Neela Scarf” highlights a different form of physical and emotional violence grounded in female isolation. Applauded for its unfiltered look into the female mind, “Neela Scarf” by Anu Singh Chaudhary is a collection of short stories published in 2014 that depicts female narratives across different classes and geographies in India (Fazili). The eponymous- ly-named short story is centered around the protagonist’s refusal to submit to the formalized heteropatriarchal violence and clinical isolation that English represents, so she revolts by only communicating through her embodied experiences. The story is centered around a newly married couple, Shambhavi and Amitesh, and the breakdown of their trust in each other and eventually their relationship. Three months into their marriage, Shambhavi gets pregnant, and Amitesh, claiming that he is not ready, forces her to get an abortion even though she wants to keep the unborn baby. After the abortion procedure, Shambhavi retreats from the marriage both mentally and emotionally. The second time she gets pregnant three years later, Amitesh wants to keep it, but there are pregnancy complications because of the previous abortion, and she must un- dergo another abortive procedure and loses her fallopian tubes in the process. After she recovers, she decides she needs a break from her strained, barely standing marriage and pursues an opportunity for a fellowship abroad. The story ends with Shambhavi not knowing whether she will return.

Although no words are written in Roman script, there are many English words integrated into the Hindi prose in Devanagari script. Categorized by frequency, English medical and physical language is the most common, followed by the language of money and business,3 and then the language of technology and departure.4 Since the medical language is the most common, this thesis will focus on analyzing that, starting with how both Amitesh and Shambhavi refer to the abortion. It is clear that one is able to note a greater level of comfort and intimacy denoted here through the use of Hindi versus English. Whenever Amitesh refers to abortion, he calls it an “अबॉर्शन” (the English word “abortion” written in Devanagari), while Shambhavi refers to it as “उसके विदा हो जाने की दुआ माँगे” (praying for its departure;5 Choudhary 107). When Amitesh uses “abortion” in English, he distances himself from the child and any emotional complications that would be associated with its loss. The constitution of the fetus’s body is negated; Amitesh’s dismissal of the baby’s body through the medicalized language becomes a “key locus for … [his] exercise of power” (Berg and Bowker 533).

However, in Shambhavi’s vernacular construction, she is already giving the child some subjectivity by wondering whether it will take some action (in this case, depart).

The third-person descriptions of her visits to the hospital are saturated with clinical English words6 such as “pregnancy kit,” “bleeding,” “ultrasound,” and “sanitary napkin” (Choudhary). Further, the diagnosis of Shambavi’s Obsessive Compulsive Disorder (OCD) is again indicative of the cold, medical Western vocabulary of scientific diagnosis and clinical procedure. This clinical English disavows the embodied experience she is going through; no thought is given to offering emotional, personal support for having gone through an abortion or for living life with OCD. Instead, in a form of epistemic violence, her own life is articulated to her in a foreign, formalized English.7 She is categorized and “configured” with English words of procedure and diagnosis (Berg and Bowker 514). Once her mental and physical “disorder[s]” are named, she is cast aside by both her husband and Western medical procedure.

Then, when she does not behave as her husband expects and begins retreating from the marriage because of the forced abortion, Amitesh uses English words

Describing Shambhavi, he says, “Formal. Curt. Ceremonious. Si- lent. Amitesh did not want to believe it”8 (Chaudhary 104). The concept of negative space plays a large role in showcasing the growing distance between the two people and also the helplessness that Shambhavi later becomes ashamed of. The auditory manifestation of this negative space is the silence present in their relationship, the physical manifestation of the space is her empty womb, and emotionally, it represents the lack of space she is allowed to take up in her and Amitesh’s marriage and home. Notably, the only way in which she is able to escape her feeling of helplessness and betrayal to her child is by leaving the space that Amitesh occupies, and she drives this point home by leaving the blue scarf she bought to impress him on one of their first dates back in the airport when she departs. She no longer has any need for her own body and subjectivity to be validated — and governed — by the specter of heteronormativity, embodied ignorance, and apathy.

However, instead of accepting the de- humanization and isolation that follows the procedural dialects of English, she rejects this language and thus refuses to obfuscate her unborn child through the medicalized English language. Instead, Shambhavi’s articulation of her state of mind and heart is through a specific discourse of the body. When she does speak or emote, it is either through embodied emotion (for example, her teary eyes) or through vernacular language that calls into being the body of her absent baby. Most of Shambhavi’s dialogue is assumed to happen off the page or is made up of curt sentences traded with Amitesh. However, here she is given the opportunity to verbalize the baby’s life into the world for the first time. Shambhavi’s longest dialogue by far is with her doctor, who tells her she is pregnant. She replies, “I know. And I also know that by this time, the heart of the child must have started to form, and the brain as well. I know that her eyelashes must have started forming, and she may too have a twist in both elbows”9 (Chaudhary 108). By listing its body parts, she characterizes the physical space and shape the baby inhabits in her womb and also the negative space that will be left when it is gone. Unlike Amitesh, who wishes to remain clinically abstracted and detached from the fetus, Shambhavi refuses to use the word “abortion” throughout the whole story. She only ever asks forgiveness from the unborn child and prays that it stays well after it “departs.” For everyone else, focusing on the humanness of the unborn body is a problem, but she insists on verbalizing it and their connection into reality.

II. Rejecting Sanskritized Shame: “Mitro Marjani” (1967) and “When I Hit You: Or, A Portrait of the Writer as a Young Wife” (2017) Supported by culturally and religiously fundamental stories such as “Draupadi,” the notion of the ideal woman as chaste, pure of body and mind, and loyal to the patriarch became the popular one. Even in contemporary literature, we see an expectation of the woman to behave this way, as well as a justification of violence towards the woman if she does not. The characterization of Mi-

8 “फ़ॉर्मल। कर्ट। औपचारिक। ख़ामोश। अमितेश मानना नहीं चाहता था।” 9 “जानती हूँ। और ये भी जानती हूँ कि इस वक़्त तक बच्चे का दिल भी बनने लगा होगा, दिमाग़ भी। जानती हूँ कि उसकी पलकें बनने लगी होंगी, दोनों कुहनियों में अबतक मोड़ भी आ गया होगा शायद।” tro in “Mitro Marjani” allows the reader to explore shame as a social discourse as well as its deconstruction by Mitro both in her articulation of her body and in her physical uncovering of it. Building upon Mitro’s exploration of her femininity, Meena Kandasamy’s “When I Hit You: Or, A Portrait of the Writer as a Young Wife” further explores the gendered language of sexuality through the protagonist’s radical rejection of her husband’s violent representation of female sexuality.

In 1967, Krishna Sobti — one of the leading female Hindi authors of the twentieth century — wrote “Mitro Marjani,” arguably her most famous work. In it, she depicts a family drama centered on the defiant daughter-in-law of a middle-class Punjabi family. The middle daughter-in- law, Sumitravanti (whose nickname is Mitro), is the most outspoken of all the daughters-in-law, constantly facing threats of violence from Sardarilal (her husband), harsh reprimands from Dhanvanti (the matriarch), and scorn from Suhag (the first daughter-in-law) for her improper behavior. The most controversial aspect of “Mitro Marjani” is the fact that the dialogue is imbued with such potent female subjectivity. At various points in the novella, Mitro speaks freely about her sexual desire and her body. After a family argument about Mitro’s behavior, she speaks to the first daughter-in-law, Suhag, mocking her husband: “Banwari [the eldest son, Suhag’s husband] says — Mitro, your body is all honey, pure honey! I tell the rascal — in this milk and honey of mine, there writhe the serpents of your own desires!”10 (Sobti trans. Yadav 17). Then after taking all of her clothes off, Mitro asks Suhag, “‘Tell me the truth, Jethani, does any other woman have breasts like these?’ Rage blazed through Suhag”11 (Sobti trans. Yadav 18). First, it is pointedly cruel of Mitro to talk about her sexual power over Suhag’s husband with Suhag. With Suhag representing the “ideal” daughter-in-law, Mitro posits herself as superior to Suhag and thus positions herself above the expectations of the household. Through the repetition of “honey,” the reader gets the sense that Mitro is reveling in her own body. Mitro is intimately aware of her body, of the physical space it takes up, and of its powerful capabilities as a sexed body; she dismisses Suhag’s normativity as simple hypocrisy.

Even while Mitro is unapologetically cele- brating the female body, she still emphasizes that the male eye is more sinful than the female body. In recognizing that and thus taking power away from the male gaze, she begins to reassert her own subjectivity. By discussing her body parts, bodily

“

Mitro is empowering herself because she is creating a space where she does not have to suppress her subjectivity and submit to sanskritized notions of purity and honor.

processes such as menstruation, and sexual innuendos, Mitro reclaims the female body for herself. She does not let the family — or any other authority — dictate what she wears, how she acts, and what she says. By not suppressing these thoughts and by verbalizing this body-centric, sexualized discourse, Mitro is empowering herself because she is creating a space where she does not have to suppress her subjectivity and submit to sanskritized notions of purity and honor.

One of the most remarkable parts of Sobti’s novella is how she constructs the clash between the patriarchal gaze and Mitro’s sexuality. In the novella, Mitro not only lays claim to her own body but also turns an accusatory eye towards Sardarilal’s body and sexuality. Her deliberate and continual provocations of Sardarilal spring from her unfulfilled sexuality. She says, “The dullard! Had [he] any manhood, [he] would have either licked me all over with relish or torn me apart like a lion” (Sobti trans. Yadav 16-7). Sobti problematizes the phallocentric view of sexuality by showing Mitro taking control of the sexual dynamic between the two; though her takeover is steeped in stereotypical images of manhood, hypermasculinity, and male sexuality, she nonetheless is able to turn a reverse gaze to Sardarilal and his supposed authority over her body. He, in turn, is thrown off guard because the sex is not on his terms. In response, Sardarilal becomes physically abusive whenever Mitro misbehaves. This violence is another manifestation of his own male insecurity due to Mitro now controlling the narrative and discourse of shame within the novel, as well as his inability to verbalize his problem with her objectification of him (Hoque). Incredibly, Mitro is able to dominate the subjectivity within their relationship through her embodied language and fully reappropriate her body through language of desire.

Written exactly half a century after “Mitro Marjani,” Meena Kandasamy’s English novel “When I Hit You: Or, a Portrait of the Writer as a Young Wife” also reveals the dynamics of a heteropatriarchal household. Similar to Mitro, this unnamed protagonist finds power in the verbaliza- tion of her body and subjectivity, with one key difference being that in Kandasamy’s novel, the protagonist’s husband uses that same female sexuality to abuse and shame her in a far more violent and explicit way than Mitro’s husband ever does. Set during the first couple of months of an increasingly manipulative and abusive marriage, the unnamed female protagonist details the burgeoning emotional, physical, and sexual violence she faces. Although the protagonist falls in love with a passionate Marxist professor in a whirlwind romance, she quickly realizes after their marriage how abusive and controlling he really is. Initially forcing her to give him her email and social media passwords, he eventually controls her internet time, clothing, job prospects, phone time with family, and every single other aspect of her life until the only respite she has left is her writing.

As the relationship gets increasingly violent, the protagonist’s husband uses specifically female sexed language to harm her because he feels threatened. Female sexuality has a negative, insatiable, and dangerous connotation because, like other independent female functions (i.e., menstruation, childbirth), it cannot be controlled by the man. Thus, it provides a significant threat to the level of control the husband wants to have over the protagonist (Viswanath 315). In an effort to “control” her, he constantly shames her for being a dirty, sexually loose woman. After getting mad that his provocations are no longer garnering a reaction from her, he rapes her so she can “prove it to [him] that [she is] not thinking of another man.” Over her screams, he continues, “You are a whore. This is what whores do. … How many men took you from behind? How many? … Fucking cheap whore” (Kandasamy, When I Hit You 102). In the whole passage, “bitch” is repeated twice, “whore” is repeated seven times, and “cunt” three times. The sheer onslaught of slurs that are meant to demolish the female spirit and to disrespect and violate the female body is significant. The husband twists the gendered language of women’s bodies in order to inflict pain and bring shame to his wife. The narrator later writes:

The coarseness of my husband’s insults makes me cringe. I’m ashamed that language allows a man to insult a woman in an infinite number of ways. … Every part of my body is a word spat out in disgust. My cunt, sequestered and quarantined, is nothing but a spittoon for his insults. Once, this language … was a secret place of pleasure (Kandasamy, When I Hit You 106).

Kandasamy reveals language to be gendered, steeped in heteropatriarchal ideology, and predetermined towards favoring the man. The narrator recalls parts of her body as if she is dismembered but also to preserve them by verbalizing them. The final body part — the cunt — is forced into submission, as if a wild animal, to take whatever the man chooses to throw at it. The image of a “spittoon” used in the quote is exacting here: the female body is dismembered and then, in turn, made into the passive receptacle for those very body parts as they are turned into insults that are hurled back at the woman.

However, the protagonist in

Kandasamy’s “When I Hit You: Or, A Portrait of the Writer as a Young Wife” is able to further reappropriate English as her own vernacular. Since the protagonist is an author by trade, this novel also discusses her shifting relationship with English, Tamil, language in general, and writing as a form of resistance and self-preservation. While an authoritative abuse of English (emerging from colonialism) is one form of perpetuated heteropatriarchal violence against women, another far older form is using the cultural discourse of female ownership under the guise of a familial bond. Where before, the protagonist was violat- ed physically by her husband and by English, she now uses English as a vernacular form of self-expression and preservation. As her husband slowly erases all semblance of autonomy from her life, including the ability to write without incurring violence, the protagonist starts writing these letters to imaginary lovers and herself as a form of private rebellion: “Each of my letters, I de- lete after I have finished typing them. Every line I have written to you is a thought- crime, a crime that does not leave a trail of evidence, a crime that is not even a crime” (Kandasamy, When I Hit You 67). The repetition of the word “crime” four times highlights the simple absurdity and desperation of a situation where writing letters would be considered an act so offensive as to be labelled a crime. The only crime is that the protagonist is daring to retain some sense of identity and subjectivity through the act of writing these love letters. Here, she is rebelliously reoccupying the English space with which she was so intimate before her marriage turned it against her. In one of her letters, she writes:

I imbue the word kiss with the idea of clandestine; I smuggle the thought of me into the word caress. You can never dislodge me from each of the words I’ve meticulously occupied. … English makes me a lover, a beloved, a poet. Tamil makes me a word huntress, it makes me a love goddess (Kandasamy, When I Hit You 60).

In regaining a semblance of power through a repossession of both of her vernaculars — English and Tamil — she begins to feel empowered once more. English becomes a space with reciprocal love and physical affection, a concept so foreign to her that she feels she must “smuggle” herself back into the word “caress.” Tamil goes one step beyond the English docility and makes her a warrior; she feels so uplifted by being able to communicate her desires and thoughts through her own vernacular that she secures in herself the subjectivity that her husband is trying to snuff out.

III. Concluding Thoughts As women writers begin to understand how our language shapes thought, they can then begin to push back and repopulate our uses of the language — their vernaculars — with their own agency/ identities instead of mirroring the male subjectivity which social discourse tends to follow. This is exactly what Mahasweta Devi and Gayatri Spivak, Anu Singh Chaudhary, Krishna Sobti, and Meena Kandasamy are able to accomplish with their produced literature. Whether in English, Hindi, a tribal language, or the language of the body, this vernacular creates space for the female subjectivity to exist and be heard in contemporary literature and society. Looking ahead, in her book of essays “My Friend, My Enemy,” Ismat Chughtai, one of India’s most foundational feminist writers in the twentieth century, writes about her wish for women in India to achieve true equality in name, in reality, and in language, stating that “the heroine of the future will be neither heartless nor op- pressed. She will be only a woman, and instead of giving her the title of ahramen [Satan] and yazdaan [God], writers will bless her with the title of woman. And then the process of construction will begin” (Chughtai and Naqvi). ◆

As women writers begin to understand how our language shapes thought, they can then begin to push back and repopulate our uses of the language
