title: Exoneration of American Violence: The Cultural Legacy of American Atrocity Against Civilians During the War in Vietnam
text:
Exoneration of American Violence:

The Cultural Legacy of American Atrocity Against Civilians During the War in Vietnam by Saidie Stone

Department of International Studies

Faculty Adviser: Prof. Lauren Stokes, Ph.D.

“I know what happened that day. I know how it happened. I know why. It was the sunlight. It was the wickedness that soaks into your blood and slowly heats up and begins to boil. Frustration, partly. Rage, partly. The enemy was invisible. They were ghosts. … But it went beyond that. Something more mysterious. The smell of incense, maybe. The unknown, the unknowable. The blank faces. The overwhelming otherness. This is not to justify what occurred on March 16, 1968, for in my view such justifications are both futile and outrageous. Rather, it’s to bear witness to the mystery of evil. Twenty-five years ago, as a terrified young PFC, I too could taste the sunlight. I could smell the sin. I could feel the butchery sizzling like grease just under my eyeballs.”

— Tim O’Brien, In the Lake of the Woods

“Well, the Oriental … doesn’t put the same high price on life as does the Westerner. Life is plentiful, life is cheap in the Orient. And as the philosophy of the Orient expresses it, life is not important.”

— General William Westmoreland, Hearts and Minds

“The Vietnamese people and Vietnamese Americans have voices. It’s simply that Americans as a whole tend not to hear them.”

— Viet Thanh Nguyen, “Anger in the Asian American Novel”

Introduction

It is Strange How War Never Ends For Those Involved.1

On March 16, 1968, American soldiers carried out a search-and-destroy operation in the Son My village of South Vietnam.2 Quang Ngai province, called Pinkville by American GIs, had a “reputation as a Viet Cong hotspot.”3 The village includes the hamlets of My Lai, My Khe, Tu Cung, and Co Luy; each hamlet includes several sub-hamlets. Though the province was supposed to be an “enemy bastion … American forces encountered no organized resistance on the morning of March 16th, either in My Lai 4 or My Khe 4.”4 US troops killed an estimated 567 Vietnamese civilians.5 Though the massacre did not occur entirely in either My Lai or My Lai 4, the atrocity is known as the My Lai Massacre.

The troops at My Lai 4 belonged to Charlie Company, led by Lt. William Calley. Calley was ultimately the only person convicted for his involvement in the massacre. Lt. Calley’s conviction was received with bipartisan backlash.6 People opposed to the verdict believed either that the military was using Calley as a scapegoat or that he had done nothing wrong. President Nixon felt justified in pardoning Calley because of the outcry. He shared “the opinion of many Americans” that My Lai was “an aberration, unrepresentative of our country.”7

However, Nick Turse argues in his book Kill Anything That Moves that the My Lai Massacre was not an aberration but “part of a consistent pattern of criminality resulting from policies set at the top.”8 In order to reframe it as an anomaly, the military and the Pentagon focused their investigations only on the killings at My Lai 4 and the subsequent cover-up of those killings; they did not investigate the killings at My Khe 4. According to Turse, the “killings of civilians … were widespread, routine, and directly attributable to U.S. command policies.”9 While there were codes of conduct that were supposed to protect noncomba- tants, they mostly functioned to give the military deniability, since actual conduct differed greatly from what was on paper.10 Officials were desperate to reach the so- called ‘crossover point,’ which was when they killed more guerilla fighters than the Viet Cong could recruit; that goal, along with the military’s intentional indoctrina- tion of racism against Vietnamese people, led to the ‘mere-gook rule,’ or MGR, which held that Vietnamese people were less than human. Success was measured by the number of Vietnamese killed-in-action, and “the mere-gook rule promised that any dead Vietnamese would do.”11

Turse’s point that the military used racism as a tool to instill in soldiers the ability to kill readily and ruthlessly connects to two concepts that Mimi Thi Nguyen

1 Spike Lee, Da Five Bloods (Netflix, 2020). 2 The intent of search-and-destroy missions was to clear a given area of all guerilla fighters. The term became synonymous with “systematic destruction,” since soldiers were given liberty to “’shoot anything that moves.’” Nick Turse, Kill Anything That Moves: The Real American War in Vietnam (New York: Picador, 2013), 51–53. 3 Howard Jones, My Lai: Vietnam, 1968, and the Descent into Darkness, Pivotal Moments in American History (New York, NY: Oxford University Press, 2017), 23. 4 Jones. My Lai, 27–96. 5 Jones, My Lai, 212. 6 Jones, My Lai, 291. 7 Jones, My Lai, 339. 8 Turse, Kill Anything That Moves, 230. 9 Turse, Kill Anything That Moves, 22. 10 Turse, Kill Anything That Moves, 53–5. 11 Turse, Kill Anything That Moves, 50–1; 28–9.

employs in The Gift of Freedom. Nguyen’s work studies how America’s promise to deliver freedom to populations around the world, often through war and violence, inevitably and inescapably colonizes the subjects of that freedom by imposing on them an unpayable debt. Nguyen deploys the Vietnamese refugee as a double target of the gift of freedom: the first time through war and the second time through refuge. Two ideas Nguyen employs are necropower and Foucault’s economy of biopower. The former is “the idea that some deaths don’t matter,” and the latter views racism as “the politics of disposability.”12 To learn to kill without hesitancy is to learn that certain people are disposable.

In the following chapter of my thesis, I examine the work of Vietnamese-American writers about the war and their experiences as immigrants in the United States. I use Mimi Thi Nguyen’s book The Gift of Freedom: War, Debt, and Other Refugee Passages to frame my close readings of Viet Thanh Nguyen’s The Sympathizer and Qui Nguyen’s Vietgone. Many Vietnamese victims of the massacre at My Lai are not living and are therefore unable to share their side of the story. Given this reason, I examine works by Vietnamese-Americans for their perspective of American involvement in Vietnam and the Vietnamese refugee experience.

Before I begin my analysis, I would like to first address how I choose to reference the war, since the name itself has inescap- able implications. Both the ‘Vietnam War,’ the term Americans use, and the ‘American War,’ the term many Vietnamese use, over- simplify the conflict. For example, Laotians and Cambodians lost their lives in massive numbers due to U.S. efforts to bomb North Vietnamese supply chains in those countries — meaning bloodshed from the conflict spilled over borders rather than staying confined to Vietnam.13 For these reasons, among others, in his book Nothing Ever Dies, Viet Thanh Nguyen refers to the conflict as “the war.” He argues, “to deny it a name … clears a space for reimagining and remem- bering the war differently. Denying this war its name also acknowledges what everyone who has lived through a war already knows: their war needs no name, for it is always simply the war.”14 Renny Christopher argues that calling the war “Vietnam” erases “all distinctions between enemy and ally and among Vietnamese individuals,” con- flating the country with “war and evil,” and is another way of victimizing U.S. soldiers by placing blame on the amalgamation of country and war itself. To challenge typical connotations associated with the name ‘the Vietnam War,’ I will instead use the term ‘the war in Vietnam,’ or simply ‘the war.’

Chapter: We Could Never Forget

We have been the subjects of that experiment they call, with a straight face, the Cold War. What a joke, given how hot the war has been for us.15

Biopower, Necropower, and PTSD American stories about the war do not depict Vietnamese people or their experiences accurately or empathetically. Whether Vietnamese people are stereotypical supporting characters or extra bodies to be blown up in the background, their lack of

12 Nguyen, Gift of Freedom, 89. 13 Viet Thanh Nguyen, Nothing Ever Dies: Vietnam and the Memory of War (Cambridge, Massachusetts: Harvard University Press, 2016), 6–7. Approximately 400,000 people in Laos and 700,000 in Cambodia were killed by U.S. bombs during the Vietnam War. 14 Nguyen, Nothing Ever Dies, 8. 15 Viet Thanh Nguyen, The Sympathizer (New York: Grove Press, 2015), 239; 344–345.

humanity and complexity suggests that they are ‘other,’ ‘alien,’ and less than white Americans. This attitude seeps into and shapes cultural narratives about the war and Vietnamese refugees. I will perform close readings of excerpts from Viet Thanh Nguyen’s The Sympathizer and Qui Nguyen’s Vietgone, using Mimi Thi Nguyen’s reading of trauma as a tool of neoliberal war-making as a framework for my analysis in order to understand how these works counteract cultural narratives that dehumanize Vietnamese people and humanize and center perpetrators of violence.

Mimi Thi Nguyen, like Nick Turse, also critiques the erasure of systemic violence from the American consciousness. She examines how the idea of trauma op- erates differently on American veterans than on Vietnamese refugees in ways that ultimately absolve not only the soldiers who committed the violence but American war-making itself. Put simply, she argues that American veterans can be divorced from their trauma, which reinforces their humanity by highlighting their mental and emotional pain. However, refugees are defined by their trauma and limited to the category of ‘displaced person,’ a permanent status which they must perpetually work to overcome but can never overcome. As Nguyen states, “to be given freedom is a process of becoming without being.”16

Foregrounding Post Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) in American veterans reframes American violence against racial others, transforming perpetrators of brutality into victims of “unimaginable pain.”17 The victimization of perpetrators humanizes them by using their pain and suffering as proof of their humanity.18 In addition, their victimhood eclipses the people toward whom they committed violence and obscures the effects of the violence inflicted on their victims. Finally, the emphasis on their pain “rescue[s] liberal empire[s] from the criminality of its wartime conduct” by framing American violence against racial others (in this case, Vietnamese civilians) as an aberration rather than a fundamental tool of American foreign policy.19 Because of the harmful psychological consequences soldiers experience after perpetrating violence, liberal war is able to claim that such violence is an anomaly. In fact, “public disclosures about cruelties committed by U.S. military forces — including the My Lai massacre … were hugely influential in the diagnosis’s codification.”20 The diagnosis of PTSD, regarded as a psychological abnormality, makes such violence seem aberrant and atypical. Using Nguyen’s understanding, it is no surprise that the My Lai Massacre is turned from “insensible destruction wrought by a supremacist empire” to “a regrettable failure to discern between the good racial subject and the bad one” and “an accident, the unfortunate symptom of soldier’s unbearable experiences.”21

In contrast, under liberal empires, the refugee cannot be separated from their trauma. The refugee becomes not only a person who is traumatized but also a

16 Mimi Thi Nguyen, The Gift of Freedom: War, Debt, and Other Refugee Passages, Next Wave: New Directions in Women’s Studies (USA: Duke University Press, 2012), 18. 17 Nguyen, The Gift of Freedom, 116. 18 As Fassin and Rechtman say in their book Empire of Trauma, “these men should therefore be considered war victims, broken by what they had witnessed and by what they themselves had done.” Didier Fassin and Richard Rechtman, The Empire of Trauma: An Inquiry into the Condition of Victimhood, trans. Rachel Gomme (United States: Princeton University Press, 2009), 91. 19 Nguyen, Gift of Freedom, 113. 20 Nguyen, Gift of Freedom, 113. 21 Nguyen, Gift of Freedom, 173.

displaced person who responds to violence ‘abnormally’ and is defined by their ar- rested potentiality. Refugees are divorced from the situations that traumatized them (i.e., political repression or war). Trauma comes to signify abnormality and failure in refugees, rather than the experiences that harmed them. Unlike veterans, refugees are burdened with the necessity of reacting to violence ‘correctly’ or ‘normally’; without a response that is deemed as such, they are seen as deficient or incapacitated.

If the American military uses racism as a weapon to engender in its soldiers the capacity to kill Vietnamese without hesitation, then PTSD absolves the system of American war-making of blame after the war ends. In other words, biopower and necropower operate both during and after the war. During the war, they enable and encourage the perpetration of violence; after, they give way to exoneration over accountability.

The Sympathizer The end of the war is near, and a little Vietnamese boy is “crowned with a Yan- kees cap … and airlifted into the heavens, his ultimate destination being [an American soldier’s] family in St. Louis, where he would be given a golden retriever and the nickname Danny Boy.”22 This quote frames the refugee’s passage from the distant nation of Vietnam to America as an act of salvation. The young boy’s passing to America is depicted as a spiritually purifying journey. “Danny Boy’s” method of travel via helicopter is an act of sanc- tification; it takes him “to the heavens.”23 The destination — in this case, St. Louis — and the gifts that await him there are wholesome and thoroughly American. His new American family welcomes “Danny Boy” with open arms, a baseball cap — a reference to America’s favorite pastime — and the most idyllic pet possible: a golden retriever. After his salvation and his picturesque homecoming, Danny Boy’s life is full of possibility.

Danny Boy’s tale comes from a story within a story, satirizing America’s refugee parable. Danny Boy is a character in The Hamlet, a fictional Hollywood blockbuster in Viet Thanh Nguyen’s novel The Sympathizer. The film parodies many aspects of American cinema and American ideology. Danny Boy’s narrative illustrates not the genuine refugee experience but rather a mocking critique of America’s idealistic understanding of what it has to offer the disadvantaged racial ‘other.’ For Mimi Thi Nguyen, America’s gift of freedom is “composed of pipe dreams, bogus concepts, and moral luck as well as violence at its origin.”24 By juxtaposing Danny Boy’s story with The Sympathizer’s main plot, Viet Thanh Nguyen exposes the refugee parable and shows that it is in fact what Mimi Thi Nguyen says it is: a “pipe dream,”

22 Nguyen, The Sympathizer, 157. 23 Nguyen, The Sympathizer, 157. 24 Nguyen, The Gift of Freedom, 24–5.

“

”

America’s involvement in Vietnam and its ‘rescue’ of South Vietnamese civilians and soldiers engenders in him a deep sense of powerlessness.

“bogus,” and born from violence. Instead of following a young child whose Vietnamese identity and experience of the war are eas- ily and effectively erased by a picturesque American welcome, the novel follows adult men who take active roles in the war and are destroyed by it.

The Sympathizer follows an unnamed North Vietnamese mole — referred to as the Sympathizer — working for a South Vietnamese general who relocates to America after the Communists take over Vietnam. The book begins days before the fall of Saigon. Though the Communists take the capital by the third chapter, the struggle over Vietnam continues for the rest of the book. The war is technically over, but it hasn’t ended strategically or emotionally for any of the Vietnamese characters. Specifically, Bon, one of the narrator’s closest friends and a true be- liever in democracy and South Vietnam, suffers a great loss just before their escape to America. The Sympathizer uses his close relationship with an Army of the Republic of Vietnam (ARVN) general to get spaces for Bon, his wife Linh, and his child Duc on a plane to America, but Linh and Duc are shot and killed as they run across the tarmac towards the plane that will take them out of Vietnam.

Bon’s story juxtaposes and undermines the refugee parable represented by Danny Boy. Bon and the Sympathizer are not ‘purified’ or ‘fixed’ by their passage to America. In contrast to Danny Boy’s passage — his salvation — after Linh and Duc are killed on the tarmac, Bon and the Sympathizer bring their bodies onto the plane. Their passage is far from purifying or healing. Bon literally carries his family’s bodies with him to America, and he is unable to leave his pain behind. Leaving their bodies is not an option: the Sympathizer takes Linh’s body and runs onto the plane without discussion. There is no question that both he and Bon will bear this pain; there is no possibility that their passage to America will heal Bon’s heartbreak.

Once in America, Bon’s loss and his experiences in the war cannot be smoothed over or forgotten. In fact, he regrets leaving Vietnam at all, and not only because Linh and Duc were killed. Fighting for his country gave him a sense of purpose that he was willing to give up in order to save his family, but he ends up losing both. To him, life in America is not a life worth living. Their apartment in Los Angeles is “a jail cell,” rather than an idyllic new home; the Americans are their rescuers, but Bon says, “they just didn’t tell us that they’d cut off our balls and cut out our tongues along the way … If we were real men, we wouldn’t have let them do that.”25 America offers Bon neither freedom nor possibility. His escape to America not only costs him his identity as a father and a husband but also his identity as a man. Bon’s anger over his lost masculinity is indicative of his lost autonomy and control. America’s involvement in Vietnam and its ‘rescue’ of South Vietnamese civilians and soldiers engenders in him a deep sense of powerlessness.

Bon’s decision to return to Vietnam underscores America’s inability to heal him. He volunteers to take part in an operation to go back to Vietnam in an attempt to overthrow the Communist government. The operation is widely acknowledged to be a suicide mission by characters in the novel. However, Bon would rather die in Vietnam than live in America. His faith in democracy has disappeared, as has his commitment to any kind of cause. Bon tells an anticommunist admiral in Thailand, “I

25 Nguyen, The Sympathizer, 223.

don’t give a damn about saving anybody, including myself. I just want to kill communists.”26 Bon no longer values his life or anyone else’s life.

Bon’s experience of coming to and living in America differs greatly from Danny Boy’s. In The Hamlet, Danny Boy leaves behind an older brother who died and a sister who was sexually assaulted by the Viet Cong and subsequently disappeared from the movie. Neither the death of his brother nor leaving behind his sister impacts Danny Boy’s quixotic salvation. His potential pain and regret for leaving them behind is never even suggested by the movie’s finale. Instead, a new life with an American family offers a simple, neat, and happy ending.

Nguyen’s novel also works against the narrative propensity to center experiences of the war around those of Americans. Though implicated, Americans are not held directly responsible for any of the main characters’ suffering. Bon’s wife and child are shot by either the North Vietnamese Army or South Vietnamese soldiers (neither is confirmed). However, Bon’s loss is just one example of intra-community violence. The protagonist’s other close friend, Man, was a Communist double agent working in the South Vietnamese Army up until the Communists took over. The day Saigon falls, Communist planes drop Napalm bombs on Man and his South Vietnamese unit. The bomb permanently disfigures him; as a result, he distances himself from his wife and children who are disgusted by and terrified of him. The Sympathizer, who is half-Vietnamese and identifies as Vietnamese (though other characters torment him for his biraciality), kills two other Vietnamese men. Additionally, the Sympathizer claims responsibility for tor- turing a Communist agent nicknamed the Watchman, and in another torture scene, South Vietnamese soldiers rape a female Vietnamese communist during an inter- rogation.27 Nguyen argues that this is how Vietnamese can “reclaim [their] subjectivity” because they “aren’t just victims, but victimizers as well.”28 He speaks about the actual rape of Vietnamese women and the metaphorical rape of Vietnam when he says that he “wanted to show that this was something that wasn’t simply happening in terms of what the West was doing to Vietnam but what the Vietnamese were doing to themselves.”29

Though the story works against the dominant American-centric narratives about the war, the novel remains very

26 Nguyen, The Sympathizer, 294. 27 Nguyen, The Sympathizer. 28 Nguyen, “Anger in the Asian American Novel,” 394. 29 Nguyen, “Anger in the Asian American Novel,” 394.

[V]iolence is not an abnormality or an exception, but rather an innate part of

American war- making and American cultural dominance worldwide. “

” critical of American involvement in Vietnam. Nguyen does not only blame the American military for violence against the Vietnamese; war is one tool of America’s contemporary empire, but it is not the only tool. There are multiple passages throughout the book that stress the cultural and political significance of The Hamlet, not as ‘just’ a movie but as a weapon of American culture. One passage laments that sometimes art becomes “more real than the real” because the film will continue to have cultural power when the war is reduced to “a paragraph in a schoolbook students won’t even bother to read.”30 While many scholars have argued for the essential role textbooks play in the cultivation and spread of national ideology, Nguyen suggests that Hollywood is more influential.

Hollywood’s ideological and cultural power are intrinsically linked to violence and exploitation in Nguyen’s novel. The Sympathizer often uses violent words and metaphors involving weapons to describe the film’s ideological rule in that the military-industrial complex and Hollywood both contribute to “the obliteration of natives.”31 He describes Hollywood as “relentlessly assaulting the mental defenses of audiences” and being “the launcher of the intercontinental ballistic missile of Amer- icanization,” which ultimately succeeds in the “lobotomization and pickpocketing of the world’s audiences.”32 Nguyen creates an association between America’s military power and its cultural power. The language itself (e.g., the phrases “relentlessly assaulting” and “obliteration”) is violent and aggressive. All of these metaphors carry unmistakable threats of destruction and equate the destructive power of the military and Hollywood.

This overt connection between American culture and exploitation points out the essentiality of violence as a tool for American power abroad. In other words, violence is not an abnormality or an exception, but rather an innate part of American war-making and American cultural dominance worldwide. Exceptional violence “is normalized as a part of the cost of the continuous government of human freedom” — an unfortunate and inevitable consequence — when in fact America “acts murderously” and “evades indictment for doing so.”33

The Hamlet also satirizes Hollywood’s “Vietnam War” movie tropes, including its inaccurate, shallow, and stereotypical portrayals of Vietnamese people. Even though The Hamlet contains speaking roles for Vietnamese characters, it denies them full humanity and cultural and ethnic specificity. The Auteur, the director of the Movie, adds Binh (nicknamed Benny by the Americans), his sister Mai, and their little brother (whose real name is never mentioned and who is nicknamed Danny Boy by the Americans). None of the Vietnamese characters are played by Vietnamese actors; instead, they are played by a Korean-American actor, a Chinese-British actress, and a Filipino actor.34 The actors’ inaccurate ethnicities and their characters’ American nicknames erase anything iden- tifiably Vietnamese about Binh, Mai, and Danny Boy. The fact that these characters are Vietnamese is ultimately not as important as the fact that they are non-white

30 Nguyen, The Sympathizer, 178. 31 Nguyen, The Sympathizer, 180. 32 Nguyen, The Sympathizer, 133, 173. 33 Nguyen, The Gift of Freedom, 175. 34 James Yoon, a Korean American plays Binh; Mai is played by Asia Soo, a mixed-race woman of Chinese and British descent; Danny Boy is played by a young Filipino actor whose name is not mentioned by the narrator. 158–9.

people protected by white people.35 Their ethnicity and culture does not matter; the film is not about them.

These Vietnamese characters are vio- lently exploited in order to add intrigue to a story about white Americans. Each of their plotlines reinforces that the film is, as the Sympathizer calls it, “an epic about white men saving good yellow people from bad yellow people.”36 Binh’s extended, grue- some death scene underlines the brutality and viciousness of the Viet Cong while his body is brutalized and tortured. Mai’s sexual assault, also perpetrated by Communist soldiers and shown in detail on screen, functions as shock value and justification for the annihilation of the Viet Cong.37 Danny Boy’s rescue establishes America’s benevolence and superiority over this war-ravaged ‘other’ country. Nguyen is clear and unequivocal in his determination that American media — specifically Hollywood — is an essential and powerful tool of American power and ideology.38

Conclusion Vietnamese-American sources regarding the war clearly counter the racist tropes of American narratives by reclaiming agency, individuality, and pain, while also recen- tering Vietnamese experiences and perspectives. The Sympathizer and Vietgone also work against America’s refugee parable, which depicts refugee passage to America as a spiritual rebirth. Furthermore, The Sympathizer criticizes Hollywood not only for the violence against and exploitation of Vietnamese people within its films but also for its powerful and destructive role as a weapon of American power.

The racism that the U.S. military inoculated in its troops during the war in Vietnam is not contained within the specific time and place of war. Mimi Thi Nguyen’s analysis shows how PTSD is used to forgive systemic American violence after wars end. That is one manifestation of racism, and outright violence is another. Anti-Asian violence and sentiment has a long history in the U.S., not beginning or ending with involvement in Vietnam.

Over the past year (2020), Anti-Asian violence in the United States has been exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic, especially in the Bay Area (San Francisco and Oakland). The Atlanta Spa shooting is one recent example, but the reports are numerous. Vicha Ratanapakdee, who was

35 I use the term ‘non-white’ rather than ‘people of color’ or ‘Asians’ to emphasize and reinforce the way whiteness is centered in The Hamlet. 36 Nguyen, The Sympathizer, 134. 37 The film leaves out her emotional and psychological reactions to the assault; she disappears from the narrative afterwards. Mai’s plot also obscures the fact that American GIs were perpetrators of sexual violence disturbingly often. There were at least 18 rapes and two gang rapes in Pinkville on the day of the massacre. Read Jones, My Lai, 79–81. 38 In my full thesis I analyze Apocalypse Now and Da Five Bloods, which serve a cultural and psychological function by asserting and representing American ideology globally.

“To end, a word about the Vietnamese murdered by American soldiers. We must learn to grieve for deaths that have been forgotten or ignored. To overlook them would be to excuse and to ignore the violence that resulted in their demise.”

84 years old, was pushed to the ground and died two days later; a 64-year-old Vietnamese mother was robbed in San Jose; and Noel Quintana, who is 61, was cut across the face with a box cutter on the New York City subway.39 American leaders are only recently beginning to name and address the issue. President Joe Biden called the attacks “wrong” and “un-American,” while Vice President Kamala Harris stated that the violence is part of a “larger issue.”40 After the Atlanta spa shootings, there has been an attempt by news outlets and across social media platforms to highlight the victims, rather than focus on the shooter.41

To end, a word about the Vietnamese murdered by American soldiers. We must learn to grieve for deaths that have been forgotten or ignored. To overlook them would be to excuse and to ignore the violence that caused their demise. Of the 504 victims in the My Lai Massacre, 165 were women, 17 were pregnant women, 117 were children, and 56 were infants.42 Some of their names are Tran Van Duc; Nguyen Thi Tau; Pham Mot Lai; Truong Nhi and his nine-year-old son Truong Ba Cu, and two of his other sons Bon and Nam; Phong Thi Chan; Le Thi Huynh and her 24-year-old sister-in-law Do Thi Can; Ba So and her teenage daughter Ba Moi; Do Hoi, Ba Phu, and Do Hut, a six-year- old; Do Thi Be, a seven-year-old; and Do Thi Nhut.43 Among the few survivors is Pham Thanh Cong, who serves as director of the My Lai Museum. title: Radical Caring: A Qualitative Study on the Role of Frontline Workers in Eradicating Gender-Based Violence in the Asian American Communities
abstract: Gender-based violence (GBV) is a prevalent issue on a global scale, but the effects of such violence upon Asian/Asian American communities in the United States is compounded by their immigrant, refugee, and/or other historically marginalized identities. While current literature recognizes GBV as a public health issue of equity and social justice, anthropology closely examines the asymmetry of power by informing a holistic view of local contexts. The research examines the perspectives of Asian-identifying frontline workers within domestic violence agencies and multi-service organizations in Chicagoland. Frontline workers, such as social workers and legal advocates, play a pivotal role in serving survivors and offering intimate local-level knowledge. Feminist ethnography grounded in Asian American Critical Race Theory (AsianCrit) guided data collection and analysis. Ethnographic fieldwork at a local domestic violence agency for six (6) weeks was conducted and fourteen (14) key informant interviews with frontline workers from five (5) non- profits across Chicagoland took place. The analysis demonstrates that their labor as influenced by personal life histories, or “radical caring,” provides agency to survivors on the individual, relationship, community, and societal levels, aligning with the WHO Socio-Ecological Framework for Violence Prevention. The positionality of frontline workers is crucial in eradicating gender-based violence and resisting the structural violence affecting all female and non-binary people of color. Highlighting the advocacy of frontline workers broadens interdisciplinary understandings of gender-based violence in anthropology, public health, critical race studies, and other social science disciplines.
text:
Radical Caring:

A Qualitative Study on the Role of Frontline Workers in Eradicating Gender-Based Violence in the Asian American Communities by Chloe Wong

Department of Anthropology Faculty Adviser: Prof. Shalini Shankar, Ph.D.

Introduction

“It wasn’t just a career choice coming to the Asian Women’s Services Center. I am also a survivor of childhood sexual abuse, so I had been working on my own healing journey in my personal life for a number of years. When the Center’s Children’s Advocate job came up, I was at the crossroads of thinking about my career but also thinking about my own personal journey of healing. Having this job come up that seemed to blend together my desire to put out energy outwards instead of just focusing on inner healing for myself — this was really crucial. I think that the combination of having experience working with children, especially children of immigrant families, and really loving that, and then also my own experience of being a survivor and wanting to advocate for families who experienced that themselves. I think those two things came together in this job for me.”1

I spoke to Sun Hee on a bright and early Saturday morning in October 2020. I received her contact information via Diana, one of her colleagues and one of my other interlocutors. I reached out to Sun Hee via email for a Zoom meeting. We originally planned for late September, but Sun Hee had work conflicts. This was a common phenomenon with many of the frontline workers that I spoke to, as well as my colleagues at my internship site during summer 2020. Meetings with staff members could be rescheduled. Meetings with clients could not be delayed and should be prioritized.

Sun Hee was born and raised in South Korea until her family moved to the Midwest when she was an adolescent. She studied art history and religion as an

1 All names and organizations in this paper (Sun Hee, Diana, Asian Women’s Services Center) are pseudonyms to protect the identities of my interlocutors.

undergraduate and began working with children in a variety of capacities after graduation — tutor, admissions counselor, ESL teacher — until she joined the Asian Women’s Services Center in April 2020 at the start of the COVID-19 pandemic.2 I asked her whether she had a defining experience that sparked her interest in helping survivors of gender violence. With little hesitation, she shared her identity as a survivor and her motivations for joining the Center, a non-profit organization that aims to eradicate gender-based violence for women and children across Asian American communities. Sun Hee’s perspective was especially valuable for understanding the role of the frontline worker because she drew strength from her past experiences of violence. While she was working, she put energy outwards to provide direct services and advocacy to other immigrant children and families. She found kinship with others of similar identities on her personal journey and became determined to serve them as a way of healing herself. Her story demonstrates the resilience and strength of frontline workers in gender-based violence and how they actively serve and survive.

This paper centers the stories and lived experiences of Asian American frontline workers in order to develop the concept of radical caring in eradicating gender-based violence. Sharmila Rudrappa (2004) coined the term “radical caring” as an amalgamation of individual and organizational motivations to care for survivors.3 Direct service professionals do the incredibly hard and emotionally draining work of serving survivors of gender violence day after day. They often make very little pay, work at organizations in dire need of continued funding, and receive very little recognition for their work. Despite this, they continue working. I hypothesized that their sense of responsibility was connected to serving survivors of similar racial identities.

This research asks the following questions: 1) How do frontline workers view their work in relation to their racial and ethnic identities?; 2) How can radical caring, professionalization of empathy, and Asian American Critical Race Theory (AsianCrit) be used as frameworks to understand the labor of frontline workers?; and 3) What is the role of frontline workers in responding to, preventing, and working towards eradicating gender-based violence? Through the

2 At the time of writing, the Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic is an ongoing pandemic of a contagious disease. 3 Rudrappa, S. (2004). Radical Caring in an Ethnic Shelter. Gender and Society, 18(5): 588–609. DOI: 10.1177/0891243204268131

“

”

Direct service professionals do the incredibly hard and emotionally draining work of serving survivors of gender violence day after day. They often make very little pay, work at organizations in dire need of continued funding, and receive very little recognition for their work. Despite this, they continue working.

lens of AsianCrit, I argue that the work of women and non-binary individuals within domestic violence and multi-service organizations continues to demonstrate radical caring and the professionalization of empathy. In this paper, I build this argument by reviewing relevant literature and offering ethnographic discussion and analysis. In claiming the sovereignty of caring for their own ethnic communities, Asian American frontline workers build emotional and physical refuges.

Literature Review Gender-based violence (GBV) is defined by the United Nations High Commission- er for Refugees (UNHCR) as:

an umbrella term for any harmful act that is perpetrated against a person’s will and that is based on socially ascribed (i.e., gender) differences between males and females. It includes acts that inflict physical, sexual or mental harm or suffering, threats of such acts, coercion, and other deprivation of liberty. These acts can occur in public or in private.4

GBV includes any type of violence that stems from gender identity or presentation, including violence against men and violence experienced by gender non-con- forming people, who are especially vulnerable due to the marginalization of their gender identity. I discuss eradicating GBV as the long-term goal in the anti-violence movement. Eradicating, eliminating, or ending GBV refers to the complete abolition and removal of all forms of gender violence. This language is adapted from the mission and vision statements of domestic violence agencies both involved in and peripheral to this research. Many international, national, and local organizations typically use prevention or interventions to characterize their work as stopping violence before it occurs. While these efforts are crucial, the ultimate goal should remain as ending all forms of gender violence and transforming the conditions that justify, engender, and perpetuate gender violence into conditions of safety for all people.

Anthropologists have historically examined violence and conflict in relation to warfare, cultural ethos, conflicts over material resources, or cultural rituals.5 Acts of GBV, such as domestic violence, were not deeply discussed or theorized in the canon. Such issues were not thought or understood to also exist within the United States. This foreshadows our following conversations about the role of culture in perpetuating

4 Inter-Agency Field Manual on Reproductive Health in Humanitarian Settings: 2010 Revision for Field Review (2010). Inter-Agency Working Group on Reproductive Health in Crises, 8. Gender-based Violence; Geneva, Switzerland. Available from: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK305160/ 5 Wies, J.R. and Haldane, H.J. (Eds.) (2011). Anthropology on the Front Lines of Gender-Based Violence. Nashville, TN: Vanderbilt University Press.

GBV is an issue of human rights, public health, and social justice that is inextricably linked to interlocked systems of oppression: imperialism, cisheteropatriarchy, racism, and capitalism. “

” assumptions regarding GBV. A noteworthy vacuum in anthropological work was the lack of connection to macrostructures that maintain and reinforce inequalities and violence. GBV is an issue of human rights, public health, and social justice that is inextricably linked to interlocked systems of oppression: imperialism, cisheteropatriarchy, racism, and capitalism.6 This is not to say that one of these components is the root of all gender violence, but GBV has been used as a tool of each system of oppression to enact violence.

It is crucial to ground this research in Critical Race Theory (CRT), specifically AsianCrit. AsianCrit explores the complex racialization of people of Asian descent in the United States, specifically the legacy of state-sanctioned violence and marginalization of Asian American perspectives in both institutional policies and informal social practices.7 I would like to highlight one of the seven tenets of AsianCrit:

Story, Theory, and Praxis is the idea that counter stories, theoretical frameworks, research, and practice are intertwined elements in the analysis of Asian American experiences and in advocacy efforts for Asian American communities. This tenet recognizes the work of Asian American scholars whose work should inform theory and practice.

Story, Theory, and Praxis emphasizes the importance of counter stories and centering in the margins. The stories of frontline workers are pivotal in informing responses to gender violence, which has already been established as a prevalent issue. Therefore, the thoughts of frontline workers add authentic representation to survivor needs.

Methodology

Feminist Ethnography and Fieldwork In this section, I provide my intellectual genealogy of utilizing feminist ethnography. Feminist ethnography grounded in CRT was employed to guide data collection and analysis for this project. Christa Craven and Dána-Ain Davis (2011) define feminist ethnography as “a project committed to documenting lived experience as it is impacted by gender, race, class, sexuality, and other aspects of participants’ lives.”8 The aim of feminist ethnography is not to presume an egalitarian relationship between research and research subjects, but to acknowledge the power dynamics at play.9 Anthropologists should be continuously interrogating their role in meeting the needs of their female and non-binary subjects. My interlocutors were generous with their time and knowledge because they believed that I was doing impactful work simply by listening to them and bringing visibility to GBV in immigrant communities through my academic research. I argue for the use of feminist ethnography because this approach can broaden our understanding of the conditions that lead to violence and map the intersections between race, ethnicity, gender, and justice.

Ethnographic Fieldwork (Participant

Can There Be a Feminist Ethnography? Women & Performance: A Journal of Feminist Theory, 5: 7–27. https://doi-org.turing.library.northwestern.edu/10.1080/07407709008571138

Observation) Participant observation involves the day- to-day aspects of people’s activities, rituals, and interactions to uncover their culture.10 While participant observation is a common component of qualitative research and ethnographic fieldwork, I resist the premise of the “self” and the “other.” In early ethnog- raphies, the “self” has historically been the detached, privileged anthropologist who is merely present to examine the peculiarities and deviations of the “other.” Given my salient identities and personal history with GBV, I questioned the prevailing dichotomy between “self” and “other.” Instead, I was focused on being an active participant who was reflexive of my own coexistence within the same context.

My ethnographic account begins with a brief history of the South Asian Support Center and continues with a description of my involvement and the shelter environment. The South Asian Support Center is located in Uptown Chicago, a north side lakeshore neighborhood home to “Asia on Argyle,” and has a concentration of Chinese, Vietnamese, Cambodian, Laotian, and Thai businesses and residents. In the 1970s, the women’s anti-violence movements gave rise to community-organizing institutions, including domestic violence shelters.11 In the United States, many Asian American women spearheaded specific organizational responses to domestic violence in the 1980s after questioning their own communities’ lack of access to mainstream programs.12 In 1989, the South

Asian Support Center was founded by five Asian women, who were established activists and professionals within Chicagoland. They became increasingly aware of domestic violence cases within the South Asian community. Although the Center was initially dedicated to serving South Asian women, the clientele eventually expanded to all immigrant communities.

I began my virtual internship in June, dedicating four days a week for six weeks to build, develop, and execute an evaluation. I was invited to work once a week from the shelter to support understaffed shelter services. Despite the 8 a.m. shift on Saturday mornings, I was eager to contribute however I could at the shelter. The shelter had just reopened and staff members followed strict COVID-safe guidelines. My primary responsibilities, in addition to my intern tasks, were to ensure the well-being of residents, meet their daily living needs, and maintain a comfortable and safe communal living environment. Staff members and my direct supervi- sor were aware of my intent as a researcher to ask questions and collect information.

My positionality as a researcher blurred with my roles as an intern and colleague. I did not interview any clients in a thesis researcher capacity, yet all of my interactions with clients created greater empathy and emotion for their stories. I experienced vicarious trauma as I spent countless hours researching gender violence and poring over transcripts of clients’ and staff members’ interviews. I was fear- ful of the physical environment outside of

My participant observation informed my reflexivity as an anthropologist and reinforced the importance of lived experiences. I also became acutely aware of the limits of compassion and the exhaus- tion of professional care, which influenced my empathy for frontline workers. In the later sections of analysis, I will discuss how the specific limits are reflected in the professional experiences of frontline workers.

Interview Process From August to December 2020, I conducted 14 semi-structured, key informant interviews with frontline workers.13 Purposeful sampling was used to recruit female or non-binary identifying frontline workers within Asian-serving agencies in Chicagoland.14 My co-workers at the South Asian Support Center connected me to other staff members within this small but mighty community. At the end of each interview, I used snowball sampling to recruit additional participants. Once interviewees had a sense of my questions, they would introduce me to their co-workers if my interviewees thought that they would be a good fit.

Interviews ranged from thirty to eighty minutes, depending on the inter- viewee. Due to the ongoing pandemic, all interviews were conducted virtually via phone or Zoom to follow COVID-safe research protocols. A pre-designed interview guide with 15 questions was used to frame the direction of the interview. Follow-up questions and tangents offered additional insights to our conversations. I took notes during all interviews, and interviews were audio-recorded. After all interviews were conducted, they were transcribed. The transcripts were analyzed in NVivo, a qualitative research software, through inductive coding and relationship building. Emerging themes existed on various scales and were then categorized into the socio-ecological framework.

Enacting Radical Care The themes discerned from the qualitative analysis will be discussed on the individual level. I employ the socio-ecological framework to highlight how the work of frontline workers is crucial and interconnected on these levels for combating GBV. The integrated socio-ecological framework for violence prevention by the World Health Organization (WHO) views GBV as the outcome of interactions at the four levels.15 This provides a holis- tic approach to understanding the needs of survivors and contextualizes the range of factors affecting the lives of women and non-binary people of color. Locating Frontline Workers. I define frontline workers as direct service professionals who “comfort, advocate for, and assist victims and survivors of gender-based violence.”16 They are the “actors who provide care and support to survivors of violence: from volunteer-run domestic violence shelters or community-based organizations to the increasingly professionalized service providers giving psychosocial,

13 Cossham, A. and Johanson, G. (2018). The Benefits and Limitations of Using Key Informants in Library and Information Studies Research. Information Research, 24(3). http://informationr.net/ir/24-3/rails/rails1805.html 14 Purposeful sampling refers to the technique in qualitative research of identifying and selecting individuals who are especially knowledgeable or experienced with the subject of interest (Palinkas et al. 2016). 15 World Health Organization (2012). Understanding and Addressing Violence Against Women. Retrieved from http://apps.who. int/iris/bitstream/handle/10665/77432/WHO_RHR_12.36_eng.pdf;jsessionid=E7B0B9B497AC762621D13A24632CAC40?sequence=1 16 Wies and Haldane 2011 therapeutic and legal aid.”17 Within this ethnography, frontline workers range from shelter advocates and counselors to program supervisors and directors. I focus on the roles that are derived from and exist within community organizations rather than public service roles (e.g., police officers), which intrinsically reproduce systems of violence and oppression. Within my research, I focus on the frontline workers of five total organizations — three multi-service organizations (Arab American Family Association, Pan-Asian Health Center, Korean Community Center) and two domestic violence (DV) agencies (Asian Women’s Services Center, South Asian Support Center).

Individual Level The first level identifies the life histories of frontline workers to understand their motivations and hopes for their work. As previously stated, they are often the first line of help in efforts to respond to GBV.

Their life histories shape their everyday work with clients because their labor often helps them make sense of their personal experiences and of the injustices that are peripheral in their lives.When examining participants’ objects of regret, we found that 24% had regrets of career choices, 23% had regrets of education, 21% expressed regrets in their marriage or romantic relationships, 17% regretted parenting or relationships with their children, 9% had regrets relating to other family members, 9% had regrets concerning friendships, 7% regretted financial issues, 6% regretted some personal character trait, and 3% had other regrets not included in our coding scheme. Many workers shared immigrant identities and/or ethnic experiences with the clients that they were serving. Munira grew up in Pakistan and came to Chicago to pursue a college educa-

Growing up in a very collectivistic culture, you hear a lot about things like, “Oh you know you’re a woman, you should be acting in a certain way” or “If a man beats you, it’s okay.” I’ve heard it and seen it to be very normalized, and it has always bothered me. I have seen the manifestations of domestic violence in my relatives. Two of these girls were actually my nieces, but they were around the same age as me. I could not understand. … I saw them after so many years. They used to be very upbeat and friendly, very jolly. After all these years, I was quite shocked, like, “What the hell happened to you, not only physically but emotionally?” I saw some nervous tics.

Although we were on a Zoom call, Munira had an urgent tone and was clearly indignant at the violence inflicted against women within her family and community. Her own training in mental health and counseling informed her understanding of how domestic violence manifests in South Asian communities. She was especially sensitive to how other members of her community responded to unhappy relationships and how her female relatives became increasingly depressed throughout the years. This motivated her to further understand the psychology of humans. I hypothesize that this may have also influenced her immigration to the United States for higher education. She was physically escaping from the culture of neglect and pain in Pakistan but found greater strength from her cultural identity at her workplace in the U.S. She directs these emotions toward assisting survivors of gender violence at the South Asian Support Center because her family members could very well be in the position of these same clients.

Anthropological scholarship has historically theorized culture in a myriad of ways. Culture refers to the values, attitudes, and behaviors that determine definitions and descriptions of norms within distinct societies. Within GBV literature, culture is often scapegoated as the primary influence of violence. It undeniably plays an important role in how such societities “view, perceive, and process sexual acts as well as sexual violence.”18 However, “culture-blaming” is an incorrect narrative that does not accurately reflect the power dynamics at play.

First, “culture-blaming” designates a perceived dichotomy between “traditional” and “modern” cultures. “Traditional” cultures, such as immigrant communities within the United States, have not fully understood the notions of modern, civi- lized culture. Therefore, it is argued that gender violence continues to occur within these communities; however, this is an oversimplified argument that overlooks social, political, and economic inequalities. Modern societies and cultures are located, both physically and imaginarily, within First World nations, many of which are former colonizers or current neo-colonizers. Reckoning with the historical implications of oppression is crucial in doing the work of radical caring. First-Generation Immigrants. Of my 14 interlocutors, seven of them — Soo Jin, Hong, Sharon, Shaima, Sun Hee, Hye Jin, and Munira — were first-generation immigrants who immigrated from Asia. By first-generation, I refer to individuals who were born to one or both parents

18 Kalra, G. and Bhugra, D. (2013). Sexual Violence Against Women: Understanding Cross-Cultural Intersections. Indian Journal of Psychiatry, 55(3): 244–249. DOI: 10.4103/0019-5545.117139 in a country outside of the U.S. and later immigrated to the U.S. for various reasons. Studies on the ethnic identity development of first-generation immigrants in educational settings19 have ascertained that students who have left the comfort of homes seek affirmation of their ethnicity and have a strong relationship between ethnic identity development and self-es- teem. I believe that my interlocutors seek similar affirmations through their current and ongoing work. By serving their cultural and ethnic communities in the U.S., they can continue to remain connected to their parent cultures despite being situated in the dominant white American culture.

Hong was born in Vietnam and came to the United States when she was 7 or 8 years old with her then-17-year-old aunt as a refugee. She recalls leaving Vietnam in the 1980s as “boat people’’ and going to refugee camps before finally arriving in the U.S. This was a formative experience for her that led to her pursuit of roles that could give back to her community. She went on to receive a bachelor’s degree in fine arts and a master’s degree in expressive art therapy. Hong is currently the Group Programs Manager at the Pan-Asian Health Center, as well as an art therapist. Her leadership role in the Behavioral Health Program includes facilitating group programs focused on developing and practicing skills in the community, supervising the caseloads of clinicians and case managers, and supporting advocacy work as needed. Almost 20 years ago, she reached out to the Director of Mental Health at the time with a desire to do art therapy for the community. Since then, she has built many relationships with individual and group clients. Hong describes how she was able to learn how to process her emotions, memories, and experiences through art therapy:

My beliefs in the process of nonverbal expression or communication mean that expressive art is not just visual art but writing and poetry; it could be music or video; it could be any form of expression a person may have to express or explore themselves, or communicate with another person or be a part of a community …

Certainly my own experience with doing art and writing for myself since I was younger and seeing the power of that. The process of working with clay and this particular process triggered a memory that I was really surprised by and just seeing how powerful that process is because I do a lot of work in understanding myself and my experiences. Firsthand I see the power of that, and it’s kind of endless with infinite possibilities.

Expressive art was an important part of her journey in understanding her own

19 Acar, E., Yigit, M.F., and Aslan, D. (2016). Ethnic Identity Development in Schools among First Generation Immigrants in the United States. Journal of Education and Training Studies, 4(4): 105–110. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1088508

“Frontline workers are critical in comprehensive, intersectional responses of preventing, eliminating, and ending GBV for all communities.” experiences. She comments that this is especially impactful for people who do not speak English or have a high education level. Given that most of her clientele is Vietnamese and she tries to build long-term relationships with clients, I hypothesize that her role as a facilitator is crucial in also maintaining her sense of self and identity.

Conclusion This research began out of my curiosities about the perspectives of female frontline workers of color within the work of combating GBV. My conversations with my 14 interlocutors — Amina, Diana, Farah, Hong, Hye Jin, Jang Mi, Jasmin, Jennifer, Keerthi, Munira, Shaima, Sharon, Soo Jin, and Sun Hee — demonstrate the complex interactions between personal, social, and professional factors that translate in their radical caring for their ethnic communities.

I have the utmost respect for the care, compassion, and labor of frontline workers in addressing and preventing GBV, often at the expense of personal trauma to themselves. In the process of combatting state and interpersonal violence, however, their stories and labor also become marginalized and co-opted through the professionalization of the anti-violence movement. Furthermore, their roles are often made invisible by the overwhelmingly white feminist anti-domestic violence movement. My research speaks to highlighting their unique positionality as counselors, therapists, lawyers, organizers, survivors, workers, students, and advocates who approach their work as women of color with marginalized identities.

While feminist anthropologists have adopted dual roles as scholar-activists on the frontlines, Asian American feminist voices remain crucial in articulating the political connectedness of their own everyday experiences.20 In the tradition of fugitive anthropology, gendered violence should also be researched and represented from the bodily experiences of Black, brown, and Indigenous women, as well as queer women of color.21 These research works restore the agency of women’s space and physical selves, even in academic spaces.

I propose that frontline workers deserve a central, integral position in the conversation of preventing and eradicating GBV, particularly in ethnographic investments of care work. The trauma-informed, culturally relevant radical care of frontline workers aims to promote the survival of their communities through their small, daily acts of labor. In the directions of decolonial feminism, deep coalitions should be formed with the providers of care as central to the movement.22 Frontline workers are critical in comprehensive, intersectional responses of preventing, eliminating, and ending GBV for all communities. ◆

title: Urban Currents: Upstream Pollution and its Impacts on Intercity Populations Along the Mississippi River
abstract: This paper investigates the historical impacts of water pollution on downstream communities along the Mississippi River during the late 19th and early 20th centuries. As industrialization and urbanization intensified, urban centers and industries along the river increasingly discharged untreated pollutants into the water, thereby transforming the river from a residential amenity into a significant disamenity. Drawing from historical surveys and census data, this study examines how changes in pollution levels influenced population shifts in downstream counties relative to their upstream counterparts. I found that increased levels of upstream pollution had significant and economically meaningful effects on downstream populations, with pollution levels correlating negatively with population sizes. These findings are robust across a range of pollution specifications. Furthermore, I found that the impact of upstream pollution became more severe between 1880 and 1900 before declining from 1910 onwards. I hypothesize that the intercity effects of upstream pollution contributed to the urban mortality penalty before declining in the early 20th century as cities began adopting modern water purification technologies to mitigate the adverse effects of pollution and water-borne diseases. This paper contributes to the broader economic discourse on environmental externalities and neighborhood amenities by detailing the intercity effects of water pollution.
text:
Urban Currents: Upstream Pollution and its Impacts on Intercity Populations Along the Mississippi River

Faculty Adviser: Dr. W. Walker Hanlon

Department of Economics by Darran Shen

Abstract This paper investigates the historical impacts of water pollution on downstream communities along the Mississippi River during the late 19th and early 20th centuries. As industrialization and urbanization intensified, urban centers and industries along the river increasingly discharged untreated pollutants into the water, thereby transforming the river from a residential amenity into a significant disamenity. Drawing from historical surveys and census data, this study examines how changes in pollution levels influenced population shifts in downstream counties relative to their upstream counterparts. I found that increased levels of upstream pollution had significant and economically meaningful effects on downstream populations, with pollution levels correlating negatively with population sizes. These findings are robust across a range of pollution specifications. Furthermore, I found that the impact of upstream pollution became more severe between 1880 and 1900 before declining from 1910 onwards. I hypothesize that the intercity effects of upstream pollution contributed to the urban mortality penalty before declining in the early 20th century as cities began adopting modern water purification technologies to mitigate the adverse effects of pollution and water-borne diseases. This paper contributes to the broader economic discourse on environmental externalities and neighborhood amenities by detailing the intercity effects of water pollution.

Introduction The Mississippi River powered commerce and industry in the United States for a significant portion of American history as early superhighways that supported trade, transportation, and industry. Urban areas and trading centers such as New Orleans and St. Louis were developed and grew along the riverbanks, aided by water access for both consumption and travel. The introduction of the Second Industrial Revolution accelerated the role of rivers: Beginning in the late 19th century, the Revolution marked a period of rapid industrialization, urbanization, and technological innovation that fundamentally transformed the American economy and society. Bodies of water, specifically rivers, suddenly offered a new kind of industrial amenity as a fertile avenue to both situate and spread innovations from the Second Industrial Revolution: Rivers offered the water required to power steam factories and machinery. The Mississippi River also offered direct access to a natural super- highway for steam-based transportation; by 1840, steam-based river transportation had made New Orleans the fourth-largest port in the world, surpassed only by London, Liverpool, and New York.1

Importantly, rivers also served as an outlet for waste disposal. Over the next century, this natural resource would become increasingly polluted as cities, factories, and industrial mills directly released pollutants into rivers, including human effluent, industrial waste, and animal byproducts. In this paper, I study how downstream populations shifted in response to upstream pollution in the late 19th and early 20th centuries to understand this phenomenon.

1 Frank Haigh Dixon, A Traffic History of the Mississippi River System (Govt. Printing Office, 1909), 15.

Are there significant differences in the size of communities living downriver compared to upriver communities? What are the channels that caused this population change? While the impact of river pollution across communities and cities is highlighted in policy debates and historical research, the economic consequences are less well-known. Even today, upstream pollution remains a concern, with its ongoing relevance reflected in the reports that regularly make the news, from conflicts over fertilizer runoffs to the dumping of forever chemicals.

I find that upstream industrial and urban pollution had a statistically and economically significant impact on downstream populations, robust across a wide range of pollution estimates. A longitu- dinal analysis of census data from 1880 to1930 further demonstrates that the adverse effects of pollution on population levels intensified between 1880 and 1900 but began to diminish after 1910 following the introduction of contemporary water treatment technologies such as filtration and chlorination which were introduced in the early 20th century. My results imply

“Upstream industrial and urban pollution had a statistically and economically significant impact on downstream populations.” that upstream pollution contributed to the urban mortality penalty with its impact diminishing concurrently with the reduction in mortality rates, aligning with existing research on the topic.

Background

What Pollution? The Second Industrial Revolution precip- itated a dramatic expansion of urban areas and industrial development along the banks of the Mississippi River, an industrial growth that was typified by the mas- sive increase of pollution in the nation’s waterways, reflecting the contemporary theory of pollution control: “The solution to pollution is dilution,” the erroneous belief that one could empty untreated sewage, waste, and effluents into the nearest fast-moving stream of water and hope that the water would clean itself. The prevailing belief that rivers could dilute any and all waste meant that every city and industrial plant dumped untreated waste and sewage into the nearest watercourse. By the mid-1920s, Minnesota had already declared the Mississippi River a health hazard; District Engineer Major Williams reported that “all of the cities and towns located on the Mississippi River from Minneapolis to Hastings now empty their untreated sewage into the Mississippi River.”2 In a 1925 study, author H.R. Crohurst concluded that industrial waste could be found over 50 miles downriver from the Twin Cities.3 Figure 1 shows a 1932 map of sewage systems in urban areas of the Upper Mississippi region.

2 Raymond H. Merritt, The Corps, the Environment, and the Upper Mississippi River Basin, Environmental Review, vol. EP 870-1-19 (United States. Army. Corps of Engineers, Historical Division, 1984), 51. 3 H. R. Crohurst and U.S. Treasury Department Public Health Service, A Study of the Pollution and Natural Purification of the Upper Mississippi River (Govt. Printing Office, 1932), 31. 4 Paul Hesterman, “The Mississippi and St. Paul: Change Is a Constant for River and the City That Shaped It,” Ramsey County History 21, no. 1 (1986): 6. 5 William W. Folwell, “The Disposal of City Cleanings,” The Minnesota Horticulturist 16 (1888): 173–89. 6 Joseph Manulik, “Establishment of the Minneapolis Waterworks, 1867–1910,” Minnesota Historical Society.

Note that most communities on the River, including the largest Upper Mississippi cities of St. Paul and Minneapolis, did not have sewage treatment of any kind and simply emptied their effluents into the river. Contemporary reports found that the combined pollution dumped into the Mississippi from the Twin Cities was now over two and a half times the volume of the flow of the river.4

The Health Calculus River pollution, then, was a well-documented phenomenon along the Mississippi, and upstream pollution was a noted problem. As early as 1888, William W. Folwell, a professor at the University of Minnesota, issued a warning in the Minnesota Horticulturist: “The spectacle of … emptying into the Mississippi river thousands upon thousands of tons of solid and liquid filth and offal yearly is one to make angels weep and men blaspheme.”5 Thus, the effects of river pollution on health were noted, even if river residents did not fully understand the relationship. In Minneapolis, where water was pumped from the Mississippi River, residents began complaining about the color and taste of their water as early as 1880.6

The most significant impact of polluted water was the spread of water-borne diseases. In 1900, these diseases accounted for nearly a quarter of all deaths from infec- tious diseases in major cities, which themselves caused 44% of total deaths. As cities discharged untreated waste into rivers, downstream communities used the same water for drinking and cooking, allowing diseases like typhoid and cholera to spread easily. Existing economics research by Cutler and Miller (2004), Ferrie and Troesken (2008), and Anderson, et al. (2022) examine how the interaction between environmental pollution and public health shaped demographic patterns and contributed to the urban mortality penalty. The concept of the “urban mortality penalty” refers to the increased risk of death associated with living in urban areas compared to rural ones; in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, rapid urbanization led to densely populated cities that struggled with inadequate sanitation infrastructure. This lack of infrastructure resulted in the direct discharge of untreated sewage into rivers, which were often the same sources from which downstream communities drew their drinking water. A lack of infrastructure and poor understanding of disease theory and bacteriology also meant that water drawn from cesspool sources allowed pathogens such as those causing typhoid and cholera to thrive and spread, exacerbating the incidence of water-borne diseases. The urban mortality penalty during this period can be attributed primarily to these diseases, which prolifer- ated due to the crowded living conditions and poor environmental management inherent to urban settings.

Literature Review My paper contributes to existing literature in several notable ways. First, it joins the substantial volume of research that looks at the negative impacts of water pollution on populations, both long-term and short-term. Second, it contributes to the body of economic history that identifies pollution as an amenity (or in this case, a disamenity) that may result in sorting or migration effects. Third, my paper adds a results-centered take on existing economics and hydrology research that looks at the upstream and downstream effects of water pollution.

Existing research has firmly identified the negative health effects of water-related pollution. Unprecedented improvements in urban health from 1900 to 1940 elim- inated the so-called “urban penalty” associated with living in cities, with mortality rates falling by 40% during this period (Cutler and Miller 2004). Cutler and Miller find that the introduction of major public health interventions and specifically new clean water technologies such as filtration and chlorination played key roles in eliminating or reducing the spread of water-borne pollution-related diseases such as typhoid, pneumonia, and tubercu- losis by preventing infected effluent from polluting clean water sources. My research expands on these findings by looking specifically at intercity water pollution, which Cutler and Miller acknowledge as an issue.

Heblich et al. (2021) look at temporal disamenities, finding that high levels of temporary pollution from coal factories during the Industrial Revolution altered the spatial organization of cities in the long run, wherein different households express their environmental preferences and willingness-to-pay through reloca- tion. Other literature that looks at air pollution-induced neighborhood sorting includes Banzhaf and Walsh (2008), who find that households will “vote with their feet” for better environmental quality, entering and leaving communities in response to environmental disamenities. My paper seeks to expand on the study of pollution-related sorting by looking at river pollution, which may offer similar environmental amenity decisions but must contrast with the inherent commercial and recreational value of rivers.

Finally, my paper contributes to research that looks at the upstream and downstream effects of water pollution. Existing research approaches water pollution with both economics and hydrology. Existing economics approaches to upstream and downstream water pollution famously address the question through the study of externalities. Lewin (1982) offers a neoclassical approach to pollution externalities by creating a theoretical framework of social costs, property rights, and optimal levels of pollution. Ferrar and Sassone (1975) and Sokoloski (1967) address the externality issue of effluent charges in the specific context of upstream and downstream firms. Cutler and Miller (2004) and Beach et al. (2016) do acknowledge, but do not substantively address, the potential issue of upriver pollution, indicating that cities that dump sewage into a river would increase future typhoid rates for cities downstream.

Research stemming from the field of hydrology grapples more with the upstream and downstream effects of pollution but is primarily focused on modeling pollution itself instead of linking pollution with economic outcomes and focusing on modern events. Shrestha and Kazama (2007) and Singh (2004) assess upstream and downstream water quality relations, focusing on modeling the quality of river water when transporting municipal and industrial wastewater and agricultural runoff. Chen et al. (2021) find that the severity of water pollution is closely related to the population size of cities. Glinska-Lewczuk et al. (2016) is one of few papers that recognizes multi-city effects, analyzing the river as an environmental path that links urban areas into an “urban river continuum.” I bridge the economic and hydrology approaches to upstream and downstream pollution, on one hand borrowing a water quality analysis framework and multi-city approach from hydrology, while focusing more on the economic impacts of water pollution.

My paper ties together the ideas of health-related water pollution effects, neighborhood choice and migration, natural disamenities, and upstream and downstream pollution models to identify how downriver counties fared in a new era of urbanization and industrialization.

This figure was more difficult to construct given the lack of historical data. Instead, I utilize a report from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, which played a significant role in river-related infrastructure projects during this period, such as constructing canals for transportation. Following the 1924 Oil Pollution Act,which mandated the Corps to investigate “pollution affecting navigation or commerce on navigable waters,” a 1926 report submitted by Major General Harry Taylor, Chief of Engineers, to the U.S. House of Representatives concluded that “as a general rule, the pollution density of the waters in any locality is directly

I construct my upstream pollution concentration figure using three elements. First, I use each county’s aforementioned population density as a measure of pollution density. This data is pulled from the U.S. Census. Second, I aggregate the pollution density measures of each county using the ordered list of counties such that the pollution “experienced” by each county includes effluents flowing from upstream counties. Finally, I use an exponential decay function to model the varying levels of pollution over distance and severity. As effluents flow through a river, they are subject to various decaying forces such as decompo- sition, oxidation (the chemical process by which organic materials are broken down when they react with oxygen), dilution, and sedimentation. In the context of my paper, I model the decay of river pollution using the recorded distances between each county so that pollution from County A will impact County B the most, County C the second most, and so on.
