Discussion The consistent direction and magnitude of my findings indicate that upstream pollution concentration had both statistically and economically significant impacts on population levels over a long period in the late 19th to early 20th centuries. A logical next step in interpreting these results would be to understand the channels by which populations declined. There are a few possibilities. First, one could interpret the decline in population to represent an increase in mortality. That is to say, increases in pollution concentration increased the incidence of deadly water-borne diseases, increasing mortality and reducing population levels. This is not unreasonable, given the findings from Cutler and Miller (2005), Ferrie and Troesken (2008), and Beach et al. (2016). In the absence of mortality data, however, it is difficult to directly prove this hypothesis. Another way to interpret the results is to argue that populations reacted to the presence of a disamenity, manifesting in the form of negative health effects or low aesthetic value, and decided to move elsewhere. This is the explanation that my amenity model predicts in section 4. Therefore, a second channel could be that populations declined as a result of migration. The most likely case is that both channels were valid and active.

It is also worth discussing my finding that the effect of water pollution on the population began declining after 1910. From 1880 to 1900, the effect of upstream pollution concentration on population levels increased in magnitude. The increasing magnitude of pollution makes sense: The river was increasingly polluted, resulting in increasing deaths from water-borne diseases. The sudden declining effect of pollution from 1910-1930 defies this explanation. I propose that one potential explanation for the observed directional change in Figure 3 may be linked to significant exogenous developments in clean water technologies. As demonstrated by Cutler and Miller (2005), breakthroughs in bacteriology and clean water technologies such as chlorination during the early 20th century played pivotal roles in reducing urban mortality rates. These technological innovations effectively mitigated the health risks posed by polluted water sources, thereby diminishing the negative impact of upstream pollution on population health. As cities and smaller communities implemented these

“A one-unit increase in upstream pollution resulted in two families moving away from the county.” new technologies, they not only curbed the prevalence of waterborne diseases but also enhanced the overall quality of life, contributing to increased amenity levels of urban environments. Consequently, the reduction in the upstream pollution coefficient can be interpreted as a response to these public health improvements and the subsequent decline of the urban mortality penalty caused by intercity pollution.

Indeed, many cities on the Mississippi River began filtering and chlorinating water in the early 20th century as part of broader trends in U.S. water treatment practices; to gain a more complete understanding of these developments, I build a timeline of water-related interventions in selected cities along the Mississippi River referencing papers published in the Journal of the American Water Works Association (Journal AWWA) as well as data drawn from local city government websites. Figure 4 shows the timeline of a selection of 12 river cities that adopted clean water practices and sanitation technologies from 1880-1940. A detailed list of cities used for this survey is listed in Appendix A. As Figure 4 shows, cities on the Mississippi River began implementing water purification technologies at around the same time the pollution coefficients in Table 1 began to decline. These findings track with both the historical record and the aforementioned research showing that such efforts to purify water sources for safe consumption were indeed effective enough to address the negative effects of water pollution.

Conclusion My paper looks at how increased urban and industrial pollution in the late 19th and early 20th centuries in the Mississippi River affected the population size of river communities. I find that upstream pollution had a statistically and economically significant impact on downstream populations. My findings add to existing economic research that (dis)amenities, and specifically environmental disamenities, have a powerful effect on where people choose to live. Furthermore, I find that the effects of water pollution worsened from 1880-1900 before declining from 1910 onwards. I argue that upstream river pollution likely contributed to the urban mortality penalty by increasingly polluting the same water sources from where downstream cities often drew their water. By the same token, the implementation of new water technologies such as filtration and chlorination in cities along the Mississippi in the early 20th century, which helped mitigate the urban mortality penalty, also explains why my pollution concentration effect declined after 1910.

This paper is one of few that look at the economic relationship between upstream and downstream communities, and there are numerous opportunities to expand and

Given more time and access to historical records (specifically local or state-level records), one could analyze the effects of pollution at a more precise scale than my existing county-level observations and also look at the differential effects of pollution between inland communities and communities on the river. I also propose future directions of study. One extension of this research may analyze the relationship between upstream pollution and population sorting

(i.e., changing income, property values, and literacy in downstream communities), which would also be an interesting application for a hedonic pricing model or externality analysis. Another extension lies in investigating the differential mortality rates of smaller industrial towns, which often lagged behind in implementing modern public health mechanisms (Leonard et al. 2012), and larger communities on the Mississippi that did implement water quality improvements. ◆

title: Revisiting the Agentic-Communal Framework: A Conjoint Analysis Approach to Understanding Bias Against Female Leaders in the Workplace
abstract: In this study, we employ a conjoint analysis to assess what factors influence the likelihood of male and female candidates being perceived as leaders. In particular, we consider the influence of agency and communality stereotypes in terms of personality, emotionality, and parental status. Participants evaluated a set of fictitious employee profiles of a consulting firm, selecting which employees they considered most deserving of being promoted to managers. Participant evaluations were then analyzed to determine the relative importance of eight study attributes in influencing the probability of managerial promotion (i.e., leadership selection). In this paper, we discuss two of our main findings. First, when emotional control is described as fair, female candidates are less likely than male candidates to be chosen as leaders. Second, certain agentic female leaders benefit from being described as mothers: bossy, but not ambitious, female candidates are more likely to be chosen as leaders when described as having children compared to when described as childless.
text:
Revisiting the Agentic- Communal Framework: A Conjoint Analysis Approach to Understanding Bias Against Female Leaders in the Workplace

Faculty Adviser: Dr. Sylvia Perry

Department of Psychology by Charlotte Cagliostro

Abstract In this study, we employ a conjoint analysis to assess what factors influence the likelihood of male and female candidates being perceived as leaders. In particular, we consider the influence of agency and communality stereotypes in terms of personality, emotionality, and parental status. Participants evaluated a set of fictitious employee profiles of a consulting firm, selecting which employees they considered most deserving of being promoted to managers. Participant evaluations were then analyzed to determine the relative importance of eight study attributes in influencing the probability of managerial promotion (i.e., leadership selection). In this paper, we discuss two of our main findings. First, when emotional control is described as fair, female candidates are less likely than male candidates to be chosen as leaders. Second, certain agentic female leaders benefit from being described as mothers: bossy, but not ambitious, female candidates are more likely to be chosen as leaders when described as having children compared to when described as childless.

Introduction Although women make up approximately half of the American workforce and earn the majority of undergraduate and master’s degrees, they are underrepresented in leadership roles, particularly in business organizations (Catalyst, 2022; Warner et al., 2018). The proportion of female leaders diminishes progressively across the corporate pipeline: while women hold a slim 36% of senior manager positions, they hold just 28% of C-suite positions (Catalyst, 2022; McKinsey & Company, 2023).

If female employees are as prevalent and as qualified as male employees, why then does there exist a disparity between men and women in positions of authority? For decades, psychologists have investigated a myriad of stereotypes as potential sources of this gap. Such research has uncovered that the traits comprising society’s traditional leadership prototype are mas- culine, and the stereotypical traits associated with women are inconsistent with this prototype (Eagly & Karau, 2002). Leaders are typically described as ambitious, independent, confident, and assertive; while men can display these traits without penalty, women face backlash. Women are expected to be warm, friendly, nurturing, and sensitive—traits that are rarely used to describe leaders. Women who violate these societal norms (e.g., by being cold or acting assertively) face various penalties for being stereotype-inconsistent (Eagly & Wood, 2002; Eagly & Wood, 2012; Rudman et al., 2008).

Thus, a woman in the workplace is subject to a double-edged sword: act too submissively, and she will not be seen as a leader, but act too dominantly, and she will not be desired as a leader. This research seeks to address how women can best navigate this paradox in order to be seen and desired as leaders.

Agency and Communality In this study, we utilize Bakan’s (1966) agentic-communal framework. Bakan’s model posits that humans can be described using two constructs: agency and communality. Agency can be understood as independence, while communality can be understood as interdependence. Although the prototypical traits used to describe successful leaders are agentic, social identities like gender appear to play a critical role in governing the effectiveness of agentic displays as a means of demonstrating leadership quality (Eagly & Karau, 2002).

Agentic stereotypes are prescribed for men and proscribed for women; hence, agentic male leaders are stereotype-congruent, while agentic female leaders are stereotype-incongruent (Eagly et al., 2020; Sczesny et al., 2018). When individuals violate their prescribed stereotypes, they prompt psychological discomfort, which often results in negative evaluations (Moss-Racusin et al., 2010). Since agentic female leaders are inconsistent with the stereotype of women being communal, they experience various forms of backlash, including being seen as less likable, hirable, and competent (Eagly & Karau, 2002; Rudman et al., 2012; Rudman & Glick, 1999). Due to this backlash, when compared directly against one another, agentic male leaders are typically perceived as better than agentic female leaders. However, when leaders are described as communal, male and female leaders are typically evaluated similarly (Heilman & Okimoto, 2007; Rudman et al., 2012).

Agentic female leaders appear to be able to mitigate the backlash they face by being mothers, or more precisely, through evaluators’ awareness of their motherhood. When agentic female leaders are described as having children, they are perceived significantly more favorably than when described as being childless[a] (Heilman & Okimoto, 2007). Having children appears to mitigate the penalties incurred by agentic women due to the fact that they are now perceived as sufficiently communal (i.e., stereotype-congruent).

Emotionality stereotypes can further explain differences in leadership perception between men and women. Communality is tied to emotional attunement, such that communal individuals are regarded as warm, sensitive, and empathetic (Keck, 2019). In that women are stereotyped as being more communal than men, they are also stereotyped as being more emotional than men (Shields, 2002). In fact, a majority of men and one-third of women believe that women are underrepresented in leadership positions in business and politics because they are too emotional (Dolan, 2014). Research, however, has shown that men and women do, in fact, experience the same amount of emotion, but since women are more likely to express it, women are commonly believed to be more emotional than men (Durik et al., 2006; LaFrance & Banaji, 1992).

As female leaders are more likely to express emotion, it is assumed that they allow their emotions to influence their thoughts and decisions. This perceived biasing effect of emotions on decision-making hurts female leaders because it is widely believed that emotion detracts from rational thought, despite a robust body of research indicating that emotion does not impede decision-making and, in some cases, actually helps it (Damasio, 2005; Shields, 2002). When leaders are described as emotional, female leaders are more likely than male leaders to be perceived as overreacting and unable to regulate their emotions [b](Shields, 1987). Even when no evidence pertaining to a leader’s emotionality is made available, individuals are still more likely to evaluate an identical managerial decision as emotion-driven and, consequently, rate that decision as inferior and that leader as less employable when told the leader is female compared to male (Brescoll, 2016).

Present Study With a novel methodological application, this research aims to fill a gap in the existing literature and contribute to a more multifaceted understanding of leadership perception. With a conjoint survey design, we examine the influence of several attributes to better assess how potential leaders are judged. This project addresses

“When agentic female leaders are described as having children, they are perceived significantly more favorably than when described as being childless.” the following overarching question: under what criteria are male and female leaders perceived differently, and how can agency and communality stereotypes explain these differences?

In previous comparable leadership studies, only a small number of variables have been examined within a single experiment. With conjoint analysis, however, it becomes possible to precisely evaluate a significantly larger number of variables, referred to as attributes. While conjoint survey experiments are common in fields such as product testing and political science research, they have never before been applied to study leadership using the agentic-communal framework, allowing us to provide novel insights.

In order to better understand the basics of conjoint analysis, consider the following example in which a group of researchers conduct an experiment to inform the development of a new smartphone. The researchers decided to evaluate three core smartphone features to determine their relative importance and the optimal combination of features (i.e., the smartphone with the highest likelihood of purchase). As such, they create a conjoint survey design with three attributes: color, length, and price. The color attribute levels are silver and black, the length attribute levels are five inches and six inches, and the price attribute levels are $600, $700, and $800. With a forced-choice conjoint survey design, participants see a series of tables each depicting two phone profiles in terms of color, length, and price, with a randomly selected level for each of the attributes. Because conjoint designs are within-subjects, the profile tables are completely randomized across participants. For each selection task, participants consider the two phone profiles and select which phone in the pair they would rather purchase. The subsequent analyses are repeated-measures comparisons of participant responses to each of the tables. In other words, respondents’ preferences are compared to each other to examine how they vary as a function of the attributes of interest. This analysis enables the researchers to determine which phone to produce based on the feature combination yielding the highest probability of selection.

Conjoint analyses allow for the calculation of average marginal component effects (AMCEs) for each attribute level. AMCEs can be understood as the individual effect of each attribute level on the probability of a profile being selected. Moreover, interaction AMCEs can be calculated to show how differing combinations of attribute levels impact the overall probability of a profile being selected. With this methodology, we were able to assess leadership perception via the agentic-communal

“When leaders are described as emotional, female leaders are more likely than male leaders to be perceived as overreacting and unable to regulate their emotions.” framework across several attributes, more than ever previously examined in a comparable singular experiment. This study tests the following hypotheses: (1) Gender and emotional control will interact to affect leadership perception, (2) Gender and personality will interact to affect leadership perception, and (3) Gender, personality, and parental status will interact to affect leadership perception.

Methodology

Participants Participants (n = 301) were recruited through the online data collection platform Prolific. The average age of participants was 39.9 years (SD = 13.54). Participants were limited to U.S. citizens 18 years and older. Although an a priori power analysis suggested that for 10 selection tasks, 200 participants were needed to detect a medium-sized effect, to increase the robustness of our study results, we increased our sample size to 301.

Design and Materials A forced-choice conjoint survey design was employed; see Table 1 for a full attribute breakdown.

In total, this design had eight attributes: race, gender, relationship status, parental status, personality, emotional control, industry experience, and highest education. Three attributes served to analyze agency and communality perception. First, the personality attribute most directly indicated the candidates’ agentic or communal nature. This attribute had four levels, two levels being communal traits (collaborative, empathetic) and two levels being agentic traits (ambitious, bossy). Second, parental status served as a potential indicator of commonality, particularly among female candidates. This attribute denoted the number of kids a candidate had with four levels (0, 1, 2, 3). Third, the emotional control attribute served to indicate agency and communality through emotionality associations. This attribute had four levels (poor, fair, good, and excellent).

In order to create a more realistic employee evaluation experience for participants, the emotional control attribute was renamed to “performance under pressure” during the experiment. Similarly, to explain how candidates’ personality traits and abilities to perform under pressure were determined, the task description explained to participants that this information was pulled from previous performance evaluations.

Procedure Participants began the experiment by reading a short passage that described a consulting firm and explained their task of evaluating current firm employees up for a promotion to a managerial role. More specifically, participants were informed that each selection task would consist of assessing a pair of candidate profiles and selecting which candidate they believed to be more deserving of a managerial (i.e., leadership) role. While this company and the employees were entirely fictitious, participants were not given this information until after completing the study. Participants completed 10 selection tasks. See Figure 1 for a sample task.

After the candidate selection component, participants provided demographic information, including two scales to assess gender bias. The Benevolent Sexism in the Workplace (BSW) scale (Warren et al., 2023) consisted of 19 items and assessed participant endorsement of complemen- tary gender differentiation (e.g., “When employees have personal problems, they prefer to go to their female coworkers to get emotional support”) and protective paternalism (e.g., “Women should work less than men so they can serve as a caretaker for their families”). For each item, participants indicated their agreement using a 7-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree); higher scores indicated stronger endorsement. A modified version of the 13-item Color-blind Racial Attitudes Scale (Neville et al., 2000), in which racial terminology was replaced with that of gender, assessed participant endorsement of gender-blind ideology (e.g., “Sexism may have been a problem in the past, it is not an important problem today”). For each item, participants indicated their agreement using a 6-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to 6 = strongly agree); higher scores indicated stronger endorsement.

Results A complete overview of the average marginal component effects (AMCEs) of all attribute levels is shown in Figure 2.

Note. Figure 2 shows percentage point change in probability of being selected. Sample size N = 301 respondents, or at candidate level N = 6020.

Candidates with college and with graduate degrees were evaluated significantly better than candidates with a high school degree, experiencing a sizable bump of about 10 percentage points (p < .001). Similarly, candidates with eight years of experience and 12 years of experience were evaluated significantly better than candidates with only four years of experience, experiencing a bump of about 10 percentage points (p < .001). Considering the personality attribute, results indicated that compared to empathetic candidates, collaborative candidates experienced a boost of about 6 percentage points (p < .001), ambitious candidates experienced a drop of about 6 percentage points (p = .002), and bossy candidates experienced an even larger drop of about 24 percentage points (p < .001).

Emotional control played a significant role in determining candidate perception. Compared to candidates with poor emotional control, candidates with fair emotional control were roughly 25 percentage points more likely to be selected for the promotion, candidates with good emotional control were roughly 36 percentage points more likely to be selected for the promotion, and candidates with excellent emotional control were roughly 51 percentage points more likely to be selected for the promotion (p < .001).

Figure 3 shows how the gender attribute interacted with each of the seven other candidate attributes to affect the probability of candidate selection. For each attribute level, the presence of a significant difference between male and female

“Female candidates with fair emotional control were evaluated roughly 7 percentage points more negatively than male candidates with fair emotional control.” candidates was determined by subtracting the interaction AMCE for male candidates from the interaction AMCE for female candidates. Thus, the right-hand panel shows the effect differences between genders; points on the left side of the axis indicate a male advantage, points on the right side of the axis indicate a female advantage, and points residing on the axis indicate no significant effect difference between genders. (see: Appendix)

Comparing the interaction AMCEs between male and female candidates across all attribute levels revealed one significant difference. When candidates were described as having fair emotional control, a significant evaluation gap between male and female candidates emerged. Female candidates with fair emotional control were evaluated roughly 7 percentage points more negatively than male candidates with fair emotional control (p = .048).

Participant characteristics generated additional insights into this interaction. Figure 4 shows the effects of the interaction between gender and emotional control when conditional on participant BSW scores. The effects for the top 50th percentile scorers (high BSW), the effects for the bottom 50th percentile scores (low BSW), and the difference between the effects (high BSW minus low BSW) are visible. (see: Appendix) Among participants with the strongest ideological adherence, female candidates with fair emotional control were significantly less likely to be promoted: high BSW participants evaluated female candidates with fair emotional control about 10 percentage points behind low BSW participants (p = .036).

Transitioning to the parental status attribute, analyses showed no significant evaluation differences between candidates with zero, one, two, or three children. However, when personality interacted with parental status, significant evaluation differences emerged within one personality trait: bossy. The interaction AMCEs between parental status and personality can be seen in Figure 5. Compared to bossy candidates without children, bossy candidates with children were evaluated significantly more favorably. (see: Appendix)

Bossy candidates with one child experienced a boost of about 9 percentage points (p = .007), bossy candidates with two children experienced a boost of about 7 percentage points (p = .022), and bossy candidates with three children experienced a boost of about 8 percentage points (p = .018). For no other personality trait did parental status produce a significant effect on the probability of candidate promotion.

Considering the influence of gender on this interaction, results showed the agentic male and female candidates experienced some key differences in evaluation. This analysis revealed that the significant evaluation boost of having children experienced by bossy candidates applied only to female candidates. Bossy male candidates were evaluated similarly with or without kids, while bossy female candidates were evaluated significantly better when described as having kids. Compared to childless bossy female candidates, bossy female candidates with one child were more likely to be promoted (13.6%, p = .003), and bossy female candidates with three children were more likely to be promoted (15.3%, p = .001). While bossy female candidates with two children were also more likely to be promoted, this effect was not quite significant (8.3%, p = .065).

Discussion The results of this study support Hypothesis 1 (Gender and emotional control will interact to affect leadership perception). While we had expected that female candidates would be evaluated more negatively than male candidates across all emotional control levels, we found only a significant gender difference within the fair level. When both were described as having fair emotional control, female candidates were significantly less likely than male candidates to be promoted, but when both were described as having poor, good, or excellent emotional control, female candidates were evaluated similarly to male candidates.

A possible explanation for this effect is that the “fair” descriptor is a rather ambiguous term to indicate a candidate’s ability to regulate their emotions, while the “poor”, “good”, and “excellent” descriptors are more explicit and tangible. In the absence of a clear indication of a candidate’s ability to regulate their emotions, participants may be forced to rely on gendered emotionality stereotypes. It is possible that as a result of subscribing to the stereotypes that (1) women are more emotional than men and (2) emotionality impedes leadership quality, individuals evaluate leadership candidates described as having “fair” emotional control more harshly when that leader is female compared to when the leader is male. In other words, when a candidate’s emotionality is left vague to individuals, they may resort to the use of gendered emotionality stereotypes to inform their decision-making, leading to female candidates suffering penalties avoided by male candidates.

Our reasoning that emotional control being described as “fair” results in biased evaluations against women due to stereotyping is further supported by our analysis of the effect of participants’ ideological beliefs. For the fair emotional control level (and this level only), a significant difference in evaluation emerges between participants with strong adherence to workplace benevolent sexist ideology and participants with weak adherence. We find that individuals who more rigidly endorse this form of sexism are significantly less likely to select a female leader over a male leader when both are described as having fair emotional control, compared to individuals lower in sexism endorsement. The lack of significant evaluation differences between these participant groups within the poor, good, and excellent levels can once again be explained using the reasoning that with more explicit indications of emotionality, individuals do not need to resort to gender stereotypes to inform their decision-making.

Our results do not support Hypothesis 2 (Gender and personality will interact to affect leadership perception). Based on previous research, we had expected that when described communally, there would be no difference in evaluation between male and female candidates, but when described agentically, male candidates would be perceived more favorably than female candidates (Rudman et al., 2012; Rudman & Glick, 1999). Our results indeed show that individuals perceive leadership capability similarly between communal male and communal female candidates. However, contrary to our expectations, our results also show that individuals perceive leadership capability similarly between agentic male and agentic female candidates. Hence, we find some evidence that may suggest that the United States populace is moving away from a dominant alpha male as its leadership prototype, such that agentic women are no longer at such a significant comparative disadvantage (Wiezel et al., 2024).

The results of this study support Hypothesis 3 (Gender, personality, and parental status will interact to affect leadership perception). While, for bossy male candidates, we find no significant evaluation differences based on whether or not they have children, we find that bossy female candidates experience significant improvements in evaluation when they are described as having kids compared to when described as childless. This evidence supports previous research indicating that agentic female leaders benefit from being described as mothers, with motherhood serving to remedy a perceived communality deficit (Heilman & Okimoto, 2007). However, we had expected that all agentic female candidates would benefit from being described as mothers, but we only see this among bossy female candidates. Ambitious female candidates do not appear to experience significant evaluation differences based on their status as mothers.

We reason that ambitious female leaders may not experience a motherhood boost because the perception of these leaders’ ambition is reduced by the knowledge that they are parents. Previous research suggests that parents are typically perceived as less committed to their jobs and less achievement-oriented than non-parents (Allen & Russell, 1999; Fuegen et al., 2004; Heilman & Okimoto, 2007). An explanation for why ambitious, but not bossy, female candidates do not experience a motherhood boost is that any improvement in perception they receive for being considered sufficiently communal is counteracted by the punishment in perception they receive for being seen as less professionally dedicated.

Building on previous studies for a more nuanced perspective, we suggest that not all agentic female leaders experience improvements in perception when described as being mothers. We reason that when female leaders are defined by motivation-based agentic traits (e.g., ambitious, dedicated, persistent, go-getter), having children calls these traits into question, resulting in similar evaluations between mothers and non-mothers. Conversely, when female leaders are defined by agentic traits tangential to motivation (e.g., bossy, decisive, assertive, dominant), having children does not call these traits into question, resulting in mothers being perceived more favorably than non-mothers.

Conclusion We hope this study can highlight the value of examining a familiar research question in an unfamiliar way. Decades of research have applied the agentic-communal framework to understand how male and female leaders experience differences, yet through novel methodological applications, we become capable of generating new insights and showing that this question remains to be fully answered. Where in most of the previous literature, leaders were either classified as agentic or communal, emotional or non-emotional, parents or non-parents, in conjoint experiments, leaders not only have more facets but also more specific levels within facets. Participant evaluations of the truly multifaceted candidate profiles unique to conjoint experiments can facilitate a more precise understanding of perception. With the results of our conjoint survey design consisting of 13,284 possible candidate profile combinations, we conclude with two testimonies to this point.

First, considering the interaction between gender and emotionality, our results show that not all female leaders are evaluated more negatively than male leaders when emotional control is held constant. When emotional control is described explicitly, we find no evaluation differences between genders, but when described ambiguously, we see that female leaders are at a disadvantage. Yet, in the real world, a person’s ability to control their emotions is ambiguous; people do not walk around with a one-word label on their shirt or a numeric score on their resume designating such an ability. Had we not included “fair” as a level and opted only for explicit levels, we would not have seen any way in which female leaders suffer a penalty, let alone the most critical way — that which is most true to life.

Second, considering the interaction between gender, personality, and parental status, our results show that not all agentic women see an improvement in leadership desirability when described as having children. While we find that bossy female leaders experience a motherhood boost, we do not find this to be the case for ambitious female leaders. If both “bossy” and “ambitious” are agentic traits, why do we see this difference? We explain this discrepancy through the reasoning that within the agency umbrella, there may exist different types of agency, and the perception of certain types can be jeopardized by the knowledge of a female leader having children. If instead of having two levels to encapsulate agentic personality, we had only used one, we would have missed out on this nuance.

These findings help to illustrate the salience of extracting and empirically evaluating multiple levels within leadership criteria. Follow-up research is necessary to sketch out more of the complexities within agency and communality. As we find evidence to support the existence of unique dimensions within agency, we are left wondering what dimensions within communality may likewise uniquely affect how leaders are perceived. When interpreting these results, it is important to keep in mind that although conjoint analyses are extremely useful in illustrating what factors influence leadership preference and factor interactions, there are critical differences between theoretical preference and real-world choice. Moreover, we can not rule out that any number of our findings would differ if we were to repeat this experiment using a participant pool made up of actual employees in the business world tasked with these kinds of leadership personnel decisions. ◆

title: The Effect of Merit Scholarships on Saving for College
abstract: State merit-based scholarships are a large source of funding for many college students, and the effects of this aid on families, students, and states’ economies is a topic of continued interest and research. There are 22 states with merit aid programs, and because eligibility includes graduating from an in-state high school, students and parents in some states can depend on this aid while others cannot. I use this variation, documented by the InforeED State Financial Aid Dataset, together with survey data on people’s decisions to save for college, provided by the National Financial Capability Survey, to assess the effect of merit aid programs on college savings. I find mixed evidence, some suggesting that living in a state with a merit aid program meaningfully decreases the likelihood of saving for college, and some suggesting that it has no effect. I assess whether the scholarships change the amount parents save using the College Savings Plan Network data on 529 accounts. My results are inconclusive, and I propose redoing my analysis with the Survey of Consumer Finances confidential dataset. My analysis is limited by the fact that data sets containing both a measure of college savings and the state of residence are difficult to obtain and/or to use because of the structure of the available data. The purpose of this paper is, in addition to quantifying the effect of scholarships on savings, to describe the potential data sources, limitations, and possible strategies, to inform future related work.
text:
The Effect of Merit Scholarships on Saving for College

Faculty Adviser: Dr. Scott Ogawa

Departments of Economics and Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences by Emilya Ershtein

Abstract State merit-based scholarships are a large source of funding for many college students, and the effects of this aid on families, students, and states’ economies is a topic of continued interest and research. There are 22 states with merit aid programs, and because eligibility includes graduating from an in-state high school, students and parents in some states can depend on this aid while others cannot. I use this variation, documented by the InforeED State Financial Aid Dataset, together with survey data on people’s decisions to save for college, provided by the National Financial Capability Survey, to assess the effect of merit aid programs on college savings. I find mixed evidence, some suggesting that living in a state with a merit aid program meaningfully decreases the likelihood of saving for college, and some suggesting that it has no effect. I assess whether the scholarships change the amount parents save using the College Savings Plan Network data on 529 accounts. My results are inconclusive, and I propose redoing my analysis with the Survey of Consumer Finances confidential dataset. My analysis is limited by the fact that data sets containing both a measure of college savings and the state of residence are difficult to obtain and/or to use because of the structure of the available data. The purpose of this paper is, in addition to quantifying the effect of scholarships on savings, to describe the potential data sources, limitations, and possible strategies, to inform future related work.

Introduction Government funding for college has the following direct effects: pushing students slightly below the margin of affording college to attend college, reducing families’ financial burden, reducing students’ financial burden, increasing student charges (increasing tuition or decreasing institutional aid), and replacing other forms of financial aid. The manner in which the funding is distributed between these areas is not, however, decided by the government. Instead, it is determined by the interaction of choices made by students, parents, universities, and various loan and scholarship providers. Theory has helped make predictions and guide the decisions of state and federal governments. But the unpredictability of preferences about college and the complexity of factors playing into funding for college make it difficult to know how exactly government funds are distributed.

In this paper, I focus on the effects of aid on family savings for college. I look at one type of government funding for college: merit-based scholarships given to undergraduate students. I use merit scholarships administered by U.S. states because eligibility for merit aid is determined by residence, and states in various regions of the country have adopted these programs. As a result, outcomes can be compared across states and over time, providing a plausible identification strategy for the treatment effect of government-funded merit-based aid.

The size of the effect on savings is relevant for several reasons. First, it is an interesting behavioral question. Do parents carefully optimize the amount they put into college savings, changing their behavior as they learn more about their child’s scholarship possibilities? Or do they go by some default idea of how much they should save, or by a worst-case scenario savings scheme? It can also be a question about information and certainty about future scholarships. Do parents know enough about merit aid programs and feel that the programs are stable and certain enough to depend on?

My question also relates to the tradeoff between benefiting colleges and helping families faced by any government funding for education. If families reduce their savings for college, and are thus expecting to pay less, this would counteract tuition increases, especially because the reduction in savings has already happened at the time that colleges set their tuition. However, if families do not reduce their savings due to uncertainty about receiving the merit aid, colleges are likely able to demand higher charges from parents.

Another reason to study this question relates to the common criticism that merit aid programs benefit wealthier families. Families that have college savings funds are often more wealthy and can afford college more easily to begin with, so a finding that aid reduces savings could confirm that criticism. The extent to which merit aid decreases savings would help clarify how much the funding is helping to reduce the burden on families who would have paid for college regardless, as opposed to making it affordable for more students.

The theory that merit aid would affect savings is simple: when parents anticipate lower future costs, they save less. It is possible that a parent would not change their saving behavior because of uncertainty about their child’s future qualification for the scholarship; however, one reason to believe that parents can reliably predict eligibility for the scholarship is that the GPA/ SAT requirements for these scholarships tend to be fairly low, so it may be clear early on whether a student will qualify. For example, for the Louisiana TOPS scholarship, which covers full tuition, a 2.5 GPA and approximately a 1000/1600 SAT or 20 ACT score are required. A 2.5 GPA is achievable with half B’s and half C’s, which is generally a very low standard for public schools in the United States. A 1000 SAT score and a 20 ACT score correspond to getting approximately half of the questions correct. The Georgia HOPE scholarship, which covers full tuition, requires a 3.0 GPA (B average). New Mexico, covering full tuition, has no requirements aside from successfully graduating. (See Table 1 for eligibility requirements of all states.) However, it is still possible that parents don’t change their savings decisions due to behavioral explanations, lack of information, or correct expectations. For example, they could correctly expect future tuition increases, lack of eligibility for need-based aid in these states, or lack of availability of other scholarships.

1 These statistics come from National Center for Education Statistics’s National Postsecondary Student Aid Study. 2 These statistics come from the Education Data Initiative.

The Status of Merit Aid Programs in the U.S. State scholarships constitute a fairly large portion of funding for U.S. college students. In 2023, 23% of students received state grants, as compared to 40% receiving federal grants, and 28% receiving institutional grants. The average state grant was $3,500, average federal grant was $4,300, and average institutional grant was $9,900.1 The average cost of in-state tuition was $9,700 and out-of-state was $27,000.2 Students received an average of around $5,000 in scholarships, with low-income students receiving more federal and state aid because much of the aid is based on demonstrated need.

Between 1991 and 2006, 27 states implemented merit aid programs, and five of them have been terminated at some point since. These programs give scholarships to seniors graduating in the state who meet certain merit criteria. The largest program is the Georgia HOPE Scholarship, followed by Tennessee HOPE and Louisiana TOPS. The first one was the Arkansas Academic Challenge Scholarship in 1991, Georgia HOPE in 1993, 12 others starting in the 1990s, and eight starting in the 2000s. The stated goals include reducing families’ and students’ financial burden, as well as increasing the number of students who attend college. Nine states have programs classified as strong by Sjoquist and Winters (2014), a classification that I borrow in this paper, which identifies large participation rates and large average awards. I add Arkansas into the strong category as they expanded in 2011, a year outside of the range that Sjoquist and Winters studied. Each program has specific eligibility requirements, but the requirement shared

“The theory that merit aid would affect savings is simple: when parents anticipate lower future costs, they save less.” by all programs is being a resident of that state at the time of graduation. Programs differ slightly in their merit criteria, but not drastically. They differ in funding amounts, number of students affected, and some have other miscellaneous rules. Table 1 gives a summary of the characteristics of each state’s program.

Literature Review One of the most common criticisms of merit aid programs is that they do not increase college access because they target students who would attend college regardless. Consequently, there are several papers assessing average effects on college enrollment and college completion. Various papers in the literature find con- tradictory results for the average effect on college enrollment, with more recent literature generally finding smaller effects.

Cornwell, Mustard, and Sridar (2006) estimated that between 1988 and 1997, the Georgia HOPE Scholarship increased college enrollment by 5.9%. This corre- sponds to 15% of HOPE recipients being people who would not have gone to a college in Georgia otherwise. These per- centages refer to increase in enrollment in Georgia, so some of the effect may be coming from students choosing to stay in Georgia instead of going out of state, and may not be reflecting enrollment of students who would have not gone to college otherwise. Dynarski (2004) estimated that merit aid programs in Georgia, Arkansas,

Florida, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, and South Carolina had an average effect on in-state enrollment of 5%. Binder and Genderton (2004) find an enrollment effect of 6% in New Mexico.

A comprehensive analysis conducted by Sjoquist and Winters (2014) uses data from 25 states, and distinguishes between weak and strong programs. It finds no effects on college enrollment as well as no effects on college completion. Most recently, Chakabarti, Nober, and Klaauw (2023) use the most granular data yet and find no effect on propensity of attending college or of degree attainment, in the general population as well as among low-income and racial minority groups.

Scott-Clayton and Zafar (2019) find that marginal recipients of the West Virginia merit scholarship have higher incomes, and are more likely to complete graduate degrees. Despite finding no effect on their enrollment in college, it appears that the scholarship decreased the time it took to complete the degree, and improved life outcomes. Cornwell and Mustard (2006) find that Georgia HOPE increased the portion of high ability students choosing to go to in-state colleges, and increased selectivity in universities.

To the best of my knowledge, there have been few attempts to examine which sources of funding the scholarships replace, and none have examined the effect on savings. Chakabarti et al. (2023) find an average effect of about -$1,000 on student

“One of the most common criticisms of merit aid programs is that they do not increase college access, as they target students who would attend college regardless.” loan originations. Long (2004) finds that the Georgia HOPE Scholarship allowed universities to increase student charges by increasing tuition, increasing room and board fees, and reducing institutional scholarships.

There is also an array of past literature looking at other unintended effects of statewide merit aid programs for college, some of which counteract some of the goals of the programs. For example, researchers have investigated if grade inflation occurred in high schools, counteracting the intended impact of improving student achievement to qualify for the scholarship. Sjoquist and Winters (2015) give evidence that merit aid scholarships have diverted students away from STEM majors, but were unable to identify the mechanism behind this trend. Cornwell and Mustard (2007) showed evidence that car regis- trations in richer counties increased as a result of HOPE, suggesting that HOPE was helping families be less burdened by college costs, allowing them to spend on other consumption goods.

Data Close to half of states, varied in demo- graphics and geography, give merit aid, which presents the opportunity to use the other half as a control group to identify the effect of merit aid on savings. The timeline of the implementation of these programs seems also to have the potential for using a difference in difference approach, but unfortunately most of the strong merit aid programs were implemented in the 1990s, and pre-2001 data on college savings is scarce. As a result, the core of my analysis uses cross-sectional data to compare

3 Note: they exclude New Hampshire and Rhode Island, nine years for Nevada, 10 years for Delaware, and one year for South Dakota, because data was not obtainable. They do not add the New Mexico merit aid money, which I manually added in from state reports.

levels of savings between states, with a set of control variables meant to mitigate omitted variable bias. I include a graphical comparison of the change over time of savings in Arkansas, the only state which has a big jump in merit aid, with other states.

I compile two main data sets for my analysis. The variables contained in each are summarized in Table 2. The 529 dataset is at the state-year level, using assets in each state’s 529 program (tax-advantaged college savings account) as a measure of college savings. The saved dummy dataset, with observations at the individual level, uses people’s answers to the question: “Are you setting aside any money for your children’s college education?” as the measure of savings. To measure merit aid, I use the InformED State Financial Aid Dataset, which was compiled by researchers looking through state financial aid reports and contacting higher education officials.3 As a result, I have detailed data on the merit aid distributed in each state. The limitations of my project, which I discuss in detail below, primarily lie with the savings data.

The saved dummy dataset contains individual level observations taken during 2009, 2012, 2015, 2018, and 2021. For each individual, the National Financial Capability Survey (NFCS) tells whether they saved for college in addition to their state of residence, income group, education level, number of children, race, household ownership, and age group. I choose these control variables following Korankye and Kalenkoski (2021) who show a significant relationship between these demographic characteristics and savings. I match this data with the amount of merit aid given per student in the respondent’s state of residence. I also add, to both data sets, a dummy for being in a state with a strong merit aid program.

The NFCS gives a binary response of whether parents saved, but it does not give a measure of how much they saved. The best measure I could use of how much they saved was data on the amount of assets in each state’s 529 program, but there are other potential sources for this. Table 3 describes potential sources and their limitations.

The 529 data set covers 2001-2021 and contains how much money is in each state’s 529 programs per resident under 20, and how much merit aid was given out that year per student. I combine data on 529 assets from the College Savings Plan Network with Census data on children under 20 to calculate the savings per child. I combine total merit aid given (InformED) with number of students enrolled in post secondary institutions multiplied by the proportion that are undergraduates4 (National Center for Education Statistics) to get merit aid per student. I combine this with FRED data on median income and World Population Review data on percentage of adults with high school and bachelor’s degrees, which serve as control variables.

Table 3 contains several sources I was not able to use. The Survey of Consumer Finances in particular could potentially be the ideal source for this project, as it contains household level data on the amount of college savings as well as state of residence, 1983–2022. However, demographic characteristics such as state of residence are not included in the publicly available dataset, and I was not able to get authorization for confidential data in the timeline of this project. I believe it is very feasible in future

4 The portion of undergraduates is not available by state, so I use the U.S. percentage each year for all states.

work to use this source to assess the effect of merit aid on savings. The Edward Jones 529 Account Survey, SavingforCollege Survey, and the College Savings Foundation also collect data from individuals about their college savings. They do not make any data publicly available, and I was not able to reach the owners, but these surveys likely also contain both data on savings and on state of residence.

529 Data The College Savings Plan Network (CSPN) works with state sponsored 529 programs to compile data on the total amount of assets and number of accounts in each 529 plan. Every 529 plan is administered by a state, and some states have multiple 529 plans. The data is provided on the CSPN website in separate PDF files for each year/quarter. The New York Fed compiles data on total assets, aggregating over states’ multiple plans into a CSV file, and this is what I use.

There are two types of 529 accounts: prepaid and savings. About 95% of 529 assets are in savings plans, and the other 5% are in prepaid plans. Prepaid plans allow you to prepay tuition, locking in current lower tuition rates for attending the participating universities in the future. Typically, participating universities include all in-state universities. If a child ends up not going to a participating university, funds can typically be transferred to other uses. Prepaid plans do not pay interest, and money must be used to pay tuition or fees. These plans have declined over the years; 22 states used to offer prepaid plans, which has decreased to nine in 2023.

The 529 savings plans, on the other hand, allow account holders to choose from a range of investment portfolio options. Money in a savings plan may be used to pay for room and board expenses in addition to tuition and fees. Incentives for putting college savings into a 529 savings account include federal tax exemptions and state tax benefits, described further in Table 4. There are also disincentives from putting savings that may not be used for educational expenses into 529 accounts. If money in either a savings or prepaid plan is used for nonqualified expenses, it incurs taxes and a 10% penalty.

The first issue with the CSPN data is that it is not available for 1991–2000, the years when some of the largest merit aid programs started, so it is not possible to use difference in difference methods. For the years covered, 2001–present, there is not a lot of variation or jumps in merit aid. I searched merit aid data from 2001– present for jumps (See Figure 1), and the only large jump is Arkansas, which jumped from about 1,000 students receiving $8,500 in their merit aid to about 35,000 students receiving $3,000.

However, data directly from 529 programs on savings prior to 2000 likely exists. Different states started their 529 programs at different times, and many states started these programs several years before a merit aid program, so if this data were obtained it might be possible to do a difference in difference analysis. Unfortunately, however, the rapidity of the uptake of these 529 programs is influenced by many different factors in different states, and so it is unclear if even this analysis would be possible.

The second issue for both panel and cross-sectional analysis is that most programs accept out-of-state account openers. As a result, the state of the 529 program doesn’t correspond perfectly to merit aid eligibility. There is still reason to believe that this data may be fairly representative of states’ residents for certain states. First- ly, 6 states (New Jersey, South Dakota, Florida, South Carolina, West Virginia, Louisiana) do not allow out of state residents to enroll in their program. Second, online sources like Morningstar, which give advice regarding choosing a 529 plan, typically suggest choosing the home state’s 529 program if that state provides tax benefits (39 states), so it is possible that many states’ residents primarily use their home 529. Even if a state’s residents use their own 529 program, the issue remains that the data could overestimate residents’ 529 savings due to out-of-state account holders. The 529 programs offer differing investment portfolio options as well as differing fee structures, making some more desirable, depending on people’s circumstances. One way to get around this issue is to exclude the states that have non-neg- ligible out of state investment. It seems as though there are a handful of states which attract the majority of out-of-state inves- tors. Morningstar provides ratings of the 529 programs, and rates only two to three of them as Gold level. Online advisory sources typically recommend one of several programs including Virginia, Maine, Nevada, and Utah. In my analysis, I exclude

“Incentives for putting college savings into a 529 savings account include federal tax exemptions and state tax benefits.” these states and make the assumption that the remaining states have no out-of-state investment. However, I do not have definitive evidence in support of this assumption, and the results of the regressions using the 529 data is very contingent.

The CSPN data is desirable for answering other questions that exploit variation among states as well; for example, Heim and Winecoff (2023) explore how state specific incentives affect people’s decisions to invest in a college savings account, but they need to assume that all 529 accounts come from in-state residents. Addressing the issue of resident/non-resident accounts could be useful for improving research on a number of topics.

Regression Specification I run several regressions with different specifications. The first set of regressions uses the NFCS survey data with the binary outcome of whether or not respondents saved for college. I run both linear probability models and logit regressions to check that the regression specification does not alter my results, and I report the linear probability results as my main results. There are various ways to measure the largeness of a merit aid program, and I use average merit aid per student and recipients as a percentage of all undergraduate students. Additionally, I use a dummy for having a strong-classified merit aid program as the input variables, because savings decisions may not be sensitive to fluctuations in the exact amounts, but may instead respond to the general knowledge that a strong merit aid program exists.

To interpret these regressions, I assume that the measure of merit aid and all controls have a linear relationship with the probability of saving. I run several ver- sions of the following regressions, where

Ms is one of the three measures of merit aid for state s:

The education control is unavailable for 2009 and 2012, so for regressions including those years,

I report regressions in which I pool the observations over the years, and sep- arately for each year. I run the analogous logit regression where f (x) = ―― . The logit regressions results can be found in the appendix.

While I control for demographic characteristics of individuals, a concern I have is that I am not able to control for policy trends. It could be the case that states with merit aid programs may also be more likely to have certain other policies that encourage or discourage savings, and this could be an important omitted variable. Unfortunately, it is difficult to identify which policies affect savings incentives, and I was not able to control for state policies. States with merit aid vary in predominant political party over time, and it is unclear whether merit aid policies are connected to specific political affilia- tions. For the purpose of my regression, I assume that merit aid programs did not

The next set of regressions use state level data on average 529 savings per child 2015-2020 as the outcome variable, and the three different measures of merit aid as input variables of interest. I assume that there is a linear relationship between merit aid and average 529 savings per child; that the only factors correlated with both are median income of the state, percent of adults with a high school degree, and that these also have a linear relationship with college savings. To relate this to general savings, I assume that some fixed percent of college savings goes into 529 accounts, and that this does not vary across states. I run the regression where Ss is savings in state s, Ms is merit aid, HSs is percent of adults with a high school degree, Bs is percent with a bachelor’s degree, and ϵs is an exogenous error term.

In addition to averaging the 2015- 2020 529 assets, I run the regression pool- ing all years, and including state and year fixed effects.

where the s subscript represents the state and the t subscript represents the year.

I choose to average over the years 2015-2020 for regression (3) because it is not clear if there is meaningful variation in merit aid in each state across time. There appears to be fluctuations around a base level (see Figure 1), so I decided to simply compare the levels of saving across states for recent years. I averaged over several years to abstract away from chance variation in any particular year. I include regression (4) as well to test if the fluctuations in merit aid do have a meaningful impact on savings decisions. Regression (4) includes state fixed effects as well as year fixed effects, so β1 should capture the effect of the fluctuations in merit aid. I include data for years 2010–2020, starting in 2010, because some 529 programs only started in the 2000s, and the variation in their initial uptake is difficult to understand and account for. The problem of endogeneity is again a concern with the difficulty of controlling for state policies.

Lastly, I graphically compare the trend of Arkansas to other states before and after it expanded its merit aid program in 2011.

Results

NFCS Data Results for regression 1 are shown in Table 4. I find small negative effects of living in a state with more merit aid per student on the probability of saving, in the pooled regressions as well as the individual year regressions for 2012 and 2015. These regressions suggest that giving an average of $1,000 in merit aid (which is approximately what the strong programs do) decreases the probability of parents saving for college by 2-7%. The coefficients are not completely consistent across regressions; the 2021, 2018, and 2009 regressions do not have statistically significant coefficients, suggesting that either the relationship is changing over time, or there are confounding variables changing over time which I am not accounting for. The coefficients are, in particular, less negative in regressions without the education control variable, suggesting that education is an important factor and regressions excluding it are less trustworthy.

Notably, that doesn’t account for the discrepancy between the 2015, 2018, and 2021 regressions. Using the percent of students with aid or the strong program dummy as the measure of merit aid also yields significant negative effects in the pooled regressions, and the 2015 and 2012 regressions, but no significant results for 2009, 2021, and 2018. The former four regressions suggest that a 10% increase in aid recipients causes around a 1% decrease in likelihood of savings. Living in a state with a strong merit aid program is associated with a 1–3% decrease in the probability of saving. All analogous logit regressions agree in coefficient sign and significance with the OLS results. See appendix A for logit results.

529 Data Table 2 summarizes the results for regressions 3–4. There are no statistically significant coefficients on the merit aid variables. However, the coefficient for median income is negative in four out of the six regressions, and the coefficient on percent of college graduates is negative in two out of six, which is very unexpected. Because the NFCS data demonstrates that people with more education and higher income typically save more, I believe the issue is that the assets in each state’s 529 account are not truly representative of the college savings of parents in that state. It is likely the case that there are a lot of out- of-state 529 accounts.

Arkansas Program Expansion In 2011, the Arkansas Academic Challenge Scholarship expanded significantly, going from funding around 1,000 incoming students per year to 30,000. The scholarship currently gives $1,000 the first year, $4,000 the second the third, and $5,000 for the fourth year. Figure 3 shows that

Arkansas is the only state to have a big jump in the amount of merit aid given out per child during the time period for which college savings data is available.

The trajectories of states’ savings measures over time are shown in Figures 2 and 3. The red lines represent strong program states, the black line is Arkansas, and the gray are all others. There is a lot of heterogeneity in the trends of states in both 529 savings and percent of people who save for college. For the percentage of parents saving, neither merit aid states nor non-merit aid states seem to have a common trend. It is unclear whether Arkansas’ trend is more like one or the other. In 529 assets, merit aid states have less overall growth 2007–present than non-merit aid states. Arkansas saw one of the smallest growth rates throughout, with no visible changes after 2011. The case of Arkansas does not give any evidence that merit aid affected college savings.

Conclusion I primarily assessed whether merit aid programs decreased the probability of parents saving for college. The National Financial Capability Survey provided the most reliable source of publicly available data on savings, and formed the core of my analysis. While results from regressions across different years had different results, the majority had statistically significant negative coefficients, and I conclude that merit aid programs likely do decrease the likelihood of parents saving by around 1–3%. $1,000 of merit aid per student decreases the probability of saving by 2–7% and a 10% increase in merit aid recipients decreases the probability of saving by around 1%. While I control for many demographic variables in my regression, there are endogeneity concerns with potential policy omitted variables.

My results tell us about the likelihood that a parent will save, but it remains unclear whether parents who do save decrease the amount that they save when they expect to benefit from a merit aid program. I attempted to assess this using 529 data, but the results appear to be unreliable. The fundamental issue with 529 data is that many people hold accounts in states they do not reside in, and thus the assets in a certain state’s 529 program does not necessarily correspond to merit aid availability. For further work, the Survey of Consumer Finances confidential data could be a good alternative way to assess this question. ◆

title: The Protect of Total War and the Minnesota Starvation Experiment, 1944-1945
abstract: When the United States (U.S.) entered World War II in 1942, 12,000 men refused uniformed service through the draft. These conscientious objectors (C.O.s) were, however, willing to perform alternative service. This project focuses on the Minnesota Starvation Experiment, which was conducted between 1944 and 1945 at the University of Minnesota’s Laboratory of Physiological Hygiene and used C.O.s as volunteer human subjects. In conducting the experiment, the doctors (led by Ancel Keys) and subjects hoped to understand the biological and psychological effects of starvation and illuminate best practices to nourish the starving populations of Europe after World War II. In order to accomplish these aims, the 36 C.O.s under- went a control period of three months, a systematic semistarvation of six months, and a rehabilitation period of three months. This project integrates the Minnesota Experiment with the social and political landscapes of an America engaged in total war, bridging a gap between scholarship that discusses the experiment as a micro- history and broader scholarships of World War II that mention it only in passing. It does so by demonstrating and analyzing the parallels between specific groups in the experiment and specific groups in the military, showing how the character of total war became part of an experiment that was defined by its separation from combat and military institutions. In demonstrating these parallels and contextualizing the experiment in the climate of total war, the Minnesota Starvation Experiment emerges as both extraordinary and unprecedented while also deeply ordinary in the context of its own time.
text:
The Protect of Total War and the Minnesota Starvation

Experiment, 1944-1945

Faculty Adviser: Dr. Ken Alder

Department of History by Aimee Flanigan

Abstract When the United States (U.S.) entered World War II in 1942, 12,000 men refused uniformed service through the draft. These conscientious objectors (C.O.s) were, however, willing to perform alternative service. This project focuses on the Minnesota Starvation Experiment, which was conducted between 1944 and 1945 at the University of Minnesota’s Laboratory of Physiological Hygiene and used C.O.s as volunteer human subjects. In conducting the experiment, the doctors (led by Ancel Keys) and subjects hoped to understand the biological and psychological effects of starvation and illuminate best practices to nourish the starving populations of Europe after World War II. In order to accomplish these aims, the 36 C.O.s under- went a control period of three months, a systematic semistarvation of six months, and a rehabilitation period of three months. This project integrates the Minnesota Experiment with the social and political landscapes of an America engaged in total war, bridging a gap between scholarship that discusses the experiment as a micro- history and broader scholarships of World War II that mention it only in passing. It does so by demonstrating and analyzing the parallels between specific groups in the experiment and specific groups in the military, showing how the character of total war became part of an experiment that was defined by its separation from combat and military institutions. In demonstrating these parallels and contextualizing the experiment in the climate of total war, the Minnesota Starvation Experiment emerges as both extraordinary and unprecedented while also deeply ordinary in the context of its own time.

Introduction Everyone agreed that the University of Minnesota’s Laboratory of Physiological Hygiene was an odd place. Due to the lab’s unassuming entrance at Gate 27 of the university’s football stadium, most people passed by without a second glance. When 36 C.O.s reported to the lab in the winter of 1944, most could not find the entrance and walked the perimeter of the stadium, or looked aimlessly around the parking lot, before finding Gate 27. Gate 27 was deeply significant, however, to the small group of people who worked at, lived in, and visited the Laboratory of Physiological Hygiene. The lab comprised a maze of tunnels located beneath the stadium. Alongside these tunnels were offices, exam rooms, and a staggering collection of laboratory equipment.1 On Saturday afternoons, the noise of fans enjoying the football game above the researchers’ heads became an ambient rumble. With its exposed pipes, drab walls, summer and winter drafts, and inconspicuous entrance, the lab was certainly utilitarian.2 Suffice it to say that decor was not a priority for the lab’s founder, Dr. Ancel Benjamin Keys.

Keys led a team of physicians who designed and conducted the Minnesota Starvation Experiment. The 36 men who arrived in 1944 were human subjects, all of them draft-age men who had declared themselves to be C.O.s and had agreed to an alternative form of wartime service: systematic starvation in the Laboratory of Physiological Hygiene at the University of Minnesota. The C.O.s volunteered for the chance to be of service and to tangibly help others. The experiment, sponsored by the

1 Henry Blackburn, If It Isn’t Fun: A Memior from a Different Sort of Medical Life (Wordpress, 2000), https://henryblackburn. wordpress.com/stories/professional-memoirs/if-it-isnt-fun-volume-i/. 2 “Medicine: The Fat of the Land,” Time, January 13, 1961, https://content.time.com/time/subscriber/article/0,33009,828721,00.html. 3 “Arsenal of Democracy,” Fireside Chat, https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/node/209416.

U.S. government, mimicked the meager diets starving Europeans suffered as a result of World War II. To study how they could most effectively be rehabilitated, the 36 C.O.s were starved together. They were then divided into four groups of nine and revived by different diets of proteins and vitamins.

Scholars have portrayed the Minnesota Starvation Experiment as an extraordinary experiment. Indeed it was, insofar as nothing quite like it has been attempted before or since. Perhaps for this very reason, scholars have largely neglected to place the Minnesota Starvation Experiment within the broader social and cultural landscape of wartime America. Rather, scholars have either touched on the experiment as a piece of evidence or have examined it in isolation. This thesis bridges this gap, integrating the Minnesota Starvation Experiment into the American story of World War II. In illustrating how the experiment took on the character of total war, this thesis ana- lyzes parallels between the experiment and wartime America to emphasize the degree to which total war permeated American society.

Central to the understanding of the project of total war is World War II’s consumption of American society. When President Roosevelt announced U.S. entry into the war on Dec. 9, 1941, he made it clear to the American public that “we are now in this war… Every single man, woman, and child is a partner in the most tremendous undertaking of our American history.”3 World War II was an era of collective commitment and absolutes that effectively rallied the country. Resources and factories were used to manufacture guns, trucks, tanks, and aircraft engines rather than Fords, Cadillacs, and Chevro- lets.4 Author Mark P. Parillo wrote that “No war before or since touched so many Americans and so many aspects and facets of their lives.”5 From Pearl Harbor until Victory in Europe Day, Americans dedicated themselves, their time, and their money to the war effort.

The 11,996 men who declared themselves C.O.s stood out from this intense and collective mobilization: they were the men who refused noncombatant, uniformed military roles but were willing to contribute to the country’s war effort through alternative forms of service. This group, of which the Minnesota men were a part, made up the Civilian Public Service (CPS).6 In 1942, the CPS allowed these C.O.s to participate as human subjects in a variety of government-sponsored medical experiments that reflected the conditions soldiers might have faced in combat.

Although the Minnesota Starvation Experiment was part of a broader network of human medical experiments that used C.O.s as human subjects, it stood out from these other ventures. The Starvation Experiment’s duration—one year living at the Laboratory of Physiological Hygiene—was much longer than other experiments in which C.O.s participated. Furthermore, every day of the experiment required significant personal effort on the part of its human subjects. Indeed, while many of the other experiments that utilized C.O.s were strictly biological, the Starvation Experiment depended not only on the C.O.s’ willingness to sacrifice their
